The chunk lease and the manual lease are its two instances on the running machine. (The Nervous System, Safety Enforcement, Supervisory Intervention)

Exposure Wall

The limit on what failure-free operation alone can establish about a rare failure rate. Under a stationary Poisson failure model, bounding a catastrophic rate \(\ConstantHazardRate = 10^{-9}\) per hour at 95 percent confidence requires about \(-\ln(0.05)/\ConstantHazardRate \approx 3.0 \times 10^9\) failure-free hours of exposure from the same configuration, an argument Butler and Finelli made for flight software. The required exposure makes direct demonstration impractical, so claims at that level also need architectural evidence, fault injection, and justified operating premises. (Verification Ceilings and the Exposure Wall, Adversarial Verification, Zero-Failure Testing and the Exposure Wall)

Extended Kalman Filter (EKF)

A recursive state estimator for nonlinear measurement or motion models that runs the Kalman filter’s predict and update steps on a first-order linearization about the current estimate. When the model curves appreciably across the prior’s spread, the reported covariance can understate the true error, so the filter’s consistency must be tested rather than assumed. (Spatial Memory)

Extreme Value Theory (EVT)

The statistical theory that supplies limiting distribution families for extremes, much as the central limit theorem supplies one for sums. Its threshold form models every observation above a high threshold with the generalized Pareto distribution; its block-maxima form models one maximum per block with the generalized extreme value distribution. (Adversarial Verification, Extreme Value Theory and Tail Risk)

title: Glossary
text:
Fallback Ladder

The ordered set of responses the permission path selects when a proposal cannot be admitted unchanged or its premises fail. Its rungs are PROJECT (minimal-intervention projection of the proposal onto the safe set), HOLD (a state-matched powered hold), STOP (a controlled, state-matched stop), and INHIBIT (drive torque inhibit with a separately rated brake). Each response requires a validated entry region and surviving hardware; selection must occur while that response remains feasible. An invalid replacement need not revoke an active trajectory whose own premises still hold. (The Fallback Ladder, Supervisory Intervention)

Flow Matching Policy

A generative policy trained to predict a vector field that transports samples from a base distribution toward a conditional action distribution. The training probability path and sample coupling determine the transport construction; straight conditional paths do not imply globally optimal transport or straight learned sample trajectories. Sampling cost depends on the trained field, numerical solver, and required accuracy, so fewer inference steps than diffusion must be demonstrated for the selected policies. (Policy Training)

Force Closure

A grasp property: every external force and torque on the held object can be balanced by contact forces that each lie inside its friction cone. Force closure says a balancing set of forces exists, not that the gripper can produce it within its force limit or without crushing the object. (Grounded Intent, Grasp mechanics: Friction cones and force closure)

Forward Invariance

A property of a dynamical system, control policy, and set \(\ForwardInvariantSafeSet\): every trajectory starting in \(\ForwardInvariantSafeSet\) remains in \(\ForwardInvariantSafeSet\) for all future time under the stated assumptions. A barrier certificate can establish this property for a modeled system with feasible controls. Applying the result to hardware requires maintaining the state, disturbance, actuation, and timing premises of the certificate. (Safety Enforcement, Safety and Control Barrier Functions)

Forward Occupancy Set

The region a tracked actor could occupy a given time after its last measurement, grown from its measured position by its speed bound and its tracking uncertainty. A proposed motion is admitted only if it stays clear of every such set over the motion and its stop. (Grounded Intent)

Four-Stream Action Tap

The tuple \((\RequestedActionTap, \MappedCommandTap, \EnforcedCommandTap, \MeasuredResponseTap)\) that records one action at each of its four causal stages, the requested action, the mapped command, the enforced command, and the measured response. Keeping all four makes any single choice of training label interpretable, provided the taps are stamped in one hardware-synchronized timebase. (Physical Data)

Free-Space Depth (\(\FreeSpaceDepth\))

The distance from a hull’s surface to the nearest place that no live evidence vouches for, read from a distance field built with every occupied, unknown, or expired cell treated as an obstacle. It is the clearance a map can certify for motion. (Spatial Memory)

Freshness Deadline (\(\TelemetryFreshnessBound\))

The largest age, counted from the capture of a measurement to the onset of the actuator’s response, that a measurement of a moving target may reach before the target’s motion alone spends the allowable position error. It equals the error tolerance divided by the fastest credible velocity of the tracked state, and every stage from exposure to torque onset shares it. (The Physical Body)

Friction Cone

The set of forces a Coulomb contact can transmit, \(\|\TangentialContactShear\| \le \CoulombFrictionCoefficient \NormalContactForce\), a cone about the contact normal with half-angle \(\arctan \CoulombFrictionCoefficient\). A nonadhesive contact can push but not pull, so a gripper holds an object only through forces inside its friction cones. (Grounded Intent, Grasp mechanics: Friction cones and force closure)

Future-State Conditioning

Generating candidate motion plans from the state anticipated at execution time rather than the stale state measured when planning began, which removes the reference jump at trajectory handoff that planning latency would otherwise create. Activation still depends on the permission path checking the seam against the current state estimate and its error bound. (Trajectory Planning)

title: Glossary
text:
Generalist Policy

A robot policy pretrained on pooled demonstrations from many robots and tasks, then post-trained on demonstrations of the target task. Pretraining supplies broad visual and motor priors; post-training supplies the task, the embodiment, and the evidence the target deployment needs. (Policy Training)

Grounded Affordance

An affordance expressed in the robot’s own frame and units, namely a feature pose in the base frame, an approach direction, an aperture, and a contact wrench ceiling, each tied to dated sensor evidence through a calibrated measurement chain. Unlike a detector box or a language label, it says where and how the gripper may make contact. A learned grasp score or a confident detection is not grounding, because neither carries a metric error bound, a wrench limit, or an evidence epoch that the permission path could admit or expire. (Grounded Intent, Sensor Perception)

title: Glossary
text:
Hardware Lease

A countdown timer on the safety microcontroller that enforces a lease’s expiry without the cooperation of the process that issued the authority. It is the mechanism behind every other lease, since a hung host cannot extend authority that a hardware timer is counting down. (Grounded Intent, Safety Enforcement)

Heterogeneous Silicon Partitioning

Allocation of learned workloads and time-critical permission or control loops to different compute resources, with hardware protection of memory and peripheral access. Separate processors and dedicated buses can remove specific interference and fault paths, but shared power, clocks, interconnects, or thermal limits can retain common-mode failures. Timing and fault-containment claims therefore require evidence for the actual partition and declared load and fault envelope. (Workload Placement, Heterogeneous SoC Mailboxes, Memory Barriers, and Zero-Copy IPC)

Human-Gated Aggregation

An interactive imitation-learning scheme in which the expert decides when to take over and only the takeover segments enter the dataset as labels. It avoids training on the learner’s own failing commands. (Physical Data)

Human Oversight Role

A duty that a design assigns to a person, such as stopping the machine, taking over a channel, or approving a motion, and that the safety argument relies on. It counts as a countermeasure only if its holder has the time, the information, and the authority to act within the time the hazard leaves; a remote assistant who serves many machines must also be free when a request arrives. (Oversight a Person Can Perform)

title: Glossary
text:
Importance Sampling

A Monte Carlo method that draws test runs from a proposal distribution that visits the failure region often, then weights each run by the ratio of the operational to the proposal likelihood to remove the bias. It estimates rare failure rates with far fewer runs than plain sampling, but only for the declared operational distribution. (Adversarial Verification)

Inevitable Collision State (ICS)

A physical system state \(\MechanicalPlantState(\TimeInstant)\) from which no admissible, physically executable control trajectory within actuator and friction limits can prevent impact with environmental obstacles over an infinite time horizon. Unlike geometric obstacle clearance, an ICS explicitly accounts for plant momentum, friction limits, dynamic obstacle trajectories, and finite actuator braking authority. A machine can enter an ICS before contact; insufficient stopping distance establishes this only when no other admissible evasive trajectory avoids impact. (The Physical Body, Trajectory Planning, Safety Enforcement)

Innovation

The difference between a measurement and the estimator’s prediction of it, which is what the measurement says that the prediction did not. A zero innovation confirms an estimate only along directions the sensors can observe. (Spatial Memory)

Intent Grounding Refusal

A typed rejection of a goal itself, returned when the referent is unresolved or no candidate grasp survives the physical checks a learned generator did not perform, such as an inverse-kinematics solution inside joint limits, jaw aperture, and a collision-free approach corridor. Unlike a planning failure, which finds no collision-free path to a valid goal, it rejects the goal before the planner is invoked, so no best guess over unresolved referents reaches trajectory generation. (Grounded Intent, Supervisory Intervention)

Intent Lease

The record, eighth in the record chain, that turns a grounded human goal into a bounded, expiring request that grants a target, a tolerance, and effort ceilings, but never a path. It expires at the earliest of its evidence horizon, its administrative lease, and its stopping deadline, and expiry withdraws the authority based on that intent and requires re-grounding or a qualified state-matched fallback. Unlike an execution lease, it bounds which trajectories may be admitted, not how long an admitted command may run. (Grounded Intent, Trajectory Planning)

Intervention Masking

An evaluation distortion in which repeated, proactive interventions by human supervisors intercept a policy before it reaches a boundary failure. Because the supervisor intervenes during nascent drift, assisted success and accident counts alone do not reveal how the unaided policy would have behaved after takeover. Logs must distinguish intervention classes, exposure, and task outcomes. Reporting these separately prevents assisted task completion from being mistaken for evidence of independent policy competence. (Supervisory Intervention, Closed-Loop Evaluation)

Intervention Rate

The number of events in a declared intervention class divided by active operating time, or by distance when a distance-based rate is reported. The rate depends on the intervention policy and exposure population; human takeovers and automatic corrections must remain distinguishable. It does not by itself establish safety or stability. (Closed-Loop Evaluation, Supervisory Intervention)

title: Glossary
text:
Jerk

The rate of change of acceleration, \(\TranslationalJerk = \Glyph{\dot{a}} = \dddot{\Glyph{x}}\), in m/s³. A jerk limit makes a brake ramp its deceleration up instead of stepping it, which spares occupants, payloads, and transmissions a shock but lengthens the stop, because full deceleration arrives later. (Trajectory Planning, The Causal Boundary, Safety Enforcement)

title: Glossary
text:
Kinodynamic Feasibility

The property that the machine can track a candidate trajectory, including its seams and its stop, while every joint stays within its position, velocity, acceleration, jerk, torque, and current limits; the kinodynamic feasibility envelope is the set of initial states from which this holds. Collision freedom is necessary but not sufficient, and checking only discrete waypoints can miss an interpolant that overshoots a limit between samples. (Trajectory Planning, The Physical Body)

title: Glossary
text:
Learner-Action Contamination

A data-collection failure in which the failing policy’s own commands enter the dataset as expert labels, so the retrained policy learns to answer the cues of an approaching hazard with the commands that caused it. (Physical Data)

Legible Intent

Motion and signals that let a person who does not know a machine’s goal infer it early enough to get out of the way, as opposed to motion that is predictable only to someone who already knows the plan. It helps the people a machine puts at risk protect themselves, and signals should promise only what measured detection supports. (Legible intent)

title: Glossary
text:
Manual Lease (\(\ManualLease\))

The execution lease of a human operator in manual mode, renewed by authenticated heartbeats. It replaces the chunk lease in the pre-brake delay while the operator drives, so it must fit the stopping reserve of the mode in which it is granted. (Supervisory Intervention)

Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI)

Active operating time divided by the number of events in a declared intervention class. MTBI is the reciprocal of the time-based intervention rate when the count is nonzero; a zero-event run requires an exposure-based statistical bound rather than a claim of infinite reliability. Interrupted trials and the intervention policy affect interpretation, so MTBI alone does not establish safety or stability. (Closed-Loop Evaluation, Supervisory Intervention)

Memory Wall

The limit on a workload’s rate that arises when its operands cannot reach the arithmetic units as fast as those units could consume them, so that the bytes moved from off-chip memory, not the operations performed, set the time per evaluation. Faster arithmetic does not move it; only fewer bytes per evaluation (fewer or narrower weights, or weights resident on chip) or more bandwidth does. It is distinct from memory capacity, since a model can fit in memory and still be too slow to stream. (The Cognitive Brain)

Metric 3D Lifting (Spatial Grounding)

The construction of a three-dimensional scene representation in physical units and a declared coordinate frame from sensor observations. Metric scale requires calibrated geometry, depth measurements, or another validated scale reference; image features and reconstruction methods alone do not resolve monocular scale ambiguity. The representation supports reachability and collision checks only within its uncertainty, coverage, and information-age bounds. (Sensor Perception, Grounded Intent)

Minimal Risk Maneuver (MRM)

A fallback maneuver intended to reduce risk after a fault or loss of nominal authority, such as a controlled stop or transition to a supported resting configuration. Its feasibility depends on the current state, available clearance, and surviving sensing, actuation, and power. The designation does not guarantee a hazard-free outcome or require every machine to reach an immediate standstill. (Safety Enforcement, Supervisory Intervention)

Minimal-Intervention Safety Shield

A safety filter that modifies a nominal control proposal only as needed to satisfy modeled safety and actuator constraints. The CBF-QP safety filter solves \(\CertifiedControlAction=\arg\min_{\ControlInput}\|\ControlInput-\NominalControlCommand\|^2\) subject to barrier and input constraints, potentially acting before the safe-set boundary is reached. Its guarantee depends on feasibility, model and state bounds, and execution timing; minimizing input deviation neither maximizes task performance nor supplies a fallback when the feasible set is empty. Its effect on the system hazard rate is conditional on the proposal rate and its interception coverage, so a shield does not remove the need to bound the proposer’s failure rate. (Safety Enforcement, Engineering Physical AI, Safety and Control Barrier Functions)

Missing Observable

The unmeasured physical quantity on which an open claim depends, such as a friction coefficient or a latch strength, stated in terms of the physical claim rather than as an out-of-distribution latent state. Naming it lets a team choose between adding sensing, establishing a physical bound, and restricting the task. (Engineering Physical AI)

Mode Averaging (Multimodality Catastrophe)

A learning failure in which a regression policy averages distinct valid action modes into an unsuitable action, potentially causing a physical hazard. Mean squared error favors the conditional mean, which can lie between valid pathways. When human demonstrators navigate around an obstacle by choosing either a left or right detour, a naive regression model averages the competing action modes, commanding an interpolation that steers the robot directly into the obstacle. Mixture models, discrete strategy choices, or generative decoders can represent distinct modes; their selected actions still require physical feasibility checks. (Policy Training, The Cognitive Brain)

Mode Confusion

A mismatch between the mode an operator believes the automation is in and the mode it is actually in, so that an action correct for the believed mode is wrong for the actual one. On a machine whose actuator channels change hands separately, the operator’s belief about one channel can be stale while the operator acts on another. Committed channel masks and per-channel announcement address it; correct ownership at the bus does not. (Supervisory Intervention)

Monitored Premise Expiration

The withdrawal of operational authority when runtime monitoring finds a required safety-case premise false or unknown, for example because measured temperature exceeds a limit or sensor packets are missing. Linking runtime telemetry to safety case warrants makes detectable premise failures grounds for restricting authority; unmonitored premises still require independent evidence. When a monitored premise expires, the system transitions autonomously into a restricted or refusal operational regime. (Deployment Release)

title: Glossary
text:
Observability

The property that the history of a machine’s sensor outputs over a finite window, together with its known inputs and dynamics, determines the state uniquely, so that distinct physical trajectories produce distinct measurement sequences. Along an unobservable direction the innovation stays zero whatever the error, so a contracting covariance there reflects the model’s assumptions rather than evidence. (Spatial Memory, Continuous Covariance Propagation and Observability)

Observation Contract

A specification of the spatial, temporal, and semantic claims a perception subsystem supplies downstream, including coordinate frames, capture times, coverage, uncertainty, and validity flags. It distinguishes deterministic bounds from statistical confidence regions and names how detectable violations revoke a claim. A contract cannot make occluded or unmonitored conditions observable; unsupported claims must remain unknown. (Sensor Perception, The Cognitive Brain)

Observational Indistinguishability

The condition in which two physical states that require different responses produce the same observation history, under every input the machine may admissibly apply, until the deadline by which a state-specific response must begin. Unlike classical unobservability, it is tied to a deadline and to the admissible inputs. A more capable classifier on the same channel cannot separate the states; only a new channel, active probing, or a response valid in both states changes the outcome. (Engineering Physical AI)

Operating Envelope

The declared set of external conditions and internal execution states, each stated with its units and tolerances, over which a machine’s protective claim must hold and at which every trial of that claim is run. It extends the operational design domain with the machine’s own state, such as processor load, drive bus voltage, and bus traffic. Values that are each in range can combine into a point outside the envelope, so its coupled corners must be tested. (Adversarial Verification, Deployment Release)

Operational Design Domain (ODD)

The object poses, surface conditions, payloads, speeds, and disturbances in which a machine is meant to operate, written down as the scenario table. A dataset supports the part of the ODD that its occupancy join covers; the rest is its known absence. The sets nest: the policy manifest claims a declared ODD within the ODD, evaluation samples a target ODD within the declared ODD, and verification extends the target ODD to the machine’s internal conditions as the operating envelope that a release verdict authorizes in whole, in part, or not at all. (Collection Policy Coverage, Policy Training, Closed-Loop Evaluation, Adversarial Verification, Deployment Release)

Operational Independence

The property that no activity, fault, or overload in the proposal domain can push the permission path’s execution past its deadline or disable its authority to refuse, through any resource the two share. Unlike spatial isolation, it also covers time, supply, clock, reset, and heat; it is the placement-level form of what functional-safety standards call freedom from interference. A separate core or chip is not independent by construction, since each shared resource is a hypothesis that needs a bound. (Workload Placement)

Moral Crumple Zone

The position of a person who absorbs blame for an outcome that a system’s design controlled, typically the operator nearest the event, named by analogy with the crumple zone of a car. A human role without the time, information, or authority to act creates one. (Oversight a Person Can Perform)

title: Glossary
text:
Paired Probing

Validating a simulator component by applying identical open-loop command sequences to the simulator and to the physical hardware, then measuring the difference between the resulting state trajectories against explicit error budgets. A difference beyond the tolerance for the operating envelope makes the simulator defective for that training task. (Policy Training)

Performance Level (PL)

The ISO 13849-1 grade, a (lowest) to e (highest), of how reliably a safety-related control function performs, based on its architecture, diagnostic coverage, and component failure rates. Standards for the application set the required level; person detection on a driverless industrial truck, for example, requires PL d. (Sensor Perception, Safety Enforcement, Deployment Release)

Permission Path

The independent mechanism with bounded latency, which the learned model cannot delay or corrupt, that alone may permit an action to reach an actuator. It checks each proposal against fresh evidence, the stopping envelope, and a fallback feasible from the current state, and refuses when any check fails. (The Machine in Five Levels, The Nervous System, Safety Enforcement)

Permission Stage

A grant that allows a named configuration of a machine to operate in a named domain, among named groups of people, on named evidence, and under named reporting duties, such as testing with a safety driver, driverless testing, or open deployment. A machine leaves a stage on evidence gathered there, and a stage is withdrawn for a configuration change, an incident, or a withheld record. (Permission in Stages)

Physical Artificial Intelligence (Physical AI)

The engineering of closed-loop machines in which learned models influence, without synchronous human approval, physical actions that change subsequent observations. A system is in scope when it combines a learned model, consequential physical feedback, and delegated physical authority. Its actions must fit the plant’s physical limits and the time available to respond, and a useful proposal still needs an independent permission decision. (The Causal Boundary, The Cognitive Brain)

Physical Plant

The apparatus being controlled, such as a robot’s wheeled base or arm, whose state keeps changing while the computer calculates. (The Causal Boundary, The Physical Body)

Problem of Many Hands

The difficulty of assigning responsibility for an outcome that many people each helped produce, so that each can truthfully point to someone else. For a physical machine, the decisions behind one admitted action (policy, enforcer, envelope, crossing rule, staffing) belong to different parties and mostly appear in no runtime log. (Decisions Behind an Admitted Action)

Proposal Boundary

The line between a learned model, which may only propose an action, and the permission path, a mechanism designed to make the actuation decision independently of the model, within a qualified latency and fault envelope. The permission path checks each proposal against fresh evidence, the stopping envelope, and a fallback feasible from the current state, and it refuses when any check fails. The proposal boundary separates the Brain from the Nervous System in the book’s five-level machine. (The Machine in Five Levels, The Nervous System, Safety Enforcement)

title: Glossary
text:
Qualification Ladder

The ordering of four qualification environments, software-in-the-loop, processor-in-the-loop (PIL), hardware-in-the-loop (HIL), and physical fault rigs, by how much of the loop from sensing through inference, buses, drives, and plant is real, and therefore by falling trial throughput. The order is not a hierarchy of evidence, because a higher rung cannot subsume a lower one. Each rung yields a distinct category of evidence and stays blind to the physical mechanisms outside its boundary, so extensive software-in-the-loop passes say nothing about clock drift, DMA stalls, interrupt jitter, or supply sag. (Adversarial Verification)

Quantization

Storing a model’s weights, and optionally its activations, in fewer bits than training used. Weight-only quantization cuts the bytes a bandwidth-bound decode step must read; it does not speed up compute-bound phases unless the processor has kernels for the lower-precision arithmetic. (The Cognitive Brain)

title: Glossary
text:
Record Chain

The sixteen records, one produced by each chapter of Parts I to IV except the one on the learned proposer and one by the conclusion, that carry the book’s assumptions and evidence from the limit record to the residual-claims register. One strand states what the plant can do and what the proposer has shown it can do; the other carries what the proposer proposes now; they meet in the enforcement record. A record makes a claim inspectable; it does not establish the claim. (The Architecture of This Book, The record register)

Reflected Rotor Inertia (\(\ReflectedRotorInertia\))

The apparent rotational inertia of an actuator rotor seen at the load-side joint output, \(\ReflectedRotorInertia = \GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia\) for transmission ratio \(\GearReductionRatio\). In high-reduction joints it dominates the apparent load, caps joint acceleration, and concentrates impact energy on the gear teeth before drive current can be interrupted. (The Physical Body)

Relative Degree

The number of times a function of the state, such as a barrier function \(\BarrierFunction(\MechanicalPlantState)\), must be differentiated with respect to time before the control input appears explicitly. Raw distance has relative degree two for torque, so a barrier written on distance alone gives the input no instantaneous control authority at the boundary. (Safety and Control Barrier Functions, Safety Enforcement)

Release Verdict

The signed decision that sets how much authority a named machine’s permission path may grant, UNCOND for the full assessed operating envelope, COND for a separately evidenced restricted envelope, or REFUSE when any required premise is missing, contradicted, or unknown, in each case only while its standing conditions hold. It is decided before operation and never moves the proposal boundary; under every verdict the permission path still admits each action. (Deployment Release)

Replacement Latency (\(\ReplacementLatency\))

The elapsed time from the capture of the observation a new proposal rests on to the admission of that proposal. It is the sum of the capture-to-dispatch observation age and the dispatch-to-admission interval \(\DispatchAdmissionInterval\). (Trajectory Planning, Workload Placement)

Rolling Shutter

An image sensor readout in which rows are reset, exposed, and read out sequentially, each row starting one row period after the previous one, so a single frame samples a moving scene at progressively later times. A global shutter instead exposes every pixel over the same interval. (Sensor Perception)

Rule of Three

The approximation that zero failures in \(\ZeroFailureTrialCount\) independent trials bounds the per-trial failure probability below about \(3/\ZeroFailureTrialCount\) at 95 percent confidence, because \(-\ln 0.05 \approx 3\). The bound holds only under the trials’ sampling assumptions. (Closed-Loop Evaluation, Zero-Failure Testing and the Exposure Wall)

title: Glossary
text:
Safe Torque Off (STO)

A drive safety function that prevents the drive from generating motor torque through its torque-producing power stage. STO does not itself brake a moving load, hold a gravity-loaded mechanism, or isolate the electrical supply. Its use in a stopping or restraint path requires a plant-specific assessment of coasting, stored energy, and any separately rated mechanical brake. (Safety Enforcement, The Physical Body)

Safety Case (Claim–Argument–Evidence)

A structured argument that a named machine, in a stated operating envelope and under a stated fault model, meets explicit physical criteria, written as claims that decompose through stated arguments into retained evidence. Unlike a test report, it states why the evidence supports a claim about conditions the machine has not yet met and names the assumptions under which the reasoning stops holding. It is written with the design, and in this book’s architecture its verdict decides what the permission path lets the machine do. (Deployment Release)

Safety Integrity Level (SIL)

The IEC 61508 grade, 1 (lowest) to 4 (highest), of the risk reduction a safety function must provide, expressed as a band of tolerable dangerous failure rates. Not to be confused with software-in-the-loop testing, which some texts also abbreviate SIL. (Deployment Release)

Safety Laser Scanner

A planar time-of-flight sensor type-tested as a protective device (IEC 61496-3) whose safety output reports only that something occupies a configured protective field. On a mobile base it carries the certified stop for a person in the path; a perception LiDAR without that rating cannot. (Sensor Perception, Safety Enforcement)

Safety Microcontroller

The small, independently clocked processor that runs the permission path’s deadline-critical checks, watchdogs, and hardware leases, and commands the drives’ stop functions. On the running machine it sits on its own board link with no memory shared with the application processor. (The Nervous System, Workload Placement)

Scenario Table

The operational design domain divided into cells over low-dimensional task and environment parameters, such as pose offsets, surface friction, payload, and lighting, so that a dataset’s measured occupancy can be joined against it. Cells the join leaves empty are the dataset’s known absences. (Collection Policy Coverage)

Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT)

Wald’s test that updates a log-likelihood ratio after each trial and stops as soon as it crosses an acceptance or rejection boundary set by the allowed error probabilities. It permits early acceptance without inflating false acceptance, provided hypotheses, outcome, and boundaries are declared before testing. (Closed-Loop Evaluation, Sequential Probability Ratio Test)

Shadow Mode Deployment

Staging in which a candidate policy runs on the live sensor streams and writes the commands it would have proposed to an isolated buffer with no actuator authority, while the incumbent controller supplies proposals and the enforcer keeps sole output ownership. Because the incumbent’s admitted commands determine the plant trajectory, agreement in shadow mode says nothing about the states the candidate’s own actions would reach. (Deployment Release, Closed-Loop Evaluation)

Shared Autonomy

A collaborative control architecture in which a human supervisor and an autonomous policy concurrently exert control authority over an embodied system’s physical degrees of freedom. Authority allocation may be realized via continuous haptic virtual fixtures, dynamic compliance blending, or task-space privilege partitioning. The central challenge of shared autonomy is maintaining an intuitive, transparent authority distribution that avoids conflicting commands while preserving the qualified safety constraints. (Supervisory Intervention)

Sim-to-Real Contact Exploit

A training failure in which a reinforcement learning policy discovers and exploits unphysical numerical artifacts in a simulator’s contact solver, such as interpenetration spring restitution, infinite friction sticking, or instantaneous impulse relaxation, to achieve high simulated reward. Because these mathematical solver relaxations do not exist in the physical world, the learned policy can lose performance or violate constraints when deployed on hardware. Mitigation can include improved contact models, randomized parameters, energy-consistency checks, and physical validation. (Policy Training)

Sim-to-Real Gap (Sim-to-Reality Gap)

The systematic discrepancy in dynamics, contact mechanics, sensor transduction, and execution latency that exists between a computational physics simulation and the real physical environment. Policies optimized purely in simulation frequently fail upon physical deployment when the selected models omit or misrepresent effects such as frictional contact, transmission backlash, compliance, or execution delay. Bridging this gap is the central challenge of simulation-based policy training in physical AI. (Policy Training, Closed-Loop Evaluation)

Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM)

Estimating a machine’s pose while building the map it localizes against. Modern systems store past poses as a graph of odometry and scan-match constraints; a loop closure adds a constraint when a place is revisited and can shift every pose and map cell at once, which is why map-anchored beliefs must carry the map revision that placed them. (Spatial Memory)

Spatial Information Age (\(\ObservationAge\))

The time elapsed between the exposure midpoint at the transducer and the consumption of the resulting observation by a policy, state observer, or control loop; running text calls it observation age. Mass keeps moving while the pipeline computes, so the age becomes travel \(\SpeedAtDetection\,\ObservationAge\) that enters the stopping budget through the pre-brake delay. A frame’s arrival timestamp in userspace understates it by the capture and transport time already spent. (Sensor Perception, Spatial Memory)

Speed and Separation Monitoring (SSM)

A collaborative-robot safety mode, set out in ISO 10218-2:2025, that slows or stops the robot so that a protective separation distance to a person is never breached. That distance covers the person’s travel over the robot’s reaction and stopping time, the robot’s own travel and stopping distance, and the position uncertainty of both. Power and force limiting, the complementary mode, instead bounds the force of a contact that is allowed to happen. (Grounded Intent, Safety Enforcement)

Standing Condition

A relied-on premise of a release verdict paired with a detector or site procedure, a checking cadence set by the physical failure mechanism rather than the software release cycle, and a validated response for when the premise becomes false or unknown. Standing conditions make a release revocable. (The Verdict's Standing Conditions)

Stopping Budget

The accounting of the distance a moving machine needs to stop, tested against the usable clearance in \(\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance\). Its elementary form is travel during the pre-brake delay plus braking travel, \(\SpeedAtDetection\PrebrakeDelay + \SpeedAtDetection^2/(2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration)\); the finished budget adds the allowances and delays that each part of the machine introduces, so added delay consumes clearance in proportion to the machine’s speed. (The Causal Boundary, The Physical Body, Sizing the composite stopping budget)

Stopping Envelope

The set of plant states, clearance and speed along each direction of travel, from which the resident braking response, begun after the accounted delay, arrests motion before the nearest boundary with the localization, protective, and tracking allowances still reserved. It turns \(\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance\) into a speed ceiling. Payload, floor friction, and winding temperature move its boundary, so an envelope computed from a datasheet deceleration overstates it when the machine is loaded. (Safety Enforcement)

Stopping Suffix

A precomputed braking trajectory reserved with an admitted motion plan to reach a controlled standstill within declared clearance and actuator limits. It is usable only from its validated entry region, with the necessary state continuity, traction, drive authority, and power available. If authority expires from another state, the permission path needs a separately qualified state-matched response. (Trajectory Planning, Supervisory Intervention)

Supervisory Intervention

The transfer of the right to propose commands on named actuator channels between a learned policy and an authenticated person, committed on a control tick and bounded by a lease, while every command continues to pass the same permission check. The operator gains only the right to propose, not the actuators, and because the transfer is a delay on a moving machine it is priced in the stopping budget. (Supervisory Intervention)

title: Glossary
text:
Takeover Reaction Budget (\(\SupervisoryTakeoverLatency\))

The supervisory waiting interval from a takeover demand to receipt of the first human command, modeled here as \(\SupervisoryTakeoverLatency=\OperatorSensoryTime+\OperatorCognitiveTime+\OperatorMotorTime+\ConsoleCommunicationTime\). The communication term includes transport and the authority handshake; plant response, braking, and any subsequent blending require separate budget terms. A takeover can be credited with preventing harm only if this complete response fits before the last feasible intervention time. (Supervisory Intervention)

Task and Motion Planning (TAMP)

Planning that couples a symbolic search over discrete actions, such as grasp and place, with geometric samplers that find the continuous grasp poses, joint configurations, and paths each action needs. Failure to find a valid sample leaves the symbolic step unverified; it does not establish that no feasible configuration exists. (Grounded Intent)

Temporal Ensembling

A filtering technique for action-chunked policies that combines predictions for the same execution time from overlapping chunks, often through an exponentially weighted average. It can reduce inter-chunk discontinuities but does not guarantee bounded jerk, preserve distinct action modes, or establish feasibility. Weighting older predictions also trades responsiveness for smoothing. (The Cognitive Brain, Policy Training, Trajectory Planning)

Temporal Logic Falsification

Verification posed as adversarial optimization, in which an optimizer searches initial conditions and time-varying disturbance trajectories within a bounded budget to minimize the quantitative robustness of a Signal Temporal Logic (STL) requirement, a real-valued measure of how far a trajectory is from violating or satisfying it. A trajectory with negative robustness is a counterexample; an unsuccessful search yields no certificate. (Adversarial Verification, Signal Temporal Logic and Continuous Robustness)

Test Oracle

The predicate, fixed in full before a trial runs, that compares each independently witnessed quantity of the trial’s trace with its bound from a declared reference event and returns the trial’s verdict. Each comparison carries a signed margin in its own unit, which lets a near miss inform the next trial. (Adversarial Verification)

Time Parameterization

Choosing the timing \(\PathCoordinate(\TimeInstant)\) along a fixed geometric path \(\GeneralizedCoordinates(\PathCoordinate)\) so that every joint velocity, acceleration, torque, and jerk stays within the body’s limits, usually to minimize traversal time. (Trajectory Planning)

Time-to-Harm (\(\HarmLeadTime\))

The predicted interval until a specified harmful event under a stated continuation of the current motion and disturbance assumptions. Comparing it with detection, decision, actuation, and braking time helps assess response urgency, but a scalar timing inequality alone does not prove clearance or forward invariance. A protective response must begin while it remains feasible; once that region is lost, initiating emergency braking cannot guarantee avoidance. (Engineering Physical AI)

Trajectory Spline Blending (\(\DifferentiabilityClass^2\) Continuity)

Interpolation across trajectory seams that matches position, velocity, and acceleration through \(\DifferentiabilityClass^2\) continuity, using suitably constrained polynomials or splines. Acceleration continuity removes acceleration steps but does not imply continuous jerk, which requires \(\DifferentiabilityClass^3\) continuity, or bound the magnitude of jerk. The blend must separately satisfy velocity, acceleration, jerk, torque, and clearance limits over the entire segment. (Trajectory Planning, The Cognitive Brain)

title: Glossary
text:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Model

A multimodal model that conditions action predictions on visual observations and language, often with robot proprioception. Outputs may be discrete action tokens, continuous controls, or trajectory chunks. Built on high-capacity transformer backbones pretrained on Internet-scale vision-language datasets and fine-tuned on robotics demonstrations, VLA models synthesize open-vocabulary semantic reasoning with spatial affordance grounding. Because their internal weights lack physical safety and stability guarantees, their outputs are treated as unprivileged candidate proposals requiring downstream kinodynamic and barrier filtering. (The Cognitive Brain, Grounded Intent)

title: Glossary
text:
World Model

An internal generative model that learns to simulate the forward transition dynamics, contact mechanics, and sensory observations of the physical environment conditioned on the agent’s prospective actions. In physical AI, world models support counterfactual trajectory evaluation and model-predictive rollouts without executing each candidate on hardware. A learned predictive model is not automatically a validated digital twin. Their reliability is limited by epistemic uncertainty over non-smooth contact changes and the sim-to-real gap. (The Cognitive Brain, Trajectory Planning, Policy Training)

Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET)

The longest time a task can take to run to completion on a given processor, over every admissible input and every state its caches, pipeline, and buses can be in, with no other task competing for the processor. It is the \(\WorstCaseExecutionTime\) term of a response bound; blocking and interference from other tasks and interrupts are separate terms with their own bounds, which a shared multicore can inflate. A measured maximum can refute a declared WCET but never establish it. (The Nervous System, Workload Placement)

title: Systems and Hardware
text:
This appendix supplies reference models for the timing, memory, communication, and electrical limits that connect learned proposals to physical actuators. Its derivations and worked estimates help readers calculate response budgets, interpret hardware measurements, and implement the record formats used by the permission path. Each model states assumptions that must hold before its result can support a physical operating limit.

Physical AI requires quantitative intuition across computation, motion, and heat. The latency hierarchy popularized by Jeff Dean1 provides a useful starting point, but a delayed physical command also consumes clearance. The tables below separate representative rates and scenario calculations from bounds that require qualification on the actual machine.
1 Jeff Dean: Google Senior Fellow and systems architect. His latency numbers originally presented with Peter Norvig around 2010 established the canonical latency hierarchy across storage, memory, and network tiers (Scott 2012). Physical AI extends this hierarchy down into electromechanical actuators, stopping kinematics, and thermal time constants.
Scott, Colin. 2012. “Numbers Every Programmer Should Know by Year.”
The fastest events are transistor switching and local memory access. Operating-system dispatch and communication add scheduling and queueing delays. Actuator current then changes over an electrical time constant, while braking and heat accumulation unfold over longer intervals. These scales overlap; a task’s assigned deadline comes from its physical consequence, not from its location in this hierarchy.

Systems Perspective 1.1: Three physical numbers that matter most

Kinetic equivalence: \(1\text{ ms} = 1\text{ mm}\) (at \(1\text{ m/s}\)): At a nominal robotic speed of \(1\text{ m/s}\), every millisecond of perception, inference, or fieldbus latency translates into exactly \(1\text{ mm}\) of blind travel before retarding torque can be applied. At highway velocity (\(30\text{ m/s}\)), each millisecond is \(3\text{ cm}\). In physical systems, software latency is not waiting time; it is physical displacement.
Thermal divergence: \(\SiliconThermalTimeConstant \sim 1\text{ ms}\) vs. \(\ThermalTimeConstant \sim 100\text{ s}\): Semiconductor junctions heat adiabatically within milliseconds during deep neural network bursts, potentially triggering thermal throttling before heat spreaders react. Electrical rail droop is a separate response to changing current demand. In contrast, electromagnetic stator windings heat over tens to hundreds of seconds, tolerating transient overcurrent for aggressive maneuvers but accumulating thermal energy that eventually limits sustained torque.
The exposure wall: \(\FailureObservationInterval = 3 / \ConstantHazardRate\): Under a stationary Poisson model, zero observed failures gives an approximate one-sided 95 percent upper rate bound of \(3/\FailureObservationInterval\) after \(\FailureObservationInterval\) operational hours (Hanley and Lippman-Hand 1983). Very small target rates demand correspondingly large exposure. Runtime barriers can support a broader assurance argument, but neither a barrier nor a finite test proves the absence of failure.





Control rates in physical AI rise steeply from the deliberative brain down to the physical body (table 1). Deliberative multimodal models (VLAs) operate at human reaction scales (\(1\text{--}5\text{ Hz}\)). Action chunking models emit future trajectory waypoints at \(10\text{--}50\text{ Hz}\). Beneath the proposal boundary, the permission path enforces safety barriers at \(1\text{ kHz}\). At the lowest levels, power electronic current loops and PWM switching operate at tens to hundreds of kilohertz to maintain electromagnetic flux and drive torque. For real-time timer schedulability and response-time analysis, see section 1.3; for inverter gate switching and dead-time modeling, see section 1.4.

Communication buses differ sharply in latency and jitter (table 6). Whereas distributed cluster fabrics (such as RoCEv2 or InfiniBand) prioritize aggregate bandwidth using credit-based flow control and statistical multiplexing, onboard physical AI buses must guarantee bounded delivery times. Industrial fieldbuses such as EtherCAT combine hardware forwarding with scheduled exchange and clock synchronization. A specific jitter claim requires the configured system’s evidence. Classical serial buses like Controller Area Network (CAN) 2.0B provide low-overhead bitwise arbitration for up to 8 bytes, but saturate rapidly under multi-joint control traffic. The Flexible Data-Rate variant, CAN FD, expands payloads to 64 bytes with accelerated data bit rates. Meanwhile, switched IEEE Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) uses scheduled transmission gates to multiplex gigabit vision streams with hard real-time actuator commands. In contrast, non-deterministic best-effort Ethernet and shared wireless channels introduce tail latencies that exceed the reaction deadlines of high-speed electromechanical machines. For IEEE 1588 PTP hardware timestamping bounds, see section 1.7; for CAN 2.0B vs. CAN FD priority arbitration and EtherCAT cycle budgets, see section 1.11.

A real-time task is correct only if it computes the required result before its deadline. Average inference latency and throughput do not establish that property. A permission task needs a bound that includes its own execution, blocking on shared resources, and interference from other work. The following single-core scheduling models separate those contributions. Their guarantees apply only under their stated task assumptions; operating-system configuration and loaded measurements must establish whether the implementation satisfies them.


In contrast to general-purpose Linux time-sharing, real-time operating systems schedule tasks based on deterministic timing contracts rather than dynamic heuristics. A periodic real-time task \(\RealTimeTaskIndex\) is characterized by its worst-case execution time (WCET) \(\WorstCaseExecutionTime_i\), relative deadline \(\TaskRelativeDeadline_i\), and period \(\TaskPeriod_i\). When multiple real-time tasks share a single core, schedulability depends on the priority assignment discipline:
Under Rate-Monotonic Scheduling (RMS), fixed-priority preemptive scheduling assigns priority inversely proportional to task period (\(\TaskPeriod_i < \TaskPeriod_j \implies \text{priority}(\RealTimeTaskIndex) > \text{priority}(\PairedTaskIndex)\)) (Liu and Layland 1973). For a set of \(\PeriodicTaskCount\) independent periodic tasks, with negligible scheduling overhead, no blocking or release jitter, and implicit deadlines (\(\TaskRelativeDeadline_i = \TaskPeriod_i\)), a sufficient condition for schedulability is the Liu and Layland utilization bound: \[ \TaskSetUtilization = \sum_{i=1}^\PeriodicTaskCount \frac{\WorstCaseExecutionTime_i}{\TaskPeriod_i} \le \PeriodicTaskCount \left( 2^{1/\PeriodicTaskCount} - 1 \right) \] As \(\PeriodicTaskCount \to \infty\), the bound converges monotonically to \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \PeriodicTaskCount(2^{1/\PeriodicTaskCount}-1) = \ln 2 \approx 0.693\) (69.3 percent). If total processor utilization does not exceed 69.3 percent, the task set is guaranteed to meet all deadlines under RMS. Task periods may instead form a harmonic set, in which every period is an exact integer multiple of every shorter period (\(\TaskPeriod_j = \HarmonicPeriodMultiple \cdot \TaskPeriod_i\) for integer \(\HarmonicPeriodMultiple \ge 1\), such as \(1\text{ ms}\), \(5\text{ ms}\), \(10\text{ ms}\), and \(100\text{ ms}\)). For a harmonic set, the utilization bound rises to 100 percent. In physical AI architectures, rate hierarchies are purposefully engineered with harmonic cadences to maximize processor utilization without sacrificing determinism.

Kopetz, Hermann. 2011. Real-Time Systems: Design Principles for Distributed Embedded Applications. 2nd ed. Real-Time Systems Series. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4419-8237-7.
When processor utilization exceeds the conservative Liu and Layland bound (\(\TaskSetUtilization > \ln 2\)), or when relative deadlines are constrained (\(\TaskRelativeDeadline_i \le \TaskPeriod_i\)), Response Time Analysis (RTA) evaluates exact schedulability from the worst-case response time \(\WorstCaseResponseTime_i\) (Liu and Layland 1973; Kopetz 2011): \[ \WorstCaseResponseTime_i = \WorstCaseExecutionTime_i + \TaskBlockingTime_i + \TaskInterferenceTime_i \le \TaskRelativeDeadline_i \] where \(\TaskBlockingTime_i\) is the maximum blocking duration induced by lower-priority tasks holding shared resources, and \(\TaskInterferenceTime_i\) is the interference from higher-priority tasks. The response time is computed via the fixed-point recurrence. The sum runs over the higher-priority task set. The ceiling counts how many releases of each such task can interfere during the current response-time estimate. An enlarged estimate may expose another release and therefore require another iteration: \[ \WorstCaseResponseTime_i^{(\ResponseTimeIterationIndex+1)} = \WorstCaseExecutionTime_i + \TaskBlockingTime_i + \sum_{j \in \HigherPriorityTasks(i)} \left\lceil \frac{\WorstCaseResponseTime_i^{(\ResponseTimeIterationIndex)}}{\TaskPeriod_j} \right\rceil \WorstCaseExecutionTime_j \] For fixed priorities, bounded blocking, no self-suspension, and zero release jitter, start with \(\WorstCaseResponseTime_i^{(0)} = \WorstCaseExecutionTime_i + \TaskBlockingTime_i\) and iterate until \(\WorstCaseResponseTime_i^{(\ResponseTimeIterationIndex+1)} = \WorstCaseResponseTime_i^{(\ResponseTimeIterationIndex)} \le \TaskRelativeDeadline_i\) (establishing schedulability) or \(\WorstCaseResponseTime_i^{(\ResponseTimeIterationIndex+1)} > \TaskRelativeDeadline_i\) (signaling deadline violation). See Comparing bus occupancy on CAN FD and EtherCAT and Response time analysis and execution variance for the role of response time variance in the nervous system.
In dynamic-priority systems, Earliest Deadline First (EDF) assigns highest priority to the active task with the closest absolute deadline \(\JobAbsoluteDeadline_{i,k} = \JobReleaseTime_{i,k} + \TaskRelativeDeadline_i\). For independent jobs on a single-core preemptive processor with no blocking and negligible scheduling overhead, EDF is optimal: if a task set is schedulable by any scheduling algorithm, it is schedulable by EDF (Liu and Layland 1973). For periodic tasks with \(\TaskRelativeDeadline_i = \TaskPeriod_i\), EDF guarantees schedulability if and only if: \[ \sum_{i=1}^\PeriodicTaskCount \frac{\WorstCaseExecutionTime_i}{\TaskPeriod_i} \le 1 \] achieving 100 percent theoretical utilization without requiring harmonic periods. When relative deadlines are strictly less than periods (\(\TaskRelativeDeadline_i < \TaskPeriod_i\)), schedulability requires the processor demand criterion over the Demand Bound Function (DBF): \[ \text{dbf}(\SchedulingIntervalLength) = \sum_{i=1}^\PeriodicTaskCount \max\left( 0, \left\lfloor \frac{\SchedulingIntervalLength - \TaskRelativeDeadline_i}{\TaskPeriod_i} \right\rfloor + 1 \right) \WorstCaseExecutionTime_i \le \SchedulingIntervalLength, \quad \forall \SchedulingIntervalLength \ge 0 \] evaluating whether cumulative execution demand exceeds available physical time across all time intervals \(\SchedulingIntervalLength\). Under Linux, EDF is exposed via the SCHED_DEADLINE policy implementing the Constant Bandwidth Server (CBS) algorithm. A CBS task declares its runtime \(\CbsRuntimeBudget_i\), deadline \(\TaskRelativeDeadline_i\), and period \(\TaskPeriod_i\) via sched_setattr(). If a task attempts to execute beyond its declared runtime \(\CbsRuntimeBudget_i\) within period \(\TaskPeriod_i\), the kernel dynamically throttles the task until its next period, protecting co-located real-time threads from execution overruns.

Reeves, Glenn E. 1997. What Really Happened on Mars? Electronic mail message, Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
In standard multi-threaded Linux, mutual exclusion primitives (such as futex-backed mutexes) assume threads will eventually yield the processor. When real-time tasks share data structures (such as seqlock mailboxes or actuator command queues) protected by naive mutual exclusion, they suffer from unbounded priority inversion (Sha et al. 1990; Reeves 1997). A low-priority task L acquires a lock; a high-priority task H becomes ready and blocks waiting for the lock; intermediate-priority tasks M that do not need the lock preempt task L, delaying task H for an arbitrary duration. To bound blocking time \(\TaskBlockingTime_i\) in the RTA recurrence, real-time operating systems use formal synchronization protocols:

Priority Inheritance Protocol (PIP): When task H blocks on a lock held by task L, the operating system temporarily elevates task L’s active priority to task H’s priority, preventing preemption by task M. Under PREEMPT_RT Linux, standard in-kernel spinlocks are converted to sleeping rt_mutex locks that enforce PIP automatically, while user-space threads configure PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT. While PIP eliminates unbounded inversion, it permits transitive blocking chains (\(\TaskBlockingTime_i \le \sum_{k} \WorstCaseExecutionTime_k\)) and potential deadlock.
Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP): Each lock is assigned a static priority ceiling equal to the highest priority of any task that may lock it. A task \(\RealTimeTaskIndex\) can lock a resource only if its priority is strictly higher than the priority ceilings of all locks currently held by other tasks. PCP prevents mutual-exclusion deadlocks and guarantees that a task is blocked at most once by at most one lower-priority critical section (Sha et al. 1990): \[ \TaskBlockingTime_i = \max_{k \in \LowerPriorityTasks(i), \CriticalSectionIndex \in \TaskCriticalSections(k)} {\CriticalSectionWcet}_{k,\CriticalSectionIndex} \] where \(\LowerPriorityTasks(\RealTimeTaskIndex)\) is the set of tasks with priority lower than task \(\RealTimeTaskIndex\), and \(\TaskCriticalSections(\BlockingTaskIndex)\) is the set of critical sections executed by task \(\BlockingTaskIndex\) with a priority ceiling at or above the priority of task \(\RealTimeTaskIndex\).


Sha, Lui, Ragunathan Rajkumar, and John P. Lehoczky. 1990. “Priority Inheritance Protocols: An Approach to Real-Time Synchronization.” IEEE Transactions on Computers 39 (9): 1175–85.



In classical embedded systems, the worst-case execution time \(\WorstCaseExecutionTime_i\) is determined via Static Timing Analysis (STA) (Hennessy and Patterson 2019). STA parses binary machine instructions, constructs a Control Flow Graph (CFG), and solves an Integer Linear Program via the Implicit Path Enumeration Technique (IPET) using cycle-accurate microarchitectural models of processor pipelines, branch predictors, and cache sets. In physical AI systems, evaluating \(\WorstCaseExecutionTime_i\) for learned vision-language-action (VLA) and diffusion policies presents three distinct architectural challenges:

Microarchitectural opacity: Modern neural accelerators (GPUs, NPUs, Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) hardware) feature multi-level shared caches, dynamic frequency scaling (DVFS), out-of-order warp schedulers, and memory crossbar contention that make a sound static bound difficult without detailed timing and interference models.
Algorithmic execution variance: Learned pipelines follow dynamic execution paths, including adaptive denoising loops in diffusion models, variable sequence lengths in autoregressive decoders, and data-dependent sparse attention kernels.
Software runtime overhead: Deep learning runtimes (e.g., PyTorch, TensorRT, Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) Runtime) introduce non-deterministic host-to-device kernel launch queueing, unified memory migration, and internal memory allocation locks. Launch overhead and jitter depend on the runtime, driver, submission path, and load; a per-kernel constant is not portable across systems.

To constrain execution variability for neural policies that cross the proposal boundary, physical AI systems enforce deterministic execution contracts and hybrid measurement bounds:

Static shape contracts: Action chunk horizons (\(\ActionChunkHorizon\)), token context lengths, and sensor input tensors are locked to fixed maximum dimensions. Dynamic input padding replaces variable-length tensors, ensuring constant compute graph geometry and eliminating dynamic kernel recompilation.
Zero runtime allocation: All execution buffers, KV caches, scratchpad memory, and direct memory access (DMA) descriptors are preallocated during initialization. Dynamic memory calls (malloc, cudaMalloc, free) are strictly forbidden on cyclic control paths.
Reduced host dispatch overhead via CUDA Graphs: Fixing denoising iterations bounds one source of algorithmic work. Capturing and instantiating a reusable graph reduces repeated per-kernel host setup, as the CUDA Graphs documentation explains. Graph launch still uses the runtime and driver, and device scheduling, frequency changes, and shared-resource contention remain. A graph does not by itself provide deterministic execution.
Extreme Value Theory (EVT) tail bounds: Because finite empirical profiling cannot expose the true maximum execution time under worst-case hardware interference, engineers apply Extreme Value Theory (Coles 2001). Under the Pickands–Balkema–de Haan theorem, execution time exceedances over a high operational threshold \(\ExceedanceThreshold\) converge asymptotically to a Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD): \[ \GpdCumulativeDistribution(\ThresholdExcess) = 1 - \left( 1 + \frac{\TailShapeParameter \ThresholdExcess}{\GpdScaleParameter} \right)^{-1/\TailShapeParameter} \] on the support \(1+\TailShapeParameter \ThresholdExcess/\GpdScaleParameter>0\), with the exponential limit at \(\TailShapeParameter=0\). Here \(\ThresholdExcess = \TailRiskObservationLevel - \ExceedanceThreshold > 0\), \(\GpdScaleParameter > 0\) is the scale parameter, and \(\TailShapeParameter\) is the shape parameter (tail index). The shape parameter characterizes the tail behavior:

\(\TailShapeParameter < 0\) (Weibull domain): Bounded upper tail with a finite model endpoint \(\TailSupportUpperEndpoint = \ExceedanceThreshold - \GpdScaleParameter/\TailShapeParameter\), under the fitted model; an estimated finite endpoint is not proof of a hardware ceiling.
\(\TailShapeParameter = 0\) (Gumbel domain): Light, exponential tail.
\(\TailShapeParameter > 0\) (Fréchet domain): Heavy, polynomial tail. The fitted sign alone neither identifies a hardware failure mechanism nor determines whether a deadline can be defended.



Coles, Stuart. 2001. An Introduction to Statistical Modeling of Extreme Values. Springer.
For an acceptable target exceedance probability \(\TargetExceedanceProbability\) (such as \(10^{-6}\) or \(10^{-8}\) per invocation), a model-based execution-time quantile \(\ExceedanceReturnLevel(\TargetExceedanceProbability)\) is computed as: \[ \ExceedanceReturnLevel(\TargetExceedanceProbability) = \ExceedanceThreshold + \frac{\GpdScaleParameter}{\TailShapeParameter} \left[ \left( \frac{\ObservedCycleCount}{\ThresholdExceedanceCount} \TargetExceedanceProbability \right)^{-\TailShapeParameter} - 1 \right] \] where \(\ObservedCycleCount\) is total sample count and \(\ThresholdExceedanceCount\) is the count of observations exceeding threshold \(\ExceedanceThreshold\). For \(\TailShapeParameter=0\), the continuous limit is \(\ExceedanceThreshold-\GpdScaleParameter\ln(\ObservedCycleCount\TargetExceedanceProbability/\ThresholdExceedanceCount)\). These are fitted quantiles, conditional on the sampling regime, threshold choice, tail model, and parameter uncertainty. They do not certify a deterministic WCET. A placement record must distinguish measured maxima, probabilistic estimates, and justified execution bounds; the permission path must remain schedulable when the proposer exceeds its estimate.



On a heterogeneous robotics system on chip (SoC), the nervous system and safety monitors execute under real-time operating systems (RTOS) or real-time Linux kernels (such as Linux patched with PREEMPT_RT). Interrupts and non-preemptible kernel critical sections can delay user-space tasks. A hard response bound requires bounding those intervals on the chosen kernel and hardware. In physical AI pipelines where control loops govern physical momentum, operating-system determinism requires eliminating non-preemptible kernel sections, bounding interrupt preemption latency, isolating execution cores, locking virtual memory, and enforcing cache locality.
Linux fair scheduling balances CPU service among runnable tasks. Its historical CFS implementation accounts for weighted execution time; newer kernels use EEVDF, which also considers eligibility and virtual deadlines. Neither policy establishes the physical deadline guarantee needed by the permission task. In physical AI systems, real-time control threads must instead be configured with POSIX static priority scheduling policies (SCHED_FIFO or SCHED_RR) across priority levels 1 to 99 (or SCHED_DEADLINE implementing Earliest Deadline First). Under SCHED_FIFO, the highest-priority runnable thread executes immediately and runs until it blocks on I/O, yields voluntarily, or is preempted by a strictly higher-priority real-time thread.
In mainline Linux kernels, disabling preemption during spinlock acquisition (preempt_disable()), executing non-preemptible softirqs, and servicing asynchronous workqueues can delay user-space execution by tens of milliseconds. When an unprivileged machine learning process or device driver holds an in-kernel spinlock, a high-priority 1 kHz real-time safety task cannot preempt the CPU, even if its timer has expired. A kernel configured with PREEMPT_RT reduces non-preemptible execution through four mechanisms, while hardware, drivers, and remaining critical sections still require timing qualification:

Sleeping Spinlocks (rt_mutex): Standard in-kernel spinlocks (spinlock_t and rwlock_t) are replaced by sleeping mutexes backed by rt_mutex with Priority Inheritance Protocol (PIP) support. When a high-priority thread waits for an rt_mutex, the waiter sleeps and the lock owner inherits its priority until it can release the lock. Raw spinlocks remain non-preemptible; interrupt masking depends on the primitive used. Their maximum hold times must be included in the platform timing analysis.
Preemptible Read-Copy Update (CONFIG_PREEMPT_RCU): RCU read-side critical sections (rcu_read_lock() / rcu_read_unlock()) become preemptible, preventing deferred memory reclamation from stalling real-time threads.
Forced Interrupt Threading: Hardware interrupt service routines (ISRs) are split into minimal top-half handlers and prioritized kernel threads (irq/<irq>-<name>) scheduled under SCHED_FIFO.
High-Resolution Timers (hrtimers): Traditional Linux timer ticks execute at coarse periodic jiffies (\(1\text{ ms}\) or \(4\text{ ms}\) granularity), introducing substantial quantization error and timer slack. PREEMPT_RT binds the timer subsystem to hardware per-CPU clock event devices (such as the ARM Generic Timer or x86 Local APIC), enabling sub-microsecond timer resolution. Real-time cyclic threads invoke clock_nanosleep(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, TIMER_ABSTIME, &next_period, NULL) using absolute monotonic deadlines, avoiding cumulative drift from relative sleeps. Wake-up jitter remains part of the response-time bound.

When an external hardware peripheral (such as an IMU, joint encoder counter, or fieldbus controller) asserts an interrupt request (IRQ), the processor halts user execution and saves register context. It then vectors to the hardware ISR via the interrupt controller (such as an ARM Generic Interrupt Controller GICv3 or x86 APIC). The worst-case interrupt latency \(\WorstCaseInterruptLatency\) to enter the hardware interrupt handler can be budgeted as: \[ \WorstCaseInterruptLatency = \LongestInterruptMaskTime + \PipelineFlushDelay + \ContextSaveTime + \sum_{j \in \HigherPriorityTasks(\text{irq})} {\IsrExecutionTime}_{j} \] This expression does not include threaded-handler work or the subsequent scheduling delay before a user-space task runs. Here \(\LongestInterruptMaskTime\) is the longest duration during which CPU interrupts were disabled across the kernel, \(\PipelineFlushDelay\) is the processor pipeline flush delay, \(\ContextSaveTime\) is the hardware register preservation time, and \(\sum {\IsrExecutionTime}_{j}\) represents the execution duration of higher-priority ISRs.
To prevent high-bandwidth sensor streams (such as GigE Vision cameras or 3D lidars streaming gigabits of packet traffic) from generating an interrupt storm that starves the 1 kHz permission path, real-time architectures strictly enforce top-half and bottom-half partitioning:

Top-half (Hardware ISR): Executes in hard-interrupt context with CPU interrupts masked. It executes the absolute minimum hardware operations: reading the peripheral interrupt status register, clearing the physical interrupt line, latching high-resolution hardware counter timestamps, and waking the associated threaded IRQ. The handler’s maximum execution time must be bounded on the target.
Bottom-half (Threaded IRQ): In PREEMPT_RT and RTOS environments, complex packet deserialization, frame CRC verification, and data copies are deferred to dedicated kernel threads (irq/<irq>-<name>). By configuring these threaded IRQs under SCHED_FIFO with priorities lower than the 1 kHz safety monitor (e.g., setting camera IRQ threads to priority 50 and the motor permission thread to priority 90), the scheduler prevents those lower-priority threads from preempting the control task. Hard-interrupt top halves and shared-memory traffic still contribute interference.

Heterogeneous multi-core robotics SoCs must also isolate deterministic control threads from background operating-system disturbances. Kernel boot parameters and memory layout rules establish strict CPU shielding and cache locality:

isolcpus=2,3: Removes cores 2 and 3 from the general kernel scheduler balancing domain, reducing automatic load balancing onto those cores; explicit affinity, cpusets, and kernel work still require configuration.
nohz_full=2,3: Enables full dynamic tickless operation. When an isolated core runs a single real-time thread, the kernel can suppress the periodic scheduling timer tick (\(100\text{--}1000\text{ Hz}\)), removing that source of periodic interruption while other interrupts and scheduling delays remain.
rcu_nocbs=2,3: Offloads RCU callback processing from isolated cores to housekeeping cores (cores 0 and 1).
IRQ Affinity Partitioning: Peripheral hardware interrupts are directed away from real-time cores by writing CPU bitmasks to /proc/irq/<id>/smp_affinity. High-rate camera MSI-X vectors and Ethernet controller interrupts are pinned exclusively to housekeeping cores, reducing controllable interrupt interference. Nonmaskable events, local timers, and platform firmware disturbances still require accounting.
Cache Line Alignment and False Sharing Elimination: Cache-line size is architecture dependent; the examples here assume 64-byte lines. When multiple CPU cores access independent variables that reside within the same 64-byte line, hardware cache coherency protocols (MESI/MOESI) repeatedly invalidate the line across core private caches upon every store, a phenomenon known as false sharing or cache line bouncing. A single false sharing interaction can stall a real-time core for 50 to 100 clock cycles. Separating independently written state into aligned, padded cache-line slots avoids false sharing; merely aligning the beginning of a larger structure does not isolate every member. The target’s remaining cache misses and contention still need timing bounds. Furthermore, real-time control paths pre-warm L1 instruction and data caches during initialization by executing a dummy pass over critical control tables before arming actuators.

Virtual memory subsystems rely on demand paging, so deterministic execution also requires locking virtual memory and eliminating page faults. When a process accesses an unmapped virtual address, the CPU raises an architectural page fault exception (#PF) and suspends execution. The kernel page-table handler then allocates a physical page frame, updates translation lookaside buffer (TLB) entries, and zeroes the memory (a minor page fault, requiring \(10\text{--}50\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\)). If the requested page was swapped to secondary flash storage, the thread blocks on disk I/O (a major page fault, requiring \(10\text{--}50\text{ ms}\)). Furthermore, Transparent Huge Pages (THP) memory compaction (khugepaged) can asynchronously stall threads for tens of milliseconds while defragmenting physical memory pages. A page fault can consume the remaining response-time margin; its mere occurrence does not imply that every deadline is missed.
The following Linux/glibc sketch illustrates initialization and absolute-period sleeping. It assumes the shown page and cache-line sizes. Production code must also validate limits and privileges, measure completion against the deadline, and enter the assessed fallback on an overrun. A late absolute sleep can return immediately; it must not trigger an uncontrolled series of catch-up actuator writes.
// Real-time process initialization, memory locking, and cyclic execution
#define _GNU_SOURCE
#include <sys/mman.h>
#include <sched.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <malloc.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <errno.h>

#define REALTIME_PRIORITY   90
#define CONTROL_CPU_CORE    2
#define STACK_PREFAULT_SZ   (256 * 1024)       // 256 KB stack
#define HEAP_PREALLOC_SZ    (16 * 1024 * 1024) // 16 MB pre-allocated arena
#define PERIOD_NS           1000000ULL         // 1 ms period (1 kHz)

// 64-byte cache-aligned telemetry slot to prevent false sharing
typedef struct __attribute__((aligned(64))) {
    uint64_t sequence_id;
    uint64_t timestamp_ns;
    float joint_torques[8];
    uint32_t status_flags;
    uint8_t reserved[12];
} realtime_telemetry_t;

static realtime_telemetry_t g_telemetry;
static volatile uint8_t *g_realtime_heap_arena = NULL;

void configure_realtime_process(int target_cpu, int rt_priority, size_t stack_size) {
    // 1. Bind execution to dedicated isolated CPU core (isolcpus / nohz_full)
    cpu_set_t cpuset;
    CPU_ZERO(&cpuset);
    CPU_SET(target_cpu, &cpuset);
    if (sched_setaffinity(0, sizeof(cpu_set_t), &cpuset) != 0) {
        perror("sched_setaffinity failed");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // 2. Configure POSIX static real-time priority (SCHED_FIFO)
    struct sched_param sp = { .sched_priority = rt_priority };
    if (sched_setscheduler(0, SCHED_FIFO, &sp) != 0) {
        perror("sched_setscheduler SCHED_FIFO failed");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // 3. Lock all current and future virtual address mappings into physical RAM
    if (mlockall(MCL_CURRENT | MCL_FUTURE) != 0) {
        perror("mlockall failed");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // 4. Disable glibc dynamic heap trimming and anonymous mmap allocation
    mallopt(M_TRIM_THRESHOLD, -1);
    mallopt(M_MMAP_MAX, 0);

    // 5. Pre-allocate and prefault the dedicated heap arena
    g_realtime_heap_arena = (uint8_t *)malloc(HEAP_PREALLOC_SZ);
    if (!g_realtime_heap_arena) {
        perror("malloc heap arena failed");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    // Touch every 4 KB page to force physical page frame allocation and TLB population
    for (size_t i = 0; i < HEAP_PREALLOC_SZ; i += 4096) {
        g_realtime_heap_arena[i] = 0;
    }

    // 6. Prefault the thread execution stack to its declared maximum depth
    volatile char stack_buffer[stack_size];
    for (size_t i = 0; i < stack_size; i += 4096) {
        stack_buffer[i] = 0; // Trigger minor page fault and populate TLB entry
    }
}

void run_periodic_control_loop(void) {
    struct timespec next_period;
    clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &next_period);

    // A real implementation warms the actual control code and data before arming.

    while (1) {
        // Compute next absolute wake epoch (eliminates cumulative drift)
        next_period.tv_nsec += PERIOD_NS;
        while (next_period.tv_nsec >= 1000000000L) {
            next_period.tv_nsec -= 1000000000L;
            next_period.tv_sec  += 1;
        }

        // High-resolution absolute sleep
        int ret;
        do {
            ret = clock_nanosleep(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, TIMER_ABSTIME, &next_period, NULL);
        } while (ret == EINTR);
        if (ret != 0) {
            fprintf(stderr, "clock_nanosleep: %s\n", strerror(ret));
            break;
        }

        // ZERO-ALLOCATION CYCLIC CONTROL LOGIC
        // 1. Ingest sensor state from lock-free shared memory
        // 2. Evaluate Control Barrier Functions (CBFs)
        // 3. Dispatch admitted setpoints to EtherCAT master
        g_telemetry.sequence_id++;
    }
}
Beyond address space locking and stack prefaulting, the cyclic 1 kHz control loop operates under a strict zero dynamic allocation invariant. In general-purpose systems programming, developers routinely rely on dynamic memory managers (malloc, free, C++ new, delete) or standard container expansions (std::vector::push_back). In a real-time control loop, however, dynamic allocation introduces three catastrophic failure modes:

Arena Mutex Contention: Modern allocators (such as ptmalloc in glibc) partition memory into multiple heap arenas protected by mutual-exclusion mutexes. If another thread in the same process acquires an arena lock, a high-priority 1 kHz real-time control thread calling malloc blocks on that mutex, suffering from priority inversion and waiting milliseconds.
Kernel Syscall Invocations: When an allocator exhausts its active arena chunk, it issues brk() or anonymous mmap() system calls. These kernel entries acquire the process’s mmap_lock (or mmap_sem), which is shared with background kernel threads such as khugepaged performing transparent huge page compaction or memory defragmentation, stalling user-space execution for tens of milliseconds.
Heap Fragmentation: Repeated cyclic allocations and deallocations fragment the heap, degrading allocation search times across segregated free lists into non-deterministic search loops.

Consequently, all message structures, matrix workspace buffers, trajectory buffers, and seqlock mailbox slots must be statically allocated at startup or drawn from fixed-size, lock-free memory pools (such as slab allocators). Furthermore, mlockall(MCL_FUTURE) must be paired with explicit memory pre-allocation and page prefaulting. Linux uses optimistic memory allocation (overcommit), so virtual address ranges returned by malloc() are not backed by physical page frames until the thread actually writes to each 4 KB page. Touching an uninitialized buffer for the first time inside the control loop triggers a minor page fault exception (#PF).
