The qualified synchronization error and arrival deadline determine when a drive may use the frame. Clock synchronization does not remove frame transit time.



While EtherCAT processes frames on the fly through specialized slave controllers, modern multi-camera and lidar robotic systems require multi-gigabit Ethernet fabrics that transport high-bandwidth vision data alongside hard real-time actuator commands. IEEE Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) provides deterministic Ethernet via standards that bound queuing jitter and reserve transmission windows:
The IEEE 802.1Qbv Time-Aware Shaper (TAS) coordinates traffic transmission using hardware-controlled transmission gates associated with each priority egress queue (traffic classes 0 to 7). A cyclic Gate Control List (GCL), synchronized across all network bridges via IEEE 802.1AS (generalized Precision Time Protocol), switches gates open or closed at precise physical time epochs. By reserving dedicated time windows exclusively for high-priority Scheduled Traffic (ST), TAS eliminates queuing interference from lower-priority Best-Effort (BE) traffic.
Standard Ethernet frames are non-preemptive: once a transmission begins, it cannot be interrupted on physical copper or optical links. If a lower-priority best-effort packet begins transmission immediately before an ST time slice opens, the scheduled frame experiences transmission blocking of up to the maximum frame duration. To prevent this, TAS enforces a guard band before each scheduled traffic window: \[ \GuardBandDuration \ge \frac{\BestEffortWireBitCount}{\LinkBitRate} \] Here \(\BestEffortWireBitCount\) is the maximum non-preemptible wire occupancy in bits, including the applicable framing overhead. A payload MTU in bytes cannot be divided directly by a bit rate. The configured guard must also cover clock error and implementation timing uncertainty. During it, a best-effort frame may start only if it can finish before the reserved window.
IEEE 802.1Qbu and IEEE 802.3br frame preemption reduce blocking by interrupting eligible traffic at permitted fragment boundaries. The remaining bound includes the maximum non-preemptible fragment and its overhead, not merely a nominal minimum fragment size. Both the link partners and the schedule must support the mechanism. Preemption saves reserved idle time at the cost of fragmentation overhead and additional configuration obligations.

For either CAN variant, sum every command and feedback frame in the required cycle, then account for competing traffic, non-preemptive blocking, and the declared error model. EtherCAT avoids a separate frame for each axis, but its process-data size and forwarding delay still grow with the topology. TSN reserves service along a path. An end-to-end bound must include each hop’s schedule, serialization, forwarding, and synchronization uncertainty. These distinct budgets, rather than a protocol name or a universal axis count, support the selection in Real-Time Command Transport and Bus Determinism.



When a producer updates multiword state read by a deadline-bound enforcer, waiting on a producer-held mutex can violate the reader’s deadline. The single-slot mailbox in algorithm 1 uses a sequence counter, which marks a single writer’s publication in progress with an odd value and a completed publication with an even value:

Writer Protocol:

Publish an odd sequence value, write the payload, and make it visible through the platform’s coherent or cache-maintained memory contract.
Publish the next even value with release ordering.

Reader Protocol:

Read \(\SequenceCounterReading_1\) with acquire ordering. If it is odd, reject this publication without waiting.
Make one bounded copy to scratch memory using the platform’s required load ordering, then read \(\SequenceCounterReading_2\).
Stage the candidate only if \(\SequenceCounterReading_1=\SequenceCounterReading_2\) and both are even, and the copied frame passes integrity, timestamp, and requested-expiry checks. Full admission remains separate. Retain the active command only while its own state, evidence, lease, and stopping margin permit; otherwise enter the state-matched fallback.


The algorithm is platform pseudocode, not portable C++ with a non-atomic payload: racing ordinary C++ loads and stores would be undefined behavior even if the sequence check later rejects the copy. The platform must define safe concurrent copying, cache maintenance, aligned counter atomicity, and wraparound behavior. On the machine’s discrete microcontroller, the writer is the link-receive interrupt and the reader is the permission tick on the same core, so the counter protocol needs only compiler ordering between them. A data memory barrier matters where a DMA engine or a second master writes the same memory. Arm M-profile cores provide that barrier only as the full-system DMB (ARM Limited 2012), so the OrderingFence steps below stand for whatever the target requires rather than an A-profile shareability option. The reader’s one-attempt execution time can be bounded on the target hardware; success probability depends on the writer’s schedule and cannot be inferred from payload size alone. Conventional Linux seqlock readers may retry, as the kernel documentation shows, but a real-time permission gate cannot use an unbounded retry loop.

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Single-Slot Trajectory Seqlock Baseline}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require proposal $P$ (proposal header with $\text{sequence\_id}$, $\text{t\_evidence\_ns}$, $\text{sync\_error\_ns}$, $\text{t\_expire\_ns}$; waypoints $\mathbf{w}_{1..H}$; $\text{crc32}$), scratch buffer $B_{\text{scratch}}$ in static SRAM reserved for this staging attempt, mailbox $(c_{\text{seq}}, \text{Slot}_{\text{shared}})$ in the microcontroller's own SRAM, written by the link-receive interrupt after the frame's CRC and sequence checks and read by the permission tick, current time $t_{\text{now}}$ and evidence-age budget $t_{\text{age,max}}$ (the configured upper-age ceiling for candidate staging), both on the safety microcontroller's clock
\Ensure candidate snapshot in $B_{\text{scratch}}$ or rejection; the active spline remains unchanged
\Function{PublishReceivedChunk}{$P$} \Comment{runs in the link-receive interrupt}
    \State $c_{\text{curr}} \gets \operatorname{AtomicLoadExplicit}(c_{\text{seq}}, \text{memory\_order\_relaxed})$
    \State $\operatorname{AtomicStoreExplicit}(c_{\text{seq}}, c_{\text{curr}} + 1, \text{memory\_order\_relaxed})$ \Comment{mark odd: write in progress}
    \State $\operatorname{OrderingFence}()$ \Comment{odd counter ordered before payload stores}
    \State $\operatorname{CopyMemory}(\text{Slot}_{\text{shared}}.\text{payload}, P, \text{sizeof}(P))$ \Comment{copy multi-word trajectory}
    \State $\operatorname{OrderingFence}()$ \Comment{payload stores ordered before even counter}
    \State $\operatorname{AtomicStoreExplicit}(c_{\text{seq}}, c_{\text{curr}} + 2, \text{memory\_order\_release})$ \Comment{mark even: publish committed}
\EndFunction
\Function{StageLatestActionChunk}{$B_{\text{scratch}}, t_{\text{now}}$}
    \State $c_{\text{start}} \gets \operatorname{AtomicLoadExplicit}(c_{\text{seq}}, \text{memory\_order\_acquire})$ \Comment{load initial counter}
    \If{$c_{\text{start}}$ is odd}
        \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_WRITER\_ACTIVE}$ \Comment{writer active; retain prior spline}
    \EndIf
    \State $\operatorname{OrderingFence}()$ \Comment{prevent payload reads hoisting before counter}
    \State $\operatorname{CopyMemory}(B_{\text{scratch}}, \text{Slot}_{\text{shared}}.\text{payload}, \text{sizeof}(\text{Payload}))$ \Comment{tentative copy; active spline unchanged}
    \State $\operatorname{OrderingFence}()$ \Comment{payload reads complete before $c_{\text{end}}$}
    \State $c_{\text{end}} \gets \operatorname{AtomicLoadExplicit}(c_{\text{seq}}, \text{memory\_order\_acquire})$ \Comment{re-read sequence counter}
    \If{$c_{\text{start}} \ne c_{\text{end}}$}
        \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_TORN\_READ}$ \Comment{concurrent write detected}
    \EndIf
    \If{$\operatorname{ComputeCrc32}(B_{\text{scratch}}.\text{bytes\_before\_crc}) \ne B_{\text{scratch}}.\text{crc32}$}
        \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_CHECKSUM\_INVALID}$
    \EndIf
    \If{$t_{\text{now}} \ge B_{\text{scratch}}.\text{t\_expire\_ns}$}
        \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_REQUEST\_EXPIRED}$ \Comment{requested expiry is absolute}
    \EndIf
    \If{$t_{\text{now}} - B_{\text{scratch}}.\text{t\_evidence\_ns} + B_{\text{scratch}}.\text{sync\_error\_ns} > t_{\text{age,max}}$}
        \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_EVIDENCE\_STALE}$ \Comment{conversion error is added to every age}
    \EndIf
    \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_CANDIDATE\_STAGED}$ \Comment{full admission must finish before activation}
\EndFunction
\end{algorithmic}

The proposal header and chunk payload of Supervisory timers and proposal wire contracts cross the proposal boundary through this mailbox (Multi-Rate Cadences). Section 1.15.1 gives their byte layout. A successful read yields a candidate in owned staging memory. Admission separately checks producer sequence and lineage, the complete trajectory and stop, and the current seam state before activation (The Trajectory Record). Scheduling that work must preserve the permission tick; the scratch slot cannot be reused while admission still reads it. At activation the MCU rereads its clock, rechecks evidence and deadlines, and records the successful admission time. A mailbox read neither renews the active lease nor resets the evidence epoch.




In computer vision for machine learning, neural models typically process normalized pixel tensors to predict 2D bounding boxes or semantic segmentation masks. In physical AI systems, however, visual observations must be grounded as physical objects in continuous Euclidean 3D metric space to evaluate spatial clearance buffers \(\ClearDistance\) and enforce collision-avoidance invariants. Perception pipelines map continuous Euclidean 3D scenes onto discrete 2D camera photosite grids, and unproject pixel detections back into metric space under quantified measurement uncertainty.


Under the standard pinhole camera model, a 3D point \(\CameraFramePoint = [\CameraFrameHorizontalCoordinate, \CameraFrameVerticalCoordinate, \CameraFrameDepth]^\top\) in camera coordinates projects onto pixel coordinates \([\PixelColumnCoordinate, \PixelRowCoordinate]^\top\) via the intrinsic calibration matrix \(\CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix\):10 \[
\HomogeneousPixelCoordinates = \begin{bmatrix} \PixelColumnCoordinate \\ \PixelRowCoordinate \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{\CameraFrameDepth} \CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix \CameraFramePoint = \frac{1}{\CameraFrameDepth} \begin{bmatrix} \HorizontalFocalLength & 0 & \PrincipalPointColumn \\ 0 & \VerticalFocalLength & \PrincipalPointRow \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \CameraFrameHorizontalCoordinate \\ \CameraFrameVerticalCoordinate \\ \CameraFrameDepth \end{bmatrix}
\] where \((\HorizontalFocalLength, \VerticalFocalLength)\) are focal lengths in pixel units and \((\PrincipalPointColumn, \PrincipalPointRow)\) is the principal point. Non-linear radial lens distortion is modeled by distortion coefficients \((\RadialDistortionCoefficient_1, \RadialDistortionCoefficient_2)\): \[ \NormalizedRadialDistance^2 = \NormalizedImageAbscissa^2 + \NormalizedImageOrdinate^2, \quad \DistortedImageAbscissa = \NormalizedImageAbscissa (1 + \RadialDistortionCoefficient_1 \NormalizedRadialDistance^2 + \RadialDistortionCoefficient_2 \NormalizedRadialDistance^4), \quad \DistortedImageOrdinate = \NormalizedImageOrdinate (1 + \RadialDistortionCoefficient_1 \NormalizedRadialDistance^2 + \RadialDistortionCoefficient_2 \NormalizedRadialDistance^4) \] where \((\NormalizedImageAbscissa, \NormalizedImageOrdinate) = (\CameraFrameHorizontalCoordinate / \CameraFrameDepth, \CameraFrameVerticalCoordinate / \CameraFrameDepth)\) are normalized image coordinates.
10 Pinhole Intrinsic Projection: The pinhole model projects 3D points onto a 2D sensor through calibrated intrinsics. Under fixed pixel noise, the lateral variance after depth unprojection grows with squared distance; depth-error and calibration terms follow their own models. Uncalibrated intrinsics can bias a clearance estimate and must be included in its error envelope.


When unprojecting a 2D pixel observation \([\PixelColumnCoordinate, \PixelRowCoordinate]^\top\) with measured depth \(\CameraFrameDepth\) into 3D camera coordinates, photosite measurement noise \(\MeasurementNoiseCovariance = \text{diag}(\PixelStandardDeviation^2, \PixelRowStandardDeviation^2, \DepthStandardDeviation^2)\) propagates through the unprojection Jacobian \(\UnprojectionJacobian\): \[
\CameraFramePoint = \begin{bmatrix} (\PixelColumnCoordinate - \PrincipalPointColumn) \CameraFrameDepth / \HorizontalFocalLength \\ (\PixelRowCoordinate - \PrincipalPointRow) \CameraFrameDepth / \VerticalFocalLength \\ \CameraFrameDepth \end{bmatrix}, \quad \UnprojectionJacobian = \frac{\partial \CameraFramePoint}{\partial [\PixelColumnCoordinate, \PixelRowCoordinate, \CameraFrameDepth]} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\CameraFrameDepth}{\HorizontalFocalLength} & 0 & \frac{\PixelColumnCoordinate - \PrincipalPointColumn}{\HorizontalFocalLength} \\ 0 & \frac{\CameraFrameDepth}{\VerticalFocalLength} & \frac{\PixelRowCoordinate - \PrincipalPointRow}{\VerticalFocalLength} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\] The propagated camera-frame spatial covariance is: \[ \CameraFramePointCovariance = \UnprojectionJacobian \MeasurementNoiseCovariance \UnprojectionJacobian^\top \] Evaluating the diagonal terms shows that lateral positional variance along the camera \(\Glyph{X}\)-axis scales with the square of depth: \[ \CameraLateralStandardDeviation^2 \approx \left(\frac{\CameraFrameDepth}{\HorizontalFocalLength}\right)^2 \PixelStandardDeviation^2 + \left(\frac{\PixelColumnCoordinate - \PrincipalPointColumn}{\HorizontalFocalLength}\right)^2 \DepthStandardDeviation^2 \] For fixed pixel noise, the first variance contribution scales with \(\CameraFrameDepth^2\), so its standard deviation grows linearly with distance. The depth-error contribution follows the depth sensor’s own model. Transforming this 3D point into the robot body frame via rigid extrinsic transform \(\CameraExtrinsicTransform = [\CameraExtrinsicRotation, \CameraExtrinsicTranslation; \ZeroVector^\top, 1]\) yields the spatial body covariance: \[ \BodyFramePointCovariance = \CameraExtrinsicRotation \CameraFramePointCovariance \CameraExtrinsicRotation^\top + \ExtrinsicCalibrationCovariance \] where \(\ExtrinsicCalibrationCovariance\) models independent extrinsic uncertainty under this first-order approximation; correlations require the corresponding cross terms. A probabilistic clearance buffer may scale with \(\sqrt{\LargestEigenvalue(\BodyFramePointCovariance)}\) at a declared tail risk. A deterministic permission check instead needs a justified bounded-error envelope; covariance alone does not give a worst-case bound.



Zhang’s calibration technique computes the camera intrinsic matrix \(\CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix\) by observing a planar calibration rig (such as a checkerboard pattern) across \(\CalibrationViewCount \ge 3\) distinct orientations (Zhang 2000). Without loss of generality, assume the model plane lies on \(\ModelPointHeight = 0\) in world coordinates. A 3D model point \(\CalibrationModelPoint = [\ModelPointAbscissa, \ModelPointOrdinate, 0, 1]^\top\) maps to a 2D image point \(\HomogeneousPixelCoordinates = [\PixelColumnCoordinate, \PixelRowCoordinate, 1]^\top\) through a \(3 \times 3\) planar homography matrix \(\PlanarHomographyMatrix\): \[
\ProjectiveScaleFactor \begin{bmatrix} \PixelColumnCoordinate \\ \PixelRowCoordinate \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix \begin{bmatrix} \CameraRotationColumn_1 & \CameraRotationColumn_2 & \CameraRotationColumn_3 & \RigidTransformTranslation \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \ModelPointAbscissa \\ \ModelPointOrdinate \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix \begin{bmatrix} \CameraRotationColumn_1 & \CameraRotationColumn_2 & \RigidTransformTranslation \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \ModelPointAbscissa \\ \ModelPointOrdinate \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \PlanarHomographyMatrix \begin{bmatrix} \ModelPointAbscissa \\ \ModelPointOrdinate \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
\] where \(\PlanarHomographyMatrix = [\HomographyColumn_1 \; \HomographyColumn_2 \; \HomographyColumn_3] = \HomographyScaleFactor \CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix [\CameraRotationColumn_1 \; \CameraRotationColumn_2 \; \RigidTransformTranslation]\) with arbitrary nonzero scalar \(\HomographyScaleFactor\).

Zhang, Zhengyou. 2000. “A Flexible New Technique for Camera Calibration.” IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence 22 (11): 1330–34. https://doi.org/10.1109/34.888718.


Because the rotation vectors \(\CameraRotationColumn_1\) and \(\CameraRotationColumn_2\) are orthonormal columns of an \(\SpecialOrthogonalGroup\) matrix (\(\CameraRotationColumn_1^\top \CameraRotationColumn_2 = 0\) and \(\|\CameraRotationColumn_1\| = \|\CameraRotationColumn_2\| = 1\)), inverting \(\CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix\) yields: \[
\CameraRotationColumn_1 = \frac{1}{\HomographyScaleFactor} \CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix^{-1} \HomographyColumn_1, \quad \CameraRotationColumn_2 = \frac{1}{\HomographyScaleFactor} \CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix^{-1} \HomographyColumn_2
\] Imposing orthonormality on \(\CameraRotationColumn_1\) and \(\CameraRotationColumn_2\) defines two algebraic constraints per homography: \[
\HomographyColumn_1^\top \CameraIntrinsicInverseTranspose \CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix^{-1} \HomographyColumn_2 = 0
\] \[
\HomographyColumn_1^\top \CameraIntrinsicInverseTranspose \CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix^{-1} \HomographyColumn_1 - \HomographyColumn_2^\top \CameraIntrinsicInverseTranspose \CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix^{-1} \HomographyColumn_2 = 0
\] The symmetric matrix \(\AbsoluteConicImageMatrix = \CameraIntrinsicInverseTranspose \CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix^{-1}\) represents the image of the absolute conic (IAC): \[
\AbsoluteConicImageMatrix = \begin{bmatrix} \AbsoluteConicImageEntry_{11} & \AbsoluteConicImageEntry_{12} & \AbsoluteConicImageEntry_{13} \\ \AbsoluteConicImageEntry_{12} & \AbsoluteConicImageEntry_{22} & \AbsoluteConicImageEntry_{23} \\ \AbsoluteConicImageEntry_{13} & \AbsoluteConicImageEntry_{23} & \AbsoluteConicImageEntry_{33} \end{bmatrix}
\] Defining the 6-vector \(\AbsoluteConicVector = [\AbsoluteConicImageEntry_{11}, \AbsoluteConicImageEntry_{12}, \AbsoluteConicImageEntry_{22}, \AbsoluteConicImageEntry_{13}, \AbsoluteConicImageEntry_{23}, \AbsoluteConicImageEntry_{33}]^\top\), each quadratic term \(\HomographyColumn_i^\top \AbsoluteConicImageMatrix \HomographyColumn_j\) can be rewritten as the linear inner product \(\HomographyConstraintVector_{ij}^\top \AbsoluteConicVector\), where: \[
\HomographyConstraintVector_{ij} = \begin{bmatrix} \HomographyColumnEntry_{i1}\HomographyColumnEntry_{j1} \\ \HomographyColumnEntry_{i1}\HomographyColumnEntry_{j2} + \HomographyColumnEntry_{i2}\HomographyColumnEntry_{j1} \\ \HomographyColumnEntry_{i2}\HomographyColumnEntry_{j2} \\ \HomographyColumnEntry_{i3}\HomographyColumnEntry_{j1} + \HomographyColumnEntry_{i1}\HomographyColumnEntry_{j3} \\ \HomographyColumnEntry_{i3}\HomographyColumnEntry_{j2} + \HomographyColumnEntry_{i2}\HomographyColumnEntry_{j3} \\ \HomographyColumnEntry_{i3}\HomographyColumnEntry_{j3} \end{bmatrix}
\] The two constraints per observed orientation become the linear system: \[
\begin{bmatrix} \HomographyConstraintVector_{12}^\top \\ (\HomographyConstraintVector_{11} - \HomographyConstraintVector_{22})^\top \end{bmatrix} \AbsoluteConicVector = \ZeroVector
\] Stacking \(\CalibrationViewCount \ge 3\) images forms the homogeneous system \(\CalibrationConstraintMatrix \AbsoluteConicVector = \ZeroVector\), where \(\CalibrationConstraintMatrix \in \mathbb{R}^{2\CalibrationViewCount \times 6}\). The right singular vector of \(\CalibrationConstraintMatrix\) corresponding to the smallest singular value provides \(\AbsoluteConicVector\) up to a scale factor. The intrinsic parameters \((\HorizontalFocalLength, \VerticalFocalLength, \PrincipalPointColumn, \PrincipalPointRow)\) and skew \(\CameraSkewCoefficient\) are then extracted, after fixing the scale and sign, via a positive-definite factorization of \(\AbsoluteConicImageMatrix\). Degenerate views or measurement noise can make that factorization invalid. Distinct orientations alone do not guarantee a well-conditioned calibration. This closed-form linear solution initializes the non-linear Levenberg–Marquardt optimization minimizing reprojection residuals over all observed fiducial corners.





In distributed systems, pipeline latency represents elapsed waiting time or queuing delay. In physical AI, end-to-end software latency converts directly into irreversible physical displacement, uninspected “blind travel,” during which an embodied machine traverses space with undiminished momentum before actuators can begin retarding motion. Halting an embodied machine transporting mass \(\Mass\) at velocity \(\SpeedAtDetection\) requires balancing sensorimotor information freshness, neural compute budgets, and fieldbus dispatch against physical mechanical braking deceleration.


For a stop triggered by a specified hazard detector and stop path, let \(\PrebrakeDelay\) bound the time from the physical state represented by the evidence until validated braking deceleration begins (Watchdog validity leases and teleoperation latency bounds gives the lease-expiry form, which charges the lease interval in place of recognition and compute): \[ \PrebrakeDelay = \ObservationAge + \DetectionInterval + \StopDecisionComputeBound + \CommandTransportTime + \ActuatorResponseTime \] The five intervals partition the pre-brake timeline without overlap:

\(\ObservationAge\) is the upper evidence age at a declared decision-start epoch, including capture/readout, completed processing and transport, and clock-conversion uncertainty.
\(\DetectionInterval\) bounds any remaining recognition or expiry-detection interval after that epoch; work already included in evidence age is not charged twice.
\(\StopDecisionComputeBound\) bounds subsequent stop-decision work and any still-required input transfer.
\(\CommandTransportTime\) bounds command dispatch and network queuing.
\(\ActuatorResponseTime\) ends when the measured actuator begins delivering the specified deceleration, not when a command register is written.

The intervals must be disjoint and ordered along the actual stop path. Clearance and motion must share a declared epoch: if the clearance is already propagated to current time, do not subtract historical travel a second time. Under the explicit simplifying assumption that speed cannot increase before brake onset, the blind travel is bounded by \(\BlindTravelDistance=\SpeedAtDetection\,\PrebrakeDelay\). If propulsion or a slope can increase speed, use its validated acceleration bound in this interval instead.



Tire-floor friction and actuator torque place upper limits on achievable deceleration. The bound \(\AchievedBrakingDeceleration\le\CoulombFrictionCoefficient \Gravity\) does not establish what braking the machine will deliver. Let \(\CredibleBrakingDeceleration>0\) be a validated lower bound on achieved deceleration throughout the stop, for the declared load, temperature, slope, brake condition, and surface. A justified friction floor \(\FrictionCoefficientFloor\) may support that bound, but does not replace brake tests. With constant or stronger braking after onset, a localization bound \(\LocalizationBound\), a fixed protective clearance \(\ProtectiveClearanceMargin\), and a tracking-error bound \(\TrackingErrorBound\), \[ \StoppingDistance(\SpeedAtDetection)=\SpeedAtDetection\,\PrebrakeDelay+\frac{\SpeedAtDetection^2}{2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration}+\LocalizationBound+\ProtectiveClearanceMargin+\TrackingErrorBound. \] Motion is admitted only when \(\StoppingDistance(\SpeedAtDetection)\le \ClearDistance\), where \(\ClearDistance\) is taken as a validated lower bound on available path clearance. This is a constant-deceleration reference model. The smooth stop in Stopping Envelopes ramps acceleration from and back to zero, so it does not satisfy a strictly positive deceleration floor throughout braking. For that profile, replace \(\SpeedAtDetection^2/(2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration)\) with the integral of its validated speed trajectory and use its full duration. The sampled controller must reserve intersample travel and a state-matched stop before the viable region is lost.



In an ideal friction-limited model, lowering \(\CoulombFrictionCoefficient\) from \(\NominalFrictionCoefficient\) to a positive \(\DegradedFrictionCoefficient\) changes the braking-distance ratio to \(\NominalFrictionCoefficient/\DegradedFrictionCoefficient\). That ratio is illustrative; actual deceleration can also be limited by brake hardware or control. If surface friction is not sensed in time, derive \(\CredibleBrakingDeceleration\) from a controlled surface condition and inspection schedule, exclude degraded surfaces, or withhold motion. For the constant-speed pre-brake model above, solving the clearance inequality gives \[ \ClearanceSpeedClamp=-\CredibleBrakingDeceleration\PrebrakeDelay+\sqrt{(\CredibleBrakingDeceleration\PrebrakeDelay)^2+2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration\left(\ClearDistance-\LocalizationBound-\ProtectiveClearanceMargin-\TrackingErrorBound\right)}. \] This clamp is valid only when \(\ClearDistance\) exceeds the three fixed allowances, the braking lower bound and timing upper bounds hold, and the speed bound is enforced before entering the hazard corridor. No positive clamp follows if the available deceleration floor is unknown or zero.

The chain has two strands. Records 1 through 5 state what the plant can do and what the proposer has shown it can do; records 6 through 9 carry what the proposer proposes now. They meet in the enforcement record. The placement record then tests whether the permission path keeps its deadline on the chosen silicon, and records 12 through 16 carry the result into governance.




A mailbox decoder needs a bounded amount of work and an unambiguous representation. The layouts below specify byte offsets, field lengths, and validation rules across the proposal boundary between application processors and the independent enforcer. Fixed headers and bounded arrays make resource requirements explicit. The chosen serialization framework alone does not determine allocation or timing behavior.

Zero Dynamic Allocation Invariant: Deserialization must never invoke dynamic memory managers (malloc, free, C++ new, delete). Dynamic heap allocators manage internal free-list bins, take global allocator mutexes, and suffer from heap fragmentation. Under memory pressure, heap operations can invoke the brk() or mmap() system calls, triggering kernel memory compaction or page faults that stall execution for tens of milliseconds. In hard real-time control, all record slots, mailbox staging areas, scratch buffers, and circular telemetry logs must be statically sized at compile time and preallocated in dedicated static SRAM or Data Tightly Coupled Memory (DTCM) pools.
Bounded Parse and Validation Work: Header fields have fixed offsets; arrays have validated counts and configured maxima. Reading one scalar is constant-time, but copying, hashing, and validating a complete record scale with its bounded length. Full trajectory admission remains interruptible and separate from the per-tick check.
Natural Alignment Across Heterogeneous ABIs: On heterogeneous SoCs combining 64-bit application processors (ARM Cortex-A or x86_64) and 32-bit real-time microcontrollers (ARM Cortex-R52 or Cortex-M7), data types must be naturally aligned. A scalar of size \(\ScalarFieldSize\) bytes must reside at an offset satisfying: \[ \text{offset} \equiv 0 \pmod \ScalarFieldSize \] Specifically, 64-bit timestamps and integers (uint64_t, float64) align on 8-byte boundaries (\(\ScalarFieldSize=8\)), 32-bit values (uint32_t, float32) align on 4-byte boundaries (\(\ScalarFieldSize=4\)), and 16-bit integers (uint16_t) align on 2-byte boundaries (\(\ScalarFieldSize=2\)). Explicit padding bytes between narrower fields maintain these alignment invariants across both 32-bit and 64-bit compilers.

An alignment violation has direct microarchitectural consequences: a core may trap an unsupported unaligned access or split it into multiple bus operations. The result depends on instruction width, memory attributes, and processor configuration. A safety integrity classification does not itself specify those semantics. Explicit reserved bytes, scalar encodings, endianness, and schema versions define the wire representation. A native C structure is not that representation by default. Use checked offsets or explicit serialization and verify layout on each ABI. Alignment alone also does not guarantee atomicity of a wide access on a narrower core.
Not every record in table 9 needs a byte layout. The layouts below cover the proposal header that every proposal carries and the records that cross a mailbox or are signed offline. Runtime proposals and evidence use bounded records where they cross mailboxes or fieldbuses, while limits, evaluation, enforcement configuration, placement evidence, and release artifacts are retained under canonical encodings and linked by digest. All records use standard little-endian byte ordering for multi-byte scalars (uint64_t, uint32_t, uint16_t, float32, float64). Lineage is established by embedding parent SHA-256 digests. Runtime corruption is caught via IEEE 802.3 CRC-32 checksums over headers and payloads. Operator authority is authenticated via AES-128 CMAC tags and Ed25519 digital signatures. The authority log is chained with HMAC-SHA-256. Offline records (placement, fault, release, approval) are identified by the SHA-256 digest of their canonical encoding, and the record that consumes one stores that digest under the consumed record’s name.

The authority-transfer protocol of Authority Transitions and Transfer Without Discontinuity runs in the enforcer’s \(1\text{ kHz}\) loop on the safety microcontroller, where the four-phase handshake, integrator pre-biasing, and the \(\Glyph{C}^2\) quintic blend become one sequence of per-state steps. Each tick writes the authority-log entry of table 16 under the state names used below. The cadence and jitter below are illustrative design targets; the target implementation must qualify them before actuator permission is granted.
Three cadence and memory invariants govern the loop:

Execution cadence: Hard real-time periodic timer interrupt (\(\SamplingRate = 1\text{ kHz}\), period \(\PermissionLoopPeriod = 1.0\text{ ms}\), hardware timing jitter \(< 1.0\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\)).
Memory invariant: Zero dynamic heap allocation (malloc/free forbidden; all state variables, mailboxes, and circular log buffers statically pre-allocated in DTCM SRAM).
Hardware authority: Exclusive write of the admitted setpoints staged for the next EtherCAT frame to the drives, and of the safe torque off (STO) hardware cutoffs.

Each \(1\text{ kHz}\) tick executes five state-machine steps:

Sample and validate plant state, available stopping reserve, independent protective inputs, and the current execution lease. An independent protective input selects its validated, state-matched stop path of The Fallback Ladder.
In AUTO, a manual request or policy handover request enters PEND; the policy may propose only while its existing permission remains valid. Set \(\HandoverTimeout\) to the smaller of the protocol ceiling and clearance-derived deadline. No later than the last permission tick before \(\HandoverTimeout\), transfer to the state-matched fallback. An invalid network packet is rejected and logged, not interpreted as a stop request.
In PEND, verify the operator credential, nonce, enabling input, target freshness, actuator limits, and full transfer-plus-stop clearance. On ACK, at the next qualified Commit tick, revoke the policy’s proposal token on the masked channels, latch \(\ControlCommand_0\) as its last admitted command, latch a checked human target \(\ControlCommand_1\), and set BLEND. The enforcer remains the only actuator writer. If the replacement fails admission, retain the current mode only while its own state, evidence, lease, and stopping checks pass; otherwise enter the independently validated fallback.
In BLEND, evaluate \(\BumplessTransferProgress = \min(1, (\TimeInstant - \TimeInstant_0) / \BlendingTransitionWindow)\) and \(\BumplessTransferBlend(\BumplessTransferProgress) = 6\BumplessTransferProgress^5 - 15\BumplessTransferProgress^4 + 10\BumplessTransferProgress^3\). The enforcer proposes \(\BlendedControlCommand = (1 - \BumplessTransferBlend(\BumplessTransferProgress))\ControlCommand_0 + \BumplessTransferBlend(\BumplessTransferProgress)\ControlCommand_1\), then checks that candidate against current state, torque/rate, and stopping limits before dispatch. These are latched endpoints, not simultaneous live policy and human actuator streams. If the lease, clearance, or tracking assumption fails, use the state-matched fallback. At \(\BumplessTransferProgress = 1\) with a live manual lease, set MAN and confirm that state to the operator.
In MAN, the enforcer checks each live human proposal. Lease expiry or enabling-device loss revokes manual proposals and transfers to the validated fallback. Log request, ACK, commit, candidate, admitted command, measured response, and clock uncertainty separately; the bounded high-rate record must not block the control tick.

For a trial aborted before injection, detector time, takeover time, and robustness margin are unavailable rather than zero. The layout stores all ones (0xFFFFFFFF) in an unavailable uint32_t time slot and a canonical quiet NaN in an unavailable float32 margin slot, and the signed evidence bundle records a validity flag for each measured field and why it is absent. The fault-injection protocol of Fault Injection on Hardware runs one hardware-in-the-loop trial on target silicon, from the precondition audit to the signed header of table 17. Every exit it takes sets one value of that header’s verdict_status. The illustrative fixture below must qualify its timing, interlocks, and measurement uncertainty before any physical trial.
Three substrate and interlock invariants govern the testbed:

Execution substrate: Hard real-time FPGA plant rig and testbed orchestrator (\(\SamplingRate = 1\text{ kHz}\), hardware timestamping jitter \(< 500\text{ ns}\)).
Memory invariant: Pre-allocated static DMA buffers in the host test orchestrator; zero runtime dynamic heap allocation on the safety microcontroller.
Safety interlock authority: Independent optical or laser truth sensors wired to hardware crowbar relays capable of cutting target actuator power within \(2.0\text{ ms}\) of a physical envelope breach.

Each hardware-in-the-loop fault trial executes five sequential stages:

Precondition audit (stage 1). Sample baseline environmental sensors via \(\TruthInstrumentSet\) (temperature, rail voltage, and wheel speed). Compare each measurement with its declared same-unit tolerance; do not take one norm across kelvin, volts, and meters per second. If any precondition fails, log ERR_PRECONDITION_OUT_OF_SPEC, set the verdict to INVALID, and abort.
Synchronization and steady-state arming (stage 2). Arm the FPGA plant simulator, power up the target two-processor system, and start the periodic control loop (\(1\text{ kHz}\)). Establish a synchronized reference clock across the logic analyzer, FPGA plant, and truth digitizers via a \(10\text{ MHz}\) PXI clock. Allow the physical plant state \(\MechanicalPlantState(\TimeInstant)\) to stabilize in the nominal operating envelope for \(\ArmingSettleDuration = 2.000\text{ s}\). If baseline tracking error \(\|\BaselineTrackingError\| > \NominalTrackingTolerance\), assert ERR_BENCH_INSTABILITY, set the verdict to INVALID, and abort.
Fault injection trigger (stage 3). At monotonic test epoch \(\InjectionTriggerEpoch\), the hardware test orchestrator asserts the trigger line to the inline injection rig and records the injection timestamp \(\FaultStartTimestamp \leftarrow \CurrentTime\) in nanoseconds on the reference clock:

Proposer stall (F1): The orchestrator kills the chunk-policy task one tick after a lease renewal.
Sensor latency or bias (F2): An FPGA interceptor latches a navigation-camera frame or holds a stale encoder payload while preserving its valid hardware timestamp.
Frame loss (F3): A fieldbus disturbance node drops or corrupts EtherCAT frames at a drive’s slave port.
Drive-bus droop (F4a): A programmable supply standing in for the pack at its depleted point steps the shared drive bus below the converter lockout of Representative hardware and cyber-physical fault classes for \(\FaultInjectionDuration = 5.0\text{ ms}\), while an independent digitizer records the permission rail and the permission path’s heartbeat.
Permission-rail feed loss (F4b): A solid-state switch opens the permission rail’s feed during the longest resident stop in the qualified loaded envelope. The illustrative all-weight inspected-floor ceiling is a screening case, not the qualified injection condition.
Actuator mechanical stall: A four-quadrant dynamometer applies step counter-torque \(\StallCounterTorque = 3.5 \times \RatedActuatorTorque\).

Enforcer response and takeover audit (stage 4). Monitor the target MCU’s safety enforcer pins, CAN bus telemetry, and gate-driver PWM lines via an isolated logic analyzer. If the external containment rig trips on a structural envelope breach, the hardware crowbar cuts actuator power; assert ERR_PHYSICAL_BREACH and carry the trial to stage 5, where the violated containment predicate returns FAIL:

Detect assertion of the non-maskable interrupt (NMI) or diagnostic flag: \(\DetectionTimestamp \leftarrow \CurrentTime \implies \FaultDetectionLatency = \DetectionTimestamp - \FaultStartTimestamp\).
Detect hardware multiplexer preemption of the motor driver: \(\FaultTakeoverTimestamp \leftarrow \CurrentTime \implies \FaultTakeoverLatency = \FaultTakeoverTimestamp - \FaultStartTimestamp\).
Independently witness powered deceleration onset and standstill, rather than inferring either from a flag or multiplexer transition. Preserve the claim’s physical reference epoch: F1 measures from the last successful lease renewal, while F4a measures from the undervoltage flag; the injection epoch remains a separate diagnostic timestamp.
Detect the physical plant’s transition to its safe bounded regime: \(\BoundedRegimeTimestamp \leftarrow \CurrentTime \implies \FaultContainmentLatency = \BoundedRegimeTimestamp - \FaultStartTimestamp\).

Robustness evaluation and record serialization (stage 5). Ingest the truth trajectory \(\ObservedPlantState(\TimeInstant)\) from independent instrumentation over the declared trial window. If required truth frames are missing, set the verdict to UNOBSERVABLE and retain the partial trace. For an observable trial, compute each precommitted predicate’s signed margin in its own unit, as the STL robustness of Signal Temporal Logic and Continuous Robustness defines it. Return PASS only when every required margin is nonnegative and all predeclared timing and travel bounds pass, including independently witnessed deceleration onset and stopping distance from the claim’s reference event. Fault-to-detection and fault-to-drive-takeover times are additional diagnostics, not substitutes for physical response; otherwise return FAIL. A dimensionless aggregate may be computed only after predeclared per-predicate normalization. Link the fixed fault-record header to the variable-length evidence bundle by digest, sign the header under the specified custody scheme, and retain both.

Every digest is SHA-256. In The Release Manifest, before the motor power stages are energized, the release gate attests the silicon state, verifies the manifest of table 18 and its image digests, and audits the standing conditions in the order below. The hardware root of trust anchors an authorized, revocable adjudicator verification-key chain. Protected storage holds the signed manifest and signed evidence graph. The signature covers every versioned manifest field, including the identity of the signing key, and the verifier checks the key chain and its revocation state before trusting the signature. The individually signed fault records of section 1.15.8 enter the manifest as one digest over the complete set in its declared order. The verifier checks each record signature, the ordering, completeness, and that root against the reviewed evidence index. A digest alone establishes neither record validity nor test adequacy.
Fail-closed authorization begins with Permit_gate = 0 and the physical plant in its assessed nonoperating state. All returned decisions use the signed enum UNCOND, COND, or REFUSE; an implementation may log a reason code separately:

Verify the adjudicator key chain and revocation status, the manifest signature, expiry, signed operating-hour and cycle budgets, and every active image digest. Any invalid, missing, or expired item returns REFUSE. A different software bank requires its own signed case and a new check of physical conditions.
Authenticate the complete set of fault records and calibration references against the signed graph. A missing fault record, bad record signature, or root mismatch returns REFUSE, even if the manifest says UNCOND. Stale calibration also returns REFUSE under the full case. It can support COND only when a separately signed restricted case explicitly covers that calibration state and all of its evidence and limits still validate.
Check the state-dependent standing conditions, including brake test, separation, timebase, and monitoring health. KNOWN_FALSE and UNKNOWN both return REFUSE while retaining distinct logged causes. Apply the approved state-matched stop or hold of The Fallback Ladder.
If every check passes and the signed verdict is UNCOND, load the signed full envelope and return UNCOND. If every restricted condition passes under a signed COND case, load its signed reduced envelope and return COND. A signed REFUSE case or any other state returns REFUSE. In both operating modes the learned policy only proposes actions; the independent enforcer checks each candidate and controls actuator permission. Force trip thresholds must include measured detection and response headroom below the contact criterion.

title: Systems and Hardware
text:
Physical AI requires quantitative intuition across computation, motion, and heat. The latency hierarchy popularized by Jeff Dean1 provides a useful starting point, but a delayed physical command also consumes clearance. The tables below separate representative rates and scenario calculations from bounds that require qualification on the actual machine.
1 Jeff Dean: Google Senior Fellow and systems architect. His latency numbers originally presented with Peter Norvig around 2010 established the canonical latency hierarchy across storage, memory, and network tiers (Scott 2012). Physical AI extends this hierarchy down into electromechanical actuators, stopping kinematics, and thermal time constants.
Scott, Colin. 2012. “Numbers Every Programmer Should Know by Year.”
The fastest events are transistor switching and local memory access. Operating-system dispatch and communication add scheduling and queueing delays. Actuator current then changes over an electrical time constant, while braking and heat accumulation unfold over longer intervals. These scales overlap; a task’s assigned deadline comes from its physical consequence, not from its location in this hierarchy.

Systems Perspective 1.1: Three physical numbers that matter most

Kinetic equivalence: \(1\text{ ms} = 1\text{ mm}\) (at \(1\text{ m/s}\)): At a nominal robotic speed of \(1\text{ m/s}\), every millisecond of perception, inference, or fieldbus latency translates into exactly \(1\text{ mm}\) of blind travel before retarding torque can be applied. At highway velocity (\(30\text{ m/s}\)), each millisecond is \(3\text{ cm}\). In physical systems, software latency is not waiting time; it is physical displacement.
Thermal divergence: \(\SiliconThermalTimeConstant \sim 1\text{ ms}\) vs. \(\ThermalTimeConstant \sim 100\text{ s}\): Semiconductor junctions heat adiabatically within milliseconds during deep neural network bursts, potentially triggering thermal throttling before heat spreaders react. Electrical rail droop is a separate response to changing current demand. In contrast, electromagnetic stator windings heat over tens to hundreds of seconds, tolerating transient overcurrent for aggressive maneuvers but accumulating thermal energy that eventually limits sustained torque.
The exposure wall: \(\FailureObservationInterval = 3 / \ConstantHazardRate\): Under a stationary Poisson model, zero observed failures gives an approximate one-sided 95 percent upper rate bound of \(3/\FailureObservationInterval\) after \(\FailureObservationInterval\) operational hours (Hanley and Lippman-Hand 1983). Very small target rates demand correspondingly large exposure. Runtime barriers can support a broader assurance argument, but neither a barrier nor a finite test proves the absence of failure.





Control rates in physical AI rise steeply from the deliberative brain down to the physical body (table 1). Deliberative multimodal models (VLAs) operate at human reaction scales (\(1\text{--}5\text{ Hz}\)). Action chunking models emit future trajectory waypoints at \(10\text{--}50\text{ Hz}\). Beneath the proposal boundary, the permission path enforces safety barriers at \(1\text{ kHz}\). At the lowest levels, power electronic current loops and PWM switching operate at tens to hundreds of kilohertz to maintain electromagnetic flux and drive torque. For real-time timer schedulability and response-time analysis, see section 1.3; for inverter gate switching and dead-time modeling, see section 1.4.

For a constant heat input and a single thermal node initially at ambient, the temperature rise above \(\AmbientTemperature\) follows \(\JouleanTemperatureRise(\TimeInstant) = \SteadyStateTemperatureRise (1 - e^{-\TimeInstant/\ThermalTimeConstant})\) with steady-state rise \(\SteadyStateTemperatureRise\) and time constant \(\ThermalTimeConstant\) (table 4). Local silicon temperature can change rapidly during a computational burst, requiring thermal qualification of the workload and cooling path. Electrical droop has a separate current-transient timescale. In contrast, electromagnetic stator windings heat over minutes, allowing transient torque overdrive if bounded by an \(\MotorPhaseRmsCurrent^2 \TimeInstant\) thermal watchdog. For first-order thermal differential equations and stator winding degradation limits, see section 1.9; for regenerative energy absorption on DC power buses, see section 1.10.

For zero observed failures in stationary Poisson exposure, the one-sided 95 percent upper rate bound is approximately \(3/\FailureObservationInterval\), where \(\FailureObservationInterval\) is total operating time (Hanley and Lippman-Hand 1983). Table 5 shows the exposure needed to put that bound at three illustrative target rates. These are statistical calculations, not a mapping from a whole-system accident rate to a safety integrity level. In particular, ISO 26262 random-hardware-failure metrics do not describe every cause of a learned system’s failure (International Organization for Standardization 2018). Correlated trials, changing operating conditions, and unobserved failures invalidate a naive accumulation of hours.

Communication buses differ sharply in latency and jitter (table 6). Whereas distributed cluster fabrics (such as RoCEv2 or InfiniBand) prioritize aggregate bandwidth using credit-based flow control and statistical multiplexing, onboard physical AI buses must guarantee bounded delivery times. Industrial fieldbuses such as EtherCAT combine hardware forwarding with scheduled exchange and clock synchronization. A specific jitter claim requires the configured system’s evidence. Classical serial buses like Controller Area Network (CAN) 2.0B provide low-overhead bitwise arbitration for up to 8 bytes, but saturate rapidly under multi-joint control traffic. The Flexible Data-Rate variant, CAN FD, expands payloads to 64 bytes with accelerated data bit rates. Meanwhile, switched IEEE Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) uses scheduled transmission gates to multiplex gigabit vision streams with hard real-time actuator commands. In contrast, non-deterministic best-effort Ethernet and shared wireless channels introduce tail latencies that exceed the reaction deadlines of high-speed electromechanical machines. For IEEE 1588 PTP hardware timestamping bounds, see section 1.7; for CAN 2.0B vs. CAN FD priority arbitration and EtherCAT cycle budgets, see section 1.11.

Required jitter follows the plant and deadline; bounded control does not universally require sub-microsecond jitter. Delivery guarantees require a traffic model, topology, arbitration analysis, and measured implementation behavior.

title: Systems and Hardware
text:
A real-time task is correct only if it computes the required result before its deadline. Average inference latency and throughput do not establish that property. A permission task needs a bound that includes its own execution, blocking on shared resources, and interference from other work. The following single-core scheduling models separate those contributions. Their guarantees apply only under their stated task assumptions; operating-system configuration and loaded measurements must establish whether the implementation satisfies them.


In contrast to general-purpose Linux time-sharing, real-time operating systems schedule tasks based on deterministic timing contracts rather than dynamic heuristics. A periodic real-time task \(\RealTimeTaskIndex\) is characterized by its worst-case execution time (WCET) \(\WorstCaseExecutionTime_i\), relative deadline \(\TaskRelativeDeadline_i\), and period \(\TaskPeriod_i\). When multiple real-time tasks share a single core, schedulability depends on the priority assignment discipline:
Under Rate-Monotonic Scheduling (RMS), fixed-priority preemptive scheduling assigns priority inversely proportional to task period (\(\TaskPeriod_i < \TaskPeriod_j \implies \text{priority}(\RealTimeTaskIndex) > \text{priority}(\PairedTaskIndex)\)) (Liu and Layland 1973). For a set of \(\PeriodicTaskCount\) independent periodic tasks, with negligible scheduling overhead, no blocking or release jitter, and implicit deadlines (\(\TaskRelativeDeadline_i = \TaskPeriod_i\)), a sufficient condition for schedulability is the Liu and Layland utilization bound: \[ \TaskSetUtilization = \sum_{i=1}^\PeriodicTaskCount \frac{\WorstCaseExecutionTime_i}{\TaskPeriod_i} \le \PeriodicTaskCount \left( 2^{1/\PeriodicTaskCount} - 1 \right) \] As \(\PeriodicTaskCount \to \infty\), the bound converges monotonically to \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \PeriodicTaskCount(2^{1/\PeriodicTaskCount}-1) = \ln 2 \approx 0.693\) (69.3 percent). If total processor utilization does not exceed 69.3 percent, the task set is guaranteed to meet all deadlines under RMS. Task periods may instead form a harmonic set, in which every period is an exact integer multiple of every shorter period (\(\TaskPeriod_j = \HarmonicPeriodMultiple \cdot \TaskPeriod_i\) for integer \(\HarmonicPeriodMultiple \ge 1\), such as \(1\text{ ms}\), \(5\text{ ms}\), \(10\text{ ms}\), and \(100\text{ ms}\)). For a harmonic set, the utilization bound rises to 100 percent. In physical AI architectures, rate hierarchies are purposefully engineered with harmonic cadences to maximize processor utilization without sacrificing determinism.

Kopetz, Hermann. 2011. Real-Time Systems: Design Principles for Distributed Embedded Applications. 2nd ed. Real-Time Systems Series. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4419-8237-7.
When processor utilization exceeds the conservative Liu and Layland bound (\(\TaskSetUtilization > \ln 2\)), or when relative deadlines are constrained (\(\TaskRelativeDeadline_i \le \TaskPeriod_i\)), Response Time Analysis (RTA) evaluates exact schedulability from the worst-case response time \(\WorstCaseResponseTime_i\) (Liu and Layland 1973; Kopetz 2011): \[ \WorstCaseResponseTime_i = \WorstCaseExecutionTime_i + \TaskBlockingTime_i + \TaskInterferenceTime_i \le \TaskRelativeDeadline_i \] where \(\TaskBlockingTime_i\) is the maximum blocking duration induced by lower-priority tasks holding shared resources, and \(\TaskInterferenceTime_i\) is the interference from higher-priority tasks. The response time is computed via the fixed-point recurrence. The sum runs over the higher-priority task set. The ceiling counts how many releases of each such task can interfere during the current response-time estimate. An enlarged estimate may expose another release and therefore require another iteration: \[ \WorstCaseResponseTime_i^{(\ResponseTimeIterationIndex+1)} = \WorstCaseExecutionTime_i + \TaskBlockingTime_i + \sum_{j \in \HigherPriorityTasks(i)} \left\lceil \frac{\WorstCaseResponseTime_i^{(\ResponseTimeIterationIndex)}}{\TaskPeriod_j} \right\rceil \WorstCaseExecutionTime_j \] For fixed priorities, bounded blocking, no self-suspension, and zero release jitter, start with \(\WorstCaseResponseTime_i^{(0)} = \WorstCaseExecutionTime_i + \TaskBlockingTime_i\) and iterate until \(\WorstCaseResponseTime_i^{(\ResponseTimeIterationIndex+1)} = \WorstCaseResponseTime_i^{(\ResponseTimeIterationIndex)} \le \TaskRelativeDeadline_i\) (establishing schedulability) or \(\WorstCaseResponseTime_i^{(\ResponseTimeIterationIndex+1)} > \TaskRelativeDeadline_i\) (signaling deadline violation). See Comparing bus occupancy on CAN FD and EtherCAT and Response time analysis and execution variance for the role of response time variance in the nervous system.
In dynamic-priority systems, Earliest Deadline First (EDF) assigns highest priority to the active task with the closest absolute deadline \(\JobAbsoluteDeadline_{i,k} = \JobReleaseTime_{i,k} + \TaskRelativeDeadline_i\). For independent jobs on a single-core preemptive processor with no blocking and negligible scheduling overhead, EDF is optimal: if a task set is schedulable by any scheduling algorithm, it is schedulable by EDF (Liu and Layland 1973). For periodic tasks with \(\TaskRelativeDeadline_i = \TaskPeriod_i\), EDF guarantees schedulability if and only if: \[ \sum_{i=1}^\PeriodicTaskCount \frac{\WorstCaseExecutionTime_i}{\TaskPeriod_i} \le 1 \] achieving 100 percent theoretical utilization without requiring harmonic periods. When relative deadlines are strictly less than periods (\(\TaskRelativeDeadline_i < \TaskPeriod_i\)), schedulability requires the processor demand criterion over the Demand Bound Function (DBF): \[ \text{dbf}(\SchedulingIntervalLength) = \sum_{i=1}^\PeriodicTaskCount \max\left( 0, \left\lfloor \frac{\SchedulingIntervalLength - \TaskRelativeDeadline_i}{\TaskPeriod_i} \right\rfloor + 1 \right) \WorstCaseExecutionTime_i \le \SchedulingIntervalLength, \quad \forall \SchedulingIntervalLength \ge 0 \] evaluating whether cumulative execution demand exceeds available physical time across all time intervals \(\SchedulingIntervalLength\). Under Linux, EDF is exposed via the SCHED_DEADLINE policy implementing the Constant Bandwidth Server (CBS) algorithm. A CBS task declares its runtime \(\CbsRuntimeBudget_i\), deadline \(\TaskRelativeDeadline_i\), and period \(\TaskPeriod_i\) via sched_setattr(). If a task attempts to execute beyond its declared runtime \(\CbsRuntimeBudget_i\) within period \(\TaskPeriod_i\), the kernel dynamically throttles the task until its next period, protecting co-located real-time threads from execution overruns.

Reeves, Glenn E. 1997. What Really Happened on Mars? Electronic mail message, Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
In standard multi-threaded Linux, mutual exclusion primitives (such as futex-backed mutexes) assume threads will eventually yield the processor. When real-time tasks share data structures (such as seqlock mailboxes or actuator command queues) protected by naive mutual exclusion, they suffer from unbounded priority inversion (Sha et al. 1990; Reeves 1997). A low-priority task L acquires a lock; a high-priority task H becomes ready and blocks waiting for the lock; intermediate-priority tasks M that do not need the lock preempt task L, delaying task H for an arbitrary duration. To bound blocking time \(\TaskBlockingTime_i\) in the RTA recurrence, real-time operating systems use formal synchronization protocols:

Priority Inheritance Protocol (PIP): When task H blocks on a lock held by task L, the operating system temporarily elevates task L’s active priority to task H’s priority, preventing preemption by task M. Under PREEMPT_RT Linux, standard in-kernel spinlocks are converted to sleeping rt_mutex locks that enforce PIP automatically, while user-space threads configure PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT. While PIP eliminates unbounded inversion, it permits transitive blocking chains (\(\TaskBlockingTime_i \le \sum_{k} \WorstCaseExecutionTime_k\)) and potential deadlock.
Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP): Each lock is assigned a static priority ceiling equal to the highest priority of any task that may lock it. A task \(\RealTimeTaskIndex\) can lock a resource only if its priority is strictly higher than the priority ceilings of all locks currently held by other tasks. PCP prevents mutual-exclusion deadlocks and guarantees that a task is blocked at most once by at most one lower-priority critical section (Sha et al. 1990): \[ \TaskBlockingTime_i = \max_{k \in \LowerPriorityTasks(i), \CriticalSectionIndex \in \TaskCriticalSections(k)} {\CriticalSectionWcet}_{k,\CriticalSectionIndex} \] where \(\LowerPriorityTasks(\RealTimeTaskIndex)\) is the set of tasks with priority lower than task \(\RealTimeTaskIndex\), and \(\TaskCriticalSections(\BlockingTaskIndex)\) is the set of critical sections executed by task \(\BlockingTaskIndex\) with a priority ceiling at or above the priority of task \(\RealTimeTaskIndex\).


Sha, Lui, Ragunathan Rajkumar, and John P. Lehoczky. 1990. “Priority Inheritance Protocols: An Approach to Real-Time Synchronization.” IEEE Transactions on Computers 39 (9): 1175–85.



In classical embedded systems, the worst-case execution time \(\WorstCaseExecutionTime_i\) is determined via Static Timing Analysis (STA) (Hennessy and Patterson 2019). STA parses binary machine instructions, constructs a Control Flow Graph (CFG), and solves an Integer Linear Program via the Implicit Path Enumeration Technique (IPET) using cycle-accurate microarchitectural models of processor pipelines, branch predictors, and cache sets. In physical AI systems, evaluating \(\WorstCaseExecutionTime_i\) for learned vision-language-action (VLA) and diffusion policies presents three distinct architectural challenges:

Microarchitectural opacity: Modern neural accelerators (GPUs, NPUs, Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) hardware) feature multi-level shared caches, dynamic frequency scaling (DVFS), out-of-order warp schedulers, and memory crossbar contention that make a sound static bound difficult without detailed timing and interference models.
Algorithmic execution variance: Learned pipelines follow dynamic execution paths, including adaptive denoising loops in diffusion models, variable sequence lengths in autoregressive decoders, and data-dependent sparse attention kernels.
Software runtime overhead: Deep learning runtimes (e.g., PyTorch, TensorRT, Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) Runtime) introduce non-deterministic host-to-device kernel launch queueing, unified memory migration, and internal memory allocation locks. Launch overhead and jitter depend on the runtime, driver, submission path, and load; a per-kernel constant is not portable across systems.

To constrain execution variability for neural policies that cross the proposal boundary, physical AI systems enforce deterministic execution contracts and hybrid measurement bounds:

Static shape contracts: Action chunk horizons (\(\ActionChunkHorizon\)), token context lengths, and sensor input tensors are locked to fixed maximum dimensions. Dynamic input padding replaces variable-length tensors, ensuring constant compute graph geometry and eliminating dynamic kernel recompilation.
Zero runtime allocation: All execution buffers, KV caches, scratchpad memory, and direct memory access (DMA) descriptors are preallocated during initialization. Dynamic memory calls (malloc, cudaMalloc, free) are strictly forbidden on cyclic control paths.
Reduced host dispatch overhead via CUDA Graphs: Fixing denoising iterations bounds one source of algorithmic work. Capturing and instantiating a reusable graph reduces repeated per-kernel host setup, as the CUDA Graphs documentation explains. Graph launch still uses the runtime and driver, and device scheduling, frequency changes, and shared-resource contention remain. A graph does not by itself provide deterministic execution.
Extreme Value Theory (EVT) tail bounds: Because finite empirical profiling cannot expose the true maximum execution time under worst-case hardware interference, engineers apply Extreme Value Theory (Coles 2001). Under the Pickands–Balkema–de Haan theorem, execution time exceedances over a high operational threshold \(\ExceedanceThreshold\) converge asymptotically to a Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD): \[ \GpdCumulativeDistribution(\ThresholdExcess) = 1 - \left( 1 + \frac{\TailShapeParameter \ThresholdExcess}{\GpdScaleParameter} \right)^{-1/\TailShapeParameter} \] on the support \(1+\TailShapeParameter \ThresholdExcess/\GpdScaleParameter>0\), with the exponential limit at \(\TailShapeParameter=0\). Here \(\ThresholdExcess = \TailRiskObservationLevel - \ExceedanceThreshold > 0\), \(\GpdScaleParameter > 0\) is the scale parameter, and \(\TailShapeParameter\) is the shape parameter (tail index). The shape parameter characterizes the tail behavior:

\(\TailShapeParameter < 0\) (Weibull domain): Bounded upper tail with a finite model endpoint \(\TailSupportUpperEndpoint = \ExceedanceThreshold - \GpdScaleParameter/\TailShapeParameter\), under the fitted model; an estimated finite endpoint is not proof of a hardware ceiling.
\(\TailShapeParameter = 0\) (Gumbel domain): Light, exponential tail.
\(\TailShapeParameter > 0\) (Fréchet domain): Heavy, polynomial tail. The fitted sign alone neither identifies a hardware failure mechanism nor determines whether a deadline can be defended.



Coles, Stuart. 2001. An Introduction to Statistical Modeling of Extreme Values. Springer.
For an acceptable target exceedance probability \(\TargetExceedanceProbability\) (such as \(10^{-6}\) or \(10^{-8}\) per invocation), a model-based execution-time quantile \(\ExceedanceReturnLevel(\TargetExceedanceProbability)\) is computed as: \[ \ExceedanceReturnLevel(\TargetExceedanceProbability) = \ExceedanceThreshold + \frac{\GpdScaleParameter}{\TailShapeParameter} \left[ \left( \frac{\ObservedCycleCount}{\ThresholdExceedanceCount} \TargetExceedanceProbability \right)^{-\TailShapeParameter} - 1 \right] \] where \(\ObservedCycleCount\) is total sample count and \(\ThresholdExceedanceCount\) is the count of observations exceeding threshold \(\ExceedanceThreshold\). For \(\TailShapeParameter=0\), the continuous limit is \(\ExceedanceThreshold-\GpdScaleParameter\ln(\ObservedCycleCount\TargetExceedanceProbability/\ThresholdExceedanceCount)\). These are fitted quantiles, conditional on the sampling regime, threshold choice, tail model, and parameter uncertainty. They do not certify a deterministic WCET. A placement record must distinguish measured maxima, probabilistic estimates, and justified execution bounds; the permission path must remain schedulable when the proposer exceeds its estimate.



On a heterogeneous robotics system on chip (SoC), the nervous system and safety monitors execute under real-time operating systems (RTOS) or real-time Linux kernels (such as Linux patched with PREEMPT_RT). Interrupts and non-preemptible kernel critical sections can delay user-space tasks. A hard response bound requires bounding those intervals on the chosen kernel and hardware. In physical AI pipelines where control loops govern physical momentum, operating-system determinism requires eliminating non-preemptible kernel sections, bounding interrupt preemption latency, isolating execution cores, locking virtual memory, and enforcing cache locality.
Linux fair scheduling balances CPU service among runnable tasks. Its historical CFS implementation accounts for weighted execution time; newer kernels use EEVDF, which also considers eligibility and virtual deadlines. Neither policy establishes the physical deadline guarantee needed by the permission task. In physical AI systems, real-time control threads must instead be configured with POSIX static priority scheduling policies (SCHED_FIFO or SCHED_RR) across priority levels 1 to 99 (or SCHED_DEADLINE implementing Earliest Deadline First). Under SCHED_FIFO, the highest-priority runnable thread executes immediately and runs until it blocks on I/O, yields voluntarily, or is preempted by a strictly higher-priority real-time thread.
In mainline Linux kernels, disabling preemption during spinlock acquisition (preempt_disable()), executing non-preemptible softirqs, and servicing asynchronous workqueues can delay user-space execution by tens of milliseconds. When an unprivileged machine learning process or device driver holds an in-kernel spinlock, a high-priority 1 kHz real-time safety task cannot preempt the CPU, even if its timer has expired. A kernel configured with PREEMPT_RT reduces non-preemptible execution through four mechanisms, while hardware, drivers, and remaining critical sections still require timing qualification:

Sleeping Spinlocks (rt_mutex): Standard in-kernel spinlocks (spinlock_t and rwlock_t) are replaced by sleeping mutexes backed by rt_mutex with Priority Inheritance Protocol (PIP) support. When a high-priority thread waits for an rt_mutex, the waiter sleeps and the lock owner inherits its priority until it can release the lock. Raw spinlocks remain non-preemptible; interrupt masking depends on the primitive used. Their maximum hold times must be included in the platform timing analysis.
Preemptible Read-Copy Update (CONFIG_PREEMPT_RCU): RCU read-side critical sections (rcu_read_lock() / rcu_read_unlock()) become preemptible, preventing deferred memory reclamation from stalling real-time threads.
Forced Interrupt Threading: Hardware interrupt service routines (ISRs) are split into minimal top-half handlers and prioritized kernel threads (irq/<irq>-<name>) scheduled under SCHED_FIFO.
High-Resolution Timers (hrtimers): Traditional Linux timer ticks execute at coarse periodic jiffies (\(1\text{ ms}\) or \(4\text{ ms}\) granularity), introducing substantial quantization error and timer slack. PREEMPT_RT binds the timer subsystem to hardware per-CPU clock event devices (such as the ARM Generic Timer or x86 Local APIC), enabling sub-microsecond timer resolution. Real-time cyclic threads invoke clock_nanosleep(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, TIMER_ABSTIME, &next_period, NULL) using absolute monotonic deadlines, avoiding cumulative drift from relative sleeps. Wake-up jitter remains part of the response-time bound.

When an external hardware peripheral (such as an IMU, joint encoder counter, or fieldbus controller) asserts an interrupt request (IRQ), the processor halts user execution and saves register context. It then vectors to the hardware ISR via the interrupt controller (such as an ARM Generic Interrupt Controller GICv3 or x86 APIC). The worst-case interrupt latency \(\WorstCaseInterruptLatency\) to enter the hardware interrupt handler can be budgeted as: \[ \WorstCaseInterruptLatency = \LongestInterruptMaskTime + \PipelineFlushDelay + \ContextSaveTime + \sum_{j \in \HigherPriorityTasks(\text{irq})} {\IsrExecutionTime}_{j} \] This expression does not include threaded-handler work or the subsequent scheduling delay before a user-space task runs. Here \(\LongestInterruptMaskTime\) is the longest duration during which CPU interrupts were disabled across the kernel, \(\PipelineFlushDelay\) is the processor pipeline flush delay, \(\ContextSaveTime\) is the hardware register preservation time, and \(\sum {\IsrExecutionTime}_{j}\) represents the execution duration of higher-priority ISRs.
To prevent high-bandwidth sensor streams (such as GigE Vision cameras or 3D lidars streaming gigabits of packet traffic) from generating an interrupt storm that starves the 1 kHz permission path, real-time architectures strictly enforce top-half and bottom-half partitioning:

Top-half (Hardware ISR): Executes in hard-interrupt context with CPU interrupts masked. It executes the absolute minimum hardware operations: reading the peripheral interrupt status register, clearing the physical interrupt line, latching high-resolution hardware counter timestamps, and waking the associated threaded IRQ. The handler’s maximum execution time must be bounded on the target.
Bottom-half (Threaded IRQ): In PREEMPT_RT and RTOS environments, complex packet deserialization, frame CRC verification, and data copies are deferred to dedicated kernel threads (irq/<irq>-<name>). By configuring these threaded IRQs under SCHED_FIFO with priorities lower than the 1 kHz safety monitor (e.g., setting camera IRQ threads to priority 50 and the motor permission thread to priority 90), the scheduler prevents those lower-priority threads from preempting the control task. Hard-interrupt top halves and shared-memory traffic still contribute interference.

Heterogeneous multi-core robotics SoCs must also isolate deterministic control threads from background operating-system disturbances. Kernel boot parameters and memory layout rules establish strict CPU shielding and cache locality:

isolcpus=2,3: Removes cores 2 and 3 from the general kernel scheduler balancing domain, reducing automatic load balancing onto those cores; explicit affinity, cpusets, and kernel work still require configuration.
nohz_full=2,3: Enables full dynamic tickless operation. When an isolated core runs a single real-time thread, the kernel can suppress the periodic scheduling timer tick (\(100\text{--}1000\text{ Hz}\)), removing that source of periodic interruption while other interrupts and scheduling delays remain.
rcu_nocbs=2,3: Offloads RCU callback processing from isolated cores to housekeeping cores (cores 0 and 1).
IRQ Affinity Partitioning: Peripheral hardware interrupts are directed away from real-time cores by writing CPU bitmasks to /proc/irq/<id>/smp_affinity. High-rate camera MSI-X vectors and Ethernet controller interrupts are pinned exclusively to housekeeping cores, reducing controllable interrupt interference. Nonmaskable events, local timers, and platform firmware disturbances still require accounting.
Cache Line Alignment and False Sharing Elimination: Cache-line size is architecture dependent; the examples here assume 64-byte lines. When multiple CPU cores access independent variables that reside within the same 64-byte line, hardware cache coherency protocols (MESI/MOESI) repeatedly invalidate the line across core private caches upon every store, a phenomenon known as false sharing or cache line bouncing. A single false sharing interaction can stall a real-time core for 50 to 100 clock cycles. Separating independently written state into aligned, padded cache-line slots avoids false sharing; merely aligning the beginning of a larger structure does not isolate every member. The target’s remaining cache misses and contention still need timing bounds. Furthermore, real-time control paths pre-warm L1 instruction and data caches during initialization by executing a dummy pass over critical control tables before arming actuators.

Virtual memory subsystems rely on demand paging, so deterministic execution also requires locking virtual memory and eliminating page faults. When a process accesses an unmapped virtual address, the CPU raises an architectural page fault exception (#PF) and suspends execution. The kernel page-table handler then allocates a physical page frame, updates translation lookaside buffer (TLB) entries, and zeroes the memory (a minor page fault, requiring \(10\text{--}50\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\)). If the requested page was swapped to secondary flash storage, the thread blocks on disk I/O (a major page fault, requiring \(10\text{--}50\text{ ms}\)). Furthermore, Transparent Huge Pages (THP) memory compaction (khugepaged) can asynchronously stall threads for tens of milliseconds while defragmenting physical memory pages. A page fault can consume the remaining response-time margin; its mere occurrence does not imply that every deadline is missed.
The following Linux/glibc sketch illustrates initialization and absolute-period sleeping. It assumes the shown page and cache-line sizes. Production code must also validate limits and privileges, measure completion against the deadline, and enter the assessed fallback on an overrun. A late absolute sleep can return immediately; it must not trigger an uncontrolled series of catch-up actuator writes.
// Real-time process initialization, memory locking, and cyclic execution
#define _GNU_SOURCE
#include <sys/mman.h>
#include <sched.h>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <malloc.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <errno.h>

#define REALTIME_PRIORITY   90
#define CONTROL_CPU_CORE    2
#define STACK_PREFAULT_SZ   (256 * 1024)       // 256 KB stack
#define HEAP_PREALLOC_SZ    (16 * 1024 * 1024) // 16 MB pre-allocated arena
#define PERIOD_NS           1000000ULL         // 1 ms period (1 kHz)

// 64-byte cache-aligned telemetry slot to prevent false sharing
typedef struct __attribute__((aligned(64))) {
    uint64_t sequence_id;
    uint64_t timestamp_ns;
    float joint_torques[8];
    uint32_t status_flags;
    uint8_t reserved[12];
} realtime_telemetry_t;

static realtime_telemetry_t g_telemetry;
static volatile uint8_t *g_realtime_heap_arena = NULL;

void configure_realtime_process(int target_cpu, int rt_priority, size_t stack_size) {
    // 1. Bind execution to dedicated isolated CPU core (isolcpus / nohz_full)
    cpu_set_t cpuset;
    CPU_ZERO(&cpuset);
    CPU_SET(target_cpu, &cpuset);
    if (sched_setaffinity(0, sizeof(cpu_set_t), &cpuset) != 0) {
        perror("sched_setaffinity failed");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // 2. Configure POSIX static real-time priority (SCHED_FIFO)
    struct sched_param sp = { .sched_priority = rt_priority };
    if (sched_setscheduler(0, SCHED_FIFO, &sp) != 0) {
        perror("sched_setscheduler SCHED_FIFO failed");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // 3. Lock all current and future virtual address mappings into physical RAM
    if (mlockall(MCL_CURRENT | MCL_FUTURE) != 0) {
        perror("mlockall failed");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // 4. Disable glibc dynamic heap trimming and anonymous mmap allocation
    mallopt(M_TRIM_THRESHOLD, -1);
    mallopt(M_MMAP_MAX, 0);

    // 5. Pre-allocate and prefault the dedicated heap arena
    g_realtime_heap_arena = (uint8_t *)malloc(HEAP_PREALLOC_SZ);
    if (!g_realtime_heap_arena) {
        perror("malloc heap arena failed");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    // Touch every 4 KB page to force physical page frame allocation and TLB population
    for (size_t i = 0; i < HEAP_PREALLOC_SZ; i += 4096) {
        g_realtime_heap_arena[i] = 0;
    }

    // 6. Prefault the thread execution stack to its declared maximum depth
    volatile char stack_buffer[stack_size];
    for (size_t i = 0; i < stack_size; i += 4096) {
        stack_buffer[i] = 0; // Trigger minor page fault and populate TLB entry
    }
}

void run_periodic_control_loop(void) {
    struct timespec next_period;
    clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &next_period);

    // A real implementation warms the actual control code and data before arming.

    while (1) {
        // Compute next absolute wake epoch (eliminates cumulative drift)
        next_period.tv_nsec += PERIOD_NS;
        while (next_period.tv_nsec >= 1000000000L) {
            next_period.tv_nsec -= 1000000000L;
            next_period.tv_sec  += 1;
        }

        // High-resolution absolute sleep
        int ret;
        do {
            ret = clock_nanosleep(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, TIMER_ABSTIME, &next_period, NULL);
        } while (ret == EINTR);
        if (ret != 0) {
            fprintf(stderr, "clock_nanosleep: %s\n", strerror(ret));
            break;
        }

        // ZERO-ALLOCATION CYCLIC CONTROL LOGIC
        // 1. Ingest sensor state from lock-free shared memory
        // 2. Evaluate Control Barrier Functions (CBFs)
        // 3. Dispatch admitted setpoints to EtherCAT master
        g_telemetry.sequence_id++;
    }
}
Beyond address space locking and stack prefaulting, the cyclic 1 kHz control loop operates under a strict zero dynamic allocation invariant. In general-purpose systems programming, developers routinely rely on dynamic memory managers (malloc, free, C++ new, delete) or standard container expansions (std::vector::push_back). In a real-time control loop, however, dynamic allocation introduces three catastrophic failure modes:

Arena Mutex Contention: Modern allocators (such as ptmalloc in glibc) partition memory into multiple heap arenas protected by mutual-exclusion mutexes. If another thread in the same process acquires an arena lock, a high-priority 1 kHz real-time control thread calling malloc blocks on that mutex, suffering from priority inversion and waiting milliseconds.
Kernel Syscall Invocations: When an allocator exhausts its active arena chunk, it issues brk() or anonymous mmap() system calls. These kernel entries acquire the process’s mmap_lock (or mmap_sem), which is shared with background kernel threads such as khugepaged performing transparent huge page compaction or memory defragmentation, stalling user-space execution for tens of milliseconds.
Heap Fragmentation: Repeated cyclic allocations and deallocations fragment the heap, degrading allocation search times across segregated free lists into non-deterministic search loops.

Consequently, all message structures, matrix workspace buffers, trajectory buffers, and seqlock mailbox slots must be statically allocated at startup or drawn from fixed-size, lock-free memory pools (such as slab allocators). Furthermore, mlockall(MCL_FUTURE) must be paired with explicit memory pre-allocation and page prefaulting. Linux uses optimistic memory allocation (overcommit), so virtual address ranges returned by malloc() are not backed by physical page frames until the thread actually writes to each 4 KB page. Touching an uninitialized buffer for the first time inside the control loop triggers a minor page fault exception (#PF). The kernel page-fault handler must then allocate physical memory, zero the page, and update the MMU page table and TLB entries, a stall of \(10\text{--}50\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) that jeopardizes sub-millisecond control deadlines. Prefaulting and successful memory locking establish page residency before arming actuators. TLB and cache entries can still be evicted, so their miss costs remain in the execution budget; copy-on-write faults and later mapping changes must also be excluded.
