In distributed computing clusters, node liveness and consensus are managed via software heartbeats and distributed leases (such as Raft heartbeats, ZooKeeper leases, or Kubernetes node probes) operating over second-scale intervals. If a worker node crashes, the cluster orchestrator reschedules containers onto alternative nodes. In physical AI systems, however, an autonomous machine traveling through physical space cannot wait seconds for a software orchestrator. If the GPU driver deadlocks, memory bus crossbars stall, or a kernel panic freezes the operating system, physical momentum continues unchecked. To detect a missed execution checkpoint, an embedded design uses a hardware watchdog timer. Its clock and response path must be independent of the monitored processor. An independent crystal oscillator or low-speed internal oscillator (LSI) completely decoupled from the main system phase-locked loop (PLL) is required.
The hardware watchdog timer comprises an autonomous down-counter register \(\WatchdogCounterReading(\TimeInstant)\) clocked at frequency \(\WatchdogClockFrequency\) (typically \(32\text{ kHz}\) from an independent on-chip RC oscillator). At system initialization, the register is loaded with a threshold value \(\WatchdogReloadCount\). Software execution threads must periodically refresh (or “kick”) the register before the count decrements to zero: \[ \WatchdogCounterReading(\TimeInstant) = \WatchdogReloadCount - \left\lfloor \WatchdogClockFrequency \cdot \TimeInstant \right\rfloor \] At expiry, the timer asserts its configured reset or fault output. A separately wired trip is required when processor reset alone is insufficient to de-energize the actuators.
In safety-critical systems, simple down-counters are vulnerable to runaway execution bugs: if a corrupted control loop enters an infinite spin-loop that happens to execute the watchdog refresh instruction, the watchdog is continually fed despite the control failure. To prevent this, robust physical AI architectures employ a Windowed Watchdog Timer (WWDG). A windowed watchdog defines both an upper counter threshold \(\WatchdogUpperWindowCount\) and a lower counter threshold \(\WatchdogLowerWindowCount\). The software refresh is valid only while the counter lies between them: \[ \WatchdogLowerWindowCount \le \WatchdogCounterReading(\TimeInstant_k) \le \WatchdogUpperWindowCount \] Because the counter falls at the fixed rate \(\WatchdogClockFrequency\), the two counter thresholds convert to the time bounds \(\WatchdogEarliestServiceTime\) and \(\WatchdogLatestServiceTime\) that The Boundary Contract uses for the service window, measured from the last reload: \[ \WatchdogEarliestServiceTime = \frac{\WatchdogReloadCount - \WatchdogUpperWindowCount}{\WatchdogClockFrequency}, \quad \WatchdogLatestServiceTime = \frac{\WatchdogReloadCount - \WatchdogLowerWindowCount}{\WatchdogClockFrequency} \] If software attempts to refresh the watchdog too early (\(\TimeInstant_k < \WatchdogEarliestServiceTime\), equivalently \(\WatchdogCounterReading(\TimeInstant_k) > \WatchdogUpperWindowCount\)), the early write indicates an abnormal loop short-circuit or clock glitch. Refreshing too early or failing to refresh before \(\WatchdogLatestServiceTime\) trips the hardware watchdog controller immediately.
Feeding the watchdog directly from a periodic timer interrupt is an unsafe anti-pattern, because the timer interrupt may continue firing even if the primary motion planning and safety monitor threads are deadlocked. To check completion of the expected software checkpoints, control software can implement multi-stage token-passing checkpointing using rolling polynomial accumulators: \[ \WatchdogToken_{k+1} = \text{CRC32}\left( \WatchdogToken_k \oplus \text{Signature}_k \right) \]

At the beginning of the 1 kHz tick, a watchdog token \(\WatchdogToken_0\) is generated from the hardware monotonic cycle counter.
Stage 1 (Sensor Ingress): Validates camera, IMU, and joint telemetry timestamps, updating the token: \(\WatchdogToken_1 = \text{CRC32}(\WatchdogToken_0 \oplus \text{sensor\_valid\_signature})\).
Stage 2 (State Estimation & Tracking): Computes joint tracking errors, updating \(\WatchdogToken_2 = \text{CRC32}(\WatchdogToken_1 \oplus \text{tracking\_valid\_signature})\).
Stage 3 (Permission Enforcer): Validates Control Barrier Functions and stopping distance envelopes, computing \(\WatchdogToken_3 = \text{CRC32}(\WatchdogToken_2 \oplus \text{enforce\_valid\_signature})\).
Stage 4 (Actuator Dispatch): Transmits admitted setpoints across the fieldbus, computing \(\FinalWatchdogToken = \text{CRC32}(\WatchdogToken_3 \oplus \text{dispatch\_valid\_signature})\).

Only if \(\FinalWatchdogToken\) matches the expected value for this tick may the watchdog refresh routine service the timer. The token detects omitted or misordered checkpoints under its fault model; a CRC is neither authentication nor proof that the computed state or command is physically correct.
A watchdog timeout must reach a validated hardware fail-safe response path independently of the processor it monitors. A CPU reset or non-maskable interrupt alone does not establish that connection. When the assessed response includes safe torque off (STO), a separately wired output disables the gate drive that generates motor torque; the wiring, response time, and diagnostic coverage require device-specific qualification. Gate disable does not establish an instantaneous mechanical stop. Winding current takes time to decay, moving axes may coast, and a gravity-loaded axis may require a holding brake or a powered stop before torque removal. The complete watchdog-to-plant response belongs in the stopping budget.2
2 Hardware Watchdog Down-Counters: A configured watchdog expires when its expected service does not occur. Its oscillator, timeout, output wiring, and plant response differ by device. Feeding it merely from an unrelated interrupt does not prove that the monitored control computation progressed; a firmware-fed reset also need not signal a drive. See the Linux watchdog API for reset behavior and The Fallback Ladder for stop selection.

title: Systems and Hardware
text:
In machine learning control frameworks (such as reinforcement learning policies, imitation learning, or model predictive control pipelines), actuator actions are formulated as continuous numerical setpoints, such as commanded joint torques \(\JointTorque^*\) or angular velocities \(\GeneralizedVelocities^*\). In physical realization, however, torque is generated by synthesizing rotating electromagnetic stator flux through high-frequency switching of power semiconductor bridges (typically at \(20\text{ kHz}\) to \(100\text{ kHz}\)). Actuator motor drives employ three-phase half-bridge inverters to convert DC bus voltage into alternating stator currents.


Bridging the digital software domain with physical power silicon requires strict microarchitectural timing interlocks. Each inverter phase comprises a half-bridge with a high-side power MOSFET (or GaN FET / IGBT) and a low-side power MOSFET connected across the DC supply rail \(\DcBusVoltage\). Microcontroller timer peripherals generate complementary pulse-width-modulated (PWM) drive signals with hardware-enforced dead-time insertion \(\InverterDeadTime\): \[ \InverterDeadTime \ge \MaximumTurnOffDelay + \GateDriverSkew - \MinimumTurnOnDelay + \DeadTimeSafetyMargin \] where \(\MaximumTurnOffDelay\) is the maximum turn-off delay of the power switch, \(\MinimumTurnOnDelay\) is the minimum turn-on delay, \(\GateDriverSkew\) is the propagation delay mismatch across isolated gate drivers, and \(\DeadTimeSafetyMargin\) is an engineering safety buffer.3
3 Inverter Dead-Time Insertion: Timer dead time is selected from switch and driver timing over temperature and load, then verified with the actual gate waveforms. An overlap can create a damaging bus short; a numeric current or fuse outcome requires the circuit impedance and protection response.Modern motor control microcontrollers (such as STM32 Advanced-control timers TIM1/TIM8 or TI C2000 ePWM modules) synthesize PWM waveforms using hardware up-down counting counters (TIMx_CNT). In center-aligned mode, the counter counts up from 0 to the auto-reload value (TIMx_ARR) and back down to 0, producing symmetrical PWM waveforms with period \(\PwmPeriod = 2 \cdot \text{ARR} \cdot \TimerClockPeriod\). Center-aligned PWM provides symmetric switching and repeatable ADC trigger opportunities. Ripple reduction and valid sampling windows depend on duty cycle, modulation, current-sensing topology, and settling time. Synchronization alone does not remove switching noise.
The timer’s hardware Dead-Time Generator (DTG) monitors the compare match outputs (TIMx_CCRx) and inserts dead-time delay cycles \(\DeadTimeCycleCount\) using an autonomous digital delay line: \[ \InverterDeadTime = \DeadTimeCycleCount \cdot \DeadTimeTickPeriod \] By latching the DTG configuration behind hardware register lock bits (BDTR.LOCK), the microcontroller guarantees that the dead-time delay cannot be altered by runaway firmware or memory corruption. Once locked at boot, the register ignores subsequent software writes until the next hardware reset.
A power MOSFET or GaN FET switch possesses input capacitance \(\SwitchInputCapacitance = \GateSourceCapacitance + \MillerCapacitance\), where \(\MillerCapacitance\) is the non-linear reverse transfer (Miller) capacitance. During gate turn-on and turn-off, charge transfer follows: \[ \TotalGateCharge = \int_0^{\SwitchingTransitionTime} \GateCurrent(\TimeInstant) d\TimeInstant = \GateSourceCharge + \MillerCharge \] During turn-off, the gate driver sinks current through gate resistance \(\TurnOffGateResistance\). The gate-source voltage \(\GateSourceVoltage\) drops to the Miller plateau voltage \(\MillerPlateauVoltage\), where it dwells while the drain-to-source voltage \(\DrainSourceVoltage\) traverses the entire DC rail: \[ \MillerPlateauDuration = \frac{\MillerCharge}{\TurnOffGateCurrent} = \frac{\MillerCharge \cdot \TurnOffGateResistance}{\MillerPlateauVoltage - \NegativeGateSupplyVoltage} \] Turn-on and turn-off times depend on gate resistance, driver strength, load, and device charge. Neither is universally longer; dead time must use the measured worst-case mismatch.
If dead time is insufficient, both high-side and low-side switches conduct simultaneously (shoot-through), creating a low-impedance short circuit directly bridging the DC rail to ground: \[ \ShootThroughCurrent = \frac{\DcBusVoltage}{2 \SwitchOnResistance + \BridgeTraceResistance} \] This resistive expression gives a prospective current, not its instantaneous value. Loop inductance limits the initial rise, and the resulting device stress depends on switching overlap, protection delay, and the circuit safe operating area.
Even when dead time is configured correctly, half-bridge legs face parasitic Miller cross-conduction. When the high-side MOSFET turns on, the phase node voltage slews at high speed (\(d\DrainSourceVoltage/d\TimeInstant \sim 10\text{--}50\text{ V/ns}\) in modern SiC and GaN bridges). This steep voltage transient forces displacement current through the low-side switch’s Miller capacitance: \[ \MillerDisplacementCurrent = \MillerCapacitance \frac{d\DrainSourceVoltage}{d\TimeInstant} \] This current flows through the low-side gate resistor \(\TurnOffGateResistance\) back to ground, inducing a parasitic gate voltage rise: \[ \InducedGateVoltage = \MillerDisplacementCurrent \cdot \TurnOffGateResistance = \MillerCapacitance \frac{d\DrainSourceVoltage}{d\TimeInstant} \TurnOffGateResistance \] If \(\InducedGateVoltage\) exceeds the gate threshold voltage \(\TransistorThresholdVoltage\) (typically \(1.5\text{--}3.0\text{ V}\) in GaN FETs), the low-side switch turns on spuriously while the high-side switch is conducting, inducing catastrophic shoot-through. Power electronics gate drivers counter this using Active Miller Clamps (AMC), an internal low-impedance switch that clamps the gate directly to the negative rail whenever \(\GateSourceVoltage\) drops below \(1.0\text{ V}\), or split gate drives (\(\TurnOnGateResistance / \TurnOffGateResistance\)) with antiparallel Schottky diodes.
While necessary for silicon survival, dead time introduces non-linear voltage distortion into stator windings. During the dead-time interval \(\InverterDeadTime\), both active MOSFETs are commanded off, and signed instantaneous phase current \(\InstantaneousPhaseCurrent\) (positive from the inverter node into the winding) is forced to freewheel through antiparallel body diodes. The sign of the phase current determines whether the inverter phase node clamps to \(\DcBusVoltage\) or ground, producing an average phase voltage error: \[ \DeadTimeVoltageError = -\operatorname{sgn}(\InstantaneousPhaseCurrent) \cdot \frac{\InverterDeadTime}{\PwmPeriod} \DcBusVoltage \] In three-phase synchronous machines, this square-wave error injects 5th and 7th harmonic voltages into the stationary reference frame. When transformed into the rotor synchronous \(\Glyph{d}\Glyph{q}\) reference frame via Park’s transformation, these odd harmonics combine into a 6th harmonic voltage disturbance. The amplitudes and phases follow the harmonic coefficients of the phase-voltage error and the chosen transformation convention. They are not equal to the fundamental square-wave coefficient. The current loop filters these voltage harmonics before they become torque ripple, creating a corresponding 6th harmonic torque ripple: \[ \SixthHarmonicTorqueRipple(6\ElectricalRotorAngle) = \frac{3}{2} \RotorPolePairCount \, \PermanentMagnetFluxLinkage \cdot \FiniteChange \TorqueProducingCurrent(6\ElectricalRotorAngle) \] Left uncompensated, this hardware-induced torque ripple produces high-frequency torque chatter that excites mechanical drivetrain resonances. Modern motor drives implement dead-time compensation algorithms in low-level firmware that inject feedforward voltage vectors opposite to \(\DeadTimeDqVoltageError\), linearizing the actuator response for high-level ML policies.

title: Systems and Hardware
text:
In data center machine learning clusters, power delivery networks (PDNs) are supported by large rack-level voltage regulator modules (VRMs) and extensive decoupling capacitor planes. On embedded physical AI compute platforms, deep learning accelerators (such as tensor cores and systolic array matrix engines) share tightly constrained power rails with CPU cores and real-time safety microcontrollers. When a deep neural network transitions from idle to full execution, current draw increases by tens of amperes within nanoseconds.


A power delivery network (PDN) has parasitic resistance and inductance in each source path. For a lumped branch with resistance \(\PdnBranchResistance\), inductance \(\ParasiticLoopInductance\), and branch current \(\PdnBranchCurrent\), its voltage drop is: \[ \SourceVoltage-\AcceleratorRailVoltage = \ParasiticLoopInductance \frac{d\PdnBranchCurrent}{d\TimeInstant} + \PdnBranchCurrent \PdnBranchResistance \] The accelerator’s load current need not equal this branch current during a transient: local decoupling supplies their difference. The rail response follows the coupled source-path and capacitor equations of section 1.10. Substituting the full load-current slew into every upstream inductance would ignore that buffering.
To prevent rail excursions from exceeding allowable voltage tolerances \(\pm \AllowableRailExcursion = \NominalSupplyVoltage \times \RailVoltageTolerance\) (typically \(\pm 5\text{ percent}\), or \(45\text{ mV}\) on a \(0.9\text{ V}\) digital core rail), the power delivery network must maintain an impedance profile strictly below the target impedance \(\PdnTargetImpedance\) across the entire operational frequency band: \[ \PdnTargetImpedance = \frac{\NominalSupplyVoltage \cdot \RailVoltageTolerance}{\MaximumLoadCurrentStep} \] For a \(0.9\text{ V}\) accelerator drawing a \(50\text{ A}\) step transient with \(5\text{ percent}\) allowable ripple, \(\PdnTargetImpedance = 45\text{ mV} / 50\text{ A} = 0.90\text{ m}\OhmUnit\) from DC up to gigahertz frequencies. Exceeding this impedance at any excitation frequency permits transient load steps to pull the supply rail outside its timing-qualified window.
Switched-mode power supplies (VRMs) have limited feedback control loop bandwidth (\(100\text{ kHz}\) to \(1\text{ MHz}\)) and cannot supply charge during nanosecond current transitions. Energy must be buffered across a multi-tier decoupling capacitor hierarchy structured by frequency response:

On-Die Decoupling (\(> 100\text{ MHz}\)): Deep trench and metal-insulator-metal (MIM) capacitors fabricated directly on the silicon die (\(\OnDieDecouplingCapacitance \sim 10\text{--}100\text{ nF}\), parasitic loop inductance \(< 10\text{ pH}\), response time \(< 0.5\text{ ns}\)) supply charge during the initial clock cycles.
Package Decoupling (\(10\text{--}100\text{ MHz}\)): Land-side capacitors (LSC) mounted under the BGA package (\(\PackageDecouplingCapacitance \sim 1\text{--}10\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{F}\), loop inductance \(\sim 50\text{--}200\text{ pH}\), response time \(1\text{--}5\text{ ns}\)).
Board-Level High-Frequency MLCCs (\(100\text{ kHz}\text{--}10\text{ MHz}\)): Low-ESL surface-mount multi-layer ceramic capacitors (0201/0402 case sizes, \(\DecouplingCapacitance \sim 0.1\text{--}10\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{F}\), loop inductance \(\sim 0.5\text{--}2\text{ nH}\), response time \(10\text{--}100\text{ ns}\)).
Bulk Decoupling (\(\text{DC}\text{--}100\text{ kHz}\)): Polymer tantalum or aluminum electrolytic capacitors (\(\BulkDecouplingCapacitance \sim 100\text{--}1000\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{F}\), response time \(1\text{--}10\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\)) sustain the rail until the active VRM regulation loop stabilizes.

Parasitic inductance and parallel capacitor branches can also create anti-resonance impedance peaks between their resonances. A simple LC frequency scale is \(\LcResonantFrequency=1/(2\pi\sqrt{\ParasiticLoopInductance \DecouplingCapacitance})\), but the peak magnitude requires the complete network, including capacitor equivalent series resistance and inductance. Excitation near a poorly damped peak can amplify supply excursions. A target-impedance check therefore needs the measured or modeled impedance spectrum, not capacitance alone.



When a \(0.90\text{ V}\) core rail sags by \(60\text{ mV}\) during an accelerator burst, transistor drive current drops and every logic gate along a critical path switches more slowly, eating into register setup slack. In sub-micron CMOS silicon, logic gate propagation delay \(\GatePropagationDelay\) is governed by the Sakurai-Newton alpha-power law:4 \[ \GatePropagationDelay(\SupplyVoltage) \propto \frac{\SwitchedCapacitance \cdot \SupplyVoltage}{(\SupplyVoltage - \TransistorThresholdVoltage)^\VelocitySaturationExponent} \] where \(\SwitchedCapacitance\) is the gate load capacitance, \(\TransistorThresholdVoltage\) is the transistor threshold voltage, and \(\VelocitySaturationExponent \in [1.2, 1.5]\) is the velocity saturation index (contrasting with \(\VelocitySaturationExponent = 2.0\) in long-channel theory).
4 Sakurai-Newton Delay Modeling: The alpha-power law models voltage-dependent gate delay; its parameters are technology dependent. The model predicts reduced setup slack during droop, while a missed deadline, register error, or reset must be established against measured path slack and device thresholds.When rail voltage droops from \(\NominalSupplyVoltage\) to \(\DroopedSupplyVoltage\), propagation delay stretches according to: \[ \frac{\GatePropagationDelay(\DroopedSupplyVoltage)}{\GatePropagationDelay(\NominalSupplyVoltage)} = \frac{\DroopedSupplyVoltage}{\NominalSupplyVoltage} \left( \frac{\NominalSupplyVoltage - \TransistorThresholdVoltage}{\DroopedSupplyVoltage - \TransistorThresholdVoltage} \right)^\VelocitySaturationExponent \] In a synchronous digital pipeline with clock period \(\ClockPeriod\), setup time \(\RegisterSetupTime\), and clock skew \(\PipelineClockSkew\), timing closure requires: \[ \GatePropagationDelay + \RegisterSetupTime + \PipelineClockSkew \le \ClockPeriod \] The following illustrative calculation evaluates the delay ratio and remaining path slack with the same voltage-dependent model. A droop consumes setup margin; whether it causes a timing violation depends on the original slack, clock response, and characterized process corner.
For a drop from 0.90 V to 0.81 V, with threshold 0.35 V and exponent 1.3, delay rises by 13.5 percent to 908.3 ps. Starting with 150 ps of slack leaves 41.7 ps. These assumptions therefore do not predict a setup violation. Some processors respond to droop with active clock stretching, increasing the clock period while the rail recovers. The supported response, detection delay, and resulting execution-time stretch require device-specific characterization. Thermal and Timing Coupling connects rail disturbance to the permission task’s timing budget.

title: Systems and Hardware
text:
In cloud machine learning clusters, GPUs use high-bandwidth memory (HBM) physically separated from host CPU memory. This separates some accelerator traffic from host DRAM, although accelerator clients still contend for those channels. In embedded robotics SoCs, however, system architectures rely on Unified Memory Architecture (UMA) to satisfy size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints. Application CPU cores, neural accelerators, GPU cores, and high-rate PCIe or CSI camera DMA engines all share a single physical DRAM interface. In these shared-memory multi-core platforms, DMA transfers and vision prefetching compete directly with the permission path for memory controller command queues and physical DRAM banks.


DRAM organizes storage into channels, ranks, bank groups, and banks; their counts and timing depend on the memory standard and device organization. Each individual bank possesses an independent row buffer consisting of sense amplifiers. A read that changes the open row can require the following sequence:

Row precharge (\(\RowPrechargeTime\)): Closes the active row and equalizes the bitlines for the next activation (18.75 ns per bank at LPDDR5-6400).
Row activate (\(\RowActivationDelay\)): Reads an entire page of storage cells (e.g., 2 KB to 8 KB) across wordlines into the bank’s open row buffer (18.75 ns at LPDDR5-6400).
Column access (read latency, \(\ColumnAccessLatency\)): Reads or writes data beats from the open row buffer onto the memory data bus. LPDDR5 specifies this latency in clock cycles that depend on the data rate, so a row hit pays only this step.

To sustain high data rates, modern DRAM organizes banks into bank groups. An LPDDR5 channel offers three bank organizations: 16 banks divided into 4 bank groups for the higher data rates, 16 independent banks, or 8 larger banks formed by merging pairs (Steiner et al. 2022). In bank-group mode, consecutive column commands to the same bank group must wait a longer column-to-column delay \(\IntraGroupColumnDelay\) than commands to different groups, which need only \(\InterGroupColumnDelay\), because banks in one group share internal data paths. An address mapping that interleaves consecutive bursts across bank groups hides the longer spacing; one that keeps a stream inside a single group exposes it.

Steiner, Lukas, Matthias Jung, Michael Huonker, and Norbert Wehn. 2022. “Unveiling the Real Performance of LPDDR5 Memories.” Proceedings of the International Symposium on Memory Systems (MEMSYS), 1–3. https://doi.org/10.1145/3565053.3565062.
When consecutive memory operations target different rows within the same physical bank (a bank conflict), the memory controller cannot immediately access the column. It must execute a precharge followed by an activate before issuing the column command, introducing a compulsory stall: \[ \BankConflictPenalty \approx \RowPrechargeTime + \RowActivationDelay \] At LPDDR5-6400 that stall is 37.5 ns. The minimum time between consecutive row activations to the same bank is also governed by the row cycle time \(\RowCycleTime = \RowActiveTime + \RowPrechargeTime\), where \(\RowActiveTime\) is the minimum time a row must stay open. Repeated conflicts in one bank are therefore spaced at least \(\RowCycleTime\) apart.
Memory controllers select between an open-page or closed-page policy to balance row-buffer locality against thrashing. Under an open-page policy, row buffers remain active after access in anticipation of spatial locality. While this maximizes bandwidth for sequential streaming (such as dense general matrix multiplication (GEMM) weight fetching or linear camera DMA writes), sporadic random accesses (such as sensor fusion state lookups or 1 kHz safety monitor checks) frequently hit different rows in active banks. When a continuous camera DMA stream writes video frames to the same DRAM bank that holds real-time safety buffers, repeated row-buffer conflicts transform low-latency reads into multi-hundred-nanosecond stalls.5
5 DRAM Bank-Conflict Penalties: A row change in one bank can add precharge and activate time. Video DMA can also queue transactions ahead of a safety read. The resulting delay must be bounded for the specific address mapping, arbitration policy, and workload; a fixed penalty per request is generally unjustified.Modern DRAM controllers employ First-Ready First-Come-First-Served (FR-FCFS) command scheduling. FR-FCFS prioritizes column read/write requests that hit currently open row buffers over older requests that require row precharge and activation, maximizing overall DRAM bus throughput. However, under high cognitive load, a continuous flood of vision DMA requests or matrix multiplication memory bursts will repeatedly hit open rows. FR-FCFS schedulers then systematically postpone isolated, latency-critical read requests issued by real-time safety threads, potentially starving those requests unless the controller enforces age or service bounds.



On-chip interconnect fabrics (such as ARM CoreLink AXI4 crossbars or Network-on-Chip (NoC) meshes) split high-bandwidth accelerator and camera DMA transactions into bounded bursts of up to \(\AxiBurstLength = 256\) beats. In a shared crossbar without real-time prioritization, transactions enter a FIFO or weighted round-robin queue. For \(\QueuedTransactionCount\) competing accelerator transactions admitted ahead of a safety-critical permission request, the queuing transfer latency is: \[ \IdealMemoryQueueDelay = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^\QueuedTransactionCount {\DataVolume}_{k}}{\SharedBusBandwidth} \] Adding physical bank-switch penalties \(\sum \BankConflictPenalty\), device-specific refresh overhead, and bus turnaround penalties increases the safety read latency. Refresh mode, temperature, address mapping, and controller policy determine the bound. To protect real-time control paths against memory contention, embedded systems implement three structural defenses:

AXI Quality of Service (QoS) Priority Elevation: The AxQOS field communicates a requested priority. The interconnect and memory controller must implement a documented service policy; the field alone does not guarantee preemption or bounded latency. Already issued transactions and refresh can still block a safety read.
DRAM Bank Partitioning and Page Coloring: The operating system memory allocator allocates physical memory pages such that real-time safety code and high-rate camera DMA buffers map to strictly disjoint physical DRAM banks, removing those bank conflicts when the physical address mapping is known and enforced. Shared channels, refresh, and controller queues remain.
On-Chip SRAM Isolation: Critical safety states, barrier function parameters, and active trajectory splines bypass external DRAM entirely, executing exclusively out of static on-chip SRAM or Data Tightly Coupled Memory (DTCM).

title: Systems and Hardware
text:
In distributed machine learning clusters, nodes synchronize system clocks via Network Time Protocol (NTP) primarily for coarse event logging and telemetry, while parallel training algorithms synchronize execution through communication barriers (such as NCCL AllReduce). In physical AI systems, however, time directly maps to physical space: when a robot moves at \(30\text{ m/s}\), a \(1\text{ ms}\) synchronization error produces \(3\text{ cm}\) of spatial displacement, warping sensor fusion point clouds and invalidating safety clearance buffers. Distributed perception pipelines must convert sensor timestamps into a common clock domain with a measured conversion-error bound.


The following end-to-end delay exchange illustrates IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP), synchronizing a follower clock (\(\Glyph{S}\)) to a leader clock (\(\Glyph{M}\)). IEEE 802.1AS uses a related timing architecture with peer-delay measurement; its exchange is not identical:

\(\PtpExchangeTimestamp_1\): Master transmits a Sync frame, recording its local transmission timestamp.
\(\PtpExchangeTimestamp_2\): Slave receives the Sync frame, recording its local arrival timestamp.
\(\PtpExchangeTimestamp_3\): Slave transmits a Delay_Req frame, recording its local transmission timestamp.
\(\PtpExchangeTimestamp_4\): Master receives the Delay_Req frame, recording its local arrival timestamp.

Under the assumption of clock stability and symmetric forward and reverse propagation delay (\(\PtpForwardPathDelay = \PtpReversePathDelay = \PtpPropagationDelay\)), the time relationships satisfy: \[ \PtpExchangeTimestamp_2 = \PtpExchangeTimestamp_1 + \ClockOffset + \PtpPropagationDelay \] \[ \PtpExchangeTimestamp_4 = \PtpExchangeTimestamp_3 - \ClockOffset + \PtpPropagationDelay \] where \(\ClockOffset\) is the slave-minus-master clock offset. The estimated clock offset is: \[ \ClockOffset = \frac{(\PtpExchangeTimestamp_2 - \PtpExchangeTimestamp_1) - (\PtpExchangeTimestamp_4 - \PtpExchangeTimestamp_3)}{2} \] The one-way network propagation delay is: \[ \PtpPropagationDelay = \frac{(\PtpExchangeTimestamp_2 - \PtpExchangeTimestamp_1) + (\PtpExchangeTimestamp_4 - \PtpExchangeTimestamp_3)}{2} \]
Slave clocks adjust their local time base using a closed-loop digital proportional-integral (PI) clock servo filter. At synchronization step \(\SynchronizationStepIndex\), the measured offset \(\ClockOffset[\SynchronizationStepIndex]\) drives frequency correction \(\ServoFrequencyCorrection[\SynchronizationStepIndex]\) applied to the hardware accumulator register: \[ \ServoFrequencyCorrection[\SynchronizationStepIndex] = -\PidProportionalGain \ClockOffset[\SynchronizationStepIndex] - \PidIntegralGain \sum_{j=0}^\SynchronizationStepIndex \ClockOffset[\PastSynchronizationStepIndex] \] Here \(\ServoFrequencyCorrection\) is added to the follower frequency, \(\PidProportionalGain,\PidIntegralGain>0\), and the sampling interval is absorbed into \(\PidIntegralGain\). A positive follower-minus-leader offset therefore slows the follower; using the opposite hardware correction convention reverses the sign.
If forward and reverse path delays are asymmetric (\(\PathDelayAsymmetry = \PtpForwardPathDelay - \PtpReversePathDelay \ne 0\)), the calculated offset incurs an unobservable systematic bias of \(\PathDelayAsymmetry / 2\). Residual clock uncertainty \(\ClockConversionBound\), combining asymmetric propagation, oscillator frequency drift between sync intervals, and hardware timestamp quantization, is explicitly bounded: \[ \ClockConversionBound \le \frac{|\PathDelayAsymmetry|}{2} + \SyncMessageInterval \cdot \left| \frac{\ResidualFrequencyError}{\NominalOscillatorFrequency} \right| + 2 \TimestampQuantizationBound \] Here \(\ResidualFrequencyError\) bounds residual frequency error after servo correction, rather than the applied correction itself; \(\TimestampQuantizationBound\) bounds timestamp quantization. Additional timestamp-reference and servo errors must be included if they are not covered by these terms. This conversion bound is stored directly in the proposal header’s sync_error_ns field (table 10) and added to every evidence-age calculation in the 1 kHz permission path: \[ \ObservationAge = (\CurrentWallClockTime - \EvidenceEpoch) + \ClockConversionBound \]



Software-based timestamping captures timestamps inside the OS network socket layer or interrupt service routine. It suffers from variable kernel queueing, driver interrupt latency, and thread scheduling jitter, which inject \(50\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) to \(5\text{ ms}\) of non-deterministic timing error. To eliminate host dispatch error, physical AI hardware uses Physical Layer (PHY) Hardware Timestamping.6 Dedicated timestamping units in the Ethernet PHY or media access control (MAC) controller capture hardware counter values at the exact instant the physical Start of Frame Delimiter (SFD) crosses the Media Independent Interface (MII / RGMII). This removes software dispatch from the capture point. Timestamp resolution, reference-plane calibration, and residual error remain device-specific and must be measured.
6 Hardware Timestamping: A compatible PHY or MAC timestamps frames closer to the wire than a software interrupt handler. Hardware timestamping removes one source of dispatch variation, while path asymmetry and clock conversion remain. Timestamp uncertainty belongs in the physical belief record and permission budget.

title: Systems and Hardware
Systems and Hardware
text:
In reinforcement learning and simulation environments (such as MuJoCo or Isaac Gym), policy actions are typically abstracted as instantaneous torque or position commands applied at discrete simulation steps. In physical systems, however, actuators convert electrical energy into mechanical work through electromagnetic Lorentz forces, subject to coupled electrical, thermal, and kinematic constraints.


A brushless permanent-magnet synchronous motor (PMSM / BLDC) phase winding has phase resistance \(\PhaseResistance\) and phase inductance \(\PhaseInductance\). Applying terminal voltage \(\WindingTerminalVoltage\) against back-electromotive force \(\BackEmfVoltage = \MotorBackEmfConstant \RotorAngularSpeed\) yields the first-order stator current ODE: \[ \PhaseInductance \frac{d\InstantaneousPhaseCurrent(\TimeInstant)}{d\TimeInstant} + \PhaseResistance\, \InstantaneousPhaseCurrent(\TimeInstant) = \WindingTerminalVoltage - \MotorBackEmfConstant \RotorAngularSpeed \]
In three-phase synchronous machines under Field-Oriented Control (FOC), the stator currents are transformed from the three-phase \(\Glyph{a} \Glyph{b} \Glyph{c}\) frame into the orthogonal rotor synchronous \(\Glyph{d}\Glyph{q}\) reference frame via the Clarke and Park transformations: \[ \DirectAxisVoltage = \PhaseResistance \DirectAxisCurrent + \DirectAxisInductance \frac{d\DirectAxisCurrent}{d\TimeInstant} - \ElectricalAngularSpeed \QuadratureAxisInductance \TorqueProducingCurrent \] \[ \QuadratureAxisVoltage = \PhaseResistance \TorqueProducingCurrent + \QuadratureAxisInductance \frac{d\TorqueProducingCurrent}{d\TimeInstant} + \ElectricalAngularSpeed \DirectAxisInductance \DirectAxisCurrent + \ElectricalAngularSpeed \PermanentMagnetFluxLinkage \] The \(\Glyph{d}\) axis rotates with the rotor magnet flux, and the \(\Glyph{q}\) axis lies perpendicular to it. This separates flux and torque-producing current. Here \(\ElectricalAngularSpeed = \RotorPolePairCount \RotorAngularSpeed\) is electrical angular velocity (\(\RotorPolePairCount\) pole pairs), \(\PermanentMagnetFluxLinkage\) is the rotor permanent-magnet flux linkage, and \(\DirectAxisInductance, \QuadratureAxisInductance\) are direct and quadrature axis inductances. Under standard constant torque-angle control (\(\DirectAxisCurrent = 0\)), electromagnetic torque is directly proportional to quadrature current: \[ \MotorTorque = \frac{3}{2} \RotorPolePairCount \, \PermanentMagnetFluxLinkage \TorqueProducingCurrent = \MotorTorqueConstant \TorqueProducingCurrent \]
For a commanded voltage step with the rotor held at rest (\(\RotorAngularSpeed = 0\)) and zero initial current, quadrature current rises exponentially: \[ \TorqueProducingCurrent(\TimeInstant) = \frac{\WindingTerminalVoltage}{\PhaseResistance} \left( 1 - e^{-\TimeInstant / \ElectricalTimeConstant} \right), \quad \ElectricalTimeConstant = \frac{\QuadratureAxisInductance}{\PhaseResistance} \] where \(\ElectricalTimeConstant\) is the electrical time constant. Current, and therefore delivered torque, reaches approximately 63 percent of its steady-state value after one time constant \(\ElectricalTimeConstant\) (Electrical time constants, back-EMF, and current clamping computes it for the running machine’s hub motors from their datasheet inductance and resistance). An unprivileged neural policy step command cannot produce an instantaneous step in physical torque.
Furthermore, achievable current is constrained by inverter voltage saturation: \[ \sqrt{\DirectAxisVoltage^2 + \QuadratureAxisVoltage^2} \le \frac{\DcBusVoltage}{\sqrt{3}} \] As rotor speed \(\RotorAngularSpeed\) rises, back-EMF \(\ElectricalAngularSpeed \PermanentMagnetFluxLinkage\) increases, consuming available quadrature voltage \(\QuadratureAxisVoltage\). At the actuator’s base speed, voltage headroom vanishes, and torque collapses unless negative direct-axis current (\(\DirectAxisCurrent < 0\), flux weakening) is commanded to oppose part of the magnet flux linkage, within current and magnet-demagnetization limits.



Current flowing through stator windings dissipates resistive Joule heat: \[ \WindingLossPower(\TimeInstant) = \frac{3}{2} \TorqueProducingCurrent^2(\TimeInstant) \PhaseResistance(\WindingTemperature) \] where copper electrical resistance increases linearly with temperature: \[ \PhaseResistance(\WindingTemperature) = \ReferenceWindingResistance \left[ 1 + \CopperTemperatureCoefficient (\WindingTemperature - \CopperReferenceTemperature) \right] \] with temperature coefficient \(\CopperTemperatureCoefficient \approx 0.00393\text{ K}^{-1}\) for copper. At an operating temperature of \(150^\circ\text{C}\), stator copper resistance is approximately \(50\text{ percent}\) higher than at room temperature (\(25^\circ\text{C}\)). To sustain the same commanded torque \(\MotorTorque = \MotorTorqueConstant \TorqueProducingCurrent\), the motor requires identical current \(\TorqueProducingCurrent\) but generates \(50\text{ percent}\) more thermal dissipation. This creates positive feedback between winding temperature and Joule heating that accelerates thermal degradation.
In a physical motor, multi-node lumped thermal networks span multiple physical interfaces with disparate thermal masses:

Stator Winding Copper: Low thermal capacitance \(\CopperThermalCapacitance\), rapid heating from Joule dissipation (\(\CopperThermalTimeConstant \sim 10\text{--}30\text{ s}\)).
Stator Iron Laminations: Moderate thermal capacitance \(\IronThermalCapacitance\), absorbing iron eddy-current and hysteresis losses \(\IronLossPower\) and heat conducted across winding insulation \(\CopperIronThermalResistance\). The iron losses depend on flux, frequency, and material.
Motor Frame and Aluminum Housing: Large thermal capacitance \(\CaseThermalCapacitance\), conducting heat into the robotic link structure and convecting to ambient air through \(\CaseAmbientThermalResistance\) (\(\CaseThermalTimeConstant \sim 10\text{--}30\text{ min}\)).

The temperature dynamics across these nodes satisfy the coupled differential system: \[ \CopperThermalCapacitance \frac{d\WindingTemperature}{d\TimeInstant} = \WindingLossPower(\TimeInstant) - \frac{\WindingTemperature - \StatorIronTemperature}{\CopperIronThermalResistance} \] \[ \IronThermalCapacitance \frac{d\StatorIronTemperature}{d\TimeInstant} = \frac{\WindingTemperature - \StatorIronTemperature}{\CopperIronThermalResistance} + \IronLossPower - \frac{\StatorIronTemperature - \CaseTemperature}{\IronCaseThermalResistance} \] \[ \CaseThermalCapacitance \frac{d\CaseTemperature}{d\TimeInstant} = \frac{\StatorIronTemperature - \CaseTemperature}{\IronCaseThermalResistance} - \frac{\CaseTemperature - \AmbientTemperature}{\CaseAmbientThermalResistance} \]
For initial temperature at ambient, a simplified single-node lumped thermal model uses effective thermal resistance to ambient \(\ThermalResistance\) (in \(\text{K/W}\)) and thermal heat capacity \(\StatorThermalCapacitance\) (in \(\text{J/K}\)). The temperature rise \(\JouleanTemperatureRise(\TimeInstant) = \WindingTemperature(\TimeInstant) - \AmbientTemperature\) satisfies:8 \[ \StatorThermalCapacitance \frac{\DerivativeOperator\JouleanTemperatureRise(\TimeInstant)}{d\TimeInstant} = \WindingLossPower(\TimeInstant) - \frac{\JouleanTemperatureRise(\TimeInstant)}{\ThermalResistance} \] Under constant power, temperature rises with thermal time constant \(\ThermalTimeConstant = \ThermalResistance \StatorThermalCapacitance\): \[ \JouleanTemperatureRise(\TimeInstant) = \WindingLossPower \ThermalResistance \left( 1 - e^{-\TimeInstant / \ThermalTimeConstant} \right) \]
8 Stator Thermal Time Constants: Resistive Joule heating elevates motor phase winding temperatures during continuous high-torque maneuvers. Because copper electrical resistivity increases linearly with temperature, hot windings have higher resistance, reducing torque output under terminal voltage saturation. Exceeding winding insulation temperature limits breaks down dielectric coatings, causing inter-turn short circuits and permanent winding damage.Continuous torque capacity \(\ContinuousTorque\) is bounded by the maximum allowable winding temperature rise \(\AllowableWindingTemperatureRise\): \[ \ContinuousTorque \le \MotorTorqueConstant \sqrt{\frac{2\AllowableWindingTemperatureRise}{3 \ThermalResistance \PhaseResistance}} \] The factor \(2/3\) follows from the three-phase loss convention above; use the winding resistance at the limiting temperature. Other motor and inverter losses reduce the available thermal margin.
Transient torque peaks \(\PeakTorque \approx 2\text{--}4 \times \ContinuousTorque\) are permitted during aggressive dynamic maneuvers only if an active digital \({\MotorPhaseRmsCurrent}^2 \TimeInstant\) thermal protection observer running on the safety microcontroller bounds the thermal integral: \[ \JouleanTemperatureRise[\DiscreteSampleIndex+1] = \JouleanTemperatureRise[\DiscreteSampleIndex] e^{-\FiniteChange \TimeInstant / \ThermalTimeConstant} + \ThermalResistance \WindingLossPower[\DiscreteSampleIndex] \left( 1 - e^{-\FiniteChange \TimeInstant / \ThermalTimeConstant} \right) \] The thermal class is an insulation service rating, not a sharp instantaneous breakdown temperature. Current derating must begin with margin below the winding and rotor limits, accounting for model error, initial temperature, and response time.



Geared electromagnetic actuators amplify delivered motor torque while multiplying rotor inertia at the joint output. For a transmission with gear reduction ratio \(\GearReductionRatio = \RotorAngularSpeed / \JointVelocity\), kinetic energy conservation dictates the reflected inertia acting at the output link: \[ \KineticEnergy = \frac{1}{2} \RotorInertia \RotorAngularSpeed^2 + \frac{1}{2} \LoadInertia \JointVelocity^2 = \frac{1}{2} (\LoadInertia + \GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia) \JointVelocity^2 \] The effective rotational inertia seen at joint coordinate \(\JointCoordinate\) is: \[ \EffectiveJointInertia = \LoadInertia + \GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia \] The joint equation of motion under motor electromagnetic torque \(\MotorTorque\) is: \[ \JointAcceleration = \frac{\GearReductionRatio \MotorTorque - \ExternalJointTorque}{\LoadInertia + \GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia} \] Differentiating \(\JointAcceleration\) with respect to gear ratio \(\GearReductionRatio\) at zero external load yields: \[ \frac{\partial \JointAcceleration}{\partial \GearReductionRatio} = \frac{\MotorTorque (\LoadInertia - \GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia)}{(\LoadInertia + \GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia)^2} \] Setting \(\frac{\partial \JointAcceleration}{\partial \GearReductionRatio} = 0\) yields the inertia-matching ratio \(\InertiaMatchingRatio = \sqrt{\LoadInertia / \RotorInertia}\). When \(\GearReductionRatio > \InertiaMatchingRatio\), counter-intuitively, increasing the gear ratio decreases delivered joint acceleration because the motor spends the majority of its torque accelerating its own rotor rather than the link.


For constant effective inertia and constant external torque, angular jerk \(\JointJerk(\TimeInstant) = \dddot{\JointCoordinate}(\TimeInstant)\) measures the time rate of change of joint acceleration: \[ \JointJerk(\TimeInstant) = \frac{\GearReductionRatio}{\LoadInertia + \GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia} \frac{\DerivativeOperator\MotorTorque(\TimeInstant)}{d\TimeInstant} \] Electromagnetic torque relates to stator quadrature current via torque constant \(\MotorTorqueConstant\): \(\MotorTorque = \MotorTorqueConstant \TorqueProducingCurrent\). From the stator electrical dynamics in this section, current slew rate is bounded by winding inductance \(\PhaseInductance\): \[ \frac{\DerivativeOperator\MotorTorque}{d\TimeInstant} = \MotorTorqueConstant \frac{d\TorqueProducingCurrent}{d\TimeInstant} = \frac{\MotorTorqueConstant}{\PhaseInductance} \left( \WindingTerminalVoltage - \MotorBackEmfConstant \RotorAngularSpeed - \PhaseResistance \TorqueProducingCurrent \right) \] For a signed voltage constrained by \(|\WindingTerminalVoltage|\le \TerminalVoltageLimit\), a conservative magnitude bound in this scalar winding model is: \[ |\JointJerk| \le \frac{\GearReductionRatio \MotorTorqueConstant (\TerminalVoltageLimit + |\MotorBackEmfConstant \RotorAngularSpeed + \PhaseResistance \TorqueProducingCurrent|)}{\PhaseInductance (\LoadInertia + \GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia)} \] Positive and negative current slew have different available voltage headroom. A tighter directional bound retains the signs in the preceding current equation. Changing external torque, coupled joint motion, and inverter limits require additional terms.
When a tracker requests a step torque discontinuity \(\FiniteChange \JointTorque\) across discrete timesteps, the commanded derivative \(\frac{\DerivativeOperator\CommandedJointTorque}{d\TimeInstant} \to \infty\) cannot be delivered instantaneously by physical silicon. The inverter enters hard voltage saturation, causing steep current slew (\(d\ConductorCurrent/d\TimeInstant\)), intense thermal stress on power MOSFETs, and shock loads across gear-tooth contact flanks (\(\GearToothBendingStress \propto \GearTangentialLoad / (\GearFaceWidth \GearModule \LewisFormFactor)\)). Synchronous pre-actuation invariant filters evaluate numerical torque derivatives \((\JointTorque[\DiscreteSampleIndex] - \JointTorque[\DiscreteSampleIndex-1]) / \FiniteChange \TimeInstant\) to ensure requested actions remain within allowable jerk envelopes before latching power stages.

title: Systems and Hardware
text:
In data center machine learning clusters, electrical power is managed by high-capacity facility uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and dedicated substation transformers. On mobile autonomous platforms, computational accelerators and mechanical actuators draw from a shared, finite DC power distribution network. A robotic platform’s electrical power distribution network must supply acceleration surges and absorb regenerative braking energy across finite bus capacitance and harness impedance.


When multiple high-torque actuators accelerate simultaneously (such as a humanoid jumping or an articulated arm bracing against an unexpected payload), total load current steps by \(\FiniteChange \LoadCurrent = \sum_{k=1}^{\ActuatorAxisCount} \FiniteChange \ConductorCurrent_k\) with steep current slew rates \(d\LoadCurrent/d\TimeInstant \sim 10^5\text{--}10^6\text{ A/s}\). The electrical wiring harness connecting the main battery to distributed joint inverters possesses parasitic loop inductance \(\PowerRailInductance\) (typically \(1\text{--}5\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{H}\) for a 1-meter harness) and harness resistance \(\PowerRailResistance\). These parasitics impede source current delivery, producing instantaneous inductive rail droop at the actuator inverter terminals: \[ \SourceVoltage(\TimeInstant)-\DcBusVoltage(\TimeInstant) = \PowerRailResistance \SourceCurrent(\TimeInstant) + \PowerRailInductance \frac{d\SourceCurrent}{d\TimeInstant} \] The capacitor is connected across this same bus node; its voltage change is not another independent series drop. For an ideal capacitor, \(\FiniteChange \BusCapacitorVoltage(\TimeInstant)=\DcBusVoltage(0)-\DcBusVoltage(\TimeInstant)\). Local inverter bus capacitance \(\DcBusBulkCapacitance\) must supply the instantaneous charge deficit between load demand and battery source current: \[ \FiniteChange \BusCapacitorVoltage(\TimeInstant) = \frac{1}{\DcBusBulkCapacitance} \int_0^\TimeInstant \left( \LoadCurrent(\IntegrationTimeInstant) - \SourceCurrent(\IntegrationTimeInstant) \right) d\IntegrationTimeInstant \]
If the DC bus terminal voltage drops below the drive’s configured Under-Voltage Lockout (UVLO) threshold \(\UvloThresholdVoltage\) (e.g., \(18\text{ V}\) on a \(24\text{ V}\) nominal bus, or \(36\text{ V}\) on a \(48\text{ V}\) bus), the gate driver IC enters UVLO fault protection. It disables gate bias within microseconds to prevent power MOSFETs from operating in their linear resistive region. The resulting loss of commanded torque can let a gravity-loaded joint descend. Current decay and the holding-brake response determine the plant motion.
If the current deficit starts at \(\LoadStepCurrentDeficit\) and decreases linearly to zero over \(\LoadStepDeficitDuration\), integrating that triangular deficit gives: \[ \DcBusBulkCapacitance \ge \frac{\LoadStepCurrentDeficit \cdot \LoadStepDeficitDuration}{2 \AllowableRailDroop} \] A constant deficit over the same interval removes the factor of two in the denominator. The source dynamics and capacitor ESR must also satisfy the terminal-voltage limit. Local capacitor banks combine low-ESR multi-layer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) for high-frequency ripple filtering (\(20\text{--}100\text{ kHz}\) inverter switching) with bulk electrolytic or polymer capacitors for transient step energy buffering. The bank must also carry the RMS ripple current of the actual switching waveform. Equivalent-series-resistance losses scale with that current squared.



During controlled regenerative deceleration or emergency stopping, mechanical kinetic energy \(\KineticEnergy = \frac{1}{2} \Mass \BodySpeed^2\) (linear platform motion) or \(\KineticEnergy = \frac{1}{2} \EffectiveJointInertia \JointVelocity^2\) (articulated joint rotation) is converted back into electrical energy by the motor acting as a generator. Current flows back through the inverter bridge into the DC bus via active synchronous rectification or freewheeling body diodes.
If the battery cannot accept this regenerative current (for example, when the battery pack reaches its chemistry-specific charge limit, when battery internal resistance rises at freezing temperatures, or when safety contactors open to isolate the pack), the returned electrical energy \(\RegenerativeRecoveryEfficiency \KineticEnergy\) is forced into the local bus capacitor \(\DcBusBulkCapacitance\). The resulting terminal voltage surge follows the ideal capacitor relationship: \[ \FiniteChange \BusCapacitorEnergy = \frac{1}{2} \DcBusBulkCapacitance \left( \FinalBusVoltage^2 - \InitialBusVoltage^2 \right) = \RegenerativeRecoveryEfficiency \KineticEnergy \] \[ \FinalBusVoltage = \sqrt{ \InitialBusVoltage^2 + \frac{2 \RegenerativeRecoveryEfficiency \KineticEnergy}{\DcBusBulkCapacitance} } \]
An overvoltage protection trip and semiconductor breakdown are different thresholds. Exceeding the configured trip requests the assessed protective response; exceeding device voltage ratings can cause avalanche stress or damage. Disabling gate commands does not by itself absorb returned energy.
To prevent overvoltage destruction, motor drives incorporate an active dynamic brake chopper. When DC bus voltage crosses a hardware clamp threshold \(\ChopperTurnOnVoltage\), a high-power semiconductor switch (MOSFET or IGBT) modulates an auxiliary low-inductance braking resistor \(\BrakeChopperResistance\) with hysteresis:9 \[ \BrakeChopperResistance \le \frac{\ChopperClampVoltage^2}{\PeakRegenerativePower} \] \[ \PeakRegenerativePower \approx \RegenerativeRecoveryEfficiency \cdot \RegenerativeBrakingTorque \cdot \PeakRotorAngularSpeed \] The chopper comparator switches the resistor on when \(\DcBusVoltage \ge \ChopperTurnOnVoltage\) and turns off when \(\DcBusVoltage \le \ChopperTurnOffVoltage\), preventing rapid oscillation. In addition to peak power sizing, the braking resistor must be rated for single-pulse adiabatic energy absorption: \[ \BrakeResistorPulseEnergy \ge \RegenerativeRecoveryEfficiency \KineticEnergy \] with a thermal cooldown time constant that prevents cumulative thermal failure during repeated stop-and-go duty cycles.
9 Dynamic Braking Choppers: A qualified chopper can dissipate returned energy when the battery is unavailable as a sink. Its threshold, switch and resistor ratings, pulse duration, and thermal recovery must be tested. Regeneration and chopper operation are not inherent to every emergency stop; safe torque off can instead leave a motor coasting.

title: Systems and Hardware
text:
In distributed machine learning clusters, networks are built on high-bandwidth fabrics (such as 100/400 Gbps RoCEv2 or InfiniBand) optimized for aggregate data-parallel throughput via credit-based flow control. In physical AI systems, however, the onboard communication fabric must simultaneously multiplex two diametrically opposed traffic classes:

High-bandwidth best-effort perception streams: Multi-gigabit video from high-resolution GMSL2/GigE Vision cameras (\(2\text{--}8\text{ Gbps}\)) and 3D lidar point clouds (\(100\text{--}1000\text{ Mbps}\)) streaming into the AI accelerator’s unified memory for foundation model inference.
Hard real-time periodic control traffic: Deterministic 1 kHz joint setpoint commands and high-resolution torque/position feedback (\(100\text{--}500\text{ kbps}\)) exchanged with distributed motor inverters.

If these two traffic classes share a naive best-effort Ethernet fabric with first-in, first-out (FIFO) queueing, multi-megabyte perception bursts cause severe queue congestion and buffer bloat. A burst of video frames can delay a motor control packet by \(5\text{--}20\text{ ms}\), violating the 1 ms control deadline, starving the inverter current loop, and tripping hardware emergency stops. Coordinating distributed drives while ingesting perception streams requires an architectural separation of fabrics, deterministic bus schedules, and bounded lock-free publication protocols.


On shared physical buses, \(\ActuatorAxisCount\) actuator drives transmit telemetry and receive setpoints cyclically. To prevent perception traffic from corrupting motor timing, physical AI architectures use dedicated deterministic fieldbuses (CAN 2.0B, CAN FD, or EtherCAT) or time-scheduled switched Ethernet (IEEE TSN).
Classical Controller Area Network (CAN 2.0B, ISO 11898-1) uses differential signaling over a shielded twisted pair (\(\CanHighLineVoltage - \CanLowLineVoltage \approx 2.0\text{ V}\) for dominant logic 0, and \(0\text{ V}\) for recessive logic 1):

Arbitration Mechanics: Nodes access the physical medium using non-destructive bitwise arbitration. When two nodes transmit simultaneously, a dominant bit overrides a recessive bit. A node transmitting a recessive bit that samples a dominant bit on the physical bus immediately ceases transmission and yields the bus to the higher-priority frame without message corruption.
Framing and Payload Constraints: Standard CAN 2.0B frames support either an 11-bit standard or 29-bit extended identifier, with payload length strictly capped at \(\FramePayloadSize \le 8\text{ bytes}\) via a 4-bit Data Length Code (DLC).
Bit-Stuffing and Latency: Classical CAN inserts an opposite bit after a run of five identical bits in the stuffed region. Serialization time includes the identifier format, payload, CRC, stuffing, and interframe spacing. Let \(\FrameWireBitCount\) be that complete bit count for frame \(\FrameIndex\); then \(\FrameTransmissionTime_i=\FrameWireBitCount/\BusBitRate\). Extended identifiers consume more bits than standard identifiers.
The Scalability Bottleneck: The necessary load condition is \(\sum_i \FrameTransmissionTime_i/\FramePeriod_i\le1\), but meeting deadlines also requires priority and blocking analysis. There is no universal utilization threshold at which CAN queueing diverges. Axis capacity depends on command and feedback packing, periods, identifiers, and tolerated retransmissions; one frame per axis is a workload assumption.

Controller Area Network with Flexible Data-Rate (CAN FD, ISO 11898-1:2015) overcomes the payload and bandwidth limits of classical CAN through dual bit-rate switching and payload expansion up to 64 bytes:

Arbitration Phase: Transmitted at the nominal bit rate \(\NominalBitRate\) (typically \(500\text{ kbps}\) or \(1\text{ Mbps}\)). The bit time \(\NominalBitTime = 1/\NominalBitRate\) must accommodate physical cable propagation delays across the robot chassis and transceiver delays (\(2 \SignalPropagationDelay + \TransceiverDelay\)), allowing non-destructive bitwise priority arbitration. Nodes drive the bus using dominant or recessive states. If two nodes transmit simultaneously, the lower numerical message identifier (higher logical priority) overwrites recessive bits, winning the bus without collision or frame destruction.
Data Phase: Once arbitration is established, the winning node asserts the Bit Rate Switch (BRS) bit, accelerating transmission to the data bit rate \(\DataPhaseBitRate\) (typically \(2\text{--}8\text{ Mbps}\)). The data phase no longer needs round-trip arbitration within each bit. Signal integrity, receiver sampling, and transceiver delay compensation still constrain its rate.
Bit-Stuffing Overhead: Dynamic stuff bits are inserted after 5 consecutive identical bits in arbitration, while the CRC field incorporates fixed stuff bits with an explicit stuff count. In the worst-case bit pattern, bit stuffing can inflate frame transmission duration by up to \(20\text{ percent}\).

The serialization duration for frame \(\FrameIndex\) is: \[ \FrameSerializationTime \approx \frac{\ArbitrationFieldBitCount}{\NominalBitRate} + \frac{\DataFieldBitCount}{\DataPhaseBitRate} + \StuffBitTime + \InterframeSpacingTime \] where \(\ArbitrationFieldBitCount\) is the arbitration field length (identifier, control bits), \(\DataFieldBitCount\) is the payload and CRC length, \(\StuffBitTime\) accounts for stuff bits, and \(\InterframeSpacingTime\) is the minimum 3-bit inter-frame spacing.
In a CAN FD response-time budget, a higher-priority release cannot preempt a frame already transmitting. For a simplified error-free fixed-priority message set with no prior instance of frame \(\FrameIndex\) pending, the following conservative recurrence charges higher-priority interference across the whole response window: \[ \FrameResponseTime_i = \FrameTransmissionTime_i + \FrameBlockingTime_i + \sum_{j \in \HigherPriorityFrames(i)} \left\lceil \frac{\FrameResponseTime_i + \FrameReleaseJitter_j + \BitTime}{\FramePeriod_j} \right\rceil \FrameTransmissionTime_j \] Here \(\FrameTransmissionTime_i=\FrameSerializationTime\), \(\FrameReleaseJitter_j\) is higher-priority release jitter, and \(\BitTime\) accounts for arbitration at the boundary. Iterate from \(\FrameTransmissionTime_i+\FrameBlockingTime_i\) to convergence or a deadline overrun. Add the message’s own release jitter if its deadline starts before it becomes ready. The lower-priority blocking term is: \[ \FrameBlockingTime_i = \max_{k \in \LowerPriorityFrames(i)} \FrameTransmissionTime_k \] Set \(\FrameBlockingTime_i=0\) when no lower-priority frame exists. This simplified test is not an exact general CAN schedulability test: queued prior instances, controller transmit-buffer behavior, errors, and retransmissions require a matching busy-period analysis. A long CAN FD payload improves packing efficiency but can also increase the non-preemptive blocking seen by a short urgent command.
For high-axis-count systems (such as humanoids with 30 to 50 degrees of freedom), EtherCAT (ETG.1000) achieves deterministic 1 kHz to 10 kHz cycle times over standard 100BASE-TX full-duplex Ethernet (\(\LinkBitRate = 100\text{ Mbps}\)). Rather than transmitting individual frames per axis, EtherCAT structures communication as an active logical ring:

The real-time master (executing on the safety microcontroller or PREEMPT_RT Linux host) transmits a single standard Ethernet frame (EtherType 0x88A4) traversing all slave drives in a physical daisy chain.
Each drive integrates an EtherCAT Slave Controller (ESC) application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) (such as Beckhoff ET1100 or field-programmable gate array (FPGA) IP). As the frame’s bits pass through the ESC’s physical shift registers, the ESC processes data on the fly:

It reads commanded setpoints (joint target position, velocity, and feedforward torque) directly from its allocated byte offset in the datagram.
It writes actual measured feedback (encoder position, phase current, and drive status flags) into the moving frame.

Each slave contributes a forwarding delay that depends on its controller and ports; the frame returns from the final slave along the return path. The example below assigns an illustrative delay per slave.

The cycle must accommodate the following round-trip budget for \(\SlaveDriveCount\) slave drives, with \(\FrameBitCount\) measured in bits and each delay bounded for the topology: \[ \FieldbusCycleTime \ge \frac{\FrameBitCount}{\LinkBitRate} + \MasterProcessingTime + \sum_{\SlaveDriveIndex=1}^\SlaveDriveCount \SlaveForwardingDelay + \SignalPropagationDelay + \CycleGuardTime \]
For 30 axes, the assumed command and feedback sizes give 600 bytes of process data. An illustrative 750 bytes frame takes 60 μs to serialize at 100 Mb/s. Charging 1 μs per slave adds 30 μs, so the subtotal is already 90 μs. Master processing, propagation, omitted wire overhead, and guard time must still fit the cycle. This partial sum is not a measured round-trip bound. EtherCAT distributed clocks align local device timers through measured offsets and propagation compensation. The qualified synchronization error and arrival deadline determine when a drive may use the frame. Clock synchronization does not remove frame transit time.



While EtherCAT processes frames on the fly through specialized slave controllers, modern multi-camera and lidar robotic systems require multi-gigabit Ethernet fabrics that transport high-bandwidth vision data alongside hard real-time actuator commands. IEEE Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) provides deterministic Ethernet via standards that bound queuing jitter and reserve transmission windows:
The IEEE 802.1Qbv Time-Aware Shaper (TAS) coordinates traffic transmission using hardware-controlled transmission gates associated with each priority egress queue (traffic classes 0 to 7). A cyclic Gate Control List (GCL), synchronized across all network bridges via IEEE 802.1AS (generalized Precision Time Protocol), switches gates open or closed at precise physical time epochs. By reserving dedicated time windows exclusively for high-priority Scheduled Traffic (ST), TAS eliminates queuing interference from lower-priority Best-Effort (BE) traffic.
Standard Ethernet frames are non-preemptive: once a transmission begins, it cannot be interrupted on physical copper or optical links. If a lower-priority best-effort packet begins transmission immediately before an ST time slice opens, the scheduled frame experiences transmission blocking of up to the maximum frame duration. To prevent this, TAS enforces a guard band before each scheduled traffic window: \[ \GuardBandDuration \ge \frac{\BestEffortWireBitCount}{\LinkBitRate} \] Here \(\BestEffortWireBitCount\) is the maximum non-preemptible wire occupancy in bits, including the applicable framing overhead. A payload MTU in bytes cannot be divided directly by a bit rate. The configured guard must also cover clock error and implementation timing uncertainty. During it, a best-effort frame may start only if it can finish before the reserved window.
IEEE 802.1Qbu and IEEE 802.3br frame preemption reduce blocking by interrupting eligible traffic at permitted fragment boundaries. The remaining bound includes the maximum non-preemptible fragment and its overhead, not merely a nominal minimum fragment size. Both the link partners and the schedule must support the mechanism. Preemption saves reserved idle time at the cost of fragmentation overhead and additional configuration obligations.
The four primary real-time communication protocols differ in framing, arbitration, clock synchronization, and axis-count scaling (table 7).
