Napkin Math 1.1: DRAM bandwidth of 3D TSDF voxel gridsPractical Engineering Question: What are the distance-and-weight payload and modeled DRAM bandwidth of sparse vs. dense TSDF representations?
1. Dense allocation. A manipulation workcell of 10 m \(\times\) 10 m \(\times\) 3 m (300 m³) at 1 cm pitch holds 300,000,000 voxels. At 4 bytes per voxel (16-bit distance plus 16-bit fusion weight), excluding occupancy, per-cell evidence epochs, and allocator overhead, the distance-and-weight payload is 1.20 GB. Refining the pitch to 5 mm for tool contact raises the count to 2,400,000,000 voxels and the partial payload to 9.60 GB, which alone exceeds an illustrative 8 GB memory budget.
2. Sparse allocation. Surfaces occupy a thin manifold within the volume. Grouping voxels into 512-voxel leaf blocks and allocating only within the truncation band, assumed to be 3 percent of the volume, gives 17,579 blocks. With a 32-byte leaf header, the payload is 36.6 MB at 1 cm and 292.5 MB at 5 mm. A full map must also budget the separate occupancy layer, per-cell epochs, block lookup and allocator metadata, and capacity for the unknown-space policy.
3. Traversal and DRAM traffic. A 640 \(\times\) 480 depth stream at 60 Hz supplies 18.432 million rays per second. Along a 3 m ray at 1 cm pitch the traversal visits 300 cells. The 294 cells before the hit receive occupancy free-ray updates, and the 6 cells near the return receive TSDF fusion. Sparse TSDF allocation saves map capacity; it removes neither the traversal nor the occupancy updates. At 8 bytes of assumed read/write traffic per update, sending every update to DRAM costs 44.2 GB/s. At an assumed 95 percent cache hit fraction for both occupancy and TSDF updates, the modeled DRAM demand falls to 2.21 GB/s, a 20× reduction. The hit rate depends on ray overlap, atomics, evictions, and writeback on the chosen hardware; it is an input to measure, not a property of the map structure.
Systems insight: Sparse allocation yields 33× less modeled TSDF payload in this surface-fraction scenario, while bus demand depends on measured locality and on all traversed-cell work. Whether that demand fits beside policy inference on a shared bus is the contention question of Contention for Shared Resources.







A sensor perturbation can change a neural action proposal even when the physical scene has barely moved. A sensitivity bound limits that change relative to the input error and supplies a quantity to compare with available actuator headroom. The bound concerns the proposal; the permission path must still check the plant state and enforce current limits.


For high-rate proprioceptive feedback loops (such as \(500\text{--}1000\text{ Hz}\) quadruped balance, bipedal locomotion, and arm impedance control), physical policies frequently employ Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs) rather than deep spatial transformers. A canonical continuous MLP policy takes a low-dimensional proprioceptive vector \(\ProprioceptiveInputVector \in \mathbb{R}^{\InputCoordinateCount}\) (joint positions \(\GeneralizedCoordinates\), velocities \(\GeneralizedVelocities\), IMU angular rates, projected gravity, and previous action history). It then evaluates a sequence of \(\LayerCount\) affine transformations interleaved with element-wise non-linear activations: \[ \HiddenActivation_0 = \ProprioceptiveInputVector, \quad \HiddenActivation_{\LayerIndex} = \ActivationFunction_{\LayerIndex}(\WeightMatrix_{\LayerIndex} \HiddenActivation_{\LayerIndex-1} + \BiasVector_{\LayerIndex}) \quad \text{for } \LayerIndex=1, \dots, \LayerCount, \quad \pi(\ProprioceptiveInputVector) = \OutputLayerWeightMatrix \HiddenActivation_{\LayerCount} + \OutputLayerBiasVector \] where \(\WeightMatrix_{\LayerIndex} \in \mathbb{R}^{\LayerWidth_{\LayerIndex} \times \LayerWidth_{\LayerIndex-1}}\) are weight matrices and \(\BiasVector_{\LayerIndex} \in \mathbb{R}^{\LayerWidth_{\LayerIndex}}\) are bias vectors.


A compact MLP can keep its weights and activations in on-chip memory, reducing interference from camera direct memory access and other DRAM clients. Capacity alone does not establish residency: cache replacement, shared clients, scheduling, and accelerator transfers determine the memory level that supplies each layer.
For a dense layer with \(\LayerInputWidth\LayerOutputWidth\) weights, a single input vector requires approximately \(2\LayerInputWidth\LayerOutputWidth\) floating-point operations. If each weight occupies \(\WeightElementStorageSize\) bytes and is read once from the memory level being analyzed, the weight-only arithmetic intensity is \[ \MlpWeightArithmeticIntensity \approx \frac{2}{\WeightElementStorageSize}\;\text{FLOP/byte}. \] Activation traffic lowers this ratio; weight reuse across inputs raises it. The relevant roofline compares this intensity with compute throughput divided by bandwidth at that same memory level. Cache-resident weights therefore change the applicable bandwidth, not the amount of arithmetic.
A deployment budgets weights, scratch buffers, and hidden activations together, preallocates runtime storage, and measures or bounds worst-case execution under interference. A short average forward pass does not by itself justify placing inference in an interrupt handler or guarantee a control deadline.




Bounding how strongly a network amplifies input perturbations requires a global sensitivity constant. A neural policy \(\pi: \ProprioceptiveInputSpace \to \ControlCommandSpace\) is \(\PolicyLipschitzBound\)-Lipschitz continuous if there exists a non-negative scalar constant \(\PolicyLipschitzBound\) such that for all \(\ProprioceptiveInputVector_1, \ProprioceptiveInputVector_2 \in \ProprioceptiveInputSpace\): \[ \| \pi(\ProprioceptiveInputVector_1) - \pi(\ProprioceptiveInputVector_2) \|_{\ControlCommandSpace} \le \PolicyLipschitzBound \| \ProprioceptiveInputVector_1 - \ProprioceptiveInputVector_2 \|_{\ProprioceptiveInputSpace} \] For a feedforward network with \(\LayerCount\) layers \(\pi(\ProprioceptiveInputVector) = \ActivationFunction_{\LayerCount}(\WeightMatrix_{\LayerCount} \dots \ActivationFunction_1(\WeightMatrix_1 \ProprioceptiveInputVector))\), let \({\ActivationLipschitzBound}_k\) bound each activation’s slope over the input domain. The composed Lipschitz bound is: \[ \PolicyLipschitzBound \le \prod_{k=1}^{\LayerCount} {\ActivationLipschitzBound}_k \| \WeightMatrix_k \|_2 \] where \(\|\WeightMatrix_k\|_2 = \LargestSingularNumber(\WeightMatrix_k)\) is the spectral norm (the largest singular value of weight matrix \(\WeightMatrix_k\)). Standard activations such as ReLU and Tanh are 1-Lipschitz in their scalar forms; exact GeLU has maximum derivative about \(1.1289\), so assigning it a factor of one would understate the bound.
The product is an upper bound, not necessarily the smallest Lipschitz constant. Its physical interpretation depends on normalization. A network receiving position and velocity in different units needs declared input scales; converting its normalized output to torque introduces another scale factor. Without those conversions, multiplying a position error by a dimensionless network bound cannot yield a torque error.
To bound policy sensitivity directly during training, spectral normalization reparameterizes each weight matrix by its spectral norm: \[ \SpectrallyNormalizedWeightMatrix_k = \frac{\WeightMatrix_k}{\LargestSingularNumber(\WeightMatrix_k)} \] where \(\LargestSingularNumber(\WeightMatrix_k)\) is estimated efficiently via power iteration during forward passes. Division by the exact nonzero spectral norm gives \(\|\SpectrallyNormalizedWeightMatrix_k\|_2=1\). Finite power iteration generally gives an estimate, not a certified upper bound; a safety argument must account for its error. Even an exact network sensitivity bound does not prove closed-loop plant stability.



In physical systems, input state \(\ProprioceptiveInputVector\) is corrupted by sensor measurement noise \(\SmallPerturbation \ProprioceptiveInputVector\) bounded by \(\|\SmallPerturbation \ProprioceptiveInputVector\| \le \SensorNoiseBound\). The resulting deviation in commanded control action is bounded by: \[ \| \SmallPerturbation \NominalControlCommand \| = \| \pi(\ProprioceptiveInputVector + \SmallPerturbation \ProprioceptiveInputVector) - \pi(\ProprioceptiveInputVector) \| \le \PolicyLipschitzBound \SensorNoiseBound \] The constant has output-units per input-unit once normalization is included. Compare \(\PolicyLipschitzBound\SensorNoiseBound\) with the actuator headroom at the current operating state. Spectral normalization bounds the network, while stability, safe torque, and sensor validity require a plant model and a state-dependent permission check.




Behavioral cloning fits a policy to demonstrator state-action pairs. Two different failures need different remedies: ambiguous demonstrations can make a point predictor average incompatible actions, while feedback can carry even an accurate predictor into states missing from its training data. The decoder derivations address the first problem; the coupling bound and DAgger address the second.


When human demonstrators steer left around a central pillar half the time (\(\ContinuousActionVector = +1.0\)) and right the other half (\(\ContinuousActionVector = -1.0\)), a policy trained with mean squared error averages the two commands to \(\ContinuousActionVector = 0.0\) and drives dead center into the pillar. To see why squared-error regression produces that collision, consider an imitation learning objective minimizing mean squared error (\(\ell_2\) loss) over demonstration distribution \(\DemonstrationDataset\): \[ \min_\pi \mathbb{E}_{(\MultimodalObservation, \ContinuousActionVector) \sim \DemonstrationDataset} \left[ \| \ContinuousActionVector - \pi(\MultimodalObservation) \|_2^2 \right] \] By the law of total expectation, decomposing the error around the conditional mean \(\mathbb{E}[\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation]\) yields an orthogonal variance decomposition: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}_{\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation} \left[ \| \ContinuousActionVector - \pi(\MultimodalObservation) \|_2^2 \mid \MultimodalObservation \right] &= \mathbb{E}_{\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation} \left[ \| (\ContinuousActionVector - \mathbb{E}[\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation]) + (\mathbb{E}[\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation] - \pi(\MultimodalObservation)) \|_2^2 \mid \MultimodalObservation \right] \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation} \left[ \| \ContinuousActionVector - \mathbb{E}[\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation] \|_2^2 \mid \MultimodalObservation \right] + \| \mathbb{E}[\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation] - \pi(\MultimodalObservation) \|_2^2 \\
&\quad + 2 \left\langle \mathbb{E}_{\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation}[\ContinuousActionVector - \mathbb{E}[\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation] \mid \MultimodalObservation], \, \mathbb{E}[\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation] - \pi(\MultimodalObservation) \right\rangle
\end{aligned}
\] Because \(\mathbb{E}_{\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation}[\ContinuousActionVector - \mathbb{E}[\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation] \mid \MultimodalObservation] = \ZeroVector\), the cross-term vanishes identically, leaving: \[ \mathbb{E}_{(\MultimodalObservation, \ContinuousActionVector) \sim \DemonstrationDataset} \left[ \| \ContinuousActionVector - \pi(\MultimodalObservation) \|_2^2 \right] = \mathbb{E}_{\MultimodalObservation} \left[ \operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Cov}(\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation)) \right] + \mathbb{E}_{\MultimodalObservation} \left[ \| \mathbb{E}[\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation] - \pi(\MultimodalObservation) \|_2^2 \right] \] The first term is the irreducible conditional variance of demonstrator behavior. The second term is non-negative and strictly minimized if and only if the policy evaluates to the conditional expectation: \[ \pi^*(\MultimodalObservation) = \mathbb{E}[\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation] = \int_{\ActionSpace} \ContinuousActionVector\, \DemonstrationActionDistribution(\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation) \, d\ContinuousActionVector \] In digital machine learning tasks (such as computer vision regression), predicting the conditional expectation over ambiguous targets produces a blurry reconstruction, a soft pixel average that remains safely confined to software memory. In physical AI systems, commanded actions cross the causal boundary into continuous Euclidean space governed by non-convex obstacles, joint limits, and irreversible contact dynamics.
Demonstrator behavior in physical manipulation and navigation is inherently multimodal:

Dodging an obstacle: an expert steers left (\(\ContinuousActionVector = +1.0\)) or right (\(\ContinuousActionVector = -1.0\)) around a central pillar with equal probability \(\Pr(\ContinuousActionVector = +1 \mid \MultimodalObservation) = \Pr(\ContinuousActionVector = -1 \mid \MultimodalObservation) = 0.5\).
Symmetrical manipulation: an end effector approaches a cylindrical object from azimuth \(\AzimuthAngle = 0^\circ\) or \(\AzimuthAngle = 180^\circ\).
Assembly routing: threading a flexible cable clockwise or counter-clockwise around a structural fastener.

Because demonstration density \(\DemonstrationActionDistribution(\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation)\) is supported on disjoint, disconnected modes separated by an obstacle, the conditional expectation computes the arithmetic mean: \[ \pi^*(\MultimodalObservation) = 0.5(+1.0) + 0.5(-1.0) = 0.0 \] This mean action lies in a region of zero demonstration probability (\(\Pr(\ContinuousActionVector = 0.0 \mid \MultimodalObservation) = 0\)). In the physical workspace, the coordinate \(\ContinuousActionVector = 0.0\) corresponds precisely to the geometric position of the central obstacle. Commanding \(\pi^*(\MultimodalObservation) = 0.0\) instructs the steering actuator to hold dead center at full cruising speed, driving the physical robot directly into the pillar. In physical autonomy, regression mode averaging does not produce a cosmetic blur; it can propose a collision unless the permission path rejects it.


A probabilistic decoder can avoid mode averaging by parameterizing the conditional action distribution \(\DemonstrationActionDistribution(\ContinuousActionVector \mid \MultimodalObservation)\) rather than its expectation. The families below trade inference cost against distributional expressiveness; none of them supplies recovery states that the demonstrations lack. Policy Training Regimes compares them by the network evaluations each chunk costs, which is where the choice reaches the control deadline.

Deterministic direct regression (MLP). A feedforward network trained with squared error predicts one action per observation and, with sufficient capacity and ideal optimization, fits the conditional mean. The restriction comes from the point-output objective, not from MLPs as a network family; an MLP can also parameterize a mixture or stochastic policy. One evaluation avoids iterative sampling cost but does not resolve ambiguous demonstrations.
Mixture density networks. A Gaussian mixture head predicts nonnegative weights summing to one, means, and positive-definite covariances: \[ \pi(\ContinuousActionVector\mid \MultimodalObservation)=\sum_{\MixtureComponentIndex=1}^\MixtureComponentCount \MixtureComponentWeight(\MultimodalObservation)\,\GaussianDistribution(\ContinuousActionVector;\MixtureComponentMean(\MultimodalObservation),\MixtureComponentCovariance(\MultimodalObservation)). \] Sampling a component or selecting a mode preserves alternatives in one network evaluation. Computing the mixture mean would restore the original averaging problem. Covariance regularization and component coverage matter because likelihood optimization can collapse a component onto a few observations.
Implicit behavioral cloning. Implicit behavioral cloning (IBC) (Florence et al. 2022) learns an energy-based model \(\ImplicitPolicyEnergyFunction(\MultimodalObservation, \ContinuousActionVector) \in \mathbb{R}\), trained with contrastive or InfoNCE objectives to assign low energy to demonstrated state-action pairs and high energy to counterfactual actions. Inference solves \[ \ContinuousActionVector^* = \arg\min_{\ContinuousActionVector} \ImplicitPolicyEnergyFunction(\MultimodalObservation, \ContinuousActionVector) \] An energy function can have several separated minima, and selecting its minimizing action can change discontinuously even when the energy network is continuous. Inference requires iterative derivative-free or gradient-based optimization whose latency and convergence depend on sample counts and accelerator parallelism, with risks of settling into suboptimal local energy minima.
Conditional diffusion and flow matching. Diffusion Policy (Chi et al. 2025) and flow-matching decoders generate entire action trajectory chunks via iterative denoising or ordinary differential equation (ODE) integration. Their training targets injected noise vectors or continuous velocity fields conditioned on corrupted states, observations, and timesteps rather than clean actions, allowing multimodal sampling instead of directly regressing a clean action mean. Approximation error and the sampling procedure still affect whether distinct modes survive. Section 1.5.2 derives both objectives and prices their sampling steps.
Latent-variable chunking. Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) (Zhao et al. 2023) predicts an action trajectory chunk \(\ActionChunk_t = (\ContinuousActionVector_{t}, \ContinuousActionVector_{t+1}, \dots, \ContinuousActionVector_{t+\ActionChunkHorizon-1}) \in \mathbb{R}^{\ActionChunkHorizon \times \ActionDimension}\) from observation \(\MultimodalObservation_{t}\) using a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE). The true objective is to maximize the conditional log-marginal likelihood of demonstrated chunks across dataset \(\DemonstrationDataset\): \[ \ln \GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\ActionChunk_t \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}) = \ln \int_{\LatentVariableSpace} \GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\ActionChunk_t, \LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}) \, \DerivativeOperator\LatentStyleVariable \] Because this marginalization is intractable, ACT introduces a variational posterior \(\CvaeRecognitionEncoder(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t)\) parameterized by a transformer encoder. Expanding the identity with \(\GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\ActionChunk_t, \LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}) = \GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\ActionChunk_t \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \LatentStyleVariable) \GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\LatentStyleVariable)\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\ln \GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\ActionChunk_t \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}) &= \int_{\LatentVariableSpace} \CvaeRecognitionEncoder(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t) \ln \GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\ActionChunk_t \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}) \, \DerivativeOperator\LatentStyleVariable \\
&= \int_{\LatentVariableSpace} \CvaeRecognitionEncoder(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t) \ln \left( \frac{\GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\ActionChunk_t, \LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t})}{\CvaeRecognitionEncoder(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t)} \cdot \frac{\CvaeRecognitionEncoder(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t)}{\GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t)} \right) \DerivativeOperator\LatentStyleVariable \\
&= \int_{\LatentVariableSpace} \CvaeRecognitionEncoder(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t) \ln \frac{\GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\ActionChunk_t, \LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t})}{\CvaeRecognitionEncoder(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t)} \, \DerivativeOperator\LatentStyleVariable + \int_{\LatentVariableSpace} \CvaeRecognitionEncoder(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t) \ln \frac{\CvaeRecognitionEncoder(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t)}{\GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t)} \, \DerivativeOperator\LatentStyleVariable \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{\LatentStyleVariable \sim \CvaeRecognitionEncoder(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t)} \left[ \ln \frac{\GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\ActionChunk_t \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \LatentStyleVariable) \GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\LatentStyleVariable)}{\CvaeRecognitionEncoder(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t)} \right] + \KlDivergence\left( \CvaeRecognitionEncoder(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t) \,\parallel\, \GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t) \right) \\
&\ge \mathbb{E}_{\LatentStyleVariable \sim \CvaeRecognitionEncoder(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t)} \left[ \ln \GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\ActionChunk_t \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \LatentStyleVariable) \right] - \KlDivergence\left( \CvaeRecognitionEncoder(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t) \,\parallel\, \GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\LatentStyleVariable) \right) \equiv \EvidenceLowerBound(\ModelParameters, \CvaeEncoderParameters)
\end{aligned}
\] Assuming standard isotropic Gaussian prior \(\GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\LatentStyleVariable) = \GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \IdentityMatrix)\) and diagonal Gaussian variational posterior \(\CvaeRecognitionEncoder(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t) = \GaussianDistribution(\LatentPosteriorMean, \operatorname{diag}(\LatentPosteriorStandardDeviation^2))\), the Kullback-Leibler divergence evaluates in closed form: \[ \KlDivergence\left( \CvaeRecognitionEncoder(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t) \,\parallel\, \GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \IdentityMatrix) \right) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{j=1}^{\LatentDimension} \left( \LatentComponentStandardDeviation^2 + \LatentComponentMean^2 - 1 - \ln(\LatentComponentStandardDeviation^2) \right) \] Sampling directly as \(\LatentStyleVariable \sim \CvaeRecognitionEncoder\) is a stochastic operation that prevents backpropagation because the node has no analytical derivatives with respect to encoder parameters \(\CvaeEncoderParameters\). ACT resolves this via the reparameterization trick: isolating stochasticity into parameter-free standard normal noise \(\ReparameterizationNoise \sim \GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \IdentityMatrix)\): \[ \LatentStyleVariable = \LatentPosteriorMean(\MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t) + \LatentPosteriorStandardDeviation(\MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t) \odot \ReparameterizationNoise, \quad \text{yielding } \frac{\partial \LatentStyleVariable}{\partial \LatentPosteriorMean} = \IdentityMatrix, \quad \frac{\partial \LatentStyleVariable}{\partial \LatentPosteriorStandardDeviation} = \operatorname{diag}(\ReparameterizationNoise) \] To parameterize the reconstruction likelihood, ACT models \(\GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\ActionChunk_t \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \LatentStyleVariable)\) as an isotropic Laplace distribution: \[ \GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\ActionChunk_t \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \LatentStyleVariable) = \frac{1}{(2\LaplaceLikelihoodScale)^{\ActionChunkHorizon \ActionDimension}} \exp\left( -\frac{\|\ActionChunk_t - \Policy(\MultimodalObservation_{t}, \LatentStyleVariable)\|_1}{\LaplaceLikelihoodScale} \right) \] Maximizing the log-likelihood is equivalent to minimizing the \(\ell_1\) norm \(\|\ActionChunk_t - \Policy(\MultimodalObservation_{t}, \LatentStyleVariable)\|_1\). Away from zero residual, \(\ell_1\) loss gives constant-magnitude gradients with respect to each predicted action component, whereas \(\ell_2\) loss gives greater influence to large residuals. Neither loss alone filters demonstrator tremor or guarantees freedom from overfitting; those outcomes depend on the data, regularization, and temporal model. Weighting the KL regularizer by hyperparameter \(\LatentKlWeight > 0\) yields the full training loss: \[ \ActVariationalObjective(\ModelParameters, \CvaeEncoderParameters) = \mathbb{E}_{(\MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t) \sim \DemonstrationDataset, \ReparameterizationNoise \sim \GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \IdentityMatrix)} \left[ \|\ActionChunk_t - \Policy(\MultimodalObservation_{t}, \LatentPosteriorMean + \LatentPosteriorStandardDeviation \odot \ReparameterizationNoise)\|_1 + \LatentKlWeight \KlDivergence\left( \CvaeRecognitionEncoder(\LatentStyleVariable \mid \MultimodalObservation_{t}, \ActionChunk_t) \,\parallel\, \GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \IdentityMatrix) \right) \right] \]
The latent variable \(\LatentStyleVariable \in \mathbb{R}^{\LatentDimension}\) can encode variation among demonstrations, while the decoder predicts all \(\ActionChunkHorizon\) actions together. Neither separated latent clusters nor kinematic smoothness follows from the architecture alone. Executing \(\ChunkExecutionHorizon\) actions before replanning reduces policy interventions, but increases the time before new observations can alter the proposal. Substituting \(\BehaviorCloningHorizon/\ActionChunkHorizon\) into the single-step compounding bound is not justified without new chunk-level error and cost assumptions.
At test time the variational encoder, which requires the future demonstration chunk, is discarded. Setting \(\LatentStyleVariable=\ZeroVector\) evaluates the decoder at the prior mean in one forward pass. That latent point is not guaranteed to select the most probable demonstrated mode. Sampling the prior can expose additional modes but also poorly trained latent regions. ACT combines overlapping chunk predictions through temporal ensembling; for example, an exponentially recency-weighted convention is: \[ \ContinuousActionVector_{t} = \frac{\sum_{i=0}^{\min(\ControlStepIndex,\ActionChunkHorizon-1)} \TemporalEnsemblingWeight\,\ActionChunk_{t-i}[\ChunkStepIndex]}{\sum_{i=0}^{\min(\ControlStepIndex,\ActionChunkHorizon-1)}\TemporalEnsemblingWeight}, \] Each weight \(\TemporalEnsemblingWeight\) decays exponentially with the offset \(\ChunkStepIndex\), so this convention favors recent predictions. Averaging incompatible chunks can still create an invalid action; the admitted command must satisfy current limits.
Discrete action tokens. Vision-language-action models such as RT-1, RT-2, and OpenVLA (Brohan, Brown, Carbajal, Chebotar, Dabis, et al. 2023; Brohan, Brown, Carbajal, Chebotar, Chen, et al. 2023; Kim et al. 2024) discretize continuous action dimensions into \(\ActionBinCount\) uniform bins (commonly 256) and emit categorical tokens: \[ \text{bin}(\ContinuousActionComponent_k) = \min\!\left(\ActionBinCount-1,\left\lfloor \ActionBinCount\frac{\ContinuousActionComponent_k-\ActionRangeMinimum}{\ActionRangeMaximum-\ActionRangeMinimum}\right\rfloor\right) \] For an action clipped to the declared range, this assigns one of \(\ActionBinCount\) equal-width bins, including the upper endpoint. Decoding to bin centers gives maximum scalar quantization error \((\ActionRangeMaximum-\ActionRangeMinimum)/(2\ActionBinCount)\). Categorical sampling or mode selection preserves alternatives; taking their mean reintroduces averaging. A decoder that emits one token per action dimension autoregressively needs \(\ActionDimension\) sequential predictions, although other tokenizations and parallel heads have different costs.

Sampling one distinct trajectory around an obstacle avoids the collision caused by averaging two paths, but running 16 sequential denoising passes through a 48-million-parameter U-Net takes \(40.4\text{ ms}\) and overruns a \(25\text{ ms}\) synchronous setpoint deadline. Continuous trajectory diffusion treats policy synthesis as generative denoising over continuous multi-step action trajectory chunks \(\ActionChunk \in \mathbb{R}^{\ActionChunkHorizon \times \ActionDimension}\) conditioned on visual and proprioceptive observation histories \(\ObservationHistory\) (Chi et al. 2025). Here \(\ActionChunkHorizon\) counts physical action steps, \(\ActionDimension\) counts action dimensions, and the later \(\DecoderEvaluationCount\) counts inference evaluations; diffusion time is not physical execution time. Rather than predicting an unconstrained point estimate via mean squared error, diffusion models represent complex multimodal action distributions without collapsing into mode averaging.
The closed-loop visuomotor diffusion pipeline has three coordinated architectural columns (figure 5). The left observation column encodes visual camera streams and proprioceptive joint history into a conditioning vector. The center denoising column applies a noise network across \(\DecoderEvaluationCount\) sequential reverse-diffusion steps to refine Gaussian noise into a candidate action chunk. The right dispatch column extracts an execution prefix from the prediction horizon and routes those candidate actions across the proposal boundary into the \(1\text{ kHz}\) permission path. It also discards the unexecuted tail before re-planning. The noise-prediction backbone \(\NoisePredictionNetwork\) is typically implemented using either a 1D Temporal Convolutional (Conv1D) U-Net or a Diffusion Transformer (DiT):

1D temporal convolutional U-Net: Convolutions across the action horizon reuse filters at many positions. Feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) supplies observation and diffusion-step conditioning. Layer widths, intermediate tensors, and accelerator tiling determine whether activations stay on chip.
Diffusion transformer (DiT): Attention connects action tokens and visual conditioning. The action horizon and conditioning length determine attention work, while kernel fusion determines how much intermediate storage reaches DRAM. Neither backbone implies a fixed parameter count or per-step latency; the worked budget below declares one illustrative configuration.







Figure 5: Diffusion policy architecture: A continuous trajectory diffusion policy for visuomotor control, denoising a candidate action chunk from Gaussian noise across \(\DecoderEvaluationCount\) iterations and dispatching only a prefix of it before re-planning. Asynchronous buffering and an independent high-rate permission path can separate slower chunk generation from actuation. Conditional denoising can represent alternative demonstrated paths without taking their direct-regression mean. (Adapted from Chi et al. (2025)).





The forward diffusion process progressively corrupts a ground-truth demonstrated action chunk \(\ActionChunk^0 \sim \DemonstrationChunkDistribution(\ActionChunk)\) with Gaussian noise across \(\DiffusionStepCount\) discrete timesteps (or continuous diffusion time \(\DiffusionTimeCoordinate \in [0, 1]\)): \[ \ForwardDiffusionDistribution(\NoisedActionChunk \mid \ActionChunk^{k-1}) = \GaussianDistribution\left(\NoisedActionChunk; \sqrt{1 - \DiffusionNoiseVariance_k} \ActionChunk^{k-1}, \DiffusionNoiseVariance_k \IdentityMatrix\right) \] where \(\{\DiffusionNoiseVariance_k \in (0, 1)\}_{k=1}^\DiffusionStepCount\) denotes a predefined variance schedule. Defining \(\DiffusionStepRetention_k = 1 - \DiffusionNoiseVariance_k\), the one-step transition evaluates to: \[ \NoisedActionChunk = \sqrt{\DiffusionStepRetention_k} \ActionChunk^{k-1} + \sqrt{1 - \DiffusionStepRetention_k} \DiffusionGaussianNoise_{k-1}, \quad \DiffusionGaussianNoise_{k-1} \sim \GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \IdentityMatrix) \] Unrolling this recursion for \(\DiffusionStepIndex = 2\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\ActionChunk^2 &= \sqrt{\DiffusionStepRetention_2} \left( \sqrt{\DiffusionStepRetention_1} \ActionChunk^0 + \sqrt{1 - \DiffusionStepRetention_1} \DiffusionGaussianNoise_0 \right) + \sqrt{1 - \DiffusionStepRetention_2} \DiffusionGaussianNoise_1 \\
&= \sqrt{\DiffusionStepRetention_2 \DiffusionStepRetention_1} \ActionChunk^0 + \sqrt{\DiffusionStepRetention_2(1 - \DiffusionStepRetention_1)} \DiffusionGaussianNoise_0 + \sqrt{1 - \DiffusionStepRetention_2} \DiffusionGaussianNoise_1
\end{aligned}
\] Because the linear combination of two independent zero-mean Gaussian random variables \(\GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \FirstSummandStandardDeviation^2 \IdentityMatrix)\) and \(\GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \SecondSummandStandardDeviation^2 \IdentityMatrix)\) is itself a Gaussian with variance \((\FirstSummandStandardDeviation^2 + \SecondSummandStandardDeviation^2)\IdentityMatrix\), the combined variance of the noise terms simplifies algebraically: \[ \DiffusionStepRetention_2(1 - \DiffusionStepRetention_1) + (1 - \DiffusionStepRetention_2) = \DiffusionStepRetention_2 - \DiffusionStepRetention_1 \DiffusionStepRetention_2 + 1 - \DiffusionStepRetention_2 = 1 - \DiffusionStepRetention_1 \DiffusionStepRetention_2 \] Defining the cumulative variance product \(\DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k} = \prod_{\CumulativeScheduleStepIndex=1}^\DiffusionStepIndex \DiffusionStepRetention_{\CumulativeScheduleStepIndex}\), mathematical induction establishes the closed-form marginal distribution at any arbitrary diffusion step \(\DiffusionStepIndex\) directly from clean action chunk \(\ActionChunk^0\): \[ \ForwardDiffusionDistribution(\NoisedActionChunk \mid \ActionChunk^0) = \GaussianDistribution\left(\NoisedActionChunk; \sqrt{\DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}} \ActionChunk^0, (1 - \DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}) \IdentityMatrix\right) \] allowing immediate sampling of noisy trajectories during training without simulating intermediate Markov chain transitions: \[ \NoisedActionChunk = \sqrt{\DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}} \ActionChunk^0 + \sqrt{1 - \DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}} \DiffusionGaussianNoise, \quad \DiffusionGaussianNoise \sim \GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \IdentityMatrix) \]



The generative reverse process synthesizes an action trajectory from pure Gaussian noise \(\PureNoiseActionChunk \sim \GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \IdentityMatrix)\) by parameterizing the conditional reverse transition distribution \(\GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\ActionChunk^{k-1} \mid \NoisedActionChunk, \ObservationHistory)\): \[ \GenerativeActionModelDistribution(\ActionChunk^{k-1} \mid \NoisedActionChunk, \ObservationHistory) = \GaussianDistribution\left(\ActionChunk^{k-1}; \ReverseTransitionMean(\NoisedActionChunk, \ObservationHistory, \DiffusionStepIndex), \ReverseTransitionCovariance_k\right) \] By Bayes’ rule, the true reverse posterior conditioned on the clean trajectory \(\ActionChunk^0\) is tractable and Gaussian: \(\ForwardDiffusionDistribution(\ActionChunk^{k-1} \mid \NoisedActionChunk, \ActionChunk^0) = \GaussianDistribution(\ActionChunk^{k-1}; \ForwardPosteriorMean_k(\NoisedActionChunk, \ActionChunk^0), \ForwardPosteriorVariance_k \IdentityMatrix)\), where: \[ \ForwardPosteriorMean_k(\NoisedActionChunk, \ActionChunk^0) = \frac{\sqrt{\DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k-1}} \DiffusionNoiseVariance_k}{1 - \DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}} \ActionChunk^0 + \frac{\sqrt{\DiffusionStepRetention_k}(1 - \DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k-1})}{1 - \DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}} \NoisedActionChunk \] Because \(\ActionChunk^0\) is unobserved at test time, the reverse process substitutes an estimate of \(\ActionChunk^0\) derived from Tweedie’s formula. For any Gaussian perturbation \(\PerturbedSignalVector \sim \GaussianDistribution(\PerturbedSignalVector_0, \PerturbationNoiseStandardDeviation^2 \IdentityMatrix)\) with prior density \(\ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector_0)\), the conditional observation density is: \[ \ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector \mid \PerturbedSignalVector_0) = \frac{1}{(2\pi \PerturbationNoiseStandardDeviation^2)^{\PerturbedSignalDimension/2}} \exp\left( -\frac{\|\PerturbedSignalVector - \PerturbedSignalVector_0\|^2}{2\PerturbationNoiseStandardDeviation^2} \right) \] Differentiating with respect to the noisy measurement \(\PerturbedSignalVector\): \[ \nabla_{\PerturbedSignalVector} \ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector \mid \PerturbedSignalVector_0) = -\frac{\PerturbedSignalVector - \PerturbedSignalVector_0}{\PerturbationNoiseStandardDeviation^2} \ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector \mid \PerturbedSignalVector_0) \] The marginal density of noisy observations evaluates to \(\ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^\PerturbedSignalDimension} \ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector \mid \PerturbedSignalVector_0) \ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector_0) \, \DerivativeOperator\PerturbedSignalVector_0\). Differentiating under the integral sign: \[ \nabla_{\PerturbedSignalVector} \ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^\PerturbedSignalDimension} \nabla_{\PerturbedSignalVector} \ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector \mid \PerturbedSignalVector_0) \ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector_0) \, \DerivativeOperator\PerturbedSignalVector_0 = -\frac{1}{\PerturbationNoiseStandardDeviation^2} \int_{\mathbb{R}^\PerturbedSignalDimension} (\PerturbedSignalVector - \PerturbedSignalVector_0) \ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector \mid \PerturbedSignalVector_0) \ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector_0) \, \DerivativeOperator\PerturbedSignalVector_0 \] Dividing both sides by the marginal density \(\ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector)\): \[ \frac{\nabla_{\PerturbedSignalVector} \ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector)}{\ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector)} = \nabla_{\PerturbedSignalVector} \ln \ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector) = -\frac{1}{\PerturbationNoiseStandardDeviation^2} \left( \PerturbedSignalVector - \int_{\mathbb{R}^\PerturbedSignalDimension} \PerturbedSignalVector_0 \frac{\ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector \mid \PerturbedSignalVector_0) \ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector_0)}{\ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector)} \, \DerivativeOperator\PerturbedSignalVector_0 \right) = -\frac{\PerturbedSignalVector - \mathbb{E}[\PerturbedSignalVector_0 \mid \PerturbedSignalVector]}{\PerturbationNoiseStandardDeviation^2} \] Multiplying by \(\PerturbationNoiseStandardDeviation^2\) and isolating \(\mathbb{E}[\PerturbedSignalVector_0 \mid \PerturbedSignalVector]\) proves Tweedie’s formula: \[ \mathbb{E}[\PerturbedSignalVector_0 \mid \PerturbedSignalVector] = \PerturbedSignalVector + \PerturbationNoiseStandardDeviation^2 \nabla_{\PerturbedSignalVector} \ln \ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector) \] Tweedie’s formula reveals that the Bayes-optimal reconstruction of clean state \(\PerturbedSignalVector_0\) equals the corrupted measurement \(\PerturbedSignalVector\) shifted along the marginal Stein score \(\nabla_{\PerturbedSignalVector} \ln \ProbabilityFunction(\PerturbedSignalVector)\) scaled by noise variance \(\PerturbationNoiseStandardDeviation^2\). Rewriting the forward diffusion marginal \(\NoisedActionChunk = \sqrt{\DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}} \ActionChunk^0 + \sqrt{1 - \DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}} \DiffusionGaussianNoise\) as \(\frac{\NoisedActionChunk}{\sqrt{\DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}}} = \ActionChunk^0 + \frac{\sqrt{1 - \DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}}}{\sqrt{\DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}}} \DiffusionGaussianNoise\), the effective noise variance is \(\PerturbationNoiseStandardDeviation^2 = \frac{1 - \DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}}{\DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}}\). At the population optimum of the noise-prediction objective, Tweedie’s formula equates the estimated clean trajectory \(\EstimatedCleanActionChunk^0\) and the Stein score \(\nabla_{\NoisedActionChunk} \ln \ProbabilityFunction(\NoisedActionChunk \mid \ObservationHistory)\): \[ \nabla_{\NoisedActionChunk} \ln \ProbabilityFunction(\NoisedActionChunk \mid \ObservationHistory) = -\frac{\NoisePredictionNetwork(\NoisedActionChunk, \ObservationHistory, \DiffusionStepIndex)}{\sqrt{1 - \DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}}} \] Substituting \(\EstimatedCleanActionChunk^0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}}} \left( \NoisedActionChunk - \sqrt{1 - \DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}} \NoisePredictionNetwork(\NoisedActionChunk, \ObservationHistory, \DiffusionStepIndex) \right)\) into the posterior mean \(\ForwardPosteriorMean_k\) reparameterizes the reverse transition mean: \[ \ReverseTransitionMean(\NoisedActionChunk, \ObservationHistory, \DiffusionStepIndex) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\DiffusionStepRetention_k}} \left( \NoisedActionChunk - \frac{\DiffusionNoiseVariance_k}{\sqrt{1 - \DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}}} \NoisePredictionNetwork(\NoisedActionChunk, \ObservationHistory, \DiffusionStepIndex) \right) \] The noise-prediction network \(\NoisePredictionNetwork\) is optimized via the simplified \(\ell_2\) denoising score-matching objective: \[ \DiffusionMatchingLoss(\ModelParameters) = \mathbb{E}_{k \sim \UniformDistribution\{1, \DiffusionStepCount\}, \DiffusionGaussianNoise \sim \GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \IdentityMatrix), (\ObservationHistory, \ActionChunk^0) \sim \DemonstrationDataset} \left[ \left\| \DiffusionGaussianNoise - \NoisePredictionNetwork\left(\sqrt{\DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}}\ActionChunk^0 + \sqrt{1 - \DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}}\DiffusionGaussianNoise, \ObservationHistory, \DiffusionStepIndex\right) \right\|^2 \right] \] By following the score function \(\nabla_{\NoisedActionChunk} \ln \ProbabilityFunction(\NoisedActionChunk \mid \ObservationHistory)\), reverse diffusion steers stochastic sampling toward high-density demonstration modes rather than averaging incompatible modes into an obstacle collision. Each denoising step commits further to a single mode of the conditional action distribution.



While standard diffusion models formulate generation as reverse stochastic differential equations (SDEs), continuous flow matching (Lipman et al. 2022) generates trajectories along deterministic probability flows defined by ordinary differential equations (ODEs): \[ \frac{\DerivativeOperator\FlowSampleVector_t}{d\FlowTimeCoordinate} = \LearnedVelocityField(\FlowSampleVector_t, \FlowTimeCoordinate, \ObservationHistory) \] The continuous vector field \(\LearnedVelocityField\) drives a source noise distribution \(\FlowProbabilityPath_0(\FlowSampleVector) = \GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \IdentityMatrix)\) to the empirical demonstration target distribution \(\FlowProbabilityPath_1(\FlowSampleVector) = \DemonstrationChunkDistribution(\FlowSampleVector)\) across continuous time \(\FlowTimeCoordinate \in [0, 1]\), governed by the continuity equation: \[ \frac{\partial \FlowProbabilityPath_t(\FlowSampleVector)}{\partial \FlowTimeCoordinate} + \nabla \cdot \left( \FlowProbabilityPath_t(\FlowSampleVector) \MarginalVelocityField_t(\FlowSampleVector) \right) = 0 \] For a straight conditional interpolation path, the continuous trajectory interpolates linearly between source noise \(\FlowSampleVector_0 \sim \GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \IdentityMatrix)\) and demonstration chunk \(\FlowSampleVector_1 \sim \DemonstrationDataset\): \[ \ConditionalFlowMap_t(\FlowSampleVector_0) = (1 - \FlowTimeCoordinate) \FlowSampleVector_0 + \FlowTimeCoordinate \FlowSampleVector_1, \quad \FlowTimeCoordinate \in [0, 1] \] The conditional velocity along each paired-sample path is constant across time: \[ \ConditionalVelocityField_t(\FlowSampleVector \mid \FlowSampleVector_1) = \frac{\DerivativeOperator}{d\FlowTimeCoordinate} \ConditionalFlowMap_t(\FlowSampleVector_0) = \FlowSampleVector_1 - \FlowSampleVector_0 \] and the trajectory acceleration vanishes identically: \(\frac{\DerivativeOperator^2}{d\FlowTimeCoordinate^2} \ConditionalFlowMap_t(\FlowSampleVector_0) = \ZeroVector\). The Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) theorem (Lipman et al. 2022) proves a gradient identity. Regressing the neural vector field \(\LearnedVelocityField\) against this conditional vector field over paired samples \((\FlowSampleVector_0, \FlowSampleVector_1)\) gives the same gradients as regressing it against the intractable marginal velocity field \(\MarginalVelocityField_t(\FlowSampleVector)\): \[ \nabla_\ModelParameters \mathbb{E}_{t, \FlowSampleVector_0, \FlowSampleVector_1} \left[ \| \LearnedVelocityField(\ConditionalFlowMap_t(\FlowSampleVector_0), \FlowTimeCoordinate, \ObservationHistory) - (\FlowSampleVector_1 - \FlowSampleVector_0) \|^2 \right] = \nabla_\ModelParameters \mathbb{E}_{t, \FlowSampleVector \sim \FlowProbabilityPath_t} \left[ \| \LearnedVelocityField(\FlowSampleVector, \FlowTimeCoordinate, \ObservationHistory) - \MarginalVelocityField_t(\FlowSampleVector) \|^2 \right] \] The network is therefore trained via direct mean squared regression: \[ \FlowMatchingLoss(\ModelParameters) = \mathbb{E}_{t \sim \UniformDistribution[0, 1], \FlowSampleVector_0 \sim \GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \IdentityMatrix), \FlowSampleVector_1 \sim \DemonstrationDataset} \left[ \left\| \LearnedVelocityField\left((1 - \FlowTimeCoordinate)\FlowSampleVector_0 + \FlowTimeCoordinate\FlowSampleVector_1, \FlowTimeCoordinate, \ObservationHistory\right) - (\FlowSampleVector_1 - \FlowSampleVector_0) \right\|^2 \right] \] The conditional paths above are straight for each sampled pair, but the learned marginal velocity averages over pairs that reach the same intermediate point. Its integrated trajectories need not remain straight, and their numerical error need not vanish. Independent noise/data pairing also does not establish globally optimal transport. Flow matching can support fewer evaluations in a measured task, but the step count must satisfy an action-quality criterion; it is not a universal consequence of the interpolation formula.

In continuous generative policies, the number of reverse evaluation steps \(\DecoderEvaluationCount\) is the governing systems lever trading off policy expressiveness at the physical plant against computational latency on accelerator hardware. The reverse trajectory discretizes a continuous probability flow ODE or reverse SDE. Discretizing this path across \(\DecoderEvaluationCount\) finite steps introduces numerical integration errors:

Sampling accuracy: Reducing the number of evaluations increases numerical approximation error for a fixed solver and learned field. How that error changes multimodal coverage, collision rate, or setpoint smoothness depends on the learned distribution and solver. The architecture alone supplies no minimum acceptable step count.
Computational latency and roofline limits: Reverse diffusion is an inherently sequential Markov chain: evaluation \(\DiffusionStepIndex-1\) requires the tensor output of evaluation \(\DiffusionStepIndex\). Denoising steps cannot be parallelized across the time dimension on GPU or NPU accelerators. Total chunk generation latency scales linearly with \(\DecoderEvaluationCount\):5 \[ \ProposerInferenceTime = \VisualEncodingTime + \DecoderEvaluationCount \cdot \DecoderPassTime \] where \(\VisualEncodingTime\) is the one-time visual feature extraction latency per chunk and \(\DecoderPassTime\) is the forward execution time of noise-prediction network \(\NoisePredictionNetwork\). A weight-transfer lower bound is \(\ParameterStreamingTime=\WeightMemory/\SustainedMemoryBandwidth\) when every evaluation reloads those weights. The roofline intensity must count all operations and traffic, including convolutional or token reuse and activation spills. Batch size alone does not make every decoder memory bound. The worked budget below evaluates this transfer bound separately from its assumed execution time.

5 Diffusion Denoising Latency Budget: Sequential reverse diffusion cannot parallelize across sampling steps because each input requires the previous step’s output. Total inference time \(\ProposerInferenceTime = \VisualEncodingTime + \DecoderEvaluationCount \DecoderPassTime\) scales linearly with step count \(\DecoderEvaluationCount\), making step reduction or asynchronous chunking essential for real-time actuation.A setpoint producer that must finish synchronously within \(\ControlSetpointPeriod\) misses its contract when \(\ProposerInferenceTime>\ControlSetpointPeriod\). The consequence depends on the controller’s defined hold, interpolation, and fallback behavior; a deadline miss does not inherently imply a torque drop. Physical AI architectures resolve this latency-expressiveness trade-off through three coordinated mechanisms:

Action chunking: The policy predicts a multi-step trajectory chunk \(\ActionChunk \in \mathbb{R}^{\ActionChunkHorizon \times \ActionDimension}\) spanning prediction horizon \(\ActionChunkHorizon\). Executing an execution horizon \(\ChunkExecutionHorizon \le \ActionChunkHorizon\) amortizes the \(\DecoderEvaluationCount\)-step generation latency over \(\ChunkExecutionHorizon \ControlSetpointPeriod\) of physical robot motion.
Fewer solver evaluations: Flow matching, improved solvers, or distillation can reduce sequential evaluations when validation shows that the resulting action quality remains adequate. Reduced compute buys timing slack at the cost of a new approximation and validation obligation.
Dual-rate asynchronous decoupling: The application processor runs the generative denoising loop asynchronously at a relaxed rate (\(10\text{--}20\text{ Hz}\)), sending each action chunk across the proposal boundary over a black-channel link that carries a checksum and sequence number. A discrete safety microcontroller, which shares no memory with the application processor, receives the chunk into its own double buffer and executes synchronously at \(1\text{ kHz}\). It interpolates spline knots, enforces slew-rate limits, and gates commands through deterministic control barrier functions (The Machine in Five Levels).

The numerical execution of this dual-rate pipeline spans both processors (algorithm 2), and its geometry, denoising trajectory, and hardware split appear across the three panels of figure 6. Panel (a) demonstrates multimodal action selection. It contrasts direct MSE regression, which averages divergent paths into an obstacle collision, against conditional diffusion, which samples distinct valid trajectory modes. Panel (b) traces the reverse-diffusion denoising sequence from isotropic Gaussian noise \(\ActionChunk^{\DecoderEvaluationCount}\) to a coherent action chunk \(\ActionChunk^0\). Panel (c) shows the asynchronous dual-rate hardware split, where the application processor streams candidate chunks over a black-channel serial link to a discrete \(1\text{ kHz}\) safety microcontroller running double-buffering, freshness checks, and spline interpolation. Policy Training Regimes uses the timing budget below to evaluate which sampler fits the control deadline. The pseudocode assumes the microcontroller’s receive path has already validated the proposal’s capture epoch, clock conversion, configuration, validity interval, and handoff continuity. An absent, expired, or rejected chunk selects the defined fallback; spline interpolation and slew clamping alone do not implement that permission decision. The transmitted action must also pass the actuator interface that converts its declared units to drive commands.

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Diffusion Policy Trajectory Chunk Denoising and Dual-Rate Actuation}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require observation history buffer $\mathbf{O}_t = (\MultimodalObservation_{t-\ObservationHistoryLength}, \dots, \MultimodalObservation_{t})$ of length $\ObservationHistoryLength + 1$, noise prediction network $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta$, noise schedule $\{\alpha_k, \DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}, \sigma_k\}_{k=1}^{N_{\text{diff}}}$, chunk horizon $H$, safety microcontroller loop period $\Delta t_{\text{mcu}}$
\Ensure line-rate joint torque setpoint / action vector $\mathbf{a}_t$
\Statex
\State \textbf{Application Processor: Asynchronous Trajectory Chunk Generation ($10\text{--}20\text{ Hz}$)}
\State $\mathbf{E}_t \gets \Call{VisualEncoder}{\mathbf{O}_t}$
\State $\mathbf{A}^{N_{\text{diff}}} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}_{H d_a})$ \Comment{sample a flattened chunk, then reshape to $H \times d_a$}
\For{$k = N_{\text{diff}}$ \textbf{down to} $1$}
    \State $\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} \gets \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{A}^k, \mathbf{E}_t, k)$
    \State $\boldsymbol{\mu}_k \gets \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_k}} \left( \mathbf{A}^k - \frac{1 - \alpha_k}{\sqrt{1 - \DiffusionCumulativeSchedule_{k}}} \hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} \right)$
    \State $\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$ \textbf{if} $k > 1$ \textbf{else} $\mathbf{z} \gets \mathbf{0}$
    \State $\mathbf{A}^{k-1} \gets \boldsymbol{\mu}_k + \sigma_k \mathbf{z}$
\EndFor
\State $\mathbf{A}_{\text{chunk}} \gets \mathbf{A}^0$
\State $\Call{SendOverLink}{\mathbf{A}_{\text{chunk}}}$ \Comment{checksum and sequence number; no shared memory}
\Statex
\State \textbf{Safety Microcontroller: Synchronous Deterministic Actuation ($1\text{ kHz}$)}
\If{$\Call{HasNewChunk}{\text{RxBuffer}}$} \Comment{receive interrupt fills the inactive buffer}
    \State $\Call{UpdateSplineKnots}{\text{RxBuffer}}$
\EndIf
\State $\mathbf{a}_{\text{raw}} \gets \Call{CubicSplineInterpolate}{\mathbf{A}_{\text{chunk}}, t_{\text{current}}}$
\State $\Delta \mathbf{a} \gets \Call{clamp}{\mathbf{a}_{\text{raw}} - \mathbf{a}_{\text{prev}}, -\dot{\mathbf{a}}_{\max} \Delta t_{\text{mcu}}, +\dot{\mathbf{a}}_{\max} \Delta t_{\text{mcu}}}$ \Comment{kinematic slew-rate governor}
\State $\mathbf{a}_{\text{clamped}} \gets \mathbf{a}_{\text{prev}} + \Delta \mathbf{a}$
\State $\mathbf{a}_t \gets \Call{SafetyGovernorClamp}{\mathbf{a}_{\text{clamped}}}$ \Comment{deterministic envelope enforcement}
\State $\Call{TransmitPwmRegisters}{\mathbf{a}_t}$
\State $\mathbf{a}_{\text{prev}} \gets \mathbf{a}_t$
\State \Return $\mathbf{a}_t$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
