A second boundary concerns which layers of the permission path carry formal safety ratings. As Certified safety functions beneath the permission path established, the only rated function within the permission path is the safety MCU’s lease-expiry and heartbeat watchdog, which asserts Safe Torque Off (STO) or Safe Stop 1 (SS1) on the motor drives when valid renewals cease. The admission checks that evaluate neural proposals carry no rating. The certified functions of the motor drives, the safety-rated laser scanner, and the arm’s safety controller sit beneath the permission path. For release, the formal protective claims for every monitored hazard therefore rest on that watchdog and that certified layer. The release argument still uses the software admission checks for operational utility and nominal hazard prevention, but any hazard claim that depends only on unrated software remains an empirical premise rather than a certified safety function.
Statutory compliance reaches physical AI through product-safety law rather than through standalone artificial intelligence rules, and its sharpest consequence for release concerns updates. Under the European Union’s Machinery Regulation (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2023), a substantial modification is any physical or digital change made after deployment that the original manufacturer did not foresee and that introduces a new hazard or raises an existing risk enough to require additional safeguarding. An organization that pushes an unverified over-the-air model update can therefore become, in law, the manufacturer of the modified machine, with every obligation that role carries (section 16.9.1). The same regulation requires third-party conformity assessment4 for machinery whose safety components have fully or partially self-evolving behavior and use machine learning to execute safety functions, so a learned safety function cannot be self-certified. Its essential requirements also constrain learning directly. The limits of each safety function must be documented in the manufacturer’s risk assessment. No rule or parameter the machine generates, even during a learning phase, may change those limits where the change could create a hazardous situation (Annex III, section 1.2.1). Keeping the learned proposer outside the permission path meets that requirement only if the safety argument does not depend on the proposer’s learned behavior. Two neighboring acts reach the same machine. The EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024a), as amended in July 2026 by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2026), places the Machinery Regulation in Section B of its Annex I, so AI-specific safety rules for machines arrive through the machinery framework. The Commission must adopt delegated acts that insert those rules into the Machinery Regulation’s Annex III and that apply by 2 August 2028. Because the robot receives network updates, it is also a product with digital elements under the Cyber Resilience Act (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024b), which requires vulnerability handling and secure updates throughout the manufacturer’s support period, at least five years unless the product is expected to be in use for less. Its duty to report actively exploited vulnerabilities applies from 11 September 2026, ahead of the rest of the act. Table 3 lists the dates from which the other obligations apply. These milestones do not alter the underlying physics or systems engineering; they set the calendar dates by which statutory authorities will demand an inspectable assurance case.
4 Conformity Assessment: The formal procedure through which a manufacturer certifies that a machine fulfills all essential health and safety requirements before affixing the CE marking (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2023). While manufacturers may self-assess conventional machinery, high-risk systems and self-evolving AI safety components require third-party evaluation by a notified body. Because the conformity assessment path is fixed before market entry, every record in the release manifest must be formatted for independent inspection.

The standards map also marks the boundary between statutory obligations and the systems architecture developed in this book. Formal standards prescribe documented arguments, rated protective functions, and independent third-party assessments. The verdicts, signed capability descriptors, and release manifest developed in the rest of this chapter are one engineering architecture for carrying those obligations into the runtime system. The safety case accepted before deployment then stays binding on the machine long after the inspectors have left the floor.

title: Deployment Release
text:
16.4 The Three Verdicts
Treating a release sign-off as an informal paper memo forces teams either to ground a useful machine over an unmeasured corner case or to wave it onto the floor with unproven assumptions. Every row of table 2 ends in an adjudication, and the release decision resolves the entire assertion DAG into one of three verdicts: unconditional operation, conditional operation, or refusal to operate. In this book’s architecture, these verdicts are cryptographically signed capability descriptors loaded into the real-time safety microcontroller before motor power stages are energized, not advisory certificates or administrative paperwork. A valid descriptor is the machine’s operating permit: while it holds, the permission path may admit the policy’s tracking commands inside the envelope the descriptor names, and when it is revoked or absent, the permission path admits none. Although safety standards do not mandate this specific mechanism (section 16.3.4), the qualified gate and permission path enforce the authenticated descriptor’s limits on physical operation. The first verdict, unconditional operation (UNCOND), authorizes tracking proposals across the full operating envelope specified in a signed release manifest, provided its standing conditions remain continuously verified. Each hazard claim in that safety case requires qualified measurements, justified analysis, or validated operating restrictions applicable to the specified physical plant, payload distribution, operational design domain, and fault set. Brake thermal capacity, stopping clearance, and tracking-error bounds must all be qualified for that envelope, and independent permission checks must stand wherever learned policy proposals can reach physical actuators. The verdict does not eliminate residual or newly emergent hazards; it authorizes operation solely under the assessed claims and requires detection and safe withdrawal within the qualified response budget whenever a physical premise fails.

Definition 16.2: Release verdict
Release verdict is the signed decision that sets how much authority a named machine’s permission path may grant: UNCOND for the full assessed operating envelope, COND for a separately evidenced restricted envelope, or REFUSE when any required premise is missing, contradicted, or unknown, in each case only while its standing conditions hold.

Significance: It turns the weakest premise of the argument into the machine’s operating limit on \(\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance\). On this book’s illustrative evidence every claim carries an unknown premise, so the warehouse machine’s verdict is REFUSE. A stipulated set of loaded stopping and floor records would support a COND at 1 m/s on inspected floors, below the 1.23 m/s optimistic all-weight partial ceiling.
Distinction: A test result records the outcome of an individual trial, whereas a degraded mode is an autonomous runtime fallback triggered during execution. By contrast, a release verdict is established before deployment: it names the qualified envelope and the empirical evidence upon which it rests, while leaving the proposal boundary fixed, since the permission path continues to validate every proposed action individually.
Common pitfall: A common misconception is that a conditional verdict (COND) can patch an incomplete safety case by ignoring an unproven claim. A restricted envelope instead demands its own dedicated evidence and analytical limits; an unresolved premise in the primary case leaves that operating mode firmly refused.




16.4.1 Restricted operation and access boundaries
When a safety case lacks evidence for full-speed aisle travel or open-floor contact, letting the robot run under an informal operating note leaves the permission path enforcing the wrong limits. The second verdict, conditional operation (COND), applies when empirical evidence supports the stated hazard claims within a restricted subset of the envelope and binds the permission path to those narrower limits. In the running machine, COND selects a pre-validated safety configuration, much like industrial safety controllers and protective optical scanners switch between pre-validated field sets5 and speed-monitoring profiles. All restricted kinematic thresholds (\(\SpeedBound \le \RestrictedSpeedBound\), \(\ProfileAccelerationBound \le \RestrictedAccelerationBound\)) and spatial geofences are evaluated and validated as one configuration before release; the runtime verdict selects among these vetted profiles rather than inventing parameters on the fly. A conditional verdict (COND) is an offline, predeployment contract that restricts the machine’s operating envelope until re-adjudication. A degraded mode is an online runtime fallback, pre-assessed and named in the signed release, that the permission path invokes when an active subsystem loses telemetry or sensor redundancy (section 16.5.3 sizes one for the base). Release then enforces physical, kinematic, or environmental boundaries that exclude unverified hazard states, such as de-rated joint speeds, a restricted illumination range, or a physical barrier that keeps humans outside the manipulator’s workspace. Where contact force cannot be bounded for unseparated co-presence, a restricted release case may require physical separation: figure 2 illustrates yellow perimeter mesh fencing around an industrial workcell. Crediting that separation requires validated access-interlock and stopping evidence showing that the protective response completes before hazardous access.
5 Safety Scanner Field Sets: A safety laser scanner stores several protective-field geometries that were configured and validated in advance, and a safety controller selects one of them from encoded speed or position inputs. The scanner never computes a new field at runtime. COND borrows the pattern, so the verdict selects a pre-assessed limit set and no untested parameter can reach the permission path.





Figure 2: Physical separation example: A yellow industrial arm works behind yellow mesh fencing. Fencing can be one condition of a restricted release when a validated access interlock and stopping test support it. (Credit: PEO ACWA, Pueblo Chemical Agent-Destruction Pilot Plant, 2012, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)



Fencing excludes unseparated contact by keeping people out of the hazardous volume. The alternative that lets people share the floor, speed and separation monitoring (SSM, Certified safety functions beneath the permission path), needs a different access claim from the stationary-person stopping claim of C1. Its separation clearance must account for human approach velocity across both system reaction time and physical deceleration, robot displacement before brake onset, the executed braking profile, and measurement uncertainty. The warehouse case retains its site crossing rule; engineering teams cannot substitute a stationary-person stopping model into this context and claim to have achieved unseparated, open-floor human-robot collaboration.
Every quantitative condition attached to a release verdict names the operational limit the permission path enforces, maintaining explicit margin below the calculated physical ceiling. Item handover illustrates this margin requirement. The contract signs a TCP speed below the absolute ceiling that the contact criterion admits under equation 12.13. The gap between these two speeds accounts for unobserved physical evolution between discrete sensor samples: velocity growth between sampling instants, encoder quantization noise, and drive lag during an enforcement clamp. A contract signed at the theoretical ceiling leaves zero margin for these physical latency terms, and the release case requires measured empirical bounds on each term before the signed operational speed can be accepted.
The inspected-floor condition follows the same discipline. Where the site inspection regime certifies a friction coefficient of only 0.12, the illustrative all-weight-on-driven-wheels screen uses the optimistic traction ceiling \(\CoulombFrictionCoefficient \Gravity =\) 0.12 \(\times\) 9.81 m/s² \(=\) 1.18 m/s² against the 2 m/s² that the dry-floor budget assumes. Actual loaded credible deceleration also depends on the driven-wheel load share, drive and geometry conditions, and qualified stopping traces. Under the all-weight screening premise, the partial budget that admits 1.44 m/s on surveyed floors admits only 1.23 m/s under this reduced traction. Visual inspection alone cannot establish this lower friction bound because a thin film of transparent oil readily escapes visual detection. The site must qualify both the friction assessment method and the operating procedures (cleaning schedules, spill isolation, and access restrictions) that preserve the assessed floor state between inspections. If that maintenance regime cannot guarantee the exclusion of contaminants over the authorized operating interval, reducing vehicle speed does not salvage the safety case; the aisle remains refused.
The third verdict, refusal to operate (REFUSE), is mandatory whenever the safety case has missing warrants, uncharacterized tail latencies, incomplete fault-injection coverage, or unmonitored failure modes. For systems where torque removal causes immediate physical harm (such as upright bipedal humanoids falling under gravity), REFUSE cannot simply de-energize motor phases to zero torque; it must execute an assessed, powered descent or seated hold. If the safety enforcer’s worst-case execution time under the designated computational placement has never been verified against its 400 μs deadline, or if the fault-injection campaign omitted common-cause failures identified in the deployment topology, the hazard remains unquantified and cannot support release. Refusal is likewise mandatory whenever physical measurements contradict the mathematical model behind a safety budget term, such as loaded stopping trials that yield decelerations below the 2 m/s² assumed by the braking model.
A refusal verdict is an actionable engineering result rather than an administrative dead end. It redirects schedule pressure toward evidence by pointing to the exact broken link in the assertion DAG. If release is refused because loaded stopping trials contradict the braking model, the engineering team does not debate risk tolerance. Developers instead repeat physical braking trials at maximum payload mass until the qualified trial campaign and its uncertainty analysis support a credible lower deceleration bound. They then re-derive the stopping budget from that lower bound and submit for re-adjudication only when the aisle budget closes on validated data. The refusal verdict names the exact empirical test that must pass before re-adjudication can proceed.
Accountability for the release decision must rest with a named lead systems adjudicator rather than being split across development teams. When a vision team signs off on perception metrics, an actuator supplier on torque ratings, and a machine learning team on policy convergence, each group can assume that another layer holds the safety margin. The lead adjudicator alone attests that the integrated, physical machine satisfies the safety case. This sign-off binds the release verdict to a specific set of technical records: cryptographic digests of verified policy weights, calibration logs for manipulator contact-force sensing, empirical brake-onset measurements paired with justified worst-case response bounds, and fully loaded stopping trials establishing credible deceleration limits. The adjudicator signs the release manifest with a private key held inside a hardware security module,6 binding the manifest to the organization’s signing key and sign-off record. The robot runtime checks this digital signature against a public key anchored in its hardware root of trust before enabling actuators.
6 Hardware Security Module (HSM): A tamper-resistant device can generate and retain a non-exportable private key and perform signing inside its own boundary. The signature identifies the signing key; authenticated access, sign-off records, and key-custody controls establish who authorized its use.
↪ The adjudicator’s signature as one of several decisions behind each admitted action, each needing a named owner, is developed in Decisions Behind an Admitted Action.

The adjudicator’s signature records the internal acceptance of the engineering organization, whereas external certification requires independent evaluation. UL 4600 requires independent assessment of the autonomous safety case (UL Standards & Engagement 2023), and machinery whose primary safety functions rely on machine learning falls under regulations, such as the European Union Machinery Regulation, that require third-party conformity assessment (section 16.3.4). An assessor who did not build the safety case brings an independent view to the assumptions that shaped its trade-offs. Organizational separation alone does not establish a probability of coincident error or the statistical independence required by equation 3. The release manifest must therefore retain the full body of raw physical evidence needed for an independent audit, not just the final verdict.
The adjudicator ultimately signs one of the three decisions summarized in table 4. A conditional verdict requires its own independently evidenced restricted envelope; an unresolved gap in the nominal argument cannot be relabeled as an operational constraint. No verdict ever moves the proposal boundary. Under both UNCOND and COND, learned policies only propose candidate actions while the deterministic safety enforcer independently admits or blocks every control command, as principle \(\ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission}\) requires. The release verdict sets the physical envelope that the permission path enforces; it never grants learned policies unchecked authority.



Table 4: Three signed release verdicts for the mobile manipulator: Full operation and restricted mode both retain independent per-action permission. Refusal is an actionable engineering result.

Each verdict in table 4 is signed against the physical state of the machine at the moment of evaluation. The right-hand column of the table therefore pairs every operational grant with an explicit expiry or refusal trigger, because a brake lining or sensor mount that passed inspection before commissioning does not stay in its commissioning state. As the physical plant wears and drifts over time, a release verdict holds only while runtime checks, scheduled measurements, and enforced site procedures continue to verify its standing premises.

title: Deployment Release
text:
16.5 The Verdict’s Standing Conditions
A signed release can lapse without any change to the underlying software. Brake linings wear down, camera brackets shift under continuous vibration, or warehouse traffic polishes concrete lanes until traction drops. When these physical premises drift, the stopping claim certified by the adjudicator no longer holds. Standing conditions bind the operational verdict to these physical baselines by defining an explicit observation cadence for each premise alongside deterministic fallback responses when a check fails. Because failure modes originate in hardware and environment, their observation schedules must follow physical degradation mechanisms rather than software sprint schedules. An assurance case maintained this way, its validity updated throughout operating life as monitored evidence shifts, is what the safety literature calls a dynamic safety case (Denney et al. 2015).

16.5.1 Degradation, drift, and observation cadence
None of the three verdicts is a permanent grant. Mechanical linkages develop backlash, friction surfaces wear, optical lenses collect dust, and operating environments change. Operating under either an unconditional (UNCOND) or conditional (COND) verdict therefore carries continuous obligations for the life of the deployment. Notebook 16.1 shows how little wear the stopping claim tolerates. A credible deceleration 31 percent below the assumed 2 m/s² spends the whole partial spare, and a smaller loss spends the reserve that remains once admission work is charged, leaving no allowance for perception latency or traction variation. A lining that wears that far is discovered at a rack end as an overrun unless the degradation first trips a standing condition, such as a scheduled loaded deceleration trial or an automated pre-shift brake diagnostic, before the machine is cleared to enter the aisle. Every operational obligation pairs a physical premise with an automated detector and an immediate mitigation, establishing a standing condition tied to the release verdict.
Sensor mounting drift can silently invalidate localization while every camera frame stays sharp and fresh. Daily thermal cycling and machine vibration alter extrinsic sensor geometry, and software rollback cannot realign a physically displaced bracket. The safety case must therefore require qualified online drift detection or scheduled physical recalibrations, setting inspection intervals from the underlying mechanical wear rates. A cryptographic checksum confirms only that the stored calibration file matches its build artifact; it gives no evidence that the physical camera still sits at that modeled pose.
A release verdict depends on physical premises with widely differing observation schedules. For instance, the mobile manipulator’s optimistic all-weight traction screen requires a floor friction coefficient of at least 0.204; the braking claim additionally requires qualified loaded wheel forces, drive conditions, and stopping traces. Dry concrete exceeds this threshold by a wide margin, at roughly 0.60, but a baseline site survey conducted before commissioning cannot guarantee surface conditions against fluid spills or traffic polishing over time. The safety case must therefore specify routine floor maintenance schedules alongside strict exclusion rules whenever surface contamination occurs, supplemented by any onboard traction monitoring. Similarly, the arm’s contact-force sensors require periodic recalibration against reference loads. Every physical premise must be rechecked continuously or periodically at a cadence matched to how fast it degrades. This is the fourth law, permission must be earned (principle \(\ref{pri-vol4-evidence-bounds-authority}\)), applied over time. The verdict grants permission contingent on operating conditions, and that permission endures only while the evidence supporting each premise remains valid.
Every runtime-monitored premise requires a dedicated detector and a pre-allocated fallback response; conversely, premises governed by facility maintenance require accountable operators and enforceable exclusion rules. If a safety case credits a navigation-camera dispatch age of 51.6 ms, the runtime monitor must measure frame arrival latency against hardware clocks, accounting for sensor readout and transport delays separately. Forwarding an unverified metadata timestamp does not confirm that the frame is fresh. Without hardware-synchronized event timestamps, unverified inputs quietly turn safety premises into ungrounded assumptions. Different premises demand different sampling frequencies. The tote-rack load, bounded by its 50 kg mechanical payload limit, can be checked at each load-changing event if access controls exclude unrecorded loading and the check completes before the changed load receives motion authority. Conversely, base velocity, position tracking, and action lease validity must be evaluated deterministically on every 1 ms safety-enforcer tick.


16.5.2 The envelope trichotomy and epistemic gaps
A naive binary health check assumes normal operation whenever no explicit error flag is asserted, mistaking a dead sensor or a diverged filter for safe clearance. Checking monitored premises at runtime instead exposes three states of envelope membership: known-true, known-false, and unknown. Membership is known-true when authenticated telemetry and hardware-referenced timestamps confirm that the plant’s bounded state-uncertainty set remains strictly inside certified envelope boundaries. Estimator convergence or small covariance matrices alone do not prove containment if model assumptions have broken down. When measured telemetry reveals a physical boundary violation, such as base tracking error exceeding the 40 mm bound reserved within the stopping envelope, the state is known-false. Finally, when an optical encoder loses serial communication, a camera frame fails its cyclic redundancy check (CRC), or an extended Kalman filter diverges, the system enters an epistemic gap. In this unknown state, the controller cannot tell whether the physical machine is safely positioned or breaching clearance margins.
When telemetry supporting active motion becomes unknown or known-false, the safety enforcer revokes trajectory tracking and executes the pre-certified fallback procedure for the plant’s dynamic state. This runtime intervention differs from rejecting an invalid future trajectory proposal, because an already active trajectory chunk can continue executing only while its supporting sensor evidence, physical bounds, and lease duration remain intact. The system’s flight recorder must log whether revocation stemmed from unobservable state telemetry or an active boundary breach, while the hardware supplies enough reserve energy and sensing capability to bring the plant to a controlled stop or hold.

Definition 16.3: Envelope trichotomy

Envelope trichotomy is the three-state epistemic classification of cyber-physical system health relative to its signed operating envelope: known-true (qualified state-uncertainty set contained inside the supported envelope), known-false (verified boundary violation triggering deterministic hardware refusal), and unknown (state uncertainty caused by sensor dropout, frame corruption, or estimator divergence).

Significance: An unknown state is not evidence of a boundary breach, yet neither condition permits continued tracking. The permission decision is refusal in both unknown and known-false states; the logged cause remains distinct and the response depends on the plant’s validated stop or hold capability.
Distinction: Unlike a binary boolean status check (is_safe == true), the envelope trichotomy separates sensor blindness from active violations, ensuring telemetry loss is never mistaken for safe clearance.
Common pitfall: Treating a stored command as indefinitely valid after communication fails. An active chunk may continue only within its own still-valid evidence and lease; otherwise the assessed fallback must take over.



The same three-state distinction applies to verification test records. A test trial marked UNOBSERVABLE or INVALID during acceptance testing (Four verdicts and the invalid-test rule) cannot establish the claim its required witnesses or test conditions failed to resolve. It leaves a gap in that coverage; other valid records remain evidence only for the conditions and claims they establish. Verified PASS records support the claims covered by their conditions and witnesses. A valid FAIL contradicts the claim tested under those conditions and withdraws any authorization that relies on it.


16.5.3 Blind travel, kinetic consequences, and cycle limits
When telemetry fails or sensors black out, a machine traveling without sensory feedback moves blind; it must execute a deterministic fallback stop before its forward travel consumes the remaining spatial clearance. How fast that clearance vanishes depends directly on vehicle speed, contact geometry, and available actuator authority. Sizing the response therefore requires calculating the kinetic energy and blind travel accumulated during each millisecond of delay, and matching each sensor loss to a pre-certified fallback path.
How the system responds when a premise cannot be checked must follow from the physics of unmonitored motion rather than from arbitrary severity categories. When the mobile manipulator traverses an aisle at 1.3 m/s with its tote rack fully loaded, its 368 kg mass carries 311 J of kinetic energy. If its primary lidar stops updating, every millisecond of blind travel carries the base 1.3 mm closer to potential obstacles. The safety case pre-certifies three possible fallback paths, two of which apply only when the signed release names them in advance. The first is a degraded mode that permits continued motion while diverse redundant sensors keep state uncertainty bounded, for example throttling the aisle speed to 0.65 m/s (half the aisle speed, a chosen value) while secondary sensors watch the path. The second is a switch to a restricted limit set that a signed COND case pre-validated for that exact sensor loss, if the release includes one. The runtime only selects that profile; it does not create a new verdict. Dead reckoning and wheel odometry may retain qualified position bounds over a brief window, but cannot verify obstacle clearance on their own. The third option, the hardware STOP response, handles complete loss of observability by executing a configured drive and brake sequence. Stopping the vehicle within available clearance margins requires calibrated response timing, sufficient drive traction, and known brake deceleration.
Action leases bound how long an admitted trajectory chunk may run without renewal. Checking this lease on every controller tick does not require re-measuring every long-term site condition. Instead, the runtime permission path checks fresh local sensor telemetry alongside the signed validity windows of slower site inspections and maintenance records. If the proposer stalls or its communication drops, task throughput suffers, but safety holds as long as the enforcer and its fallback path remain decoupled, responsive, and intact.
Any standing condition governing physical motion requires an enforcement path with a measured detection and response budget. In this book’s architecture, an independent safety enforcer checks trajectory proposals and monitored premises before issuing actuator permissions, re-evaluating system state on every 1 ms control tick. A subsystem failure reaches this enforcer along one of two paths: a silent proposer that stops transmitting is caught only when its existing action lease expires, whereas an actively monitored hardware fault raises an immediate interrupt flag. Because detection delays differ between these paths, so does the distance the base travels blind (notebook 16.2).



The lease dominates: a silent proposer reaches brake onset in 82 ms, a flagged premise in 22 ms.

Napkin Math 16.2: The silent-proposer windowProblem: The base runs the aisle at 1.3 m/s. How far does it travel before brake onset when the proposer falls silent, how far when a monitored premise fails and its flag reaches the enforcer at once, and how late may that flag arrive before monitoring stops the base no sooner than the lease would?
Variables:

Aisle speed \(\SpeedAtDetection =\) 1.3 m/s (Chosen), so 1.3 mm of travel per millisecond
Chunk lease 60 ms and permission tick 1 ms (Chosen); bus transfer 1 ms and brake onset 20 ms (Illustrative)
Flag latency \(\FailureFlagLatency\) from the physical failure to a flag the enforcer can read (Unknown; the detector’s qualification must bound it)

Math:

Silent proposer: 60 ms \(+\) 1 ms \(+\) 1 ms \(+\) 20 ms \(=\) 82 ms, and 1.3 m/s \(\times\) 82 ms \(=\) 106.6 mm.
Monitored premise, immediate flag: 1 ms \(+\) 1 ms \(+\) 20 ms \(=\) 22 ms, and 1.3 m/s \(\times\) 22 ms \(=\) 28.6 mm.
Crossover: \(\FailureFlagLatency +\) 22 ms \(=\) 82 ms at \(\FailureFlagLatency =\) 60 ms, the length of the lease itself.

Result: Monitoring can save up to 78 mm of travel, but only for a flag that arrives within 60 ms of the failure; a slower flag stops the base no sooner than waiting out the lease.
Systems insight: The 22 ms local subtotal is not a complete detection-to-stop time; it reflects only controller cycle delay, communication transfer, and physical brake engagement. The decisive term governing whether an active monitor preserves physical clearance is \(\FailureFlagLatency\), the hardware detection latency. If an architectural budget fails to bound \(\FailureFlagLatency\), the safety case cannot claim proactive protection. Every millisecond spent detecting a fault carries the loaded vehicle another 1.3 mm toward whatever the failed premise was protecting against.


When an operating premise transitions to unknown or known-false, the enforcer revokes trajectory tracking and commands the appropriate rung of the fallback ladder, and the signed safety case must specify both this fallback selection and its measured timing. For the mobile base, the certified stopping sequence uses controlled, powered deceleration to bring the wheels to rest before applying electromechanical holding brakes. Because digital controller logic and brake-coil hold-up capacitors cannot deliver drive motor torque, the safety case must confirm drive energy, feedback sensing, and inverter continuity across every fault condition expected to use this active deceleration profile. By contrast, a raw torque-inhibit or free-wheeling cutoff is a different physical response; it cannot inherit stopping-distance guarantees calculated for controlled electrical braking.
Entering an unknown or known-false state also triggers local black-box logging. The onboard recorder must preserve the telemetry window leading up to refusal alongside the execution of the fallback trajectory, even if the initiating fault cuts external networking or primary bus power. These records are essential for root-cause investigation, but writing them to nonvolatile storage must never delay the hard real-time safety stop; section 16.9.5 sizes the capture path.
On longer timescales, even when every runtime heartbeat succeeds, the release verdict carries an operational cycle and inspection budget.7 Operating hours and mechanical fatigue wear components in ways that high-frequency telemetry cannot observe directly (such as surface pitting on gear teeth, elastomer seal stiffening, or fastener preload relaxation). Once this cycle budget expires, the release case must be re-adjudicated before autonomous motion can resume. Across every timescale, a deployment verdict remains valid only while its supporting standing conditions remain demonstrably known-true, checked at intervals matched to physical wear rates and backed by pre-certified fallback stops with measured latencies. Claims, verdicts, and revocation conditions are now defined. The six claims of the warehouse mobile manipulator can be adjudicated against the physical evidence assembled across this book.
7 Mechanical Fatigue Budget: A cumulative-damage model such as Miner’s rule (\(\sum_i \AppliedLoadCycleCount_i/\FatigueLifeCycleCount_i\)) (Miner 1945) can organize a measured load spectrum against component-specific fatigue data; it is an approximation, not a universal failure deadline. The assessed loads, uncertainty, inspection evidence, and stopping consequences determine any signed payload derating and cycle limit. An expired limit revokes the applicable release case rather than silently extending service.
Miner, Milton A. 1945. “Cumulative Damage in Fatigue.” Journal of Applied Mechanics 12 (3): A159–64. https://doi.org/10.1115/1.4009458.

title: Deployment Release
text:
16.6 Adjudicating the Safety Case
An algebraically exact stopping equation or contact-force bound still fails to protect a machine if the physical premise beneath its warrant has never been measured on hardware. Adjudicating a safety release case requires checking each warrant against the qualified measurements, justified analysis, or validated operating restrictions that support it. For the warehouse mobile manipulator, the adjudicator takes each of the six claims of table 2 in turn, names the physical premise under its warrant, and grades the evidence behind that premise. This isolates the exact boundary where mathematical deduction ends and physical measurement must take over.
The door-opening branch of C1 shows the procedure in full. The contact enforcement record supplies the branch’s underlying mechanics (Intentional contact and in-contact energy barriers). At the guarded approach velocity of 0.03 m/s, equation 12.11 yields an impact force at physical braking onset of 39 N, well below the 100 N latch limit. From there, equation 12.12 leaves the latch plate with only 0.15 mm of additional allowable compression. Bringing the arm to rest within this narrow mechanical travel requires a deceleration of approximately 3 m/s² over a brief 10 ms stopping window. By contrast, at the unconstrained approach velocity of 0.10 m/s, the force at braking onset rises to 95 N, and avoiding structural damage demands a deceleration of 400 m/s², more than an order of magnitude above standard gravity. While this kinematic calculation specifies the stopping performance required for release, mathematical derivation alone cannot prove that the physical arm actuators can deliver it. Consequently, the operating envelope (table 1) excludes the high-speed approach. Raising approach speeds sharply escalates contact braking demands, whereas the system’s training demonstrations offer zero empirical evidence for safe high-speed contact (Choosing a tractable coverage table).



Raising the approach from 0.03 m/s to 0.10 m/s multiplies the arm stop needed 136-fold.
Neither result is in doubt as arithmetic; the algebraic deduction is exact. Formal engineering release, however, cannot rest on closed-form kinematic models alone. The door branch fails authorization because its safety warrant depends on an unverified physical premise. Whether the physical manipulator, carrying its link momentum, payload mass, and reflected rotor inertia, can actually deliver 3 m/s² of deceleration within a fraction of a millimeter depends on transient joint torque limits, motor electrical time constants, and structural stiffness. Without calibrated hardware traces measuring these dynamic properties under load, this mechanical premise remains unknown, and the adjudicator must refuse the claim.
The remaining claim branches fail on similar grounds:

Base braking corridor (C1): The base stopping budget of 969.0 mm omits dispatch-to-admission delay and rests on illustrative values for braking deceleration, brake onset, path-tracking error, and localization uncertainty. Its remaining margin of 131.0 mm can be exhausted by the illustrative deceleration shortfall in step 4 of notebook 16.1, and step 5 leaves still less once admission work is charged.
Object handover (C1): The mug handover branch fails on three separate premises. First, the calculated contact force falls below the criterion only for an unconstrained, free-moving hand, and it comes from a standardized biomechanical body model rather than a force measurement of this contact. Second, the evidence packet does not show that the coworker’s hand cannot be trapped against a rigid fixture, so the non-clamping geometry is unproven. Third, perceptual grounding remains unverified: a proposal that mistakes a clear glass jar for the target mug satisfies every geometric affordance check, and no trace in the runtime logs disambiguates the object.
Enforcer timing (C2): The timing warrant for the runtime safety enforcer assumes a worst-case execution time (WCET) of 250 μs against an unloaded baseline of 135 μs and a 400 μs deadline. The WCET is declared without architectural analysis and loaded stress evidence supporting it under peak memory bus saturation.
Traction and environmental state (C3): Claim C3 requires a qualified friction floor across every authorized aisle; 0.204 is only the optimistic all-weight traction screen, not a sufficient loaded stopping qualification. A clean concrete floor can be validated through baseline skid testing, but the onboard cameras cannot reliably distinguish dry concrete from a thin film of transparent oil, and no sensor on the machine can exclude liquid contamination ahead of the braking contact.
Perception pipeline latency (C4): The 51.6 ms dispatch age combines nominal datasheet readout times with uncharacterized pipeline delays rather than verified end-to-end telemetry.
Permission independence (C5): The placement record’s loaded test report, which would show the enforcer’s maxima under the proposer’s worst interference and test the common causes of Two Paths and the Resources They Share, is described in this book but not produced. Without it, the credited enforcement isolation is unsubstantiated; even supporting isolation records would not by themselves establish statistical independence of every failure event.
Authority transfer (C6): The argument cites PASS fault records for authority transitions A1 through A4, and no such records exist yet. Local operation could drop the remote-channel cases, but not the local ones.

Because every claim rests on at least one unverified physical premise, the adjudicator must render a verdict of REFUSE. This refusal does not imply that the robot is inherently dangerous. The book’s supporting inputs are illustrative models rather than empirical validation logs, so the verdict is illustrative as well; it models how release is adjudicated and shows why ungrounded claims cannot license physical deployment. The fourth law, permission must be earned, requires an operational restriction wherever the available evidence cannot support a premise. Here, every branch contains an unverified premise. A principled refusal must therefore specify the exact measurements required to turn an unverified assumption into an accepted warrant. Table 5 lists these evidentiary requirements, naming the physical premise each measurement settles and the operational restriction a supporting result would lift.

Neural network inference latency primarily governs system availability rather than baseline safety. An inference overrun will not violate physical containment so long as the independent hardware safety path and powered fallback controllers remain operational; however, repeated deadline misses will degrade throughput and stall task progress. Conversely, resource contention across shared memory, PCIe buses, or CPU caches that delays the runtime enforcer or starves its sensor feeds represents a direct safety failure under claims C2 and C5. Finally, while local autonomous operation can safely omit validation trials for unused remote teleoperation links, deployment still requires verified software placement records, comprehensive common-cause fault coverage, and passing test records for every local authority transition.

16.6.1 Worked restricted service with stipulated evidence
Without calibrated hardware measurements, the mobile manipulator remains locked out under a REFUSE verdict. To see how an engineering organization moves from initial refusal to conditional deployment without relaxing its structural safety limits, consider a stipulated release case in which an engineering packet supplies the measured traces specified below. (The uncalibrated evidence currently available in this book continues to dictate REFUSE.)
The target application is restricted inspected-route mug delivery. The robot retrieves a declared mug from a singulated feeder and traverses a designated, surveyed warehouse aisle at a velocity capped at 1 m/s. It then pauses the mobile base to open an equipment cage latch using the guarded contact trajectory and hands the mug to a consenting human coworker under the accept_item primitive at 0.10 m/s. Operational authority remains strictly local. The feeder mechanism physically prevents accidental object substitutions, recognizing that singulation alone cannot authenticate identity. Similarly, strict access controls prevent personnel from stepping into the robot’s active stopping corridor during transit.


↪ The difference between a coworker who consents to a machine’s risk, as this one does, and people who bear it without choosing, is developed in Who Bears the Risk.
For claim C1, the safety case stipulates empirical stopping traces under full payload mass, measured tracking and localization variance, dynamic latch-stopping performance, and instrumented handover contact forces that satisfy the bounded thresholds in table 5. For claims C2 and C5, the case stipulates independent hardware fault-injection logs and worst-case execution timing traces gathered under peak synthetic computational load. These records must account for common-cause hardware failures, support the enforcer’s permission deadlines and actuator reaction latencies, separate controlled motor deceleration from passive mechanical braking at rest, and confirm isolated drive-energy cutoff and sensor integrity under all credited fault modes.
For claim C4, the case stipulates synchronized end-to-end hardware timestamp telemetry, bounded clock skew, and a verified upper bound on dispatch-to-admission latency. This latency must be deducted from the dynamic stopping distance budget so that a strictly positive safety margin remains; a theoretical kinematic velocity ceiling cannot authorize transit speeds on its own. Because sensor data ages continuously throughout execution, the chunk lease starts only when a plan is admitted, never when it is computed. The qualification packet must also check the time between admitted plans against the lease renewal deadline rather than assuming that nominal policy inference frequency guarantees admission. For claim C6, the packet stipulates verified PASS audit records across every state transition exercised by the local autonomous executive, while disabling the unverified remote teleoperation interface entirely.
Claim C3 requires substantially more than visual inspection or reduced transit velocity. The case stipulates a qualified site friction survey showing a friction coefficient of at least 0.12 across the surveyed transit corridor, reinforced by active cleaning protocols, chemical containment barriers, and physical access gates that maintain floor integrity throughout the authorized inspection interval. Stopping trials at maximum payload must confirm deceleration on this specific friction surface with the loaded wheel distribution and drive settings of the signed configuration. The complete restricted stopping distance, including the verified dispatch-to-admission delay bound and a positive safety margin, must fit inside the surveyed physical clearance with a positive reserve, the same accounting as step 5 of notebook 16.1. The operating velocity of 1 m/s sits below the partial ceiling of 1.23 m/s, but that comparison is only an initial feasibility filter. The active transit permit is revoked immediately upon any reported spill, expired maintenance inspection, or perimeter breach. If unmonitored oil or other fluid can enter the corridor during the deployment window, the stipulation is invalidated and the verdict reverts to REFUSE. A lower speed cannot repair that premise, because the restricted speed was sized for the inspected friction floor of 0.12, not for a film near 0.05 that removes most of it.
The task capability packet is similarly stipulated. Before evaluation begins, the facility operator defines binding acceptance criteria in the verification plan: a minimum mission completion rate, an upper bound on end-to-end cycle time, and a maximum allowable operator intervention rate, accompanied by sample-size requirements, confidence intervals, and statistical decision rules. A successful mission requires maintaining object identity and physical integrity from retrieval through coworker handover. Cycle time accounting includes transient safety stops, crossing delays, and autonomous replanning; human rescues and aborted deliveries are tracked as explicit mission failures. The safety case stipulates that closed-loop trials of this exact restricted configuration satisfy all three benchmarks. The qualification dossier separates raw neural policy autonomy, system-level task success, and safety interventions into independent metrics, the separation What a Physical Success Rate Measures drew between the policy’s own completions and the completions that protection made possible. Minimal-intervention safety filtering may run during nominal task execution; its clamps are counted separately, so they neither mask the policy’s shortcomings nor count as safety violations.
With these stipulated evidence packets in hand, the adjudicator can sign a verdict of COND (conditional release) for restricted inspected-route mug delivery. The physical records support claims C1 through C6 solely within the restricted operating envelope, while the task evaluation shows acceptable operational utility under identical constraints. The adjudicator binds both the physical safety dossier and the capability evaluation to the release manifest, leaving full-speed autonomous transit and remote teleoperation unauthorized. The result is a conditional safety case, not a blanket deployment permit. Invalidating any underlying assumption or breaching a boundary condition immediately returns the verdict to REFUSE; conversely, gathering qualified operational telemetry and physical measurements over time can justify expanding the envelope toward full-scale release.

Checkpoint 16.2: Refusal and the path to conditional release
Before approving a conditional release of the machine, verify your understanding of how a premise, rather than a calculation, decides a claim:

Premise vs. arithmetic: Can you explain why the calculated latch force at physical braking onset is not in doubt while the door branch of C1 is still refused?
Unsupported approach: Can you use equation 12.11 and equation 12.12 to show why the operating envelope admits only the guarded door approach?
Refusal as a deliverable: Can you name, for one refused claim, the measurement that would lift it and the restriction that would remain after a supporting result?
Measured-deceleration estimate: Suppose loaded stopping trials put the low tail of the deceleration at 1.6 m/s² under the same jerk bound. Can you rerun notebook 16.1 at 1.3 m/s and decide whether that aisle speed can still be signed once \(\DispatchAdmissionInterval\) is charged?

title: Deployment Release
text:
16.7 Adversarial Review
Confirmation bias steers an engineering team’s data collection toward nominal conditions where learned models succeed, leaving edge-case hazards untested until live operation exposes them. Suppose the measurements listed in table 5 arrive and, as in the stipulated branch, appear to support a conditional (COND) authorization for the mobile manipulator. Before signing, the safety adjudicator submits the safety case to an independent adversarial review tasked with falsifying its warrants. Rather than ratifying a brief, the reviewer actively searches for unsupported warrants, uncharacterized physical transitions, and environmental edge cases that violate the release contract. If an argument collapses on paper when an adversary probes for physical violations, the machine cannot be expected to withstand the hazards of live service.
The review interrogates every evidentiary node in the argument tree using four structured probes. The first challenges empirical sufficiency: whether the physical trials reached the extremes of the operating envelope. Stopping trials with the loaded base on dry concrete, at a friction coefficient near 0.60, support the warrant that the base achieves its certified deceleration under ideal conditions. The restricted operational mode, however, admits facility floors that the site’s inspection regime certifies only down to 0.12, such as an aisle polished smooth by traffic. In those zones, the base may run at the restricted velocity 1 m/s, below the 1.23 m/s ceiling. If the trial set contains no loaded stops on such degraded floors at that speed, the warrant for the restricted mode is unsupported. A coverage audit finds on paper the gap that unvetted service would otherwise find against a warehouse rack. The reviewer also checks whether validation trials covered transient execution states across an A/B partition swap, when a newly flashed software bank takes over from the incumbent one (section 16.9.1). The same check applies to cold-start sensor characteristics before cameras and inertial measurement units reach thermal equilibrium. It applies as well to the operating boundaries of canary units, the small subset of the fleet that first runs a candidate policy (section 16.9.2). Finally, the reviewer asks whether site procedures actually keep fluid films out of the corridor throughout the authorized interval, since listing oil outside the envelope does not exclude it from the floor.
The second probe examines domain transfer, targeting claims where synthetic simulation substitutes for direct physical measurement. A vision-based human detector may achieve high recall across synthetic, ray-traced warehouse environments, yet fail on physical hardware when encountering coworkers partially obscured by stretch-wrapped pallets whose specular reflections blind the camera’s auto-exposure algorithm. Benchmark recall on curated offline datasets is an indirect proxy metric that scores isolated frames rather than the closed-loop physical causal chain running from visual detection to an arrested base. Likewise, a simulation that omits linkage compliance or fieldbus jitter cannot establish tolerance to those physical mechanisms. The reviewer demands empirical evidence from paired hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) trials on target SoC devices connected to chassis dynamometers8 and physical bus emulators under real facility illumination, dust, and reflective geometry.
8 Chassis Dynamometer: Powered rollers under the drive wheels absorb or supply torque, so the base can run at aisle speed on a bench while its drive and braking torques are measured. The rollers, not the floor, set the traction. Dynamometer stops can therefore qualify drive and brake response but say nothing about the friction premise of C3.The third probe attacks structural independence, asking whether the learned model and safety enforcer share hardware resources whose contention could delay sensor delivery or actuation cutoff. On modern robotics edge platforms where neural inference engines and real-time safety enforcers share a single system-on-chip die, internal crossbar interconnects, shared caches, and DRAM memory controllers, unconstrained direct memory access (DMA) transfers from large model forward passes can saturate memory channels. This memory contention induces tail latency spikes that starve deterministic safety enforcer execution ticks, directly invalidating the 51.6 ms observation-age chain of C4. Stress tests and hardware timing analysis under peak synthetic compute and bus loads must establish the worst-case interference bound; unit tests on an otherwise idle bus provide zero evidence of non-interference. The reviewer also checks whether writing frozen edge telemetry ring buffers to non-volatile storage competes with real-time fieldbus DMA buffers across the internal bus fabric. The reviewer inspects watchdog reset circuits for single points of failure and verifies whether the supercapacitor power hold-up circuit supplies enough energy to flush in-flight telemetry buffers to persistent flash when an emergency stop opens the main DC bus contactors.
The fourth probe identifies unmonitored state drift. Mechanical wear alters gearbox compliance9 and disrupts the dynamic relationship between commanded motor torque and physical joint motion. The reviewer therefore demands paired wear-state braking and contact traces before accepting the arm-stop premise of the door branch of C1 (section 16.6). A static motor-current threshold alone cannot prove that a mechanically worn drive train remains inside certified force and stopping limits. The reviewer also checks whether over-the-air updates preserve the persistent hardware calibration partition intact across schema migrations, or whether an OS reflash can silently reset camera extrinsics and joint zeroes to unverified factory defaults. Finally, the probe checks whether thermal bracket motion stays inside the localization allowance; fresh timestamps and unchanged calibration files on disk cannot establish that physical fact.
9 Strain-Wave Gear Wear: The arm’s joints use strain-wave reducers (Transmission compliance, contact impedance, and tooth fracture), and in service their flexspline teeth and wave-generator bearing wear. Wear raises lost motion and torsional hysteresis, which adds phase lag between motor and link, so the arm begins to decelerate later and its first contact peak rises.Reviewers turn these vulnerabilities into concrete tests by constructing explicit defeaters for each warrant. The hardest failure modes to catch combine minor anomalies that each stay inside their own tolerance bands, the compound faults that Compound faults and coupled disturbances derives from shared causes. Consider the mobile manipulator’s navigation camera operating with three simultaneous sub-threshold degradations. A light film of dust coats its lens. A mount whose fasteners relaxed within tolerance vibrates as the base crosses floor joints. An interconnect harness flexes at those joints and elevates the bit-error rate across its serializer/deserializer (SerDes) link. Each individual check reads normal. The optical transmission score exceeds its 85 percent alarm threshold. The mount deflection registers below its 0.15-degree hardware fault limit. SerDes cyclic redundancy check error counters remain below their warning tripwire. Their timing effects remain contained only if the independent permission path strictly enforces the event-specific observation-age and clock-uncertainty checks of The Observation Contract and retains its validated response time. Any hardware or bus interference that defeats that deterministic path is a safety violation under C5, not a benign availability-only event.
The same anomalies compound within spatial estimation. Dimmed contrast reduces tracked visual features, mount vibration adds motion blur and persistent pose bias, and frame drops extend intervals of uncorrected dead reckoning. A systematic pose bias can quietly erode the localization allowance without forcing estimated filter covariances or innovation residuals to breach trip thresholds. The release reviewer therefore challenges the combined error against the qualified uncertainty bound, rather than inferring containment from individually passing scalar diagnostics. A breach of the combined bound consumes part of the stopping reserve and invalidates the release warrant; exhausting the entire stopping margin requires a quantified combined-error scenario. Statistical residual monitoring protects against only the specific faults its qualification shows it can detect, leaving site operational restrictions or independent physical checks to cover the remaining biases.
The review also audits the execution integrity of the permission path, checking whether inference loops or background services can bypass, corrupt, or starve the enforcer or human overrides, the latter covered by claim C6 of table 2. Below the proposal boundary, both safety monitors and manual overrides maintain non-preemptible execution priority over learned models. The reviewer asks concrete systems questions: whether a runaway policy thread can exhaust shared memory channels, whether an accelerator-runtime exception can lock a kernel spinlock, and whether a telemetry logging burst can brown out a regulated power rail. The reviewer accepts permission path independence, and the held-up power rail that carries it on the mobile manipulator, only after reviewing physical fault-injection trials. These trials must show survival under bus saturation, active feed removal, and an abruptly killed proposer task (fault F1), and they must appear in the signed fault records, because C2 claims only the faults the permission path demonstrably survives. A user-space implementation without qualified scheduling, resource isolation, and response mechanisms cannot supply the justified execution bound and fault isolation the reviewer requires.
When an adversarial probe succeeds, the case cannot be salvaged by editing claim descriptions or inserting arbitrary safety margins. The broken warrant is traced to its root systems failure (an uncharacterized physical boundary, an inadequate dataset, or an unmodeled bus latency), and the defect returns to the owning engineering subsystem. For example, a motor-current observer that fails under gearbox compliance returns to the mechanical specification as wear limits and runtime compliance estimation, while bus contention that delays the enforcer returns to the compute architecture as memory partitioning and real-time scheduling. The case returns to the engineering team with its broken warrants named, and only updated boundaries, re-derived stopping distances, and renewed verification reopen formal adjudication.
Adversarial review must also recur periodically, because a case accepted once can erode in service without any single discrete event forcing a new audit. The normalization of deviance names that operational erosion, in which anomalies that cause no immediate harm come to be treated as acceptable operating noise rather than as evidence against a warrant (Leveson 2011; Vaughan 1996) (war story 16.1).10 On the mobile manipulator, this erosion unfolds silently across months of fleet operation. Localization residuals creep toward the edge of their tolerance. Observation-age watchdog trips are dismissed as nuisance stops. Stopping distances end slightly longer than the initial trials did. Enforcer trips are cleared on the floor without a trace review. When thresholds are widened, margins trimmed for throughput, and alarms suppressed because nothing has yet gone wrong, the gap between the signed envelope and the machine’s actual physical behavior widens until a routine disturbance exhausts what remains. The defense is to fix each watched quantity’s threshold and response before service begins, as the safety performance indicators of section 16.9.5 do, so that a run of harmless readings cannot move it.

Leveson, Nancy. 2011. Engineering a Safer World: Systems Thinking Applied to Safety. MIT Press.
10 Normalization of Deviance: The sociologist Diane Vaughan coined the term in her study of the Challenger launch decision (Vaughan 1996). It names a process rather than a decision, in which each anomaly that caused no harm widened what the next review accepted as normal.
Vaughan, Diane. 1996. The Challenger Launch Decision: Risky Technology, Culture, and Deviance at NASA. University of Chicago Press.

War Story 16.1: Challenger and experience limits (1986)Context: The Space Shuttle’s solid rocket motors were assembled from cylindrical steel segments whose field joints were sealed by primary and secondary O-rings (Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident 1986). No learned model appears in this chain. The adjudication failure it records is the exact failure this chapter’s verdicts exist to prevent: a launch approved for conditions that the evidence did not cover.
Mechanism: The ambient temperature at launch was \(36^\circ\text{F}\), 15 degrees colder than any previous launch. O-ring resiliency falls with temperature, and a cold ring returns to shape too slowly to follow the joint gap as ignition pressure opens it. On the eve of launch, engineers at Morton Thiokol, the motor’s contractor, recommended against launching below \(53^\circ\text{F}\), the O-ring temperature of the coldest previous flight, whose joints had shown the worst blow-by to date. That limit was the outer edge of flight experience, not a qualified bound. NASA managers countered with a qualification temperature that applied to the propellant’s bulk temperature rather than to the joint seals.
Impact: A combustion gas leak through the right booster’s aft field joint, beginning at or shortly after ignition, weakened or penetrated the External Tank. The vehicle broke up about 73 seconds after launch, and all seven crew members died.
Response: The presidential Commission attributed the failure to “a faulty design unacceptably sensitive to a number of factors,” and temperature heads its list of those factors. It recommended that the joint be changed and that the new design be certified by tests “over the full range of operating conditions, including temperature.”
Systems lesson: Thiokol management reversed its engineers’ recommendation at the urging of NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center. Thiokol’s vice president of engineering testified, “We had to prove to them that we weren’t ready.” The burden of proof had inverted: rather than requiring proof that the joint was safe inside its evidence, adjudicators demanded proof that it was unsafe outside the evidence, where no data existed. The Commission also found that O-ring erosion had recurred on earlier flights and that NASA and Thiokol “accepted escalating risk apparently because they ‘got away with it last time’” (Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident 1986), so the flight record itself had been read as evidence of safety. A release verdict keeps the burden where the envelope trichotomy puts it. A condition outside the evidence, such as a seal temperature below all flight experience, is unknown, and the verdict refuses it.


The Tempe collision analyzed in When the Responsibilities Fail Together rested on an unmeasured premise of the same kind as Challenger’s seal temperature. Its vehicle operator was the countermeasure the whole system leaned on, so the premise was that the operator was watching, and nothing measured whether that held. A release case that relies on such a premise must bind its operational response, whether an outright refusal or a restricted case, to verified physical limits, as claim C6 does for authority transfer. Even a case that survives this adversarial review has had its warrants tested only in principle while its verdict still lives on paper. The release manifest turns the surviving argument and the verdict it supports into a signed, tamper-evident record that the machine itself checks before it moves.


↩︎ The operator-monitoring failures that a human-takeover premise invites, from mode confusion to authority ambiguity, are established in Authority Handover Failure Modes.

title: Deployment Release
text:
16.8 The Release Manifest
A safety case that lives only in static documents or procedural sign-off sheets cannot stop a robot from booting with an unverified policy checkpoint or stale sensor calibrations. To make the verdict enforceable on hardware, the adjudicator’s decision is recorded in the release manifest, the fourteenth record in the book’s record chain. This signed, tamper-evident data structure binds every upstream engineering contract, the Goal Structuring Notation argument graph, the operating envelope limits, and live standing conditions to the adjudicator’s verdict by cryptographic digest. The target platform refuses physical motion whenever runtime binary images, silicon attestation measurements, or underlying qualification data diverge from these signed digests.11
11 Cryptographic Manifest and Silicon Attestation: One-time programmable electronic fuses (OTP/eFuse) store the adjudicator’s public verification key in silicon, preventing unauthorized software updates from replacing the root of trust. Secure bootstrap validates each early boot stage before handing over execution control (Arbaugh et al. 1997), while measured boot extends cryptographic measurements into Trusted Platform Module Platform Configuration Registers (TPM PCRs). The hardware verifier checks these measurements against the digests specified in the signed manifest; any unsigned or modified binary image fails attestation and never receives an operational permit.
Arbaugh, William A., David J. Farber, and Jonathan M. Smith. 1997. “A Secure and Reliable Bootstrap Architecture.” Proceedings of the 1997 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 65–71. https://doi.org/10.1109/SECPRI.1997.601317.

↪ The residual-claims register, the record that follows the release manifest and ties each premise it leaves open to an operational restriction, is developed in A residual-claims register.

The release manifest gathers the engineering contracts established throughout this book. Each upstream record defines an operating boundary or contributes empirical data that the safety case must check; a signature on an isolated contract does not validate the system as a whole. Instead, the manifest links reviewed snapshots of these records into a single argument graph:

Physical plant and timing base: The limit record (The six elements of a limit record) documents torque, velocity, and thermal dissipation bounds alongside their qualification data. The proposer’s payload requirements (Information the proposer must supply) specify candidate action horizons that feed the handoff record rather than standing as an isolated contract. The handoff record (The Handoffs Matrix) establishes deterministic fieldbus jitter, cycle deadlines, and real-time communication premises.
Data, policy, and behavioral bounds: The provenance record (The Dataset Schema) captures dataset calibrations, sensor configurations, and operating-domain coverage. The policy manifest (The Policy Manifest) binds frozen neural network weights to the empirical behavioral bounds proven for that candidate model. The evaluation record (The Evaluation Record) details closed-loop task success rates, human intervention tallies, and stress-tested operational conditions.
Perception, belief, and planning: The observation contract (The Observation Contract) enforces observation freshness and multi-sensor synchronization windows. The belief record (The Spatial Memory Handoff and State Invariants) specifies geometric state estimates, state covariance, and validity domains. The intent lease (The Intent Handoff and Bounded Authority) records task objectives, spatial tolerances, and preemption conditions. The trajectory record (The Trajectory Record) encodes motion profiles, kinematic seam continuity, execution deadlines, and safe stopping continuations.
Deterministic containment, execution, and verification: The enforcement record (The admitted command schema) logs the command stream admitted by runtime safety filters, cleanly separated from the signed enforcement contract that specifies barrier functions and fallback triggers. The placement record (The Placement Record) documents the qualified compute scheduling, memory isolation, and processor affinity. The authority record (The Authority Record) documents arbitration switches and fallback outcomes. The fault records (Fault Records for Release) index tested fault-injection scenarios alongside known coverage gaps.

Beyond linking these upstream contracts, the release manifest adds its own fields. It carries the root claim, the cryptographic digest of the Goal Structuring Notation argument graph, and binary hashes across all deployed software (spanning learned policy weights, the deterministic enforcer logic in both nominal and restricted modes, and the real-time operating system kernel). It also carries sensor calibration tables, the adjudicator’s digital signature, mandatory standing operational conditions, an accumulated lifecycle wear budget of operating hours and load cycles, and a calendar expiration timestamp. All evidence links must resolve to these exact reviewed record digests, organized hierarchically beneath a single evidence root structured as a Merkle hash tree (Merkle 1988). Each parent digest is computed from its children’s digests, so changing an evidence leaf changes the root that the manifest signs. Only when the hardware root of trust authenticates this complete cryptographic tree will it permit the motor power stages to energize. While traditional release notes or post hoc compliance certificates summarize safety after the fact, the release manifest is an active, machine-checked gate. The robot checks it before closed-loop control begins, and its runtime monitors revoke motor tracking within a bounded detection-and-response window if any underlying evidence or environmental condition expires.

Merkle, Ralph C. 1988. “A Digital Signature Based on a Conventional Encryption Function.” Advances in Cryptology — CRYPTO ’87, Lecture notes in computer science, vol. 293: 369–78. https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-48184-2_32.

↪ Byte layout: The release manifest’s fields, types, and digests are given in Release manifest.

Figure 3 routes every release attempt through authentication and physical standing checks before an operating permit can issue. The release gate authenticates the manifest, binary images, and complete set of fault records before verifying current sensor calibration, mechanical maintenance thresholds, and operational design domain conditions. Only an exact cryptographic and physical match enables the plant’s certified startup sequence. Table 6 lists the gate result for each combination of signed case and standing check, including the single path by which stale calibration still reaches COND. A separately signed COND case can tolerate a named stale calibration only when its restricted envelope either locks out the motions that depend on that sensor, such as prohibiting base transit when the tote-rack scale is stale, or widens the uncertainty allowance and derates speed to cover worst-case calibration drift. During active motion, any breached condition commands an assessed safe fallback before any switch of software partition (the A/B banks of section 16.9.1) or electrical isolation.


↪ Protocol: The gate’s step-by-step authorization protocol is given in Release-gate protocol.






Figure 3: Fail-closed release pipeline: The signed verdict and evidence root pass key, image, and complete fault-record authentication, then current calibration, brake, and operating-envelope checks. Every failure path ends in REFUSE. A valid case reaches UNCOND or COND according to what was signed, and stale calibration reaches COND only through a separately signed restricted case; either way, each proposed action is still checked by the permission path.
