Each empirical evidence leaf in the assurance Merkle tree must identify its raw sensor trace, instrumentation hardware, calibration log, machine configuration, and automated test harness script. Analytical leaves retain their derivations and assumptions; procedural leaves retain the accountable procedure and its validation for the signed envelope. Measured latency profiles enter the safety case as empirical percentiles, whereas deterministic real-time execution guarantees demand the analytically justified upper bounds specified in Real-Time Command Transport and Bus Determinism. Similarly, collaborative object-handover criteria require load-cell time series recorded against standardized anthropomorphic surrogates across specified contact geometries. By cryptographically anchoring these primary records, an independent auditor or verification engine can reproduce the experimental test suite and pinpoint the exact operating boundaries where each safety claim ceases to hold.
The release manifest bounds the physical envelope and hardware configuration under which its verdict remains valid. Modifying a neural policy checkpoint, altering a real-time thread priority, updating a device driver, or replacing an actuator with an unverified component revision immediately invalidates the manifest, requiring a re-adjudicated safety case. On the warehouse mobile manipulator, for example, the manifest enforces signed wear thresholds on harmonic-drive backlash and electromagnetic brake lining thickness derived from stopping-distance and payload trials. Operating envelope tripwires trigger immediate refusal: on-board load cells detect tote-rack overloading beyond rated payload capacity, while facility procedures prevent operation on unmapped or unsurveyed floor surfaces (table 1). The manifest also encodes the isolated, energy-buffered power rail of the permission path as a standing invariant, running a diagnostic self-test on the hold-up capacitor bank before granting boot authorization. Whenever a runtime sensor detects that a state variable has breached a signed threshold, the hardware permission path interrupts closed-loop trajectory tracking within its certified detection-and-response deadline and brings the system to an assessed fallback state.
To preserve traceability across time, the manifest binds all operational telemetry directly to the exact hardware-software revision that generated it. High-resolution local ring buffers capture boundary excursions for post-incident diagnostics, whereas fleet-wide telemetry summaries reveal systematic mechanical drift across hundreds of operating hours. The curation pipelines examined in section 16.9.5 must preserve this cryptographic lineage whenever field data is promoted to support a later release case.
During daily operation, edge telemetry logs motor torque residuals, control-loop cycle times, and safety enforcer interventions for trend analysis, while the hardware permission path checks physical invariants on every 1 ms permission tick. If a routine maintenance check measures a stopping distance exceeding the signed clearance budget, or if a camera calibration certificate expires, the release verdict is revoked automatically. Re-flashing an older firmware image cannot compensate for worn mechanical friction pads. Unless an engineer deploys a separately signed restricted case (COND) that explicitly accommodates that degraded physical state, the controller executes an assessed emergency stop and locks out autonomous motion until certified maintenance and re-adjudication take place (table 6).
Once its powered stop has brought the base to rest, the warehouse mobile manipulator can reach a quiescent state only after the arm and payload are supported and the assessed holding brakes are engaged before drive power is removed. The base rests stably on the floor, but that support alone does not secure its gravity-loaded arm. For other morphologies, severing motor power is itself the hazard, because the machine collapses under gravity once torque is removed (perspective 16.1).

Systems Perspective 16.1: When removing torque causes the harm
Question: Which verdict applies when removing torque causes the harm?
A supported wheeled base at rest eliminates its translational kinetic hazard, though its arm and payload still require qualified support. In contrast, an upright bipedal humanoid retains substantial gravitational potential energy. While resting in a support gantry before standing up, a REFUSE verdict safely holds the robot in its mechanically supported state. Once balanced upright, however, revoking locomotion authority cannot simply de-energize the actuators without inducing an immediate dynamic fall; safe shutdown requires an active, validated arrest or controlled descent strategy.

Torque removal can cause a fall. An unsupported biped with backdrivable transmissions will collapse if motor currents drop to zero: torque removal leaves gravity-loaded joints without support (Actuation Authority), and an upright biped without active balance diverges like an inverted pendulum (Coupling the distance, lease, and supply budgets). Consequently, such physical plants cannot treat torque removal as a fail-safe stopping condition unless accompanied by certified passive catches, lock-up brakes, or an external tether.
The fall-arrest response is itself an actuation. Executing a controlled squat, brace, or step-down to bring the robot to rest is itself an active trajectory that requires validated sensorimotor claims, verified timing margins, and fault-tolerance guarantees. In this regime, executing a safe REFUSE action depends on the very control systems maintaining upright stability.
Wear revokes the running permit. Degradation in foot-sole rubber traction or increased backlash in planetary gearheads alters the dynamic margin required for emergency balancing. When telemetry signals that physical wear has crossed the threshold certified in the safety case, the runtime supervisor must revoke high-speed dynamic locomotion well before the safety-critical arrest maneuvers degrade below their qualifying safety margins.




Checkpoint 16.3: Deriving a verdict from your own measurements
Table 5 lists the measurements needed to support a release case but supplies no raw trial results. Make a copy with columns for value, source, provenance, and premise status, fill those columns with empirical data from hardware trials on your own robotic platform or an illustrative benchmark scenario, and evaluate the resulting release verdict:

Provenance and premise status: For each row, record measured, derived, datasheet, or illustrative provenance; label selected operating requirements as chosen. A derived result retains its inputs and assumptions and remains illustrative when those inputs are illustrative. A selected substitute for an unmeasured brake value is illustrative, whereas a chosen speed cap needs qualified evidence that it fits. A manufacturer’s rating is datasheet evidence, not a measurement of this unit. Separately apply the Reader Guide’s five premise statuses: established by measurement or derivation, assumed, decided by accountable judgment, unsupported, or outside the threat model. Explain why each credited assumption or restriction is warranted for the signed envelope; a status label grants no authority. Runtime known-true, known-false, and unknown describe current envelope membership, not provenance.
Verdict derivation: A COND case requires adequate support for every relied-on premise: qualified measurements, justified analysis, or validated operating restrictions. Illustrative values alone still support only an actual REFUSE. Recompute the base’s budget and spare margin from your values. If every relied-on premise has adequate support, name the envelope the COND case signs and the premise that keeps the normal mode unsigned. If a relied-on premise lacks adequate support, derive the verdict the table would support given the missing evidence, and label that verdict hypothetical.
Artifact label: Mark the filled table as your own work, whose values license no physical machine.



A release manifest binds the verdict to an explicit, reviewed system configuration. Any later modification, whether retraining a perception head, tightening an actuator torque limit, or swapping a camera lens, breaks that closure and reopens some of the underlying claims. The question the rest of the chapter answers is which ones, and how the machine stays contained while the reopened claims are requalified.

title: Deployment Release
text:
16.9 Maintaining Release Through Updates
Continuing the stipulated warehouse branch, suppose the mobile manipulator’s restricted mug-delivery policy is retrained to reduce hesitation at the controlled pick station. Pushing that updated checkpoint directly to the fleet would invalidate the signed manifest and expose the machine to unverified bus loads and contact trajectories. Before the candidate neural policy can issue commands to physical actuators, it must pass back through the release decision. A signed safety case establishes which historical evidence remains valid, which hardware-in-the-loop tests must run again, and how the machine maintains physical containment throughout the update.


↩︎ Every updated checkpoint is a new policy whose earlier evaluations no longer apply, the rule established in Real-Robot Fine-Tuning and Residual Control that gives each one its own manifest and regression evidence.

16.9.1 Modular safety cases and over-the-air updates
Retraining a policy directly alters capability evidence, and neural modifications often introduce side effects across the shared hardware platform: increased neural accelerator memory bus traffic, altered sensor frame processing latency, or modified contact force trajectories. An engineer must trace these cross-subsystem dependencies before deciding which containment records remain valid. While over-the-air (OTA) updates swap out a named software payload, modular safety cases isolate dependencies by recording how each claim relies on specific evidence items and platform assumptions (Denney et al. 2015). Whenever an update alters an underlying dependency, the modular case shows exactly which safety claims are reopened.
The containment argument is the defense against physical harm. It binds together the plant model, physical sensor limits, worst-case execution budgets, and the independent permission path. Key engineering premises include the bounded tracking error tube \(\TrackingErrorBound\), the emergency stopping budget, the passivity barrier for physical contact, and hardware watchdog timing margins. Historical verification records for these containment claims remain valid only if the proposed update preserves the exact operating conditions under which they were measured. For example, replacing a backbone network with a higher-capacity model can increase memory bus contention or cause voltage droop on the power rail even if the deterministic safety-filter binary remains byte-for-byte identical. An unchanged enforcer binary does not imply an unchanged containment argument; its guarantees remain bounded by the validated dynamic envelope \(\ForwardInvariantSafeSet\) and the system-level timing margins established during qualification.


↩︎ The tracking-error tube \(\TrackingErrorBound\) that the containment argument consumes as an invariant is established in The Tracker Handoff and Dynamic Reference Envelopes.
In parallel, the capability argument shows that the robot reliably fulfills its mission within its certified operational design domain. Candidate benchmarking, passive shadow traces, and geofenced closed-loop trials test whether a retrained policy reduces hesitation or improves task throughput. While the low-level enforcer can continuously clamp or reject invalid control proposals to maintain safety, an enforcer that constantly intervenes degrades the robot into an unusable, halting machine. Release engineering therefore evaluates capability and containment together. An update qualifies for fleet dispatch only when the candidate configuration delivers acceptable task performance without undermining the empirical premises supporting its containment envelope.
Modern physical AI platforms preserve configuration integrity during deployment through dual A/B OS partitioning. The update agent streams the candidate image onto the inactive storage bank (Bank B) while the incumbent controller continues executing from the active bank (Bank A). Activating the newly flashed partition requires an assessed stationary update state. The robot must be parked with its payload supported. Battery reserves must exceed with margin the energy needed for re-flashing and post-boot self-tests. The independent safety supervisor must hold all motor drives unpowered or mechanically locked so the robot cannot move during bootloader cutover. Hardware watchdogs govern the runtime decision to commit or abort this cutover (section 16.9.4). A single fleetwide signing key is a single point of compromise, because an attacker who extracts that key from one compromised endpoint could sign arbitrary firmware for every robot in the field. Update architectures therefore use role-separated signing structures where distinct root, targets, and release keys live on separate, hardware-isolated machines. The Update Framework (TUF) pioneered this design, and Uptane extended it to automotive and robotics systems where heterogeneous electronic control units require independently authenticated firmware images (Samuel et al. 2010; Kuppusamy et al. 2016).
Overwriting firmware must never destroy the physical calibration history of an individual robot. Persistent hardware calibration parameter retention separates machine-specific measurements from generic operating system binaries, preventing a calibration clashing failure. Camera intrinsic matrices (\(\CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix\)), extrinsic sensor transformations (\([\DirectionalCosineMatrix \mid \RigidTransformTranslation]\)), kinematic joint zero-point offsets, and motor torque constants (\(\MotorTorqueConstant\)) reflect the mechanical and electrical geometry of an individual machine and drift over time with vibration, thermal cycling, and wear. Storing these values in a dedicated, wear-leveled, non-volatile parameter partition keeps calibration intact when an OS image is flashed. When a firmware update introduces a revised parameter schema, the migration utility writes the transformed schema into a new record while preserving the legacy block, allowing direct rollback to the prior image-parameter pair. Cryptographic checksums verify the bit-level integrity of these stored calibration blocks, while physical self-tests at field release verify that the stored parameters still match the physical machine.
Finally, forensic traceability links every running OS image, policy checkpoint, and calibration partition to its training provenance, compiler flags, and reviewed HIL regression records through the signed release manifest (section 16.8). When an unexpected field intervention or trajectory excursion occurs, these links let incident investigators reconstruct the exact configuration running at that millisecond and determine which safety warrants need re-examination. While a cryptographic digest confirms identity, isolating the physical root cause requires detailed sensor traces and causal analysis.


16.9.2 Staging candidate policies before release
Software simulation models timing and electrical behavior only to the accuracy of its mathematical approximations; it cannot catch memory-bus contention, fieldbus noise, or inverter thermal sag on the real processor and drive electronics. A candidate policy must therefore repeat the hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) regression gates affected by its changes on a physical test bench under full thermal and electrical load. The bench tests the specific interference and fault mechanisms on which release claims depend:

Worst-case execution time (WCET) and scheduling jitter: Profiling whether safety filter evaluations complete within their hard real-time deadlines (\(\WorstCasePermissionCycleTime \le \CompletionDeadline\)) while neural workloads drive peak memory crossbar contention and DMA transfers, the falsification campaign of Empirical Verification of Silicon Isolation.
Deterministic bus arbitration: Measuring fieldbus communication jitter and cyclic transmission integrity across physical EtherCAT or CAN FD networks under simulated telemetry broadcast floods and electrical noise injection.
Power-stage thermal dynamics and current ripple: Verifying that high-frequency control chatter or torque ripple proposed by the candidate policy does not induce excessive inverter switching losses, DC rail voltage sag, or thermal runaway in motor windings (Thermal Duty Cycles).
Hardware fault-injection survivability: Validating that physical line breaks, power supply brownouts, or deserializer frame dropouts deterministically trigger the hardware watchdog and safe-stop sequence within certified timing budgets before motor power stages can be damaged.

A candidate policy advances through bench staging only when every required regression test passes and empirical records confirm that timing and physical margins remain intact. Observing zero deadline overruns during a finite bench campaign does not by itself establish a mathematical upper bound on worst-case execution time, nor does it show how the policy will behave on the warehouse floor. In cloud software engineering, blue-green deployment can reduce downtime by preparing a replacement cluster and redirecting traffic after readiness checks. In physical AI, however, blue-green cutover cannot happen mid-stride or at speed. Swapping active control authority between an incumbent controller and a candidate policy while mass is moving requires managing actuator state continuity, motor winding back-EMF, and dynamic tracking tubes (Command steps and mechanical drivetrain shock). De-energizing motor windings or inducing sudden torque steps causes severe mechanical shock loads (\(\GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia \LinkAngularAcceleration\)) and loss of traction. An unvalidated policy also cannot be granted partial motor authority in a populated warehouse to “canary test” edge-case performance.
Safe predeployment staging instead relies on shadow mode deployment, the shadow-operation evidence regime of The four evaluation evidence regimes applied to a release candidate. The incumbent controller \(\pi_{\text{incumbent}}\) supplies proposals, while the independent enforcer retains sole actuator-output ownership and checks each command before fieldbus dispatch. Concurrently in the background, the candidate neural policy \(\pi_{\text{candidate}}\) executes on the host compute SoC, consuming identical live sensor streams \(\MultimodalObservation_{t}\) within its qualified shared-resource budget and computing what control command \(\CandidateControlCommand_t \sim \pi_{\text{candidate}}(\MultimodalObservation_{t})\) it would have proposed. The candidate writes its outputs to an isolated telemetry buffer that grants no actuator authority. Consumers can read that record, but neither the buffer nor the candidate can bypass the enforcer. Shadow inference and recording must stay within the interference and power budgets that preserve the active case. Discrepancies between candidate proposals and the incumbent’s admitted commands are logged as high-rate telemetry events without admitting any candidate command to the drives.
Shadow-mode telemetry monitors two instantaneous divergence metrics:

Action discrepancy (\(\FiniteChange\ControlCommand_t\)): The Euclidean (or angular) distance between the candidate proposal and the incumbent control action, measured here by the Euclidean norm: \[\|\FiniteChange\ControlCommand_t\|_2 = \| \CandidateControlCommand_t - \IncumbentControlCommand_t \|_2.\] Sustained spikes in \(\|\FiniteChange\ControlCommand_t\|_2\) identify behavioral divergence where the candidate policy introduces unmodeled bias, high-frequency control jitter, or erratic steering commands. In addition, the discrepancy analyzer monitors the command-rate norm \(\|\CandidateControlCommandDerivative_t\|_2\), which is a torque-rate norm only when \(\ControlCommand\) is a torque command, to detect unmodeled control chatter that would excite mechanical resonances.
Safety barrier margin discrepancy (\(\FiniteChange \BarrierFunctionRate_t\)): The differential proximity to forward-invariant safety boundaries under a control barrier function \(\BarrierFunction(\MechanicalPlantState)\) (Safe Sets as Conditional Permission): \[\FiniteChange \BarrierFunctionRate_t = \BarrierFunctionRate(\EstimatedPlantState_t, \CandidateControlCommand_t) - \BarrierFunctionRate(\EstimatedPlantState_t, \IncumbentControlCommand_t),\] where \(\EstimatedPlantState_t\) is the state estimated from the sensor streams \(\MultimodalObservation_{t}\). A negative \(\FiniteChange \BarrierFunctionRate_t\) means the candidate has a smaller modeled barrier derivative than the incumbent. Both derivatives can still be positive, so the sign alone does not imply decreasing clearance or a violated boundary of \(\ForwardInvariantSafeSet\) (defined by \(\BarrierFunction(\MechanicalPlantState)\)).

The two discrepancies answer different questions. A large action discrepancy \(\|\FiniteChange\ControlCommand_t\|_2\) can reflect an alternate useful action, while \(\FiniteChange \BarrierFunctionRate_t\) indicates how the proposals differ in their modeled effect on the barrier. Neither sign alone supplies a verdict; review must consider the current margin, uncertainty, and the condition that the independent enforcer would require.
Shadow mode nevertheless has a limit that more traces cannot remove, the trajectory confinement of that evidence regime, which a release reviewer encounters as counterfactual divergence. Because admitted incumbent proposals determine the plant trajectory, the historical state trajectory \((\DecisionProcessState_0, \IncumbentControlCommand_0, \DecisionProcessState_1, \IncumbentControlCommand_1, \dots)\) is conditioned entirely on incumbent actions, and the candidate’s proposals \(\CandidateControlCommand_t\) never alter it. Conflating open-loop agreement with deployment safety is the open-loop replay fallacy: assuming that high action agreement during passive trace replay guarantees closed-loop dynamic stability. The \(\CovariateDriftBound\) result in Recovery and Compounding Error is an expected-cost bound under its stated imitation-learning assumptions, not a universal law for physical tracking error. A candidate that agrees on incumbent trajectories can still visit unfamiliar states or excite unmodeled dynamics when it closes the loop, the covariate shift that interactive imitation learning was designed to correct (Ross et al. 2011). Shadow mode is an essential pre-filter for gross behavioral anomalies, but never a substitute for closed-loop dynamic qualification.

Ross, Stéphane, Geoffrey Gordon, and J. Andrew Bagnell. 2011. “A Reduction of Imitation Learning and Structured Prediction to No-Regret Online Learning.” Proceedings of the Fourteenth International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS) 15: 627–35.
12 Canary (the miners’ sentinel bird): Miners carried caged canaries because the birds succumb to carbon monoxide before people do, so a bird’s distress warned the crew to leave. The metaphor carries this section’s warning. The canary is the unit exposed to the hazard first, so on a physical fleet its exposure must be bounded by containment, not by how few units are chosen.Phased canary fleet rollouts12 expose the candidate to closed-loop operation under a separately supported restricted case. Selecting fewer machines limits exposure but does not bound the consequence of any one action. The restrictions must address the physical hazard:

Geofenced operational containment: Canary units operate exclusively within dedicated, surveyed low-risk corridors, such as wide transit aisles devoid of blind rack corners, reduced pedestrian density, and high-friction surveyed concrete (\(\CoulombFrictionCoefficient \ge\) 0.60).
Enforced kinematic derating: The real-time safety enforcer clamps candidate policy velocity and acceleration below nominal ratings (\(\SpeedAtDetection \le \CanarySpeedBound < \NominalRatedSpeed\)), expanding stopping distance margins and suppressing transient kinetic energy.
Supervised human oversight: High-readiness human supervisors equipped with wireless remote emergency-stop (tele-stop) pendants maintain line-of-sight monitoring over canary units, backed by an active-lease watchdog.
Targeted regression observability: The trial measures tracking error variance \(\CandidateTrackingErrorStandardDeviation^2\), drive torque ripple, and enforcer intervention frequency to reveal service regressions. The permission path retains only the containment claims validated for the restricted envelope.

Expansion requires predeclared acceptance criteria tied to the service and physical claims. Intervention-rate non-inferiority13 and tracking variance \(\CandidateTrackingErrorStandardDeviation^2 \le \IncumbentTrackingErrorStandardDeviation^2\) are possible capability criteria, with their comparison conditions and statistical assumptions stated. The non-inferiority margin \(\NoninferiorityRatioMargin\) is fixed before the trial, so that the upper one-sided 95 percent confidence bound on the rate ratio \(\CanaryInterventionRate/\IncumbentInterventionRate\) must fall below \(1+\NoninferiorityRatioMargin\). With a zero margin, that upper-bound criterion requires evidence that the candidate is better, which may demand more exposure than a small canary provides. The trial arithmetic of Trial Budgets, Stopping Rules, and Comparisons sets how much operation a given \(\NoninferiorityRatioMargin\) requires. A sequential test can stop expansion as soon as the evidence suffices. None of these criteria replaces the evidence for stopping, observation, or containment. An enforcer intervention also needs causal review, because suppressing legitimate clamps to improve a rollout metric would weaken the release argument.
13 Non-Inferiority Testing: The design comes from clinical trials, where failing to find a difference proves nothing, so a new treatment must instead be shown worse than the standard by no more than a margin fixed before any data arrive (Blackwelder 1982). A canary can therefore pass on modest exposure without proving the candidate better, but only if \(\NoninferiorityRatioMargin\) was not chosen after the result was seen.
Blackwelder, William C. 1982. “‘Proving the Null Hypothesis’ in Clinical Trials.” Controlled Clinical Trials 3 (4): 345–53. https://doi.org/10.1016/0197-2456(82)90024-1.

↩︎ The sequential probability ratio test, which stops a trial campaign as soon as the evidence crosses a precalibrated boundary, is established in Sequential probability ratio testing.



16.9.3 From qualification to a new manifest
Reducing a policy’s hesitation rate at the pick station does not justify relaxing its contact-force limits or floor-friction restrictions. If the retrained mug-delivery candidate were promoted on task speed alone, it would bypass the containment premises that keep the restricted route safe. Instead, the reviewer repeats closed-loop capability evaluation under the restricted route and feed conditions, and repeats the loaded timing and fault tests whose dependencies changed. Unaffected plant evidence remains reusable only while configuration, calibration, wear, and site premises still match.
Assume, still within the stipulated branch, that those results satisfy the predeclared capability criteria and preserve the containment claims. The adjudicator issues a new manifest binding the candidate, retained and repeated evidence, current calibration, and the same restricted mission. At the assessed stationary cutover state, the gate authenticates that manifest and checks current standing conditions before admitting new proposals. Field monitoring then compares the running service with the same success, cycle-time, rescue, and protection criteria. Failed qualification leaves the incumbent case unchanged; a failed standing condition withdraws the affected grant.


16.9.4 Over-the-air staging and watchdog-enforced rollbacks
A candidate written to the inactive bank inherits no operating grant from its predecessor, and rolling back to the prior software image cannot repair a worn brake or a stale calibration. Hardware watchdog rollback triggers must therefore distinguish a failure to boot from a failure during motion. Before tracking is enabled, failed image authentication, startup tests, or fieldbus synchronization can reject the candidate and select the retained image, which must still pass current calibration and standing-condition checks before receiving a permit.
During motion, the independent supervisor first commands the assessed fallback within its measured response budget. Where that response ends in torque removal, the supervisor asserts Safe Torque Off after the required controlled stop; a plant needing a powered hold retains the authority needed for that hold. Unlike a conventional compute watchdog that resets the processor immediately upon a timeout, a missed enforcer heartbeat withdraws tracking permission and triggers the hardware-controlled stop without resetting the processor mid-motion. Only after the plant has come to rest in its validated update state may the boot selector change banks.
The image and its compatible calibration schema form the rollback unit. If either record is missing, corrupted, or physically stale, the gate selects REFUSE unless a separately signed restricted case covers the actual state and its limits, such as \(\SpeedAtDetection \le \RestrictedSpeedBound\). Retaining the prior binary image provides an immediate rollback target, but operators must re-validate standing physical conditions before the recovered binary receives an operating permit.


16.9.5 Event-triggered telemetry and safety performance indicators
An enforcer trip can reveal a policy failure, a changed physical premise, or both, and the field record must let the reviewer distinguish those causes before choosing retraining, maintenance, or a narrower envelope. Because wireless summaries alone cannot reconstruct the observations and actuator response around the event, detailed traces are retained locally. Edge event-triggered telemetry captures the sensor, proposal, permission, actuator, and timestamp chain around an intervention or boundary excursion. A local rolling buffer preserves the lead-up, and capture continues through the physical response whenever the qualified recording power path survives. Buffer length, write bandwidth, and hold-up energy are sized from the required reconstruction window and verified under the same contention and power faults as the permission path. A logic-rail capacitor does not guarantee that the full sensor and storage path survives, and recording must never delay the stop.
UL 4600 calls the field measurements that keep a claim alive safety performance indicators (SPIs). Each is a metric tied to a named claim, with a threshold and a predeclared response when the threshold is crossed (UL Standards & Engagement 2023). On the running machine, every standing condition of section 16.5 has one. Measured stop distance at scheduled trials and enforcer trips per operating hour watch the base’s stopping claim, age refusals per operating hour watch the observation-age claim, and localization residuals against their allowance watch the sensor geometry. An SPI whose threshold is crossed withdraws or narrows the grant it watches; one that drifts toward its threshold triggers review before it is crossed, which is the defense against the normalization of deviance of section 16.7.
During routine operation, compact health summaries support fleet monitoring while required incident records retain full provenance locally until transfer succeeds. Learning-data filters may prioritize unfamiliar events for training, provided they never discard required safety evidence or hide repeated failures. Once the traces arrive, a reviewer distinguishes policy hesitation from calibration drift, surface contamination, and mechanism wear before assigning the repair: qualified recovery traces can enter the experience pipeline, whereas reconstructed simulations extend test coverage only over their modeled conditions. A captured event therefore changes the release argument only after its physical cause and operating conditions are established. Reconstructed scenes and retraining can improve a candidate policy, yet neither automatically repairs a physical warrant, so the revised claim must return through the relevant qualification stages before a new manifest grants authority. Because the traces the machine keeps also record the people around it, each record that identifies a person carries standing conditions of its own: a declared purpose, a retention period, and a list of readers, audited like any other premise.


↪ The declarations that govern records identifying people, and the access and retention audit that enforces them, are developed in Recorded people as a standing condition.


16.9.6 Fleet evidence and accountable release
Teams break the safety warrant when they pool dissimilar routes into a single fleet mileage total or treat an operator intervention count as a collision rate. Fleet exposure can reveal recurring failures, but interpreting it requires knowing the operating domain, the intervention definition, and the exact system configuration. The release reviewer uses fleet records to challenge the same capability and containment claims, rather than replacing them with a mileage ranking. One public fleet record shows what an interpretable version looks like. Waymo publishes its rider-only crash rates by outcome, each against a human-driven benchmark adjusted to the same locations and each with a confidence interval. It republishes them as rider-only mileage accumulates (Waymo 2026; Kusano et al. 2025). Figure 4 plots the latest release and the history of two of its outcomes.

Kusano, Kristofer D., John M. Scanlon, Yin-Hsiu Chen, Timothy L. McMurry, Tilia Gode, and Trent Victor. 2025. “Comparison of Waymo Rider-Only Crash Rates by Crash Type to Human Benchmarks at 56.7 Million Miles.” Traffic Injury Prevention 26 (sup1). https://doi.org/10.1080/15389588.2025.2499887.














Figure 4: Exposure licenses claims one outcome at a time: (a) Percent change in crash rate against a location-adjusted human benchmark for each outcome in the latest public release, with 95 percent confidence intervals and the number of fleet crashes behind each estimate; orange marks outcomes with fewer than 20 crashes. (b) The same estimate and interval for two outcomes at each release, against cumulative rider-only miles. Common outcomes converge to narrow intervals; the serious-injury and fatal estimates rest on a few events, so their intervals stay wide however favorable the point estimate. Data from Waymo (2026).


Waymo. 2026. Waymo Safety Impact Data Hub.


In the June 2026 release, after 271 million rider-only miles, the injury estimate rests on 183 crashes and its interval spans a reduction of 79 to 85 percent. The serious-injury estimate rests on 3 crashes and spans 83 to 99 percent, and the fatal estimate rests on 2 and spans 18 to 98 percent. The same mileage therefore licenses a tight claim about common crashes and only a loose one about the outcomes a release decision cares about most, because rare events accumulate slowly however many miles the fleet drives. That is the fourth law, permission must be earned (principle \(\ref{pri-vol4-evidence-bounds-authority}\)), measured on a real fleet. Each outcome’s claim may extend only as far as its own interval, and a reviewer reads the interval before the point estimate.
The signed release manifest records the engineering decision and its accountable owner, and together with the records it binds, it lets an investigator follow one admitted action back to the person who signed for it. The enforcement record logs the admitted command. The manifest in force at that moment names by digest the policy weights, the enforcer and real-time operating system binaries, the calibration tables, and the operating envelope behind it. The signature on that manifest, made with a key held in a hardware security module, is bound to the sign-off record that names the lead systems adjudicator who accepted that configuration or the update that installed it. The manifest does not itself establish regulatory compliance or determine legal liability. Applicable requirements depend on the machine, intended use, and jurisdiction; the release manifest must preserve the evidence needed for that separate assessment. Throughout this lifecycle, release remains a decision about a named machine under named conditions. Shadow traces, staged trials, and field records can strengthen the next argument only when their operating conditions and limits are explicit, while the manifest and independent permission path retain the restrictions that the evidence supports.


↪ Who answers for each decision the manifest binds, and the duty to report an incident completely and on time, are developed in The Approval Record.

title: Deployment Release
text:
16.10 Fallacies and Pitfalls
In purely digital software, a deployment bug manifests as a silent crash, a corrupted database row, or a dropped network packet; in physical AI, software decisions drive heavy actuators through real space where errors bend steel, destroy machinery, and injure coworkers. Releasing an embodied AI system therefore requires uncovering hidden assumptions before kinetic energy is coupled to physical mass. The following fallacies and pitfalls highlight recurring mistakes where teams confuse software statistical confidence with cyber-physical safety.

Fallacy: Statistical coverage substitutes for deterministic architectural warrants.
Engineering teams frequently present millions of simulated hours and thousands of incident-free test cycles as primary justification for deployment release. While physical and simulated exposure provides valuable empirical evidence regarding typical operating regimes, proving the ultra-low catastrophic failure rate required by a safety release claim demands far more operational hours than any physical test campaign can execute. Simulation environments also depend on idealized models, such as rigid-body dynamics, simplified Coulomb friction, and linear actuator response. Empirical performance and architectural warrants answer different questions. A large trial count cannot substitute for architectural enforcement, such as an independent permission path that revokes motion and executes a certified safe stop. The safety case must establish how deterministic runtime guards actively constrain actuator authority to provably safe physical limits when the learned policy encounters out-of-distribution inputs.
Statistical sampling bounds hazard rates only under observed operational distributions; trial volume cannot substitute for deterministic architectural mechanisms that constrain actuator authority.
Architect’s countermeasure: Couple learned policy evaluation with independently qualified safety monitors. Explicitly state the hazard models, plant dynamics, execution deadlines, and safe-stop fallback conditions under which the system’s safety invariants are deterministically enforced.


Fallacy: A release verdict is a permanent certification of safety.
A machine passes formal validation and enters production under a signed safety case. Over months of operation, brake friction material wears down and lengthens stopping distances, kinematic calibration drifts under daily thermal cycling, and dirt or optical scratches degrade sensor fidelity. Even when the deployed software binaries remain bit-for-bit identical, the physical assumptions underpinning the original release case gradually erode. A signed release verdict certifies safe operation only within a bounded maintenance window and under strict operational thresholds. To maintain safety, the release manifest must establish explicit invalidation triggers and scheduled maintenance intervals tied to hardware lifecycle counters, physical wear measurements, and calibration drift estimates. Once these operational limits are exceeded, the system must automatically restrict its capabilities or halt operation until recalibration and service occur.
Software bit-exactness cannot prevent mechanical wear, material fatigue, or sensor degradation.
Architect’s countermeasure: Treat release manifests as perishable operational leases bounded by operating hours, calendar age, and mechanical cycle counts. Implement automated recalibration self-tests at boot, and require diagnostic verification before energizing high-power motor stages.


Pitfall: Relying on unstated environmental assumptions to support a safety claim.
During commissioning, a team verifies a mobile base’s stopping distance in brightly lit warehouse aisles on clean concrete, documenting floor friction in the safety case while leaving ambient lighting unstated. In production, when the robot enters a dimly lit cross-aisle, longer camera exposure times increase image processing latency, which an age check flags at runtime (section 16.3). Concurrently, sparse visual feature matches degrade state estimation accuracy, introducing unmonitored localization drift that consumes the clearance buffer calculated from well-lit testing (section 16.7). The mechanical brake engages exactly as specified and low-level controller diagnostics report all systems nominal, yet the actual stopping distance margin quietly vanishes. Safety claims depend on operational surroundings. If an environmental boundary is omitted from the safety case, the deployment architecture can neither verify the operating conditions at release nor enforce them at runtime.
Unstated operating assumptions silently erode safety margins until an ordinary environmental fluctuation precipitates a collision.
Architect’s countermeasure: Formally document every environmental assumption (such as ambient illuminance in lux, surface friction coefficients, and ambient thermal bounds) as an explicit premise in the release manifest. Pair each premise with a deterministic runtime detector or an enforced facility operational specification.


Fallacy: Shadow-mode qualification guarantees closed-loop dynamic stability.
An engineering team evaluates a candidate neural policy in shadow mode across thousands of fleet operating hours, recording near-zero action discrepancy (\(\|\FiniteChange\ControlCommand_t\|_2 \approx 0\)) between the candidate policy and the certified incumbent controller. The team infers that high behavioral fidelity during open-loop playback proves the candidate policy is ready for autonomous deployment. However, because the incumbent controller retains active authority over the plant, the state distribution is entirely dictated by the incumbent’s dynamics. The candidate policy never experiences the compounding physical consequences of its own commands. Even minor discrepancies in control output can excite unmodeled mechanical resonances, induce severe actuator chattering, or generate phase lag that destabilizes the physical plant the moment control authority is transferred to the closed loop.
Open-loop trace replay conceals covariate shift, compounding autoregressive errors, and unmodeled plant resonances.
Architect’s countermeasure: Treat shadow mode strictly as an initial filter to catch gross algorithmic discrepancies, never as proof of dynamic stability. Require closed-loop Monte Carlo sweeps across perturbed plant models, followed by supervised canary execution in isolated physical test facilities, before granting live actuation authority.


Fallacy: Web-style canary traffic routing is directly applicable to physical machines.
In cloud engineering, canary deployments safely route a small fraction of live network traffic to a newly deployed service, rolling back the deployment if error rates exceed a set threshold. Attempting to mirror this practice by assigning a percentage of live operational missions to an unvetted neural policy overlooks the physical reality of mass and momentum. A 368 kg vehicle moving at 1.3 m/s carries 311 J of kinetic energy. If an unverified model issues an erratic actuation command near an operator, the resulting collision cannot be mitigated by rolling back a container image or tearing down a replica set.
Kinetic energy and physical momentum render live production canary routing hazardous without deterministic architectural containment.
Architect’s countermeasure: Restrict canary deployments to physically geofenced zones devoid of human personnel. If testing in active production environments is necessary, encapsulate the unvetted policy within an independent, non-preemptible runtime safety enforcer. This permission path must deterministically maintain the vehicle within its certified viable state space across all declared sensing, plant, timing, and fault models, relying on hardware watchdog leases and certified safe-stop drive functions to override invalid actions.


Fallacy: Over-the-air updates can be treated as stateless software deployments.
In web architectures, stateless services restart cleanly from immutable container images. Treating OTA updates on physical robots as simple container replacements ignores the reality of hardware-bound state. Every physical machine possesses unique hardware calibrations: camera extrinsic matrices, joint zero-position encoder offsets, and load-cell tare values, alongside individual mechanical wear profiles. If an OTA update overwrites non-volatile storage or fails to migrate calibration schemas, the updated model executes with distorted sensor transformations. Even minor coordinate offsets introduce spatial localization errors that rapidly deplete geometric clearance budgets and invalidate the stopping guarantees established in the safety case.
Embodied systems are stateful; software updates cannot be decoupled from machine-specific physical calibration.
Architect’s countermeasure: Decouple machine-specific calibrations into an isolated, schema-versioned non-volatile partition (such as EEPROM or write-protected flash) that persists across operating system bank swaps. Use dual A/B system partitions paired with hardware watchdogs that transition the plant into a safe, depowered, or mechanically locked state before changing the active bank. Require automated calibration validation and power-on self-tests before transferring motion authority to the updated partition.


Fallacy: Continuous high-bandwidth wireless telemetry streaming is superior to edge event-triggered buffering.
To achieve comprehensive operational visibility, an engineering team attempts to stream raw multimodal sensor data (high-resolution video, dense lidar point clouds, and 1 kHz motor current logs) continuously over facility Wi-Fi or cellular networks to cloud dashboards. In dense fleet deployments, wireless channel contention, radio frequency (RF) shadowing in industrial bays, and access-point roaming cause severe packet loss and queue bloat precisely during rapid, safety-critical dynamic events. Continuous network serialization also consumes substantial CPU time, DMA channels, and memory bus bandwidth, creating bus contention that can starve real-time safety controllers of deterministic execution guarantees.
Wireless bandwidth is physically constrained and vulnerable to RF fading; continuous raw streaming alone cannot guarantee preservation of telemetry during critical dynamic anomalies.
Architect’s countermeasure: Transmit only compact, low-bandwidth health heartbeats and summary metrics over wireless networks during routine operation. Maintain continuous, high-rate circular telemetry buffers in local non-volatile storage. When a safety fault, anomalous dynamic event, or emergency stop occurs, latch the pre-trigger and post-trigger event windows locally. Size storage write bandwidth and write endurance to prevent memory bus interference with real-time safety enforcers, and offload event packages once the machine establishes a dedicated, high-bandwidth maintenance link.

title: Deployment Release
text:
16.11 Summary
A deployment release formalizes which physical claims the empirical evidence licenses for a specific physical machine, under what operating conditions, and for how long. For the warehouse mobile manipulator examined across these chapters, release resolves to three concrete physical inequalities. The mobile base stops within surveyed clearance. The manipulator unlatches the cage door below the latch’s mechanical force limit. A mug handover remains strictly below the contact criterion for an unconstrained human hand. A formal claim-argument-evidence safety case links each inequality to its supporting premises and experimental evidence within a clearly demarcated operating envelope. Because required premises combine conjunctively, an argument is no stronger than its least supported premise; empirical confidence cannot be averaged across heterogeneous requirements. Independent sufficient legs strengthen support in the stipulated probability model, which estimates neither this robot’s hazard rate nor calibrated assurance confidence. In the physical argument, a policy error cannot breach a monitored invariant only while the qualified enforcement, plant, sensing, timing, and fault premises hold; C5 isolation evidence does not by itself establish statistical independence. Recognized machinery safety standards govern this argumentation structure. Within the permission path, only the safety microcontroller’s lease-expiry timer and heartbeat watchdog are rated safety functions; the other formal protective claims rest on the certified drive, scanner, and arm safety functions beneath it.
An adjudicator evaluates the safety case to deliver one of three definitive verdicts: unconditional release (UNCOND), conditional release (COND), or refusal (REFUSE). If release is granted, standing conditions enforce operational boundaries in real time, automatically withdrawing authorization whenever any relied-upon premise becomes false or unobservable. Records that identify people carry standing conditions of their own, declared and audited like the physical premises (Recorded people as a standing condition). Against this book’s illustrative input datasets, every primary claim contains at least one ungrounded premise, compelling a verdict of REFUSE. A separately stipulated branch illustrates the empirical evidence that would justify restricted conditional service (COND). Before final authorization, an adversarial review must try to break the entire argument, and that scrutiny must recur throughout the operational lifespan. A cryptographically signed manifest binds the release verdict to reviewed software and calibration artifacts by cryptographic digest, failing closed if any binary or configuration changes. Any subsequent model or firmware update must return through the same safety case, because open-loop shadow operation cannot evaluate the physical consequences of unexecuted closed-loop control actions. Table 7 collects the load-bearing equations governing deployment release, detailing the physical or statistical boundary each expression establishes and noting where each was derived in earlier chapters.



Table 7: Key equations of deployment release: Each load-bearing equation of the chapter, the physical boundary it bounds or decision it settles, and the equation where it is derived. Stopping, contact, latch, and exposure relationships originate in preceding chapters; the release case incorporates their mathematical guarantees as foundational premises.










Equation
What it bounds or decides

The three physical criteria every release claim must evidence: stopping clearance, contact force, and execution timing
equation 1


\(\SpeedAtDetection\,\PrebrakeDelay + \ResidentStopDistance(\SpeedAtDetection) + \LocalizationBound + \ProtectiveClearanceMargin + \TrackingErrorBound \le \ClearDistance\)

Key Takeaways: Deployment release and safety cases

The envelope bounds the claim: A release claim covers only the speeds, payloads, surface friction coefficients, clearances, and contact scenarios for which empirical evidence was systematically collected. Every dimension of the operational design domain requires an active runtime monitor or a strictly enforced site procedure.
Doubt accumulates along required premises: A conjunctive argument (\(\bigwedge_i \RequiredPremiseClaim_i\)) is no stronger than its weakest required premise and is often strictly weaker; confidence cannot be averaged across premises. High empirical accuracy in perception cannot offset an unmonitored braking margin or an uncharacterized tail latency. Independent sufficient legs reduce doubt under the stipulated probability model. Policy validation and an isolated permission path do not automatically constitute such legs; the physical containment claim still requires qualified plant, sensing, timing, and fault premises.
Standing conditions make release revocable: Every relied-upon premise requires an active detector or operational procedure, an explicit checking cadence, and a validated safety action triggered whenever the premise evaluates to false or unknown. The signed safety case binds these obligations directly to the machine across its operational life.
Updates return through the release argument: Shadow deployment reveals policy divergence without testing the closed-loop physical consequences of those divergent actions. Rigorous closed-loop qualification and a re-evaluated manifest still govern deployment authorization; every update must preserve machine-specific calibration and execute a validated stop or hold during software cutover.
An unknown premise refuses, and refusal names the next work: In safety argumentation, unknown envelope membership refuses exactly as a measured violation does, while its cause is logged separately. On this book’s illustrative walkthrough, the mobile manipulator receives an explicit verdict of REFUSE. A structured refusal is productive: it isolates the missing measurements, identifies the claims they would ground, and defines the residual operational envelope that remains once those gaps are closed.
Useful service needs its own evidence: The stipulated restricted mug-delivery workflow achieves COND only by satisfying concrete task-success, cycle-time, and human-intervention criteria alongside safety claims C1–C6. Safety filtering can preserve high task completion rates even when raw proposer policy autonomy is comparatively modest.
No verdict moves the proposal boundary: Under both UNCOND and COND, learned policies merely propose actions while the hardware permission path decides physical admission. Within that permission path, only the safety MCU’s lease-expiry and heartbeat watchdog is a rated safety function; the admission checks are not rated. Entering a restricted operational mode requires its own signed release case, never an informal or ad hoc runtime downgrade.



The fourth law, permission must be earned (principle \(\ref{pri-vol4-evidence-bounds-authority}\)), establishes that permission to operate must derive strictly from recorded evidence and expire whenever that evidence lapses. Standing conditions transform this principle into an active software and hardware mechanism. Each condition couples a required premise with a dedicated detector, a monitoring cadence, and an enforced safety response. Consequently, the loaded stopping trials that would support a conditional release for the warehouse mobile manipulator become binding empirical warrants whose invalidation immediately terminates authorization. Under this book’s illustrative records, that grant is never issued, because each of the six primary claims relies on at least one premise that remains ungrounded or unknown. The stipulated delivery branch demonstrates how empirical field trials could substantiate useful restricted service and specifies the runtime conditions necessary to sustain that grant. Just as a manual lease restricts human or teleoperation authority to the validity window of its evidence, and precommitment binds test evaluation to rules established before observations occur, deployment release binds fleet deployment to verifiable physical limits. Release is the widest operational authority granted in this book, and even it never reaches the actuators directly. Every motion it licenses still crosses the causal boundary only through the permission path and the rated functions beneath it.


↩︎ The manual lease that bounds human authority to the validity window of its evidence is established in Arbiter execution and manual-lease heartbeats.

title: Deployment Release
text:
16.12 Historical Perspective and Further Reading
Long before it became an engineering artifact, the modern safety case originated in the philosophy of practical reasoning. Toulmin (1958) decomposed argument structures into concrete elements: an explicit claim, the ground data offered to support it, an inferential warrant that licenses the logical step from data to claim, and the rebuttals that identify conditions under which the warrant fails. That structural anatomy survives almost unchanged in modern deployment release arguments. In the late 1990s, safety engineers translated these philosophical foundations into auditable systems practices. The Claim-Argument-Evidence (CAE) methodology introduced by Bishop and Bloomfield (1998) and the Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) formalized by Kelly (1998) transformed implicit engineering convictions into graph-structured arguments that an independent reviewer can inspect link by link. Later, the autonomous vehicle community adapted this goal-based assurance framework in ANSI/UL 4600 (UL Standards & Engagement 2023), requiring explicit argumentation over positive and negative evidence, concrete safety performance indicators, and rigorous independent assessment.

UL Standards & Engagement. 2023. ANSI/UL 4600 Ed. 3-2023: Standard for Evaluation of Autonomous Products. UL Standards & Engagement.

Butler, Ricky W., and George B. Finelli. 1993. “The Infeasibility of Quantifying the Reliability of Life-Critical Real-Time Software.” IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 19 (1): 3–12. https://doi.org/10.1109/32.210303.

Kalra, Nidhi, and Susan M. Paddock. 2016. “Driving to Safety: How Many Miles of Driving Would It Take to Demonstrate Autonomous Vehicle Reliability?” Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice 94: 182–93. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tra.2016.09.010.

Bloomfield, Robin, and Bev Littlewood. 2003. “Multi-Legged Arguments: The Impact of Diversity Upon Confidence in Dependability Arguments.” Proceedings of the 2003 International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks, 25–34. https://doi.org/10.1109/DSN.2003.1209913.
Two foundational results established the statistical limits of empirical testing, shaping what a release argument can claim. First, Butler and Finelli (1993) proved that the ultra-low failure rates demanded of life-critical software cannot be validated through testing alone; verifying a rate of \(10^{-9}\) failures per operational hour demands on the order of \(10^9\) failure-free test hours. Decades later, Kalra and Paddock (2016) applied that same arithmetic to embodied autonomy, showing that an autonomous fleet would have to drive billions of operational miles to establish statistical parity with human drivers. A hazard mitigation claim therefore cannot rest solely on driving miles; it requires an architectural warrant, such as formally verified runtime safety envelopes and deterministic interlocks, alongside empirical testing. Second, redundancy cannot be assumed to yield statistical independence. The classic empirical study by Knight and Leveson (1986) demonstrated that independently written software implementations suffer correlated failures far more often than independent probability models predict. As a result, a multi-legged safety argument (Bloomfield and Littlewood 2003) must provide empirical and architectural evidence for the independence of its redundant legs rather than treating diversity as an axiom. On the running machine, claim C5 carries that burden.
The final historical lesson concerns the temporal fragility of assurance. The Rogers Commission report on the Space Shuttle Challenger disaster (Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident 1986) and Diane Vaughan’s subsequent sociological analysis (Vaughan 1996) revealed that safety cases rarely collapse from an isolated blunder. Instead, arguments degrade through the “normalization of deviance,” a slow organizational erosion in which unexplained anomalies are repeatedly rationalized until a catastrophic threshold is breached. Dynamic safety cases (Denney et al. 2015) counter this failure mode by maintaining the argument as an active runtime process, continually validating underlying assumptions against operational telemetry. Because embodied systems require continuous post-deployment evolution, compromise-resilient update frameworks such as TUF (Samuel et al. 2010) and Uptane (Kuppusamy et al. 2016) established that the software delivery channel is itself a primary attack surface. The release architecture developed here joins these lines of work. The deployment verdict is cryptographically bound to a signed manifest validated by the target controller before motion begins, and every environmental assumption remains a standing operational condition whose violation revokes execution authority within the qualified detection-and-response bound.

Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident. 1986. Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident. U.S. Government Printing Office.

Denney, Ewen, Ganesh Pai, and Ibrahim Habli. 2015. “Dynamic Safety Cases for Through-Life Safety Assurance.” 2015 IEEE/ACM 37th IEEE International Conference on Software Engineering, 587–90. https://doi.org/10.1109/ICSE.2015.199.

Samuel, Justin, Nick Mathewson, Justin Cappos, and Roger Dingledine. 2010. “Survivable Key Compromise in Software Update Systems.” Proceedings of the 17th ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS), 61–72. https://doi.org/10.1145/1866307.1866315.

Kuppusamy, Trishank Karthik, Akan Brown, Sebastien Awwad, Damon McCoy, Russ Bielawski, Cameron Mott, Sam Lauzon, André Weimerskirch, and Justin Cappos. 2016. Uptane: Securing Software Updates for Automobiles. Paper presented at the 14th Embedded Security in Cars Conference (escar Europe).
Six foundational works reward careful study, each anchoring a distinct dimension of the release argument:

Toulmin (1958) introduces the claim, warrant, backing, and rebuttal framework that underpins modern structured argumentation, establishing why inferential warrants must be scrutinized independently from raw empirical data.
Bishop and Bloomfield (1998) articulates the Claim-Argument-Evidence (CAE) framework for critical software systems, providing the structural basis for the assurance scorecard in table 2.
Kelly (1998) introduces Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) and formalizes pattern-based approaches for managing safety cases across system lifecycles, establishing the graphical formalism illustrated in figure 1.
Knight and Leveson (1986) provides empirical evidence of correlated failures in diverse redundant software, demonstrating why claims of subsystem independence must be actively verified rather than taken as an architectural postulate.
Vaughan (1996) reconstructs the organizational and technical breakdown of the Challenger launch decision, defining the concept of normalization of deviance that runtime safety performance indicators are designed to detect and arrest.
Koopman and Wagner (2016) identifies inductive machine learning among the core challenges confronting autonomous vehicle validation, proposing phased operational envelope expansion, hardware-isolated runtime monitors, and systematic fault injection, the triad that this chapter’s release protocol builds on.


Bishop, Peter, and Robin Bloomfield. 1998. “A Methodology for Safety Case Development.” In Industrial Perspectives of Safety-Critical Systems: Proceedings of the Sixth Safety-Critical Systems Symposium, edited by Felix Redmill and Tom Anderson. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4471-1534-2_14.

Kelly, Timothy Patrick. 1998. “Arguing Safety: A Systematic Approach to Managing Safety Cases.” PhD thesis, Department of Computer Science, University of York.

Koopman, Philip, and Michael Wagner. 2016. “Challenges in Autonomous Vehicle Testing and Validation.” SAE International Journal of Transportation Safety 4 (1): 15–24. https://doi.org/10.4271/2016-01-0128.

What’s Next: From release to responsibilityWho answers for the decisions behind a signed manifest? The manifest names the adjudicator who accepted the configuration and its operating envelope. Yet the crossing rule, the staffing of the remote assistant, the permit under which the machine runs, and the uses of the records it keeps were each decided by someone else, and none of them appears in a per-tick log. Responsible Physical AI traces those decisions to named owners. It tests whether each human role the safety argument relies on is one a person can perform. It converts gaps in how well the machine detects different groups of people into gaps in stopping distance. It collects all of it in an approval record that the release gate reads, so that a decision with no owner refuses operation the way an unknown premise does.

title: Supervisory Intervention
text:
Purpose



Physical AI stack focus for this chapter.
Why can handing a moving robot to a human operator cause the collision the handover was meant to prevent?
Most deployed robots keep a person in reserve for the situations their learned policies cannot handle, and that reserve is usually treated as the final safeguard. A person, however, needs a large fraction of a second to respond even while watching closely and several seconds after only monitoring. A machine moving at walking pace covers meters in that time, so a request for help can consume the very clearance the help was meant to protect. Taking over also creates hazards of its own. Two controllers that each believe they hold a joint can command it at once, a controller that believes the other still holds it can leave it unattended, and an abrupt switch between their commands jolts the drivetrain and the load it carries. A takeover that grants unchecked control lets a startled or lagging operator drive the machine into a rack. A log that does not mark who commanded each instant can neither settle what caused an incident nor keep the machine’s own near-failures out of the demonstrations it later learns from. Authority can change hands within a single control cycle, but the momentum already delivered across the causal boundary cannot be recalled, so a takeover must be engineered as a control action with its own deadline, its own limits, and its own record.


Learning Objectives

Specify operator permissions through capability matrices that bind each authenticated role’s operations to physical channels, preemption tiers, and clearance-derived deadlines
Select a state-dependent local fallback that remains physically feasible while human intervention is pending
Calculate the latest fallback time and takeover speed ceilings from human reaction latency and remaining physical stopping clearance
Evaluate the inherited chunk lease and the chosen manual lease against their modes’ stopping reserves and available fallback mechanisms
Design authority handshakes that keep one owner on each actuator output and size fixed-endpoint \(\Glyph{C}^2\) command blends within each channel’s rate limit
Diagnose mode confusion in split-channel handovers and specify the per-channel annunciation that keeps an operator’s model of ownership current
Evaluate whether an authority record provides the cryptographic and kinematic evidence needed to reconstruct post-incident fault causality
