14.3.4 Arbiter execution and manual-lease heartbeats
Once a channel reaches \(\text{Human-Manual}\), a dropped wireless link or a distracted assistant who leaves the console would let the last manual command keep running unless the machine checks that the operator is still present. The safety microcontroller bounds that risk with a hardware-timed manual lease. Depending on the console, presence detection may use a capacitive grip sensor, eye tracking, or continuous joystick deflection past a deadband, chosen for their sensor coverage and false-drop rates. Manual authority is sustained exclusively through authenticated keep-alive heartbeats streamed from the operator console to the safety microcontroller. The manual lease \(\ManualLease\) of section 14.3.1 is the longest silence the microcontroller tolerates between them. Two bounds set its length. From below, the lease must outlast the heartbeat period plus the link’s jitter and at least one lost packet, or ordinary wireless loss would drop a healthy operator into fallback. That floor is why the heartbeats must run at a rate several times the lease’s inverse. From above, the lease replaces the chunk lease inside \(\PrebrakeDelay\) while the operator holds MAN, so the travel it adds over the chunk lease, \(\SpeedAtDetection(\ManualLease - \ChunkLease)\), must fit the clearance left after the takeover. The reference implementation chooses 100 ms. Section 14.4.6 checks that value against the upper bound at the in-loop request speed, and only the site’s measured heartbeat loss can show that it clears the lower one.
Each heartbeat packet carries a strictly increasing 64-bit sequence counter \(\HeartbeatSequenceCounter\), a monotonic hardware timestamp \(\HeartbeatTimestamp_k\), an authenticated operator credential, and a keyed message authentication code (AES-128 CMAC, evaluated in section 14.5). In the age calculation below, \(\HeartbeatTimestamp_k\) represents the sender’s timestamp translated into the local clock domain. The receiver tracks the bounded clock-synchronization uncertainty interval and computes freshness relative to the oldest plausible timestamp; an unqualified clock mapping cannot safely establish packet freshness. The nominal local-clock age is: \[\HeartbeatAge = \HeartbeatReceiptTime - \HeartbeatTimestamp_k.\] These fields combine communication checks used in black-channel safety architectures (International Electrotechnical Commission 2021) with cryptographic security over an untrusted wireless link. The sequence counter detects transmission loss and replay attacks. The timestamp and bounded lease act as a communication watchdog against excessive latency. The cryptographic tag authenticates the claimed credential. The safety communication checks and the security mechanism require separate qualification.

International Electrotechnical Commission. 2021. IEC 61784-3:2021: Industrial Communication Networks, Profiles, Part 3: Functional Safety Fieldbuses, General Rules and Profile Definitions. International Electrotechnical Commission.

↩︎ The proposal header that applies the same black-channel safeguards to every learned proposal is established in Supervisory timers and proposal wire contracts.

A heartbeat packet may renew authority only while its conservative age falls within the configured freshness window. The active manual lease expires deterministically on the local hardware clock at its committed deadline; stale or out-of-order network traffic cannot extend that horizon. Similarly, an autonomous action chunk expires strictly according to its admitted local deadline. A packet that fails cryptographic verification is immediately discarded. It cannot renew the lease, but it does not revoke currently valid authority either; the existing timer runs down on its own. Upon lease expiration, the microcontroller automatically revokes the operator’s proposal token, drops into Fallback, and executes a pre-validated holding or stopping trajectory. Once a lease lapses, the state machine prohibits any immediate return to \(\text{Autonomous}\) or \(\text{Human-Manual}\). The robot must satisfy strict recovery conditions: it must come to a complete mechanical standstill, resolve and acknowledge the relevant faults without erasing their evidence, and undergo an authenticated four-phase re-admission handshake initiated from rest.
When multiple control sources propose concurrent commands, the permission path resolves candidate selection through a fixed priority hierarchy evaluated deterministically every 1 ms control cycle below the proposal boundary. This mechanism adopts the layered priority structure of subsumption architectures (Brooks 1986), but applies it strictly to input source selection rather than behavioral synthesis. The independent enforcer then admits, modifies, or rejects the winning candidate to ensure compliance with configured physical limits. In the \(\text{Human-Manual}\) state with a valid lease, the human proposal takes precedence over learned model proposals, while remaining bounded by barrier certificates and actuator limits. In \(\text{Autonomous}\), the learned policy generates candidate actions for safety screening. Because fixed-state arbitration requires bounded work per tick (\(\mathcal{O}(1)\) computational complexity), it eliminates runtime negotiation or dynamic bargaining between software proposers.

↩︎ The proposal boundary, above which a learned component may only propose and below which the permission path alone admits commands, is established in The Machine in Five Levels.

Two properties of the protocol show only when the states and handshake are drawn together (figure 5). Every active state has an edge to Fallback, so no failure of the network or the operator can leave a channel without a defined owner, and the only edge out of Fallback is a reset from standstill. The hardwired Protective input sits outside the protocol entirely and preempts every state.






Figure 5: Authority states and their guards: Each box is one value of the per-channel authority state, with its code name above its plain name. A handover runs from request through acknowledgment to a commit on a control tick; from then on the enforcer owns the blend between latched endpoints, and manual proposals begin only when the profile completes with a live manual lease. Timeout, lease lapse, or an invalid state leads to the validated fallback, whose only exit is a reset from rest with a fresh re-admission. The hardwired protective input preempts every state.



Here the state machine decouples physical bus ownership from protocol progress. An acknowledgment prepares the transition. The local hardware commit (REVOKE_PROPOSAL_TOKEN()) strips the autonomous policy of its proposal token on the committed channels and grants the enforcer sole ownership of the blend. The enforcer admits live manual proposals only after the interpolation profile completes under an active manual lease. An unconfirmed transition therefore leaves only the console uncertain, as the Confirm phase states. A delayed handover request or a dropped heartbeat, in contrast, runs down its local timer and invokes the validated fallback without waiting for network consensus.
Assigning a single writer resolves authority unambiguously at each control tick, but an instantaneous switch can still produce hazardous dynamic transients. If the autonomous policy’s last admitted joint torque diverges significantly from the operator’s initial target, directly swapping setpoints across a single tick boundary requests an unachievable step change in torque, risking mechanical shock or actuator saturation. The enforcer avoids this discontinuity by using the latched boundary conditions to generate a dynamically feasible interpolation profile that preserves stopping margins throughout the transition.

Checkpoint 14.2: Authority transitions and timeout boundsBefore moving from who owns each channel to how its command changes value, verify your understanding of leases, transition state machines, and timeout dynamics:

State-dependent fallback: Can you explain why the moving base and the loaded arm need different validated responses when a lease lapses, and why Safe Torque Off alone provides neither?
Finite-state transition semantics: Can you trace the deterministic progression among the Autonomous, Handover-Pending, Blend, Human-Manual, and Fallback states, and name the guard and the single actuator owner on each edge?
Timeout bound: At the aisle speed the configured protocol ceiling is 500 ms and the clearance-derived deadline after charging the dispatch-to-admission allocation is 37.5 ms. Can you state which one sets \(\HandoverTimeout\), by how many milliseconds it is the tighter, and how many whole 1 ms permission ticks the arbiter may wait before it dispatches fallback?
Asymmetric preemption hierarchy: Can you explain why the qualified local protection path must meet its measured deadline, while restoring autonomous authority requires a fresh admission handshake?
Fallback on a lapsed handover: Can you explain why a lapsed or unacknowledged handover goes to the validated stop rung rather than back to the degraded policy that requested it?

If any transition paths permit unhandled timeouts or undefined intermediate states, the authority protocol is vulnerable to mode confusion and runaway actuation. Review this section before proceeding to smooth command blending.

title: Supervisory Intervention
text:
14.4 Transfer Without Discontinuity
At commit time \(\TimeInstant_0\), the enforcer latches the last admitted policy command \(\ControlCommand_0\) and a checked human target \(\ControlCommand_1\). Switching them in one permission tick may exceed the channel’s allowed command rate. In classical process control, bumpless transfer between manual and automatic modes is achieved by making the inactive controller track the active one’s output, so its internal state, including its integrator, already agrees at the switch (Åström and Hägglund 2006). Section 14.4.3 applies that tracking to the console-side controller that turns operator input into a command. Here bumpless transfer also names a second mechanism layered on top, which spreads the remaining command change across a finite window while matching the required endpoint derivatives. The quintic seam bridges of Quintic splines and C^2 boundary matching provide the construction; takeover adds a new admission decision because waiting for the operator has already consumed some clearance.

14.4.1 Command steps and mechanical drivetrain shock
A step change in torque or acceleration excites torsional resonances and snaps gearboxes across their backlash, while a slower blend lowers the command rate at the cost of stopping reserve. Because the \(\PowerRailInductance\,d\ConductorCurrent/d\TimeInstant\) coupling to the DC supply also turns a current step into a voltage sag on the shared rail, the command transition must satisfy the drive’s rate limits while leaving enough clearance for fallback. A smooth profile therefore needs both a rate bound and a check against the remaining physical envelope.


↩︎ The \(\PowerRailInductance\,d\ConductorCurrent/d\TimeInstant\) coupling through which a current step sags the shared DC bus is established in Power distribution impedance, transient droop, and brownout resets.

Definition 14.2: C² bumpless authority transfer ramp
\(\Glyph{C}^2\) bumpless authority transfer ramp is the enforcer-owned command profile between two checked, latched references \(\ControlCommand_0\) and \(\ControlCommand_1\). It is parameterized by a monotonic weighting function \(\BumplessTransferBlend(\TimeInstant) \in [0,1]\) with vanishing first and second boundary derivatives (\(\BumplessTransferBlendRate = \BumplessTransferBlendAcceleration = 0\)) over a finite blending window \(\BlendingTransitionWindow\). The profile keeps that command and its first two derivatives continuous across the fixed-endpoint handoff. When the command is acceleration, its first derivative is commanded jerk; when it is torque, the first derivative is torque rate.

Significance: A setpoint step has an unbounded ideal derivative. A \(\Glyph{C}^2\) command profile removes that discontinuity; measured actuator tracking and plant limits still decide physical feasibility.
Distinction: Unlike a linear interpolation ramp whose derivative jumps at both endpoints, a \(\Glyph{C}^2\) quintic spline enforces vanishing first and second derivatives (\(\BumplessTransferBlendRate = \BumplessTransferBlendAcceleration = 0\)) at entry and exit, making the interpolated command and its first two derivatives continuous for stationary endpoint derivatives. The physical meaning of those derivatives depends on the command channel.
Common pitfall: Choosing a window shorter than the rate limit allows for a fixed acceleration-command change (the bound equation 7 derives below) breaches the stated command-jerk limit even though the profile is smooth. Resonance, slip, and stopping distance require plant tests.





14.4.2 Sizing the blend window and the stopping-distance cost
Smoothing an acceleration command from cruising speed to emergency braking delays the onset of maximum deceleration, so bumpless transfer consumes clearance. It trades stopping reserve for lower mechanical stress, and sizing the blend window means balancing the actuator’s jerk limit against the clearance that remains.
The enforcer blends with the quintic smoothstep. For normalized progress \(\BumplessTransferProgress = (\TimeInstant - \BumplessTransferStartInstant) / \BlendingTransitionWindow \in [0, 1]\), the polynomial weighting function is: \[\BumplessTransferBlend(\BumplessTransferProgress) = 10\BumplessTransferProgress^3 - 15\BumplessTransferProgress^4 + 6\BumplessTransferProgress^5. \tag{6}\] The polynomial in equation 6 is the fixed-endpoint result derived in Smooth Trajectories and Bumpless Transfer. Its derivative \(\BumplessTransferBlendSlope(\BumplessTransferProgress) = 30\BumplessTransferProgress^2(1-\BumplessTransferProgress)^2\) peaks at \(\BumplessTransferProgress = 1/2\) with value \(30/16 = 1.875\), so the profile’s peak slope is \(1.875/\BlendingTransitionWindow\) and an acceleration change must satisfy: \[\BlendingTransitionWindow \ge \frac{1.875 \lVert \FiniteChange \ControlCommand \rVert}{\JerkLimit}. \tag{7}\]
For a torque command, replace the acceleration difference and jerk ceiling with the torque difference and torque-rate ceiling. The illustrative 15 N·m joint-torque change under a 750 N·m/s ceiling therefore requires 37.5 ms, rounded up to 38 ms on the permission clock. These bounds assume stationary endpoint derivatives; a transfer from a moving ramp must match its boundary state explicitly.6
6 Nonzero Boundary Derivatives: The \(1.875/\BlendingTransitionWindow\) peak derivative factor assumes stationary endpoint derivatives. A general quintic can match the command value, first derivative, and second derivative at both endpoints, including nonzero values (Quintic splines and C^2 boundary matching). Its interior rate extrema must then be checked; the fixed-endpoint smoothstep factor does not automatically apply.Increasing \(\BlendingTransitionWindow\) reduces the profile’s peak commanded jerk, but delays the full human target and can lengthen the stopping trajectory. Consider the remote assistant’s takeover of the mobile manipulator’s base, committed while the machine cruises at the \(\SpeedAtDetection =\) 0.75 m/s it slowed to before requesting it (section 14.2.4). Suppose the assistant commands a stop at the scenario’s braking deceleration, a fixed step of \(\lvert \FiniteChange \BaseAccelerationCommand \rvert =\) 2 m/s² from the latched cruise command. The enforcer holds the blend to \(\JerkLimit =\) 7.11 m/s³, the jerk bound of the resident jerk-limited stop. That bound is a stipulated property of the loaded base, not of its speed, so the blend window does not depend on the speed at which the takeover commits. Measured load response still requires qualification. The smoothstep bound then sets a minimum blending window of 527.34 ms, longer than the 281.25 ms the resident stop spends ramping its deceleration at the same jerk bound, because the smoothstep reaches its peak slope only at mid-window. The smoothstep weight averages one half over the window, so the base would leave the blend at 0.22 m/s after traveling 316.1 mm. Integrating the smoothstep weight a first time subtracts one half of \(\lvert \FiniteChange \BaseAccelerationCommand \rvert\,\BlendingTransitionWindow\) from the entry speed \(\SpeedAtDetection\), whereas integrating that speed profile across the window subtracts only one seventh of \(\lvert \FiniteChange \BaseAccelerationCommand \rvert\,\BlendingTransitionWindow^2\) from the unbraked travel \(\SpeedAtDetection\,\BlendingTransitionWindow\) because most of the deceleration occurs in the second half of the ramp. Braking from there at the full target would take another 12.4 mm, for 328.4 mm to zero speed in this partial model. It holds full deceleration until rest, then switches acceleration to zero instantaneously. The value is therefore a lower-bound comparison for the ramp followed by ideal braking, not a complete smooth stopping trajectory. A feasible terminal transition needs its own distance and boundary-state check.
An instantaneous step takeover would stop in 140.6 mm, so even this partial ramp-and-brake model adds 187.8 mm of travel. The partial model is also 82.4 mm longer than the 246.1 mm resident stop from the same speed. For the one-dimensional model starting at zero acceleration and ending at rest with zero acceleration, the resident profile is a minimum-distance stop under the stated deceleration and jerk bounds (The C^2 stopping suffix and jerk-limited braking), so a different complete transition into braking must be checked against that baseline. The partial comparison above lacks the required terminal transition and is not itself a competing complete profile. For a braking command the resident stop is already the bumpless transfer. The base’s blend window therefore governs base command changes that do not stop the machine, such as the first manual command after an automatic stop, where the blend starts from rest and the enforcer still checks the resident stop from every blended state. An idealized step stop is mathematically shorter. Executing an unblended emergency stop, however, risks wheel lockup, dynamic rollover, or load shedding (such as throwing a loaded tote off the manipulator rack), which can increase the actual physical stopping distance beyond the ideal theoretical rigid-body stop. Command smoothing limits the requested rate; physical stability and sufficient clearance still require qualification. The enforcer admits each blended tick only while the resident stop from the resulting state still fits. Where no blend fits, the base receives the resident stop itself, the suffix the fallback ladder’s stop rung executes. Bypassing the blend window by applying the acceleration step within a single 1 ms permission tick would instead request a command jerk of about 2,000 m/s³ over that tick. The idealized step is only a comparison baseline.



Under the stated stopping model, the blend adds travel beyond the resident stop.


14.4.3 Initial condition matching and integrator pre-biasing
Command blending removes the chosen output discontinuity, but it cannot remove one that a controller upstream of the blend produces. On the remote assistant’s side that controller is the console-side tracking loop, the software that turns joystick deflection, or a measured guiding force (the force-guided input that section 14.4.4 describes next), into a velocity target for the channel. While the policy still owns the channel, that loop runs against a plant it does not drive, and its integrator accumulates the difference between its target and a motion that never follows. At commit it would emit that accumulated correction as a jump in the manual target, a step the blend window was never sized to absorb. Initial condition matching pre-biases that loop against the measured state before commit, so its internal controller state matches the output required at transfer rather than releasing accumulated error. It does not force the deliberate human target to equal the last policy command. The enforcer latches both endpoints, sizes the blend for their actual difference, and checks the resulting command and stopping reserve throughout transfer.7
7 Mid-Blend Re-Intervention Abort: If an operator commands a secondary protective stop while a bumpless transfer blend is actively underway (\(0 < \BumplessTransferProgress < 1\)), the enforcer does not wait for \(\BlendingTransitionWindow\) to complete. It uses the measured plant position, velocity, and acceleration, together with the active command and their uncertainty, to select a qualified state-matched fallback. A new polynomial seeded only from the intermediate command does not establish that the physical plant can execute it.To verify a transfer, record the command profile, motor current, encoder motion, and chassis inertial response on a shared timebase with bounded alignment error. In the ideal model, a step command has an infinite derivative at the switch, which excites high jerk, unmodeled compliance, and drivetrain ringing in physical hardware. A fixed-endpoint quintic polynomial removes the command discontinuity by zeroing the boundary derivatives, so its command rate stays bounded across the whole window \(\BlendingTransitionWindow\) instead of concentrating in one impulse (figure 6). The measured plant response, not the command profile, establishes whether the handover met its physical limits.






Figure 6: Step vs. quintic command transfer: A step and fixed-endpoint quintic blend are compared. The solid line is the command. The step’s ideal derivative is a red impulse, the quintic’s bounded derivative is dashed slate, and the gray ringing is schematic. The profile bounds the commanded rate for the assumed endpoints.



The two panels distinguish the command’s mathematical continuity from the plant’s measured response. Removing the step bounds the requested rate under the stated endpoint assumptions; it does not establish that the drive tracks the command or that the load remains stable. Those measurements decide whether the selected blend window is acceptable.
The enforcer’s 1 kHz loop gathers the four-phase handshake, integrator pre-biasing, and the \(\Glyph{C}^2\) quintic blend into one protocol on the safety microcontroller. Each tick it samples plant state, stopping reserve, protective inputs, and the active execution lease. It commits an ownership change only on the qualified commit tick that follows a verified acknowledgment, blends only between latched endpoints and checks every blended candidate before dispatch, and falls back on a lapsed lease or a failed clearance check.


↪ Protocol: The enforcer’s cadence, memory and write invariants, and per-state execution steps are given in Authority-transfer protocol.


14.4.4 Mapping operator input to arm motion
Once the operator holds the arm channel, commanding a rigid position target into a bin wall or rack upright builds contact force until the enforcer trips, whereas guiding the arm through measured contact force lets the wrist comply. Position streaming supplies kinematic targets directly; force guiding uses measured contact force to generate a motion target through an admittance controller8 (Hogan 1985). Either mapping remains subject to the arm’s qualified limits. The choice also changes the logged learning target, so the record must retain whether a sample is a requested pose, a force measurement, or an admitted command.
8 Admittance and Impedance Control: Hogan (1985) framed interaction control as programming the relation between force and motion at the contact. An impedance controller answers imposed motion with a commanded force; an admittance controller is its dual, turning a measured force into commanded motion, which suits stiff, highly geared arms whose position loops are accurate but which cannot render force directly. On such an arm a force-guided target is still a motion command, so it passes the same enforcer checks as a streamed pose.
Hogan, Neville. 1985. “Impedance Control: An Approach to Manipulation: Part i–Theory, Part II–Implementation, Part III–Applications.” Journal of Dynamic Systems, Measurement, and Control 107 (1): 1–24.


14.4.5 Bilateral teleoperation and haptic feedback passivity
A force-reflecting console adds an actuated device at the operator’s hands. Delayed feedback9 can destabilize that coupled loop even when authority ownership is correct (Anderson and Spong 1989). Such a console therefore needs a separate interaction-energy argument, including its port conventions, controller sampling, delay and loss assumptions, and actuator saturation. The energy-storage condition and wave-variable construction are developed in Passivity and Energy-Bounded Interaction; they do not replace the clearance or force limits. The basic warehouse takeover does not require bilateral force reflection. If a site adds it, pre-biasing and ramping the console’s force output must prevent a command step at the operator’s hand within its own measured limits, because the arm’s accepted blend duration does not automatically qualify the console. Whichever input mapping and console a site chooses, the session that carries them must still fit the clearance left after the operator’s response.
9 Delayed Teleoperation: Ferrell (1965) found that operators working through a transmission delay fall back on a move-and-wait strategy, so task time grows with the delay. Force reflection through the same delay proved unstable until Anderson and Spong (1989) used scattering theory to make the communication channel passive, a construction that Niemeyer and Slotine (1991) recast as wave variables. For a force-reflecting console the delay budget is therefore a stability term as well as a latency term.
Ferrell, William R. 1965. “Remote Manipulation with Transmission Delay.” IEEE Transactions on Human Factors in Electronics HFE-6 (1): 24–32. https://doi.org/10.1109/THFE.1965.6591253.

Anderson, Robert J., and Mark W. Spong. 1989. “Bilateral Control of Teleoperators with Time Delay.” IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control 34 (5): 494–501. https://doi.org/10.1109/9.24201.

Niemeyer, Günter, and Jean-Jacques E. Slotine. 1991. “Stable Adaptive Teleoperation.” IEEE Journal of Oceanic Engineering 16 (1): 152–62. https://doi.org/10.1109/48.64895.


14.4.6 Admitting the remote-assistant session
Every interval priced so far in this chapter now draws from the same finite stopping reserve when a remote session begins. Admitting the remote assistant requires bounding four timing parameters against the machine’s limits: the operator reaction budget (the takeover latency \(\SupervisoryTakeoverLatency\) of equation 1 for the takeover mode in use), the handshake protocol latency \(\HandshakeProtocolLatency\), the manual lease \(\ManualLease\), and the minimum blending window \(\BlendingTransitionWindow\). Table 6 states them for the machine’s two command channels, the base and the arm, which one remote-assistant session commands together.


↪ How many machines one remote assistant can serve before requests wait minutes for a person is developed in One person, many machines.



Table 6: Blending windows on the mobile manipulator: One remote-assistant session commands both channels, and each window is rounded up to whole 1 ms permission ticks. The rate ceiling \(\CommandRateCeiling\) bounds the derivative of each command. The base window is the same at every speed, because the jerk bound belongs to the loaded base. At the in-loop request speed a braking blend does not fit the clearance that remains, so the base receives the resident stop and its window applies only to non-braking changes. Every lease and pending deadline must fit the state-dependent stopping reserve.

Consider an illustrative remote-assistant in-loop takeover, requested after the mobile manipulator has slowed to 0.75 m/s with the assistant’s manual_drive entry. The four parameters take the values already derived. The reaction budget \(\SupervisoryTakeoverLatency\) is the 605 ms in-loop takeover of section 14.2.2, which already includes transport and the 31 ms four-phase exchange of table 5, so the handshake is part of \(\SupervisoryTakeoverLatency\), not an addition to it. The manual lease, the longest silence tolerated from the assistant before the permission path falls back, is 100 ms, and table 6 gives the blending window for each channel.
An in-loop session at 0.75 m/s closes its complete budget by only a few centimeters, and only because the base takes its resident stop rather than a braking blend. A session that begins at the 0.15 m/s crawl or from standstill has far more room, so those are the configurations worth qualifying. Three rows of the table decide that verdict. The remainder after the takeover, the 146.6 ms by which the takeover beats \(\FallbackDeadline\) (section 14.2.4), bounds the transfer itself. Any further delay before a stop could begin while authority is changing hands must fit inside it, and the enforcer checks the resident stop against it at every tick of the transfer. The lease row exists because, once the assistant holds MAN, the manual lease replaces the 60 ms chunk lease inside \(\PrebrakeDelay\), so its extra length becomes travel. The row is the upper bound on the lease set out in section 14.3.4, and the chosen value passes it. The blend row fails. Blending the step to braking from 0.75 m/s grows the travel plus the resident stop from the blended state by up to 157.0 mm, well past the remainder, so in this session the base receives the resident stop and only the arm blends. This conservative per-tick check charges a fresh resident stop starting from zero deceleration at each blended speed rather than the partial model’s 82.4 mm constant-deceleration tail, because any fallback triggered during the blend begins from the standard resident profile.
