The first line of defense against dynamics mismatch is empirical measurement. System identification9 calibrates the simulator’s parameter values (link masses, friction coefficients, torque constants, and transport delays) against paired command-response traces recorded on the physical robot. When a physical subsystem resists accurate first-principles modeling, engineers can replace analytical equations with data-driven approximations. In quadrupedal locomotion work, Hwangbo et al. (2019) trained an actuator network that predicted physical joint torque directly from a rolling history of position errors and joint velocities, executing this neural network inside the simulation loop instead of an idealized torque actuator. Similarly, delta-action residual models learn state-dependent corrections from physical rollouts, adjusting simulated commands so that simulated trajectories track physical behavior (He et al. 2025). In the cage-door latch task, these techniques help reconcile actuator response and bus transport latency, yet they share one limit. A learned correction model is valid only across the empirical state distribution visited during data collection, and outside that distribution the model is uncharacterized. Consequently, any learned simulator correction must enter the policy manifest’s omission log with its own explicitly bounded domain of validity.
9 Identification Experiments: System identification treats the input excitation signal as part of the experiment design. Signals such as step functions, swept-frequency sines (chirps), and pseudo-random binary sequences (PRBS) must persistently excite the relevant mechanical and electrical modes, since nominal closed-loop operation rarely activates them (Ljung 1999). Paired physical probing follows this discipline: it drives both the simulator and physical hardware with identical open-loop excitation trajectories rather than relying on passive operational logs, where feedback regulation actively keeps the machine away from the boundary contact dynamics listed in the omission log. 
Ljung, Lennart. 1999. System Identification: Theory for the User. 2nd ed. Prentice Hall.

He, Tairan, Jiawei Gao, Wenli Xiao, Yuanhang Zhang, Zi Wang, Jiashun Wang, Zhengyi Luo, et al. 2025. “ASAP: Aligning Simulation and Real-World Physics for Learning Agile Humanoid Whole-Body Skills.” Robotics: Science and Systems XXI. https://doi.org/10.15607/RSS.2025.XXI.066.
10 Domain Randomization: The technique originated in computer vision, where Tobin et al. (2017) randomized textures, lighting, and camera poses so that physical scenes appeared as ordinary variations to a detector trained purely on synthetic renders. Peng et al. (2018) extended the concept to dynamics, randomizing link masses, friction coefficients, joint damping, and transport latencies for robotic manipulation. Appearance and dynamics differ in how a policy can exploit history. Appearance variation changes instantaneous visual observations, whereas dynamics variation changes how the physical plant responds to control inputs, a discrepancy that a policy with temporal memory can infer online. 
Tobin, Josh, Rachel Fong, Alex Ray, Jonas Schneider, Wojciech Zaremba, and Pieter Abbeel. 2017. “Domain Randomization for Transferring Deep Neural Networks from Simulation to the Real World.” 2017 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS), 23–30. https://doi.org/10.1109/IROS.2017.8202133.

Peng, Xue Bin, Marcin Andrychowicz, Wojciech Zaremba, and Pieter Abbeel. 2018. “Sim-to-Real Transfer of Robotic Control with Dynamics Randomization.” 2018 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA), 3803–10. https://doi.org/10.1109/ICRA.2018.8460528.
Repeatedly training against a single point estimate of physical parameters, such as an assumed strike-plate stiffness, encourages a policy to overfit to that exact numerical value. Domain randomization10 addresses parameter uncertainty by perturbing modeled simulation parameters across plausible distributions during training, forcing the policy to encounter varied physical responses (Tobin et al. 2017; Peng et al. 2018). However, sampling from a parameter distribution merely defines training weights; it does not constitute a formal certificate of robustness across the parameter set. How effectively a policy handles this diversity depends heavily on whether its architecture incorporates memory.
In standard reinforcement learning, a policy maximizes expected return within a single nominal simulation environment parameterized by the static vector \(\SimulationParameterVector_0\): \[\ExpectedReturnObjective(\ModelParameters; \SimulationParameterVector_0) = \mathbb{E}_{\RolloutStateSequence, \RolloutActionSequence \sim \PolicyTrajectoryDistribution(\cdot \mid \SimulationParameterVector_0)} \left[ \sum_{k=0}^\Time \DiscountFactor^\RolloutStepIndex \Reward(\PhysicalWorldState_{k}, \CognitivePolicyAction_{k}) \right].\] Domain randomization reformulates the physical environment as a distribution over plausible Markov Decision Processes parameterized by physical vector \(\SimulationParameterVector \sim \ProbabilityFunction(\SimulationParameterVector)\), where \(\SimulationParameterVector\) encompasses link masses, centers of mass, surface friction coefficients, joint damping, transport delays, and sensor noise variances. The domain randomization objective maximizes the expected return marginalized across this distribution: \[\DomainRandomizationObjective(\ModelParameters) = \mathbb{E}_{\SimulationParameterVector \sim \ProbabilityFunction(\SimulationParameterVector)} \left[ \ExpectedReturnObjective(\ModelParameters; \SimulationParameterVector) \right] = \int_{\SimulationParameterSet} \left( \mathbb{E}_{\RolloutStateSequence, \RolloutActionSequence \sim \PolicyTrajectoryDistribution(\cdot \mid \SimulationParameterVector)} \left[ \sum_{k=0}^\Time \DiscountFactor^\RolloutStepIndex \Reward(\PhysicalWorldState_{k}, \CognitivePolicyAction_{k}) \right] \right) \ProbabilityFunction(\SimulationParameterVector)\,\DerivativeOperator\SimulationParameterVector. \tag{10}\] Marginalizing over \(\ProbabilityFunction(\SimulationParameterVector)\) incentivizes policies to maintain performance across sampled physical configurations rather than collapsing to a single operating point. Nevertheless, optimizing expected return can mask catastrophic control failures occurring in low-probability regions of the distribution; high average reward does not imply uniform stability across the support \(\SimulationParameterSet\).
An alternative formulation adopts a minimax objective from robust control, optimizing performance against the worst-case modeled configuration: \[\max_\ModelParameters \min_{\SimulationParameterVector \in \SimulationParameterSet} \ExpectedReturnObjective(\ModelParameters; \SimulationParameterVector).\] Here, the inner minimization identifies the worst-case return within the bounded uncertainty set \(\SimulationParameterSet\), while the outer optimization searches for policy parameters \(\ModelParameters\) that maximize this floor. Minimax optimization targets the worst return within the modeled set, but this remains an optimization statement over modeled rewards rather than a physical stability proof. Neither distribution-averaging nor minimax optimization can protect against physical mechanisms that the simulator omits.
Two constraints govern domain randomization. First, hardware operating outside the sampled support (\(\HardwareParameterVector \notin \text{supp}(\ProbabilityFunction(\SimulationParameterVector))\)) is entirely unrepresented during training. Second, parameter randomization cannot compensate for structural omissions in the physics engine: no amount of variation in link mass or friction will expose a policy to the unmodeled lost motion of a harmonic drive or the preemptive jitter of a real-time operating system. Within the modeled support, the operational effect of broad randomization depends on whether the policy maintains temporal state. A memoryless feedforward network receives only the current observation \(\MultimodalObservation_{t}\). When different parameter instances produce indistinguishable observations but require different actions, the policy cannot adapt its choice to the active instance. Optimizing average return may then favor a compromise, and neither conservatism nor stability across the envelope is guaranteed. Conversely, a policy that conditions on a temporal history of observations and actions can infer physical plant dynamics online from the system’s transient response, effectively performing implicit system identification. For this reason, recurrent policies trained across randomized dynamics transfer with substantially higher fidelity than memoryless architectures (Peng et al. 2018), and memory is what lets a wider randomization range produce adaptation to the real plant rather than conservative detuning.
In engineering practice, parameter distributions are configured through two distinct strategies grounded in different forms of evidence. In calibration-first engineering, developers measure nominal masses, torque constants, bus latencies, and friction parameters directly on test benches. Randomization bounds are then derived from known physical mechanisms. For example, motor winding thermal limits determine the envelope of torque-constant variation, and surface degradation models govern friction bounds. These ranges represent verifiable physical claims about the robot and its environment. In contrast, automatic domain randomization (ADR) initializes the simulator at calibrated values and dynamically expands parameter ranges as the policy’s training performance at the distribution boundaries exceeds predefined success thresholds (OpenAI et al. 2019). ADR parameter bounds reflect the limits of what the reinforcement learning optimization can master rather than physical properties of the hardware, often expanding to unphysical extremes. The dexterity achieved by ADR in robotic in-hand manipulation relied on a recurrent policy learning to adapt online to these artificially broad dynamics. Regardless of the scheduling strategy, paired hardware traces must ultimately audit each channel against explicit error budgets before deployment; discrepancies exceeding tolerance require simulator revision rather than blind parameter widening. A randomization range expanded by an automated training curriculum represents an optimization scaffold, not an empirical characterization of the hardware, and therefore cannot expand the declared ODD.
Where domain randomization and simulation fidelity reach their physical limits, deterministic safety mechanisms must enforce system invariants. Every action proposed by a learned policy must pass through an independent permission path before reaching hardware actuators. Within this execution layer, hard force-derivative clamps, torque slew-rate limiters, and velocity-dependent stopping governors restrict commands to the envelope supported by verified sensing and braking capabilities.


↪ The Control Barrier Function filter that minimally corrects unverified policy proposals on every permission tick is developed in The Minimal Intervention Principle and Optimization Filters.
Decomposing the reality gap channel by channel divides the operating space in two. Inside the region where paired traces match simulation within verified tolerances, the simulated experience counts as support. Every unmodeled phenomenon, uncalibrated parameter, and unrepresented disturbance outside it becomes an entry in the omission log, the policy manifest’s record of what the simulator leaves out (section 6.8). The log therefore holds two kinds of entry, mechanisms the simulator omits and parameters no paired probe has yet calibrated, because an uncalibrated parameter leaves the simulated experience just as unsupported until a probe bounds it. For the latch, one of each heads the log: the strike-plate stiffness, a parameter the penalty spring sets far softer than the plate, and the transport latency of the actuator bus, a mechanism the simulator omits. No paired probe has yet closed either, so the high-speed contact states they govern fall outside what the simulation supports. Each entry also states a requirement for a runtime monitor or safety filter, which must detect when execution leaves the regime where the policy’s simulated training remains valid. Calibrating or randomizing simulator parameters still leaves a second gap: the simulator exposes exact contact forces, friction coefficients, and fixture offsets during training that the physical robot’s onboard sensors cannot directly measure at run time.

6.5.1 Teacher-student privileged state distillation and asymmetric actor-critic
While policy training can exploit privileged simulator state, such as ground-truth contact wrenches, friction coefficients, and exact strike-plate offsets, the onboard policy proposer must execute exclusively from the noisy, bandwidth-limited sensors installed on the physical machine. In actor-critic reinforcement learning, the actor proposes control actions while the critic evaluates expected future returns to compute policy gradients. Systems engineers bridge this sensor gap through two main architectures. Asymmetric actor-critic grants privileged observations exclusively to the critic during training. Teacher-student distillation first trains a privileged teacher policy and subsequently trains a sensor-limited student policy to imitate the teacher’s actions. Both architectures require validating whether the runtime observation stream delivered to the student contains enough information to reconstruct or compensate for the missing state.
The core challenge stems from partial observability, which casts physical robot control as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP).11 Identical sequences of measured joint positions and velocities can produce drastically different physical trajectories depending on whether a footpad grips dry concrete or slips on wet oil. A conventional critic \(\CriticReturnEstimate(\MultimodalObservation_{t})\) conditioned solely on instantaneous sensory observations cannot distinguish between these physical regimes, producing high-variance or biased value estimates. In simulation, exposing hidden contact wrenches \(\ContactWrench\), friction coefficients \(\CoulombFrictionCoefficient\), terrain profiles, and payload inertias directly to the critic stabilizes temporal-difference learning without burdening the onboard runtime actor.
11 Partially Observable MDP: Åström (1965) formulated optimal control under incomplete state information, proving that an optimal controller must act on the conditional probability distribution of the state given the observation history (the belief state) rather than solely on the instantaneous observation. Reinforcement learning formalized this framework three decades later (Kaelbling et al. 1998). An onboard student network’s temporal observation history serves as a learned approximation of this belief state; its temporal window must span sufficient duration for physical contact and load dynamics to become observable in the sensor stream. 
Åström, Karl Johan. 1965. “Optimal Control of Markov Processes with Incomplete State Information.” Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications 10 (1): 174–205. https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-247X(65)90154-X.

Kaelbling, Leslie Pack, Michael L. Littman, and Anthony R. Cassandra. 1998. “Planning and Acting in Partially Observable Stochastic Domains.” Artificial Intelligence 101 (1–2): 99–134. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0004-3702(98)00023-X.

Pinto, Lerrel, Marcin Andrychowicz, Peter Welinder, Wojciech Zaremba, and Pieter Abbeel. 2018. “Asymmetric Actor Critic for Image-Based Robot Learning.” Robotics: Science and Systems XIV. https://doi.org/10.15607/RSS.2018.XIV.008.

Lee, Joonho, Jemin Hwangbo, Lorenz Wellhausen, Vladlen Koltun, and Marco Hutter. 2020. “Learning Quadrupedal Locomotion over Challenging Terrain.” Science Robotics 5 (47): eabc5986.

Kumar, Ashish, Zipeng Fu, Deepak Pathak, and Jitendra Malik. 2021. “RMA: Rapid Motor Adaptation for Legged Robots.” Robotics: Science and Systems XVII. https://doi.org/10.15607/RSS.2021.XVII.011.
Asymmetric actor-critic and teacher-student distillation deploy privileged information through contrasting computational pipelines (Pinto et al. 2018; Lee et al. 2020; Kumar et al. 2021). Under asymmetric actor-critic, the actor receives only the onboard sensor history available at runtime, while the critic receives full privileged simulation state. Because the critic is discarded after training, the deployed actor architecture remains clean and lightweight. However, training an unprivileged actor directly against complex, contact-rich tasks can suffer from high sample complexity.
Distillation splits the work across the proposal boundary (figure 8). Everything privileged stays on the simulation side, and only the frozen student’s proposals, built from the machine’s own sensor history and renewed every 50 ms, cross to the permission path. In Phase 1, the privileged teacher policy \(\pi_{\text{teacher}}(\CognitivePolicyAction_{t} \mid \PrivilegedSimulatorState, \MultimodalObservation_{t})\) learns an effective control strategy via standard reinforcement learning, exploiting full access to contact forces and surface friction. In Phase 2, the student policy \(\pi_{\text{student}}(\CognitivePolicyAction_{t} \mid \ObservationHistoryWindow)\) is trained via supervised imitation learning (such as DAgger or behavioral cloning) to reproduce the teacher’s proposed actions using only a sliding history of onboard observations. While this two-phase approach simplifies reinforcement learning exploration, it introduces a transfer bottleneck. If the teacher’s control strategy relies on distinctions that cannot be reconstructed from the onboard observation history \(\ObservationHistoryWindow\), the student cannot replicate the teacher’s behavior. Privileged information accelerates training convergence, but it cannot make physically unobservable states identifiable on hardware.
Consider the cage-door latch mechanism. A student network equipped with a temporal history can compare commanded motor efforts against observed joint accelerations over recent timesteps, inferring changes in contact stiffness or friction through the resulting mechanical resistance. However, identical joint kinematics can arise from multiple distinct physical causes, and an unobserved geometric offset in the strike plate cannot be inferred simply because the simulation teacher possessed that knowledge. A temporal convolutional network or transformer encoder can output a learned latent embedding of the environment, but its accuracy must be audited against physical ground truth. Adding auxiliary loss functions to predict privileged parameters during distillation regularizes the representation, but an auxiliary loss cannot create physical information that is absent from the underlying sensor stream.






Figure 8: Teacher-student privileged state distillation: A schematic two-phase transfer pipeline. The teacher uses simulator state during training, and the student learns from onboard observations and their history. The training advantage does not establish that every privileged quantity is identifiable from those observations. On the machine, the frozen student renews a proposal every 50 ms and crosses the proposal boundary to the independent permission path; it still requires physical validation.



Selecting the observation history length \(\ObservationHistoryLength\) (distinct from the chunk horizon \(\ActionChunkHorizon\)) involves a trade-off in real-time estimator design. A window that is too short cannot filter high-frequency sensor noise or integrate enough kinematic evidence to distinguish sudden payload changes from transient disturbances. Conversely, an excessively long window increases onboard memory footprint, inflates neural inference latency, and risks diluting transient signals, such as the exact moment of initial mechanical contact, under an accumulation of pre-contact free-space observations. System qualification for the cage-door latch policy must verify contact-onset braking dynamics under the chosen history length while accounting for real hardware sensing delays. Buffering a longer temporal history in memory does not inherently add latency to incoming sensor frames, but the temporal encoder must be structured so that the newest observation immediately influences the output action.

Checkpoint 6.2: Simulator fidelity and transfer
A simulator supplies cheap experience only for the mechanisms it models, and the evidence that it models them comes from the machine.
Sizing the gap

Parameter error vs. omitted mechanism: Can you classify the rotor-inertia error, unmodeled backlash, and a missing transport lag of this chapter, say which of them domain randomization can cover, and explain why the latch’s penalty stiffness, a parameter error, still sits in the omission log until a paired probe calibrates it?
Compliance estimate: Suppose the push test returned exactly the break-even robot-side stiffness of notebook 6.3. How long after touch would a drive that keeps pushing at the fast approach reach the latch limit, and how does that compare with the plate-only contact yield deadline and the contact loop’s response?

Crediting the result

Randomization range: Can you explain why a range widened by a success threshold never enlarges the declared ODD, while a range set from a measured mechanism can be checked against the plant?
Privileged information: Can you say which of the latch teacher’s privileged quantities the student can recover from its observation history, and why it cannot infer an unobserved plate offset merely because the teacher knew it?



Even after system identification, domain randomization, and privileged state distillation, residual discrepancies persist in high-precision, contact-rich operational regimes. For the latch, both omission-log entries remain open. Engineers can resolve certain localized kinematic and friction mismatches through fine-tuning directly on the physical fixture. Physical training, however, consumes hardware operational life through mechanical wear and reopens qualification claims that depend on changed proposer behavior, timing, interfaces, or physical conditions. Every updated policy checkpoint produced by on-robot training demands fresh qualification evidence before it can be cleared for autonomous operation.

title: Policy Training
text:
6.6 Real-Robot Fine-Tuning and Residual Control
Fine-tuning a simulation-trained policy directly on a physical robot to absorb a small fixture offset can fix the local contact error while overheating the motor windings, spending gearbox fatigue life on exploratory impacts, and silently corrupting the free-space approach trajectories that had already passed qualification. Mechanical assemblies rarely match their models exactly: on a warehouse cage door, for example, the physical strike plate may sit at a small mounting offset relative to its nominal position in the simulation model. By computing gradient updates directly from physical rollouts, on-robot fine-tuning adapts policy parameters to the true structural compliance, contact dynamics, and bus latencies of the hardware. However, because end-to-end policy gradients optimize cumulative task return rather than identifying individual system parameters, they do not isolate or quantify specific physical mechanisms. Unmodeled simulation discrepancies, such as an idealized contact spring or an omitted communication transport lag, therefore remain open in the engineering omission log until dedicated system-identification probes characterize them.
Furthermore, physical adaptation exacts a concrete hardware toll. In simulation, sampling aggressive state transitions near the boundaries of stability costs only compute cycles. On physical hardware, the exploratory actions and gradient updates that correct a contact error consume mechanical fatigue life and generate substantial heat in the motor windings. Every exploratory rollout risks driving the mechanism into an unrecoverable contact jam or an over-current trip, and unconstrained parameter updates can silently degrade nominal, previously certified behaviors.
Consider adapting the baseline policy latch-sim-02 into latch-res-03, a residual candidate that adds a gated learned correction to the frozen latch-sim-02 setpoints. This adaptation is motivated by the physical reality of the hardware fixture: the physical strike plate sits 1.5 mm away from its modeled location in simulation. The physical mechanism must guide a spring-loaded latch past this plate, where non-smooth Coulomb friction, cam surface geometry, and spring preloads produce sharp stick-slip transitions. The policy outputs setpoints every 25 ms (40 Hz). To adapt its control commands to the strike plate’s contact dynamics, an on-robot fine-tuning routine collects 20,000 interaction steps, totaling 500 s of active contact and near-contact operation.
During exploration, stochastic perturbations can inject force transients faster than the low-level controller can reject them. If 1.5 percent of the sampled steps breach the 15 N contact tripwire, the fine-tuning run records 300 above-threshold samples. However, engineers must not mistake these raw sample counts for independent mechanical collisions. Consecutive over-threshold steps typically belong to a single sustained contact episode rather than multiple distinct impacts. Accurately counting mechanical shocks and evaluating their damage potential requires temporal event segmentation alongside continuous force-time telemetry.
Every mechanical impact transmits impulsive loads directly into the drivetrain. Translating that cumulative stress into an estimated expenditure of actuator service life requires an empirical, drive-specific load spectrum and fatigue life model. Actuator thermal dynamics impose a second, equally rigid operational boundary. Stochastic exploration dither elevates the root-mean-square current passing through the motor coils. Without explicit cooling intervals scheduled between training episodes, this continuous Joule heating can push motor windings to their thermal derating threshold within minutes.
Demonstrating improved performance on a specific contact fixture does not prove that the overall manipulation task remains sound. An optimization step yielding a parameter update \(\FiniteChange\ModelParameters\) produces an entirely distinct model checkpoint. Empirical evaluations gathered on the prior policy \(\ModelParameters_0\) remain historical observations of \(\ModelParameters_0\) alone; they do not substantiate safety claims for the updated weights. Gradient updates that successfully minimize contact forces on the strike plate can inadvertently distort free-space approach trajectories or degrade emergency stopping profiles in operational regions absent from the fine-tuning rollouts. Because physical trials consume valuable robot runtime and cause mechanical wear, requalification protocols must be strictly prioritized to verify both the targeted contact improvement and the baseline capabilities the update could destabilize.
Each updated checkpoint must carry its own explicit configuration manifest and regression evidence before deployment. Moreover, while optimization progresses on physical hardware, the safety permission path must actively evaluate every candidate action proposed by intermediate policies. Restricting where learned corrections may act keeps unconstrained weight updates from corrupting verified behaviors.

6.6.1 Residual policy architectures and bounded authority
To let latch-res-03 adapt to the strike plate without perturbing its free-space approach, residual architectures freeze the base policy weights and multiply the learned additive correction by an independently enforced binary gate: \[\NominalControlCommand(\DecisionProcessState) = \pi_{\text{base}}(\DecisionProcessState) + \ResidualGate(\DecisionProcessState)\,\FiniteChange\Policy(\DecisionProcessState), \tag{11}\] where \(\pi_{\text{base}}\) is the frozen base controller, \(\FiniteChange\Policy\) is a learned contact correction trained via reinforcement learning on the physical machine against the latch reward of equation 1, and \(\ResidualGate(\DecisionProcessState)\in\{0,1\}\) is an independently evaluated deterministic gate that equals one only within the certified contact envelope.
Both the base policy and the composite controller require explicit verification, because freezing an unverified base policy such as latch-sim-02 does not make it qualified for deployment. Instead, the role of the gate \(\ResidualGate(\DecisionProcessState)\) is structural: it forces the residual correction to evaluate identically to zero in free space and across all non-contact states. There, an absence of reward gradients during training would still allow a function approximator to output nonzero values on out-of-distribution inputs. Before any command reaches physical actuators, the permission path verifies the validity of the current state estimate (the machine’s fused estimate of its own configuration, developed in Spatial Memory) and audits the proposed composite action.
Relying on a soft training loss, such as an action-norm penalty \(\|\FiniteChange\Policy(\DecisionProcessState)\|^2\), merely biases the optimizer toward modest corrections during nominal rollouts; it offers no deterministic runtime guarantee. In contrast, the independent gate explicitly revokes residual authority whenever the robot operates outside designated regimes. Even with an architectural gate, the verification suite must evaluate transient switching behaviors at gate boundaries, state-estimation latency, execution timing jitter, and joint torque limits under the combined controller.
Imposing an output magnitude ceiling, \(\|\ResidualGate(\DecisionProcessState)\FiniteChange\Policy(\DecisionProcessState)\|\le\ResidualCorrectionCeiling\), restricts only one dimension of authority. A production permission path must also enforce slew-rate limits on the correction delta, prevent joint limit violations, verify multi-axis dynamic feasibility, and invoke the qualified fallback when active execution loses valid state, evidence, or lease. A late replacement proposal does not revoke a still-valid active prefix; that prefix may continue only within its own validity conditions. Furthermore, the authorized residual envelope must lie strictly within the verified stability margin of the combined closed-loop system across its intended operating envelope; checking an isolated torque limit against an idealized, single-axis specification is never sufficient. For the latch fixture, for instance, the architecture activates residual corrections exclusively during confirmed physical contact, enforces a hard zero via the gate throughout the free-space approach, and clamps joint torque slew rates. Following each optimization step on hardware, an automated regression suite must re-verify free-space trajectory tracking, contact engagement forces, emergency stopping, thermal duty cycles, and drivetrain shock profiles before granting operational authority to the new checkpoint. An improperly verified residual, even when clipped in magnitude, can still induce limit-cycle oscillations or drive the actuator gearboxes into saturation. Freezing the base policy and gating an additive residual is the most localized way to refine a policy with rewards; other post-training regimes modify the decoder’s input noise or update every weight in the network, widening the regression scope accordingly.


6.6.2 Reinforcement learning after pretraining
The gated residual is one member of a broader family of post-training regimes. Every method that refines a pretrained policy using environmental rewards must specify which parameters are allowed to change, because updating shared weights to double throughput on one fixture can silently degrade baseline behaviors elsewhere. That choice determines how much regression evidence is required to re-qualify the resulting checkpoint. Modern robotic systems use four primary post-training strategies (table 3):

Residual control freezes the base policy weights and learns an additive correction term, exactly as demonstrated by latch-res-03. This strategy has been successfully deployed to refine frozen chunked imitation policies for high-precision assembly, training the residual policy via PPO in simulation (Ankile et al. 2025). Residual architectures are straightforward to bound because independent hardware permission logic can directly gate, saturate, and rate-limit the additive output.
Noise-space steering freezes every parameter of an underlying diffusion or flow-matching policy, training an auxiliary policy only to predict the initial latent noise vector supplied to the reverse diffusion trajectory. Every proposed trajectory still passes through the frozen generative decoder, so steering is restricted to outputs that decoder can generate. This restriction does not establish that those outputs lie within demonstrated support or satisfy physical limits. Furthermore, the optimizer requires only black-box sampling access to the base policy (Wagenmaker et al. 2025). Here, the support of the base distribution constrains the proposed behaviors; the independent permission path must still determine whether those proposals may execute.
Advantage-conditioned post-training updates all network weights using supervised learning conditioned on advantage estimates. A learned critic evaluates the advantage of candidate actions across human demonstrations, autonomous rollouts, and real-time human interventions; the policy is then trained on this mixed corpus conditioned on target advantage and queried for high-advantage actions at run time. Rather than weighting gradients by the advantage or discarding failed trials, this formulation supplies an advantage indicator token as an additional conditioning input during supervised training so the network learns to associate suboptimal trajectories with negative advantage and successful recoveries with positive advantage, allowing runtime inference to prompt the policy with the positive-advantage indicator. Applied to generalist robot manipulation models, this approach more than doubled throughput and halved failure rates on the reported physical manipulation tasks (Physical Intelligence et al. 2025). However, because gradient updates modify every weight in the network, all nominal behaviors remain subject to drift.
Policy-gradient fine-tuning in simulation applies reinforcement learning techniques (section 6.4.1) to update the weights of a pretrained vision-language-action policy using sparse or binary success rewards in parallel simulation (Li et al. 2025). Like advantage conditioning, this paradigm modifies all network parameters; in addition, it inherits every physical approximation and contact-solver idealization present in the underlying simulation environment.

Regression scope follows where the composite output can change and which execution assumptions the update affects. An independently enforced residual gate localizes the changed output, but regression still covers its active region, boundary transitions, combined closed-loop behavior, and timing and resource effects. Noise-space steering can change sampling throughout the base domain despite frozen decoder weights, so every affected operating mode requires regression unless a separate gate establishes a narrower scope. Full-weight updates can also alter behaviors across the entire operational envelope. A newly fine-tuned full-weight model demands complete end-to-end regression testing across all previously validated operational modes, and the system’s adaptation_wear_log must document every modified parameter group. Whether adaptation rollouts accumulate physical machine wear on hardware or incur modeling dependencies in simulation, each rollout must be recorded in the policy manifest. No model can legitimately claim expanded operational authority without concrete validation data recorded in the system audit log.

Bounded residual authority restricts the influence of an exploratory policy during execution, but it cannot alone prevent mechanical damage or eliminate latent vulnerabilities introduced during earlier training phases. Every stage of policy synthesis, from demonstration ingestion and simulation contact mechanics to residual adaptation, leaves a distinct behavioral signature on closed-loop execution. When an embodied machine develops high-frequency chattering, thermal derating, or semantic drift, systems engineers can trace that failure behavior directly back to the training assumptions, solver compromises, and architectural trade-offs that created it.

title: Policy Training
section: 6.7 Training Failure Modes and Permission-Path Interceptors
text:
6.7 Training Failure Modes and Permission-Path Interceptors
A physical failure in a learned policy is rarely arbitrary. When an end-effector collides with a strike plate, that command reflects optimization over a specific dataset, loss formulation, and simulator dynamics, and the two failures that opened the chapter can now be traced back to theirs. The assumptions baked into that optimization leave a structural footprint on policy behavior, one that engineers can trace and mitigate before hardware ever runs. The policy vulnerability inference chain makes this causal trace explicit across five links: (\(\text{Exposure} \to \text{Dependency} \to \text{Violated Assumption} \to \text{Observable Signature} \to \text{Permission-Path Interceptor}\)). Training exposure establishes a learned dependency. An unmodeled deployment condition violates that dependency. The violation produces a measurable signature in the commands or physical plant telemetry. That signature names the specific runtime interceptor that the execution permission path requires. Reading the three latch checkpoints back through this chain shows how distinct optimization regimes produce different failure modes.
For latch-bc-01, behavioral cloning relies on the teleoperated openings. These demonstrations only support nominal plate alignment during the guarded approach; the data-collection campaign never demonstrated a displaced or misaligned plate. A sagging door frame directly violates that geometric dependency. The resulting failure signature is compounding covariate shift. Because behavioral cloning optimizes an open-loop supervised objective over expert trajectories, small drift errors compound at each control step. Individual motion proposals often remain physically plausible right up until the gripper mechanically binds against the frame. To prevent mechanical damage, a support monitor must evaluate runtime observations against the empirically supported demonstration cells and revoke policy authority outside them. Predeployment qualification follows directly from the known coverage gap that the scenario table of Choosing a tractable coverage table recorded: bench trials with deliberately displaced plates must confirm that the support monitor trips reliably before the mechanism binds.
For latch-sim-02, training inside a physics simulator instills strong dependencies on idealized contact dynamics and negligible actuation lag. A physical steel plate violates both assumptions, generating sharp contact forces and unmodeled transport delays that produce the overforce transients quantified in section 6.4.2. Paired contact probes expose this dynamical mismatch before hardware deployment. If the physical contact deadline leaves insufficient time for closed-loop deceleration, a reactive force tripwire arrives too late. Detecting a force excursion confirms that an impact occurred, but actuator inertia and mechanical compliance will continue driving the mechanism into the plate before the brakes can arrest motion. The interceptor is therefore the pre-contact stopping envelope of section 6.4.2, which guarantees a full stop at the standoff before the plate and hands engagement beyond it to the separately qualified guarded contact mode.
For latch-res-03, adaptation concentrates real-robot experience on the contact states of a single hardware rig. Localized fine-tuning targets tight-tolerance contact dynamics on that specific fixture, but it does not qualify the frozen base across the rest of the operational state space. Unlike full-weight fine-tuning, which can introduce catastrophic forgetting, this gated residual retains the base weights and holds corrections at zero in free space; its primary regression risks arise from contact corrections and gate-boundary transitions. Before updated weights receive operational authority, they must clear a frozen regression suite that evaluates both nominal latch engagement and free-space flight. In addition, an architectural residual gate must hold corrections at zero outside the designated contact phase, preventing fine-tuned offsets from destabilizing the free-space approach. Physical exploration during real-machine tuning (section 6.6) also imposes mechanical shock and motor winding heat. The runtime supervisor must monitor these thermal and structural thresholds continuously to ensure that task reward improvements do not mask hardware degradation.
Subsequent training stages do not automatically heal the unresolved dependencies of earlier stages. In the simulation-and-residual lineage (latch-sim-02 through latch-res-03), simulation artifacts persist until physical hardware evidence explicitly closes them. Conversely, the recovery-imitation branch adopts an alternative architectural path. The checkpoint latch-bc-recovery-02 incorporates targeted, human-guided recovery demonstrations for a named displaced-plate condition, expanding the operational envelope without relying on an uncalibrated simulator. Its remaining engineering uncertainties, chiefly closed-loop trajectory stability and potential regression on nominal openings, are made explicit through targeted qualification requests.
Ultimately, each inference chain connects a specific training assumption to an empirical test and an active execution limit. The policy manifest preserves these connections alongside the checkpoint’s source data, simulator configuration, optimization objective, and architectural constraints. By maintaining this end-to-end traceability, verification suites can systematically evaluate candidate policies against the exact physical vulnerabilities created by their training history.

title: Policy Training
text:
6.8 The Policy Manifest
Handing a candidate checkpoint to an evaluation team with only its weight file and a training curve hides whether its behavior on a displaced plate comes from human recovery demonstrations, uncalibrated simulator rollouts, or pure network extrapolation. The candidate selection must distinguish nominal behavior supported by demonstrations, newly taught recovery, and contact behavior that still depends on unverified simulation. The failure chains of section 6.7 make that distinction concrete for each checkpoint; the record accompanying the candidate into evaluation preserves the reasoning, including the assumptions that remain open.
The policy manifest records how a checkpoint was produced (table 4). It lists the training stages and the data support the checkpoint inherits from the provenance records. It also lists the simulator versions, together with the omission log of mechanisms they leave out and mismatches paired probes have not closed. Finally, it records the wear incurred during adaptation and the operating domain the checkpoint declares. These fields state what evaluation must test and what runtime enforcement must accommodate. The runtime safety supervisor can check the manifest against its validated configuration before enabling a checkpoint. A declared boundary does not automatically generate a reliable detector or a safe clamp; those mechanisms require their own engineering and evidence.
The manifest separates optimization results from the conditions the policy may be asked to operate in. The declared ODD is the part of the ODD from Collection Policy Coverage that the policy manifest claims: the supported cells of the data join, minus every state the omission log excludes. High training reward or low offline loss does not show that the policy is safe outside it. The declared ODD is therefore computed from the join and the log, never from the training curve, and a convergent metric cannot stand in for clearance over regimes nobody characterized.
The separate latch-bc-recovery-02 manifest consumes the original provenance and the stipulated latch-recovery-02 archive, adding the positively displaced-plate cell at the guarded approach to the candidate domain with the expert recovery labels and held-out sessions identified by digest. Its qualification request asks whether the updated policy completes that recovery and preserves nominal service under the same physical limits. The original archive remains unchanged, and negative displacement and the fast approach remain excluded. Current provenance bounds the evidence already available, whereas collecting and qualifying new experience expands the machine’s useful competence.

For the original latch campaign and its simulation-residual lineage, a compact manifest links the fields into one decision:

regime_sequence: demonstration checkpoint latch-bc-01 → latch-sim-02, a student initialized from latch-bc-01 and distilled from a simulator teacher trained by reinforcement learning on privileged state (privileged contact wrenches \(\ContactWrench\) distilled into an 8-step observation-history buffer) → gated residual candidate latch-res-03. Retain each checkpoint hash, loss or reward specification, and stop rule.
base_checkpoint: no pretrained robot policy underlies the latch checkpoints, which descend from latch-bc-01 as regime_sequence records; any pretrained image encoder they use belongs here by digest. A candidate post-trained from the machine’s intent model would record that model’s weight digest, its pretraining mixture as a known unknown, and its action-space mapping, and would inherit the same declared ODD (section 6.2.8).
policy_inference_contract: specify checkpoint weights hash \(\text{hash}(\ModelParameters)\), the machine’s 80M-parameter ACT architecture with one decoder pass per chunk, chunk prediction horizon \(\ActionChunkHorizon =\) 16 setpoints at 25 ms, and the 40 ms p99 inference target. Record the selected execution prefix separately from the 50 ms proposal-renewal deadline and the selected chunk lease. Each renewed prefix requires valid evidence and a feasible continuation or fallback; the prediction horizon is not the active lease.
data_support: cite the latch campaign’s provenance records and its scenario table by digest; their join supports the nominal strike plate at the guarded approach, and lists the displaced plate and the faster approach, whose cells hold no demonstrations, as known absences with no recovery label.
simulation_provenance: record the actual solver build and contact parameters.
omission_log: the example simulator models strike-plate contact with a penalty spring far softer than the plate and omits actuator transport lag, so the contact states those two departures govern are unverified for the checkpoints trained in simulation.
negative_event_registry: cite by digest the authority-record entry, with its pre-trigger ring-buffer trace, for every fixture-shoulder strike, operator veto, or permission-path clamp with its event classification, without treating rejected learner commands as expert targets. Mark episodes an operator truncated, so that an update does not score an aborted command as a success.
adaptation_wear_log: associate latch-res-03 with the specific rig, above-threshold samples and separately identified contact events, motor-current history, modified residual weights, and free-space regression result.
declared_odd_boundary: the supported cells minus the states the omission log excludes, here the nominal plate at the guarded approach of 0.03 m/s. The contact states governed by the two omissions stay outside the declared ODD for every simulation-refined checkpoint, latch-sim-02 and latch-res-03 alike, until paired probes close them. The displaced plate and the 0.10 m/s approach lie outside it, and the fast approach would stay outside even with demonstrations, because its contact deadline (section 6.4.2) leaves almost nothing beyond the contact-loop response. There the permission path must impose the guarded approach or refuse policy authority.

A qualification review would withhold operational authority from latch-res-03 until paired contact probes quantify the contact-stiffness error and the omitted lag, and the combined controller passes contact, free-space, stopping, and wear-budget tests. With only the original campaign, the same rule leaves latch-bc-01 as the checkpoint evaluation may sample, provided the support monitor of its chain refuses policy authority off the nominal plate (section 6.7). Trained without a simulator, it carries no omission-log exclusions, so its declared ODD keeps the door’s contact states at the nominal plate and the guarded approach. The manifest records that decision and its evidence rather than converting a training score into permission.
The manifest references the collector, plant, calibration, and action taps through the provenance record of The Dataset Schema. The cited digests preserve which data and scenario table produced the checkpoint; later changes require a new record rather than silently updating its lineage. Simulator provenance similarly fixes the solver and timestep12 used during optimization. Its separate omission log carries unresolved discrepancies from section 6.5 into evaluation’s coverage gaps and fault-injection tests.
12 Penalty-Contact Timestep: The contact timescale scales as \(\sqrt{\EffectiveImpactMass/\EffectiveSeriesStiffness}\). For the latch’s 9 kg moving mass it is about 24 ms against the soft penalty spring and 4.7 ms against the real plate, so a timestep sized to resolve the simulated contact is about 5× too coarse once the spring is stiffened to match the plate. The integrator, damping, and solver tolerances set the final step, which is refined until contact onset, peak force, and impulse converge. Downstream engineering teams consume the manifest throughout the design, evaluation, and release lifecycle. The evaluation record of The Evaluation Record consumes it directly. Its target ODD is sampled from inside the declared ODD, and its catalog of coverage gaps inherits the known absences and the omission log, so evaluation suites probe the specific failure modes each training regime predicts. Targeted exploratory tests outside the candidate domain can also identify gaps, but they do not establish an operational claim there without new support and qualification. The permission path takes the declared ODD as the outer limit of the region in which it admits policy proposals, and uses the recorded support to parameterize out-of-distribution detectors. Verification and the safety case draw on the manifest to establish the provenance of every parameter update and to confirm that each omission is bounded by an independent physical interlock.


↪ The omission log becomes one of the upstream records from which fault records are compiled for release, developed in Fault Records for Release.

Checkpoint 6.3: Policy manifests and declared ODDs
Before releasing a trained policy checkpoint to physical verification, confirm the following relationships between the policy manifest, its omission log, and the declared ODD:

Complete the latch record: A fixture-shoulder strike appears after latch-res-03 was trained with a soft penalty contact and no actuator lag. Which omitted mechanism belongs in omission_log, and which paired probe and admission decision must the manifest record?
Confining the declared ODD: Suppose demonstrations were collected at the fast approach and every omission-log entry were closed by paired probes. Why would the latch policy’s declared ODD still exclude the fast approach, which timing comparison decides it, and what must the permission path impose on a proposal that arrives at that speed?
Negative event logging: Why does the manifest keep the pre-trigger trace of an operator veto or fixture strike as labeled failure evidence rather than as an imitation target?
Declared operational boundaries: latch-bc-01 proposes to open the door while the strike plate sits displaced from its nominal mount. How does the permission path use the data_support field to classify that state as ungrounded extrapolation rather than demonstrated competence, and why does a confident policy output not change the classification?



The manifest turns a training history into a claim with stated limits. The original record sends latch-bc-01 to evaluation and keeps latch-res-03 out of service until paired probes and regression tests close its gaps. The stipulated recovery record sends latch-bc-recovery-02 with a wider, explicitly testable candidate claim. The common ways that decision goes wrong all let a training score stand in for that evidence.

title: Policy Training
text:
6.9 Fallacies and Pitfalls
Minimizing loss on an offline demonstration split or maximizing cumulative return in simulation measures compliance with training assumptions rather than physical competence on hardware. When an objective rewards behavior that exploits a curated demonstration distribution or a simulator approximation, the ranking of candidates established in training can invert on deployment. The candidate that scored highest in simulation finishes lowest on hardware, through unsupported state drift, contact-force spikes past the structural limit, or torque oscillations that grow into resonant chatter (figure 9). Virtual environments forgive maneuvers that physical hardware penalizes with tripwires, resonance, or thermal overload, so the causal assumptions connecting a training metric to physical execution have to be tested before a policy receives actuator authority.






Figure 9: Illustrative policy ranking inversion: (a) A constructed slope graph shows how a candidate favored by a simulated score can lose its advantage under physical evaluation. (b) Possible causes include unsupported recovery states, contact mismatch, and actuator chatter. The rankings are a teaching example, not measured results for the latch checkpoints.




Pitfall: Sanitizing recovery episodes to achieve lower offline validation loss.
Suppose an archive of latch manipulation demonstrations includes human recovery maneuvers, and two separate policies train on competing subsets of this corpus. One policy trains on the full archive, including episodes where a human teleoperator backed off the gripper and re-aligned the jaws after the latch cam caught on the strike plate. The second policy trains on a sanitized subset stripped of all hesitation and retries, achieving a markedly lower loss on its held-out validation split. When deployed on the physical cell, both policies eventually encounter a misaligned cam. The first policy recognizes the contact anomaly, backs off, and seats the latch successfully. The second policy relentlessly drives along the nominal path, building contact force until the safety supervisor’s force tripwire halts the cell. Because the sanitized dataset excluded off-nominal recoveries, the lower validation loss proves only that predicting smooth nominal trajectories is easier to fit than handling physical disturbances. Pruning corrective demonstrations simplifies the loss score at the exact price of removing the feedback behaviors the physical controller needs off the nominal path. Filtering out recovery trajectories to drive down offline prediction loss strips the policy of the corrective demonstrations required to escape compounding physical errors.
Architect’s countermeasure: Retain all authority-record entries during dataset ingestion and admit, as training targets, only the stabilized, human-reviewed segments of attributable expert recoveries. Never prune demonstration corpora to minimize offline validation loss, and mandate closed-loop physical perturbation benchmarks to verify recovery competence before signing off on deployment candidate checkpoints.


Fallacy: Transitioning from human demonstrations to simulation reinforcement learning removes the failures training left in the policy.
An assembly team switches from behavioral cloning to simulation reinforcement learning to eliminate lateral drift during automated gasket seating. The resulting policy cures the drift in the virtual environment but commands joint torque oscillations at 65 Hz. The physics simulator permits this aggressive chatter because its rigid-body solver assumes massless motor rotors and instantaneous torque reversal. On the physical machine, this high-frequency command excites drivetrain mechanical resonance and rapidly heats the motor windings toward their thermal trip point via \(\TorqueProducingCurrent^2 \ElectricalResistance\) Joule losses. The drive electronics throttle current to prevent permanent motor damage, causing the assembly stroke to stall before seating completes. Shifting training regimes solved an imitation drift problem by introducing a high-frequency chatter exploit that the simulator did not penalize. Qualification must therefore evaluate the full physical task under sustained cyclic operation, verifying simulator dynamics assumptions against physical hardware telemetry. Switching to simulation reinforcement learning substitutes numerical solver shortcuts and unmodeled mechanical dynamics for human demonstration deficits.
Architect’s countermeasure: Require paired-trace validation across all four reality gap channels before deploying simulation-trained policies. Enforce low-level hardware rate limiters and digital low-pass action filters (\(\ActionFilterCutoffFrequency \le\) 20 Hz) within the embedded motor drives to suppress high-frequency chatter originating from unmodeled rotor inertia.


Fallacy: Assuming online gradient updates preserve predeployment safety envelopes.
When a simulation-trained policy shows steady-state positioning error on a physical assembly fixture, an engineer might enable online policy-gradient fine-tuning directly on the robot. After 5,000 gradient steps, the arm successfully eliminates contact positioning error at the fixture, prompting the team to declare the updated model production-ready. Applying parameter updates \(\FiniteChange\ModelParameters\) directly to the policy network, however, produces an entirely new checkpoint with changed weights. The behavioral trials accumulated during predeployment qualification remain observations of the original checkpoint and do not establish performance of the updated one. Independent permission and fallback properties may remain applicable only while their plant, timing, authority, isolation, and realization premises hold; integration must check those premises after the update. While local contact accuracy improves, unconstrained backpropagation into shared representations triggers catastrophic forgetting in rarely visited state-space regions. As a result, the fine-tuned policy may lose stability during high-speed free-space slews or corrupt its emergency deceleration profiles. Because physical robot time and mechanical wear preclude repeating full-scale testing suites on hardware, regression suites must isolate and verify every operational envelope that gradient updates might perturb. Online gradient updates require fresh behavioral qualification and reopen every assurance claim that depends on the changed checkpoint or execution conditions.
Architect’s countermeasure: When a bounded correction suffices, use gated residual policy architectures (\(\NominalControlCommand = \pi_{\text{base}} + \ResidualGate(\DecisionProcessState)\,\FiniteChange\Policy\)) with an externally enforced binary gate (\(\ResidualGate(\DecisionProcessState) \equiv 0\) in free space) to localize real-world adaptation. Mandate automated, frozen non-regression suites that verify trajectory tracking and stopping profiles before granting execution authority to updated parameters.


Fallacy: Believing that widening parameter distributions can substitute for missing physical mechanisms.
When an assembly policy repeatedly fails on physical hardware, an engineering team might attempt to brute-force sim-to-real transfer by radically widening the simulator’s domain randomization bounds. They randomize link masses by ±50 percent and vary surface friction coefficients across the extreme interval from 0.05 to 1.5. On the physical test bench, however, the trained policy behaves poorly: it moves sluggishly through free space and hesitates indefinitely upon initial contact. Randomization perturbs coefficients exclusively within the governing differential equations already hardcoded in the physics engine. It cannot synthesize missing physical phenomena such as gearbox backlash, joint cable compliance, Stribeck friction, or sensor transport jitter. When dynamically incompatible virtual plants produce indistinguishable observations, a memoryless policy cannot choose separately for each plant; average-return optimization may favor a slow compromise or may sacrifice low-probability cases. While recurrent or history-conditioned architectures can adapt to wide parametric variations by estimating system properties online, even an adaptive policy cannot identify or compensate for physical mechanisms that never existed in its training simulator. Expanding parameter randomization bounds merely shifts the probability distribution across existing simulator equations; it cannot synthesize unmodeled physical dynamics.
Architect’s countermeasure: Calibrate baseline physics engine parameters against real hardware test fixtures before introducing domain randomization. Explicitly document whether parameter distributions derive from empirical instrument measurements or heuristic curricula such as automatic domain randomization. Enumerate known physical omissions, including transmission elasticity and actuator deadbands, in the policy manifest’s omission log, ensuring that hardware-level safety watchdogs bound operations within verified modeling assumptions.


Fallacy: Assuming multi-step generative decoders can execute synchronously within inner actuator control loops.
Aiming to capture multimodal trajectory distributions observed in offline demonstration logs, an engineer replaces the single-pass ACT feedforward decoder in latch-bc-01 with an iterative 16-step diffusion denoising head. The team deploys the new architecture synchronously into the robot’s real-time inner control loop, scheduling a complete iterative sampling cycle for every 25 ms actuator setpoint. Under the hardware inference budget evaluated in section 6.2.6, executing all denoising steps consumes 48 ms, exceeding the allowable control step deadline. Because the synchronous dispatch pipeline stalls awaiting model convergence, the system routinely misses setpoint deadlines. The low-level controller must either freeze on stale command setpoints or trip safety watchdogs on every iteration overrun. The weight-streaming floor of The memory wall bounds each evaluation from below, and Action chunking shows that re-reading the action head on every evaluation can dominate the decoder’s cost. Each of the 16 dependent evaluations pays that floor, so the sum misses the setpoint deadline before scheduling jitter is even counted. Deploying multi-step generative policies into high-rate actuator loops requires decoupling iterative trajectory generation from real-time setpoint tracking through asynchronous execution contracts.
Architect’s countermeasure: Decouple iterative policy inference from high-frequency actuator control loops whenever measured inference latency approaches the control period. Formally partition the pipeline into an asynchronous planner generating trajectory chunks and an inner controller tracking them under qualified execution leases. Explicitly track prediction horizons, executed setpoint prefixes, and proposal renewal deadlines. Buffering trajectory chunks never grants permanent operational authority: the execution engine continuously validates physical safety invariants and triggers safe stopping profiles whenever a lease expires without a fresh proposal.

title: Policy Training
text:
6.10 Summary
A policy’s weights keep what its training experience rewarded and forget which experience that was, so each regime is best remembered by the dependency it leaves behind. Demonstrations leave a dependency on coverage: a point-regression head averages valid modes into an action no one chose, and even a multimodal head drifts into states the demonstrations never recovered from. A reward-labeled log leaves a dependency on the support of the logged actions, and a pretrained base on someone else’s embodiment. Trial on the machine pays for its experience in calendar time, winding heat, and drivetrain life. Simulation pays almost nothing per trial but inherits every approximation in its contact solver and every mechanism it omits. Fine-tuning on the machine creates a new checkpoint that needs its own behavioral evidence and review of affected assurance premises. None of these dependencies shows in a validation loss or a simulated return.
Orthogonal to the source of experience, every policy must deliver its proposal inside the machine’s deadline \(\CompletionDeadline\). The decoder that represents several modes buys that representation with dependent evaluations, and what decides whether it can run is renewal slack against the jitter allowance, not mean latency. When slack runs out, the chunk lease, not the decoder, bounds how long an admitted prefix keeps moving the arm.
The policy manifest gathers these dependencies into one claim with stated limits. Its declared ODD is the supported cells of the data join minus every state the omission log excludes, never a region read off a training curve. For the latch, that rule sends latch-bc-01 to evaluation at the nominal plate and the guarded approach. It holds the simulation-refined checkpoints until paired probes bound the contact and timing omissions. It also lets latch-bc-recovery-02 carry a wider claim that new recovery experience has to earn. An admitted action crossing the causal boundary carries no guarantee beyond the evidence that qualifies it, and the load-bearing relations behind that evidence are collected in table 5.
