Checkpoint 3.3: Proposals that arrive on time and are wrong
A proposal can meet every deadline and still target the wrong thing, so the receiver needs evidence the proposer cannot supply about itself.

Classical vs. learned: For the welding cell and the conveyor mug pick, which approach would you use to propose motion in each, and which properties could you still prove or measure for each?
Interface checkability: Can you explain why the permission path can enforce this geometric intent lease on a target pose with a capture time but not on an ungrounded latent vector alone?
Hallucination vs. staleness: For the grasp on the carton photograph and for a smooth chunk that arrives after \(\EvidenceHorizon\), which payload field or independent measurement lets the receiver refuse each?
Threshold estimate: Assuming every attempt in a regime receives its tabulated confidence score, if the receiver admitted every proposal scoring above the far-OOD confidence in table 4, which regimes would pass, and what stipulated fraction of near-OOD attempts would fail?

title: The Cognitive Brain
text:
3.7 Fallacies and Pitfalls
Learned models expand the behavioral repertoire of robotic systems, but their predictions remain ungrounded hypotheses until verified against physical dynamics and environmental constraints. In deployed systems, critical failures emerge when software architectures treat statistical confidence, numerical formatting, or kinematic smoothness as an unconditional license to command hardware. Avoiding these hazards requires separating candidate generation from deterministic safety enforcement.

Fallacy: An engineering team must choose entirely between formal classical safety proofs and learned empirical capability.
Engineers often frame robot control as a mutual exclusion: either adopt a classical controller with provable stability guarantees, or deploy an expressive neural policy that achieves broad task coverage through empirical learning. Consider an assembly plant routing flexible wiring harnesses. A classical model-based controller enforces rigid kinematic constraints and workspace boundaries, yet it struggles to model the nonlinear dynamics of deformable cables. Conversely, a learned diffusion policy navigates cable deformation successfully, but occasionally proposes motions that exceed physical clearance limits.
The proposal boundary dissolves this dilemma. The diffusion policy proposes, and an independent minimal-intervention filter corrects any command that would cross a clearance limit before it reaches the actuators. The correction preserves the modeled safety constraint without guaranteeing completion of the harness insertion, so systems architects must track task completion, proposer error distribution, and protective intervention frequency as independent performance metrics.



↪ The minimal-intervention filter, which replaces an inadmissible command with the smallest correction that satisfies the physical constraints, is developed in The Minimal Intervention Principle and Optimization Filters.

Pitfall: Allowing a neural model’s high confidence to bypass deterministic geometric boundaries.
A cleanroom manipulator handling reagent vials mistakes specular glare on a transparent glass partition for open workspace and plans a reach directly through the barrier. The resulting action packet satisfies standard transport validation: joint coordinates are finite and in range, the command arrives on schedule, and the neural proposer reports an output confidence of \(\ProposerConfidenceScore = 0.98\). However, a high score indicates only that one output dominated the alternatives. Section 3.6.2 showed that a network can be most confident on inputs far from anything it was trained on. The same specular reflection that deceived the perceptual front-end also corrupts the confidence head, producing an assertive proposal for an impossible motion.
Actuation permission must always derive from deterministic geometric validation rather than statistical self-assessment. Before energizing motor drives, the real-time execution monitor must validate candidate trajectories against qualified local geometric boundaries derived from independent sensors, such as acoustic rangefinders, time-of-flight sensors, or calibrated structural keep-out zones. Because an isolated microcontroller or real-time checker lacks the memory and compute budget to evaluate a full host-resident 3D occupancy grid, the boundary handoff contract must deliver explicit spatial bounds along with verified validity intervals before motors receive current.


Fallacy: Raw softmax probabilities or predicted confidence scores reflect true physical success rates.
An industrial bin-picking policy can assign near-unity scores to grasp candidates that fail immediately under altered lighting or surface conditions. The softmax function merely transforms unbounded real-valued logits into an artificial probability distribution that sums to one across the discrete candidate set. This mathematical normalization quantifies relative preference across the model’s training distribution rather than mechanical stability in physical contact.
Post-hoc calibration methods, such as temperature scaling, align predicted probabilities with empirical accuracy only while operating under conditions identical to the calibration distribution. As the illustrative gaps in table 4 depict, calibration can degrade sharply when lighting, surface friction, or geometry shifts out of distribution. Relying on an abstention threshold applied to raw model scores will silently allow unstable grasps or collisions during operational shifts. Production systems must backstop model proposals with independent physical verification, including tactile slip sensing, force-torque thresholds, and deterministic geometric checks.


Pitfall: Coupling high-frequency semantic classifications directly to motor setpoints without continuous filtering.
A delivery robot navigates past reflective tarps flapping over traffic cones. At every perception update (\(20\,\text{Hz}\)), the vision pipeline alternates its discrete classification between an open corridor, a rigid obstacle, and a compliant drape. If the motion planner maps these discrete classification switches directly into motor setpoints, perceptual noise commands instantaneous velocity reversals. Each reversal is a step in velocity reference, which a PD servo loop turns into the derivative-gain torque step that the temporal ensembling jerk trap computed for a single chunk seam, repeated at every flip. Chattering commands of this kind saturate motor drive currents, cause mechanical backlash wear, and excite dangerous structural resonances throughout the chassis.
Physical architectures must decouple discrete semantic classification from continuous motor control. Engineers introduce temporal debouncing, Bayesian belief filters, or hysteresis thresholds to suppress semantic switching noise. Furthermore, the permission path’s interpolator must hold setpoints within explicit acceleration and jerk limits before dispatching them to the drives. Even when the resulting trajectory appears smooth, the real-time execution engine must verify dynamic feasibility against hardware torque and thermal limits.


Fallacy: A numerically valid and smooth action chunk can safely be executed whenever it arrives.
Modern action-chunking architectures generate sequences of future setpoints to bridge the rate mismatch between slow neural inference on an application processor and fast motor control loops. Consider a mobile manipulator grasping an item from a moving conveyor. A host policy computes a smooth, multi-step arm trajectory toward the target, but operating system scheduling jitter, memory paging, or bus stalls delay packet delivery beyond the sensor evidence horizon. When the action chunk finally reaches the motor controller, its waypoints remain mathematically continuous and within joint kinematic limits. Meanwhile, conveyor motion has shifted the actual object outside the grasp envelope.
Executing an outdated chunk causes the arm to track a phantom path. A motor controller must reject stale packets regardless of their internal smoothness. Action chunks must carry explicit timestamps and temporal validity leases tied to the freshness of their underlying sensor observations. The real-time receiver may execute an active trajectory only while its lease remains valid. If an expected chunk fails to arrive before the lease expires, the controller must execute a qualified deceleration or compliant hold to keep the hardware within safe operational limits. Kinematic smoothness cannot compensate for expired temporal validity.

title: The Cognitive Brain
text:
3.8 Summary
Learned representations give the mobile manipulator what hand-authored geometry could not, the ability to recognize and act on objects no engineer enumerated, and the machine pays for that breadth in memory traffic, arithmetic, and time. A fresh evaluation splits into a compute-bound prefill and a bandwidth-bound decode, so weight-only quantization shortens one term and leaves the other, and a large intent model on an embedded processor renews only a few times per second. Supply and validity are therefore separate budgets. A chunk keeps the arm supplied between renewals, but every setpoint in it descends from one observation, so the time the target stays within tolerance, not the length of the chunk, bounds how much of it may run. What the slow proposer hands the fast one decides what the permission path can check, and because a proposal can arrive on time and still be wrong, every proposal must carry its capture time, validity limit, and provenance so that it remains refusable. Six core quantitative relations govern these trade-offs across the chapter, each bounding a distinct stage of proposal generation and expiration (table 6).



Table 6: Key equations of the cognitive brain: The bounds that price a learned proposer on the machine’s processor and size its chunks against a moving target, with the place each is derived.










Equation
What it bounds or decides
Derived




\(\ProposerEvaluationRate \le \SustainedMemoryBandwidth/\WeightMemory\)
The memory wall: the peak renewal frequency when every evaluation cycle streams nonresident weights from memory before performing additional work
equation 2


\(\ArithmeticIntensity = \text{FLOPs}/\text{bytes transferred}\)
Arithmetic intensity vs. the processor ridge point, determining whether a workload phase is bandwidth-bound or compute-bound (batch-1 decode sits near one FLOP per byte; prefill approaches \(\SequenceLength\) FLOPs per byte)
equation 3


\(\ProposerInferenceTime \approx \max\!\left(\frac{\PrefillOperations}{\EfficiencyHw\,\PeakRate}, \frac{\WeightMemory}{\SustainedMemoryBandwidth}\right) + (\EmittedTokenCount-1)\frac{\WeightMemory}{\SustainedMemoryBandwidth}\)
The latency of a complete evaluation, combining compute-bound prefill with bandwidth-bound decode sweeps; weight-only quantization reduces only the second term
equation 4


\(\KvCacheMemory = 2 \times \LayerCount \times \HiddenDimension \times \SequenceLength \times \ElementStorageSize\)
The memory capacity occupied and reread by retained context, scaling linearly with the preserved token sequence length
equation 1


\(\MinimumChunkSetpointCount = \left\lceil (\ChunkRenewalPeriod + \ProposerInferenceTime)/\SetpointStepInterval \right\rceil\)
The minimum setpoint count an action chunk must deliver to keep actuators supplied across a complete replanning and inference cycle
equation 6


\(\EvidenceHorizon = \sqrt{2(\PositionalTaskTolerance - \InitialTrackingError)/\SlipAccelerationBound}\)
The evidence horizon during which target tracking remains within physical tolerance; the total latency span \(\ChunkRenewalPeriod + \ProposerInferenceTime\) must fit inside this limit
equation 5







Key Takeaways: Learned proposers and deliberation limits

Memory traffic and arithmetic both bound fresh inference: When an evaluation cycle streams nonresident weights from memory, the total weight footprint and sustained memory bandwidth establish a hard latency floor. Fetching the intent model’s 14 GB of FP16 weights requires 98.0 ms. Input token prefill operates in the compute-bound regime, whereas per-token autoregressive decoding is bandwidth-bound. Consequently, even with INT4 weights, a single evaluation consumes approximately 336 ms. This supports the selected intent renewal rate of 2 Hz, which is far too slow to drive real-time actuator chunk renewal directly.
Chunking supplies motion without refreshing evidence: Generating a chunk of 16 setpoints amortizes a single backbone evaluation across 400 ms of candidate motion. Although this amortizes memory bus traffic across waypoints, the robot executes that motion without incorporating new visual evidence until the subsequent policy evaluation completes.
Supply and validity bound different horizons: In the conveyor pick task, actuator continuity requires a minimum supply horizon of 4 setpoints to bridge neural renewal intervals, whereas target drift constrains the sensory evidence horizon to approximately 219 ms. A deeper queue of setpoints cannot extend that validity. A setpoint stays eligible only while the evidence behind it holds and the active chunk lease runs, and when renewal stops, the chunk lease bounds how far the arm continues.
Retained context competes with current sensing: Retaining the hypothetical five-second history at the stated sampling rate occupies 21.0 GB of key-value cache memory. Because storing and rereading past attention state directly contends for DRAM bandwidth with incoming sensory observations and proposal generation, temporal context retention must be explicitly managed within the system timing and memory budget.
Proposer interfaces dictate runtime verifiability: An opaque latent embedding passed from a high-level intent model to a low-level policy cannot be cross-referenced with measured workspace geometry or aged against target drift. Conversely, an explicit Cartesian target pose accompanied by an observation timestamp provides a checkable contract. This auditable geometric interface allows the machine’s permission path to enforce its intent lease alongside the high-rate chunk lease.
Reported confidence requires independent physical validation: A softmax probability or normalized confidence score emitted by a learned model cannot guarantee physical execution success under real-world distribution shift. While calibration validates score reliability across known operating regimes, runtime safety demands independent geometric constraints, kinematic limits, and physical contact monitoring.
Proposals must remain rejectable: Trajectory proposals must bundle explicit observation timestamps, kinematic assumptions, and validity envelopes alongside their raw setpoints. The Nervous System combines these proposer constraints with real-time body state measurements to validate trajectory headers, manage handoffs between successive chunks, and enforce fail-safe execution windows.



The conveyor pick separates two kinds of inadequacy that call for different fixes. A proposer that cannot renew before its evidence expires has design remedies: fewer input tokens, a smaller or differently quantized model, more bandwidth, or a slower target. A proposer that renews in time and still proposes a wrong grasp is not repaired by any of them, which is why its output stays a proposal however fast it arrives. Both cases end at the first law (principle \(\ref{pri-vol4-irreversibility}\)). Motion executed on evidence that has gone stale, or toward an affordance that does not exist, delivers energy that cannot be recalled. The time a proposal may keep driving the machine therefore has to be set below the proposer, from the body’s stopping budget, rather than by the proposer’s own schedule.

title: The Cognitive Brain
text:
3.9 Historical Perspective and Further Reading
The two-speed architecture developed throughout this chapter, which couples a slow deliberative proposer with a high-frequency execution loop that continuously services the actuators, is robotics’ recurring answer to a timing constraint. Physical machines have wrestled with this division since Shakey’s deliberative planning (Nilsson 1984), Brooks’ reactive subsumption layers (Brooks 1986), and ALVINN’s direct learned steering (Pomerleau 1989). The classical industrial pipelines examined in section 3.2 retained explicit geometric representations by restricting robot operation to structured, calibrated workcells where rigid kinematic models hold, while end-to-end learning gained broad behavioral coverage from data at the cost of formal analytical guarantees.

Nilsson, Nils J. 1984. Shakey the Robot. Technical Note No. 323. Artificial Intelligence Center, SRI International.

Pomerleau, Dean A. 1989. “ALVINN: An Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 1: 305–13.

↩︎ The lineage from Shakey’s deliberative planning through Brooks’ subsumption layers to ALVINN’s learned steering is established in From Prediction to Action.

Vaswani, Ashish, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Łukasz Kaiser, and Illia Polosukhin. 2017. “Attention Is All You Need.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 30.

Jacob, Benoit, Skirmantas Kligys, Bo Chen, Menglong Zhu, Matthew Tang, Andrew Howard, Hartwig Adam, and Dmitry Kalenichenko. 2018. “Quantization and Training of Neural Networks for Efficient Integer-Arithmetic-Only Inference.” 2018 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, 2704–13. https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr.2018.00286.

Lin, Ji, Jiaming Tang, Haotian Tang, Shang Yang, Wei-Ming Chen, Wei-Chen Wang, Guangxuan Xiao, Xingyu Dang, Chuang Gan, and Song Han. 2024. “AWQ: Activation-Aware Weight Quantization for on-Device LLM Compression and Acceleration.” Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems 6: 87–100.

The hardware bottlenecks that govern modern policy inference stem from a parallel evolution in computer architecture. Wulf and McKee (1995) identified the widening memory wall, observing that processor speed was improving far faster than DRAM access time. Williams et al. (2009) formalized this relationship into the roofline model, establishing operational arithmetic intensity, the ratio of floating-point operations performed to memory bytes transferred, as the metric that reveals whether an execution phase is memory-bandwidth-bound or compute-bound. Modern autoregressive models collide directly with these bandwidth ceilings. The Transformer architecture requires every newly generated token to attend over cached keys and values from all preceding context tokens (Vaswani et al. 2017). As Pope et al. (2023) demonstrated through analytical modeling of distributed Transformer inference, generating one token at a time splits execution into a compute-bound prompt prefill phase, which processes all input tokens together, and a memory-bandwidth-bound autoregressive decoding phase. In embodied setups, where real-time interactive control requires generating action tokens with a batch size of 1, the memory wall dominates the decode, as notebook 3.1 prices for the machine and checks against a published measurement on its processor. To alleviate this memory traffic, integer-only quantization demonstrated that low-precision arithmetic could run efficiently on mobile processors with small accuracy loss on the vision networks it evaluated (Jacob et al. 2018). As the intent-model measurements of table 1 show, however, the cost of a given bit width depends on the method, the kernels, and the task. Modern weight-only formats such as AWQ protect salient weight channels while cutting the bytes transferred across the memory bus on each decoding pass (Lin et al. 2024).
Learned proposers emerged when these sequence architectures were adapted to robot sensorimotor trajectories. The Vision Transformer demonstrated that self-attention could replace convolutional feature extractors on raw image patches without losing spatial coherence (Dosovitskiy et al. 2021). RT-1 and RT-2 extended this foundation to robotics by tokenizing continuous physical actions directly into the vocabulary of large vision-language models (Brohan, Brown, Carbajal, Chebotar, Dabis, et al. 2023; Brohan, Brown, Carbajal, Chebotar, Chen, et al. 2023), while OpenVLA established an open, reproducible seven-billion-parameter architecture that enabled systematic hardware profiling and fine-tuning (Kim et al. 2024). However, evaluating large transformer backbones autoregressively at every single control step proved computationally impractical for low-latency physical loops. Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) and Diffusion Policy resolved this bottleneck by shifting the unit of prediction from isolated steps to short trajectories (Zhao et al. 2023; Chi et al. 2025), amortizing inference latency over multiple timesteps and reducing the compounding of per-step errors. Advancing this approach, \(\pi_0\) coupled a high-capacity vision-language backbone with a flow-matching action expert capable of generating high-frequency motor commands (Black et al. 2024). Real-time action chunking hid the inference delay behind execution by freezing the setpoints that run during inference and generating the rest of the next chunk to agree with them (Black, Galliker, et al. 2025), a formulation that recasts classical receding-horizon model predictive control through the lens of deep learning (Mayne et al. 2000). Modern embodied platforms, including Helix (Figure AI 2025) and GR00T N1 (Bjorck et al. 2025), adopt the same two-speed separation. The contract between the two tiers remains an open design question. Deployed systems pass latent vectors, language, or geometry from the slow model to the fast one (table 2). This chapter’s case for a checkable geometric target, together with the invariants a real-time monitor must enforce on it, is one position in that question rather than a settled standard.

Dosovitskiy, Alexey, Lucas Beyer, Alexander Kolesnikov, Dirk Weissenborn, Xiaohua Zhai, Thomas Unterthiner, Mostafa Dehghani, et al. 2021. “An Image Is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

Brohan, Anthony, Noah Brown, Justice Carbajal, Yevgen Chebotar, Joseph Dabis, Chelsea Finn, Keerthana Gopalakrishnan, et al. 2023. “RT-1: Robotics Transformer for Real-World Control at Scale.” Robotics: Science and Systems (RSS). https://doi.org/10.15607/RSS.2023.XIX.025.

Brohan, Anthony, Noah Brown, Justice Carbajal, Yevgen Chebotar, Xi Chen, Krzysztof Choromanski, Tianli Ding, et al. 2023. “RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2307.15818.

Black, Kevin, Noah Brown, Danny Driess, Adnan Esmail, Michael Equi, Chelsea Finn, Niccolo Fusai, et al. 2024. “\(\pi_0\): A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2410.24164.

Black, Kevin, Manuel Y. Galliker, and Sergey Levine. 2025. “Real-Time Execution of Action Chunking Flow Policies.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS).

Figure AI. 2025. Helix: A Vision-Language-Action Model for Generalist Humanoid Control. Figure AI technical report (web).

Bjorck, Johan, Fernando Castañeda, Nikita Cherniadev, Xingye Da, Runyu Ding, Linxi Fan, Yu Fang, et al. 2025. “GR00T N1: An Open Foundation Model for Generalist Humanoid Robots.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2503.14734.
Six works trace this lineage from reactive robotics to modern vision-language-action architectures:

Brooks (1986) introduces the subsumption architecture, organizing autonomous robots into layered, asynchronous behaviors that each close their own sensorimotor loop. The paper presents the foundational systems argument that fast reactive loops must never block on deliberative planning, establishing the conceptual basis for modern two-speed execution.
Williams et al. (2009) introduces the roofline model, a visual bound relating arithmetic intensity to processor compute and memory bandwidth ceilings. The paper provides the standard methodology for diagnosing whether an inference kernel is memory-bound or compute-bound before undertaking hardware optimization.
Pope et al. (2023) models Transformer inference from first principles, demonstrating how batch size, sequence length, and tensor partitioning dictate whether execution binds on memory bandwidth or arithmetic execution units. This analysis underpins the performance characterization of batch-size-1 policy inference explored throughout this chapter.
Zhao et al. (2023) introduces Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) and temporal ensembling for precise bimanual manipulation. The authors demonstrate that predicting action sequences rather than individual steps dampens compounding tracking errors and stabilizes learned policies, establishing the trajectory chunking approach that real-time learned policies now rely on.
Chi et al. (2025) develops Diffusion Policy, demonstrating why multimodal human demonstrations with multiple valid solutions require expressive generative decoders rather than unimodal regression. The paper explicitly characterizes the systems cost of iterative refinement, quantifying the computational latency required to evaluate multiple diffusion steps per action chunk.
Kim et al. (2024) provides a complete, open-source seven-billion-parameter vision-language-action model, detailing its training pipeline, data mixture, and deployment trade-offs. The paper includes 4-bit and 8-bit quantization benchmarks, which make it a common reference point for profiling learned embodied policies on edge hardware.


Brooks, Rodney. 1986. “A Robust Layered Control System for a Mobile Robot.” IEEE Journal on Robotics and Automation 2 (1): 14–23.

Williams, Samuel, Andrew Waterman, and David Patterson. 2009. “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures.” Communications of the ACM 52 (4): 65–76.

Pope, Reiner, Sholto Douglas, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Jacob Devlin, James Bradbury, Jonathan Heek, Kefan Xiao, Shivani Agrawal, and Jeff Dean. 2023. “Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference.” Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems (MLSys) 5: 606–24.

Zhao, Tony Z., Vikash Kumar, Sergey Levine, and Chelsea Finn. 2023. “Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware.” Robotics: Science and Systems (RSS). https://doi.org/10.15607/RSS.2023.XIX.016.

Chi, Cheng, Zhenjia Xu, Siyuan Feng, Eric Cousineau, Yilun Du, Benjamin Burchfiel, Russ Tedrake, and Shuran Song. 2025. “Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion.” The International Journal of Robotics Research 44 (10-11): 1684–704. https://doi.org/10.1177/02783649241273668.

Kim, Moo Jin, Karl Pertsch, Siddharth Karamcheti, Ted Xiao, Ashwin Balakrishna, Suraj Nair, Rafael Rafailov, et al. 2024. “OpenVLA: An Open-Source Vision-Language-Action Model.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2406.09246.

What’s Next: From learned proposals to the permission pathA physical machine cannot allow a candidate proposal to continue driving hardware indefinitely when its successor fails to arrive. The mobile manipulator’s chunk policy targets a proposal period of 50 ms, whereas the intent model updates at a slower cadence, and either level can stall, miss its deadline, or misjudge the target object. A check that waits on the proposer it checks stalls along with it. The Nervous System therefore begins with where the permission path must run to stay independent of the learned models. It next derives each tier’s rate from a physical time constant and passes proposals between tiers without letting a slow writer block a fast reader. Only then does it price the chunk lease from the body’s stopping budget and the proposer’s renewal floor, ensuring that an admitted chunk commands the joints for a bounded interval before a deterministic fail-safe response begins.

title: The Machine Anatomy
text:
The Machine Anatomy
Every physical AI system acts through a body with limited capacity to move, stop, exert force, and dissipate heat. The first law of The Four Bedrock Laws holds that this apparatus cannot take back the work it delivers, and Part I turns that law into numbers. It asks how quickly the machine’s evidence ages, how far the machine travels before it stops, how much torque its drives can deliver, and how much winding heat and supply-voltage drop they tolerate. The Body establishes what motion the hardware can physically support. The Brain, the learned proposer, establishes what computation can supply and how long its answers stay true. The Nervous System must therefore connect them within the time the stopping budget allows. Following this physical order lets the engineer derive an architectural requirement before selecting its implementation.

Principle 1: The irreversibility lawInvariant: Once a permitted command crosses the causal boundary, the energy it delivers becomes motion, strain, or heat that no software action can recall. At steady speed, during a pre-brake delay \(\PrebrakeDelay\) the machine travels \(\SpeedAtDetection\,\PrebrakeDelay\) before any response begins. A stop therefore requires \(\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance\), with every term of \(\StoppingDistance\) taken from a measured limit of this machine under stated conditions (Kinetic Momentum).
Implication: Each part of the machine carries budgets in time, distance, torque, heat, and voltage. The checks needed to admit a command must finish before its execution and inside those budgets. A design is admissible only when it can say which budget binds first, how that budget was established, and what the machine does when it is exhausted.



The Physical Body (The Physical Body): Decides which physical budget binds first and how its value was established, and produces the limit record from which every later record descends.
The Cognitive Brain (The Cognitive Brain): Decides what a learned proposer can deliver on time and what memory and latency that costs, and derives the machine’s two-speed split, a slow intent model above a fast chunk policy. It produces no record of its own; its proposer limits, and the payload every proposal must carry, enter the handoff record.
The Nervous System (The Nervous System): Decides where the permission path must run to stay independent of the proposer, how often it must check, and how long a proposal may drive the actuators. It produces the handoff record together with the header that every proposal carries. The independence it requires leads it to adopt a two-processor split as the hypothesis the machine is built on; whether that split holds on real silicon is decided in Workload Placement.

Part I hands forward three linked artifacts across these chapters. On the physical side, The Physical Body establishes the limit record, the six-element form in which every budget that can end in damage states its operating conditions and its evidence category. The chapter then fills that form on the running machine for the credible deceleration behind the stopping distance, the drive torque that must deliver it, and the input lockout of the converter on the shared drive bus. Against those physical bounds, The Cognitive Brain characterizes the proposer’s supply by pricing how many future setpoints one chunk covers, how long a new chunk takes, and how quickly the evidence behind it ages, showing why a chunk keeps the arm supplied without keeping that evidence fresh. Joining demand and supply, The Nervous System produces the handoff record: the lease the permission path derives from the stopping budget, the tick at which it checks, the handoffs between proposer and permission path, and a worked budget that couples all three chapters on the running machine. That worked example selects a candidate configuration. Qualification still requires bounds on each interval, including dispatch to admission, evidence that the protective response remains physically available, and loaded tests showing that the permission path’s isolation from the proposer holds. Part II inherits both records as preconditions on the demonstrations the machine collects while its permission path is watching.

title: Notation
text:
Physical AI draws on three disciplines at once. Machine learning supplies the foundation models, vision-language-action architectures, diffusion policies, and action chunking that propose what a robot should do. Robotics and control supply the mechanics that decide what it can do: articulated dynamics, the Lie group \(\SpecialEuclideanGroup\), contact and friction, Lyapunov stability, control barrier functions, and actuator electromechanics. Embedded and real-time systems supply the machinery that decides when it happens, from interconnect and memory contention through zero-order hold, real-time scheduling, leases, hardware watchdogs, and functional safety.
Because each discipline developed its mathematical conventions independently over decades, combining them creates symbol collisions that cyber-physical systems engineering has long lived with. For example, writing \(\nabla_{\Glyph{\theta}} \Policy(\Glyph{\mathbf{a}} \mid \Glyph{\mathbf{q}})\) when \(\Glyph{\theta}\) also denotes joint angles, or writing \(\Glyph{\mathbf{a}}_t\) for an action when \(\Glyph{\mathbf{a}}\) denotes Cartesian acceleration or barrier constraints, confuses spatial mechanics with parameter optimization and control execution authority.
The sections that follow state the cross-discipline disambiguation rules, the governing relationships of embodied systems, and the symbol tables used throughout this book. Every symbol of the series core keeps its foundational meaning: \(\Time\) is time, \(\Bandwidth\) bandwidth, \(\Latency\) latency, \(\PeakRate\) peak rate, \(\Operations\) operations, \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) arithmetic intensity, \(\DataVolume\) bytes moved, \(\LossFunction\) loss, \(\LearningRate\) learning rate, and \(\mathcal{O}(\cdot)\) asymptotic cost. Serving and memory arithmetic on the robot’s onboard computer uses those symbols, with a subscript naming the instance (\(\SustainedMemoryBandwidth\), \(\PrefillOperations\)).


When physical plant dynamics meet deep neural networks and real-time embedded hardware, common mathematical shorthand breaks down. The conventions below resolve these cross-domain collisions systematically:










Symbol
Canonical Convention
Colliding Meaning
Disambiguation Rule




\(\Glyph{\theta}\)
Learned model (policy) parameters, as in \(\Policy\)
Joint angle, trajectory polynomial \(\Glyph{\theta}(\Glyph{t})\), heading, azimuth, attitude or mounting error, clock offset, or thermal resistance \(\Glyph{\theta_{JA}}\)
Bare \(\Glyph{\theta}\) is always the parameter collection of a learned model, set italic (never bold), as the series core defines it. A geometric angle always carries a subscript that names it: \(\JointAngle\) for one joint (\(\Glyph{\theta_{\text{motor}}}\) and \(\Glyph{\theta_{\text{link}}}\) on either side of a reducer, \(\EncoderAngle\) for an encoder reading), \(\HeadingAngle\) for planar heading, \(\AzimuthAngle\) for azimuth, \(\AttitudeError\) for attitude error, \(\ExtrinsicMisalignmentAngle\) for extrinsic misalignment, \(\TiltAngle\) for tilt from vertical, \(\OrientationTolerance\) for an orientation tolerance, and \(\ElectricalRotorAngle\) for the electrical rotor angle; increments keep the subscript (\(\FiniteChange\JointAngle\), \(\SmallChange\EncoderAngle\)). Joint configurations are the generalized coordinates \(\GeneralizedCoordinates \in \mathbb{R}^\GeneralizedCoordinateCount\) with entries \(\JointCoordinate_i\), and a joint trajectory polynomial is \(\JointCoordinate(\TimeInstant) = \sum \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_k \TimeInstant^{\Glyph{k}}\) with boundary values \(\JointCoordinate_0, \JointCoordinate_1\) (never \(\Glyph{\theta}(\Glyph{t})\)). A clock offset is \(\ClockOffset\) (in seconds). Thermal resistance is \(\ThermalResistance\) or \(\JunctionAmbientThermalResistance\) (in \(\text{K/W}\)), never \(\Glyph{\theta_{JA}}\).

Physical intelligence operates subject to thermodynamic, mechanical, kinematic, and communications constraints. The relationships below state those constraints in the symbols this book uses. They are working relationships, not laws: the book’s four bedrock laws are the ones The Four Bedrock Laws states.


Delay converts directly into travel before any retarding force begins. The pre-brake delay \(\PrebrakeDelay\) runs from the capture of the frame that first shows a hazard to retarding force, excluding the dispatch-to-admission interval \(\DispatchAdmissionInterval\), which the stopping budget charges against its timing allowance. The stop it leaves, whose travel is \(\ResidentStopDistance(\SpeedAtDetection)\), must fit inside the clear distance, and the spare that remains must pay for \(\SpeedAtDetection\,\DispatchAdmissionInterval\):
\[\PrebrakeDelay = \ObservationAge + \ChunkLease + \PermissionLoopPeriod + \CommandTransportTime + \ActuatorResponseTime\]
\[\SpeedAtDetection\,\PrebrakeDelay + \ResidentStopDistance(\SpeedAtDetection) + \LocalizationBound + \ProtectiveClearanceMargin + \TrackingErrorBound \le \ClearDistance\]
Inference time is spent on the proposal side of the proposal boundary. It ages the evidence behind a proposal, which the permission path checks against the proposal’s expiry. It is neither a term of \(\PrebrakeDelay\) nor part of the permission loop’s period \(\PermissionLoopPeriod\), because the fallback does not wait for the proposer.
The appendices regroup the same interval for two specific stop paths, and each form defines its own terms. For a stop triggered by lease expiry, \(\PrebrakeDelay = \ChunkLease + \DetectionInterval + \FallbackHold + \ObservationAge + \ActuatorResponseTime\); for a stop triggered by a hazard detector, \(\PrebrakeDelay = \ObservationAge + \DetectionInterval + \StopDecisionComputeBound + \CommandTransportTime + \ActuatorResponseTime\).

Large neural policies that stream their weights from memory may exceed a kilohertz control period. Action chunking predicts an action trajectory of horizon \(\ActionChunkHorizon\) at a lower cognitive frequency \(\Glyph{f_{\text{policy}}}\), while the chunk’s waypoints are consumed at \(\ActionExecutionRate\). In the serial model with one weight-streaming pass per chunk and no additional fixed overhead, memory streaming must fit inside the chunk execution window after reserving the compute term \(\Glyph{T_{\text{compute}}}\) of the single-device decomposition:
\[\ParameterStreamingTime = \frac{\WeightMemory}{\SustainedMemoryBandwidth} \le \frac{\ActionChunkHorizon}{\ActionExecutionRate} - \Glyph{T_{\text{compute}}}\]
A decoder that streams its nonresident weights once per emitted token spends, for \(\EmittedTokenCount\) emitted tokens, the inference time
\[\ProposerInferenceTime \approx \max\!\left(\frac{\PrefillOperations}{\EfficiencyHw\,\PeakRate},\ \frac{\WeightMemory}{\SustainedMemoryBandwidth}\right) + (\EmittedTokenCount - 1)\,\frac{\WeightMemory}{\SustainedMemoryBandwidth}\]
which caps the fresh-evaluation rate at \(\ProposerEvaluationRate \le \SustainedMemoryBandwidth/\WeightMemory\) when every evaluation streams the weights. The symbols are those of the single-device decomposition: \(\PrefillOperations\) counts the prefill’s operations, \(\PeakRate\) is the processor’s peak rate at the activation precision, \(\EfficiencyHw\) is the fraction of it the prefill achieves, and \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) is the arithmetic intensity that decides which term binds.

For the stopping-based safety envelope, the machine must retain enough clearance to arrest its approach before crossing the protected boundary. The relationship below specializes the resident stop to one-dimensional motion starting and ending at zero acceleration, with symmetric jerk ramps and a constant-deceleration segment. \[\StoppingDistance(\SpeedAtDetection) = \SpeedAtDetection\,\PrebrakeDelay + \ResidentStopDistance(\SpeedAtDetection), \qquad \ResidentStopDistance(\SpeedAtDetection) = \frac{\SpeedAtDetection^2}{2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration} + \frac{\SpeedAtDetection\,\CredibleBrakingDeceleration}{2\JerkLimit} \quad (\SpeedAtDetection \ge \CredibleBrakingDeceleration^2/\JerkLimit)\]

Catastrophic failure rates in embodied systems cannot be certified through stochastic testing alone. For a defined hazard class \(\HazardClassIndex\), verified interception coverage and independently bounded residual faults constrain the system’s hazard rate. Under a constant-rate Poisson exposure model, zero-failure exposure follows the Rule of Three:
\[\SystemHazardRate \le \HazardousProposalRate (1 - \ShieldInterceptionCoverage) + \HardwareCommonCauseRate \le \TargetHazardRate, \qquad \FailureObservationInterval \ge \frac{-\ln \HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel}{\TargetHazardRate}\]
Here \(\FailureObservationInterval\) is the zero-incident operating exposure, in hours. For independent trials with a common success probability, per-trial campaigns use the same bound in probability form, \(\ZeroFailureTrialCount \ge \ln\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel/\ln \TargetTrialSuccessProbability \approx 3/(1 - \TargetTrialSuccessProbability)\).

Independently bounded hardware-fault and common-cause hazard rate the shield cannot intercept; the floor \(\SystemHazardRate\) reaches when \(\ShieldInterceptionCoverage = 1\).


\(\TargetHazardRate\)
Target Hazard Rate
\(\text{h}^{-1}\)
Tolerable dangerous failure rate assigned to the safety function by risk assessment, in the band its governing standard defines.


\(\DiagnosticCoverage\)
Diagnostic Coverage
Dimensionless
Rate-weighted fraction of hardware faults whose hazardous effect is mitigated, \(\UnmitigatedHardwareFaultRate = \RawHardwareFaultRate(1 - \DiagnosticCoverage)\); the hardware counterpart of \(\ShieldInterceptionCoverage\), which covers policy proposals.


\(\TrialFailureProbability, \TargetTrialSuccessProbability\)
Per-Trial Probabilities
Dimensionless
Per-trial failure probability, and the per-trial success probability a campaign must demonstrate; trial counts follow \(\ZeroFailureTrialCount \ge \ln\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel/\ln \TargetTrialSuccessProbability\).


\(\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel\)
Statistical Significance Level
Dimensionless
Type I error threshold (\(\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel = 1 - \text{CL}\), e.g., \(\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel=0.05\) for 95% confidence where \(-\ln(0.05) \approx 3.0\)).


\(\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate\)
Type II Error Allowance
Dimensionless
Probability of rejecting an acceptable candidate (\(1-\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate\) is the power); with \(\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel\) it sets the SPRT boundaries \(\SprtUpperBoundary\) and \(\SprtLowerBoundary\). Diffusion schedules use indexed \(\Glyph{\beta_s}\); a KL weight \(\Glyph{\beta}\) stays local to its objective.


\(\ZeroFailureTrialCount\)
Zero-Failure Trial Count
Trials
Required number of incident-free trials to substantiate \(\TargetTrialSuccessProbability\); for exposure measured in hours, the bound is on \(\FailureObservationInterval\) instead.


\(\SequentialLogLikelihoodRatio\)
Sequential Log-Likelihood Ratio
Dimensionless
After \(\ObservedTrialFailureCount\) failures in \(\SequentialTrialCount\) trials, \(\SequentialLogLikelihoodRatio = \ObservedTrialFailureCount\ln(\HypothesizedTrialFailureProbability_1/\HypothesizedTrialFailureProbability_0) + (\SequentialTrialCount-\ObservedTrialFailureCount)\ln\frac{1-\HypothesizedTrialFailureProbability_1}{1-\HypothesizedTrialFailureProbability_0}\) for per-trial failure probabilities \(\HypothesizedTrialFailureProbability_0\) (unacceptable) and \(\HypothesizedTrialFailureProbability_1\) (acceptable); SPRT stops when it leaves \((\SprtLowerBoundary, \SprtUpperBoundary)\).


\(\SprtUpperBoundary, \SprtLowerBoundary\)
SPRT Boundaries
Dimensionless
Upper and lower stopping thresholds on \(\SequentialLogLikelihoodRatio\), \(\SprtUpperBoundary \approx \ln((1-\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate)/\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel)\) and \(\SprtLowerBoundary \approx \ln(\StatisticalFalseNegativeRate/(1-\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel))\); never bare \(\Glyph{A}\) and \(\Glyph{B}\).


\(\AssuranceClaim\)
Assurance Claim
Proposition
Top-level safety claim of an assurance argument. Under an independent-premise probability model, its confidence \(\Pr(\AssuranceClaim)\) is the product of the premise confidences for a conjunctive argument, and one minus the product of the legs’ failure probabilities for a multi-legged one.







Untethered mobile manipulators and autonomous robots operate under strict battery energy reserves and peak thermal dissipation ceilings. Total mission energy (distinct from the ML workload’s \(\Glyph{E_{\text{total}}}\)) splits across mechanical actuation work, edge neural computation, and auxiliary sensor payloads. The compute energy expended by edge inference system-on-chip (SoC) devices decomposes into data movement and arithmetic operations according to the core energy corollary:
\[\MissionEnergy = \Glyph{E_{\text{act}}} + \Glyph{E_{\text{total}}} + \Glyph{E_{\text{aux}}}, \qquad \Glyph{E_{\text{total}}} \approx \DataVolume \times \Glyph{E_{\text{move}}} + \Operations \times \Glyph{E_{\text{compute}}}\]
For constant loss power in the single-node thermal model, resistive heating in stator windings \(\WindingLossPower \approx \sum \TorqueProducingCurrent^2 \ElectricalResistance(\WindingTemperature)\) sets the steady-state rise \(\JouleanTemperatureRise = \WindingLossPower \ThermalResistance\). Transient heating during shorter acceleration or contact bursts follows the coupled first-order thermal balance above.

Force and moment the environment applies at the end effector, in newtons for the force and newton-meters for the moments; it maps into joint torques through the transposed manipulator Jacobian.


\(\ExternalContactTorque\)
External Contact Torque Vector
\(\text{N}\cdot\text{m}\)
Joint torques produced by external contact forces acting on the manipulator.


\(\ExternalJointTorque\)
External Joint Torque
\(\text{N}\cdot\text{m}\)
Torque the environment applies at one joint’s output; the scalar counterpart of the external contact torque vector \(\ExternalContactTorque\).


\(\FrictionCoefficientFloor\)
Friction Coefficient Floor
Dimensionless
Lowest friction coefficient a braking or contact premise assumes the surface provides; an unobserved oil spill can invalidate it.


\(\GraspForceCeiling\)
Grasp Force Ceiling
\(\text{N}\)
Largest grasp contact force the object tolerates without crushing or deforming.


\(\GraspForceFloor\)
Grasp Force Floor
\(\text{N}\)
Smallest grasp contact force that holds the object against slip; the grasp must stay between this floor and \(\GraspForceCeiling\).


\(\GraspMap\)
Grasp Map
Matrix
Linear map from contact forces to the wrench they exert on the grasped object; indexed by contact when one contact is meant; not the Kalman gain.


\(\GravityCenterHeight\)
Center-of-Gravity Height
\(\text{m}\)
Height of a vehicle’s center of gravity above the floor; it sets the tip-over ceiling on deceleration.


\(\GravityVector\)
Gravity Vector
\(\text{m/s}^2\)
Gravitational acceleration as a vector pointing down with the magnitude of surface gravity; the scalar is the gravitational acceleration, and it is not the vector of gravitational joint torques.


\(\ImpedanceControlledPosition\)
Impedance-Controlled Position
\(\text{m}\)
Measured position of the point an impedance controller regulates; its deviation from \(\ImpedanceEquilibriumPosition\), times the stiffness, is the spring term.


\(\ImpedanceControlledVelocity\)
Impedance-Controlled Velocity
\(\text{m/s}\)
Measured velocity of the regulated point, the time derivative of \(\ImpedanceControlledPosition\).


\(\ImpedanceEquilibriumPosition\)
Impedance Equilibrium Position
\(\text{m}\)
Virtual rest point of the emulated spring that an impedance controller pulls the controlled point toward.


\(\ImpedanceEquilibriumVelocity\)
Impedance Equilibrium Velocity
\(\text{m/s}\)
Velocity of the virtual equilibrium; its difference from \(\ImpedanceControlledVelocity\), times the damping, is the damper term.


\(\KineticEnergy\)
Kinetic Energy
\(\text{J}\)
Energy a moving body carries, one half its mass times its speed squared (plus rotational terms where stated); not the standard’s limit on energy transferred to a person.


\(\MassCenterHeight\)
Center-of-Mass Height
\(\text{m}\)
Height of a body’s center of mass above its support or contact point; it sets the natural frequency of the linear inverted pendulum, \(\sqrt{\Gravity/\MassCenterHeight}\), and is not a camera-frame coordinate.


\(\PenetrationDepth\)
Penetration Depth
\(\text{m}\)
Depth by which one body penetrates or compresses another at a contact, measured along the contact normal; penalty and compliant contact models compute normal force from it. Shares its glyph with the Huber threshold of the training chapters.


\(\PenetrationRate\)
Penetration Rate
\(\text{m/s}\)
Time rate of change of the penetration depth \(\PenetrationDepth\) at a contact; zero at the instant of maximum compression.


\(\LatchApproachSpeed\)
Latch Approach Speed
\(\text{m/s}\)
Speed at which the arm presses into the cage-door latch plate; the enforcement and release chapters use the same latch scenario.


\(\LatchForceLimit\)
Latch Force Limit
\(\text{N}\)
Structural force limit of the door latch the arm pushes against.


\(\LatchPlateStiffness\)
Latch Plate Stiffness
\(\text{N/m}\)
Spring stiffness of the cage-door latch plate the arm compresses.


\(\LeadingSupportDistance\)
Leading Support Distance
\(\text{m}\)
Horizontal distance from a vehicle’s center of gravity forward to its leading ground support; it shrinks when an arm extends forward.


\(\IntrusionDistance\)
Intrusion Distance
\(\text{m}\)
Distance a body part can intrude past the sensing field before detection; a term of the ISO/TS 15066 protective separation distance.


\(\PersonApproachTravel\)
Person Approach Travel
\(\text{m}\)
Distance a person travels toward the robot during the robot’s reaction and stopping time; a term of the ISO/TS 15066 protective separation distance.


\(\PersonPositionUncertainty\)
Person Position Uncertainty
\(\text{m}\)
Position uncertainty of the person from the sensing system; a term of the ISO/TS 15066 protective separation distance.


\(\KnownComponentStopDistance\)
Known-Component Stop Distance
\(\text{m}\)
Stopping travel that the known components of the stopping budget add up to at a given speed on a dry floor: delay travel, braking, jerk ramps, and fixed overheads; the clear distance minus it is the spare the stopping claim holds in reserve.


\(\PreImpactNormalVelocity\)
Pre-Impact Normal Velocity
\(\text{m/s}\)
Normal contact velocity just before an impact, negative while the bodies approach; the restitution law links it to the post-impact velocity.


\(\PostImpactNormalVelocity\)
Post-Impact Normal Velocity
\(\text{m/s}\)
Normal contact velocity just after an impact, equal to minus the restitution coefficient times the pre-impact normal velocity.


\(\RobotStructuralStiffness\)
Robot Structural Stiffness
\(\text{N/m}\)
Stiffness of the manipulator side of a contact, its pads, linkages, and joint elasticity acting as one series spring; it combines in series with the stiffness of the struck body.


\(\SlipAccelerationBound\)
Slip Acceleration Bound
\(\text{m/s}^2\)
Bound on the residual acceleration of a tracked object slipping relative to its carrier; it widens the evidence horizon of a target estimate.







Every measurement a robot uses arrives in some frame, and every command leaves in another. These symbols name the frames, the rigid transforms between them, and the camera models that project the world onto a sensor.










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\SpecialEuclideanGroup\)
Special Euclidean Group
Lie Group
Group of 3D rigid-body spatial transformations (translations and rotations: \(\mathbb{R}^3 \rtimes \SpecialOrthogonalGroup\)).


\(\SpecialOrthogonalGroup\)
Special Orthogonal Group
Lie Group
Group of \(3 \times 3\) proper orthogonal rotation matrices (\(\DirectionalCosineMatrix^\top \DirectionalCosineMatrix = \IdentityMatrix, \det(\DirectionalCosineMatrix) = +1\)).


\(\WorldReferenceFrame, \BodyReferenceFrame, \Glyph{\mathcal{F}_E}\)
Coordinate Reference Frames
Reference
Fixed World frame (\(\WorldReferenceFrame\)), mobile robot Base/body frame (\(\BodyReferenceFrame\)), and End-effector frame (\(\Glyph{\mathcal{F}_E}\)).


\(\CartesianPosition \in \mathbb{R}^3\)
Cartesian 3D Position
\(\text{m}\)
Position vector \([\Glyph{x}, \Glyph{y}, \Glyph{z}]^\top\) expressing point coordinates in a stated frame.


\(\RigidTransformTranslation \in \mathbb{R}^3\)
Rigid-Transform Translation
\(\text{m}\)
Translation part of a rigid transform between two frames (the offset of one frame’s origin in the other).


\(\DirectionalCosineMatrix \in \SpecialOrthogonalGroup\)
Directional Cosine Matrix
Matrix
\(3 \times 3\) orthonormal matrix parameterizing spatial attitude and orientation.


\(\UnitQuaternion \in \Glyph{\mathbb{H}}\)
Unit Quaternion
Dimensionless
Hypercomplex orientation vector \([\Glyph{w}, \Glyph{x}, \Glyph{y}, \Glyph{z}]^\top\) satisfying \(\lVert \UnitQuaternion \rVert = 1\).


\(\Pose \in \SpecialEuclideanGroup\)
Pose
Matrix
Rigid-body pose of a named frame, such as a grasp, the tool center point, or a target (\(\Glyph{\Pose_{\text{grasp}}}\), \(\Glyph{\Pose_{\text{TCP}}}\)); the transform between two frames is \(\HomogeneousTransform\) below.


\(\HomogeneousTransform \in \SpecialEuclideanGroup\)
Homogeneous Transform
Matrix
\(4 \times 4\) matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} \TransformRotationBlock & \TransformTranslationBlock \\ \ZeroVector^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) mapping coordinates from frame \(\Glyph{B}\) into frame \(\Glyph{A}\).


\(\AngularVelocity, \AngularAcceleration \in \mathbb{R}^3\)
Angular Velocity & Acceleration
\(\text{rad/s}, \text{rad/s}^2\)
Spatial angular velocity and angular acceleration vectors of a rigid body.


\(\SensorLeverArm \in \mathbb{R}^3\)
Sensor Lever-Arm Vector
\(\text{m}\)
Displacement vector from body rotation origin \(\Glyph{O}\) to displaced sensor location \(\Glyph{P}\); its length, or a link’s lever arm, is the scalar \(\LeverArmLength\).


\(\FundamentalMatrix, \EssentialMatrix\)
Fundamental and Essential Matrices
Matrix
Two-view epipolar constraint \(\HomogeneousPixelCoordinates_2^\top \FundamentalMatrix\HomogeneousPixelCoordinates_1 = 0\) with \(\EssentialMatrix = [\RigidTransformTranslation]_\times \DirectionalCosineMatrix\); the subscript keeps it distinct from the transition matrix \(\StateTransitionMatrix\).


\(\CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}\)
Pinhole Camera Intrinsics
Pixels
Calibration matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} \HorizontalFocalLength & 0 & \PrincipalPointColumn \\ 0 & \VerticalFocalLength & \PrincipalPointRow \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) parameterizing focal lengths and principal center.


\(\CameraIntrinsicInverseTranspose\)
Inverse-transpose intrinsic matrix
Matrix
Transpose of the inverse of the camera intrinsic matrix \(\CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix\), which carries an essential matrix into the pixel-coordinate fundamental matrix.


\(\CameraFramePoint = [\CameraFrameHorizontalCoordinate, \CameraFrameVerticalCoordinate, \CameraFrameDepth]^\top\)
Camera-Frame 3D Coordinate
\(\text{m}\)
Metric coordinates of a spatial point in the optical camera frame (\(\CameraFrameDepth\) is optical depth).


\([\PixelColumnCoordinate, \PixelRowCoordinate]^\top\), \(\HomogeneousPixelCoordinates\)
Image Plane Pixel Coordinates
Pixels
Discrete sensor pixel coordinates (\(\PixelColumnCoordinate \sim \HorizontalFocalLength \frac{\CameraFrameHorizontalCoordinate}{\CameraFrameDepth} + \PrincipalPointColumn\), \(\PixelRowCoordinate \sim \VerticalFocalLength \frac{\CameraFrameVerticalCoordinate}{\CameraFrameDepth} + \PrincipalPointRow\)), italic as scalars; the homogeneous image point is \(\HomogeneousPixelCoordinates = [\PixelColumnCoordinate, \PixelRowCoordinate, 1]^\top\), never bold \(\Glyph{\mathbf{u}}\).


\(\ExposureDuration\)
Exposure Duration
\(\text{ms}\)
Integration time of one camera frame; the frame’s timestamp belongs at its midpoint, \(\ExposureDuration/2\) after exposure starts.


\(\BeliefInvalidationHorizon\)
Belief Invalidation Horizon
\(\text{ms}\)
Time since the last supporting evidence after which a belief can no longer be shown to lie inside its task tolerance; a belief expires at \(\TimeInstant_0 + \BeliefInvalidationHorizon\).


\(\FreeSpaceDepth\)
Free-Space Depth
\(\text{m}\)
Distance from a hull’s surface to the nearest cell that is occupied, unknown, or expired, read from an ESDF built with all three treated as obstacles; the budget motion may spend there (Volumetric metric maps and distance fields).


\(\RollingShutterRowReadout\)
Rolling Shutter Row Readout
\(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\)
Exposure time delta between adjacent CMOS sensor scanlines; row \(\SensorRowIndex\) starts at \(\TimeInstant(\SensorRowIndex) = \FrameExposureStartTime + \SensorRowIndex\,\RollingShutterRowReadout\).


\(\RollingShutterDistortion(\SensorRowIndex)\)
Rolling Shutter Distortion
\(\text{m}\)
Kinematic skew displacement \(\RollingShutterDistortion = \Velocity \cdot \SensorRowIndex \cdot \RollingShutterRowReadout\) induced by high-velocity platform motion.


\(\Glyph{\text{tsdf}}(\VoxelCenterPosition)\)
Truncated Signed Distance
\([-1, +1]\)
Normalized volumetric distance \(\Glyph{\text{tsdf}}(\VoxelCenterPosition) = \text{clamp}(\Glyph{d}(\VoxelCenterPosition)/\TsdfTruncationBand, -1, 1)\) of the voxel centered at \(\VoxelCenterPosition\) to the nearest surface.


\(\TsdfTruncationBand\)
TSDF Truncation Band
\(\text{m}\)
Metric thickness of the spatial surface interface band stored in voxel memory.


\(\TsdfAccumulatedDistance_t(\VoxelCenterPosition), \TsdfAccumulatedWeight_t(\VoxelCenterPosition)\)
TSDF Accumulated Volume
Mixed
Running weighted signed distance and accumulated visibility weight at the voxel centered at \(\VoxelCenterPosition\).


\(\InitialTrackingError, \PositionErrorCeiling\)
Initial and Ceiling Error
\(\text{m}\)
Position error of an estimate when its evidence is fresh, and the largest error the task tolerates; \(\Glyph{E}_0\) and \(\Glyph{E_{\max}}\) stay energies.


\(\PositionalTaskTolerance\)
Positional Task Tolerance
\(\text{m}\)
Radius within which a target estimate must lie for the task to succeed; paired with the orientation tolerance \(\OrientationTolerance\).


\(\GoalSet\)
Geometric Goal Set
Subset of \(\SpecialEuclideanGroup\)
Admissible terminal poses within the positional and angular tolerances of the task; the spatial component of an intent lease \(\IntentLease\).


\(\TargetTravelDistance\)
Distance to Target
\(\text{m}\)
Straight-line distance from the measured end-effector position to the admitted target, \(\lVert \TargetPosition - \CartesianPosition_0 \rVert\), in the intent-lease reachability test; distinct from the hidden width \(\HiddenDimension\).


\(\AttitudeError\)
Attitude Error
\(\text{rad}\)
Angular error in an estimated attitude, which leaks gravity into the horizontal acceleration.


\(\AzimuthAngle\)
Azimuth Angle
\(\text{rad}\)
Angle of a direction measured in the horizontal plane about the vertical axis; the book may state values in degrees.


\(\BaseCameraTransform\)
Base-to-Camera Transform
Matrix
Rigid transform mapping camera coordinates into the robot base frame.


\(\BodyFramePoint\)
Body-Frame Point
\(\text{m}\)
Position of a perceived point expressed in the robot body frame, the camera-frame point carried through the extrinsics.


\(\BodyFramePointCovariance\)
Body-Frame Point Covariance
\(\text{m}^2\)
Covariance of a perceived point’s position error in the robot body frame, the spatial covariance an observation contract carries; rotated camera-frame covariance plus the extrinsic term, not the covariance of a state estimator.


\(\CameraExtrinsicRotation\)
Camera Extrinsic Rotation
Dimensionless
Rotation part of a camera’s extrinsic calibration, taking camera-frame vectors into the body frame; the rotation block of \(\CameraExtrinsicTransform\).


\(\CameraExtrinsicTransform\)
Camera Extrinsic Transform
Matrix
Rigid transform of a camera’s extrinsic calibration, mapping camera-frame coordinates into the body frame; mixed rotation and translation blocks.


\(\CameraFramePointCovariance\)
Camera-Frame Point Covariance
\(\text{m}^2\)
Covariance of a point’s position error in the camera’s optical frame, after unprojection of its pixel and depth measurement; rotated into the body frame by \(\CameraExtrinsicRotation\).


\(\CartesianXCoordinate\)
Cartesian X Coordinate
\(\text{m}\)
First Cartesian component of a three-dimensional position.


\(\CartesianYCoordinate\)
Cartesian Y Coordinate
\(\text{m}\)
Second Cartesian component of a three-dimensional position.


\(\CartesianZCoordinate\)
Cartesian Z Coordinate
\(\text{m}\)
Third Cartesian component of a three-dimensional position.


\(\ClearanceInset\)
Clearance Inset
\(\text{m}\)
Separation a consumer holds between an estimated obstacle position and the machine’s envelope so the true obstacle stays the required clearance away, except with a stated tail probability; a field of the observation contract.


\(\DepthStandardDeviation\)
Depth Standard Deviation
\(\text{m}\)
Standard deviation of the depth a stereo or range sensor reports for one point; for stereo it grows with the square of the range.


\(\DisparityStandardDeviation\)
Disparity Standard Deviation
pixels
Standard deviation of the disparity a stereo matcher measures; it feeds the stereo depth term \(\DepthStandardDeviation\).


\(\ElevationAngle\)
Elevation Angle
\(\text{rad}\)
Angle of a direction above the horizontal plane; not the encoder parameters of a variational autoencoder, which render the same glyph.


\(\ExtrinsicCalibrationCovariance\)
Extrinsic Calibration Covariance
\(\text{m}^2\)
Covariance of a sensor’s calibrated mounting extrinsic.


\(\ExtrinsicMisalignmentAngle\)
Extrinsic Misalignment Angle
\(\text{rad}\)
Angular error of a sensor’s extrinsic calibration relative to its true mounting.


\(\FocalLength\)
Focal Length
pixels
Focal length of a pinhole camera in pixels, the scale from normalized image coordinates to pixels; a rectified pair shares one value.


\(\HorizontalFocalLength\)
Horizontal Focal Length
pixels
Camera focal length in pixels along the horizontal image axis, one entry of the intrinsics.


\(\FrameExposureStartTime\)
Frame Exposure Start Time
\(\text{s}\)
Instant at which the first row of a rolling-shutter frame begins its exposure.


\(\FrameReadoutTime\)
Frame Readout Time
\(\text{s}\)
Time a camera takes to read its pixels out after exposure.


\(\EvidenceCaptureInstant\)
Evidence Capture Instant
\(\text{s}\)
Instant, on a monotonic clock, at which the sensor evidence behind an observation or proposal was captured; observation age and proposal validity are measured from it.


\(\EvidenceEpoch\)
Evidence Epoch

Capture instant of the most recent measurement that constrained a stored belief; republishing or predicting never advances it.


\(\FreshEvidenceTime\)
Fresh Evidence Time
\(\text{s}\)
Capture time of the fresh physical evidence that renews a belief’s evidence epoch \(\EvidenceEpoch\).


\(\CurrentTime\)
Current Time

Wall-clock time at which a consumer evaluates a stored record; evidence age is the current time minus \(\EvidenceEpoch\).


\(\DispatchObservationAge\)
Dispatch Observation Age
\(\text{s}\)
Elapsed time from the sensor exposure midpoint to dispatch of the processed observation. Current consumer evidence age additionally includes elapsed time after dispatch.


\(\FreeConfigurationSpace\)

Set
Configurations at which the robot touches no obstacle, the configuration space minus the obstacle set.

Inverse Depth

Reciprocal of a point’s depth along the optical axis, the parameterization that lets a landmark at infinity enter an estimator at zero; linear in disparity.


\(\ObstacleSeparationDistance\)
Obstacle Separation Distance
\(\text{m}\)
Distance between the machine and the nearest obstacle or boundary at a given time, the signal a clearance predicate scores; written as a function of time.


\(\OccupancyLogOdds\)
Occupancy Log-Odds
Dimensionless
Natural logarithm of the odds of a voxel’s occupancy probability, the quantity an occupancy map stores per cell; indexed by step, with the prior at step zero.


\(\MeasuredTrackedPosition\)
Measured Tracked Position
\(\text{m}\)
Measured Cartesian position of the tracked point, which the tracking error compares against the reference.


\(\LastMeasurementTime\)
Last Measurement Time

Capture time of the most recent measurement that updated a track or map cell.


\(\InitialVelocityStandardDeviation\)
Initial Velocity Standard Deviation
\(\text{m/s}\)
Standard deviation of the velocity error of an estimate, here at the onset of occlusion.


\(\PixelStandardDeviation\)

Pixels
Standard deviation of a measured image position, in pixels; the image-plane noise that propagates into depth and position error.


\(\PrincipalPointColumn\)
Principal Point Column
Pixels
Horizontal pixel coordinate of the principal point, where the optical axis meets the image.


\(\PrincipalPointRow\)
Principal Point Row
Pixels
Vertical pixel coordinate of the principal point, where the optical axis meets the image.

Stereo Baseline

Distance between the optical centers of a stereo camera pair; depth is focal length times baseline over disparity.

Pixels
Horizontal pixel offset between the images of one scene point in the two views of a rectified stereo pair; not a travel distance or a sightline range, which share the glyph.
