title: About the Author
text:
Vijay Janapa Reddi is the Gordon McKay Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Engineering at Harvard University and a Visiting Professor at ETH Zurich in the Integrated Systems Laboratory (IIS), D-ITET. He is a founding member and Vice President of MLCommons and the author of the open-source reference text Machine Learning Systems.
His research sits at the intersection of computer architecture, machine learning systems, and edge robotics, focusing on how computing hardware and learned software co-design to interact with the physical world. Over the past decade, his work has concentrated on democratizing applied systems through open-source education and reproducible benchmarks, connecting first-principles silicon constraints directly to accessible, bench-verified learning.


Every textbook reflects the intellectual lineage, biases, and lens of its author. I want to make the viewpoint behind this book explicit.
I am not a classical control theorist, nor a mechanical kinematics specialist, and I do not pretend to be one. I bring the perspective of a computer systems architect and machine learning systems (MLSys) researcher going after first principles.
My intuition for this domain dates back to my undergraduate mechatronics capstone. As an electrical and computer engineering student, that capstone was the first time I had to integrate analog circuits, sensor conditioning, microcontrollers, motor drivers, mechanical linkages, and embedded software into a single working machine. It was the moment I realized that software cannot be designed in isolation from physical reality: motor coils heat up, power rails droop under sudden acceleration, and sensor measurements age the instant physical transduction occurs. For over twenty years, my work has sat at the boundary where software meets silicon and energy constraints: mobile System-on-Chip performance architecture and edge AI silicon at Google, co-founding MLCommons and MLPerf to set empirical benchmarking standards for AI accelerators, and helping start TinyML, which compresses neural networks to run on milliwatt microcontrollers.
Physical AI brings me back to that mechatronics capstone, with one difference. In classical mechatronics, we closed the loop using hand-crafted, deterministic logic: PID controllers, state machines, and analytical models. In Physical AI, we are embedding high-capacity neural networks (foundation models, diffusion policies, and learned decoders) into that exact same unforgiving loop. Their proposals may be sampled or deterministic, but neither form alone establishes that an action is safe. The engineering challenge now extends beyond making the machine move to closing the loop safely around a learned brain, using deterministic systems and safety principles.
That background shapes what I want students to understand. A model’s proposed action must pass through a computing system before the physical machine can carry it out. I want readers to trace that path and ask what could prevent an action from being carried out as intended. The timing of computation, the body’s capabilities, and the assumptions behind command checks all matter to that assessment. The explanations should make these interactions understandable before specialized mathematics or implementation detail is needed.
This textbook is my attempt to share that foundational systems perspective with the next generation of engineers, roboticists, and computer scientists. It is the book I wish my own students had when bridging machine learning systems to the physical world.



This first-principles systems work spans three major eras. Each era extended the same hardware-to-software discipline to a tighter physical operating envelope:

Silicon Reality & Mobile Architecture: Grounded in computer architecture, low-power microarchitectures, and mobile System-on-Chip (SoC) design (including edge AI silicon performance architecture at Google). This work addressed the physical realities of computing: memory bus contention under high-bandwidth camera streams, thermal throttling under strict power and thermal envelopes, and interrupt latencies under hard real-time deadlines.
ML Systems & The TinyML Movement: Bridging algorithmic machine learning abstractions to silicon execution. He co-founded MLPerf to establish the global standard for benchmarking ML hardware and software, and pioneered the TinyML movement, developing the Harvard CS249r curriculum and the HarvardX TinyML program (reaching over 100,000 learners globally) to bring deep neural models onto milliwatt microcontrollers.
Closing the Sense-and-Act Loop in Physical AI: Extending this systems perspective to machines whose learned models propose physical actions. The focus is on how sensing, computation, and the body’s response interact, and on the conditions under which a proposed action can be executed.




Development of the hands-on bench laboratories and the reference hardware platform (the Physical AI Kit on Arduino UNO Q Dual-Brain) is a collaboration with Dr. Andrea Mattia Garavagno, postdoctoral researcher in the Integrated Systems Laboratory (IIS), D-ITET at ETH Zurich. This work aims to translate the systems ideas in the book into firmware and software exercises that students and practitioners can reproduce and examine on the bench.

title: Author’s Note
text:
Author’s Note

When a server returns an error for a page request, the reader can try again. A robot approaching an obstacle keeps moving while its computer decides whether to brake. Restarting the computation cannot recover the distance already traveled.
In a page-serving application, an unhandled exception or late result may produce a log entry, a dropped frame, or a retry button. In physical AI, software commands matter, momentum, and energy. The unit of engineering is the action crossing the causal boundary. Delay is paid in millimeters, and failure results in cracked composite, burned motor coils, or physical harm.
To build machines that survive this reality, we must give up the idea that a high-capacity network can drive a physical plant, the apparatus being controlled, directly. In the machine this book builds, the learned model proposes; only the permission path permits, and only for as long as its evidence holds.
I write these chapters as an active systems researcher exploring how the laws of computing intersect with the laws of Newtonian mechanics, thermal dissipation, and functional safety. Concrete systems tasks, hardware measurements, and first-principles napkin math guide our progression; formal continuous-control derivations and proof machinery provide optional depth in the appendices.
This book is an open, working notebook. Step across the causal boundary with me, and let us explore how to engineer machines that sense, act, and survive in the physical world.
— Vijay Janapa Reddi
Cambridge, Massachusetts
2026

title: Physical AI
text:
This is an active draft. Physical AI systems connect learned models to actuators that move mass, deliver torque, and interact with the physical world. When a learned proposal crosses the causal boundary into physical force, delay becomes distance traveled, and work delivered cannot be rolled back.
    This book builds an embodied system in the order its physics imposes: body limits, learned proposers, deterministic permission, sensorimotor learning, real-time execution, and evidence-based governance, treating physical embodiment as an architectural systems discipline.

title: Preface
text:
This book is for senior undergraduates and beginning graduate students in computer science, robotics, electrical engineering, and machine learning, and for practicing engineers who build, deploy, or certify physical AI systems. It is written for the engineer who has watched an embodied policy succeed in simulation or a scripted demonstration and now has to ship a machine that moves mass among people, day after day. That machine must not collide with a coworker, damage a payload, burn out a motor winding, or run away on a network timeout.
The reader should understand basic programming in Python and machine learning intuition, and be comfortable with introductory Newtonian physics, linear algebra, and basic probability. The book assumes no prior book in this series. It develops physical AI concepts where they are first used and derives the timing, control, and hardware-placement relationships needed to reason about embodied workloads without requiring specialist background in nonlinear control theory or application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) microarchitecture.



A reasonable engineer might look at the current wave of robot foundation models and ask a skeptical question. Is physical artificial intelligence a genuine systems discipline with durable principles, or is it simply classical robotics with a transformer bolted on, or an end-to-end neural network running on an onboard computer?
The skepticism is fair. Much of what is written about embodied AI highlights impressive single-task demonstrations, such as a dexterous hand folding laundry or a humanoid walking through a lab. Demonstration, however, is not deployment. In the field, failure rarely comes from the raw expressiveness of the model. What fails is the system around it, as when an observation arrives 50 milliseconds too late, an action proposal demands more torque than the joint drives can deliver, or an unmodeled delay turns a braking command into an impact.
Traditional machine learning systems center on disembodied prediction. A model evaluates static inputs in an open loop and returns advisory labels, rankings, or tokens without acting directly on the world. Because a person or downstream service must still decide what to do with that output, an erroneous prediction can be discarded or recalculated before it causes harm, and systems engineering centers on balancing training cost against serving latency, memory, and throughput. Agentic machine learning systems move from single predictions to sequential action: a model formulates multi-step plans, inspects feedback, and invokes software tools in a closed loop. As long as that loop stays inside a digital environment, however, virtual time can be paused, execution can be sandboxed, and failed transactions can be rolled back.
Physical AI systems bring agency into continuous physics. When an autonomous model commands actuators, computation crosses the causal boundary into mass, momentum, friction, and heat. In continuous physics, virtual sandboxes do not exist: time cannot pause while a foundation model deliberates, and Newtonian work cannot be rolled back after an impact. A larger model cannot shorten a stopping distance, cool an electric winding, or recover clearance spent while it computed. Physical AI therefore requires an architectural discipline. Learned models propose, while an independent permission path, with its own timing and its own fallback, decides what may cross into the physical world.
This book teaches how to design, measure, and govern that machine. Its central question is what an embodied task needs around a learned model to produce useful physical service supported by the required evidence. Readers should leave able to translate physical limits into computational budgets, design sensorimotor policies that close the loop under real-time deadlines, enforce runtime assurance independently of the learned proposer, and justify release through an assurance case that links claims to empirical evidence.



The unit of engineering in this book is the causal boundary, the interface where an admitted digital command becomes current in a motor winding, torque on a shaft, and physical force delivered to the world. Accuracy on a held-out dataset is not the measure of a physical AI system. The measure is whether closed-loop actions achieve task goals within verified physical limits, supported by evidence independent of the learned model’s self-report, and at what cost in latency, energy, thermal margin, and compute.
Four governing laws anchor the book’s architecture. Each law pairs a physical or statistical constraint with the systems mechanism required to bound it:

The First Law: Irreversibility. Software cannot roll back physical consequences. Every check that admits a command must finish before the machine spends its remaining clearance, so physical limits become strict budgets in time, distance, torque, heat, and voltage.
The Second Law: Endogenous Data. A physical machine’s actions choose its next observations. The states a deployed policy visits are conditioned on its own previous actions, so competence is a claim bounded by the operating envelope that closed-loop evaluation actually verified.
The Third Law: Proposal Is Not Permission. A learned model may propose motion; only an independent permission path may admit it. The permission path evaluates state whose age is bounded, executes within a deterministic deadline set by the plant physics, and maintains a feasible fallback that does not depend on the learned proposer.
The Fourth Law: Permission Must Be Earned. Permission to operate is granted per operating condition on recorded evidence, and it expires when that evidence does.

The first of these is a physical law. The other three are design principles, the embodied counterparts to covariate shift, runtime assurance, and the assurance case. This book elevates them to bedrock laws because a production machine that violates them incurs predictable physical risks.
Two relations quantify these obligations throughout the book. Delay is distance governs the stopping budget: if a machine moving at velocity \(\SpeedAtDetection\) takes reaction time \(\PrebrakeDelay\) to sense, compute, and actuate before decelerating at rate \(\CredibleBrakingDeceleration\), the total stopping distance is \(\StoppingDistance = \SpeedAtDetection \cdot \PrebrakeDelay + \frac{\SpeedAtDetection^2}{2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration}\). Every millisecond of latency is distance spent before braking can begin. Evidence expiration governs the validity of state: an observation or state estimate carries an expiration timestamp derived from the plant’s maximum rate of change, after which it cannot justify a safety assertion.
The machine’s architecture separates five roles: the Brain (learned models that propose goals and motion), the Nervous System (deterministic communication and the independent permission path), the Body (drives, transmissions, windings, and power systems), the Boundary (register writes and sensor captures), and the World (continuous physical dynamics, obstacles, and people). A warehouse mobile manipulator that navigates an aisle shared with workers, opens a spring-latched door, and handles a fragile payload serves as the running reference machine in every chapter. A humanoid example at the end of each part tests whether the reasoning survives a body that couples balance, joint torque, and thermal dissipation.



The book builds understanding in physical dependency order: anatomy, teaching, running, governing. Each part adds responsibilities that the preceding material prepares the reader to evaluate, and reference appendices supply the supporting mathematical, control, and hardware derivations:

Introduction: The Causal Boundary (The Causal Boundary) prices delay at the causal boundary, defines the five-level machine architecture, and establishes the four governing laws.
Part I: The Machine Anatomy turns the first law into physical budgets. The Physical Body measures what the body can do before damage, The Cognitive Brain characterizes the learned proposer and how quickly its evidence ages, and The Nervous System derives how frequently the permission path must tick and how long a proposal may drive the actuators.
Part II: Teaching the Machine applies the second law to sensorimotor learning. Physical Data records demonstrations with their operating conditions, Policy Training analyzes training regimes and the dependencies they hide, and Closed-Loop Evaluation bounds the policy’s competence through finite-trial closed-loop evaluation.
Part III: Running the Machine applies the third law at runtime. It follows dated sensor measurements through perception (Sensor Perception), spatial memory and state estimation (Spatial Memory), intent grounding (Grounded Intent), and trajectory planning (Trajectory Planning) to runtime enforcement (Safety Enforcement), and tests whether real-time hardware keeps that path on time (Workload Placement).
Part IV: Governing the Machine applies the fourth law to operational authority. Supervisory Intervention governs how authority passes between the machine and an operator. Adversarial Verification injects physical and computational faults to prove containment. Deployment Release constructs the assurance case that justifies release under named conditions. Responsible Physical AI names who answers for each decision behind an admitted action, which human roles a person can actually perform, and which people bear the machine’s risk and appear in its records.
Conclusion: Engineering Physical AI (Engineering Physical AI) synthesizes the complete methodology, transfers the reasoning to an unfamiliar machine, and establishes the open research frontier.

Reference appendices provide background on machine learning foundations (Machine Learning Background), control and dynamics (Control and Dynamics), systems and hardware (Systems and Hardware), sensorimotor troubleshooting (Physical AI Production Troubleshooting Matrix), and a unified glossary. Each appendix is organized as a lookup reference so that readers can consult a specific derivation without losing the thread of the main text.



The book is written to be read in order. Each chapter uses only ideas introduced earlier or defined where they appear, and each owns its concepts. Every chapter opens with the physical problem it solves, develops the mechanism as the answer, and closes with a summary and a handoff to the next chapter. Classical systems mechanisms (watchdog leases, safety filters, interlocks, fail-safe fallbacks, and real-time scheduling) appear as concrete solutions to physical hazards rather than as abstract theory.
Readers with a particular focus can tailor their depth after the introduction. Four tracks correspond to the primary engineering roles that collaborate on a physical AI deployment:

Core systems curriculum: Follow the complete sequence from The Causal Boundary through Engineering Physical AI to integrate physical limits, learning, runtime design, and operational evidence.
ML systems and learned runtimes: Focus on the common foundation, sensorimotor training and evaluation (Physical Data through Closed-Loop Evaluation), perception and planning (Sensor Perception through Workload Placement), and release (Deployment Release).
Embedded systems and silicon: Focus on the common foundation, runtime placement (Workload Placement), communication timing (The Nervous System), and fault verification (Adversarial Verification).
Robotics, control, and assurance: Focus on the common foundation, state estimation and planning (Spatial Memory through Trajectory Planning), runtime enforcement (Safety Enforcement), human intervention (Supervisory Intervention), and responsibility for the people around the machine (Responsible Physical AI).

Evidence flows from physical anatomy through training and runtime execution to operational release, and the chapter dependencies across the six divisions of the book follow that progression (figure 1). Every arrow in the map represents a concrete record or physical bound handed forward from one engineering stage to the next.






Figure 1: Chapter Dependency Map: Arrows show chapter dependencies across the book’s divisions. Solid-arrow weight follows the citation-count bands in the legend: 5–9, 10–19, and 20 or more citations; dashed arrows mark light links. Transitive links are omitted for clarity.





The margins carry small visual aids beside the prose where a quantitative relationship, scale gap, or threshold is easiest to see. Each visual follows one of five recurring forms:

Ladders span orders of magnitude (such as sensor ingestion bandwidths or execution loop rates).
Threshold knees mark the point where a physical relationship changes regime (such as reflected rotor inertia dominating gear trains or contact stiffness spiking forces).
Budget envelopes set competing demands against a deadline (such as diffusion denoising steps against control periods, or operator takeover latencies).
Sequence strips illustrate multi-phase timing (such as receding-horizon chunk execution or fault handshakes).
Causal chains trace fault propagation from sensor error to physical consequence.

















Alongside these visual notes, unnumbered marginal navigation pointers trace architectural connections across chapters. Three symbols distinguish whether a pointer looks back to a foundation, ahead to a downstream consumer, or across to a contrasting design:

↩︎ Backward pointer: Directs the reader back to the earlier chapter where a physical bound, hardware contract, or clock cadence was established.
↪ Forward pointer: Directs the reader ahead to the later chapter, or to an appendix, where the idea is developed, measured, or enforced.
⇄ Contrast: Marks a place where two chapters or machine classes treat the same problem differently.

A pointer only orients. When an argument depends on another chapter, the reference stays in the text.




This is not a ROS 2 or middleware manual. Middleware and messaging frameworks change, whereas the physical requirements they must satisfy (bounded latency, deterministic serialization, and fault isolation) do not. The book therefore introduces real-time protocols and message queues only as mechanisms to meet stated physical deadlines. Nor is it a mechanical CAD manual or a motor design treatise, because it characterizes actuators, transmissions, and thermal limits through the software budgets they impose rather than through their mechanical fabrication. For the same reason, simulation appears here not as a benchmark leaderboard, where open-loop scores stand in for deployment, but as a tool for generating hypotheses and training data. Its claims must still be verified on the physical machine. Software agents that act solely behind digital APIs without physical actuators remain outside our scope.



Robot form factors, neural network architectures, and motor drive silicon will evolve, some before this book reaches print. The text therefore emphasizes the principles that survive those transitions: the causal boundary as the unit of engineering, the four governing laws, the separation between learned proposers and deterministic permission paths, and the discipline of grounding operational authority in empirical evidence. Current platforms and models appear throughout to make the concepts concrete, but the principles stand independently of any specific vendor, model, or hardware platform. Where a question is actively unsettled in the field, such as how best to verify generalist policies against rare corner cases, the book presents the problem as an open engineering challenge rather than settled doctrine.



The worked examples and derivations draw on five foundational areas. Readers should be comfortable with:

programming in Python and working with numeric arrays;
core machine learning concepts, including supervised training, loss functions, and inference;
introductory Newtonian mechanics (position, velocity, acceleration, force, torque, inertia);
linear algebra (vectors, matrices, coordinate transformations); and
undergraduate probability and basic statistics.

Deeper background in classical control theory, real-time operating systems, or robotics kinematics is beneficial but not required; the book develops the necessary control, estimation, and real-time concepts where they are first needed. Every specialized tool is introduced from first principles at the point where a concrete systems decision depends on it.

title: Preface
Reader Guide and Prerequisites
text:
Physical AI: Machine Learning Systems That Sense and Act is an independent textbook for advanced undergraduate students, graduate researchers, and practicing engineers who want to build machines that sense and act. Readers may arrive from machine learning, software systems, electrical engineering, or robotics. The common goal is to connect learned behavior to physical execution and explain the conditions under which that connection can be trusted.


A physical AI systems engineer must reason across disciplines, but need not enter with specialist training in all of them. The starting point is programming experience, basic machine learning intuition, and introductory mechanics, supported by undergraduate mathematics. Prior study of another volume in this series is not required.
The following competencies support the worked examples. Each area supplies a practical skill that the chapters build on rather than a prerequisite in advanced theory:

Programming: Read and modify a short program, follow its data flow, and interpret experimental output. The executable calculations use Python; familiarity with C or C++ helps with implementation examples but is not the entry requirement.
Machine learning intuition: Distinguish training from inference, understand a learned model as a mapping fitted from data, and recognize why performance on held-out examples may differ from deployment. Experience building a large model or using a particular framework is not required.
Mathematics: Work with algebra, vectors, matrices, derivatives, and elementary probability. These tools support coordinate transformations, rates of change, and uncertainty estimates. More specialized notation is introduced with the mechanism that needs it.
Physical reasoning: Relate force to acceleration, speed to distance traveled, and electrical power to energy use. Introductory Newtonian mechanics supplies the starting intuition for stopping, contact, and actuator limits.
Experimental practice: Interpret a measurement with its units and conditions, distinguish an assumption from an observation, and compare a calculation with a test. The book develops this practice into evidence for operating a machine.

Specialized control theory, robot kinematics, real-time scheduling, and accelerator architecture are subjects of study here, rather than a second set of admission requirements. Some derivations require a slower pass or background reading. The local appendices provide machine learning background (Machine Learning Background), control and dynamics (Control and Dynamics), and systems and hardware (Systems and Hardware). When a failure spans perception, planning, and actuation, Physical AI Production Troubleshooting Matrix maps the symptom to measurements that distinguish competing causes.


Readers from different backgrounds enter this loop from different sides. An ML practitioner starts from the consequences of a proposed action and works toward the mechanics and timing that constrain it. An embedded systems engineer starts from a hardware deadline and learns how training data and policy behavior shape the workload that must meet it. A roboticist starts from a model of the plant and examines what changes when a learned proposer supplies goals and trajectories. Each reader brings one part of the foundation and meets the others where the system connects them.
On a first pass through a dense derivation, identify the physical quantity being bounded, the assumptions the bound needs, and the decision it changes. Then work through the example before returning to the derivation. A formal guarantee may require that deeper mathematical treatment; understanding the systems decision still begins with the concrete failure the mechanism is meant to prevent.




The sequential path is the default for learning the whole discipline. Specialist tracks select an emphasis within that path. They do not make the common physical model or the evidence limits optional.
All tracks begin with The Causal Boundary and the machine anatomy in The Physical Body, The Cognitive Brain, and The Nervous System. These establish physical budgets, learned proposals, and the independent path that decides whether a proposal may act. Later chapters repeatedly use those foundations. After that common start, readers can concentrate their deeper study along one of four role-specific tracks (table 1).

When a track omits a chapter from detailed study, its opening, worked handoff, and summary provide the context needed downstream. For example, a planning exercise still needs dated observations and a current state estimate; a release decision still needs evidence about human authority and fault response. Instructors can select technical depth while retaining those dependencies. The full sequence contains more detail than every course will cover at equal depth.



The curriculum builds toward an end-to-end engineering judgment about a machine performing a specified task. Its parts contribute different capabilities:

In Part I, determine which physical budget binds, estimate what the learned proposer can supply, and derive the timing requirements that connect computation to actuation.
In Part II, collect demonstrations with their operating conditions, choose a training regime, and evaluate behavior in the feedback loop where actions change subsequent observations. Use failures to collect new experience and test whether a changed candidate expands competence without losing established behavior.
In Part III, turn measurements into dated state estimates, grounded goals, and feasible trajectories; then check proposals against physical limits and place the runtime on resources that can meet its deadlines.
In Part IV, design human intervention, challenge the integrated system with faults, and justify useful service within the conditions the evidence covers, assessing task performance and physical containment separately.

The conclusion synthesizes those engineering capabilities and tests whether they transfer to an unfamiliar machine. The records accumulated along the way preserve the reasoning behind a design: what was measured, what was assumed, which decision followed, and what would invalidate it. Filling in a record is useful only when the underlying engineering argument is sound.



The evidence behind a number determines what it can support. Four categories distinguish observations and calculations from ratings and illustrative inputs; a fifth label identifies a design choice:

Measured: A calibrated observation of a particular machine. It names its instrument, its operating conditions, its sample count, and, for a distribution, the percentile it reports. Only a measured number, or a number derived from measured ones, can support a safety margin.
Derived: Computed from stated inputs through a physical or statistical model. It carries that model’s assumptions, input provenance, and propagated uncertainty. A result derived from illustrative inputs remains illustrative evidence.
Datasheet: A manufacturer’s rating under the manufacturer’s conditions. It says what to expect and what to test, and it is not evidence about the unit on the bench.
Illustrative: Selected to show arithmetic or scaling. It supports no margin, timeout, or release decision.

A budget or requirement, such as a lease duration or a clearance margin, belongs to none of the four. It is a design decision, labeled chosen, and it means something only when it is checked against the measured or derived number it must fit, as a chosen lease is checked against the derived ceiling on pre-brake delay.
A worked design in this book shows a decision procedure. When its inputs are illustrative, the decision it reaches is illustrative too. It shows how the machine’s speed, lease, or verdict would be set, and it would bind a real machine only after its physical and timing premises are qualified. Some examples stipulate a supporting evidence packet to teach how successful learning or restricted service could be justified. Such branches are hypothetical throughout; their assumed trial counts and outcomes are not measurements of the book’s machine.
When a number decides something, such as a speed limit, a timeout, or a release, the book keeps it as a limit record with six elements. The record pairs the nominal value (or distribution) and its measurement uncertainty with the operating conditions under which that value holds (payload, temperature, supply voltage, surface, concurrent workload, and firmware). Alongside the engineering margin between the operating target and the breakdown threshold, it names the runtime detector that catches an excursion while the machine runs and records the value’s provenance, meaning its label and the instrument or model that produced it. A limit holds only under its stated conditions. When wear, heat, a new payload, or a new build changes them, the limit must be established again before it is reused.
Before using a worked value to justify a decision, establish both its category and the conditions attached to it, because an unlabeled value does not become a measured limit merely by appearing in a calculation. Every result holds only under the assumptions stated with its example. A statistical bound from finitely many trials depends on its sampling assumptions and proves nothing beyond them. A measured percentile describes only the tested workload rather than a true worst case. In a release argument (Deployment Release and Engineering Physical AI), each premise therefore carries an explicit status: established by qualified measurements or derivations, assumed, decided by accountable judgment, unsupported, or outside the threat model.



The book develops specialist mechanisms to the depth needed for systems decisions, introducing each topic from first principles inside the chapter whose decision depends on it and stopping there. In the anatomy and learning chapters, model quantization is introduced where it sets the intent model’s latency (Quantizing the intent model), while reinforcement learning fundamentals and the pretrain-then-post-train recipe appear when the arm learns the spring-latched door task (The latch task as a reward problem, Pretrained generalist policies and post-training). In the runtime chapters, perception stops at the qualified measurement and hands state estimation to spatial memory (Spatial Memory). Spatial memory builds from the discrete and extended Kalman filters, multi-target tracking, and delayed updates (Estimating State from Dated Measurements) to localization and SLAM in the planning map (Localization drift and map frames that jump). Task and motion planning grounds abstract goals in feasible geometry (Task Operators and Geometric Samplers), while manipulator kinematics, time parameterization, and mobile-base planning build the trajectory record (The Planning Handoff and the Trajectory Record, Time parameterization under torque and jerk bounds, Mobile-base planning under nonholonomic constraints) and worst-case execution time analysis tests hardware isolation (Empirical Verification of Silicon Isolation). Finally, the governance chapters introduce importance sampling where rare-failure rates must be estimated (Estimating a rare failure rate by importance sampling) and functional safety standards where the release argument is assembled (The standards map for the running machine).
What the book omits is the remainder of each of those fields. It does not provide an exhaustive catalog of manipulator geometries or grasp analysis, or a complete course in nonlinear or optimal control. It omits the convergence theory of reinforcement learning and the construction of large-scale SLAM back ends. It also leaves out the internals of static timing-analysis tools and a comprehensive theory of deep learning optimization, and it is not a substitute for the text of a safety standard. Specialized derivations appear where they explain a bound or trade-off, and the appendices provide supporting background.
Implementation examples expose timing, memory, communication, and actuation mechanisms. They are not tutorials for a particular robotics middleware package or simulation product. The intended result is the ability to reason about a new machine and recognize when its design needs additional specialist analysis or measurement.

title: Reader Guide and Prerequisites
text:
A physical AI systems engineer must reason across disciplines, but need not enter with specialist training in all of them. The starting point is programming experience, basic machine learning intuition, and introductory mechanics, supported by undergraduate mathematics. Prior study of another volume in this series is not required.
The following competencies support the worked examples. Each area supplies a practical skill that the chapters build on rather than a prerequisite in advanced theory:

Programming: Read and modify a short program, follow its data flow, and interpret experimental output. The executable calculations use Python; familiarity with C or C++ helps with implementation examples but is not the entry requirement.
Machine learning intuition: Distinguish training from inference, understand a learned model as a mapping fitted from data, and recognize why performance on held-out examples may differ from deployment. Experience building a large model or using a particular framework is not required.
Mathematics: Work with algebra, vectors, matrices, derivatives, and elementary probability. These tools support coordinate transformations, rates of change, and uncertainty estimates. More specialized notation is introduced with the mechanism that needs it.
Physical reasoning: Relate force to acceleration, speed to distance traveled, and electrical power to energy use. Introductory Newtonian mechanics supplies the starting intuition for stopping, contact, and actuator limits.
Experimental practice: Interpret a measurement with its units and conditions, distinguish an assumption from an observation, and compare a calculation with a test. The book develops this practice into evidence for operating a machine.

Specialized control theory, robot kinematics, real-time scheduling, and accelerator architecture are subjects of study here, rather than a second set of admission requirements. Some derivations require a slower pass or background reading. The local appendices provide machine learning background (Machine Learning Background), control and dynamics (Control and Dynamics), and systems and hardware (Systems and Hardware). When a failure spans perception, planning, and actuation, Physical AI Production Troubleshooting Matrix maps the symptom to measurements that distinguish competing causes.


Readers from different backgrounds enter this loop from different sides. An ML practitioner starts from the consequences of a proposed action and works toward the mechanics and timing that constrain it. An embedded systems engineer starts from a hardware deadline and learns how training data and policy behavior shape the workload that must meet it. A roboticist starts from a model of the plant and examines what changes when a learned proposer supplies goals and trajectories. Each reader brings one part of the foundation and meets the others where the system connects them.
On a first pass through a dense derivation, identify the physical quantity being bounded, the assumptions the bound needs, and the decision it changes. Then work through the example before returning to the derivation. A formal guarantee may require that deeper mathematical treatment; understanding the systems decision still begins with the concrete failure the mechanism is meant to prevent.

title: Reader Guide and Prerequisites
text:
The sequential path is the default for learning the whole discipline. Specialist tracks select an emphasis within that path. They do not make the common physical model or the evidence limits optional.
All tracks begin with The Causal Boundary and the machine anatomy in The Physical Body, The Cognitive Brain, and The Nervous System. These establish physical budgets, learned proposals, and the independent path that decides whether a proposal may act. Later chapters repeatedly use those foundations. After that common start, readers can concentrate their deeper study along one of four role-specific tracks (table 1).

title: A Note on AI Assistance
text:
A Note on AI Assistance






CautionWorking draft



This text is an evolving working draft. As I collect ideas and organize this cross-disciplinary material, these chapters represent an active work in progress. While I develop each section carefully from foundational control literature, robotics principles, and verified computation cells, I have not yet reached the stage of stress-testing these frameworks with external domain specialists. I am sharing this draft openly to organize my thoughts and invite early community feedback as the curriculum takes shape.


This book is released as an open-access, living textbook; it is not yet under contract with a commercial publisher. In digital machine learning, computation operates behind glass: an unhandled exception produces a log trace, and latency costs user patience. In Physical AI, computation commands matter, momentum, and current. Latency is paid in millimeters of uncontrolled travel, and software decisions carry direct kinetic consequences.
Crossing that boundary required reconciling two engineering traditions that rarely speak the same language. On one side stands classical robotics and control theory, built on state-space dynamics, kinematics, and formal stability proofs. On the other stands modern machine learning systems, built on statistical optimization, memory hierarchies, and massive hardware acceleration.
Bridging these disciplines is difficult because their literatures are deeply siloed. In developing this curriculum, I used generative AI as an interactive research translator and cross-domain synthesis engine. Large language models served as a lateral search tool, querying across disparate bodies of robotics, control, and systems literature to connect classical methods with modern learned representations. The tool helped surface historical precedents, identify relevant mathematical formulations across disciplines, and explore alternative pedagogical framings.
Yet an AI tool cannot test whether a control loop survives contact with physical hardware. Discovering mathematical parallels between neural networks and control theory is easy; deciding which abstractions hold under real sensor noise, actuator saturation, and hard millisecond deadlines requires human systems judgment. Translating these cross-disciplinary connections into a disciplined, first-principles textbook required months of intensive analysis, iterative drafting, and building executable models.
Authorship in this domain is stewardship: uniting two historically divided fields into a cohesive curriculum and assuming responsibility for the result. The breakthroughs belong to the control theorists, roboticists, and systems researchers cited throughout these pages. My name is on the cover so that readers and engineers have a single human being to hold accountable, someone to reach out to for debates, clarifications, and corrections.
Because physical systems carry real-world consequences, this text should be approached as an evolving working draft. While our executable Python cells verify numerical consistency and automated test suites check cross-references, I am actively refining these connections before formally stress-testing them with robotics and control specialists. I invite readers, roboticists, and control engineers to engage with these ideas, report errors on GitHub, and help refine this material as the curriculum takes shape. The principle holds with absolute finality at the physical boundary: the tool can propose, and the tool can tutor, but only the human engineer can ratify and take responsibility.




 Back to top

title: The Causal Boundary
text:
Purpose



Physical AI stack focus for this chapter.
Why can a better prediction still produce a worse physical action?
A learned model can recognize a task correctly and still act too late to stop a moving machine or prevent excessive contact force. Once a command produces motion or heat, replacing the prediction cannot undo the work already delivered. The engineer must therefore connect model quality to the body’s limits, the time available to respond, and the evidence supporting the next action. An independent permission path must be able to refuse a proposal and carry out a feasible fallback even when the model stalls. At the causal boundary, where commands become physical work, irreversibility makes these responsibilities part of the system’s architecture.


Learning Objectives

Trace how machine learning systems evolved from disembodied prediction through digital agency to physical embodiment, and explain why that progression gives data, compute, evaluation, and deployment physical stakes
Explain why an action that crosses the causal boundary requires reasoning about consequences that software rollback cannot undo
Calculate how response delay consumes a moving machine’s stopping clearance
Apply the scope test to distinguish physical AI from advisory learning and classical control
Distinguish learned proposals from permission to execute them in the five-level machine
Diagnose how perception, response timing, and missing redundancy interacted in the Tempe collision
Relate the four laws to their established names in the field and to the book’s four parts

title: The Causal Boundary
text:
1.1 Artificial Intelligence Beyond Glass
When an image classifier mislabels a warehouse photograph on a server, a downstream filter can discard the label before any machine moves; when a mobile robot’s policy misjudges aisle clearance and drives its wheel motors, the chassis is already accelerating toward the rack. Across offline advisory prediction, digital agency, and physical embodiment, computation acquires different consequences as its outputs enter an action loop, and physical AI diverges from the other two in how agency, time, and recovery behave (table 1).
In the offline or advisory case, a model delivers predictions against a static dataset before any downstream action closes a feedback loop. Whether classifying an image, predicting customer churn, estimating a bounding box, or ranking search results, the model operates in open loop. Its input distribution is exogenous, because the predictions it emits do not alter the process that generates later test examples. Because those requests arrive independently, throughput-oriented serving can batch many inputs together (\(\BatchSize \gg 1\)) across pipeline stages, performing many arithmetic operations for every byte of weights fetched from memory (its arithmetic intensity). The advisory model exercises no agency of its own. Before a person or downstream service acts on the output, an incorrect label or irrelevant search result can be ignored, filtered, or recalculated without having done physical work.
The emergence of agentic machine learning marked an architectural transition from passive, single-shot prediction to active, sequential decision-making. Endowed with reasoning loops and test-time deliberation, an agentic model formulates multi-step plans, maintains internal state across execution traces, and autonomously invokes external tools. These tools execute database queries, call web APIs, run generated code in execution environments, and coordinate software subagents. In this regime, the execution loop is closed. An action taken at step \(\TurnIndex\) alters the state of the software environment, so subsequent observations \(\TrajectoryObservation_{t+1}\) depend directly on prior decisions \(\TrajectoryAction_t\). The system possesses genuine agency.
Within a controlled software environment, this agency can operate inside a protective envelope, “behind the glass.” Such environments can grant agentic systems three structural privileges, though external services and consequential tool calls may fall outside that envelope:

Elastic virtual time: A controlled software environment can wait while the model computes. Whether an agent requires \(200\text{ ms}\) or \(30\text{ s}\) of test-time compute to plan its next tool call, the environment can hold its simulated state until the action is emitted. External services continue evolving on their own clocks.
Transactional rollback and sandboxing: Tool execution can occur within isolated containers, virtual machines, or transactional databases. When an action produces an error inside this envelope, software exceptions catch the fault, database transactions roll back, or the container restarts from a clean snapshot. These mechanisms cannot undo consequences already delivered outside it.
Discrete symbolic interfaces: Actions are structured strings, JSON schemas, or API payloads whose syntax and validity can be verified by deterministic compilers and linters before execution.

Physical artificial intelligence represents the arrival of agency in the physical world. A physical AI system does not invoke a software API inside a virtual sandbox; its outputs cross the causal boundary into physical actuators. A learned model’s output becomes a setpoint (the target value a low-level controller drives toward), the setpoint becomes electrical current in a motor phase winding (one of the stationary copper coils whose current turns the motor), and the current becomes electromagnetic torque. The torque accelerates physical mass through gearboxes, linkages, and contact surfaces sharing space with people and objects. That physical embodiment strips away every digital privilege:

Continuous time: Physical time advances under Newtonian mechanics regardless of processor state. The physical plant, the apparatus being controlled such as a robot’s wheeled base or arm, does not pause while a neural network deliberates. In a moving robot, computational latency is not a software delay. A machine moving at speed \(\BodySpeed\) that takes a time \(\PrebrakeDelay\) to begin braking covers \(\BodySpeed\,\PrebrakeDelay\) toward an obstacle under unguided momentum. Delay is physical distance.
Mechanical and thermodynamic irreversibility: Physical state transitions admit no software rollback. Once software commands current through an inverter (the power electronics that switch a DC supply into the motor’s phase currents), electromagnetic force accelerates mass, dissipating irreversible Joule heat (\(\PhaseJoulePower = \MotorPhaseRmsCurrent^2 \PhaseResistance\) in each phase winding) and altering mechanical contact states. Kinetic energy (\(\KineticEnergy = \frac{1}{2}\Mass \BodySpeed^2\)) cannot be garbage-collected, and a mechanical impact cannot be undone by restoring a checkpoint. A command that has moved a machine can be answered only by another physical action, which itself consumes time, clearance, and energy.
Single-batch, hard real-time execution: On the running machine, each new action proposal depends on observations shaped by prior motion, so the live loop does not accumulate independent observations into a throughput batch (\(\BatchSize=1\)). Control loops must also meet hard real-time deadlines across several coupled timescales: motor current loops at tens of kilohertz, loops near a kilohertz that check motion and regulate contact force, learned policies renewing at tens of hertz, and slower models interpreting the scene a few times per second. Section 1.7 gives the running machine’s rates. A missed deadline does not degrade user experience; it can destabilize the physical plant.

Losing these privileges forces an architectural response. Deep neural networks are statistical function approximators, vulnerable to distribution shift, sensor noise, and hallucination, so they cannot be granted unmediated authority over physical actuators. Physical AI therefore separates proposal from permission. High-capacity learned models act only as proposers in an unprivileged tier (the Brain). An independent, deterministic permission path (in the Nervous System) checks each proposal against the machine’s physical limits and admits (accepts for execution) only the proposals that pass. It also keeps an executable fallback ready on isolated real-time hardware. The permission path does all of this before any action crosses the causal boundary into the plant (the Body).



Table 1: Three deployment regimes of machine learning systems: The selected arrangements progress from offline advisory prediction to digital agency to physical embodiment. The unit of engineering shifts from advisory prediction to digital tool execution, and finally to irreversible physical action across the causal boundary.

Physical AI did not arrive solely through the scaling of language models. It represents the convergence of two long-standing engineering traditions: robotics and control, which learned to act reliably on a physical world that pushes back, and machine learning, which learned to extract representations from data at scale. Over eighty years, the learned model has moved step by step from the periphery of the machine toward its actuators, and each step shifted what the surrounding systems architecture had to guarantee. That history explains what physical AI inherits from classical control and digital learning, and why its central systems challenge is new.

title: The Causal Boundary
text:
1.2 From Prediction to Action
The acting line begins with feedback. Wiener’s cybernetics described animals and machines alike as systems that measure the result of their own action and use it to correct the next one (Wiener 1948), and control theory soon learned to estimate a moving system’s state from noisy measurements (Kalman 1960). The first industrial robots needed little of this at the level of the task. In 1961 a Unimate arm began stacking hot die-cast parts at General Motors by replaying step-by-step commands stored on a magnetic drum (Computer History Museum 1961). Nothing in that program could notice a person in the arm’s path, so protecting people meant keeping them out of its reach. The machine acted, but it did not perceive, and nothing in it was learned. Robotics and control learning to act and machine learning mastering prediction run as the upper and lower lanes of figure 1 until they merge.

Wiener, Norbert. 1948. Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine. Wiley.

Kalman, Rudolph Emil. 1960. “A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems.” Journal of Basic Engineering 82 (1): 35–45. https://doi.org/10.1115/1.3662552.

Computer History Museum. 1961. 1961: UNIMATE, the First Mass-Produced Industrial Robot, Begins Work at General Motors. Timeline of Computer History.






Figure 1: From prediction to action: Robotics and control (top) learned to act on the physical world, and machine learning (bottom) learned to predict from data; the two lines merge in learned action. The band beneath the time axis shows where the learned output lands in typical deployed systems of each era, from no learned component, to learned perception feeding hand-written planners, to learned motor commands, to pretrained models that propose motion. The time axis widens after 2005.



Shakey, developed at SRI from 1966 through 1972, joined perception to planning (Nilsson 1984). It took camera images and range-finder readings, kept a model of its surroundings, and used a planner called STRIPS to compose sequences of actions that would achieve a stated goal. This organization, later summarized as sense-plan-act (S·P·A), treats acting as the last step of a computation. Shakey moved slowly, and its designers treated its motion as running asynchronously to the programs directing it (Nilsson 1984). The world was assumed to wait while the computer thought. Shakey also carried a detail that anticipates this book’s architecture. When one of its catwhiskers touched an obstacle, the robot stopped by a reflex action beneath the planner.

Nilsson, Nils J. 1984. Shakey the Robot. Technical Note No. 323. Artificial Intelligence Center, SRI International.

↪ The sense-plan-act paradigm, and the failure taxonomy it organizes, is developed in The Sense–Plan–Act Paradigm.

Brooks, Rodney. 1986. “A Robust Layered Control System for a Mobile Robot.” IEEE Journal on Robotics and Automation 2 (1): 14–23.
1 Moravec’s Paradox: Moravec (1988) observed that computers could be made to perform at an adult level on intelligence tests or at checkers far more easily than they could be given a one-year-old’s perception and mobility, and he traced the gap to evolutionary age, since sensorimotor skill was refined over a far longer history than abstract reasoning. For a physical machine the hard part is therefore the part that touches the causal boundary, perceiving a changing world and acting on it before a deadline, which is where learning and this book both concentrate. 
Moravec, Hans. 1988. Mind Children: The Future of Robot and Human Intelligence. Harvard University Press.

Brooks inverted that organization. His subsumption architecture built control from layers of simple, asynchronous behaviors, each coupling sensing to action. Higher layers could suppress the outputs of lower ones, but the lower layers continued to run as higher ones were added (Brooks 1986). A fast layer that keeps working while a slow one is busy or wrong is an ancestor of the permission path this book develops. Neither organization, however, made perception or dexterous motion easy to write by hand, and the planners and behavior layers alike stalled on exactly the skills a toddler has. That difficulty has a name. Moravec’s paradox1 observes that sensorimotor skills people perform with little conscious effort can be difficult to reproduce computationally, which is why learning became attractive for physical tasks.
Learning had already entered the loop. In 1989 ALVINN, a small neural network, mapped camera and laser range images to the direction a vehicle should steer, and followed real roads under some field conditions (Pomerleau 1989). Through the 1990s robotics also made uncertainty explicit. Probabilistic robotics represents what a machine believes about itself and its surroundings as probability distributions, updated as actions and measurements arrive (Thrun et al. 2005). The DARPA Grand Challenge tested these ideas at scale. In the first race, in 2004, no vehicle covered more than a small fraction of the desert course. In 2005 five vehicles finished, and the winner, Stanford’s Stanley, relied predominantly on machine learning and probabilistic reasoning (Thrun et al. 2006). In systems of this kind, learning mostly estimated what the world was like, and hand-written planners and controllers decided what to do. A decade later, the DARPA Robotics Challenge Finals asked robots to work at a simulated disaster site, driving a vehicle, opening a door, turning a valve, and climbing stairs. The organizers deliberately degraded the communications link to the remote human operators, so that each robot had to carry out parts of every task under supervised autonomy rather than direct teleoperation (Krotkov et al. 2017). Even at that stage, a person remained close to the loop.

Deep learning then changed how much a machine could perceive. In 2012 a deep convolutional network trained on GPUs classified ImageNet photographs with error well below the previous state of the art (Krizhevsky et al. 2012), and learned detectors spread into the perception systems of robots and automated vehicles. The architecture around them usually stayed modular, with a learned percept feeding a planner written as rules or as an optimization. The learned outputs were still predictions, yet no person stood between them and the brakes. The Tempe vehicle examined in section 1.8 was a machine of this kind.
Learning reached the actuator itself in the following years. Levine and colleagues trained convolutional networks that mapped raw camera images directly to the torques at a robot’s motors, for tasks such as screwing a cap onto a bottle (Levine et al. 2016). Grasping systems learned from hundreds of thousands of their own attempts, gathered by groups of robot arms working in parallel (Levine et al. 2018; Kalashnikov et al. 2018). Deep reinforcement learning (training a network by trial, error, and a numerical reward) in simulation produced controllers for a legged robot and a dexterous hand that transferred to hardware (Hwangbo et al. 2019; OpenAI et al. 2019). With that step the data changed character. A robot that learns from its own attempts chooses the states it will see, so its training data depends on its own behavior.

Imitation learning, which trains a policy to reproduce recorded demonstrations, made human demonstration a practical route to new manipulation skills, and two ideas shaped the policies now in use. Action chunking predicts a short sequence of future actions from each observation, a design its authors motivated partly by the way a cloned policy’s errors compound over time (Zhao et al. 2023). Diffusion policies generate action sequences by iterative denoising, which lets one policy represent the several different ways a demonstrator might complete the same task (Chi et al. 2025). The learned output had become a short plan of future motion, executed by controllers beneath it.
The latest step changed where learned proposals come from. In digital software systems, foundation models matured as agentic reasoning engines capable of decomposing abstract goals, generating plans, and invoking external tools. Bringing that agentic reasoning into physical embodiment required grounding multimodal representations in spatial geometry, continuous dynamics, and motor coordination. Large multitask datasets collected on many robots prepared the ground (Brohan, Brown, Carbajal, Chebotar, Dabis, et al. 2023; Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al. 2024), and between 2023 and 2025 several groups showed that a model pretrained on web-scale images and text can be fine-tuned to emit robot actions directly. These vision-language-action (VLA) models share one mechanism. A pretrained vision-language backbone encodes the camera images and an instruction, and an action head converts the backbone’s output into motor commands. The head either decodes actions as discrete tokens, the way a language model decodes words (Brohan, Brown, Carbajal, Chebotar, Chen, et al. 2023; Kim et al. 2024), or produces a continuous action chunk, a short sequence of future setpoints from one inference (Black et al. 2024). A backbone with billions of parameters cannot run at a controller’s rate, so recent designs split the work across rates. A slow model interprets the scene, and a fast action model or on-robot decoder emits chunks that controllers execute (Bjorck et al. 2025; Gemini Robotics Team 2025). These systems are dated instances of one step, in which a pretrained general-purpose backbone, rather than a policy trained for one task on one robot, proposes the motion. The sizes and rates their authors report are collected later in State of practice in learned proposers, as of 2026. The running machine adopts the same hierarchy with two proposers: an intent model, the slow vision-language model that reads the scene and chooses the goal, and a chunk policy, the fast learned policy that emits action chunks toward that goal. Their rates are fixed on its machine card (section 1.4.2). Because a general-purpose learned model can now propose motion for a general-purpose machine, deciding which component may permit that motion becomes a design question for every machine that adopts one.

The scale of that transfer from web-scale pretraining is easy to overstate. In the Epoch AI database, the open robot action policies trained on hundreds to thousands of times less compute than the largest language models of their year (figure 2) (Epoch AI 2026). The gap is about 350 times less for a 2024 vision-language-action model and about 7,000 times less for a 2025 open robot foundation model, and only 25 robotics models in the database carry a compute estimate at all. Physical AI is therefore not a smaller copy of the language-model scaling story. Its learned proposers are bounded by what can be collected from machines acting in the world and by what can run on the machine itself, two constraints that Parts I and II of this book treat as first-class.
