The proposal boundary is where all four laws meet in one architecture. Irreversibility requires that every check complete before a command alters the plant, and endogenous data prevents offline training metrics from certifying a proposer in the closed loop. For these reasons, the third law (proposal is not permission) places that check on an independent permission path that the model cannot delay or corrupt. The fourth law (permission must be earned) then confines admitted proposals to the operating conditions that empirical evidence has verified. Scaling up model capacity does not relax these constraints; on the contrary, it intensifies physical pressure on the system. Although general machine learning methods deliver superior performance as compute expands (Sutton 2019), the running mobile machine must supply its onboard compute within a finite electrical and thermal budget. Every additional neural layer, attention head, or diffusion step draws against fixed physical allocations of memory bandwidth, electrical power, and thermal dissipation. Inference latency on the stopping path is travel that braking cannot recover. On the running machine at its drive limit, each millisecond costs 1.5 mm of clearance, as the stopping notebook showed. This compute, thermal, and temporal ceiling forms the physical wall confronting every learned proposer.

Sutton, Richard S. 2019. “The Bitter Lesson.” Incompleteideas.net 43.

↪ The memory-bandwidth and latency bottlenecks confronting onboard learned proposers are developed in The Cost of a Fresh Evaluation.

Finally, rejecting an inadmissible command must have an explicit physical realization. In traditional software, an unhandled exception or failed assertion can simply terminate a thread. On a moving robot, halting a software process leaves physical momentum untouched. A refusal is meaningful only if the execution runtime immediately dispatches an admissible fallback (a dynamic braking maneuver, a compliant hold, or a controlled stop) that the physical body can safely execute within its remaining stopping clearance. Translating the four laws and their runtime mechanisms into an engineered system takes the four parts of this book, each producing records that later parts rely on.

title: The Causal Boundary
text:
1.11 The Architecture of This Book
Moving a learned proposal, such as the running machine’s trajectory to open a warehouse cage door, from an abstract task requirement to safe, justified physical operation requires a disciplined four-stage progression. The engineer must first bound what the hardware plant can physically achieve and characterize what the learned proposer has demonstrated under rigorous testing. The engineer must then build an isolated runtime monitor to intercept live proposals and establish the operational conditions under which continued execution remains justified. Each stage corresponds to one of the four laws. The system of records illustrated in figure 9 formalizes this progression, capturing operating assumptions and empirical evidence so that downstream runtime decisions can inspect and rely on them. Conceptually, these records trace two converging pipelines. One strand establishes offline physical limits and verified competence; the second processes online sensor observations and real-time candidate actions. Both pipelines converge at the permission decision, where the system admits or rejects a proposed trajectory. In From a Better Prediction to Useful Service, this architecture synthesizes both strands to resolve the book’s central challenge of engineering dependable, high-performance physical systems out of unverified learned models and unforgiving mechanical hardware.
A record is a machine-checkable artifact that downstream safety and runtime decisions can verify and trust. The initial stopping calculation (notebook 1.1) already sketches the first record in the chain: a limit record, with the six elements the reader guide introduces (nominal value, operating conditions, uncertainty, margin, runtime detector, and provenance). Its nominal value is the derived stopping distance under stated operating conditions of loaded payload mass, dry concrete, a stationary obstacle, and constant approach speed. Because those inputs are illustrative scalars rather than calibrated distributions, however, its uncertainty remains unquantified. The apparent buffer between the obstacle and the machine is therefore only an arithmetic difference between provisional figures rather than a verified safety margin. The calculation also lacks a runtime detector (no sensor yet monitors whether floor traction drops or cargo shifts outside the assumed envelope, The six elements of a limit record), and its provenance rests on baseline assumptions rather than calibrated hardware logs. An ungrounded calculation becomes operational engineering evidence only when all six fields are populated and backed by empirical data. Every numbered box across the four part bands in figure 9 establishes a machine-checkable record of this rigor for a distinct architectural decision.






Figure 9: The spine of the book: Each part is led by one law, and each chapter of Parts I to IV except The Cognitive Brain (Chapter 3) produces a record that a later one consumes. What the plant can do and what the proposer has shown it can do run as one strand, what the proposer proposes now as another, and the two meet at the permission decision.



Part I, The Machine Anatomy, translates physical irreversibility into rigid architectural limits. The Physical Body profiles the mechanical plant to quantify its physical budgets (measurement freshness, stopping distance, deliverable torque, winding heat, and supply voltage). The Cognitive Brain measures the throughput and inference latency of the learned proposer to determine what it can deliver before deadlines expire. The Nervous System links compute to the actuators across deterministic buses, structuring a permission path whose timing guarantees derive from the plant’s stopping requirements. Together, the limit record and handoff record make every physical and temporal assumption explicit. Part II, Teaching the Machine, confronts the reality that physical actions continuously alter future sensor observations. Physical Data, Policy Training, and Closed-Loop Evaluation build the evidentiary chain required to collect demonstrations, train control policies, and bound policy performance to a declared operational design domain. Across this pipeline, the provenance record, policy manifest, and evaluation record document both the empirical competence demonstrated by the model and the operational boundaries where its statistical guarantees break down.
Part III, Running the Machine, enforces at runtime the separation between proposing an action and permitting it to execute. From Sensor Perception through Workload Placement, the chapters trace candidate commands through the online runtime. They qualify sensor measurements in observation contracts and maintain state estimates in a belief record. They bound a goal with an intent lease (a time-limited grant of a target, never of a path, and distinct from the chunk lease that bounds one motion segment). They check candidate trajectories against real-time physical constraints before admission and dispatch, then test whether the hardware keeps the permission path independent. Part IV, Governing the Machine, enforces the principle that permission must be earned. Supervisory Intervention, Adversarial Verification, and Deployment Release govern how authority transfers between the machine and a human operator, how fault injection tests whether protective responses hold, and how deployment decisions are assembled into release manifests. Responsible Physical AI then names who answers for each decision behind an admitted action. It also tests whether each human role the design relies on is one a person can perform, and it counts the people who bear the machine’s risk and appear in its records. Finally, Engineering Physical AI brings the framework to bear on an unfamiliar machine, synthesizing what an engineering team can construct and formally justify while identifying the residual risks that require further mitigation. Across these parts, the warehouse mobile manipulator introduced here provides a single concrete machine on which to ground each architectural decision. Its records render design assumptions fully inspectable, though an engineer must remember that assembling a record documents an explicit claim rather than guaranteeing its physical truth. The system record register in The record register catalogs all sixteen records, noting their producing chapters and the specific invariants they bind, while the machine card in section 1.4.2 specifies the foundational physical parameters of the robot itself. Together, this four-stage route forms a repeatable discipline for making learned behavior dependable in physical space, guarding against the common misconceptions that arise when digital assumptions are carried across the causal boundary.

title: The Causal Boundary
text:
1.12 Fallacies and Pitfalls
The misconceptions that follow arise when assumptions from pure software engineering, statistical learning, or classical control theory are imported into embodied machines. In digital systems, an erroneous state can typically be trapped, rolled back, or restarted. Across the causal boundary, however, software outputs become physical forces that alter the world irrevocably. Preventing physical harm requires hard deterministic guarantees that learning objectives, human operators, and asynchronous recovery routines cannot provide on their own.

Fallacy: Safety constraints can be trained into the policy.
Engineering teams often attempt to enforce physical safety by adding penalty terms, barrier penalties, or negative rewards to the training objective. While penalty shaping suppresses undesirable actions over the training distribution, it provides no mathematical guarantee on the actions emitted during deployment. Deep neural networks remain uncalibrated function approximators when exposed to out-of-distribution inputs, sensor degradation, or novel environmental dynamics. A statistical loss function optimizes expected performance, but safety requires hard invariants that hold on every control cycle. For this reason, deterministic safety enforcement must sit downstream of the policy, operating as an independent permission path that filters proposed commands before they reach actuator driver registers, exactly where the third law places the boundary gate.


Pitfall: Treating human supervisory intervention as instantaneous in shared-autonomy systems.
In shared-autonomy designs, such as a robotic surgical tool providing haptic guidance from a learned anatomical model, system designers sometimes treat the human operator as a failsafe catch-all. This assumption ignores the physiological limits of human reaction time, which ranges between 150 ms and 250 ms for simple tactile or visual reflexes and grows under cognitive load. Once console video and a handshake are added, the running machine’s card budgets an in-loop takeover at 605 ms. Over that interval, an actuator running on a 1 kHz control loop can execute hundreds of unchecked cycles, generating enough force to tear soft tissue or damage a mechanical workpiece before the operator can intervene. Delegating authority to a human supervisor does not eliminate the machine’s capacity for harm during the supervisory lag. The permission path must enforce local force, velocity, and displacement envelopes autonomously, preserving the established physical envelopes under their operating assumptions without relying on timely human overrides.


Pitfall: Assuming software latency merely degrades performance gracefully.
In purely digital systems, inference latency or scheduler jitter increases response time or degrades service quality. In physical systems, timing is a functional correctness requirement. If a learned policy stalls, whether from accelerator kernel contention, memory allocation pauses, or network serialization delays, allowing its previous command to persist across subsequent control cycles turns stale intent into physical danger. For example, a mobile manipulator that repeats its last forward-velocity command during a 100 ms inference hiccup can collide with an unmapped obstacle. Actuation commands must therefore carry bounded temporal validity, enforced by hardware or real-time software watchdogs. When that validity window (the chunk lease of the stopping budget) expires without a verified update, the low-level controller must begin a fallback within its established response budget. The selected stop or hold must remain feasible for the current mechanism, state, and surviving resources.


Fallacy: Assuming physical actuation is reversible through subsequent software compensation.
Transactional software architectures rely on rollbacks and compensation routines to undo erroneous operations. In embodied systems, thermodynamics and materials science break this equivalence. If a robotic arm applies excessive torque to a workpiece, issuing a reverse motor command cannot unbend plastically deformed metal, repair fractured composite, or recover the electrical energy dissipated as heat in the motor windings (\(\MotorPhaseRmsCurrent^2 \PhaseResistance\)). Anomaly detection routines that react after physical contact can only truncate ongoing damage; they cannot undo the mechanical work already transferred across the causal boundary. Preventive verification, such as checking proposed trajectories against workspace boundaries, torque limits, and kinetic energy caps before dispatch, must serve as the primary defense. Reactive recovery strategies remain necessary for unexpected disturbances, but they function as a secondary backstop rather than a substitute for preventive enforcement.

title: The Causal Boundary
text:
1.13 Summary
Physical AI converges two historically distinct engineering disciplines: classical robotics and modern machine learning. As learned models move progressively closer to direct actuator control, the boundary between digital computation and physical reality sharpens at the causal boundary, the interface where an admitted command becomes an irreversible physical effect. In purely software systems, state rollbacks and retries can recover from algorithmic faults; in the physical world, software cannot undo kinetic energy, momentum, or impact. Safe recovery requires an executable, physically feasible countermeasure.
Physical dynamics also do not pause while neural networks compute. Because a machine continues to travel during sensing and processing delays, safety requires deterministic admission checks upstream of any consequential actuation. As the warehouse mobile manipulator’s stopping budget and the Tempe collision show, prediction quality offers no protection once response delay has spent the clearance. The architecture resolves this tension by separating proposal from permission and giving an independent, bounded-latency permission path the authority to refuse. Four laws, one physical and three design principles, organize the framework the rest of the book develops, while the elementary stopping budget and its crossover speed form this chapter’s quantitative core (table 4).



Table 4: Key equations of the causal boundary: The elementary stopping budget and its crossover speed, with the place each is derived.










Equation
What it bounds or decides
Derived




\(\StoppingDistance = \SpeedAtDetection\PrebrakeDelay + \dfrac{\SpeedAtDetection^2}{2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration} \le \ClearDistance\)
Whether a moving machine can stop within its observed clearance: distance traveled during response delay plus braking distance, prior to allowances added in later chapters
equation 1


\(\StoppingCrossoverSpeed = 2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration\PrebrakeDelay\)
The crossover speed at which delay distance equals braking distance; below \(\StoppingCrossoverSpeed\), delay travel is larger, while above it, braking travel is larger
From equation 1, section 1.4.3







Key Takeaways: Engineering across the causal boundary

Useful behavior requires an integrated machine: Physical AI combines learned decision-making, physical dynamics, and delegated mechanical authority. Delivering reliable autonomous operation requires co-designing task competence with physical body limits, real-time compute runtimes, and the operational evidence supporting deployment.
Response delay consumes physical margin: The elementary stopping budget \(\StoppingDistance = \SpeedAtDetection\PrebrakeDelay + \SpeedAtDetection^2/(2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration) \le \ClearDistance\) partitions stopping distance into latency-induced travel and mechanical braking. Below the crossover speed \(\StoppingCrossoverSpeed = 2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration\PrebrakeDelay\), response delay dominates stopping distance; above \(\StoppingCrossoverSpeed\), braking deceleration dominates. For the warehouse mobile manipulator at its drive limit, pre-braking travel adds 35.6 percent to braking distance. The decisive delay belongs to whichever path triggers the protective response, which can operate independently of the learned proposer’s inference time.
Proposal and permission serve distinct architectural roles: The learned proposer (the Brain) generates goal-directed actions, while an independent permission path admits, modifies, or rejects them before they cross the causal boundary. Safety enforcement relies on validated sensor inputs, physical kinematic envelopes, strict real-time deadlines, and verifiable fallback maneuvers.
Evidence governs safe operation and systematic refinement: Four laws structure this book. Irreversibility is a physical law; the other three (endogenous data, proposal is not permission, and permission must be earned) are design principles that translate covariate shift, runtime assurance, and the assurance case into systems practice. Together they link physical hardware, embodied learning, real-time execution, and operational governance, establishing verified service within defined operational envelopes while identifying the targeted evaluations needed to expand them.



Before judging whether a proposed action is right, an engineer should establish what physical response would remain if the proposal were wrong, stale, or never arrived, and whether the machine still holds the clearance, the time, and the authority to carry that response out. A design that cannot answer from its own measured limits has handed safety to prediction quality, and the stopping budget showed that prediction quality cannot buy back clearance once delay has spent it. The answer therefore starts from what the plant can do under stated conditions, never from what the model believes.

title: The Causal Boundary
text:
1.14 Historical Perspective and Further Reading
In physical artificial intelligence, moving learned models directly into the actuation loop creates severe timing and safety hazards. The engineering principles that resolve these challenges originate in embedded systems, real-time control, and safety engineering. General-purpose computing treats execution time as a mere performance optimization, assuming that correctness depends solely on logical input-output relationships. Cyber-physical systems theory overturned this assumption, holding that physical dynamics and computational processes must be modeled jointly because a command dispatched at the wrong time is physically incorrect (Lee 2008). This insight forms the foundation of the causal boundary. Similarly, separating command proposal from execution permission stems from runtime assurance architectures. The Simplex architecture demonstrated that an industrial control system could safely run an unverified, high-performance controller if paired with a certified baseline controller and deterministic switching logic capable of taking back the plant before safety boundaries were violated (Seto et al. 1998; Sha 2001). Modern safety filters in embodied machine learning generalize this design, validating neural network proposals against mathematical certificates of safe states (control barrier functions or reachability envelopes, which Safety Enforcement develops) before granting actuator permission (Hsu et al. 2024).

Seto, Danbing, Bruce Krogh, Lui Sha, and Alongkrit Chutinan. 1998. “The Simplex Architecture for Safe Online Control System Upgrades.” Proceedings of the 1998 American Control Conference (ACC) 6: 3504–8. https://doi.org/10.1109/ACC.1998.703255.

Hsu, Kai-Chieh, Haimin Hu, and Jaime F. Fisac. 2024. “The Safety Filter: A Unified View of Safety-Critical Control in Autonomous Systems.” Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems 7: 47–72. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-control-071723-102940.

Kelly, Timothy Patrick. 1998. “Arguing Safety: A Systematic Approach to Managing Safety Cases.” PhD thesis, Department of Computer Science, University of York.
Many foundational safety principles in physical systems emerged from forensic investigations of catastrophic failures. The Therac-25 radiation therapy disasters demonstrated the fatal peril of replacing mechanical interlocks with software routines (Leveson and Turner 1993). When race conditions bypassed software checks, the machine administered lethal radiation overdoses, proving that software reliability does not imply system safety. Systems-theoretic safety subsequently recast accidents not as isolated component breakdowns, but as failures of the overall control structure to enforce safety constraints on the interactions among components, feedback loops, and human operators (Leveson 2011). This shift led directly to the assurance case, a structured argument demonstrating that concrete evidence satisfies defined safety claims within explicit operating environments (Kelly 1998). The UL 4600 standard adopted this structure as its central framework for autonomous products (UL Standards & Engagement 2023), abandoning arbitrary road-testing mileage in favor of verifiable, claim-based arguments. Public accident records, particularly the National Transportation Safety Board investigation of the 2018 Tempe autonomous vehicle collision (National Transportation Safety Board 2019), remain the field’s most complete documentation of how safety arguments unravel when classification changes, a response delay chosen in software, and reliance on a human fallback interact in the field.

Cyber-physical systems (Lee 2008). Lee articulates why classical computing abstractions fail when computation interacts with physical processes. General-purpose computer architectures deliberately abstract away time, treating execution speed as a performance consideration rather than a correctness specification. Lee demonstrates that for physical interactions, the timing of an actuation command is inseparable from its physical meaning, providing the conceptual foundation for treating the causal boundary as an explicit systems interface.
Runtime assurance (Sha 2001). Sha’s paper on the Simplex architecture is the place to see how the switching logic decides when to take the plant back from the unverified controller, and why that logic must be simpler than what it supervises. It is the pattern behind this book’s separation of proposal from permission.
Therac-25 (Leveson and Turner 1993). Leveson and Turner’s forensic analysis traces the specific race conditions and the development and reporting practices that let the overdoses recur, detail the summary above omits. It remains the essential case study in why protective functions need justification independent of the software they supervise.
Systems-theoretic safety (Leveson 2011). Leveson introduces the STAMP accident model, reframing safety as a continuous control problem rather than a collection of component failure probabilities. Accidents occur when the control structure fails to enforce safety constraints across component interactions, sensor delays, and feedback loops. This text provides the theoretical basis for enforcing safety invariants as dynamic runtime constraints rather than static design assumptions.
The Tempe investigation (National Transportation Safety Board 2019). The National Transportation Safety Board report on the fatal 2018 Tempe autonomous vehicle crash offers the most thorough empirical record of an embodied AI safety failure. The report details how classification changes that discarded tracking history, a one-second action suppression meant to limit responses to false alarms, the separate deactivation of the vehicle’s factory emergency braking over possible radar interference, and reliance on an operator whose attention nothing monitored combined in the collision. The event timeline and sensor telemetry provide vital reading for anyone building real-time perception-action loops.


Lee, Edward A. 2008. “Cyber Physical Systems: Design Challenges.” Proceedings of the 11th IEEE International Symposium on Object and Component-Oriented Real-Time Distributed Computing (ISORC), 363–69. https://doi.org/10.1109/ISORC.2008.25.

Sha, Lui. 2001. “Using Simplicity to Control Complexity.” IEEE Software 18 (4): 20–28.

Leveson, Nancy G., and Clark S. Turner. 1993. “An Investigation of the Therac-25 Accidents.” Computer 26 (7): 18–41.

Leveson, Nancy. 2011. Engineering a Safer World: Systems Thinking Applied to Safety. MIT Press.

What’s Next: From the causal boundary to physical limitsA permission decision needs a physical limit against which to judge the proposed action. The Physical Body begins Part I with the five budgets the permission path must check before it commits torque (measurement freshness, stopping distance, deliverable torque, winding heat, and supply voltage) and asks which binds first for a given maneuver, under what stress, and on what evidence. Each budget ends as a limit record, the six-element form this chapter sketched from its stopping calculation. The Cognitive Brain then examines the learned proposer’s capabilities and timing, and The Nervous System uses both sets of constraints to design the handoff and independent permission path. The progression starts with what the machine can sustain and ends with how computation may safely request it.

title: The Physical Body
text:
Purpose



Physical AI stack focus for this chapter.
Why can a correctly chosen action still demand more than the machine’s body can deliver?
A mobile manipulator can recognize an obstacle correctly and still strike it if its body cannot stop within the remaining distance. The same machine can hold a payload without moving while its motor windings overheat, or lose its controller when a sudden demand for current pulls the supply voltage too low. These failures arise from limits that prediction accuracy alone cannot reveal. Physical AI engineering requires connecting a proposed action to the motion, heat, and electrical demand it creates, then establishing which limit the assembled machine reaches first. Measurements must also establish the conditions under which those limits hold, because a change in payload, floor surface, cooling, or battery state changes what the machine can deliver. The body’s limits therefore govern what the permission path may admit before a command crosses the causal boundary and produces irreversible physical work.


Learning Objectives

Calculate observation freshness limits from measurement age and the machine’s allowable motion
Calculate stopping distance and the admissible speed ceiling from pre-brake delay, credible deceleration, and clearance overheads
Evaluate actuator and transmission choices against response limits, reflected inertia, and mechanical impedance
Estimate sustainable motor duty cycles from heat generation, cooling, and operating conditions
Budget electrical supply margins for simultaneous actuation, computation, and regenerative braking
Specify the elements of a limit record that states a measured limit’s conditions, uncertainty, margin, runtime detector, and evidence category
Evaluate maneuver-specific binding budgets from qualified evidence and justify holding up the permission supply through covered faults

title: The Physical Body
text:
2.1 The Five Physical Budgets
Every action a learned model proposes ultimately manifests as electrical current flowing through a motor winding, and from that instant physics governs execution. Machine learning practice rarely contends with this transition. Policies trained in simulation typically interact with idealized plants where commanded torque appears instantaneously, heat never accumulates in windings, and direct current (DC) bus voltages never sag under load. A physical machine honors none of these simplifications. The physical body is the coupled assembly of actuators, mechanical transmissions, structural linkages, power electronics, and sensors that translates digital commands into mechanical motion. Its physical dynamics bound what even a mathematically optimal policy can achieve. An emergency brake command requires finite time to develop mechanical retarding force and clearance distance to dissipate kinetic energy. Similarly, commanding a manipulator to hold a heavy payload motionless draws continuous phase current, dissipating resistive heat into the stator even though the joint does zero mechanical work.
The proposal boundary in The Machine in Five Levels assigns the permission path responsibility for admitting action, and the body provides the concrete physical envelopes that make that gating decision meaningful. Before committing a command to hardware registers, the permission path must evaluate five physical budgets. It must confirm that the sensor observation remains fresh, that the moving machine can stop within available clearance, that the actuator can deliver the required torque trajectory, that the winding can tolerate the resulting thermal rise, and that the electrical bus can support the transient current demand. These mechanisms form a direct causal chain. Sensor and pipeline latencies consume allowable stopping distance. Arresting momentum demands delivered actuator torque. Generating that torque dissipates heat in motor coils and pulls current from a shared power rail. For any given maneuver, the governing systems question is which of these physical budgets binds first, under what operational stress, and on what empirical evidence.

Measurement freshness (\(\ObservationAge\)): The observation must remain valid until the mechanical plant responds. Latency accumulated across sensor exposure, data transport, neural inference, and low-level drive dispatch consumes allowable tracking margins as the physical world continues to move.
Kinetic momentum (\(\KineticEnergy, \LinearMomentum\)): A moving machine carries kinetic energy (\(\KineticEnergy = \frac{1}{2} \Mass \BodySpeed^2\)) and linear or angular momentum (\(\LinearMomentum = \Mass \BodySpeed\)). Bringing the plant to rest demands applying retarding force over finite distance and time; safe operating velocity must therefore preserve a stopping envelope well within available physical clearance.
Actuator bandwidth and reflected inertia (\(\GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia\)): Winding inductance and supply voltage limit the rate at which torque can change. A gearhead with reduction ratio \(\GearReductionRatio\) multiplies delivered torque by \(\GearReductionRatio\), but it also scales the motor rotor’s inertia \(\RotorInertia\) by \(\GearReductionRatio^2\) as seen at the joint output (section 2.4.3), which constrains instantaneous acceleration.
Thermal capacity (\(\EstimatedWindingTemperature\)): Resistive losses (\(\WindingLossPower = \TorqueProducingCurrent^2 \EffectiveLossResistance\), with \(\EffectiveLossResistance\) the winding’s effective loss resistance) deposit thermal energy directly into the stator windings and inverter switching stages. Heat dissipation limits sustained continuous torque, while the thermal mass of the coils constrains the magnitude, duration, and repetition rate of transient torque bursts.
Electrical power integrity (\(\DcRailVoltage\)): Onboard compute clusters and motor inverters draw from a shared DC power rail. Peak motor accelerations must not drag the bus voltage below digital logic thresholds, while regenerative braking must provide an electrical sink so returned kinetic energy does not overvoltage the bus.

Under the simultaneous admission invariant, motion permission requires a non-negative margin in every budget before the permission path commits torque to hardware registers. Each margin must be checked in its own units; time, distance, torque, temperature, and voltage are separate constraints, not interchangeable quantities: \[\begin{aligned}
\ObservationAge &\le \TelemetryFreshnessBound, \\
\StoppingDistance &\le \ClearDistance, \\
|\CommandedJointTorque| &\le \OutputTorqueCeiling, \\
\EstimatedWindingTemperature &\le \WindingTemperatureLimit, \\
\MinimumRailVoltage &\ge \ConverterLockoutVoltage.
\end{aligned}\] Here \(\CommandedJointTorque\) is requested torque and \(\OutputTorqueCeiling\) is the maximum deliverable output torque under current electrical and thermal conditions. The estimated winding temperature \(\EstimatedWindingTemperature\) must remain below its limit, while the lowest rail voltage \(\MinimumRailVoltage\) must remain above the undervoltage-lockout threshold \(\ConverterLockoutVoltage\) at which the supply regulator shuts down. The fifth line checks only undervoltage. Permission must also require regenerative braking to stay below the qualified upper operating-voltage limit of the supplied components, with an available absorption or dissipation path. Two lines state their budgets in derived form. The kinetic budget appears as the stopping distance it demands, \(\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance\). The actuator line checks only torque magnitude, because the slew-rate limit that winding inductance and reflected inertia impose enters the stopping line instead, through the brake-onset term of the pre-brake delay \(\PrebrakeDelay\). All five inequalities must hold simultaneously. A surplus in four budgets cannot compensate for a deficit in the fifth. A fresh observation cannot prevent a stop from overrunning if kinetic energy exceeds available clearance, and abundant battery energy cannot prevent an actuator from burning out if thermal dissipation limits are violated.

Systems Perspective 2.1: Why physical limits bound physical AI architectureThe permission path requires concrete bounds on physical behavior, not abstract software promises. Accepting a torque command does not guarantee that the inverter can deliver the requested current against the back electromotive force (back-EMF) the spinning motor induces in its own windings, nor does cutting motor power guarantee that friction will arrest the plant before it breaches a clearance zone. The five physical budgets bridge this gap, tying software proposals to verifiable, empirical responses under declared operating conditions.


The warehouse mobile manipulator that this book follows draws on all five. Loaded to at most 368 kg and moving at its 1.5 m/s drive limit (illustrative; see the Reader Guide), it carries 414 J of kinetic energy through aisles it shares with people. Each budget establishes an empirical operating boundary on the assembled machine under declared thermal and electrical stress. Each ends the chapter as a limit record, the six-element record that The Architecture of This Book sketched from the stopping notebook: a value, the conditions under which it holds, its uncertainty, the margin defended, a runtime detector, and the provenance of its evidence. The first budget is the age of the measurement on which every command rests, which runs from physical transduction, well before any software process receives the raw sensor data.

title: The Physical Body
text:
2.2 Measurement Freshness
Software benchmarks in machine learning frequently report latency as isolated accelerator execution time, for example 18.5 ms for the vision backbone of the arm’s wrist-camera grasp path on an edge neural processing unit (NPU), a different pipeline from the navigation backbone that the stopping budget of Delay consumes stopping clearance charges. This narrow focus fosters the illusion of an agile 54.1 Hz control loop. In physical AI systems, however, that compute kernel represents only one intermediate segment in an end-to-end silicon-to-plant dataflow pipeline. A sensor measurement begins decaying the moment physical transduction occurs; what governs physical performance is its total age when torque actually appears at the actuator joint. That physical age spans the entire interval from the moment photons strike a photodiode array, magnetic flux sweeps past a Hall sensor, or strain deflects a piezoresistor to the moment motor inverter switches build stator magnetic flux that alters link acceleration. If a perception policy evaluates an obstacle bounding box in 18.5 ms, while exposure integration, sensor readout, Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe) transport, kernel scheduling, fieldbus dispatch, and motor current rise consume an additional 16.5 ms at the median, the true physical age of the observation when the joint accelerates is 35 ms. The distribution tail extends farther still.
Throughout that capture-to-onset window, the physical environment continues to evolve unobserved. In distributed data systems, read-after-write consistency windows govern whether a client observes stale or linearized state. In physical AI, the physical plant acts as an autonomous, unpausable concurrent writer: spatial position \(\CartesianPosition(\TimeInstant)\) evolves along continuous trajectories at velocity \(\Velocity(\TimeInstant)\). An observation age \(\ObservationAge\) converts directly into unobserved physical displacement \(\FiniteChange \CartesianPosition \approx \int_0^{\ObservationAge} \Velocity(\TimeInstant)\,d\TimeInstant\). High-speed machines inevitably act on historical state.
The rate of world-state change dictates how long a measurement remains valid before acting on it introduces intolerable error. Let \(\PositionErrorCeiling\) denote the maximum acceptable error in a tracked state, such as a joint angle or the position of a part on a conveyor, and let \(\SpeedBound\) denote the fastest credible velocity at which that state can evolve. The freshness deadline \(\TelemetryFreshnessBound\) is the upper bound on measurement age before a control action based on that measurement becomes invalid, defined by the inequality \[\TelemetryFreshnessBound \le \frac{\PositionErrorCeiling}{\SpeedBound} \tag{1}\]

Definition 2.1: Freshness deadline
Freshness deadline (\(\TelemetryFreshnessBound\)) is the largest age, counted from the capture of a measurement to the onset of the actuator’s response, that the measurement of a moving target may reach before the target’s motion alone spends the allowable position error \(\PositionErrorCeiling\) (equation 1).

Significance: It converts a spatial tolerance into a time budget that every stage from exposure to torque onset must share. A 12 mm tolerance on a target moving at 0.20 m/s leaves 60 ms for sensing, inference, transport, and current rise together.
Distinction: Unlike an inference-latency budget, which times one stage, the deadline bounds the age at onset; unlike a control-loop period, it is set by the target’s speed and the tolerance rather than by the loop rate. When the machine moves toward a stationary obstacle instead, the same age becomes the first term of the pre-brake delay \(\PrebrakeDelay\) and is paid as blind travel \(\SpeedAtDetection\,\PrebrakeDelay\) in the stopping distance.
Common pitfall: Treating the deadline as a property of the sensor or the model. It changes whenever the target moves faster or the tolerance shrinks, so a pipeline qualified on a slow conveyor can miss on a faster one without any change in its own timing.





↪ The same deadline applied to a stored belief, which lapses once its region falls out of view, is developed in Forward State Propagation and Occlusion Decay.
The running machine meets this bound at its pick station, where the arm grasps a mug from a moving conveyor. The belt carries the mug at speeds up to \(\ConveyorSpeed =\) 0.20 m/s, and the gripper mechanism tolerates \(\PositionalTaskTolerance =\) 15 mm of position error. Initial handle-pose estimation already consumes \(\InitialTrackingError =\) 3 mm of this margin. Consequently, the mug’s physical motion may spend at most \(\PositionErrorCeiling = \PositionalTaskTolerance - \InitialTrackingError =\) 12 mm, with \(\SpeedBound = \ConveyorSpeed\). Notebook 2.1 evaluates this resulting deadline against the ages an integrated camera-to-joint pipeline delivers in practice. The deadline governs any target that moves while its observation ages. For moving workpieces, it limits motion-induced tracking drift under bounded relative velocity and valid initial observations. Sensing and state-estimation noise consume separate slices of the tolerance budget, just as \(\InitialTrackingError\) does here. Conversely, when the robot approaches a stationary obstacle, such as a person standing in a warehouse aisle, the target does not move. Instead, the mobile base drives toward the person during the latency interval. Observation age then converts directly into unguided vehicular travel before braking begins, which section 2.3 charges against the kinetic stopping envelope.

2.2.1 Transduction physics, quantization noise, and Nyquist limits
If a 12-bit magnetic encoder jumps by a single count between two 1 ms servo ticks, backward differencing reports a sudden 88°/s velocity spike. If an unshielded cooling fan vibrates an inertial unit above half its sampling rate, the vibration folds into the low-frequency band and looks like chassis acceleration. Every sensor trades error tolerance against time: it must resolve the physical state of interest, and the analog filtering, sampling, or serial scanning needed to extract a clean signal must fit inside the freshness deadline. Four physical mechanisms set this trade:

Optical Encoders and Velocity Quantization Noise: An encoder measures joint position in discrete angular increments. An \(\EncoderBitCount\)-bit encoder discretizes the continuous \(2\pi\text{ rad}\) circle into an angular resolution of \(\QuantizationStep \EncoderAngle = \frac{2\pi}{2^\EncoderBitCount}\). For an 18-bit absolute optical encoder, \(\QuantizationStep \EncoderAngle \approx 2.4 \times 10^{-5}\text{ rad}\) (\(0.0014^\circ\)); for a 12-bit magnetic encoder, \(\QuantizationStep \EncoderAngle \approx 1.53 \times 10^{-3}\text{ rad}\) (\(0.088^\circ\)). Feedback controllers, which compute each command from the measured difference between the desired and the actual state, estimate joint velocity from successive position samples across a discrete control cycle \(\FiniteChange \TimeInstant\): \[{\EncoderVelocityEstimate{}}_{k} \approx \frac{{\EncoderAngle}_{k} - {\EncoderAngle}_{k-1}}{\FiniteChange \TimeInstant}\] Backward differencing acts as an effective high-pass filter, scaling high-frequency position fluctuations by \(1/\FiniteChange \TimeInstant\). Under an idealized model where successive quantization errors are independent and uniformly distributed across one encoder count, each sample has variance \((\QuantizationStep\EncoderAngle)^2/12\). Differencing two independent samples sums their variances to \((\QuantizationStep\EncoderAngle)^2/6\), yielding a velocity-error standard deviation of \(\EncoderVelocityNoise = \frac{\QuantizationStep\EncoderAngle}{\sqrt{6}\,\FiniteChange \TimeInstant}\). At a \(1\text{ kHz}\) servo update rate (\(\FiniteChange \TimeInstant = 1\text{ ms}\)), a single-count jump on a 12-bit encoder (\(1.53\text{ mrad}\)) registers as an abrupt velocity spike of \(1.53\text{ rad/s}\) (\(88^\circ/\text{s}\)). If routed directly into velocity feedback loops or neural policy state inputs, these discrete impulses cause severe torque chatter and excite mechanical resonances. Downstream low-pass filters or state observers (models that infer a quantity such as velocity from a stream of measurements) smooth this quantization noise, but filter group delay introduces phase lag, consuming milliseconds of the freshness budget.
Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) and Nyquist Aliasing: An inertial measurement unit measures linear acceleration and angular velocity. Sampling must isolate macroscopic body dynamics from high-frequency structural vibration. Under the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem (Nyquist 1928; Shannon 1949), continuous signals require a sampling frequency strictly greater than twice their highest spectral component (\(\SamplingRate > 2 \HighestSignalFrequency\)). Mechanical sources, including gear mesh harmonics, cooling fans, and motor inverter switching, generate vibrations reaching kilohertz frequencies. Without adequate analog anti-aliasing filters before the analog-to-digital converter (ADC), structural vibrations above the Nyquist frequency fold back into baseband frequencies (\(1\text{--}20\text{ Hz}\)). The state estimator, which combines sensor readings into an estimate of the machine’s motion, cannot distinguish these aliased artifacts from genuine chassis acceleration, introducing cumulative drift into dead-reckoning integrations. Raising downstream software loop rates cannot reconstruct information already corrupted at the sensor hardware interface.
Tactile Sensor Arrays and Scanning Bandwidth: Tactile arrays measure contact pressure across a robot gripper using discrete sensing elements called taxels. To minimize cabling across robotic wrists, hardware architectures multiplex taxels across shared row and column lines. Scanning these elements sequentially forces an entire frame to span the multiplexing period. This serial scan time adds directly to the measurement age and limits the bandwidth for detecting rapid contact events, such as the onset of localized slip. Increasing the taxel density without scaling the underlying ADC readout rate produces older tactile observations.
Cameras and Rolling-Shutter Readout: A rolling-shutter CMOS camera exposes and transfers pixel rows sequentially, so a single frame spans its entire readout duration. Image timestamps must therefore anchor to a defined reference, such as the exposure midpoint of a designated row, rather than the frame-arrival interrupt.

Across all four mechanisms, a measurement begins aging at physical transduction, milliseconds before any software driver receives a buffer. Bounding how much of the freshness deadline remains at actuation therefore requires tracing the signal across every stage between transduction and motor current.


↪ Rolling-shutter distortion on the navigation camera, and its compensation before images enter the state estimator, is developed in Capture Physics and Calibration.


2.2.2 The end-to-end sense-to-actuation latency pipeline
A measurement’s physical age begins at capture, the moment of physical transduction, rather than when an operating system process first receives the data buffer. Three subsequent boundary events demarcate the pipeline from transduction to mechanical work. Dispatch is when perception publishes dated perceptual evidence to the action proposer. Admission is when the real-time permission path validates and accepts a proposal built using that evidence. Onset is when electrical current in the motor stator windings begins driving physical acceleration at the joint. The four events recur throughout the book, and The capture-to-brake-onset timing budget of the running machine later budgets the intervals between them for the running machine. For the freshness deadline, capture and onset form the bounding endpoints, and the deadline limits the cumulative delay between them.
An illustrative camera-to-joint pipeline reveals how latency compounds across physical and digital boundaries (table 1). Between capture and dispatch, the CMOS sensor integrates exposure and reads out raw scanlines over MIPI CSI-2.1 Direct memory access (DMA) transfers the frame into host memory, and the vision backbone executes. In this representative architecture, the policy network executes in the same inference pass as the backbone, spanning the dispatch boundary. Between dispatch and admission, inter-process communication (IPC) transmits the proposed trajectory to the safety microcontroller, a dedicated real-time processor that executes the deterministic permission path. Between admission and onset, an EtherCAT fieldbus2 delivers target setpoints to individual motor drives, where power-inverter gate drivers switch to ramp up stator current. Neural inference occupies one of the eight stages. Under memory bus contention and scheduling delays, the peripheral system stages expand the latency tail substantially more than the neural network execution itself.
1 MIPI CSI-2 (Camera Serial Interface 2): The Mobile Industry Processor Interface camera link carries raw frames from the image sensor to the system-on-chip and marks the start and end of each frame with short packets. Latching a hardware timestamp on the frame-start packet ties the frame to a fixed offset from its exposure rather than to the moment software first sees it, which is what lets transduction time, not arrival time, anchor the age budget.2 EtherCAT: An industrial Ethernet fieldbus in which one frame passes through every drive on the segment, each node reading and writing its own slice of the frame as it passes. Frame length and node count, not contention for the wire, fix the cycle time, which is why the fieldbus row of table 1 has equal \(\text{p50}\) and \(\text{p99}\). Comparing bus occupancy on CAN FD and EtherCAT sizes that cycle for the running machine.3 Quantile Convolution: In general, the quantile of a sum of delays does not equal the sum of their individual quantiles (\(\LatencyQuantileFunction(\UpstreamStageLatency + \DownstreamStageLatency) \ne \LatencyQuantileFunction(\UpstreamStageLatency) + \LatencyQuantileFunction(\DownstreamStageLatency)\)). Even when stages are independent, adding their \(\text{p99}\) values is not a worst-case bound, and shared buses and queues correlate the stages so that the end-to-end tail must be measured across the whole pipeline.Systems engineers sometimes estimate worst-case pipeline latency by summing the 99th-percentile (\(\text{p99}\)) latencies of individual stages. However, the percentile of a sum does not equal the sum of the percentiles.3 In embedded system-on-chip (SoC) architectures, shared hardware resources couple stage delays. For example, PCIe DMA bursts during camera readout contend for memory-controller bandwidth with neural accelerators, while CPU cache evictions during kernel message passing induce thread scheduling jitter. The end-to-end distribution of sense-to-torque latency must therefore be profiled empirically on the integrated hardware platform under concurrent production workloads. Furthermore, an empirical percentile remains a statistical measurement; it does not replace the formal worst-case bounds required for hard real-time safety guarantees. Under continuous inference load, each stage in table 1 carries its own tail, and the two bottom rows separate the arithmetic column sums from the end-to-end age the system actually delivers.



Table 1: Illustrative sense-to-actuation latency decomposition: Stage and system-level timings show why the arithmetic sum of stage percentiles is not the end-to-end tail. The 50 ms sum of individual stage percentiles overstates the system-level \(\text{p99}\) latency of 46.2 ms because pipeline stages rarely experience worst-case contention simultaneously. For the same reason, the sum of the stage maxima enters the end-to-end row only as an upper bound within the stated illustrative profile and conditions. A measured maximum needs a separately justified allowance or bound before it can support a hard real-time deadline. Coupling pushes the other way. Stages that slow down together, because they contend for the same memory controller or scheduler, fatten the end-to-end tail toward the stage sum, while stages that vary independently usually leave that sum pessimistic, as here. The end-to-end median in the table is set equal to the stage-median sum, a simplification of the illustrative profile that a measured one need not share.
