The four timing events of table 1 sit on this grid’s handoffs, capture within \(\SignalHandoff_1\), dispatch at \(\SignalHandoff_2\), admission at \(\SignalHandoff_4\), and brake onset at \(\SignalHandoff_5\). The grid’s latency column therefore follows the same single execution path as the timing table, and every time in it is expressed on the safety microcontroller’s clock. Together, those rows show that the chunk lease at \(\SignalHandoff_4\) cannot be chosen in isolation from the stopping distance below it or the inference renewal rate above it.

4.9.1 Coupling the distance, lease, and supply budgets
Shortening the chunk lease to save stopping distance, without checking how fast the proposer renews, causes the lease to expire before the next chunk arrives, so the robot stutters from stop to stop. Lengthening the lease to ride out slow renewals lets the robot overrun its rack-end clearance before braking begins. The machine’s physical, cognitive, and nervous subsystems therefore meet at a single shared budget, with the chunk lease at their point of convergence. In Kinetic Momentum, the loaded machine moving at its 1.5 m/s drive limit had to come to a complete stop within the 1.10 m clearance available at a rack end. Accounting for deceleration mechanics and fixed braking overheads left 258.3 ms for all computational and communication activities preceding brake onset. Section 4.4 then allocated a portion of this window: when a proposer stalls, it retains motion authority for one chunk lease before the emergency stop command reaches the motor drives one tick and one bus cycle later, bringing the running stopping budget to 835.5 mm.
Because the proposer needs enough time to renew that lease before it expires, The Cost of a Fresh Evaluation sets the lower bound from what each learned model can supply. The intent model’s INT4 weights require 24.5 ms just to stream across the memory bus. A complete inference pass of compute-bound prefill followed by bandwidth-bound autoregressive decoding consumes 336 ms, so at 2 Hz the intent model cannot renew proposals on tens-of-milliseconds timescales. By contrast, the action chunking policy streams its parameters in 1.12 ms, and its target 20 Hz cadence supplies a fresh trajectory chunk every 50 ms. Its illustrative 40 ms \(\text{p99}\) inference latency makes this cadence a feasible nominal supply target rather than a guaranteed worst-case bound, so intercepting late, dropped, or corrupt renewals remains the responsibility of the independent permission path.




The lease must outlast renewal and expire well before the stopping budget runs out.
These constraints dictate the lease rule for the machine. For continuous, uninterrupted trajectory tracking, the lease duration must exceed the proposer’s renewal interval plus an allowance for tail jitter. Simultaneously, to guarantee physical safety, the lease must fit within the pre-brake ceiling of equation 2 once detection latency, bus transport, actuator brake onset, and sensor evidence age at admission are deducted: \[\ChunkRenewalPeriod + \RenewalJitterAllowance < \ChunkLease \le \frac{\ClearDistance - \LocalizationBound - \ProtectiveClearanceMargin - \SpeedAtDetection^2/2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration}{\SpeedAtDetection} - \PermissionLoopPeriod - \CommandTransportTime - \ActuatorResponseTime - \ObservationAge \tag{4}\] where \(\ChunkRenewalPeriod\) is the chunk policy’s nominal renewal period, \(\RenewalJitterAllowance\) is the margin allocated for interarrival timing variations, and \(\ObservationAge\) is charged as the evidence’s age at admission, rows 1 and 2 of table 1 together, not its age at dispatch alone. This inequality captures the coupled cyber-physical budget in a single mathematical relation. The left side reflects compute supply, bounded by the neural proposer. The first term on the right reflects physical mechanics, governed by vehicle speed, workspace clearance, and braking deceleration. The remaining subtractive terms account for detection and communication delays, actuator brake onset, and the observation age accumulated across the perception pipeline. A faster vehicle, a less aggressive brake, or a tighter workspace lowers the upper bound; a slower or more jitter-prone neural network raises the lower bound. If the two bounds cross, no lease can preserve both uninterrupted proposal tracking and the stopping guarantee at that velocity; the permission path must interrupt tracking before authority expires.
On the mobile manipulator, the lower bound evaluates to the 55 ms renewal floor derived in notebook 4.1. The upper bound provides 236.3 ms prior to deducting observation age; subtracting the 51.6 ms capture-to-dispatch age allocated in row 1 of table 1 leaves 184.7 ms. Because the observation must also traverse the dispatch-to-admission pipeline before execution, charging that interval’s budget from table 1 increases total evidence age at admission to 114.9 ms, leaving an effective upper limit of 121.4 ms. This is the same subtraction as the notebook’s, taken in a different order. The notebook charged the lease first and left 176.3 ms under the ceiling for evidence age and the stop profile; the lease rule charges the age first and leaves this limit for the lease. The selected 60 ms lease sits just above the lower renewal bound, reflecting the physical reality that every additional millisecond of lease duration consumes 1.5 mm of stopping clearance at maximum drive velocity. This value remains an unverified allocation until the physical vehicle demonstrates that all constituent intervals fit within budget under load. Artificially inflating the lease duration to mask software latency spikes merely consumes stopping clearance, trading mechanical safety margin for compute slack.
Because each chunk packages base velocities and arm joint targets together, the architecture enforces a single shared chunk lease across both subsystems. When that lease expires, each physical body must execute a kinematically feasible, state-matched fallback maneuver. The base’s 258.3 ms pre-brake ceiling governs this allocation; it does not imply that the arm possesses surplus margin. The arm analysis in The Planning Handoff and the Trajectory Record evaluates stopping distance and response travel against its own localized workspace clearances. Validating the shared lease requires verifying timing, evidence age, dynamic state, and fallback limits simultaneously across both base and manipulator. The goal the intent model supplies is governed by a different timer, the intent lease, which limits how long a high-level goal remains active before it must be renewed and is sized in its own chapter, not from this stopping budget.


↪ The intent lease and its contract are developed in The Intent Lease Specification and Contract.

Checkpoint 4.3: The handoffs matrix and physical budgets
Before testing the lease on a humanoid and reviewing the engineering fallacies, verify your understanding of system-wide interface contracts:

Signal handoff classification: Can you identify the five canonical handoffs (\(\SignalHandoff_1\text{--}\SignalHandoff_5\)) bridging physical plant mechanics to high-level deliberative reasoning?
Binding physical constraints: Can you explain why sensory handoffs bind first on bandwidth and exposure latency, whereas actuation handoffs bind first on determinism and heat?
Handoff record provenance: Can you describe why every numerical limit in an autonomous system must record its evidence category, operating conditions, bound kind, and verification status?
The lease rule: Can you state the two limits on the chunk lease, one set by successful-admission interarrival and one by the pre-brake ceiling, and explain why a p99 inference time alone proves neither?




Systems Perspective 4.2: A deadline set by a fall
Question: Does the split among proposer, lease, and permission path still hold when the deadline comes from a fall rather than a stop?
An upright biped diverges from balance on the characteristic timescale \(\BalanceDivergenceTime = \sqrt{\MassCenterHeight/\Gravity}\), where \(\MassCenterHeight\) is its center-of-mass height. The biped is modeled in the sagittal plane as an inverted pendulum of point mass \(\Mass\) pivoting above a contact point at height \(\MassCenterHeight\) (the linear inverted pendulum model that Kajita et al. (2001) introduced for walking-pattern generation). Newton’s second law for a small angular deflection \(\TiltAngle\) from vertical then yields: \[\Mass \MassCenterHeight^2 \BipedTiltAcceleration = \Mass \Gravity \MassCenterHeight \sin\TiltAngle \implies \BipedTiltAcceleration \approx \frac{\Gravity}{\MassCenterHeight} \TiltAngle\] The characteristic equation \(\BipedTiltAcceleration - \PendulumNaturalFrequency^2 \TiltAngle = 0\) yields natural divergence modes \(e^{\pm \PendulumNaturalFrequency \TimeInstant}\) with natural frequency \(\PendulumNaturalFrequency = \sqrt{\Gravity/\MassCenterHeight}\). The growing exponential mode governs how quickly an unrecovered perturbation tilts out of control, with characteristic divergence timescale: \[\BalanceDivergenceTime = \frac{1}{\PendulumNaturalFrequency} = \sqrt{\frac{\MassCenterHeight}{\Gravity}}\] For an adult-scale humanoid with its center of mass near hip height (\(\MassCenterHeight =\) 0.9 m) and gravitational acceleration \(\Gravity = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2\), this evaluates to \(\BalanceDivergenceTime = \sqrt{0.9 / 9.81} \approx 0.303\,\text{s} = 303\,\text{ms}\) (about 303 ms). This figure represents a characteristic divergence rate, not an absolute recovery deadline. The actual time available to recover depends on the biped’s initial angular deflection, its angular velocity, support polygon geometry, and available kinematic reach. Nonetheless, this timescale demonstrates why deliberative inference cannot be placed in the feedback loop governing local balance: an explicit, state-dependent recovery calculation must define the hard real-time deadline.
The architectural partition between proposer, lease, and permission path remains valid for bipeds, but the recovery deadline becomes dynamic and state-dependent. Rather than bringing drives to a standstill, balance recovery requires placing a foot at the dynamic capture point (Pratt et al. 2006), a process demanding both finite swing time and peak joint torque. The interface lease must accommodate these physical demands:

The lease is sized from the dynamic capture-point deadline. On a wheeled base, an expired lease triggers mechanical braking to bring the vehicle to rest (\(\SpeedAtDetection \cdot \ChunkLease\)). On an underactuated biped, locking the joints mid-stride makes the fall worse, because engaging holding brakes while the center of mass moves forward causes the torso to pivot forward into an uncontrolled ground impact. Where reach, swing-time, torque, and energy limits permit recovery, the lease fallback action must therefore execute an emergency capture-point step. The chunk lease, permission tick, fieldbus transit, and observation age must all fit within the dynamic recovery budget while reserving sufficient time to swing and plant the foot. The characteristic fall timescale frames this constraint but cannot substitute for dynamic simulation.
The proposer must meet the recovery budget. An inference renewal period that consumes a major fraction of the characteristic fall timescale cannot safely participate in posture stabilization. High-level intent models must remain decoupled from balance reflexes. Whether a mid-level chunk policy can safely control locomotion depends on whether its renewal interval and tail jitter leave adequate margin for fallback step execution.
Actuator thermal limits and supply sag constrain the recovery step. Executing an emergency recovery step demands simultaneous peak torque across multiple leg joints. This surge draws a large transient current, inducing resistive heating in motor windings and risking DC bus voltage collapse (Power distribution impedance, transient droop, and brownout resets). Consequently, the permission path must evaluate candidate recovery trajectories against instantaneous thermal and electrical reserves before admission.




Pratt, Jerry, John Carff, Sergey Drakunov, and Ambarish Goswami. 2006. “Capture Point: A Step Toward Humanoid Push Recovery.” Proceedings of the 6th IEEE-RAS International Conference on Humanoid Robots (Humanoids), 200–207. https://doi.org/10.1109/ICHR.2006.321385.

Kajita, Shuuji, Fumio Kanehiro, Kenji Kaneko, Kazuhito Yokoi, and Hirohisa Hirukawa. 2001. “The 3D Linear Inverted Pendulum Mode: A Simple Modeling for a Biped Walking Pattern Generation.” Proceedings of the 2001 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) 1: 239–46. https://doi.org/10.1109/IROS.2001.973365.
Whether the deadline comes from a warehouse rack end or a biped’s fall, the handoff matrix and the lease rule only protect the machine if the hardware and firmware underneath them honor the boundaries the equations assume. In practice, subtle implementation shortcuts in watchdog servicing, calibration ports, state feedback, and middleware configurations routinely bypass those boundaries without triggering a compile or bench error.

title: The Nervous System
text:
4.10 Fallacies and Pitfalls
A block diagram draws a clean boundary between high-level deliberation and low-level real-time enforcement, but physical boards and firmware routinely couple the two through shared power rails, common clock domains, interrupt lines, or auxiliary diagnostic ports. When a planning subsystem crashes or misbehaves, those hidden couplings decide whether the safety enforcement loop actually survives.

Pitfall: Servicing a safety watchdog inside a high-priority timer interrupt rather than an application-verified safety loop.
The mobile manipulator relies on a hardware self-watchdog to trigger the Safe Torque Off path of section 4.6 if it receives no feed within 5 ms. Because an enforcer that stops executing can no longer command a coordinated stop, this immediate hardware cutoff is required. A dangerous design mistake occurs when engineers service this watchdog from a high-priority hardware timer interrupt rather than directly from the safety loop. If the lower-priority enforcement task deadlocks on a mutex or crashes, the hardware timer interrupt continues firing every 1 ms tick. The watchdog remains fed while the enforcer has silently lost its ability to evaluate torque limits, kinematic clearances, and lease budgets.
In distributed systems engineering, this error is known as the confusion of liveness with correctness. A node responding to network ping heartbeats can be livelocked, thrashing on memory allocation, or deadlocked on an internal mutex. Servicing a watchdog must never signify mere scheduler activity. Instead, every refresh pulse must be conditioned on the successful, sequential retirement of all required verification stages, for example by requiring a monotonic task-completion token before a windowed hardware watchdog is serviced. An independent timer tick confirms only that interrupt dispatching still operates; it provides zero evidence that the controller has safely evaluated the machine’s physical state (section 4.4.1).
Architect’s countermeasure: Bind watchdog refresh pulses strictly to the verified completion of the safety loop’s invariant checks, deploying windowed hardware watchdogs that trip on both execution underruns and spurious early feeds.


Pitfall: Leaving auxiliary diagnostic or calibration interfaces unmediated in production operation.
Suppose the mobile manipulator validates base velocity proposals through its permission path, yet its drive-wheel motor drives retain an unmonitored serial calibration interface. If a diagnostic daemon writes a \(35.0\text{ A}\) test value directly into an inverter register through that port, the proposal mailbox continues reporting zero velocity. Checking the mailbox reveals nothing about the bypassed command, yet the drive wheels produce torque that no motion safety check ever evaluated or approved. Actuation authority is not defined by a logical software diagram; it encompasses every physical wire, bus transceiver, and digital interface capable of changing a power-stage register. Service interfaces must therefore incorporate operational interlocks or hardware jumpers that prevent calibration writes from bypassing the enforcer during production runs.
Architect’s countermeasure: Electrically isolate, physically jumper, or cryptographically interlock all auxiliary diagnostic and calibration ports during operational modes, routing all register writes exclusively through the real-time enforcer.


Fallacy: Evaluating safety barrier invariants on commanded trajectory setpoints is equivalent to evaluating physical plant state.
Suppose an arm controller evaluates safety using a control barrier function (Ames et al. 2019), a scalar function \(\BarrierFunction\) of the state space that remains positive within the safe set and is kept from going negative by filtering unacceptable control inputs. To conserve fieldbus bandwidth, an engineer might evaluate \(\BarrierFunction\) using commanded joint positions rather than load-side encoder feedback. If a transmission gear strips or a drive belt shears, the trajectory interpolator continues generating valid, smooth setpoints. The enforcer calculates that the system remains safely inside the barrier set (\(\BarrierFunction(\CommandedJointConfiguration) > 0\)), even while the decoupled arm collapses into an obstacle. Safety enforcement belongs at the causal boundary, which means it must ingest ground-truth physical state measurements through dependable sensory channels and account for sensor noise and latency. Auditing the command stream reveals what the planner intended, but only independent physical feedback captures where the machinery actually moves.

Ames, Aaron D., Samuel Coogan, Magnus Egerstedt, Gennaro Notomista, Koushil Sreenath, and Paulo Tabuada. 2019. “Control Barrier Functions: Theory and Applications.” 2019 18th European Control Conference (ECC), 3420–31. https://doi.org/10.23919/ECC.2019.8796030.
Architect’s countermeasure: Close safety barrier evaluations strictly around verified, independent sensor measurements (such as optical load encoders and current shunts) rather than planned trajectory setpoints.



↪ The control barrier function and the safety filter that keeps it nonnegative are developed in Safe Sets as Conditional Permission.

Fallacy: Nominal, fault-free operating logs are sufficient to prove physical architectural isolation.
Logging thousands of operating hours without a missed deadline demonstrates nominal stability, but clean telemetry cannot expose hidden cross-subsystem couplings that awaken only during failure modes. Subsystem isolation often breaks down under unmodeled physical interactions, such as supply-rail voltage sags when multiple inverters switch simultaneously, bus contention storms, or memory corruption spilling across addressing domains. Rigorous qualification requires deliberate fault injection: inducing power transients, flooding communication buses, corrupting policy memory, and mechanically locking motor shafts on a dynamometer. Each experiment must evaluate an explicit, quantitative response bound, such as locked-rotor detection clamping motor current within \(2.0\text{ ms}\), rather than treating the mere absence of an operating system crash as validation. Fault experiments support the isolation claim within their stated fault and load coverage when the system maintains invariant enforcement or reaches the specified fallback within the quantitative response bounds. They do not establish coverage of untested fault combinations.
Architect’s countermeasure: Validate fault-domain independence through active fault-injection regimes (power sags, clock glitches, bus flooding, and memory corruption) with quantitative pass-fail response bounds.


Pitfall: Assuming zero packet loss in robotics middleware equates to deterministic real-time delivery.
A publish-subscribe transport configured for reliable delivery attempts to recover lost packets, but successful recovery does not establish deterministic real-time delivery. After congestion or interference, a reliable transport delivers the burst of queued, obsolete setpoints that section 4.3.2 traced, each describing a robot state that no longer exists. While switching to a freshest-sample policy prevents queue backlogs, dropping stale frames does not inherently bound scheduling jitter, serialization delay, or driver execution latency. The cycle-critical actuation path requires two separate guarantees: an engineered worst-case delivery bound across the physical communication bus and an explicit freshness deadline enforced by the receiver before executing any torque command.
Architect’s countermeasure: Budget the complete transport response under declared traffic and fault conditions, enforce deadline-based freshness at the consumer, and isolate cycle-critical commands from supervisory middleware traffic regardless of the bus architecture.

title: The Nervous System
text:
4.11 Summary
The Physical Body derived the physical stopping budget for the loaded machine, and The Cognitive Brain established the operational cadences for proposal generation and evidence age. This chapter introduced the real-time permission path designed to enforce those constraints, establishing a two-processor architecture whose physical isolation still awaits evaluation under load. To guarantee deterministic safety, the permission path holds exclusive write access to the motor drive registers. It communicates with the unprivileged proposal engine through a lock-free mailbox that never stalls the high-frequency control tick, while communication and computation delays mandate closing joint-level feedback loops directly within the drives. By evaluating command interfaces, from joint positions to operational-space impedances, the permission path prices each check against available stopping clearance. Combining these constraints yields a bounded time window during which an action proposal is permitted to drive physical actuators. On the running machine, this analysis produces a chunk lease that exceeds the proposer’s renewal interval while fitting within the pre-brake delay budget. The resulting handoff record documents this lease alongside its validity conditions and evidence requirements. This lease and the mechanisms behind it remain claims until they are verified under worst-case compute jitter, bus contention, malformed proposals, sensor faults, and degraded braking. Table 5 summarizes the four governing relations that define the nervous system’s timing, lease duration, and response guarantees, along with the engineering decisions they resolve.



Table 5: Key equations of the nervous system: The four relations behind the chapter’s rate, lease, and response decisions, with the place each is derived. \(\PrebrakeDelayCeiling\) is the right side of the pre-brake ceiling.










Equation
What it bounds or decides
Derived




\(\DelayPhaseLag = \CrossoverFrequency\left(\dfrac{\SamplingPeriod}{2} + \EnforcerComputeTime + \CommandTransportTime\right)\)
The phase lost to sample-and-hold, computation, and transport delay at crossover, dictating whether a control loop can close across the network bus or must reside inside the drive
equation 1


\(\PrebrakeDelay \le \dfrac{\ClearDistance - \LocalizationBound - \ProtectiveClearanceMargin - \SpeedAtDetection^2/2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration}{\SpeedAtDetection}\)
The pre-brake ceiling: the maximum allowable delay before braking onset that still guarantees stopping within available clearance
equation 2


\(\ChunkRenewalPeriod + \RenewalJitterAllowance < \ChunkLease \le \PrebrakeDelayCeiling - \PermissionLoopPeriod - \CommandTransportTime - \ActuatorResponseTime - \ObservationAge\)
The lease rule, bounding chunk lease duration between the proposer’s renewal floor and the ceiling imposed by detection, transport, brake onset, and evidence age
equation 4


\(\WorstCaseResponseTime_i = \WorstCaseExecutionTime_i + \TaskBlockingTime_i + \TaskInterferenceTime_i \le \TaskRelativeDeadline_i\)
Worst-case response-time schedulability for hard real-time tasks, verifying that execution, blocking, and interference fit within the task deadline
equation 3







Key Takeaways: The permission path and determinism

The permission path alone writes the drives: Learned models act only as unprivileged proposal engines (\(\CandidateProposal_t\)). Write access to the motor drive registers belongs to the deterministic real-time enforcer alone, hosted on silicon whose isolation from the proposer must be verified experimentally.
Cadence is dictated by physics, not software: The four-tier concurrency hierarchy (20 kHz FOC current regulation, 1 kHz kinematic enforcer checks, 20 Hz action-chunk renewal, and 2 Hz multimodal deliberation on the running machine) is governed by physical time constants (\(\ElectricalTimeConstant = \PhaseInductance/\PhaseResistance\)), total loop delay, exposure horizons, and model execution budgets. The total loop delay appears as a phase lag \(\DelayPhaseLag = \CrossoverFrequency(\SamplingPeriod/2 + \EnforcerComputeTime + \CommandTransportTime)\), which keeps the joint loops in the drives.
The exchange never waits, and every proposal expires: The permission path reads the mailbox in a single bounded attempt per tick, retaining the currently active, independently admissible chunk if a write collision occurs. Every proposal carries an evidence timestamp and an explicit expiration horizon that terminates its authority even if an explicit cancellation never arrives.
Stopping dynamics dimension the chunk lease: For the mobile manipulator operating at its drive limits, the pre-brake ceiling is 258.3 ms. Sizing the lease at 60 ms places it just above the proposer’s renewal floor. The interval from the final admitted chunk to brake onset takes 82 ms. Its lease path brings the stopping budget’s running total to 835.5 mm of the 1.10 m clear distance before evidence age and the remaining stop margins are charged (row 4 of The warehouse mobile manipulator's stopping budget).
Worst-case bounds outrank empirical distributions: Tail-latency percentiles such as \(\text{p99}\) cannot establish real-time safety. Deterministic enforcement requires bounding worst-case computation, blocking, and interference (\(\WorstCaseResponseTime_i = \WorstCaseExecutionTime_i + \TaskBlockingTime_i + \TaskInterferenceTime_i \le \TaskRelativeDeadline_i\)) under rigorously qualified operating conditions.
The permission path is only as independent as what it shares: If the permission path shares a clock source, power rail, memory bus, or silicon die with the proposal engine, faults in the proposer can compromise the enforcer. The two-processor split is an architectural hypothesis that requires empirical validation through stress testing and fault injection (Empirical Verification of Silicon Isolation), not an assumed property of separate software processes.
The command interface sets what the permission path must check: Joint position targets express kinematic intent that the enforcer can verify geometrically, but they cannot bound contact forces. Velocity interfaces require a bounded motion projection, while torque interfaces require dynamic bounds and a feasible fallback. Impedance targets bound steady-state interaction forces, but only if the enforcer validates the stiffness and damping gains alongside the reference trajectory.
Locate interface regressions at their handoff: The system handoff record maps every timing and clearance limit to one of five architectural boundaries, binding each to operational preconditions, evidence categories, and bound types. When performance regresses, engineers can isolate the offending subsystem against its allocated budget using like-for-like evidence.



Physical stopping limits, inference renewal rates, and the Nervous System’s response delays converge on one governing parameter, how long an admitted proposal may command the actuators. When a timing question arises on a new machine, the first diagnostic is to price that parameter, converting the lease path to distance at the operating speed and comparing it with what the stopping budget has left. A lease that cannot fit between the renewal floor and the pre-brake ceiling cannot sustain uninterrupted proposal tracking at that speed, and a faster processor helps only if it lets the renewal period, and with it the floor, shrink.
This chapter closes Part I, and with it the argument that the first law, irreversibility (principle \(\ref{pri-vol4-irreversibility}\)), set in motion. The Body turned irreversibility into distances and limit records, the Brain into proposals that arrive late and expire, and the Nervous System into a rule of authority. Motion that cannot be undone may be granted only for as long as the stopping budget can still guarantee the stop. The chunk lease is that rule written as a number, and the handoff record is where the number is kept. Everything the machine later learns or is permitted to do inherits this bound, including the demonstrations it collects while the permission path is watching.

title: The Nervous System
text:
4.12 Historical Perspective and Further Reading
The phase-margin arguments that keep high-bandwidth joint feedback loops inside local motor drives predate digital computing. Nyquist (1932) established the foundational stability criterion that determines whether a closed-loop feedback amplifier will oscillate, and Bode (1945) formalized these dynamics into the gain and phase margins that control engineers budget today. When mechanical and analog controllers transitioned to software, sampled-data control theory formalized how digital sample-and-hold stages, discrete computation steps, and communication transport introduce pure time delays that consume this margin (Franklin et al. 1998). High-bandwidth feedback-loop placement in this chapter follows directly from this phase accounting: a control loop must close physically close to its sensors and actuators because any transport latency erodes phase margin that high-bandwidth physical dynamics cannot spare.

Joseph, Mathai, and Paritosh Pandya. 1986. “Finding Response Times in a Real-Time System.” The Computer Journal 29 (5): 390–95. https://doi.org/10.1093/comjnl/29.5.390.

Audsley, Neil, Alan Burns, Mike Richardson, Ken Tindell, and Andy J. Wellings. 1993. “Applying New Scheduling Theory to Static Priority Pre-Emptive Scheduling.” Software Engineering Journal 8 (5): 284–92. https://doi.org/10.1049/sej.1993.0034.

Reeves, Glenn E. 1997. What Really Happened on Mars? Electronic mail message, Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
Predictable execution and real-time scheduling supply the second pillar of this architecture. Liu and Layland (1973) proved that assigning static priorities monotonically by rate guarantees schedulability for periodic task sets up to a theoretical utilization bound. Subsequent response-time analysis transformed this sufficient condition into an exact test by summing worst-case execution time, resource blocking, and higher-priority task interference (Joseph and Pandya 1986; Audsley et al. 1993). When shared resources threatened these guarantees with priority inversion, Sha et al. (1990) bounded the duration of blocking through priority inheritance and the priority ceiling protocol. The Mars Pathfinder mission in 1997 demonstrated precisely what the absence of such bounds costs in production, when unmanaged priority inversions triggered repeated system resets on the Martian surface (Reeves 1997). Extending predictability to distributed embedded systems, Kopetz (2011) established the foundations of time-triggered design. That work argued that safety-critical systems must remain statically analyzable prior to execution, and it introduced the concepts of state messages and temporal accuracy that govern the proposal headers in this chapter.
The lock-free coordination between the high-level policy proposer and the low-level safety permission path descends from foundational work on sharing state without waiting. Lamport (1977) demonstrated that a concurrent reader can detect an overlapping write using version sequence numbers alone. Simpson (1990) developed the asynchronous four-slot mechanism for flight-control avionics running on unrelated clocks, Herlihy (1991) formalized the theoretical hierarchy of wait-free synchronization, and Kopetz and Reisinger (1993) formulated the non-blocking write protocol specifically for real-time readers. Industrial networks confronted similar timing and isolation challenges on the wire: Controller Area Network (CAN) bus architectures resolved medium access through deterministic, bitwise priority arbitration (International Organization for Standardization 2015). The functional-safety profiles of IEC 61784-3 established the black-channel principle, which encapsulates integrity and freshness guarantees within the messages so that the transmission medium itself need not be trusted (International Electrotechnical Commission 2021). Finally, the concept of bounded temporal leases originated in distributed systems, where Gray and Cheriton (1989) restricted how long a client could rely on cached data so that an unresponsive client blocked the server for at most one lease period. Physical AI systems adapt this lease mechanism to an entirely different physical objective: rather than preserving distributed cache consistency, the lease is bounded by the kinetic stopping budget and renewal deadlines of the safety monitor.

Kopetz, Hermann, and Johannes Reisinger. 1993. “The Non-Blocking Write Protocol NBW: A Solution to a Real-Time Synchronization Problem.” Proceedings of the 1993 Real-Time Systems Symposium, 131–37. https://doi.org/10.1109/REAL.1993.393507.

International Organization for Standardization. 2015. ISO 11898-1:2015: Road Vehicles, Controller Area Network (CAN), Part 1: Data Link Layer and Physical Signalling. International Organization for Standardization.

International Electrotechnical Commission. 2021. IEC 61784-3:2021: Industrial Communication Networks, Profiles, Part 3: Functional Safety Fieldbuses, General Rules and Profile Definitions. International Electrotechnical Commission.

Gray, Cary G., and David R. Cheriton. 1989. “Leases: An Efficient Fault-Tolerant Mechanism for Distributed File Cache Consistency.” Proceedings of the Twelfth ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP), 202–10. https://doi.org/10.1145/74850.74870.
For readers seeking deeper exploration, six works trace the lineage from classical feedback theory to modern real-time permission paths:

Franklin et al. (1998) provides the definitive treatment of digital and sampled-data control, analyzing how zero-order hold circuits, computation time, and transport latencies introduce phase lag. This analysis forms the theoretical foundation for the multi-rate cadence decisions in section 4.3.
Liu and Layland (1973) is a concise, classic paper that remains the clearest demonstration of how rate-monotonic priority assignment guarantees schedulability under worst-case task arrival patterns.
Sha et al. (1990) formalizes the priority inheritance and priority ceiling protocols alongside their mathematical blocking bounds. This work explains both the recovery strategy deployed on Mars Pathfinder and the derivation of the blocking term \(\TaskBlockingTime_i\) in equation 3.
Buttazzo (2011) offers an authoritative textbook treatment of hard real-time systems, fixed-priority and deadline-driven scheduling, and response-time analysis, complete with concrete task sets that readers can verify by hand.
Kopetz (2011) develops real-time architectures from the time-triggered perspective. Its chapters on real-time entities, temporal accuracy, and communication clarify why our proposal mailbox exchanges idempotent state messages rather than transient event queues.
Simpson (1990) presents the four-slot mechanism in its original flight-critical avionics context, demonstrating how four memory slots decouple an asynchronous reader and writer without locking, waiting, or sample loss.


Franklin, Gene F, J David Powell, and Michael L Workman. 1998. Digital Control of Dynamic Systems. 3rd ed. Addison-Wesley.

Sha, Lui, Ragunathan Rajkumar, and John P. Lehoczky. 1990. “Priority Inheritance Protocols: An Approach to Real-Time Synchronization.” IEEE Transactions on Computers 39 (9): 1175–85.

Buttazzo, Giorgio C. 2011. Hard Real-Time Computing Systems: Predictable Scheduling Algorithms and Applications. 3rd ed. Real-Time Systems Series. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-0676-1.

Kopetz, Hermann. 2011. Real-Time Systems: Design Principles for Distributed Embedded Applications. 2nd ed. Real-Time Systems Series. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4419-8237-7.

Simpson, H. R. 1990. “Four-Slot Fully Asynchronous Communication Mechanism.” IEE Proceedings E (Computers and Digital Techniques) 137 (1): 17–30. https://doi.org/10.1049/ip-e.1990.0002.

What’s Next: From anatomy to closed-loop learningWhen an embodied machine modifies or rejects a human command before execution, the recorded demonstration no longer reflects unconstrained intent. The Body, the Brain, and the Nervous System establish physical limits, learned proposals, and a timed permission path. During data collection, such as teleoperated openings of the spring-latched cage door, that path may clamp, rate-limit, or refuse an operator’s request, while the body may deliver motion that differs from the admitted command. The limit and handoff records preserve the conditions behind those interventions. In Part II, Physical Data begins from the reality that a physical machine manufactures its own training data, so each executed action changes the observations that follow. Each record carries what the operator requested, what the permission path admitted, and what the body delivered. It then establishes what a demonstration must retain so that a policy can learn the task without mistaking the collecting machine’s limitations for intended behavior.

title: Physical Data
text:
Purpose



Physical AI stack focus for this chapter.
Why can a large archive of successful demonstrations leave a robot unable to recover from its first mistake?
A successful demonstration shows how one machine completed a task under one set of conditions. It shows almost nothing about what to do after a slip, a shifted fixture, or a worn gripper, yet a learned policy’s first error carries it into exactly those states, where the archive holds no instruction. Repeating the demonstration enlarges the archive without filling that gap. The recorded motion also carries the operator’s delay, the machine’s limits, and every correction the permission path applied, so a training process that cannot separate these influences learns a safeguard’s intervention or a mechanical limitation as if it were skill. Gathering the missing experience costs operator time and component life, and the collection itself must stay within the machine’s physical limits. Physical data must therefore be engineered, from the choice of experiences to the meaning, timing, and physical origin of every label and the conditions the archive leaves uncovered. Because every collected action crosses the causal boundary, its irreversible costs decide what a machine can learn and where its evidence stops.


Learning Objectives

Explain how endogenous covariate shift yields the conditional quadratic imitation-cost bound, and distinguish dataset occupancy from evaluated closed-loop competence
Select the action tap a dataset imitates and align multi-rate sensor and action streams to hardware exposure-midpoint timestamps within the task’s spatial tolerance
Estimate usable demonstration yield from collection time, operator rest, and physical reset overhead, and budget the mechanical component wear a campaign consumes
Identify collection gaps by joining empirical state-action occupancy against a required scenario table
Separate failed autonomous actions from admissible human recovery across the divergence, takeover, and stabilization timestamps of an intervention episode
Evaluate whether an embodiment’s mechanical, sensing, and timing assumptions transfer to another machine without falling into the normalization fallacy
Detect silent calibration and plant drift in a demonstration archive using kinematic reprojection and repeated excitation trajectories
Design an immutable provenance record linking each observation to its four-stream action taps (\(\RequestedActionTap, \MappedCommandTap, \EnforcedCommandTap, \MeasuredResponseTap\)) and to the collecting plant

title: Physical Data
text:
5.1 Endogenous Experience
In most machine learning, the dataset exists before the engineering begins. A text corpus or an image benchmark is gathered independently of the model, costs little per additional example, and does not change in response to anything the model predicts. A physical machine has no such corpus. Collecting demonstrations on the robot consumes operator time and component life; robot-free and synthetic sources avoid that robot wear but still require qualification for the target machine. Every telemetry record reflects who commanded the action, what the permission path admitted, and how the physical body moved. Because each executed action changes the physical state of the system, it dictates what subsequent observations can reveal. Physical data is therefore an engineered artifact. The central challenge of physical data engineering is deciding which experiences to collect, and what to record about them, so that a policy learns the task rather than the idiosyncrasies of its collection. Answering this challenge requires four elements: accounting for collection costs in operator time and hardware wear, defining an unambiguous meaning for every recorded action label, establishing a metric for state-space coverage independent of the archive’s internal contents, and explicitly auditing what the archive omits.
Consider a warehouse mobile manipulator tasked with opening a spring-latched cage door. The robot can flawlessly enforce its low-level motion limits and yet fail because it lacks the operational experience to unlatch the door. During a demonstration, a human operator commands motion, the safety permission path checks and filters it, and the robot’s physical body drives against the mechanical latch. The onboard sensor log captures the output of that entire coupled loop. The limits and handoffs recorded earlier for this machine, in the limit record of The six elements of a limit record and the handoff record of The Handoffs Matrix, therefore become preconditions on the training data fed to the learned policy proposer. Every logged command was shaped by them before the body moved. Choosing which physical experiences to collect demands a rigorous accounting of how control inputs shift future sensory states. Choosing what to imitate requires cleanly separating the operator’s raw request from the safety-filtered command and the measured physical response.
A policy fit by supervised imitation to nominal, clean teleoperated demonstrations of door openings (behavioral cloning, defined below) can execute flawlessly in simulation yet jam the latch during its first autonomous deployment. The primary culprit is the distribution shift that the machine’s own closed-loop actions induce. Unlike passive inference on a fixed benchmark, an action executed within an embodied Markov decision process (MDP), in which the next state depends on the current state and action, physically alters the robot’s spatial trajectory, camera viewpoint, and contact states. That displacement changes the probability distribution of every subsequent sensory observation (\(\DecisionProcessState_{t+1} \sim \EnvironmentTransitionDistribution(\DecisionProcessState \mid \DecisionProcessState_{t}, \CognitivePolicyAction_{t})\)).


↪ The Markov decision process, with its transition model and reward, is developed for the latch task in The latch task as a reward problem.

Definition 5.1: Endogenous covariate shift
Endogenous covariate shift is the closed-loop distribution discrepancy wherein an embodied agent’s executed actions alter its subsequent physical states and sensory observations (\(\DecisionProcessState_{t+1} \sim \EnvironmentTransitionDistribution(\DecisionProcessState \mid \DecisionProcessState_{t}, \CognitivePolicyAction_{t})\)), driving the system into state-space regimes unsupported by its training demonstrations.

Significance: Explains how offline behavioral cloning can fail during closed-loop physical execution: a perturbation may drive the system into states where the policy lacks training support.
Distinction: Unlike exogenous dataset shift caused by changing ambient lighting or seasonal weather, endogenous shift is actively generated by the agent’s own closed-loop actions altering its subsequent observation distribution.
Common pitfall: Attempting to fix closed-loop policy failure by collecting more nominal expert demonstrations, which only increases data density along the success manifold without providing the corrective recovery data needed to escape boundary excursions.



This distribution shift is how the second law, endogenous data (principle \(\ref{pri-vol4-endogenous-drift}\)), shows up in data collection, where the machine’s own actions choose the states its archive must later answer for. An archive composed exclusively of flawless executions without recovery trajectories becomes an operational liability. The moment the autonomous policy commits its first sub-millimeter tracking error, the robot enters states never encountered during training. Two distinct physical mechanisms govern how fast that departure grows (section 5.2).

title: Physical Data
text:
5.2 Mechanics of Endogenous Covariate Shift
When an image classifier misidentifies a dog as a cat, the mistake does not alter the pixels of the next photograph in the test set. When a door-opening policy misses the latch centerline by a millimeter, that motion shifts the camera viewpoint, changes the contact geometry, and alters every observation that follows. Classical empirical risk minimization assumes the first setting, drawing independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) samples from an exogenous, stationary distribution \(\ExogenousDataDistribution\). Even when passive machine learning studies covariate shift, it treats the shift as an open-loop observational change: the marginal input distribution \(\InputDistribution\) shifts (such as evaluating a daytime-trained vision model at night) while the conditional data-generating function \(\ConditionalDistribution\) stays fixed. Because a passive model’s predictions \(\PassiveModelPrediction\) exert no physical back-action on the world, an inference error never mutates the next input. Imitation learning on a machine operates inside the closed-loop counterpart to this setting.


↩︎ The closed loop through which a flawed proposal carries the machine into states missing from its training distribution is established in From a proposed action to motion.
In an embodied physical system, two distinct mechanisms distort what the learner encounters. The first shifts the states that the policy visits even when the hardware stays unchanged; the second alters how the physical plant responds to any given control input:

Endogenous state distribution shift: The policy’s executed actions \(\CognitivePolicyAction_{t} = \Policy(\MultimodalObservation_{t})\) directly drive the physical state transition \(\DecisionProcessState_{t+1} \sim \EnvironmentTransitionDistribution(\DecisionProcessState \mid \DecisionProcessState_{t}, \CognitivePolicyAction_{t})\), choosing the sensory observations \(\MultimodalObservation_{t+1}\) the robot sees next. A single control error moves the body into an unvisited region of the state space and changes the incoming observation distribution on the next tick.
Active physical plant drift: The physical plant is a continuous dynamical system governed by differential equations of motion \(\PlantStateRate = \PlantDynamicsFunction(\MechanicalPlantState, \ControlInput; \PlantDynamicsParameters(\TimeInstant))\) whose parameters drift over operational time. Actuator Joule heating (\(\TorqueProducingCurrent^2 \ElectricalResistance(\WindingTemperature)\)) raises winding temperature and copper resistance via \(\ElectricalResistance(\WindingTemperature) = \ElectricalResistance_0(1 + \CopperTemperatureCoefficient \JouleanTemperatureRise)\), compressing the motor drive’s voltage headroom and capping peak torque at high joint speeds. Over extended operating cycles, continuous loading degrades strain-wave gearbox lubrication, lowering torsional stiffness and expanding mechanical lost motion. Compliant elastomer gripper pads wear down and deform, shrinking the Coulomb friction cone (\(\lVert \TangentialContactShear \rVert \le \CoulombFrictionCoefficient \NormalContactForce\)). Finally, physical workpieces vary in mass, center of gravity, and surface texture across trials, perturbing both the inertial loads the arm accelerates and the gravitational torques the joints sustain.

Together, the policy’s closed-loop actions and the plant’s response induce an endogenous state visitation distribution \(\LearnerStateVisitationDistribution(\DecisionProcessState)\), the expected fraction of time steps that a rollout of policy \(\pi\) spends in state \(\DecisionProcessState\). When an agent is trained by offline behavioral cloning on demonstrations from an expert policy \(\pi^*\), empirical risk minimization fits the imitation objective only over the expert’s occupancy distribution \(\ExpertStateVisitationDistribution(\DecisionProcessState)\). During autonomous execution, the learned policy instead acts under its own induced distribution \(\LearnerStateVisitationDistribution(\DecisionProcessState)\). Wherever \(\LearnerStateVisitationDistribution\) departs from \(\ExpertStateVisitationDistribution\), the policy encounters states that hold no demonstrated corrective action.

Definition 5.2: Behavioral cloning
Behavioral cloning is imitation learning posed as supervised learning: a policy is fit to map each recorded observation to the action the demonstrator took there, with the loss weighted by the demonstrator’s own state occupancy \(\ExpertStateVisitationDistribution\).

Significance: Training error is measured only on states the demonstrator visited, while deployment cost accrues on the states the learned policy visits. Under a 0–1 action loss (one whenever the policy’s action differs from the expert’s, zero otherwise) the worst-case excess cost can therefore grow with the square of the horizon \(\BehaviorCloningHorizon\), the episode length in control steps, rather than linearly, as the next section derives.
Distinction: Unlike corrective aggregation, which obtains expert labels at states the learner itself reaches (section 5.8 develops it), behavioral cloning never observes the consequences of its own mistakes; unlike reinforcement learning, it needs demonstrations but no reward.
Common pitfall: Reading a low held-out loss as evidence of closed-loop competence. A held-out split drawn from the same demonstrations shares their occupancy, so it cannot contain the states the policy’s first error reaches.



Because behavioral cloning weights its loss solely by the demonstrator’s occupancy \(\ExpertStateVisitationDistribution\), a single step off the demonstrated path places the policy in states where training never penalized an error. How fast that first departure compounds over an episode depends on whether the archive holds any actions that steer the machine back (section 5.3).

title: Physical Data
text:
5.3 Recovery and Compounding Error
Opening a latch from a nominal centered approach and recovering from an off-axis sideways slip require different physical actions (figure 1). Every retained demonstration guides the gripper forward along the narrow corridor centered on the strike plate, which populates the archive with thousands of forward-progress actions. The archive contains zero demonstrations that start from a gripper displaced a few millimeters toward the fixture and return it to the centerline. Because a skilled human operator rarely lets the gripper drift into those boundary regions, and because teleoperation runs that drifted noticeably were aborted or discarded during curation, nothing in the training data constrains the policy’s output at such a displaced state.1 The recoverability problem is this absence of demonstrated corrective actions that steer the system back into the nominal corridor.
1 ALVINN (Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network): Pomerleau’s road-following network learned to steer from a human driver who kept the van centered, so its training images held almost no off-center views (Pomerleau 1989). His remedy shifted each camera image sideways in software and corrected the steering label to match, synthesizing recovery examples about 20 years before Dataset Aggregation (DAgger, section 5.8) (Pomerleau 1991). A warp could fill that gap because the missing state was only a viewpoint of a flat road, whereas a gripper displaced toward the fixture also lacks contact forces that no image transform can manufacture, so its recoveries must be demonstrated or collected.
Pomerleau, Dean A. 1989. “ALVINN: An Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 1: 305–13.

Pomerleau, Dean A. 1991. “Efficient Training of Artificial Neural Networks for Autonomous Navigation.” Neural Computation 3 (1): 88–97. https://doi.org/10.1162/neco.1991.3.1.88.






Figure 1: The latch corridor seen from above: Retained demonstrations supply dense forward-progress actions inside a narrow corridor centered on the strike plate. A gripper displaced toward the fixture sits where the archive holds no demonstration, so nothing in the data specifies the action that returns it to the corridor, and an unconstrained output can carry it farther toward contact.



Whether this missing return action leads to task failure depends on the closed-loop dynamics of the complete physical plant. Because the robot’s physical state encompasses joint coordinates, joint velocities, motor drive currents, contact wrenches (combined three-axis contact forces and torques), and raw camera streams, a nominal demonstration traces an infinitesimally thin manifold through a high-dimensional state space. Almost any unmodeled disturbance displaces the system off this path. If the physical plant and its low-level joint controllers inherently restore small lateral displacements toward the centerline through compliant passive dynamics, an imperfect policy output near the corridor boundary will naturally attenuate. If the system dynamics lack this self-centering stability, the tracking error will persist or compound until a learned recovery policy, the safety permission path, or a human supervisor intervenes. While production demonstration archives often contain occasional human corrections, their coverage cannot be assumed; it must be audited against an explicit scenario table (section 5.7).
The quadratic worst-case scaling of behavioral cloning can be derived through a discrete summation over horizon steps. Suppose an autonomous agent follows the expert trajectory until encountering its first execution error at step \(\FirstErrorStepIndex \in \{1, \dots, \BehaviorCloningHorizon\}\). If this error propels the system into an unsupported state from which it never recovers, the agent incurs an adverse task cost at every remaining step (\(\BehaviorCloningHorizon - \FirstErrorStepIndex\)). Assigning each time step an upper bound \(\SingleStepImitationError\) on the probability of committing a first error and normalizing the per-step cost to unity (\(\ImmediateTaskCostScore_t = 1\)) yields the following worst-case cost accumulation. This discrete summation serves as an upper-bound derivation rather than an exact expectation over independent failure events: \[\sum_{\FirstErrorStepIndex=1}^\BehaviorCloningHorizon \SingleStepImitationError (\BehaviorCloningHorizon - \FirstErrorStepIndex) = \SingleStepImitationError \left( \BehaviorCloningHorizon^2 - \sum_{\FirstErrorStepIndex=1}^\BehaviorCloningHorizon \FirstErrorStepIndex \right) = \SingleStepImitationError \left( \BehaviorCloningHorizon^2 - \frac{\BehaviorCloningHorizon(\BehaviorCloningHorizon+1)}{2} \right) = \frac{\BehaviorCloningHorizon(\BehaviorCloningHorizon-1)}{2} \SingleStepImitationError \approx \frac{1}{2} \BehaviorCloningHorizon^2 \SingleStepImitationError.\] In open-loop supervised learning, by contrast, if per-step inference errors were independent and exerted zero feedback on subsequent model inputs, an error rate of \(\SingleStepImitationError\) per step would scale linearly over \(\BehaviorCloningHorizon\) steps as \(\sum_{t=1}^\BehaviorCloningHorizon \SingleStepImitationError = \BehaviorCloningHorizon\SingleStepImitationError\). The extra factor of \(\BehaviorCloningHorizon\) appearing in \(\CovariateDriftBound\) is the mathematical signature of closed-loop endogenous feedback.
This quadratic bound characterizes the accumulation of task cost over time, not the physical trajectory of the machine. The result does not imply that spatial tracking errors grow quadratically as \(\TimeInstant^2\). Closed-loop contact forces, mechanical compliance, and actuator saturation govern how physical trajectories evolve; the derivation formalizes only the cost of operating in states where the policy lacks training support.
Writing \(\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi)\) and \(\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi^*)\) for the expected cumulative task costs of the learned policy \(\pi\) and expert policy \(\pi^*\) over those \(\BehaviorCloningHorizon\) steps, let \(\SingleStepImitationError\) bound the single-step action disagreement across expert-visited states under a 0–1 action loss: \(\mathbb{E}_{\DecisionProcessState \sim \ExpertStateVisitationDistribution} [\IndicatorFunction(\pi(\DecisionProcessState) \ne \pi^*(\DecisionProcessState))] \le \SingleStepImitationError\). Assuming per-step task costs lie in \([0,1]\), behavioral cloning admits the worst-case bound (equation 1) derived by Ross and Bagnell (2010) and restated by Ross et al. (2011): \[\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi)-\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi^*) \le \BehaviorCloningHorizon^2\SingleStepImitationError. \tag{1}\] The published theorem carries a constant of one rather than the sketch’s one half; both are worst-case bounds, and their quadratic dependence on the horizon is the same.
In practice, this theoretical bound can exceed the maximum possible cost achievable in a finite episode. Because per-step costs are bounded in \([0,1]\), the excess cost is trivially bounded by \(\BehaviorCloningHorizon\); hence, \(\min(\BehaviorCloningHorizon, \BehaviorCloningHorizon^2\SingleStepImitationError)\) represents the operational upper bound. Once the quadratic expression surpasses \(\BehaviorCloningHorizon\), it provides no meaningful prediction regarding physical failure rates or contact severity. The practical engineering value of this bound lies in exposing why behavioral cloning has no defense in states its demonstrations never reached, rather than in predicting exact physical collision rates.


↪ The full derivation of the quadratic bound, with its loss and cost assumptions, is developed in Imitation Learning and Compounding Covariate Shift.

Foster, Dylan J., Adam Block, and Dipendra Misra. 2024. “Is Behavior Cloning All You Need? Understanding Horizon in Imitation Learning.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 37: 120602–66. https://doi.org/10.52202/079017-3834.

Simchowitz, Max, Daniel Pfrommer, and Ali Jadbabaie. 2025. “The Pitfalls of Imitation Learning When Actions Are Continuous.” Proceedings of the Thirty Eighth Conference on Learning Theory (COLT), Proceedings of machine learning research, vol. 291: 5248–351.
The actual scaling with horizon length depends heavily on the chosen loss function, the action space, and the closed-loop plant stability. Consequently, equation 1 reflects a classical result for discrete 0–1 loss rather than an absolute law for all imitation architectures. When trained under logarithmic loss (minimizing the negative log-probability assigned to expert actions) over a well-specified policy class containing the expert, behavioral cloning can achieve a sample complexity that does not grow with the horizon length. This result holds provided total reward is bounded and the policy class capacity is controlled (Foster et al. 2024). Continuous action spaces, however, introduce the opposite challenge. Even when the physical closed loop is exponentially stable (small mechanical perturbations decay at a fixed rate) and the expert policy is smooth and deterministic, any smooth, deterministic imitator can accumulate closed-loop execution errors that scale exponentially with horizon length relative to its training loss (Simchowitz et al. 2025). The same analysis identifies two ways around this compounding (Simchowitz et al. 2025). The first changes the policy class. A policy that is non-smooth, that is non-Markovian (its action depends on recent history rather than solely the current observation), or whose action distribution is multimodal (it can place probability on several distinct actions at once, rather than averaging them) escapes the result. Action chunking and diffusion decoders have these properties. The second changes the data, using demonstrations deliberately spread across a wide tube surrounding the nominal trajectory. That second remedy is a data-collection decision, and section 5.8 returns to it as noise injection during teleoperation. Because the mobile manipulator operates in a continuous control space, closed-loop success ultimately hinges on whether the combined policy and low-level controllers actively restore a displaced gripper to the nominal path.


↩︎ Action chunking, in which the policy emits a short sequence of setpoints per inference, is established in Action chunking.
Collecting more nominal expert demonstrations does not resolve endogenous covariate shift. Adding another thousand hours of clean, centered door openings merely increases sample density along the nominal trajectory; the empirical support outside this narrow tube remains strictly zero (\(\ExpertStateVisitationDistribution(\DecisionProcessState) = 0\)). This pitfall is the nominal demonstration trap. Beyond this coverage limitation, logging physical robot experience carries direct hardware costs. While a web crawler scrapes static text with zero marginal mechanical wear, every recorded second of robot telemetry consumes actuator fatigue life, heats motor windings (\(d\WindingTemperature/d\TimeInstant\)), wears down gearbox teeth, and depletes battery reserves. In practical data-collection campaigns, required pauses for operator fatigue, sensor recalibration, scene resets, and discarded trials often leave less than one quarter of scheduled workcell time as usable demonstration data (section 5.6). Physical telemetry is scarce, wear-intensive, and costly; collecting it without modeling closed-loop recovery dynamics compromises policy training.


↩︎ Actuator thermal dissipation (\(d\WindingTemperature/d\TimeInstant\)) and winding damage limits are established in Thermal Duty Cycles.
A physical command also changes meaning as it crosses the control stack toward the actuators. In a system partitioned by the proposal boundary, an operator’s or policy’s requested action is mapped into a trajectory setpoint, checked and potentially clamped by the safety permission path, and executed by the physical plant to produce a measured response. Logging only the raw requested action trains the policy on commands the plant may be physically incapable of executing; logging only the measured plant response teaches the policy to copy link flexure, gear backlash, and contact stalls as if they were intentional human skill. A physical data-collection campaign must therefore settle two decisions before recording its first trajectory. The first is which collection path generates the actions (section 5.4). The second is which of the four representations of one command (the request, the mapped setpoint, the admitted command, or the measured response) the dataset preserves as its training label (section 5.5).


↩︎ The proposal boundary, which separates a learned proposer from the permission path that alone may admit an action, is established in The Machine in Five Levels.

title: Physical Data
section: 5.4 Physical Telemetry Sources and Collection Paths
text:
5.4 Physical Telemetry Sources and Collection Paths
When an engineer records demonstrations of the warehouse cage-door latch, the choice of collection rig decides which contact forces, hesitations, and recovery maneuvers ever reach the archive. Guiding the robot arm by hand gives the demonstrator direct tactile feel of the binding latch, but the demonstrator’s torso blocks the onboard cameras. Puppeteering the arm over a network clears the camera view, but display delay makes the operator inch forward in a stop-and-go hunt. Running a scripted spline produces clean, repeatable approaches that jam the moment the strike plate shifts by a millimeter. Because every attempt on the physical robot spends facility hours, joint life, and human effort, choosing a collection path trades collection cost against the behaviors the resulting archive can support. Seven collection paths appear in practice, six on physical hardware and a seventh in simulation:

In kinesthetic teaching, a colocated human demonstrator physically grasps and guides the unpowered or gravity-compensated links of the mechanism. The logging pipeline records joint encoder positions at the native controller rate without network transport delays. However, human biomechanics govern the motion’s bandwidth, moving far more slowly than the controller’s sampling loop, while labor costs scale \(1:1\) with demonstrator time. The demonstrator’s body also frequently occludes onboard camera views, introducing systematic visual distribution shifts relative to autonomous operation.
In teleoperation, a remote operator manipulates an input device to puppet the follower robot across a network fabric.2 Teleoperation interfaces differ in how operator inputs map to robot actuators and how much physical contact information reflects back to the human. Joint-space leader-follower arms such as ALOHA (Zhao et al. 2023) and GELLO (Wu et al. 2024) mirror the follower’s joint topology, often at reduced scale, streaming joint angles directly to the follower without inverse kinematics (computing the joint angles that place the tool at a commanded pose). In contrast, tracked spatial controllers and rate-controlled space mice command Cartesian tool poses or velocities that require inverse kinematics solvers at runtime, while force-reflecting bilateral arms actively transmit measured contact forces back to the operator’s hands. Table 2 compares these interfaces and names the artifact each leaves in the recording.
In scripted collection, a deterministic trajectory generator executes automated motion primitives, such as cubic splines or impedance-governed state machines. Ingestion rates are high and predictable (\(50\text{--}500\text{ Hz}\)), but trajectories traverse rigid, repetitive manifolds. Because these paths fail to generate corrective recovery data during off-nominal contact, the manipulator risks jamming whenever workpiece dimensions deviate by even a millimeter.
In exploratory collection, an active neural policy or reinforcement learning agent selects actions to maximize an information-theoretic objective, such as epistemic entropy or intrinsic curiosity. Although data throughput matches the robot’s peak policy cadence (\(50\text{--}100\text{ Hz}\)), unconstrained exploratory actions risk high-energy collisions, tripping hardware safety tripwires or degrading mechanical gearboxes through repeated high-torque shock loads.
In autonomous deployment logging, production policies control actuators during routine factory or warehouse operation, streaming multimodal telemetry into local circular buffers in situ. This channel yields zero-marginal-labor data at the system’s full execution rate (\(10\text{--}50\text{ Hz}\) for high-level policies, \(1\text{ kHz}\) for joint servos). However, runtime safety barriers heavily censor the recorded state distribution, capturing almost exclusively nominal operating regimes while excluding boundary failures.
In robot-free demonstration, the operator carries a hand-held gripper fitted with a wrist camera and performs tasks directly in the physical environment, as in the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) (Chi et al. 2024). Collection incurs zero robot operating hours or actuator wear, allowing a single demonstrator to gather data across locations where no robot is deployed. The engineering cost shifts to label synthesis: because the hand-held rig records its own Cartesian trajectory and visual feed without robot joint states, actions must be expressed relative to the gripper’s pose frame and executed downstream through the target robot’s controller. The deployed robot’s observation and actuation latencies must also be calibrated to match the recording timing (section 5.5.2).

2 Bilateral Telemanipulation: Raymond Goertz’s 1949 master-slave manipulator at Argonne National Laboratory moved tongs behind radiation shielding in exact correspondence with a master handle, and its mechanical linkage returned the forces at the tongs to the operator’s hand (Goertz 1949; Hokayem and Spong 2006). Remote manipulation therefore began with contact force inside the loop. A demonstration recorded through an interface that drops that force channel cannot contain the contact corrections the operator would have made by feel.
Goertz, Raymond C. 1949. Master-Slave Manipulator. ANL-4311. Argonne National Laboratory. https://doi.org/10.2172/1054625.

Hokayem, Peter F., and Mark W. Spong. 2006. “Bilateral Teleoperation: An Historical Survey.” Automatica 42 (12): 2035–57. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.automatica.2006.06.027.
A seventh source removes physical hardware entirely. Simulation pipelines eliminate mechanical wear by substituting a numerical contact model for the physical plant, generating synthetic demonstrations at scale. Trajectory generators can expand a few hundred human seed demonstrations across novel object poses and scene layouts, replaying them in physics engines to synthesize tens of thousands of varied trajectories (Mandlekar et al. 2023). Downstream policies can then co-train on simulated and real telemetry at a specified mixing ratio. However, these synthetic streams require rigorous metadata tagging: records must log their source generator, physics engine build, integrator step size, and contact solver parameters. The dataset’s scenario table, the list of required operating conditions that section 5.7.1 builds, must also flag every condition covered solely by synthetic rollouts, ensuring that training diagnostics can isolate simulation artifacts from measured physical plant behavior. The provenance requirements for synthetic telemetry appear under dataset degradation (section 5.10.2).
Because the collection source determines how the machine interacts with its physical environment, these data streams occupy disjoint state-action manifolds even when executing identical manipulation tasks. Consider releasing the warehouse mobile manipulator’s cage-door latch. A colocated demonstrator guiding the arm feels the latch bind through direct tactile resistance and immediately adjusts wrist compliance, whereas a remote teleoperator watching a compressed video stream lacks haptic feedback and falls into step-and-wait hunting, pausing repeatedly to check strike-plate contact. By contrast, a scripted controller advances along a fixed geometric path at constant velocity and produces the same rigid contact-force spike on every repetition, while an exploratory policy approaches at oblique angles that bind the latch until safety tripwires abort the trial. Far from representing noisy variations of a single ground-truth trajectory, these recorded streams reflect distinct dynamical systems with different bandwidths, transport latencies, and mechanical compliance profiles, as summarized in table 1.
