Spatial memory consumes this record to update its world model, while trajectory planning uses \(\ClearanceInset\) to inflate collision boundaries. Both modules evaluate evidence age, verify kinematic coordinate frames, and bound spatial uncertainty before allowing an observation to influence a control decision.
The tuple is the same object as the error-qualified claim \((\BodyFramePoint, \BodyFramePointCovariance, \ClearanceInset, \DispatchObservationAge)\) that section 8.6 assembled, now wrapped for transport. The claim’s point travels in \(\ObservationPayload\), its covariance in \(\BodyFramePointCovariance\), and its inset in \(\ClearanceInset\). Its age is deliberately not stored, because each consumer computes the current evidence age from \(\CaptureTimestamp\) and \(\ClockConversionBound\) on its own clock.
This contract does not replace binary serialization formats such as Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers, or ROS 2 IDL; any of these serialization systems can transmit the underlying struct over shared memory or bus fabrics. While transport schemas standardize memory layout and data types, the observation contract establishes verifiable physical invariants: monotonic temporal progression, bounded clock skew, active calibration validity windows, and rigorous spatial uncertainty limits. Table 5 serializes the tuple as named fields, details each one alongside its validation rule, and populates the schema for the mobile manipulator’s navigation camera. It splits \(\CaptureTimestamp\) and \(\text{clock\_id}\) into capture_timestamp_ns and capture_clock_id, carries the calibration behind \(\text{frame\_id}\) in calibration_metadata, and adds a sequence_index and a provenance_digest that the tuple leaves out.



Table 5: Observation contract schema: Compact fields needed to date and frame a claim, evaluate its uncertainty, bounding envelope, and health flags, and check the bytes and generating revision. The last column fills the fields this chapter computes for the mobile manipulator’s navigation camera; its dispatch age and clock-conversion bound are illustrative. A keyed authenticator is a separate requirement if the threat model includes malicious modification.

The fields detailed in table 5 anchor each observation in physical time, geometric space, and software revision history. The capture timestamp \(\CaptureTimestamp\) must refer to a strictly monotonic hardware timer rather than wall-clock time (such as nanoseconds since the UNIX epoch), which remains vulnerable to stepping backward during network time adjustments. Because rolling-shutter sensors read out scan lines sequentially, any spatial claim derived from a rolling-shutter imager must explicitly identify the image row or region corresponding to that capture instant. The transport-level sequence_index counter detects frame drops and out-of-order deliveries directly on the bus, independently of clock readings. When the safety MCU operates in a separate clock domain from the camera host, an active synchronization daemon provides a versioned affine mapping \(\MicrocontrollerClockTime = \ClockConversionSlope \CaptureTimestamp + \ClockConversionIntercept\), an expiration window, and an empirical sync-error bound \(\ClockConversionBound\), characterized as described in section 8.6.2.
Systems engineering demands precise conventions when accounting for sensor latency. The handoff matrix and the perception latency budget evaluate the sensor’s latency contribution under different row conventions, and the observation contract must explicitly state which convention governs the record. The handoff matrix allots \(\SignalHandoff_1\) one frame period (16.7 ms at 60 Hz) and references the entire frame by its middle row. Because rolling-shutter rows stagger their exposures at the exact rate they read out, the middle row finishes its own exposure halfway through the frame’s readout window and waits only the remaining \(\SensorReadoutTime/2\) for the bottom half of the array to clock off the die, so measuring from that middle row’s exposure midpoint to the completion of sensor readout yields a sensor-side latency of \(\ExposureDuration/2 + \SensorReadoutTime/2 =\) 16.3 ms, which falls well within the handoff allotment. Conversely, the perception latency waterfall charges for the top row: \(\ExposureDuration/2 + \SensorReadoutTime =\) 24.6 ms. Because a physical hazard such as a warehouse rack upright can appear in the very first scan lines, a safety-certified stopping budget must charge for the oldest sensory evidence underpinning the spatial claim. Under this oldest-row convention, the navigation camera exceeds the handoff allotment by 7.9 ms. The two numbers answer different questions, and the stopping budget governs. The \(\SignalHandoff_1\) allotment is a design budget for the sensing handoff, stated in the middle-row convention, and the camera meets it. The safety charge is row five, which uses this chapter’s oldest-row waterfall. The 7.9 ms is already inside the 51.6 ms that row five charges, so nothing is missing from the stopping budget. What the mismatch does require is a record that says which convention dated it. The capture metadata therefore stamps the reference row index, so that a consumer checking \(\SignalHandoff_1\) and a consumer checking clearance each read the age they need from the same field.
Upon dispatching an observation, the producer records an upper bound on its observation age at dispatch as \(\McuDispatchTime - \McuCaptureTime + \ClockConversionBound\). That metric reflects only the latency accumulated up to the producer’s egress boundary. By the time the permission path admits the record, the evidence has aged further by the dispatch-to-admission transit delay \(\DispatchAdmissionInterval\), and it ages further still before actuators execute a command. The permission path must evaluate freshness using its local monotonic clock against the original capture epoch; treating a static dispatch timestamp as if time had frozen violates basic physical causality. Submitting a new trajectory proposal derived from a previously buffered observation does not refresh the underlying sensory evidence.
For the navigation camera, the dispatch-local threshold equals the budgeted observation age 51.6 ms plus the 0.2 ms clock-conversion bound, yielding 51.8 ms. The threshold sits exactly at the budget because row five of the stopping budget charges exactly that age; admitting an older frame would spend travel that no row accounts for. A frame that meets every stage budget therefore reaches dispatch with zero spare margin, and any host contention, pipeline queuing, or batching beyond those budgets pushes it past the threshold. The stage values are allocations each stage must meet at its tail, not typical latencies, so a pipeline that meets them refuses only the frames that overrun them. In the vehicle’s stopping budget, the 51.6 ms perception delay maps directly to physical travel distance at cruising velocity. The 0.3 mm displacement associated with the clock-conversion uncertainty bound is absorbed into the localization uncertainty parameter \(\LocalizationBound\). Neither accounting choice eliminates the ongoing physical aging that occurs after dispatch.
Admitting an observation into the motion-planning safety pipeline requires an empirically qualified current-age limit that accounts for the dispatch-to-admission bound \(\DispatchAdmissionInterval\) while reserving sufficient execution time for the active motion lease and physical braking response. Because this partial budget has not yet bounded \(\DispatchAdmissionInterval\), the populated record in table 5 illustrates correct structural field construction rather than an admitted full-speed trajectory. Once engineers measure and bound \(\DispatchAdmissionInterval\) across all inter-process channels, they can either close the stopping budget or reduce maximum vehicle velocity to restore safety margins. Latency accounting conserves time. Whether an engineer anchors the timeline at physical capture or measures from the admission gate by summing prior evidence age with the active lease, each elapsed interval appears exactly once in the stopping budget.
The transform identifier sensor_frame_id and its calibration revision key the observation into the robot’s kinematic transform tree.14 The provenance digest records the exact SHA-256 hash of the vision model weights and camera firmware, providing an auditable record of software configuration. Concurrently, payload_crc32 guards against transmission glitches across shared-memory rings or serial buses. Data integrity is not semantic truth. Checksums and build digests detect accidental bit flips and firmware mismatches, but they cannot verify whether an image is optically uncorrupted, nor do they prevent adversarial tampering without a keyed cryptographic signature.
14 Stereo Baseline Thermal Drift: For a stereo baseline \(\StereoBaseline =\) 0.20 m and an unmodeled change \(|\SmallPerturbation \StereoBaseline| =\) 0.1 mm, first-order geometry gives \(|\SmallPerturbation \CameraFrameDepth|/\CameraFrameDepth\approx|\SmallPerturbation \StereoBaseline|/\StereoBaseline\). At \(\CameraFrameDepth =\) 20 m, the corresponding depth bias is about 10 mm, assuming focal length and disparity are otherwise unchanged. Temperature compensation must be checked against the actual mount and calibration.The health_bitmask structures failure reporting across three architectural layers. The lowest bits report hardware-level faults, such as clock synchronization loss, DMA ring buffer overruns, or physical link dropouts. The intermediate bits signal environmental degradation, including sensor saturation from direct sunlight, optical blooming, and aerosol backscatter from dust or fog. The upper bits represent perceptual validity concerns, such as severe field-of-view occlusion or out-of-distribution (OOD) sensory inputs that fall outside the training support tested during system evaluation. When any safety-critical bit is set, downstream motion planners and trackers must immediately reject spatial claims derived from that frame.
An explicit observation schema also creates a systematic interface for automated fault injection. Verification harnesses can deterministically alter capture timestamps, drop sequence numbers, artificially inflate covariance diagonals, or assert occlusion bits, confirming that downstream consumers reject or gracefully degrade unviable observations within their budgeted time limits. These software mutations demonstrate consumer responses for the tested corruptions under the tested budgets; evaluating resilience against physical phenomena such as optical flare, mounting deflection, and actuator dynamics requires hardware-in-the-loop testing regimes.


↪ Hardware-in-the-loop testing of physical phenomena is developed in Fault Injection on Hardware.

Brohan, Anthony, Noah Brown, Justice Carbajal, Yevgen Chebotar, Xi Chen, Krzysztof Choromanski, Tianli Ding, et al. 2023. “RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2307.15818.

Kim, Moo Jin, Karl Pertsch, Siddharth Karamcheti, Ted Xiao, Ashwin Balakrishna, Suraj Nair, Rafael Rafailov, et al. 2024. “OpenVLA: An Open-Source Vision-Language-Action Model.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2406.09246.

Black, Kevin, Noah Brown, Danny Driess, Adnan Esmail, Michael Equi, Chelsea Finn, Niccolo Fusai, et al. 2024. “\(\pi_0\): A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2410.24164.
Learned policies require explicit contract metadata just as much as classical state estimators do. An end-to-end policy \(\CognitivePolicyAction_{t} = \pi(\CapturedSensorObservation)\) that receives only sensory pixels or point clouds cannot distinguish two identical images consumed under radically different pipeline latencies. Widely used vision-language-action (VLA) models do not receive these quantities. RT-2 and OpenVLA condition on visual tokens and a language prompt (Brohan et al. 2023; Kim et al. 2024), and \(\pi_0\) adds proprioceptive joint state (Black et al. 2024), but none of them is given capture age, extrinsic transforms, or measurement covariance as input. To integrate learned models safely into real-time control loops, this book presents an observation tokenizer that projects the full observation contract into the token space of a VLA policy or neural estimator. The sensory modality dictates the raw payload encoding (patch tokens from vision transformers, range tokens from lidar arrays, spike tokens from event cameras, or stress fields from tactile arrays), while the tokenizer interface preserves the capture epoch, geometric frame, and measurement uncertainty associated with that payload.
Under this architecture, the observation tokenizer pairs the sensory feature tokens \(\SensorFeatureTokens\) with continuous Fourier temporal embeddings (\(\CaptureAgeEmbedding = \text{Fourier}(\CurrentWallClockTime - \TimeInstant_0)\)), coordinate frame prefix embeddings (\(\CoordinateFrameEmbedding = \text{MLP}(\CameraExtrinsicTransform)\)), and spatial covariance embeddings (\(\SpatialCovarianceEmbedding = \text{MLP}(\text{vec}(\BodyFramePointCovariance))\)) (equation 13): \[\ObservationTokenSequence = [\SensorFeatureTokens, \CaptureAgeEmbedding, \CoordinateFrameEmbedding, \SpatialCovarianceEmbedding] \tag{13}\] A forward-propagated state token \(\PredictedStateEmbedding = \text{MLP}(\CurrentStateEstimate)\), generated by the state estimator that spatial memory maintains, can accompany these tokens so the policy conditions on the robot’s predicted state at the instant of actuation rather than its historical configuration at sensor exposure. Because the observation contract preserves the exact capture epoch, delayed frames do not become worthless garbage. When network congestion or compute preemption delays delivery, a state estimator can ingest an out-of-order observation at the precise historical instant it captured and propagate corrections forward to the current state, a technique that spatial memory develops in Applying a delayed observation. While this embedding scheme exposes physical time, frame geometry, and uncertainty directly to transformer attention layers, engineers must verify that the model actually attends to these tokens in closed-loop operation. Demonstrating that a policy uses temporal embeddings requires rigorous ablation experiments that inject artificial latency into held-out evaluation trials and measure resulting closed-loop tracking error. Embedding metadata as neural tokens also does not substitute for deterministic safety gating. The permission path must continue to verify clock bounds, extrinsic calibration envelopes, innovation residuals (the gap between each measurement and the estimator’s prediction of it), and health status bits before any network output is permitted to drive the physical actuators.

Checkpoint 8.3: Observation contract checks
A consumer can refuse only what the record lets it check, and it must check before it reads the payload.

Record triage: Can you explain why a health bit, checksum, valid clock conversion, and freshness check must precede consumption of a spatial claim?
Timestamp corruption vs. dropped packets: Can you describe why receiving a sensory frame with a desynchronized timestamp degrades spatial state estimation and policy grounding far more severely than dropping the packet entirely?
Deterministic fault injection: Can you distinguish between physically perturbing optical sensors vs. deterministically mutating fields in the shared-memory observation contract during automated hardware-in-the-loop verification?
Age on the consumer’s clock: Can you explain why the permission path must recompute evidence age on its own monotonic clock from the capture epoch, rather than trusting the age stamped at dispatch, and why its 51.8 ms dispatch-local threshold is not the limit it applies at admission?

title: Sensor Perception
text:
8.9 Fallacies and Pitfalls
Passing contract triage and computing state updates still does not make an observation semantically true in the physical world, and the most common perception errors come from treating a syntactically valid record as a statement about the present scene. Perception must describe the physical world within the strict temporal deadlines demanded by closed-loop control. In embodied systems, high semantic confidence and fine spatial resolution cannot compensate for pipelines that deliver stale observations, fuse asynchronous exposures, or treat average I/O bandwidth as a bound on single-frame latency.

Fallacy: Accepting an observation because its semantic classification confidence is high, regardless of its age.
Consider a mobile manipulator that receives an observation indicating with high semantic confidence that the rack end ahead is clear. If a scheduling stall in the vision pipeline delivers that observation several frames late, a warehouse worker who stepped into the aisle after the camera exposure will not appear in the image. The confidence score describes only the classifier’s assessment of past sensory input, not current physical clearance. Treating an overdue packet as present state risks commanding actuators directly into occupied space. The perception interface must verify measurement age against its freshness limit (section 8.8) and reject observations that exceed the threshold. Furthermore, any state propagation that continues without fresh data must inflate kinematic uncertainty covariances, incorporating heavy-tailed residuals or reachability bounds on dynamic obstacles. This growth forces downstream controllers to contract their safety envelopes and slow the robot as sensory evidence ages. High softmax confidence reflects internal model certainty on an acquired image, but it guarantees neither temporal freshness nor true physical clearance.


Pitfall: Fusing multi-sensor observations without a clock bound derived from the tolerated spatial error.
Suppose two cameras on the mobile manipulator observe the same rack upright while the mobile base travels at its 1.5 m/s velocity limit, but their internal clocks differ by an uncorrected skew \(\InterSensorClockSkew\). If downstream fusion treats the two exposure times as simultaneous, the physical upright appears displaced by \(\BodySpeed\,\InterSensorClockSkew\) between the two sensor frames. Downstream track association can split this single physical obstacle into two conflicting tracks (“ghosting”), corrupting the world model. Spatial calibration cannot correct an uncharacterized temporal offset. Instead, the allowable clock synchronization error must follow directly from the tolerated spatial position error \(\ToleratedPositionError\) and the maximum operational velocity \(\SpeedBound\), yielding the relation \(\InterSensorClockSkew \le \ToleratedPositionError / \SpeedBound\). Hardware synchronization at exposure time makes that bound enforceable. Selecting a network timing technology such as the IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP) without first deriving this spatial error budget leaves the sensor fusion pipeline ungrounded.


Pitfall: Inferring a critical read’s deadline from average camera bandwidth.
A comfortable average utilization figure says nothing about how long a critical read stalls behind synchronized sensor capture and inference bursts. On the mobile manipulator, safety permission checks execute on a dedicated real-time microcontroller reading from local memory, shielding the immediate control path from host bus contention. The danger instead appears on the application processor, where concurrent DMA transfers, memory bus saturation, and inference bursts delay the sensor ingestion pipeline (section 8.5). This contention inflates the capture-to-dispatch age of the perceptual observation and stretches the renewal interval between successive updates. System architects must verify worst-case capture-to-dispatch age and end-to-end renewal intervals under peak burst conditions rather than relying on average throughput metrics.


Fallacy: Assuming an end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy implicitly learns to compensate for rolling shutter and sensor latency without explicit temporal tokenization.
Deep imitation learning often assumes that large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies trained on extensive robot teleoperation datasets will automatically learn action corrections that compensate for sensor distortion and communication latency. In practice, demonstration datasets aggregate trajectories collected across fluctuating chassis velocities, camera frame rates, and host bus loads. If the model receives only raw pixel arrays without capture timestamps or row readout schedules, it cannot distinguish true physical obstacle geometry from rolling-shutter scanline shear or motion lag. Unresolved temporal ambiguity degrades closed-loop trajectory tracking and induces control oscillations. The quadratic compounding bound of equation 5.1 describes how per-step imitation error grows over a horizon, but it assumes a stationary Markov process rather than unmodeled phase lags and sensor dynamics. Providing explicit timing metadata, such as capture time deltas (\(\FiniteChange \TimeInstant = \CurrentWallClockTime - \TimeInstant_0\)), readout offsets, and forward-propagated kinematic states, gives the network the causal context required to resolve these distortions. Even with temporal tokenization, empirical evaluation must verify closed-loop stability, and independent out-of-band safety permission checks remain mandatory.


Pitfall: Treating neural depth network outputs as calibrated geometric covariances without empirical residual validation.
Monocular depth estimation backbones and bird’s-eye-view (BEV) lifting transformers output continuous depth fields or discrete depth-bin categorical distributions. Engineers often mistake these softmax spreads or secondary network confidence heads for calibrated geometric uncertainties (\(\BodyFramePointCovariance\)), passing them directly into a state estimator such as an extended Kalman filter or a safety filter such as a control barrier function. In practice, raw neural confidence scores correlate poorly with true physical error distributions. When presented with unfamiliar textures, specular reflections, or occluding object silhouettes, depth networks produce gross multimodal outliers that deviate by tens of standard deviations from physical ground truth. Downstream clearance insets (\(\ClearanceInset\)) must never rely on raw neural variance. Safe execution requires empirical validation against heavy-tailed residual distributions and hard spatial bounds cross-verified by active ranging sensors such as LiDAR or radar.


Pitfall: Relying exclusively on line-of-sight optical sensing for manipulation without tactile contact feedback.
During reaches and grasps, the robot’s own fingers, palm, and wrist occlude the contact interface. Optical cameras cannot observe local normal forces, shear stress distributions, or incipient micro-slip at the boundary between the gripper and the object. Relying exclusively on high-resolution visual perception to ensure grasp stability leads to dropped objects from undetected slipping or crushed workpieces from excessive actuator torque. Tasks that involve physical interaction and delicate object handling require direct contact feedback. Elastomeric tactile sensors and optical skin arrays can track surface shear and incipient micro-slip, while other applications may rely on wrist force-torque transducers, compliant passive mechanics, or fixtured tooling. Sensor selection must reflect the physical contact dynamics of the manipulation task rather than defaulting to line-of-sight optical cameras.


Fallacy: Assuming active LiDAR and depth sensors are immune to specular reflections and multipath interference in built environments.
A common misconception is that active time-of-flight LiDAR and depth sensors are immune to optical artifacts because they project their own structured energy. In industrial facilities and built environments, surfaces routinely violate the diffuse Lambertian scattering assumption. Polished concrete floors, metallic shelving, architectural glass partitions, and shrink-wrapped pallet freight cause severe specular reflection. Emitted laser pulses deflect away from the receiver at shallow incidence angles, causing complete signal loss and creating artificial dropouts (“puddle black holes”) on polished or wet floors. Conversely, multi-bounce reflections bounce pulses across multiple reflective surfaces before returning to the detector, generating phantom obstacles that appear meters behind solid walls or beneath the floor plane. The observation pipeline must validate return intensity distributions and cross-corroborate surface geometry against complementary inertial and radar channels.

title: Sensor Perception
text:
8.10 Summary
A perception measurement is actionable only when its capture epoch, clock synchronization bound, coordinate frame, and spatial uncertainty match the kinematic requirements of the intended motion. Sensor selection begins with the physical quantity demanded by the control decision: photometric appearance, metric range, Doppler radial velocity, or contact deformation. Physical capture constraints then determine the exact temporal and geometric validity of that measurement. For rolling-shutter cameras, row-by-row readout creates geometric distortion that must be compensated before triangulation, while an optical bearing ray provides directional bearing but no distance until stereo disparity or active time-of-flight ranging resolves depth. Furthermore, calibration matrices remain valid only within the physical and environmental envelopes under which they were characterized. Latency between exposure and downstream dispatch directly consumes the vehicle’s stopping budget. At the drive limit, the first five rows of that budget leave 187.1 mm of the 1.10 m clear distance, a remainder that must still absorb the dispatch-to-admission interval, the jerk-limited stop, and the tracking inset. Whether the machine may drive at that speed is therefore a question this chapter hands forward to The board-link budget and the dispatch-to-admission interval and Stopping Envelopes, which close the budget. The warehouse mobile manipulator's stopping budget lists every term with the chapter that prices it. Because an embodied system continues to travel while sensor data moves through serialization, transport, neural inference, and planner admission, unmeasured pipeline delays erode physical clearance margins just as severely as spatial measurement error.
Spatial error deducts from that same physical clearance budget. Stereo depth uncertainty scales quadratically with distance under fixed disparity noise, while angular extrinsic misalignment introduces lever-arm errors that widen linearly with range. System designers cannot rely on nominal datasheets or raw model outputs to establish safety bounds. Zero-mean covariance matrices frequently ignore systematic calibration biases, and classification confidences or learned depth logits do not represent calibrated tail probabilities. Establishing a rigorous 99th-percentile clearance inset requires empirical residual quantiles evaluated directly against ground-truth measurements across the operational domain. Perception delivers individual dated, localized, and qualified measurements; integrating these discrete observations into a coherent state estimate that remains reliable between sensor arrivals is the responsibility of spatial memory.
Silent failures present the most severe operational hazards in physical systems, precisely because dropped frames or overt hardware faults trigger immediate system alerts, whereas misdated frames, saturated detectors, or hallucinated traversable paths arrive without raising error flags. To guard against corrupted data, the perception pipeline enforces an explicit observation contract. Downstream consumers inspect and validate the capture timestamp, clock synchronization bound, reference frame, calibration identifier, error model, and hardware health flags before reading payload buffers. Even with rigorous contracts, confirming semantic truth requires corroboration across independent, complementary sensing modalities. Seven relations carry the chapter’s quantitative argument, and table 6 records what each bounds or decides.

Key Takeaways: Spatial perception and age of information

Observation age begins at capture and is paid in travel: Hardware-latched exposure timestamps, row readout schedules, and bounded clock conversion enable downstream consumers to compute a qualified upper age bound. Every microsecond elapsed from photon arrival to actuator response translates directly into unobserved travel (\(\BlindTravelDistance = \SpeedAtDetection \cdot \PrebrakeDelay\)) deducted from the physical clearance margin.
Choose the measurement for the decision: Photometric appearance, metric range, Doppler radial velocity, high-rate edge transitions, and tactile contact deformation address distinct physical questions. Multi-sensor fusion improves system resilience only when sensor spatial coverage and correlated common-cause failure modes are rigorously qualified.
Fix the geometry before interpreting it: Rolling-shutter readout shears geometric edges under vehicle motion (\(\FiniteChange \CartesianXCoordinate = \BaseTravelSpeed \cdot \SensorRowIndex \cdot \RollingShutterRowReadout\)), requiring per-row pose compensation prior to spatial triangulation. Mechanical vibration and thermal cycling also induce extrinsic calibration drift. An extrinsic shift of 0.005 rad at 10 m projects to 50 mm laterally, as large as the entire localization allowance \(\LocalizationBound\). Consequently, every calibration record must carry an explicit validity envelope that consumers verify prior to inference.
A wrong timestamp is worse than a lost frame: A dropped frame is an overt failure that triggering systems can handle gracefully, whereas a plausible but misdated frame silently displaces an obstacle’s reconstructed position while reporting deceptively narrow uncertainty. Hardware capture timestamps, clock synchronization error bounds, sequence continuity checks, and age validation must always precede payload interpretation.
Claimed error must be measured: Softmax classification confidences and depth-bin logits do not characterize spatial tail risk, and zero-mean covariance matrices fail to capture systematic calibration bias. Bounding collision risk requires empirical residual quantiles evaluated against high-precision ground truth across operational conditions to establish defensible clearance insets.
The contract bounds what a consumer can refuse: The observation contract packages capture epoch, clock conversion bounds, reference frame, calibration identity, error bounds, and hardware health flags so the planning permission path can reject untrustworthy claims before reading payload data. Even a fully operational sensor can report a clear path that does not exist, and structured observation tokens do not guarantee that downstream policies compensate for transport latency. Establishing semantic truth requires independent cross-modal verification, and spatial memory must synthesize these dated snapshots into a coherent state that persists through occlusion.



Perception supplies the grounded evidence that physical action needs: detected obstacles, identified affordances, and measured range and velocity across complementary modalities. Its output is still a sequence of isolated measurements, each bound to a capture epoch and a sensor frame, and each qualified for the instant it was captured. A qualified measurement states where something was, how old that knowledge is, and how far to trust it. It never states where that thing is now, and when a worker steps behind a rack upright, direct perception falls silent.
The observation contract is where Part III’s law, proposal is not permission, first takes physical form. A confident detection does not grant permission to move. The permission path admits motion only on evidence whose age, frame, and error it can check against the clearance that remains, and it refuses everything else before reading the payload. Every later stage in this part inherits that discipline, because each one consumes a dated claim that it did not produce and cannot refresh.

title: Sensor Perception
text:
8.11 Historical Perspective and Further Reading
The geometric foundations of computer vision trace back to photogrammetry and geodesy, where surveyors established rigorous mathematical formulations for optical distortion and perspective projection long before digital processors or mobile robots existed. In the late 1980s, Tsai (1987) made accurate geometric calibration feasible on off-the-shelf industrial cameras and lenses by developing computationally efficient two-stage optimization algorithms. A decade later, Zhang (2000) democratized the process by demonstrating that a camera could recover its intrinsic parameters and radial distortion from a planar checkerboard pattern observed at several unconstrained orientations. This formulation transformed camera calibration from an exotic cleanroom procedure into a practical workshop routine. Concurrently, Hartley and Zisserman (2003) codified the multiple-view projective geometry that underpins stereo disparity, epipolar constraints, and triangulation error. As cameras mounted directly onto robotic manipulators, hand-eye calibration techniques (Shiu and Ahmad 1989; Tsai and Lenz 1989) resolved the rigid kinematic transformations relating camera frames to robot end-effectors. Furgale et al. (2013) generalized this problem to continuous-time systems by integrating temporal delay estimation directly into spatial extrinsics, demonstrating that camera-to-inertial sensor time offsets must be estimated as dynamic parameters rather than assumed to be zero. Together, these developments established that sensor calibration is never a static constant retrieved from an assembly drawing, but an evolving state estimate bounded by physical drift, mechanical compliance, and thermal expansion.

Tsai, Roger Y. 1987. “A Versatile Camera Calibration Technique for High-Accuracy 3D Machine Vision Metrology Using Off-the-Shelf TV Cameras and Lenses.” IEEE Journal on Robotics and Automation 3 (4): 323–44. https://doi.org/10.1109/JRA.1987.1087109.

Thrun, Sebastian, Mike Montemerlo, Hendrik Dahlkamp, David Stavens, Andrei Aron, James Diebel, Philip Fong, et al. 2006. “Stanley: The Robot That Won the DARPA Grand Challenge.” Journal of Field Robotics 23 (9): 661–92. https://doi.org/10.1002/rob.20147.

Lamport, Leslie. 1978. “Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System.” Communications of the ACM 21 (7): 558–65. https://doi.org/10.1145/359545.359563.

IEEE. 2002. IEEE Std 1588-2002: IEEE Standard for a Precision Clock Synchronization Protocol for Networked Measurement and Control Systems. IEEE. https://doi.org/10.1109/IEEESTD.2002.94144.

IEEE. 2020a. IEEE Std 1588-2019: IEEE Standard for a Precision Clock Synchronization Protocol for Networked Measurement and Control Systems. Institute of Electrical; Electronics Engineers. https://doi.org/10.1109/IEEESTD.2020.9120376.
Sensor hardware diversified along a parallel trajectory as real-time autonomy demanded richer, faster environmental feedback. The autonomous driving competitions of the mid-2000s established scanning laser rangefinders as the primary metric sensor for navigation in unstructured environments (Thrun et al. 2006). Mechanically spinning multi-beam LiDAR systems delivered direct, dense depth measurements, yet their physical rotation introduced significant motion distortion across individual scan lines, which requires per-point timestamping and motion unwinding as detailed in section 8.4.2. To overcome the bandwidth and latency limits of synchronous frame-based sensing, neuromorphic engineering (Mead 1990) introduced event-based vision sensors featuring independent pixels that emit asynchronous signals only when local log-intensity changes exceed a threshold (Lichtsteiner et al. 2008). Over the subsequent decade, algorithmic frameworks for event cameras (Gallego et al. 2022) revealed their microsecond-level temporal resolution and high dynamic range. The same work exposed their central limitation, complete blindness to static scenes in the absence of relative motion. Operating several high-rate sensors of different types at once required rethinking temporal coordination. Clock synchronization had evolved as a classical problem in distributed computer systems (Lamport 1978), but physical embodiment demanded hardware-level precision. The IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (IEEE 2002, 2020a) addressed this requirement by embedding hardware timestamping directly into the network physical layer, enabling modern LiDARs, cameras, and compute nodes to align their measurement epochs to a shared master clock that real-time safety monitors can verify.
The third pillar of reliable physical perception is the formal qualification of error. Traditional robotic state estimation frequently assumed Gaussian noise models that systematically underestimated the probability of catastrophic tracking failures in complex environments. Conformal prediction (Vovk et al. 2005) addressed this vulnerability by proving that exchangeable calibration residuals yield distribution-free prediction regions with exact, non-asymptotic coverage guarantees. Angelopoulos and Bates (2023) made these theoretical foundations accessible to systems practitioners, establishing split-conformal methods as practical tools for safety-critical clearance verification. Observation contracts unite these three lineages. Each contract packages recent calibration revisions, formal network synchronization bounds, and empirical residual distributions. Downstream planning controllers and safety monitors can verify these empirical bounds explicitly rather than placing blind trust in raw transducer outputs.

Vovk, Vladimir, Alex Gammerman, and Glenn Shafer. 2005. Algorithmic Learning in a Random World. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/b106715.
For further reading, six foundational works elaborate on the geometric modeling, hardware timing, and statistical error qualification developed across this chapter:

Hartley and Zisserman (2003) is the classic reference for projective geometry, epipolar constraints, and triangulation, providing the theoretical basis for the stereo depth uncertainty relations analyzed in section 8.6.
Szeliski (2022) offers an exhaustive survey of computational image formation, camera calibration, and stereo correspondence from the computer vision perspective, detailing the optical aberrations and sensor transduction phenomena underlying section 8.2.
Zhang (2000) presents the ubiquitous planar-pattern calibration method, outlining the closed-form solutions and nonlinear refinement procedures that generate the intrinsic calibration records used throughout production pipelines.
Furgale et al. (2013) demonstrates continuous-time batch state estimation for multi-sensor suites, proving why temporal offsets between cameras and inertial measurement units must be modeled and optimized as explicit unknowns.
Gallego et al. (2022) provides a thorough review of event-based sensing, tracing hardware architectures from analog pixel circuitry to contemporary tracking and SLAM algorithms while outlining the latency-bandwidth trade-offs relevant to high-speed robotic safety.
Angelopoulos and Bates (2023) serves as a lucid, practical guide to conformal prediction and distribution-free risk control, clearly articulating the exchangeability conditions that physical distribution shifts such as floor wear, rain, or abrupt lighting changes can compromise in real-world deployment.


Hartley, Richard, and Andrew Zisserman. 2003. Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision. Cambridge university press.

Szeliski, Richard. 2022. Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications. 2nd ed. Springer.

Zhang, Zhengyou. 2000. “A Flexible New Technique for Camera Calibration.” IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence 22 (11): 1330–34. https://doi.org/10.1109/34.888718.

Furgale, Paul, Joern Rehder, and Roland Siegwart. 2013. “Unified Temporal and Spatial Calibration for Multi-Sensor Systems.” 2013 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS), 1280–86.

Gallego, Guillermo, Tobi Delbruck, Garrick Orchard, Chiara Bartolozzi, Brian Taba, Andrea Censi, Stefan Leutenegger, et al. 2022. “Event-Based Vision: A Survey.” IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence 44 (1): 154–80. https://doi.org/10.1109/TPAMI.2020.3008413.

Angelopoulos, Anastasios N., and Stephen Bates. 2023. “Conformal Prediction: A Gentle Introduction.” Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning 16 (4): 494–591. https://doi.org/10.1561/2200000101.

What’s Next: From sensory photons to spatial memoryHow long may a dated measurement keep authorizing motion after the scene that produced it goes out of view? Perception answers only for the instant of capture. When the mobile manipulator pivots past a rack upright, the cross aisle leaves the cameras’ view, and a worker can step into the corridor that the last frame recorded as clear. Spatial Memory takes the observation contracts this chapter produced and fuses them, each at its own capture epoch, into a state estimate whose uncertainty grows while no new evidence arrives. That growth sets the deadline after which a remembered empty aisle can no longer support motion, and past that deadline the permission path refuses any proposal that relies on it.

title: Grounded Intent
text:
Purpose



Physical AI stack focus for this chapter.
Why is recognizing the right object insufficient to authorize a robot to reach for it?
A spoken request names an outcome, not a motion. Between the word and the grasp lie questions no label settles: which feature of the object to touch, where that feature sits in metric space, how hard to squeeze it, and how long the observation behind the answer stays true. A model can name the right object while misplacing its handle by more than the gripper tolerates, can locate it precisely a moment before a conveyor carries it away, or can report high confidence about the wrong object altogether. Once any of these answers becomes a coordinate it looks exactly like a correct one, and the drive that tracks it cannot tell the difference, so a machine that lets such a proposal command motion turns an error in meaning or timing into force against ceramic, glass, or a person. A learned target is safe to pursue only when it arrives bounded in space, effort, and time, with refusal available whenever the evidence cannot support it. Those bounds keep learned intent on the proposal side of the causal boundary, where a mistake can still be refused rather than delivered as motion that cannot be undone.


Learning Objectives

Ground natural-language directives and symbolic task operators into metric affordance frames, continuous motion predicates, and verified geometric goal sets
Emit the intent lease from parent belief records with explicit error envelopes, task tolerances, and effort ceilings
Calculate intent lease expiry as the earliest of the evidence horizon, the administrative lease, and the stopping deadline
Decide when grounding ambiguity or a wrong-object premise requires refusal rather than admission
Evaluate terminal reachability within one evidence window, screen approach corridors against the forward occupancy of moving people, and select guarded, renewed stages for a longer approach
Design hardware lease expiry that revokes motion authority even when the issuing process hangs or crashes

title: Grounded Intent
text:
10.1 Grounded Affordances
An operator tells the warehouse mobile manipulator to “pick the red mug” from an active takeaway conveyor. The request names an outcome and leaves the grasp pose, approach velocity, contact force, and execution deadline unspecified. Spatial memory has already done its part by recording a belief about the mug’s handle with an evidence epoch, an initial error of 3 mm, and a growth law. Under that law, the moving belt carries the handle outside the 15 mm grasp tolerance 60 ms after capture. Because that record says only where the handle is and how long the claim holds, it neither specifies what the machine may do with the handle nor authorizes actuator torque. Intent bridges this gap by binding the spoken request to an admissible, time-bounded physical goal that the motion planner can pursue.


↩︎ The belief record a lease consumes (evidence epoch, initial error, growth law) is established in The Belief Record Schema.
The reach does not stay inside the arm. On the running machine a slow intent model sits above a fast chunk policy that proposes base velocity and arm targets together in one whole-body stream (Two proposers and the evidence horizon). A wrong or stale mug target can steer the base as well as the wrist. What the permission path grants in answer to the request is therefore deliberately narrower than motion. It grants an intent lease (section 10.8), a record that names a target and effort ceilings but never a path. For the mug, the lease binds the parent belief record’s digest and evidence epoch to a target pose in the handle’s affordance frame, a goal region of spatial and angular tolerances around that pose, and ceilings on tool speed, acceleration, and contact wrench. Alongside those geometric and dynamic bounds, it records the motion predicates already validated, an expiration deadline on the safety controller’s own clock, and the fallback that controller engages when the deadline passes.
Friction cones, force closure, and symbolic planners matter in this layer only because each supplies a field that the safety controller can check without re-running the upstream model: grasp mechanics fix the target pose, goal region, and wrench ceiling below; task operators (section 10.2) and open-vocabulary grounding (section 10.3) determine which predicates and error envelopes accompany a candidate target; and belief drift (section 10.5) paired with kinematic reachability (section 10.6) bounds the expiration deadline and dynamic limits.
This grounding step is where a learned model’s output first turns into physical coordinates and contact limits that the robot can execute. Open-vocabulary object detectors, language models, and vision-language-action policies let operators specify manipulation tasks in plain words rather than through hard-coded skill libraries. What those neural networks emit, however, is only a statistical hypothesis, such as a bounding box, a semantic token, an uncalibrated point coordinate, or a chunk of normalized actions. An objective function that knows nothing of metric clearance, actuator torque limits, or physical time produced it. On the running machine, the division of responsibility is therefore strict: the learned Brain proposes candidate actions, and the deterministic permission path checks and admits them before any drive receives current.


↩︎ The proposal boundary and the permission path are established in The Machine in Five Levels.
Before the permission path admits a proposed target for planning and execution, the target must satisfy three physical requirements:

Metric physicality: The target cannot remain a symbolic label; it must resolve to an explicit geometric feature carrying a six-degree-of-freedom pose, a gripper aperture, and a bounded contact wrench profile.
Bounded error: The proposal must include a certified spatial error envelope that fits strictly within the task tolerances and mechanical effort limits of both the manipulator and the workpiece.
Temporal expiration: Every target must carry an explicit evidence epoch, bounding its valid lifespan as target objects shift and sensory observations grow stale during compute cycles.

Every request traverses an explicit pipeline to meet these three requirements. Sensory perception resolves symbolic task operators into measurable physical predicates, and calibration transforms image regions into metric poses. The permission path then evaluates effort limits, evidence age, kinematic reachability, and dynamic obstacle clearances before committing the target to the motion planner. A vision-language-action (VLA) model (Brohan, Brown, Carbajal, Chebotar, Chen, et al. 2023) can propose the mug’s target directly, but its deliberative inference loop is slow. The running machine’s intent model executes at 2 Hz and requires 336 ms (derived in The memory wall) to autoregressively decode 7 target values. These values are a 3D position, a three-value orientation (which the producer converts to the quaternion the wire format carries), and an open-close gripper command. The machine therefore splits proposal across two speeds (Two proposers and the evidence horizon). The intent model names the target, and a smaller chunk policy streams motion toward it between intent inferences.

Brohan, Anthony, Noah Brown, Justice Carbajal, Yevgen Chebotar, Xi Chen, Krzysztof Choromanski, Tianli Ding, et al. 2023. “RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2307.15818.
That split keeps the joints supplied with setpoints, but it does not keep the target true. If the conveyor moves while one intent inference runs, every chunk aims at where the mug was when the model’s frame was captured. One inference outlasts the handle’s 60 ms evidence window more than five times over. When target evidence expires between model inferences, the system must either switch to a high-rate local visual tracker or arrest motion entirely. Section 10.5 quantifies these expiration dynamics. Safe physical agency demands dated geometric evidence, explicit capability limits, and an autonomous permission path capable of revoking execution authority whenever the neural model lags or stalls.


↩︎ The machine’s multi-rate cadences, from motor current loops through safety screening to deliberative planners, are established in Physical time constants and sampling phase lag.
1 Affordance (from the verb to afford): Gibson (1979) coined the noun for what an environment offers an animal able to act on it, and the sense is relative to the agent. A handle affords a grasp only to a gripper whose aperture and wrench ceiling fit it, so the affordance record carries the gripper’s limits as well as the mug’s geometry. 
Gibson, James J. 1979. The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception. Houghton Mifflin.
2 Special Euclidean Group: “Euclidean” because its elements preserve distances, “special” because the rotation part has determinant \(+1\), which excludes mirror reflections. A learned regressor carries no such constraint. An unnormalized quaternion or a matrix with determinant \(-1\) is a valid tensor and an impossible pose, so admission rechecks quaternion normalization (section 10.8) instead of trusting the output head.Grounding the mug grasp starts with naming which physical feature the gripper will touch, expressing that feature in the robot’s base frame, and bounding the forces of contact. In ecological psychology, Gibson coined the term affordance for what an environment offers an agent capable of acting on it (Gibson 1979).1 Robotics turns that qualitative idea into four measurable quantities for the mug handle. The first is a target grasp pose \(\GraspPose = (\GraspOrientation, \GraspPosition) \in \SpecialEuclideanGroup\) in the robot base frame (where \(\SpecialEuclideanGroup\) is the Special Euclidean group of 3D rigid-body positions and \(\SpecialOrthogonalGroup\) rotations).2 The others are a unit approach vector \(\ApproachDirection\), a jaw aperture \(\JawAperture\) in meters, and an allowable contact wrench envelope \(\ContactWrenchEnvelope\) bundling three-axis forces in newtons and three-axis torques in newton-meters. Because each usable site on an object imposes different geometry and force limits, each site defines its own affordance frame \(\AffordanceFrame\) attached to the object’s body coordinates. A single mug offers several distinct affordance frames across its surface. Its thin rim tolerates little normal force, its cylindrical wall requires a wide jaw span, and its handle requires a full six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) alignment that threads the fingers through the loop without collision.
Contact mechanics dictates the allowable contact wrench. Under the classical Coulomb friction model, tangential contact forces \(\FingerTangentialForce\) remain stable without slipping only when constrained within a friction cone: \[\|\FingerTangentialForce\| \le \CoulombFrictionCoefficient \FingerNormalForce\] where \(\FingerNormalForce\) represents the normal contact force and \(\CoulombFrictionCoefficient\) is the static coefficient of friction. For an idealized two-finger parallel gripper, Nguyen established that a grasp resists arbitrary in-plane disturbance forces if and only if the line connecting the two contact points lies strictly within the interior of both friction cones (Nguyen 1988).
The general formulation operates in wrench space. For each contact point \(\ContactPointIndex\), a grasp map \(\GraspMap_i\) transforms the local contact force \(\ContactPointForce_i\) into an object wrench composed of the force and its moment \(\GraspContactDisplacement_i \times \ContactPointForce_i\) about the object reference frame. Here \(\GraspContactDisplacement_i\) denotes the displacement from the reference origin to the contact point. Mapping the extremal rays of every friction cone into wrench space yields a set of primitive contact wrenches. The grasp achieves force closure when the origin of wrench space lies strictly within the interior of the convex hull of these primitive wrenches, guaranteeing that admissible contact forces can equilibrate any external disturbance wrench. Because fingers can only push into the surface, the net wrench they apply is a nonnegative scaling of a point inside that convex hull, and enclosing the origin strictly inside the hull ensures that a ray pointing opposite to any external disturbance wrench intersects the hull interior so the fingers can scale up their normal forces to cancel disturbances from every direction. Ferrari and Canny formalized this condition into a scalar quality metric. The metric is the radius of the largest origin-centered ball inscribed within that convex hull, and it represents the minimum disturbance wrench the grasp resists per unit of applied normal force (Ferrari and Canny 1992).
Force closure, however, remains an idealized geometric property that specifies stability without bounding magnitude. A physical grasp requires finite capacity. The normal squeeze force must counter the mug’s gravitational load and dynamic accelerations during transit while remaining strictly below structural limits that would fracture ceramic or spill contents. Grasp mechanics: Friction cones and force closure derives the lower bound on squeeze force from Newton’s second law and develops friction cones and force closure from first principles. These dynamic bounds constitute the effort envelope that the Brain proposes and the permission path enforces.
Turning a spoken request into a checkable physical target is the robotic form of the symbol grounding problem (Harnad 1990), which asks how arbitrary symbols connect to measurable sensorimotor states.3 For the mug, that connection runs through the calibrated transform chain from the camera frame to the manipulator base, the handle’s affordance frame, and the contact wrench bounds. An uncalibrated detection box or an autoregressively sampled coordinate carries none of those bounds. The permission path must therefore catch and reject an unsupported model proposal (a hallucination, in machine learning terms4) deterministically, regardless of the model’s reported confidence. When a spatial feature instead bundles a calibrated base-frame pose, certified wrench limits, and an evidence timestamp, it forms a grounded affordance.
3 Symbol Grounding Problem: Harnad (1990) compared the problem to learning Chinese from a Chinese-to-Chinese dictionary alone, in which every definition points only to more undefined symbols. A model’s text embedding is that dictionary. Only a calibrated camera-to-base chain breaks the circle for the mug, so the proposal must carry its evidence record and not only its label.
Harnad, Stevan. 1990. “The Symbol Grounding Problem.” Physica D: Nonlinear Phenomena 42 (1-3): 335–46.
4 Hallucination: In text generation the word names fluent output that the source does not support (Maynez et al. 2020). For a robot the unsupported output is a coordinate, and nothing in its format marks it as unsupported. Containment therefore has to be a check on evidence that the model does not produce.
Maynez, Joshua, Shashi Narayan, Bernd Bohnet, and Ryan McDonald. 2020. “On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization.” Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL), 1906–19. https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2020.acl-main.173.

Definition 10.1: Grounded affordance
Grounded affordance is an affordance expressed in the robot’s own frame and units: a feature pose in the base frame, an approach direction, an aperture, and a contact wrench ceiling, each tied to dated sensor evidence through a calibrated measurement chain.

Significance: It turns a label into quantities the permission path can check. The mug handle’s grounded affordance is a pose that must land inside a 15 mm task tolerance from evidence with a 3 mm initial error, and on the moving belt that evidence stays valid for only 60 ms (section 10.5).
Distinction: Unlike a detector box or a language label, which designates where an object appears in image space or what it is called, a grounded affordance defines where and how an end effector may establish contact. Unlike Gibson’s perceptual affordance, it is bound to one gripper’s limits and to one capture time.
Common pitfall: Treating a learned grasp score or a confident detection as grounding. Neither carries a metric error bound, a wrench limit, or an evidence epoch, so neither can be admitted or expired.



A high-level task action like Grasp(Mug, Handle) specifies an operational objective, but its preconditions require rigorous physical verification. Perceptual noise and latency prevent open-loop execution from guaranteeing that the handle remains unobstructed or that the jaws are properly aligned. Motion predicates formalize these physical prerequisites by mapping abstract conditions to measurable geometric tolerances and wrench readings:

Pre-contact approach predicate: \(\ApproachPredicate(\ToolCenterPointPose) \iff \|\ToolCenterPointPosition - \PregraspPosition\| \le \PositionalTaskTolerance \land \arccos(\ToolCenterPointAxis \cdot \ApproachDirection) \le \OrientationTolerance\), requiring the tool center point (TCP) frame \(\ToolCenterPointFrame\), whose origin sits between the gripper fingertips, to align with the affordance approach axis \(\ApproachDirection\) within spatial tolerance \(\PositionalTaskTolerance\) and angular orientation tolerance \(\OrientationTolerance\).
Guarded contact predicate: \(\GuardedContactPredicate(\ContactWrench) \iff \GraspForceFloor \le \FingerNormalForce \le \GraspForceCeiling\), checking a normal squeeze band under the illustrated parallel-jaw model. Here the contact-force magnitude denotes the relevant normal squeeze at each finger, measured or conservatively inferred under qualified contact geometry; a generic force-vector norm or net wrench does not establish that quantity. The task profile sets the band from friction, payload load and acceleration, and crush limits. Passing it supports retention under those premises but does not establish object identity or task completion.
Spatial clearance predicate: \(\SpatialClearancePredicate(\CartesianPosition, \SpatialMemoryMap) \iff \min_{\ObstaclePoint \in \SpatialMemoryMap} \|\CartesianPosition - \ObstaclePoint\| \ge \PointClearanceMargin\), evaluating candidate point \(\CartesianPosition\) against obstacle geometry stored in the spatial memory map \(\SpatialMemoryMap\). This point clearance test serves as a fast preliminary check. Certifying the physical gripper, manipulator links, and their swept transit volumes requires a continuous path collision query during trajectory synthesis.

Together, the spatial and angular tolerances delineate an admissible geometric goal set \(\GoalSet \subset \SpecialEuclideanGroup\): \[\GoalSet = \left\{ \Pose = (\DirectionalCosineMatrix, \CartesianPosition) \in \SpecialEuclideanGroup \;\middle|\; \|\CartesianPosition - \TargetPosition\|_{\ToleranceEllipsoidMatrix} \le 1, \; \angle(\DirectionalCosineMatrix, \TargetOrientation) \le \OrientationTolerance \right\} \tag{1}\] Contact and obstacle clearance predicates operate as distinct, phase-specific execution constraints outside this static pose volume. Within equation 1, the weighted ellipsoidal norm \(\|\CartesianPosition - \TargetPosition\|_{\ToleranceEllipsoidMatrix} = \sqrt{\sum_{i \in \{\Glyph{x},\Glyph{y},\Glyph{z}\}} \left(\frac{\PositionComponent_i - \TargetPositionComponent}{\TaskToleranceSemiAxis_i}\right)^2}\) bounds spatial deviation within an ellipsoid whose principal semi-axes are \(\TaskToleranceSemiAxes = (\XTaskToleranceSemiAxis, \YTaskToleranceSemiAxis, \ZTaskToleranceSemiAxis)\). Here \(\PositionalTaskTolerance\) denotes the corresponding semi-axis \(\TaskToleranceSemiAxis_i\) along any individual coordinate direction. The rotation error metric \(\angle(\DirectionalCosineMatrix, \TargetOrientation) = \arccos\left(\frac{\operatorname{tr}(\DirectionalCosineMatrix^\top \TargetOrientation) - 1}{2}\right)\) bounds geodesic orientation divergence on \(\SpecialOrthogonalGroup\), equivalent to \(2 \arccos(|\UnitQuaternion \cdot \TargetUnitQuaternion|)\) when unit quaternions represent orientations. Terminal grasp poses falling outside \(\GoalSet\) lead directly to task aborts or damage. Translational errors exceeding \(\TaskToleranceSemiAxis_i\) cause gripper fingers to impact the ceramic rim or close on empty space, while angular misalignments exceeding \(\OrientationTolerance\) jam the fingers against the handle opening, tripping joint torque protection or shattering the object.
For the warehouse mug, the nominal task profile assigns all three ellipsoidal semi-axes to the 15 mm grasp tolerance. A terminal TCP offset of 10 mm along the \(\Glyph{x}\)-axis yields a normalized ellipsoidal distance of 0.67, remaining well within the admissible goal set. Conversely, an offset of 20 mm yields a normalized distance of 1.33, falling outside the set and triggering immediate rejection. Checking angular alignment requires the angular tolerance \(\OrientationTolerance\) specified in the verified task profile, which the mug model registers during commissioning.
This goal set is an operational task specification rather than an estimate of target pose. The task tolerance region defines the maximum terminal error that the physical grasp can absorb; state estimator covariance captures uncertainty in the target’s actual pose. For the mug pick, the approved task profile permits at most 15 mm of translational discrepancy. The proposed affordance must therefore supply a conservative target error bound that fits inside this envelope, leaving sufficient headroom for the motion controller’s dynamic tracking error. Artificially expanding the task tolerance to accept an uncertain perception estimate corrupts the safety invariants of the physical task.
Generating candidate affordances prior to intent proposal packaging typically relies on a learned 6-DoF grasp generator applied to an incoming point cloud. Architectures such as Contact-GraspNet predict grasp poses anchored directly to surface points in cluttered point clouds (Sundermeyer et al. 2021). Frameworks like AnyGrasp predict dense \(\SpecialEuclideanGroup\) grasp distributions with learned quality scores and track them across temporal observation sequences (Fang et al. 2023). The generator outputs a set of candidate grasp configurations paired with scalar confidence scores. However, a learned score merely reflects the network’s predictive confidence relative to its training distribution. It provides neither an analytic stability metric like the Ferrari-Canny radius nor a measured empirical grasp success rate for this specific gripper and workpiece geometry.
Candidate poses surviving initial filtering must satisfy rigorous downstream physical constraints that learned generators omit:

Kinematic feasibility: The manipulator must possess a valid inverse kinematics (IK) solution that avoids joint position and velocity limits. A well-conditioned kinematic Jacobian does not guarantee clearance from mechanical joint stops, making explicit joint travel verification mandatory.
Geometric compatibility: Gripper jaw stroke must exceed workpiece thickness at the grasp site with sufficient clearance margin.
Corridor clearance: The approach trajectory must provide an unobstructed approach vector clear of surrounding bin walls and adjacent cargo.

When no candidate grasp satisfies these constraints, or when target identification remains unresolved across ambiguous visual candidates, the control pipeline must not execute an argmax guess. Instead, the proposal’s producer on the application processor issues an explicit intent grounding refusal (ERR_GROUNDING_AMBIGUITY), signaling a typed rejection of the goal itself. A planning failure means that the planner has not produced a collision-free path to a valid, well-formed goal. An intent grounding refusal halts execution earlier. It rejects an ungrounded or ambiguous goal before invoking the motion planner, which prevents unverified guesses from generating physical trajectories. When a symbolic task planner sits above the grasp generator, its discrete task operators must discharge these same geometric and contact predicates before any step of the plan is admitted.

title: Grounded Intent
text:
10.2 Task Operators and Geometric Samplers
A symbolic task planner can emit the discrete action Grasp(Mug, Handle) and mark the mug as held in its internal state even when no collision-free inverse kinematics solution reaches the handle, a bin wall blocks the approach, or the mug has not been separated from adjacent items on the belt. The high-level action Grasp(Mug, Handle) inherits from classical planning traditions, where actions are formalized as operators defined by preconditions, an add list, and a delete list. The formalism traces back to the STRIPS5 framework (Fikes and Nilsson 1971) and was standardized by the Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) (McDermott et al. 1998). A discrete world state \(\SymbolicPlanningState\) consists of a set of grounded predicates. An operator \(\PlanningOperator\) is applicable in state \(\SymbolicPlanningState\) if its preconditions hold, \(\text{pre}(\PlanningOperator) \subseteq \SymbolicPlanningState\), producing the successor state \[\SuccessorPlanningState = \left(\SymbolicPlanningState \setminus \text{del}(\PlanningOperator)\right) \cup \text{add}(\PlanningOperator) \tag{2}\] A symbolic planner searches sequences of operators, advancing states by the delete-then-add update of equation 2 until reaching a state satisfying the target goal predicates. For the warehouse pick, an operator pick(mug, handle, conveyor) requires preconditions Reachable(handle), Clear(approach), Singulated(window), and HandEmpty, where a singulated window holds exactly one separated candidate object. Upon execution, it adds Holding(mug) and deletes HandEmpty.
5 STRIPS (Stanford Research Institute Problem Solver): The formalism was built to plan for Shakey, a physical mobile robot at SRI (Nilsson 1984), so symbolic planning began on a machine that moved. Its operators treat an action’s listed effects as certain, an assumption that slipping wheels and a misreading camera cannot grant. The gap that geometric samplers and motion predicates close is therefore as old as the formalism itself.
Nilsson, Nils J. 1984. Shakey the Robot. Technical Note No. 323. Artificial Intelligence Center, SRI International.

Garrett, Caelan Reed, Tomás Lozano-Pérez, and Leslie Pack Kaelbling. 2020. “PDDLStream: Integrating Symbolic Planners and Blackbox Samplers via Optimistic Adaptive Planning.” Proceedings of the International Conference on Automated Planning and Scheduling (ICAPS) 30: 440–48. https://doi.org/10.1609/icaps.v30i1.6739.
Abstract symbols disguise the primary computational challenge: verifying whether a predicate like Reachable(handle) holds requires finding a continuous end-effector pose, a valid inverse kinematics solution, and a collision-free joint trajectory. A symbolic planner cannot evaluate these continuous constraints natively. Integrated task and motion planning (TAMP) resolves this disconnect by coupling discrete symbolic search with geometric samplers, computational routines that sample continuous configuration spaces (proposing candidate grasps, inverse kinematics configurations, and transit paths) to certify symbolic preconditions (Kaelbling and Lozano-Pérez 2011; Garrett et al. 2021). For instance, PDDLStream treats each geometric sampler as a generator stream whose continuous outputs certify symbolic facts. The task planner can then make optimistic symbolic progress, backtracking or branching when a sampler fails to find a valid configuration (Garrett et al. 2020). A sampler failure means that the search has not found a collision-free grasp for the given base pose; unless the sampler certifies infeasibility, it does not prove that none exists. The symbolic planner can spend more search effort, reposition the mobile base, or select an alternate interaction sequence.
Large language models (LLMs) increasingly generate the symbolic layer. Systems such as LLM+P prompt an LLM to translate natural-language task specifications into formal PDDL domain and problem instances, subsequently delegating resolution to a classical symbolic planner (B. Liu et al. 2023). While this decouples linguistic parsing from plan generation, neither the language model nor the symbolic planner verifies geometric feasibility or sensorimotor validity against real-world scene observations. Bridging this gap requires mapping each symbolic precondition to a verifiable motion predicate or geometric certificate evaluated against live physical measurements, as summarized in table 1.



Table 1: From task operator to motion predicate: Each fact the symbolic pick operator requires or predicts for the mug maps directly to a predicate over measured physical quantities and to an explicit verification check in the execution pipeline.

In this execution architecture, the predicted effect Holding(mug) remains a conditional hypothesis until the declared terminal pose, contact, and retention checks pass following finger closure. The guarded contact predicate \(\GuardedContactPredicate\) supplies the normal squeeze check under the task profile; it cannot alone confirm that the intended mug is held. A symbolic task plan operates as an intent proposal in the same manner as a neural VLA target. It asserts the preconditions and effects it intends to achieve, while the deterministic permission path verifies whether calibrated physical evidence supports execution.
Grounding an open-ended directive therefore yields a structured, time-stamped intent proposal. The immediate systems design challenge is converting an identified image region into a calibrated metric target without corrupting its semantic identity, understating its measurement uncertainty, or obscuring its evidence epoch. Once packaged with these invariants, the proposal enters the independent permission path to verify physical admissibility, effort bounds, and expiration limits before execution begins.

title: Grounded Intent
section: 10.3 Semantic Request Translation to Geometric Proposals
text:
10.3 Semantic Request Translation to Geometric Proposals
When an operator asks for the red mug and the vision backbone instead binds the word “mug” to an adjacent table fixture, the coordinate that crosses the proposal boundary arrives in the trajectory pipeline indistinguishable from a valid handle target. Low-level motor drives monitor encoder counts, winding temperatures, and phase currents, so they have no way to tell whether the setpoint they track belongs to a mug or a bolted bracket. Any unmodeled arm compliance or thermal expansion also adds metric bias that a high semantic confidence score never reveals. Before any motion planner accepts a target, the grounding pipeline must therefore turn the model’s selection into a geometric proposal that carries bounded spatial uncertainty, dated selection evidence, and an explicit expiration time.

10.3.1 The four-stage open-vocabulary grounding pipeline
Passing a detector’s 2D bounding box or an uncalibrated pixel coordinate straight to a motion planner hides two failures at once. Two identical mugs can both score high without triggering an ambiguity warning, and a small depth error along the camera ray can stretch into centimeters of pose error in the robot base frame. To expose each failure where it can be checked, the four-stage open-vocabulary grounding pipeline separates semantic referent selection from metric localization and physical actuation:

Stage 1: Visual encoding: RGB-D frames from static or eye-in-hand cameras enter a vision backbone running at batch size one on the machine’s accelerator, transforming raw image patches into dense feature embeddings.
Stage 2: Referent selection: Given a prompt such as “pick the red ceramic mug,” an open-vocabulary detector such as Grounding DINO or OWL-ViT proposes candidate bounding boxes and scores each against the text prompt (S. Liu et al. 2023; Minderer et al. 2022). The model evaluates each candidate independently without global normalization across boxes (OWL-ViT trains with a sigmoid focal loss (Minderer et al. 2022), while Grounding DINO filters tokens against an absolute threshold). Two identical mugs can therefore both yield high confidence, or a lone glass jar can score above threshold even when no mug is present. A promptable segmentation model such as SAM 2 can refine the chosen box into an object mask and track it across video frames (Ravi et al. 2024). However, a 2D bounding box or segmentation mask provides only image-space localization without metric depth, surface normals, or wrench limits. It indicates where the object projects onto the camera sensor, leaving contact dynamics and grasp mechanics completely unspecified.
Stage 3: Metric lifting: Calibrated camera intrinsics, depth measurements, and the hand-eye extrinsic transformation lift the selected pixels into 3D points in the robot base frame, while propagating sensor noise into a base-frame covariance matrix. For stereo and structured-light systems, depth error grows quadratically with range, \(\DepthStandardDeviation \approx \CameraFrameDepth^2\DisparityStandardDeviation/(\StereoBaseline \FocalLength)\) for baseline \(\StereoBaseline\) (the stereo term of equation 8.6), focal length \(\FocalLength\), and disparity error \(\DisparityStandardDeviation\), whereas lateral error grows only linearly, \(\PixelStandardDeviation \CameraFrameDepth/\FocalLength\). Their ratio, approximately \((\CameraFrameDepth/\StereoBaseline)(\DisparityStandardDeviation/\PixelStandardDeviation)\), scales with range and baseline rather than remaining constant, while time-of-flight sensors have their own range-dependent error profiles. The resulting uncertainty ellipsoid elongates dramatically along the optical line of sight. Any unmodeled extrinsic error from wrist compliance or mounting deflection tilts this elongated ellipsoid directly into the robot’s clearance margin.
Stage 4: Affordance parameterization: The lifted 3D geometry transforms into candidate actions. Depending on the architecture, these candidates may take the form of scored 6-DoF grasp sets from a learned grasp generator, 3D attraction and repulsion cost fields (Huang et al. 2023), parameterized motion primitives (Liang et al. 2023), or decoded action tokens (Brohan, Brown, Carbajal, Chebotar, Dabis, et al. 2023). Stage 4 filters these candidates against the kinematic reachability, gripper aperture, and collision clearance criteria detailed in section 10.1. It then constructs a goal tolerance set \(\GoalSet\) around each surviving affordance frame and assigns the required motion predicates. Finally, it serializes these hypotheses into a fixed-size, statically verified proposal structure (table 2) and carries them across the physical silicon boundary between the non-real-time Linux Application Processor (AP) and the hard real-time Safety MCU.


↪ The pinhole camera model and the propagation of pixel and depth noise into a base-frame covariance are developed in Camera Projective Geometry and Covariance Propagation.

↪ Byte layout: The intent payload’s fields, types, and offsets are given in Intent payload.
