Every row leaves admission the same two questions, whether the metric estimate is tight enough for the task and whether it belongs to the right object. The mug’s handle shows how each can fail while the other holds.


10.3.3 Imprecise estimates and wrong objects
When the wrist camera views the red mug from across the workstation before the arm begins its reach, depth uncertainty along the optical ray stretches the 95 percent error region to more than twice the handle’s grasp tolerance. Closing the gripper on that single-frame estimate can therefore drive the fingers into the ceramic rim. Under an illustrative calibrated Gaussian sensor model for that pre-approach wrist-camera frame, the principal standard deviations in the camera frame are 4 mm and 5 mm laterally, and 12 mm along the optical depth axis. Because the optical axis aligns with the gripper’s approach vector, range uncertainty directly challenges position control. A 95 percent statistical region surrounding the estimated handle coordinate \(\CartesianPosition_0\) is defined by the Mahalanobis squared distance \((\CartesianPosition-\CartesianPosition_0)^\top\PerceptionDepthCovariance^{-1}(\CartesianPosition-\CartesianPosition_0)\le\PositionConfidenceEllipsoidRadius^2\). With the three-degree-of-freedom chi-square quantile \(\PositionConfidenceEllipsoidRadius^2 =\) 7.815, the distribution expands into principal semi-axes of 11.2 mm, 14.0 mm, and 33.5 mm.
Against the mug’s 15 mm physical grasp tolerance (figure 4, panel a), the ellipsoid fails on one axis only. While both lateral semi-axes fall comfortably within the mechanical tolerance window, the depth semi-axis of 33.5 mm substantially exceeds the allowed threshold. Consequently, the admission gate rejects the proposal, because the controller cannot guarantee that closing the gripper fingers at that estimated setpoint will capture the handle rather than collide with the rim.
The remedy, worked through in section 10.6, decomposes the reach into distinct phases. The system first admits an intermediate, collision-checked inspection waypoint, allowing the arm to travel closer to the workspace. Once positioned nearby, a second wrist-camera observation constructs a refined belief record, reducing the initial position uncertainty to 3 mm. Because a Gaussian probability region retains an unbounded asymptotic tail, statistical distributions alone cannot certify absolute spatial clearance. The downstream intent proposal therefore needs independently justified conservative error envelopes in the robot base frame before requesting trajectory tracking. Covariance alone supplies only a statistical region.






Figure 4: Localization uncertainty and authority expiry: Panel (a) draws the handle estimate’s 95 percent region to scale against the 15 mm grasp tolerance: the lateral semi-axis of 11.2 mm fits, while the 33.5 mm depth semi-axis along the camera ray does not. Panel (b) sketches speed against time: renewals keep the lease alive, and when they stop the lease expires, the drive takes 22 ms to begin braking, and a jerk-limited stop follows. The shaded area is the stopping distance, which must fit the clearance that remains; the dashed trace is motion with no lease, which never stops.



While a configured statistical gate cleanly rejects detections with large variance envelopes, it cannot catch an entirely incorrect object identified with high semantic confidence. This is a different case from the jar beside the mug, where both candidates entered the prediction set and the producer refused. Consider instead the jar in place of the mug, where a fragile, thin-walled glass jar sits on the workstation where the ceramic mug was expected and no mug is present. When prompted to pick the mug, the vision-language model misidentifies the jar with strong semantic certainty, generating a sharp, low-variance geometric proposal centered on the glass container. The downstream trajectory planner accepts the coordinate, solves inverse kinematics in \(\SpecialEuclideanGroup\), verifies joint position and velocity limits, and confirms that the approach path clears all static obstacles in the occupancy map. Because the requested motion satisfies all kinematic and wrench envelopes, the real-time permission path authorizes execution. However, if the gripper applies the clamping force required to hold a heavy ceramic mug, the jaws crush the thin glass container upon contact despite clearing every geometric check.



A confident wrong object passes every geometric check until the gripper closes.
This scenario marks the boundary between physical verification and semantic premises. The deterministic permission path enforces coordinate envelopes, kinematic limits, actuator torque thresholds, and obstacle clearance against known geometric occupancy grids. These physical invariants cannot confirm whether a given coordinate actually corresponds to the requested object. The premise that the targeted item is indeed the requested ceramic mug remains an unverified upstream assumption outside the hardware controller’s reach. Establishing that premise requires distinct task-level perceptual evidence, which must be tracked through the handover release case (Adjudicating the Safety Case) and recorded in the residual-claims register (A residual-claims register). A learned task filter upstream cannot close this gap either. The AutoRT deployment showed that a language-model task filter improved the fraction of sensible task proposals while unsafe commands still passed it. Human teleoperators therefore had to intervene and halt execution (war story 10.1) (Ahn et al. 2024).

War Story 10.1: AutoRT task filtering and supervision (2024)Context: AutoRT deployed foundation models to propose and filter physical manipulation tasks for fleets of mobile manipulators operating in unstructured human office environments (Ahn et al. 2024).
Mechanism: In a sample of 259 proposed tasks, human annotators judged 228 (88 percent) acceptable. A second LLM pass then filtered the tasks against a robot “constitution” of safety and embodiment rules. Of the 214 tasks it kept, 200 (93 percent) were acceptable. The filter rejected 17 of the 31 unsuitable tasks, a recall of 55 percent, and passed the other 14.
Impact: All 14 misses arose during teleoperated collection. Although the filter raised overall proposal quality, human supervisors had to intervene to intercept every unsafe proposal before robot execution.
Response: The system architecture placed physical safety outside the model’s domain. Deployments supplemented learned proposals with hardware joint-force limits, physical emergency stop buttons, and direct human line-of-sight supervision or physical perimeter barricades.
Systems lesson: A learned task filter can improve proposal quality, but it cannot serve as a safety referee. An independent, deterministic permission and fallback path must validate every physical action against real-time plant limits before execution.



Ahn, Michael, Anthony Brohan, Noah Brown, Yevgen Chebotar, Omar Cortes, Byron David, Chelsea Finn, et al. 2024. “AutoRT: Embodied Foundation Models for Large Scale Orchestrating of Robotic Agents.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2401.12963.
The distant view and the glass jar mark two distinct verification boundaries. The distant view fails on metric uncertainty along the depth axis, whereas the jar in place of the mug fails on an unverified semantic premise, because metric precision does not establish object identity. A safe geometric proposal must therefore carry both dated physical evidence and task-specific selection evidence across the silicon boundary. By this point the mug proposal holds most of what the lease will carry. The grounded affordance has fixed the target pose and its goal region, and the squeeze bounds of the grasp analysis have set the wrench ceiling. The operator table has named the predicates the grasp must discharge, and the handle’s error envelope has been compared with the task tolerance. Carrying these values is not yet holding authority, however. The proposal still lacks a grant, a deadline, and a stop that works without the proposer, and turning it into bounded authority over the arm is the work of the handoff.

title: Grounded Intent
section: 10.4 The Intent Handoff and Bounded Authority
text:
10.4 The Intent Handoff and Bounded Authority
If a deliberative host could stream raw joint trajectories or actuator currents directly to the drives, a two-millimeter depth error into a rigid latch plate or a stalled inference thread mid-reach would drive motor currents to saturation before any host process could intervene. When the arm reaches for the red mug, the deliberative host instead submits a candidate intent specifying a bounded target region, an expiration deadline, and explicit physical effort ceilings. The region and the ceilings are the grounding results packaged for transit, the affordance pose with its goal set and the grasp’s wrench and speed limits, and the requested deadline is computed from the parent belief record’s evidence epoch. An independent real-time supervisor intercepts this proposal, vetting each requested parameter against retained sensor evidence and configured plant dynamics. Granting a target lease merely authorizes downstream trajectory planning within certified safety bounds. The deliberative model remains isolated from low-level actuator registers.
This permission path validates every requested target constraint before any motion planner can generate trajectory setpoints. Rather than forcing memory-constrained microcontrollers to maintain full scene representations, host-side spatial engines export compact geometric evidence across a strictly typed interface. The supervisor verifies four mandatory invariants against this evidence:

Spatial containment invariant: The proposed geometric goal set \(\GoalSet \subset \SpecialEuclideanGroup\) must lie strictly within the robot’s reachable workspace manifold \(\ReachableWorkspace\). The bounded spatial uncertainty envelope \((\XPositionErrorEnvelope, \YPositionErrorEnvelope, \ZPositionErrorEnvelope)\) must fit inside the task tolerance \((\XTaskToleranceSemiAxis, \YTaskToleranceSemiAxis, \ZTaskToleranceSemiAxis)\) without intersecting persistent obstacle geometry in spatial memory \(\SpatialMemoryMap\).
Temporal freshness invariant: The sensor evidence epoch \(\MonotonicClockInstant_0\) must match a retained parent belief record. The unobserved elapsed time on the Safety MCU’s monotonic hardware clock must not exceed the evidence horizon \(\EvidenceHorizon\) that section 10.5 takes from the parent belief record.
Dynamic effort invariant: Requested tool-center-point velocity \(\SpeedBound\), acceleration \(\ProfileAccelerationBound\), and contact wrench \(\ContactWrenchCeiling = [\ContactForceCeiling, \ContactTorqueCeiling]^\top\) must remain strictly within actuator thermal ratings, link inertia limits, and workpiece structural yield thresholds.
Certified deterministic fallback invariant: The robot must possess an independently verified, pre-computed stopping or hold trajectory that brings all moving links to rest within current physical obstacle clearance (\(\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance\)) if authority is abruptly revoked.

The first three invariants turn the requirements that opened the chapter into checks: metric physicality and bounded error become spatial containment and the effort ceiling, while temporal expiration becomes freshness. The fourth adds the obligation those requirements left implicit, a stop that works without the proposer. Each invariant guards against a distinct failure mode in physical interaction. Loose target bounds can exceed kinematic grasp tolerances, and stale sensor evidence risks collision with a displaced object. Excessive commanded effort can shatter a workpiece, and an unvetted handoff leaves moving mass without a safe recovery trajectory. The resulting intent lease records the validated envelope that survives these four checks and constrains the downstream trajectory planner, which must synthesize path timing and deceleration profiles that satisfy supervisory admission criteria (section 10.8). Pairing the evidence epoch with a finite lease expiration keeps the temporal bound deterministic even if the host crashes, because the safety controller compares its own clock against the admitted deadline rather than waiting for a cancellation packet (section 10.5).
Spatial and temporal bounds alone cannot guarantee safety if the downstream controller commands unbounded effort. Every intent proposal must therefore declare explicit effort ceilings covering tool-center-point velocity, acceleration, and contact wrench. Consider a depth perception error of two millimeters that places a target goal slightly inside a rigid workpiece. An unrestricted position controller will drive actuator currents to saturation trying to eliminate tracking error, imposing severe mechanical stress on the gear train. During a guarded approach to a spring-latched cage door, for example, the host proposes a 15 N tripwire ceiling, well below the 100 N structural latch threshold, paired with an approach velocity capped at 0.03 m/s. The permission path evaluates these values against hardware torque-speed curves and environmental thresholds, admitting only parameters that guarantee structural integrity.
Downstream of the permission path, an impedance controller shapes interaction dynamics, answering a position error with the restoring force of the virtual spring-damper established in Transmission compliance, contact impedance, and tooth fracture. Under quasi-static contact, scaling the virtual stiffness along the approach vector directly limits steady-state contact force for a given positional error. Transient impacts, however, demand more than static stiffness modulation; containing peak collision forces requires coordinating approach velocity, passive mechanical compliance, sensor latency, and actuator closed-loop bandwidth.
Omitting spatial, temporal, or dynamic boundaries leaves physical hardware vulnerable during communication dropouts or perception stalls. Stopping distance scales linearly with the reaction delay preceding brake engagement and quadratically with operating velocity (equation 2.2). For a mobile base navigating within physical obstacle clearances, a silent or stalled proposer inflates this reaction window by the entire lifespan of the active command lease. As established in Chunk Lease Sizing from the Stopping Budget, this chunk lease duration directly extends the unbraked latency parameter \(\PrebrakeDelay\). The verified safety envelope must therefore maintain obstacle clearance greater than the total stopping distance, factoring in sensor pipeline latency, transport jitter, and state estimation uncertainty. Furthermore, powered deceleration requires electrical bus energy and closed-loop control authority to survive an upstream fault. Logic-level power alone cannot generate mechanical braking torque.
The intent lease defines the temporal horizon over which a deliberative goal remains valid. It operates alongside the chunk lease of Chunk Lease Sizing from the Stopping Budget rather than replacing it, because the two hold different kinds of authority even though the Safety MCU’s permission path checks both. The chunk lease authorizes motion. It allows an admitted chunk to drive the actuators only for its short lease unless the chunk policy renews it at its own rate. By contrast, the intent lease authorizes a goal, fixing which target that motion may pursue, how hard it may press, and until when, and only newer evidence can renew it. Consequently, each lease ends authority from its own side. When the chunk lease lapses, motion stops even though the goal remains valid. When the intent lease lapses, nominal tracking toward the goal ends at once, even if the current chunk still has lease time left, and the MCU engages the validated fallback (The trajectory record and its deadlines). A rejected proposal is the gentler case, because it revokes nothing and leaves already admitted motion running until its own leases lapse. The physical stopping budget must accommodate the cumulative delay across perception, communication, actuator response, and mechanical braking in every case.



A 200 ms unbraked stall drives the latch to 2,400 N, far past its limit.

Napkin Math 10.1: What the latch ceilings buyProblem: The intent lease for the cage door requests a 15 N tripwire and a 0.03 m/s approach speed against a 100 N latch limit. With the local contact loop in place, what force does the latch see when the brake command issues, and what would it see in a counterfactual design with no local contact trip, where pressing stops only when the proposer or the intent lease acts?
Variables:

Tripwire 15 N and approach speed \(\LatchApproachSpeed =\) 0.03 m/s, the requested ceilings; latch limit 100 N (Illustrative)
Plate stiffness \(\LatchPlateStiffness =\) 400 N/mm (Illustrative) and contact-loop response 2 ms
Unbraked stall \(\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant =\) 200 ms (Illustrative), shorter than one 500 ms intent period

Math:

Force at brake command: The tripwire fires at 15 N, and the plate keeps compressing while the 2 ms contact loop responds, so the force when the brake command issues is \(\BrakeCommandForce = \ContactTripwireForce + \LatchPlateStiffness\,\LatchApproachSpeed\,\ContactLoopResponseTime =\) 15 N \(+\) 400 N/mm \(\times\) 0.03 m/s \(\times\) 2 ms \(=\) 39 N. The arm stop that follows has only a fraction of a millimeter of compression left to spend; Intentional contact and in-contact energy barriers derives that stop (equation 12.11).
Stall travel (counterfactual, no local trip): \(\FiniteChange \ApproachPosition = \LatchApproachSpeed\,\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant =\) 0.03 m/s \(\times\) 200 ms \(=\) 6 mm past first contact.
Stall force: \(\LatchStallForce = \LatchPlateStiffness\,\FiniteChange \ApproachPosition =\) 400 N/mm \(\times\) 6 mm \(=\) 2,400 N.

Result: The contact loop brakes at 39 N. Without the local trip, a stop that waited on the proposer would let the arm press on, and the spring model predicts 2,400 N.
Systems insight: The predicted force lies far past the 100 N limit, beyond the point where the spring model applies at all; the latch has failed. Sizing and arresting transient contact within milliseconds is the duty of the high-rate, low-latency contact loop. The intent lease supplies the operational boundaries (velocity caps and force tripwires) that keep dynamic loads within the contact loop’s braking envelope, ensuring physical safety even when upstream deliberative proposers stall across multiple intent cycles.


Both the mug grasp and the latch engagement depend on a privilege separation boundary.7 While deliberative models propose goal targets and operational bounds, an independent supervisor enforces safety invariants and executes certified fallback maneuvers whenever evidence expires or contact states change unexpectedly. This design decouples deliberative reasoning from real-time physical protection, inverting the classical priority hierarchy found in early reactive control systems (Brooks 1986).
7 Subsumption Architecture: In the classic subsumption architecture of Brooks (1986), a higher layer subsumes a lower one by suppressing its inputs or inhibiting its outputs. Physical AI systems invert that priority. The lower, real-time layer retains absolute veto authority over deliberative proposals because its timing, stability, and failure behavior can be strictly bounded.
Brooks, Rodney. 1986. “A Robust Layered Control System for a Mobile Robot.” IEEE Journal on Robotics and Automation 2 (1): 14–23.
Structured intent handoffs explicitly disentangle task tolerance, sensor uncertainty, actuator effort limits, and fallback trajectories. External dynamic processes, however, dictate how long these static bounds remain valid. On a moving conveyor, for instance, a correctly localized workpiece drifts continuously after perception capture. The mathematical model governing this uncertainty growth establishes the strict temporal deadline that the independent safety controller must enforce.

title: Grounded Intent
section: 10.5 Expiring Goals and Temporal Validity Leases
text:
10.5 Expiring Goals and Temporal Validity Leases
Suppose the host application processor hangs while the robotic arm reaches for the red mug on the moving belt. The fault that makes canceling the reach necessary is the very fault that prevents a cancellation command from being sent. An explicit abort requires a working sender, scheduler, and network link, while the belt carries the mug beyond the grasp tolerance regardless of when the model last published a coordinate. An intent lease must therefore expire autonomously from the physics of environmental drift. Autonomous expiry applies the third law, proposal is not permission (principle \(\ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission}\)), to physical goals, so that the permission side and not the proposer decides when authority ends. In distributed systems, Gray and Cheriton (1989) introduced leases to maintain cache consistency: a coordinator grants time-bounded authority that lapses unless explicitly renewed, preventing a crashed client from blocking others indefinitely. That correctness proof assumes bounded clock drift between client and coordinator. In an embodied system, the Safety MCU enforces this assumption by transforming every incoming timestamped epoch into its own local monotonic timebase with a strictly bounded synchronization error. The physical domain raises the stakes, because an expired cache lease merely delays a read, whereas an unexpired motion lease lets moving mass keep consuming physical clearance unchecked. The privileged Safety MCU acts as coordinator, issuing a transient tracking lease to the unprivileged deliberative host. If the host stalls during inference, pauses for garbage collection, or experiences an operating system kernel panic, the Safety MCU’s local hardware countdown expires and automatically engages a validated fallback response. This requires no network packet or cancellation command from the failed host.8
8 Watchdog Timer: An independently clocked down-counter that forces a hardware reset or a safe fallback output unless software reloads it before reaching zero. Because a crashed host cannot reload it, the lease countdown runs on the isolated Safety MCU rather than in the host process it supervises.9 Monotonic Clock: A counter that only advances forward at a fixed nominal rate, such as POSIX CLOCK_MONOTONIC or a free-running microcontroller timer. A lease evaluated against wall time could gain or lose its entire remaining window in a single clock adjustment. Every measurement in this chapter is therefore evaluated on the Safety MCU’s monotonic counter and converted from external clocks with a bounded synchronization error.Lease duration is measured exclusively against the Safety MCU’s monotonic hardware clock.9 Network time-synchronization daemons or operator adjustments can step wall-clock time abruptly backward or forward, while host-level software watchdogs can freeze alongside the user-space process they are designated to monitor. Furthermore, no inference pipeline, regardless of its mean throughput, completely eliminates long-tail p99 scheduling stalls. Placing the lease countdown on an isolated, hardware-timed MCU counter ensures that target authority is revoked locally the instant the lease expires. This hardware isolation decouples expiry detection from host operating system jitter, although total physical stopping distance must still account for fieldbus transmission, drive response, and kinematic deceleration.
The deadline the lease enforces is the evidence horizon \(\EvidenceHorizon\) of Two proposers and the evidence horizon put to a new use. There it bounded how long the evidence behind a chunk keeps the tracked mug within tolerance (equation 3.5). Here the intent lease starts from the same quantity, and memory supplies its value. The mug-handle belief record carries an invalidation horizon \(\BeliefInvalidationHorizon\) (equation 9.14), the elapsed time before its error growth law (equation 9.12) reaches the task tolerance. The lease reads that horizon with the grasp tolerance \(\PositionalTaskTolerance\) as the error ceiling and the initial sensor error \(\InitialTrackingError\) as the starting bound.
For a conveyor pick, the growth law charges two bounded effects against that ceiling: \[\PositionErrorBound(\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant) = \InitialTrackingError + \DriftVelocityBound\,\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\SlipAccelerationBound\,\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant^2 \tag{4}\] Here \(\DriftVelocityBound\) bounds the relative velocity between the gripper frame and the target, including both conveyor motion and unmodeled mobile-base odometry drift, and \(\SlipAccelerationBound\) bounds the residual slip acceleration of the mug on the belt. The evidence-only horizon is the elapsed time at which \(\PositionErrorBound(\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant)\) reaches \(\PositionalTaskTolerance\). The numerical examples in this chapter evaluate this upper ceiling with zero additional controller tracking reserve. An admission gate, however, must first subtract a separately qualified nonnegative scalar tracking reserve from \(\PositionalTaskTolerance\). It then solves equation 4 against the reduced budget. It refuses immediately if the initial target error plus that reserve already reaches the tolerance (alongside the full 3D error-set containment check of section 10.8). The two limiting regimes are horizons derived earlier in the volume. With no tracker, the horizon is the linear horizon of equation 9.15, with belt speed as its growth rate. With a tracker that cancels belt velocity, the horizon is the slip-only root of equation 3.5. In this chapter’s symbols they read \[\UntrackedEvidenceHorizon = \frac{\PositionalTaskTolerance - \InitialTrackingError}{\DriftVelocityBound} \quad (\SlipAccelerationBound = 0), \qquad \TrackedEvidenceHorizon = \sqrt{\frac{2(\PositionalTaskTolerance - \InitialTrackingError)}{\SlipAccelerationBound}} \quad (\DriftVelocityBound = 0) \tag{5}\] These evidence-only roots are upper ceilings on target lifetime. When drift velocity and slip acceleration act together, \(\EvidenceHorizon\) is the positive root of \(\PositionErrorBound(\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant) = \PositionalTaskTolerance\) in equation 4, which is strictly shorter than either single-effect root.
If \(\PositionalTaskTolerance \le \InitialTrackingError\), the target is inadmissible at the moment of perception. Initial measurement uncertainty alone consumes the entire task tolerance, which obligates the safety controller to reject dependent motion commands immediately. Even when the evidence horizon is strictly positive, granting motion permission requires a separate geometric verification. The system must verify that current physical clearance accommodates total sensing latency, permission evaluation time, fieldbus transmission delay, mechanical brake engagement, and physical braking distance.
For a red mug carried on a takeaway conveyor, the untracked linear root dictates the evidence deadline. Sizing the control pipeline requires determining whether deliberative intent models can refresh targets rapidly enough to renew authority before this window elapses. While the evidence-horizon calculation in Two proposers and the evidence horizon sized the low-level chunk execution policy against this horizon, deliberative intent models evaluate on a substantially slower cycle.

Napkin Math 10.2: The cadence gapProblem: The conveyor carries the mug at 0.20 m/s. Can the 2 Hz intent model keep the target inside its tolerance by re-proposing it, and how slowly would the belt have to run for a model-only renewal to suffice?
Variables:

Grasp tolerance \(\PositionalTaskTolerance =\) 15 mm and initial handle error \(\InitialTrackingError =\) 3 mm (Illustrative)
Belt speed \(\DriftVelocityBound =\) 200 mm/s (Illustrative)
Intent period \(\IntentProposalPeriod =\) 500 ms (Chosen, 2 Hz) and inference \(\ProposerInferenceTime =\) 336 ms (Derived, The memory wall)

Math:

Horizon (equation 5): with no tracker, \(\EvidenceHorizon = \UntrackedEvidenceHorizon =\) (15 mm \(-\) 3 mm) \(/\) 200 mm/s \(=\) 60 ms.
Error at one period: 3 mm \(+\) 200 mm/s \(\times\) 500 ms \(=\) 103 mm, 88 mm past the tolerance. Inference alone overruns the horizon by 336 ms \(-\) 60 ms \(=\) 276 ms.
Renewal ceiling: Each model-only renewal installs a target computed from a frame captured one inference earlier, and that target stays in force until the next renewal replaces it one period later. Just before the replacement, the evidence behind it is \(\IntentProposalPeriod + \ProposerInferenceTime =\) 836 ms old (the reaction latency of Action chunking, here for the intent model), so the drift it can keep up with is (15 mm \(-\) 3 mm) \(/\) 836 ms \(=\) 14.4 mm/s.

Result: The model alone could renew the target only on a belt running at 7.2 percent of its speed. Even a slow settling drift of 20 mm/s, such as a mug still sliding to rest after the belt stops, whose 600 ms horizon is charted against inference latency in figure 6, is too fast for it.
Systems insight: Physical drift and allowable tolerance dictate \(\EvidenceHorizon\), independent of computing performance. An intent renewal can extend operational authority only if the sum of its dispatch period and inference latency fits entirely within this window. Artificially inflating the lease duration to cover inference delay leaves the pose estimate outside its declared tolerance envelope for 276 ms. Without a qualified, high-frequency local tracker, the system must either slow or stop the conveyor, or refuse the pick task entirely.


The 60 ms limit is a physical evidence deadline that only fresh sensor observations, validated against current motion, can extend. Faster deliberative inference does not lengthen this physical evidence horizon, although a sufficiently fast capture-to-admission pipeline and renewal cadence can fit inside it.
Deploying a qualified local tracker changes these dynamics. By re-measuring the mug in every camera frame and matching conveyor velocity, the local tracking loop prevents conveyor speed from driving error growth. While the initial perception uncertainty of 3 mm still counts against the grasp tolerance, it leaves a target-only error margin of 12 mm for unmodeled physical perturbations before reserving controller tracking error. Sizing against an illustrative worst-case residual slip acceleration of 0.50 m/s², this remaining margin yields the same 219 ms tracked horizon that Two proposers and the evidence horizon computed for the chunk policy. Because the local tracking pipeline runs at high frame rates, only the tracker’s brief period plus sensing latency must fit within this expanded horizon. The tracker also changes who renews the lease. Each tracked frame yields a newer belief record of the same handle, and the producer re-proposes the same referent against it. The Safety MCU therefore receives renewals with a newer capture epoch on the tracker’s cadence rather than the model’s. Relieved of geometric tracking, the deliberative intent model only re-confirms semantic identity (which mug to grasp) at its own rate, and no renewal waits for a fresh inference. The lease attaches its target to the handle’s affordance frame, whose base-frame pose under a qualified tracker follows the belt. The goal set therefore moves with the mug. The tolerance bounds only how far the handle departs from the tracked estimate under residual slip, rather than how far it departs from a fixed point in the base frame. Whichever horizon governs the active operating mode caps the duration of the intent lease granted for that target (section 10.8).
Examining a host processor stall illustrates the protection each horizon provides. Suppose the robotic arm reaches toward the red mug under a target admitted without local tracking, and the application processor stalls during neural network inference. If the system held that unvalidated target across a 200 ms stall, the actual mug position would drift 43 mm away from the commanded setpoint, causing the gripper to close on empty air or strike the rim. The Safety MCU does not rely on host health to catch this fault. In the ideal zero-additional-reserve case, at 60 ms the lease expires automatically, commanding braking to begin within 22 ms (accounting for one permission evaluation tick, one fieldbus cycle, and actuator brake onset), even if the current chunk’s own lease has time left. In contrast, under a qualified local tracker, an identical 200 ms stall leaves the target estimate displaced by only 13 mm, inside the target-only tolerance budget, because the ideal tracked horizon extends to 219 ms. Delegating fast geometric updates to local tracking is what allows a 2 Hz deliberative intent model to operate safely in a dynamic physical environment.
On one clock, the proposer’s timing loses to both horizons (figure 5). Both idealized zero-additional-reserve countdowns end before the 336 ms inference returns and well before the next proposal at 500 ms, so the model can renew neither lease. Absent other renewals, each expiry is followed by the 22 ms stop onset. Under a qualified tracker the tracked countdown restarts with every tracked frame, long before it reaches 219 ms, so the tracked bar in the figure shows what happens only when those renewals stop, as they do when the host stalls. What follows that expiry is still motion, as panel (b) of figure 4 sketches in speed against time. The drive begins braking 22 ms after expiry, and the stopping distance under the falling curve must already fit the clearance that remains. This is why the lease carries the stopping deadline as a term of its own (section 10.8).














Figure 5: Mug lease against the intent model’s timing: The top lane charges the conveyor mug’s modeled target error against the 15 mm grasp tolerance. Without tracking, belt speed exhausts it at 60 ms; with a tracker that cancels belt velocity, residual slip exhausts it at 219 ms. The bottom lane puts idealized countdowns with zero additional controller reserve on the Safety MCU’s clock beside the 336 ms inference and the 500 ms proposal period; each expiry is followed by the 22 ms stop onset (hatched). Neither lease can wait for the next proposal. After a 200 ms host stall the untracked target sits 43 mm off and the tracked one 13 mm.









Figure 6: Target-evidence horizon and early filters: Panel (a) plots the bound \(\EvidenceHorizon\le(\PositionalTaskTolerance-\InitialTrackingError)/\DriftVelocityBound\) for the 15 mm tolerance and 3 mm initial error; the shaded region below the curve means only that the target remains within the task tolerance. The machine’s computed 336 ms intent inference sits far above the 60 ms conveyor horizon and below the 600 ms settling horizon. Panel (b) shows early rejection stages that precede the full path and stopping checks.



Panel (a) of figure 6 generalizes the cadence gap across drift speeds. The 336 ms inference alone fits under the 600 ms horizon of slow settling drift but far exceeds the 60 ms conveyor horizon, and adding the proposal period, as the cadence-gap notebook showed, breaks even the settling case. Panel (b) previews the cheap early filters (sequence and evidence, workspace, transit lower bound, and ambiguity) that reject impossible proposals before the planner spends compute on them. Sustaining continuous tracking safely requires fresh physical evidence, not merely retransmitting a new packet computed from stale sensor observations. Every renewal must derive from an independent physical capture and reach the Safety MCU before the active lease expires. The end-to-end timing budget must account for image capture, inference processing, fieldbus transmission, clock synchronization uncertainty, and permission verification. The timing condition \(\IntentProposalPeriod + \Latency < \EvidenceHorizon\) serves only as a necessary scheduling check. When a renewed proposal arrives, the trajectory planner computes a jerk-limited splice originating from the measured physical state. The safety controller admits this spliced trajectory only if the new swept volume, refreshed evidence validity, and emergency stopping reserves remain fully verified. An abrupt target displacement that violates kinematic or clearance bounds triggers immediate refusal or a controlled stop.
Safely executing a bounded lease presupposes that the commanded geometric target is physically achievable by the robot. If a proposed coordinate falls outside kinematic reach or demands joint velocities that exceed actuator limits across the lease window, granting the lease squanders control authority. It also risks tripping drive overcurrent protection as motor controllers saturate attempting to reach unattainable velocities. Determining whether an incoming goal is kinematically and dynamically admissible must precede trajectory generation, establishing a physical admissibility filter between high-level deliberative intent and real-time execution.

title: Grounded Intent
text:
10.6 Admissible Goal Sets
If the red mug rides past on the far side of the belt, beyond the arm’s physical reach from where the base is parked, no sequence of joint torques can bring the gripper to its handle. In an embodied ML system, this physical impossibility must be intercepted at the proposal boundary, before the target enters the trajectory optimization queue. When an upstream vision-language model or diffusion policy emits a candidate Cartesian coordinate, treating that output as an unverified proposal protects the real-time motion pipeline from executing physically impossible trajectories and from wasting compute cycles attempting to solve them.
A reachability screen also protects the planner’s computational budget. When a target cannot be reached at all, the trajectory optimizer faces an empty feasible set. Local nonlinear solvers cannot certify infeasibility quickly. They typically exhaust their entire iteration budget before timing out, transforming an upstream geometric hallucination into compute starvation on the planning core. Similarly, a requested terminal move that cannot complete before its supporting sensory evidence expires must fail before entering detailed planning. Long-horizon tasks should instead request guarded progress under renewable evidence leases rather than attempting an ungrounded terminal grasp on a single sensor capture.
To avoid spending the planning budget on an already impossible request, the admission layer evaluates proposals against two low-cost preliminary checks:

Static Workspace Manifold Check (\(\TargetPose \in \ReachableWorkspace\)): Geometric workspace analysis defines the closed spatial manifold \(\ReachableWorkspace \subset \SpecialEuclideanGroup\) of reachable end-effector configurations given link dimensions, joint travel limits, and mounting geometry (Craig 2005; Lynch and Park 2017).10 An analytical reachability check evaluates whether the target \(\SpecialEuclideanGroup\) pose \(\TargetPose\) resides inside this workspace manifold \(\ReachableWorkspace\), while an occupancy lookup in spatial memory confirms that the target volume does not intersect persistent static obstacles.
Dynamic Reachability Transit Check: Even when a target lies inside the static workspace manifold \(\ReachableWorkspace\), it may be physically unreachable within the finite window during which its sensor evidence remains valid. This check evaluates whether the end effector can transition from its measured state \((\CartesianPosition_0, \Velocity_0)\) to the target pose within the remaining window \(\IntentLeaseExpiry - \CurrentMonotonicTime\) while respecting its velocity, acceleration, jerk, and thermal torque limits.


Craig, John J. 2005. Introduction to Robotics: Mechanics and Control. 3rd ed. Pearson Prentice Hall.

Lynch, Kevin M, and Frank C Park. 2017. Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control. Cambridge University Press.
10 Workspace vs. Singularity: Membership in \(\ReachableWorkspace\) says that some joint configuration reaches the pose, not that the arm can move freely there; inside the workspace the Jacobian can still lose rank at a singular configuration, where some Cartesian velocities become unattainable. A workspace screen therefore rejects unreachable targets early, leaving singularities to the configuration and path checks; Forward kinematics and singularities develops the Jacobian rank loss behind them.Whatever continuous trajectory profile the actuators follow, no physical move covers distance \(\TargetTravelDistance = \|\TargetPosition - \CartesianPosition_0\|\) faster than its maximum speed ceiling allows. Here both \(\CartesianPosition\) terms are translation vectors in the same Cartesian frame, not full \(\SpecialEuclideanGroup\) poses; orientation feasibility requires a separate check. For terminal completion before the current expiry, a necessary condition is: \[\frac{\TargetTravelDistance}{\SpeedBound} \le \IntentLeaseExpiry - \CurrentMonotonicTime. \tag{6}\] Actuator acceleration limits, jerk ceilings, and motor torque-speed curves only lengthen the required transit time beyond this kinematic floor. A proposal that violates this inequality cannot promise terminal completion in that window. A request for an intermediate guarded segment may remain feasible if its executed motion and stopping fallback fit the current authority, deferring continuation to newly admitted evidence. Dynamic Reachability, Intent Envelopes, and Differential Games gives triangular and trapezoidal transit bounds and explains how jerk limits change the complete-move check.
The scalar lower bound is an early rejection test, not a trajectory generator. It avoids optimizing a terminal request that is already too late, leaving detailed acceleration profiles, obstacle avoidance, and stopping reserves to the fuller motion check. Equation 6 couples spatial distance to evidence lifetime, so dynamic reachability evaluates the target and its supporting evidence together rather than the spatial coordinate alone.


↪ Resolving the admitted goal region into a timed trajectory is developed in Replacement Timing and the Planning Horizon.

Definition 10.2: Dynamic reachability
Dynamic reachability is the property that the end effector can move from its measured state to a target pose, within its velocity, acceleration, jerk, and thermal limits, before the evidence supporting that target expires.

Significance: It prices a target in time as well as space. At the arm’s 1 m/s TCP limit, equation 6 allows at most 219 mm of travel inside the mug’s 219 ms tracked evidence window, so a handle 300 mm away is dynamically unreachable on one capture even though it lies well inside the workspace.
Distinction: Static reachability evaluates geometric feasibility alone (whether any joint configuration can achieve the pose). Dynamic reachability introduces the clock and actuator dynamics. Unlike the dynamic obstacle forecasting of section 10.6.1, which bounds where external actors might move, dynamic reachability bounds where the robot’s end effector can safely travel within a bounded lease.
Common pitfall: Attempting to resolve an unreachable target by stretching its evidence deadline in software. Only fresh sensor measurements can renew an expiring window; the remedy is a staged approach whose segments each fit their own evidence and fallback.



On the arm, the mug’s evidence under the qualified tracker stays valid for 219 ms after its capture. At the 1 m/s TCP speed limit, the gripper could cover at most 219 mm even if the entire window remained. A terminal proposal issued with the gripper 300 mm from the handle needs at least 300 ms of transit. It therefore receives ERR_DYNAMIC_TIME_INSUFFICIENT if it promises completion on that record. Without the tracker, the full window is only 60 ms and the corresponding speed-only reach is 60 mm. Processing and transport consume part of either window. Acceleration further reduces the reachable distance.
This bound and the fuller checks behind it assume that actuators stay within their nominal thermal ratings, that encoders report the initial state \((\CartesianPosition_0, \Velocity_0)\) correctly, and that the payload matches the inertial model. When winding temperatures cross the thresholds of Thermal capacity and insulation breakdown thresholds, or a force measurement reveals a payload mismatch, the permission path lowers \(\ProfileAccelerationBound\) and \(\SpeedBound\) (thermal derating). It then evaluates new proposals against the reduced limits and rechecks any admitted path that the derating may have made infeasible.
A rejection must not simply discard the packet, which would leave the reasoning model waiting for a task timeout. The intent filter returns a structured diagnostic across the proposal boundary: the classification (ERR_WORKSPACE_OUT_OF_BOUNDS, ERR_DYNAMIC_TIME_INSUFFICIENT, or ERR_OCCUPANCY_BLOCKED) and the numerical margin of failure. A dynamic failure reports the shortfall between the transit bound and the remaining window; a workspace failure reports the nearest reachable point on the boundary of \(\ReachableWorkspace\). The reasoning layer can then seek fresher evidence, choose another approach, slow the process, or propose moving the base. It cannot extend the evidence horizon without new sensor data.
The diagnostic makes a staged approach possible. Consider a setup where the pre-contact corridor and its stopping reserve are qualified, a closer wrist observation supports the 3 mm error bound, and the tracker holds the declared slip bound. The rejected terminal promise becomes a pre-contact observation goal. A separately checked corridor carries the gripper toward a better view while keeping a stop outside contact, and the closer capture supplies the mug-handle belief record whose error fits the 15 mm tolerance.
Better sensing does not shorten the physical transit floor. The 300 mm approach still takes at least 300 ms, longer than the 219 ms horizon of any one capture, so it needs at least 2 fresh captures. The planner executes guarded segments under chunk leases, and each continuation is checked against the current intent, target evidence, corridor, and fallback. The predicted route beyond the admitted segment carries no authority. Once the last segment and the closure pass the full trajectory check, the gripper completes the grasp inside the tolerance and moves to the admitted hold for handover. If the closer observation fails, identity becomes unresolved, or a renewal arrives late, the next segment is refused, and existing motion continues only while its own evidence, authority, and fallback remain valid.


↪ The staged approach, with each trajectory segment re-anchored to a fresh wrist-camera capture, is developed in Tail latency budgeting across a mission.


The 300 ms reach outlasts one 219 ms evidence window; it needs 2 captures.


10.6.1 Dynamic obstacle forecasting and forward occupancy
Even when the mug handle lies within kinematic and dynamic reach, a coworker may be about to cross the approach corridor, a conflict that the static workspace and transit tests alone cannot reject. Dynamic obstacle forecasting carries the perception and memory estimates forward into regions that moving obstacles could occupy so the intent stage can reject blocked corridors early, before the planner and permission path check the complete timed trajectory. Because this forecast predicts only where people might move and says nothing about whether those people can tell where the machine will move, it covers only one half of how coworkers and robots stay clear of one another.


↪ Motion and signals that let the people around a machine infer its goal early enough to yield are developed in Legible intent.
The intent filter consumes the dynamic track manifest \([(\text{ID}_k, \EstimatedPosition_k, \EstimatedVelocity_k, \EstimationErrorCovariance_k, \LastMeasurementTime, \text{state})]\) published by the multi-object tracker, alongside tentative detections, raw occupied regions, and unknown-space evidence, because failure to confirm an identity does not make its occupied region clear. For each confirmed or coasting track \(\ManifestTrackIndex\), the admission engine constructs a forward occupancy set \(\ForwardOccupancySet_k(\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant)\), the region the actor could occupy \(\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant\) after its last measurement: \[\ForwardOccupancySet_k(\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant) = \left\{ \CartesianPosition \in \mathbb{R}^3 \;\middle|\; \|\CartesianPosition - \EstimatedPosition_k\| \le \ActorBodyRadius_k + \HumanWalkingSpeedBound \FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant + \OccupancyCoverageMultiplier \TrackPositionDeviation(\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant) \right\} \tag{7}\] Here \(\ActorBodyRadius_k\) is a declared body envelope that covers torso, limbs, and carried objects. The term \(\HumanWalkingSpeedBound\) is a validated bound on the actor’s speed. The term \(\OccupancyCoverageMultiplier\) is a selected multiplier whose joint spatial coverage must be calibrated rather than read off a scalar Gaussian rule. The term \(\TrackPositionDeviation(\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant)\) is the root-mean-square position deviation of the propagated track covariance. That deviation need not grow monotonically during coasting, so the check needs a conservative bound over the whole interval. \(\ForwardOccupancySet_k(\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant)\) is called an occupancy set rather than a reachability set because dynamic reachability bounds where the robot can get in time, whereas forward occupancy bounds where a person might be. A tracker with a validated acceleration bound can instead center the set on the predicted position \(\EstimatedPosition_k + \EstimatedVelocity_k \FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant\) and grow it with \(\frac{1}{2} \ActorAccelerationBound \FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant^2\), which is tighter over short intervals. The speed-bound form is the conservative one that safety standards use.


↩︎ The dynamic track manifest and the tentative, confirmed, and coasting track lifecycle are established in Multi-object tracking and data association.

International Organization for Standardization. 2025. ISO 10218-2:2025: Robotics, Safety Requirements, Part 2: Industrial Robot Applications and Robot Cells. International Organization for Standardization.

International Organization for Standardization. 2016. ISO/TS 15066:2016: Robots and Robotic Devices, Collaborative Robots. International Organization for Standardization.

Marvel, Jeremy A., and Rick Norcross. 2017. “Implementing Speed and Separation Monitoring in Collaborative Robot Workcells.” Robotics and Computer-Integrated Manufacturing 44: 144–55. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rcim.2016.08.001.
11 Approach-Speed Constant: The standard’s speed describes a design person walking toward a safeguard, not a measured coworker, and the standard applies a higher constant to hand and arm reach at short separations (International Organization for Standardization 2024). A forecast built on the walking value is valid only for the motion it describes. A coworker who runs or reaches across the corridor lies outside that bound, and the growth term must therefore be validated for the site rather than copied from the standard.
International Organization for Standardization. 2024. ISO 13855:2024: Safety of Machinery, Positioning of Safeguards with Respect to the Approach of the Human Body. International Organization for Standardization.
Equation 7 is the human half of speed and separation monitoring (SSM), a certified safety function that runs beneath the permission path and keeps a protective separation distance between the moving robot and a person. Certified safety functions beneath the permission path sizes that distance under ISO 10218-2:2025, which incorporates the collaborative-application requirements formerly published as ISO/TS 15066 (the technical specification itself remains published and is under revision) (International Organization for Standardization 2025, 2016; Marvel and Norcross 2017). The separation calculation assumes the ISO 13855 walking approach speed11 of 1.6 m/s for an approaching person (International Organization for Standardization 2024). The intent stage uses the same speed bound for an earlier and coarser purpose, rejecting a corridor before the planner spends time on it.


↩︎ The mapping of the robot’s protective-separation terms onto its stopping-distance budget is established in Kinematic stopping distance and pre-brake delay.
Screening a corridor means sweeping the robot’s candidate transit volume \(\RobotTransitVolume(\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant)\) forward in time beside every person’s set. On the aisle of figure 7, the coworker’s set grows at the ISO 13855 walking speed from 96 mm over the untracked horizon to 351 mm over the tracked one, and the corridor enters the larger disc, so the screen refuses it. Under declared motion bounds, the early screen requires the candidate transit volume to remain disjoint from every active occupancy set across the execution window. Here \({\ObservationAge}_k\) is the upper age of actor \(\ManifestTrackIndex\)’s last measurement at the current admission epoch, including bounded clock-conversion error, and \(\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant\) is additional future time: \[\RobotTransitVolume(\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant) \cap \ForwardOccupancySet_k({\ObservationAge}_k + \FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant) = \emptyset \quad \forall \FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant \in [0, \IntentLeaseExpiry - \CurrentMonotonicTime], \;\; \forall \ManifestTrackIndex \tag{8}\] Full trajectory admission must extend the exclusion check through the response delay and the complete stopping fallback. If a candidate corridor violates equation 8 by intersecting an expanding set, the early screen can return ERR_DYNAMIC_OCCUPANCY_CONFLICT and request a different corridor or a yield. The refusal diagnostic returns the earliest predicted conflict time \(\FiniteChange \EarliestConflictTime\) and the conflicting actor identifier \(\text{ID}_k\). Passing this screen does not establish a collision-free trajectory. The planner must supply the timed motion, and the permission path must check its swept volume and stopping reserve against evidence that remains valid. The arithmetic of this linear growth is simple; what decides the outcome is the horizon over which it runs.

Napkin Math 10.3: The freezing radiusProblem: A coworker walks in the 1.30 m aisle while the arm screens its corridor. How far can the growth term of equation 7 carry that person’s set over the mug’s evidence horizons and over a 2 s planning horizon, and beyond what horizon does one person’s set alone span the aisle?
Variables:

Approach speed \(\HumanWalkingSpeedBound =\) 1.6 m/s (Datasheet, ISO 13855 design value)
Evidence horizons 60 ms untracked and 219 ms tracked (Derived, equation 5); planning horizon 2 s (Illustrative)
Aisle width \(\AisleWidth =\) 1.30 m (Illustrative)

Math:

Evidence horizons: 1.6 m/s \(\times\) 60 ms \(=\) 96 mm, and 1.6 m/s \(\times\) 219 ms \(=\) 351 mm.
Planning horizon: 1.6 m/s \(\times\) 2 s \(=\) 3.2 m.
Crossover: The growth term reaches the aisle width when \(\HumanWalkingSpeedBound\,\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant = \AisleWidth\), at \(\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant =\) 1.30 m \(/\) 1.6 m/s \(=\) 0.81 s.

Result: Over the evidence horizons the set grows by centimeters to decimeters; past 0.81 s a single person’s set covers the full aisle before the body envelope and tracking terms are even added.
Systems insight: The duration of the screening horizon dictates whether the robot can plan feasible motion. Extending a dynamic forecast beyond the admitted motion and its complete stopping fallback can reject a corridor for possible human movements outside the current commitment. In narrow operating aisles, unnecessarily long forecast horizons can block otherwise admissible progress. The shorter screen must still cover response delay and deceleration; evidence expiry does not end physical motion.


A set that outgrows the aisle is the root of the freezing robot problem. Trautman and Krause showed that when a planner predicts each person independently and lets that uncertainty grow, the predicted occupancy of a crowd covers every path, and the robot stops even though people would make room for it (Trautman and Krause 2010). Three choices reduce unnecessary conservatism, and none permits shrinking a physically justified bound merely to obtain motion:

Short receding horizons: Screening over the evidence horizon rather than seconds ahead keeps the growth term near 351 mm instead of meters. The forecast must still cover the entire executed prefix and the physical fallback, including response delay and deceleration; shortening the lease does not shorten an actor’s possible motion while the robot stops.
Re-centering on fresh evidence: A qualified tracker re-centers each set on new measurements (\(\MonotonicClockInstant_0 \leftarrow \FreshEvidenceTime\)), resetting the growth term and the propagated covariance, provided its accuracy and latency support the required bound.
Interaction-aware prediction: Trautman and Krause’s own remedy predicts the people and the robot jointly, so that each accounts for how the others will respond. Such predictions are learned or modeled proposals, and they may narrow a set only after their error has been bounded by the same kind of evidence the permission path demands of any other input.















Figure 7: Forward occupancy sets on the aisle: A top-down view of a candidate corridor screened against a coworker’s forward occupancy sets, centered on the last measured position. The discs show only the growth term \(\HumanWalkingSpeedBound\FiniteChange \MonotonicClockInstant\) at the ISO 13855 speed of 1.6 m/s: 96 mm over the untracked 60 ms horizon and 351 mm over the tracked 219 ms horizon; the body envelope \(\ActorBodyRadius_k\) and the tracking term \(\OccupancyCoverageMultiplier\TrackPositionDeviation\) add to every radius. The corridor enters the tracked set (red segment), so the screen refuses it and asks for a detour or yield. Over a 2 s horizon the set grows to 3.2 m and spans the aisle.



The discs are centered on the coworker’s last measured position, so the tracker’s lifecycle sets their age. A confirmed track receives fresh measurements, while a coasting track accumulates propagated uncertainty and widens the exclusion region as its evidence ages. A goal proposal cannot refresh a stale track without incoming sensor data, and a detour proposed after a refusal needs its own timed check. When a person walks out of view, terminating the software track does not make the occluded space free. Memory already erodes certified free space behind an occlusion at the same walking-speed bound (Forward State Propagation and Occlusion Decay), and that unknown-space policy remains in force until new observations justify a different claim.

Checkpoint 10.1: Evidence windows and reach
A target is admissible only while its evidence lasts, and every early screen in this section is sized by that window.

Evidence-horizon estimate: Suppose the mug drifts at 50 mm/s instead of riding the belt, with the same 15 mm tolerance and 3 mm initial error. Can you compute the untracked evidence horizon and decide whether the 2 Hz intent model could renew it without a tracker?
Transit bound: Can you explain why a terminal move inside the static workspace can still fail admission, and what a staged approach changes about it and what it cannot change?
Occupancy vs. reachability: Which question does a forward occupancy set answer that dynamic reachability does not, and why does screening over the evidence horizon rather than seconds ahead keep the robot from freezing?
Stretched deadlines: Why can neither faster processing of the same old frame nor a longer requested lease extend a target whose evidence has expired?



Reachability and corridor filters reject provably impossible requests before planning begins. The survivors remain candidates, carrying the target bounds and obstacle evidence needed for the full motion check. The remaining challenge is distinguishing between failures these physical checks can expose and errors in task meaning that geometry and kinematics alone cannot resolve.

title: Grounded Intent
section: 10.7 Intent Grounding Failure Modes and Their Checks
text:
10.7 Intent Grounding Failure Modes and Their Checks
Whether an error arises from physical drift or from task misunderstanding, a vision-language model or multimodal transformer emits the same \(\SpecialEuclideanGroup\) target pose for a physical manipulator. A specular reflection in empty air, a stale coordinate from a moving belt, or a bolted fixture mistaken for a handle all arrive across the proposal boundary as the same clean seven-number pose:

Phantom target (hallucination): Attention concentrates on a specular glare, a shadow, or a transparent surface, and the pipeline predicts an object where none exists. Missing or corrupted depth returns then place the target in empty space or inside a transparent barrier, and an admitted proposal sends the arm into air or into glass.
Stale target (pipeline latency or temporal drift): The physical workpiece shifts on a conveyor, vibrates on a feeder tray, or is displaced by a human coworker while the multi-stage perception pipeline buffers, batches, and decodes frames. The machine’s intent model takes 336 ms per inference, longer than the 60 ms untracked horizon before any tail latency is added. A chunked action stream can keep the arm moving throughout, but on the target the model last saw. The resulting proposal arrives downstream with mathematically valid coordinates that describe where the object used to be rather than where it is, consuming physical clearance before motion begins.
Semantic ambiguity (bimodal posterior or argmax failure): Two visually identical candidate objects (e.g., two red mugs) reside within the pick zone, and both score high because the detector scores each box independently. The calibrated prediction set holds both (\(|\ConformalPredictionSet| = 2\)). Keeping only the top box or averaging the candidates’ centroids commands an arbitrary choice or drives the end effector toward the empty midpoint between the objects, risking a dual-object collision.
Misclassified affordance: A bolted fixture is taken for a movable handle, or a thin-walled container for a robust one, and the requested grip force destroys it. The approach can be collision-free while the contact wrench is wrong.
Dynamic unreachability (kinematic transit shortfall): A requested terminal move is geometrically within the static workspace manifold \(\ReachableWorkspace\), but the transit time demanded by actuator velocity and acceleration limits exceeds the remaining sensor evidence window (\(\TerminalTransitTime > \IntentLeaseExpiry - \CurrentMonotonicTime\)). The terminal request must be rejected or replaced with guarded stages supported by fresh observations; extending its old evidence deadline cannot make it feasible.

All five failures arrive across the proposal boundary in the same format: a candidate position \(\CartesianPosition \in \mathbb{R}^3\) and orientation \(\DirectionalCosineMatrix \in \SpecialOrthogonalGroup\). While a pose in empty air leads to a futile reach and a pose inside a fixture leads to contact unless path and permission checks intervene, the wrong-object case can satisfy every geometric and kinematic check while targeting the wrong item. Because the independent permission path checks only what it can measure (freshness, coverage, geometry, current state, and actuator limits), it makes no claim to verify the task’s meaning. The Safety MCU enforces physical feasibility, not semantic truth. A goal can be collision-free, kinematically smooth, and torque-limited, yet wrong for the task. Semantic verification therefore belongs to upstream task monitoring and operator oversight, and the same boundary holds under adversarial attack, where an injected instruction or a printed patch in the camera view still yields a well-formed pose.


↪ What the permission path can and cannot catch when the proposer itself is attacked is developed in Physical sensor spoofing and proposer injection.

Sajjan, Shreeyak, Matthew Moore, Mike Pan, Ganesh Nagaraja, Johnny Lee, Andy Zeng, and Shuran Song. 2020. “ClearGrasp: 3D Shape Estimation of Transparent Objects for Manipulation.” Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA), 3634–42. https://doi.org/10.1109/ICRA40945.2020.9197518.
A fresh depth observation can reject a proposed grasp when required object evidence is absent inside a covered, visible region, whereas missing returns in an occluded or unobserved region leave that space unknown. On this station, the singulation rule goes further by requiring independently qualified depth evidence of a single candidate in the pick window, even when the grounding model reports high confidence. Because the Safety MCU holds no scene representation with which to count objects, this check runs in a separate station component before any proposal is forwarded. The component routes any window with multiple candidates to a coworker for manual selection (a scoped station policy; another qualified operating mode could select a uniquely identified mug among several objects). Counting itself depends on validated sensor coverage and segmentation, so it shares a failure mode with phantom targets. Touching items can merge into a single cluster, and transparent objects such as the glass jar return little or no depth (Sajjan et al. 2020). The counter’s qualified domain must therefore exclude those cases or route them to a manual pick. Even when the count finds a single cluster, it still cannot verify that the lone object is a mug, and while the producer’s calibrated ambiguity filter may refuse earlier, it cannot replace the station’s independent check.
Table 5 groups these failures by the check that can expose them. Dynamic transit insufficiency can be rejected before motion, whereas a misclassified affordance may first become observable through contact residuals. The table separates admission checks from responses after motion or contact has begun. At the cage-door latch of notebook 10.1, the 2 ms contact-loop response already leaves 39 N at brake-command onset, and the peak comes later. Precontact speed and force limits, actuator response, compliance, and available clearance therefore determine whether the full contact trace stays within the validated contact limits.



Table 5: Grounding failure modes and their evidence limits: Each check addresses a different failure class. The table separates proposal rejection from a response to an already moving plant.











Failure mode
Evidence or check
Admission or response
Physical limit to verify




Phantom target: image artifact in empty space
Fresh depth evidence and target-region occupancy, with coverage and occlusion checked
Reject the proposal when the required object evidence is absent; request another view if the region is unknown
Rejection precedes motion only if the proposal has not already been admitted. Missing returns alone do not prove empty space.


Stale target: workpiece moved after capture
Converted capture time, bounded clock error, local tracking, and target-error envelope
Revoke dependent tracking when the evidence limit fails; select the validated fallback
Total detection, communication, actuation, and braking delay must fit the measured clearance.


Station singulation failure: multiple candidates in the pick window
Independent count of candidates in the pick window from fresh depth evidence; calibrated prediction-set size as an earlier producer-side signal
Refuse admission and route the item to the coworker for a manual pick
A single wrong object passes the count, and a confident model can return a singleton set; independent physical checks remain necessary.


Misclassified affordance: bolted fixture selected as graspable
