Operating near an active safe-set boundary can produce chattering. If a learned policy repeatedly proposes an unsafe command, sampled enforcement may switch the active constraint across successive 1 ms ticks. Depending on the plant and controller, rapid torque changes can excite a structural mode or increase motor heating and transmission wear. A tested boundary layer or hysteresis can reduce switching, but its added tracking error must fit inside the validated stopping margin.
The intervention vector \(\FiniteChange \ControlInput = \CertifiedControlAction - \NominalControlCommand\) also measures upstream policy health. A rising intervention frequency or magnitude can indicate proposal drift, a changed task, or a changed plant. Normal filtering can also preserve successful whole-machine service while reducing unassisted proposer autonomy; the log must distinguish these outcomes rather than count every correction as a task failure. Summed over an illustrative rolling window of \(\InterventionWindowDuration =\) 500 ms as \(\sum_{k} \|\CertifiedControlAction_k - {\NominalControlCommand}_k\| \FiniteChange \TimeInstant\), the metric lets the permission path flag divergence for logging or operator notification while the per-tick limits still protect the plant.


12.6.2 Intentional contact and in-contact energy barriers
Once the manipulator arm reaches the cage-door strike plate (\(\AngularClearance = 0\)), the spatial kinetic barrier (equation 5) reduces to \(\BarrierFunction(0, \JointAngularSpeed) = -\JointAngularSpeed^2 / (2\NetAngularBrakingDeceleration) \ge 0\), which admits only zero speed (\(\JointAngularSpeed = 0\)) and freezes the gripper before it can depress the latch. A spatial kinetic barrier operates under the premise that the robot’s objective is to avoid collision (\(\AngularClearance > 0\)), whereas manipulation, grasping, and assembly require intentional physical contact (\(\AngularClearance = 0\)). While the spatial barrier can admit arrival at contact with zero approach speed, it does not govern the subsequent force-controlled interaction where geometric separation no longer supplies the relevant margin. Once the warehouse mobile manipulator’s gripper meets the strike plate at the guarded approach, the arm must push against the latch spring, and the margin that matters is the energy and force it delivers there.
Enforcing safety during intentional contact requires transitioning from a spatial clearance barrier to an energetic passivity barrier. When physical clearance is zero (\(\ClearDistance = 0\)), safety cannot mean zero velocity; it means bounding mechanical energy exchange and normal contact force \(\NormalContactForce\). A controller in physical contact interacts with an unmodeled, potentially stiff environment. If tracking errors or neural policy oscillations pump unmeasured energy into the interface, the closed-loop system undergoes contact chattering, limit cycles, or high-force impact spikes that damage both the workpiece and the robot’s transmission.
To bound active energy exchange, the enforcer augments the controller state with an energy tank \(\EnergyTankLevel(\TimeInstant)\)12 (Ferraguti et al. 2013; Hogan 1985) grounded in passivity. A passive system can return no more energy than its initial stored energy plus the energy it absorbs, so a power-preserving interconnection with a passive environment retains a passive energy balance (while a stability claim additionally requires the appropriate dissipation and state-observability conditions). The tank enforces that property by bookkeeping, acting as a software tally of work rather than a physical store of energy. Every joule that virtual damping removes from the arm’s motion is credited to the tank, and the controller may spend actively only what the tank holds, namely its accumulated credits plus a fixed initial reserve. In this contact formulation, \(\ActiveControlTorque\) denotes the active torque component excluding damping, so the total controller torque is \(\ActiveControlTorque-\VirtualDampingMatrix\GeneralizedVelocities\). The damping term can credit the tank only to the extent that the actuator actually realizes the corresponding dissipative work, and using total torque in the debit while also crediting damping would count the same dissipation twice. With those components separated, the modeled balance is: \[\EnergyTankPower = \GeneralizedVelocities^\top \VirtualDampingMatrix\,\GeneralizedVelocities - \ActiveControlTorque^\top \GeneralizedVelocities \tag{9}\] where \(\GeneralizedVelocities^\top \VirtualDampingMatrix\,\GeneralizedVelocities \ge 0\) is the dissipative power credited under qualified torque tracking and \(\ActiveControlTorque^\top \GeneralizedVelocities\) is active mechanical power. Saturation, delay, or tracking error requires conservative bounds on realized work rather than credit for an unrealized damping request. The enforcer then defines the energy-tank barrier certificate of equation 10: \[\EnergyTankBarrierFunction(\MechanicalPlantState, \EnergyTankLevel) = \EnergyTankLevel - \EnergyTankReserve \ge 0 \tag{10}\] where \(\EnergyTankReserve > 0\) is a reserved baseline. Combined with a hard contact-force limit \(\ContactForceBarrierFunction(\MeasuredContactForce) = \ContactForceLimit - \|\MeasuredContactForce\| \ge 0\), the enforcer establishes the in-contact viable set \(\InContactViableSet\). While \(\EnergyTankLevel > \EnergyTankReserve\) and \(\|\MeasuredContactForce\| < \ContactForceLimit\), candidate neural actions are admitted to perform manipulation. If the task consumes the allocated energy budget (\(\EnergyTankLevel \to \EnergyTankReserve\)) or contact force approaches \(\ContactForceLimit\), the barrier filter clamps active energy injection (\(\ActiveControlTorque^\top \GeneralizedVelocities \le 0\)), restricting active work under the modeled power balance. This energy constraint does not by itself bound contact force, because a passive interaction with a stiff surface can still produce a large force. The force channel needs its own sensing-error, response-delay, and actuator bounds before the combined constraints can justify continued contact.
12 Dissipativity: Willems (1972) generalized circuit passivity to any dynamical system with a storage function, an energy-like quantity that can grow no faster than the power supplied to the system. Interconnected passive systems inherit that bound, which is why contact with an unknown but passive environment can be kept stable without a model of the environment. The energy tank is a storage function that the controller keeps explicitly in software, so the bound holds only as far as the tank’s bookkeeping matches the work the actuators actually do. 
Willems, Jan C. 1972. “Dissipative Dynamical Systems Part I: General Theory.” Archive for Rational Mechanics and Analysis 45 (5): 321–51. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00276493.
For a contact command, integrating the work balance in equation 9 over one control interval \(\FiniteChange \TimeInstant\) supplies the energy allowance for the same least-change decision. Suppose the current tank level is \({\EnergyTankLevel}_0\ge \EnergyTankReserve\), a conservative lower bound on damping power actually realized is \(\RealizedDampingPower\), and a bounded contact-direction speed \(\ContactDirectionSpeed>0\) is held over this simplified interval. The spendable work is then \({\EnergyTankLevel}_0-\EnergyTankReserve+\RealizedDampingPower\FiniteChange \TimeInstant\). Because a proposed constant force \(\ProposedContactForce \ge 0\) debits \(\ProposedContactForce \ContactDirectionSpeed \FiniteChange \TimeInstant\), the energy allowance caps force at \(\EnergyLimitedContactForce=({\EnergyTankLevel}_0-\EnergyTankReserve+\RealizedDampingPower\FiniteChange \TimeInstant)/(\ContactDirectionSpeed\FiniteChange \TimeInstant)\). Letting \(\ContactForceCap\) denote the smaller of the deliverable force and the contact-force ceiling after sensing and delay allowances, the admitted command under these stipulated scalar conditions is \(\AdmittedContactForce = \min(\ProposedContactForce, \EnergyLimitedContactForce, \ContactForceCap)\), whose debit leaves \({\EnergyTankLevel}_1={\EnergyTankLevel}_0+\RealizedDampingPower\FiniteChange \TimeInstant-\AdmittedContactForce \ContactDirectionSpeed\FiniteChange \TimeInstant\ge \EnergyTankReserve\) while keeping force below the independent cap. The controller can therefore continue useful contact with a reduced force instead of abandoning the task. At the reserve with no credited damping, however, no positive active work is admitted. Zero speed requires a separate force check rather than division by speed, and delayed or uncertain power requires conservative work bounds over the interval.
The force channel’s own bounds can be computed for the running machine’s two contacts: the cage door, which the arm pushes on purpose, and the coworker’s hand, which it must never press too hard. Each calculation turns a force limit into a speed that the enforcement record carries as a channel ceiling, and each rests on premises that only a measurement can settle. They are derived here, where the channel is enforced; the release decision consumes the results as premises.


↪ Contact force and speed ceilings are enforced as release premises in Physical Criteria for Release.
At the door the quantity that matters is how fast force rises. Against a strike plate of stiffness \(\LatchPlateStiffness\), an arm approaching at \(\LatchApproachSpeed\) raises the contact force at \(d\NormalContactForce/d\TimeInstant = \LatchPlateStiffness\,\LatchApproachSpeed\), which at the guarded 0.03 m/s against the 4.0 × 10⁵ N/m plate is 12 N/ms. The contact tripwire fires at \(\ContactTripwireForce =\) 15 N, but the contact loop needs \(\ContactLoopResponseTime =\) 2 ms for detection, command delivery, and torque rise, and the plate keeps compressing by \(\LatchApproachSpeed \ContactLoopResponseTime\) before deceleration begins. The force at physical braking onset is therefore \[\BrakingOnsetContactForce = \ContactTripwireForce + \LatchPlateStiffness\,\LatchApproachSpeed\,\ContactLoopResponseTime \tag{11}\] which evaluates to 39 N, well inside the 100 N latch limit. The limit still binds the stop that follows, because the plate goes on compressing while the arm sheds its remaining kinetic energy: \[\MaximumPlateIndentation = \frac{\BrakingOnsetContactForce}{\LatchPlateStiffness} + \frac{\LatchApproachSpeed^2}{2\ArmStoppingDeceleration} \le \frac{\LatchForceLimit}{\LatchPlateStiffness} \tag{12}\] Against time since first contact (figure 8), force climbs through the tripwire and across the loop-response window to 39 N at brake onset; the commanded stop then bends the curve over to finish at the 100 N latch limit, while an unbraked run crosses the limit within a few milliseconds. The braking term ignores the plate’s spring work, which would help decelerate the arm, so the bound is conservative. Below the limit the plate can compress only 0.15 mm further, and stopping within that distance requires about 3 m/s², an illustrative stop of about 10 ms.














Figure 8: Latch contact force against time: Force on the strike plate rises at 12 N/ms from first contact. It crosses the 15 N tripwire, but the 2 ms contact-loop response lets it reach 39 N before the brake command. A stop at about 3 m/s², lasting about 10 ms, brings the arm to rest exactly at the 100 N limit; without the brake, force crosses the limit within a few milliseconds. The plate is modeled as a linear spring and the arm as rigid.



The same two equations show why the approach speed is an enforced channel rather than a preference. At the chunk policy’s proposed 0.10 m/s (section 12.5), equation 11 already gives 95 N at braking onset, and equation 12 then demands an arm deceleration of 400 m/s². The faster approach spends the response interval on force that the stop can no longer absorb. This is the physical half of the refusal in section 12.5; the evidential half is that no trial sampled this speed. Both results treat the arm as rigid and the plate as the whole contact stiffness. Gripper, wrist-sensor, and joint compliance in series lower the effective stiffness and slow the rise, while a geared joint reflects rotor inertia into the moving mass. Whether this arm achieves the required deceleration within a fraction of a millimeter depends on joint torque, drive rise time, and structural stiffness that only arm stopping trials establish. A compliant element placed in series on purpose turns that softening into passive protection. Springs in series add their compliances, so the combined stiffness falls below that of the softer element and the force rises more slowly, a protection that holds even when the enforcer cannot stop in time. The stiffness of that element is therefore part of the contact margin, and Responses when the state remains hidden sizes it for this latch.
The coworker’s hand is the opposite case, a contact the task tolerates only up to a bounded peak force. The force depends first on which contact occurs. In a transient contact the hand is free and recoils, so both bodies move and the collision acts through their reduced mass \(\ReducedImpactMass\). In a clamped (quasi-static) contact the hand is trapped against a rack upright or the robot’s own body, cannot recoil, and receives the full robot-side effective mass at the tool center point, \(\EffectiveImpactMass =\) 12 kg. The biomechanical body model of ISO/TS 15066:2016, whose collaborative-application requirements ISO 10218-2:2025 now incorporates (section 12.8.3), assigns the hand and fingers an effective mass \(\BodyRegionMass\) of 0.6 kg and an effective spring constant \(\HertzianContactStiffness\) of 75 N/mm (International Organization for Standardization 2016, 2025b; Kirschner et al. 2022). This worked example estimates the robot-side mass as half the arm’s moving mass plus its payload capacity; it does not compute the configuration- and direction-dependent mass reflected through the contact Jacobian. In an unbraked elastic contact the peak force is \[\UnbrakedImpactForce = \ContactApproachSpeed\,\sqrt{\HertzianContactStiffness\,\ReducedImpactMass}, \qquad \ReducedImpactMass = \left(\frac{1}{\BodyRegionMass} + \frac{1}{\EffectiveImpactMass}\right)^{-1} \tag{13}\] This is the spring-mass bound of equation 6.7, which equated a moving mass’s kinetic energy to the peak elastic energy of the contact, with one change: two bodies move. Momentum conservation keeps the pair’s common (center-of-mass) motion unchanged through the contact, so only the kinetic energy of their relative motion, \(\frac{1}{2}\ReducedImpactMass \ContactApproachSpeed^2\) for a closing speed \(\ContactApproachSpeed\), can compress the hand, and the reduced mass takes the place of the single moving mass. For this hand and arm, \(\ReducedImpactMass\) is 0.57 kg, because the light hand dominates the sum; a clamped hand is the limit \(\BodyRegionMass \to \infty\), in which \(\ReducedImpactMass\) becomes \(\EffectiveImpactMass\). Solved for speed at a force criterion \(\HandForceCriterion\), the equation gives the channel ceiling \(\ContactApproachSpeed = \HandForceCriterion/\sqrt{\HertzianContactStiffness\,\ReducedImpactMass}\). The peak follows the assumed masses and stiffness; the model establishes neither an impact duration nor a pressure or injury limit.

Kirschner, Robin Jeanne, Nico Mansfeld, Saeed Abdolshah, and Sami Haddadin. 2022. “ISO/TS 15066: How Different Interpretations Affect Risk Assessment.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2203.02706.

↩︎ The single-mass spring-impact bound that this reduced-mass form extends is established in The sim-to-real contact exploit.

At the arm’s 1 m/s free-space limit even the transient model predicts 207 N, or 4.1× the 50 N criterion, so the arm cannot enter an unseparated contact at that speed. At the handover speed the two contact cases bound the approach very differently (notebook 12.3).

Napkin Math 12.3: The clamped-hand penaltyProblem: The arm approaches the coworker’s hand at the handover speed. What peak force does equation 13 predict for a free hand that recoils and for a hand clamped against a rack upright, and what approach speed does the force criterion allow in each case?
Variables:

\(\EffectiveImpactMass =\) 12 kg (Derived; the simplified half-arm-mass plus payload-capacity estimate used above).
\(\BodyRegionMass =\) 0.6 kg and \(\HertzianContactStiffness =\) 75 N/mm (Datasheet; the ISO/TS 15066 hand body model).
\(\ContactApproachSpeed =\) 0.10 m/s (Chosen; the handover approach while the coworker holds the accept_item grant that Human Authority, Reaction Time, and Clearance defines).
\(\HandForceCriterion =\) 50 N (Chosen; the handover force criterion).

Math: For a free hand, \(\ReducedImpactMass =\) (1/0.6 + 1/12)\(^{-1} =\) 0.571 kg, and with \(\HertzianContactStiffness =\) 75,000 N/m the stiffness term is \(\sqrt{\HertzianContactStiffness\ReducedImpactMass} =\) 207 N per m/s. The peak force is \(\ContactApproachSpeed\sqrt{\HertzianContactStiffness\ReducedImpactMass} =\) 0.10 \(\times\) 207 \(=\) 20.7 N, and the criterion admits \(\HandForceCriterion/\sqrt{\HertzianContactStiffness\ReducedImpactMass} =\) 50 \(/\) 207, or 0.24 m/s. A clamped hand cannot recoil, so \(\ReducedImpactMass\) becomes \(\EffectiveImpactMass\) and \(\sqrt{\HertzianContactStiffness \EffectiveImpactMass} =\) 949 N per m/s. The same approach then delivers 0.10 \(\times\) 949 \(=\) 94.9 N, and the criterion admits only 50 \(/\) 949, or 0.053 m/s.
Result: The free hand sees 20.7 N, inside the criterion; the clamped hand sees 94.9 N, which fails it.
Systems insight: Clamping multiplies the force at any speed by \(\sqrt{\EffectiveImpactMass/\ReducedImpactMass} =\) 4.6, because the whole arm-side mass, not the light hand, sets the collision. A speed ceiling derived for a free hand is therefore a geometric premise as much as a kinematic one.





At one handover speed a free hand passes the force criterion and a clamped hand fails it.
The handover channel is therefore a transient-contact ceiling. It holds only while the handover geometry excludes clamping, with the handover point in free space and no rack upright, tote edge, or link of the arm within reach of the hand along the approach. Both contacts end the same way. The arithmetic is exact; what it cannot supply is the premise it rests on, whether an achievable arm deceleration, a contact stiffness, or a clamp-free geometry. The enforcement record keeps each ceiling beside that premise, and the same discipline governs every barrier in this chapter.


12.6.3 The conditions forward invariance rests on
Unmodeled friction loss, actuator saturation, solver overruns, or inter-sample drift under a held torque command can each push a physical plant across a barrier boundary even when the continuous-time inequality is satisfied at the sample instant. The containment claim provided by both spatial and energetic barrier calculations is therefore strictly conditional. A forward-invariance claim requires a feasible barrier and the following bounded conditions; the list is necessary for this design, not an exhaustive if-and-only-if test:

Model Fidelity: The nominal plant dynamics \(\ControlAffineDriftField(\MechanicalPlantState)\) and \(\ControlAffineInputField(\MechanicalPlantState)\) must capture the true system dynamics within a validated parameter error bound.
Disturbance Bounds: External forces and unmodeled friction acting on the mass must remain strictly within the modeled disturbance envelope \(|\ExternalDisturbanceForce(\TimeInstant)| \le \DisturbanceForceBound\).
Actuation Authority: Physical actuators must possess sufficient voltage, current, and thermal headroom to realize the commanded corrective force within a qualified delivered-effort error and response-delay envelope, as well as without saturation (\(\ActuatorEffort^* \in [\MinimumActuatorEffort, \MaximumActuatorEffort]\)).
Solver Determinism: The optimization solver or projection algorithm must terminate strictly within its allocated execution budget (\(\FilterSolveTime \le \FilterSolveBudget < \PermissionLoopPeriod\)).
Discretization Invariance: The discrete sampling interval \(\PermissionLoopPeriod\) must be sufficiently small that inter-sample state drift does not breach the continuous-time invariance boundary.

The approach-acceleration upper bound is a separate premise from the lower bound on available braking, and equality of their illustrative magnitudes does not identify their roles. Each of the five conditions maps to a dedicated engineering budget: model fidelity and disturbance bounds come from system identification and bench load testing, actuation authority from dynamometer curves and thermal limits, solver determinism from static worst-case execution time analysis on the MCU, and discretization from the loop period itself. Because the drive holds the last admitted command between samples (a zero-order hold13), the plant drifts for one full period before the next check can act on it. The drift covers at most \(\FiniteChange \ZohHoldTravel = \BodySpeed \PermissionLoopPeriod + \frac{1}{2} \ProfileAccelerationBound \PermissionLoopPeriod^2\) at speed \(\BodySpeed\), where the worst case is the highest speed the base can reach rather than the ceiling \(\SpeedBound\) that admission enforces. At the 1.5 m/s drive limit, an independently stipulated 2 m/s² upper bound on approach acceleration, and \(\PermissionLoopPeriod =\) 1 ms, that drift is 1.501 mm, a small fraction of \(\ProtectiveClearanceMargin\). Tightening a raw-clearance check by this displacement preserves geometric separation over the hold interval under the stated motion bounds, whereas a kinetic or energy barrier requires a bound on its own evolution throughout the interval.
13 Zero-Order Hold: The order counts the derivatives the hold carries forward. A zero-order hold keeps the command’s value constant until the next sample, while a first-order hold would also extrapolate its slope. For one control tick the plant therefore integrates a torque the controller can no longer change, which is the source of the drift buffer \(\BodySpeed \PermissionLoopPeriod + \frac{1}{2}\ProfileAccelerationBound \PermissionLoopPeriod^2\); Discrete-time sampling and zero-order hold phase lag develops the hold’s delay. A condition that no detector watches is an assumption, so the permission path attaches one to each. A disturbance observer compares predicted with measured acceleration on every cycle. Inverter status registers and current shunts report actuator saturation. A hardware watchdog and cycle counter time the solver against its deadline. Timestamp counters on the sensor bus catch jitter and missed samples. When a detector invalidates a premise, the enforcer cannot restore permission by substituting optimistic parameters. It selects a response whose sensing, effort, and clearance premises survive, as developed in section 12.8. Both the free-space projection and contact decision must finish before the physical margin reserved for computation is spent.


12.6.4 Execution timing in the sub-millisecond loop
A correct barrier calculation delivered after the permission deadline cannot protect the margin reserved for that deadline. The whole cycle must therefore have a bounded execution time (Wilhelm et al. 2008), including state acquisition and the final drive transfer. A real-time operating system can reduce scheduling delays, but its name does not establish a bound on shared-memory or peripheral interference. The permission path’s implementation must be qualified under the competing workloads that can delay it, so the declared cycle allocation below is a timing requirement carried into loaded placement tests rather than a measured trace or a platform-independent solver guarantee.
In this heterogeneous design, the shield executes inside a 1 kHz timer interrupt routine on the MCU. An unloaded cycle of acquisition, validation, and a typical active-set solve completes in about 135 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\), an illustrative estimate rather than a bound. The candidate path instead declares a worst-case execution-time requirement of 250 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) for the whole cycle, divided among the stages below, and the whole sequence must finish inside the 400 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) deadline:



The QP solve takes 150 of the 250 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) declared cycle, inside a 400 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) deadline.

Interrupt Entry & State Acquisition (30 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\)): The hardware timer triggers the interrupt service routine (ISR), and firmware latches the wheel and joint encoder registers and the latest inertial measurement unit (IMU) sample.
Proposal & Lease Verification (15 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\)): The MCU makes one bounded read of its local mailbox, which the link receiver fills outside this routine, validates the checksum, and confirms sequence order before checking evidence age, the active chunk lease, and the host heartbeat timer. In the evidence-age check, the evidence’s age at dispatch is the difference between the source frame’s evidence timestamp and the host dispatch timestamp in the proposal header (Supervisory timers and proposal wire contracts). That age may not exceed 51.8 ms, which combines the 51.6 ms observation age charged in row 5 of table 1 with 0.2 ms of clock uncertainty (The Observation Contract). Passing that test qualifies the evidence only at dispatch, so the MCU also reconstructs the evidence’s current age from its source epoch and elapsed time and checks it against the evidence’s own validity deadline and the remaining physical margin. Inference, admission, waiting, and transfer after dispatch must already be reserved once in that margin through the dispatch-to-admission allocation inside the timing allowance. Otherwise fresh evidence is required before activation, because a new proposal timestamp cannot renew old evidence. The MCU then verifies that elapsed time since valid admission or renewal has not exceeded the 60 ms active chunk lease and reads the host heartbeat timer, which marks the host silent once no heartbeat has arrived within the 30 ms timeout.
Tracking Contract Verification (10 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\)): Firmware evaluates instantaneous tracking error norm \(\|\TrackingErrorDistance(\TimeInstant)\| = \|\CartesianPosition(\TimeInstant) - \ReferencePosition(\TimeInstant)\|\) against the qualified bound \(\TrackingErrorBound\).
CBF-QP Safety Shield Solve (150 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\)): An active-set QP solver14 running in pre-allocated static SRAM, the MCU’s tightly coupled data memory, evaluates active barrier inequalities and computes \(\CertifiedControlAction = \arg\min_{\ControlInput \in \mathbb{R}^\ControlInputDimension} \frac{1}{2}\|\ControlInput - \NominalControlCommand\|^2\). A fixed iteration cap limits the work count; meeting the allocation also requires bounded per-iteration arithmetic, memory access, interrupt interference, and output service, including ill-conditioned constraint geometry. Dynamic memory allocation is forbidden on this path so that heap service is excluded from that timing obligation. In this two-processor design no memory is shared with the host, so camera direct memory access (DMA) streams cannot reach the memory this cycle uses. The couplings that remain are the link receiver, whose DMA writes into the MCU’s own memory, and any shared supply rail or clock; The Placement Record measures that residual interference and tests whether the isolation holds under load.
Output Selection & Admitted Command Staging (15 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\)): If the QP is feasible and constraints hold, the enforcer emits the admitted command. The drives close the velocity and current loops. Because industrial servo drives running in position mode choose torque direction internally from position tracking error while an unsigned torque limit clips only the magnitude of each joint’s effort symmetrically, a position setpoint plus an unsigned torque limit does not by itself realize the signed braking effort or coupled multi-axis half-space the QP requires. This interface needs a qualified mapping from the staged command to delivered effort, with bounded realization error and response delay. The filter tightens each commanded half-space by the largest possible projection of that effort error along its normal, so every effort the drive may realize still satisfies the delivered-effort constraint. Near full braking, that allowance may remove feasibility and require earlier intervention. The drive configuration and qualification evidence must establish these bounds; this example supplies no measured error or delay. During the response interval, a previously held command must remain valid and the intersample/response allowance must cover its effect, charging each delay once. If the position/limit interface cannot satisfy this contract, the design needs a qualified effort interface or a stricter qualified operating envelope and fallback. The next position setpoint and per-axis torque limit travel in the next EtherCAT frame only under that realization contract. Drive-reported torque on the following tick can detect a breach but cannot retroactively certify the preceding interval; an invalid replacement leaves previously admitted setpoints in force only while their own evidence, lease, state, and stopping reservation remain valid.
Completion & Reserve (30 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\)): The MCU checks the register write and services its own watchdog only after the cycle succeeds. The reserve absorbs variation in the stages above; a cycle that has not completed by the deadline requires a qualified preempting timer or an independent mechanism to select the resident fallback before the next tick. The overrunning ISR cannot be assumed to detect and recover from its own stall. Only with that bounded transfer does a missed tick cost the base 1.3 mm of travel at the aisle speed. Empirical Verification of Silicon Isolation tests whether the declared WCET holds under load, so that ticks are not missed.

14 Active-Set QP: An active-set solver guesses which constraints hold with equality, solves the resulting linear system, and adds or drops one constraint per iteration. Dual variants such as that of Goldfarb and Idnani (1983) start from the unconstrained optimum, here the nominal command itself, and add only violated constraints, so a proposal that already satisfies every barrier costs almost nothing. The iteration count is bounded by the combinations of the constraint set rather than by a clock, so a fixed iteration cap bounds steps while the time per step must still be measured under interference. 
Goldfarb, Donald, and Ashok Idnani. 1983. “A Numerically Stable Dual Method for Solving Strictly Convex Quadratic Programs.” Mathematical Programming 27 (1): 1–33. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02591962.

↪ The schedulability analysis that a declared WCET and deadline feed is developed in Real-Time Timers, Watchdogs, and Schedulability.

Stage 5 is also where refusal takes effect. Any of several conditions triggers it. The chunk lease may have expired, the host heartbeat may have fallen silent, the shared drive bus may report undervoltage, tracking error \(\|\TrackingErrorDistance(\TimeInstant)\|\) may exceed \(\TrackingErrorBound\), actuator saturation may render the feasible control set empty (\(\SafeControlSet = \emptyset\)), or an operating-contract detector such as the disturbance observer or the solver deadline may trip. In any of these cases, the output selector withholds the admitted command, revokes policy authority, and selects the state-matched stop. At standstill, lease or heartbeat expiry selects HOLD, the powered standstill hold that section 12.8 defines, only while powered support remains available. Undervoltage instead requires a qualified transition to mechanical restraint before that support expires. In motion, STOP under undervoltage remains conditional on drive survival.

Checkpoint 12.2: Barrier, projection, and cycle budget
The barrier fixes which commands preserve the stop; the filter and its cycle decide whether the chosen command arrives in time.

Relative degree: Why does a barrier on raw distance give torque no control authority at the boundary, and what does the kinetic barrier of equation 5 add to restore it?
Projection vs. clamp: Why can clamping each joint separately leave a coupled half-space violated, while equation 8 satisfies it with the smallest torque change?
Projection estimate: Treat the latch approach as a one-dimensional speed command whose half-space is the 0.03 m/s target-ODD ceiling. What are \(\BarrierProjectionMultiplier^*\) and the admitted speed when the chunk policy proposes 0.10 m/s?
Timing premise: Which of the five forward-invariance conditions do the declared 250 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) WCET and the 400 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) deadline defend, and what must select the fallback when a cycle overruns?



Every stage of this cycle assumes that the solve returns a feasible command. When saturation empties the admissible torque set, the lease lapses, or the cycle overruns its deadline, projection has nothing to return, and the permission path must already hold a response it can execute without the proposer. Executing that check deterministically while surviving proposer faults requires placing the enforcer where the host processor cannot preempt or bypass it.

title: Safety Enforcement
section: 12.7 Admission, Cyclic Checking, and Monitor Independence
text:
12.7 Admission, Cyclic Checking, and Monitor Independence
A planned waypoint can clear a warehouse rack upright in the planner’s geometric check while the physical manipulator overshoots into the steel during execution, and an instantaneous motor torque well within electrical limits can accelerate the arm past the point where its remaining stopping reservation can arrest motion. Relying on trajectory admission alone misses in-flight tracking overshoot and saturation, whereas checking only single-step torque commands without a verified stopping continuation lets the arm enter an inevitable collision state before the local filter reacts. Robust safety enforcement therefore demands both layers (the per-tick cycle of section 12.6.4 on a dedicated MCU and full-plan admission before motion begins). That raises three structural questions: why neither layer can replace the other, where the cyclic checker sits relative to the command stream, and how independent of the proposer the MCU must actually be.
Full-plan admission judges the candidate trajectory, its seams, its swept clearance, and its verified stopping continuation before the machine commits to motion. The expensive geometry behind that judgment (queries of global occupancy octrees, signed distance fields, or mesh collision models) cannot run inside a 1 ms control interrupt merely because the MCU owns final actuation privilege. It therefore runs on the host as a separately scheduled, bounded job, and its result reaches the MCU as the trajectory record. The MCU’s own admission check then verifies that record against bounded, qualified local evidence (the resident stop suffix, its entry state, and the commitment deadline) without traversing the global map. The hard real-time cyclic path evaluates current joint state, remaining lease validity, and available actuator effort on every tick before selecting and dispatching the next physical command.
An in-line checker places its worst-case execution time directly inside the control-loop deadline, consuming a portion of the available compute tick. A parallel monitor instead operates asynchronously alongside the proposal pipeline, avoiding added forward latency during nominal execution but contributing detection latency and trip delay to the physical response budget. Either architectural placement must ensure privilege isolation. The untrusted proposer must never be able to bypass the selected output, and the system must preserve the dedicated sensing and actuation channels required by the fallback controller. As Two Paths and the Resources They Share will show from the resources each candidate placement shares, isolating these execution domains across memory spaces or heterogeneous processing cores is what allows the safety monitor and its fallback mechanisms to survive the very proposer faults that trigger an intervention. The physical stopping budget supplies the non-negotiable temporal and spatial boundaries that this hardware split must satisfy.

Systems Perspective 12.3: The monitor independence ruleAny valid safety claim must explicitly define which proposer failure modes its sensing, compute, and actuation pathways survive. Placing a monitor on a separate physical core or processor does not establish true independence if that monitor shares a power rail, a memory bus, a sensor link, or an unisolated clock domain with the untrusted proposer. Shared hardware resources require provably bounded interference or a qualified, survivable fallback state. Any environmental condition that the monitor cannot observe directly must remain an explicit, documented operating premise rather than an unstated assumption.


The running example assumes qualified drive, scanner, and arm safety functions and a rated lease/heartbeat watchdog; the release case must name the scoped evidence supporting those functions. Independence, however, is not certification. The runtime permission path is not the machine’s certified functional safety layer, and beneath it sit the certified safety functions embedded within motor drives, safety laser scanners, and the dedicated safety controller. These hardware-interlocked mechanisms carry the formal integrity claims that certification bodies audit against industrial standards. The primary operational duty of the software permission path is to regulate the learned proposer proactively so that the robot never trips those certified hardware interlocks during normal operation. Section 12.8.3 maps each dynamic response developed throughout this chapter onto that underlying certified safety floor once the complete response hierarchy is established, and names the one narrow MCU function that does carry a rating.

12.7.1 Where the thesis bends
When a learned locomotion or manipulation policy emits raw joint targets or motor torques at the control rate instead of handing the permission path a multi-step trajectory, the enforcer loses the ability to verify a collision-free stopping continuation before motion begins. It must then either run an active fallback model on every tick or watch its projections induce distributional shift and boundary chattering. Admission and the cyclic check in this chapter both assume that the proposer hands the permission path a plan it can judge before motion: kinematic intent lives in the learned policy, and deterministic motor drives close the torque loops. Much of contemporary robot learning practice abandons this classical division, outputting joint targets at the control rate above stiff proportional-derivative loops (Lee et al. 2020) or emitting motor torques end-to-end. The third law, proposal is not permission (principle \(\ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission}\)), does not disappear in such direct control designs. Instead, the range of physical guarantees that the runtime permission path can uphold narrows in precise, quantifiable ways.

Lee, Joonho, Jemin Hwangbo, Lorenz Wellhausen, Vladlen Koltun, and Marco Hutter. 2020. “Learning Quadrupedal Locomotion over Challenging Terrain.” Science Robotics 5 (47): eabc5986.
Four guarantees survive because each acts directly on raw commands at the causal boundary, without requiring a forward plan. A per-tick limit on rate and amplitude bounds torque slew and joint velocity at the hardware register interface. The kinetic barrier of equation 6 operates directly in effort space, so a CBF-QP can filter the policy’s output without converting it to an intermediate kinematic setpoint. The passivity-based energy tank of section 12.6.2 monitors power exchange and bounds the physical work the policy can inject into the environment during contact. Beneath all of these, low-level geofencing, safely-limited speed monitoring, and torque removal backed by mechanical spring brakes remain permanently active under the software stack. Communication timing improves along one dimension. If a qualified freshness deadline is selected at one tick and an independent watchdog enforces it, policy silence is detected within that tick plus bus transport delay, which reduces the lease-expiration travel row of table 1 from 80.6 mm to 2.6 mm at the aisle speed.
What is lost is admission. Without an explicit multi-step trajectory, the system cannot verify the collision-free stopping suffix before the robot commits to motion. The enforcer must instead evaluate the machine’s dynamic stopping reservation on every tick against an active fallback controller that maintains its own internal braking model. On a wheeled mobile base, that fallback is straightforward to formulate. The controller executes a qualified service-braking response along the current heading, followed by wheel restraint after confirmed standstill. On an underactuated balancing machine, such as a bipedal humanoid, the fallback is itself an active balance controller; cutting motor torque produces an immediate uncontrolled fall rather than a safe state.
Runtime projection also alters the closed sensorimotor loop under which the policy was trained. Every time the enforcer projects a proposed action onto the admissible set, it delivers a state to the environment that the policy never intended, precipitating distributional shift in subsequent observations. This penalty surfaces directly in task performance, as quantified by the intervention metrics of section 12.6. Frequent overrides cause the machine to chatter erratically along safety boundaries or freeze conservatively short of its goal. To reconcile this tension, modern architectures adopt filter-aware policy training, incorporating the safety filter directly into the training objective so that the neural network learns to avoid the boundary rather than encountering the enforcer for the first time on physical hardware (Hsu et al. 2024). The core thesis still holds at the causal boundary, where untrusted proposals never bypass runtime enforcement. What bends is how much of the safety argument can be settled mathematically before motion begins vs. how much performance the machine must sacrifice to settle the remainder while moving.

title: Safety Enforcement
text:
12.8 The Fallback Ladder
A safety filter must select its fallback before the admissible control set becomes empty. Once the chosen filter has an empty feasible intersection, it cannot maintain its modeled invariant. A qualified alternate response may mitigate damage or support its own narrower containment claim, but selecting it does not restore the lost guarantee. Furthermore, physical systems cannot rely on a single, binary kill switch. Abruptly severing DC bus power whenever a control proposal approaches a barrier boundary induces uncontrolled deceleration, mechanical shock, and incessant false-positive mission aborts. Conversely, complex software optimization is futile during a hardware fault such as an inverter shoot-through, because the fault destroys gate-driver field-effect transistors (FETs) milliseconds before an interrupt handler can even dispatch.
To resolve these competing physical realities, the permission path maintains a deterministic ladder of resident protective responses. The runtime arbiter evaluates plant kinematics, remaining sensor validity, and hardware integrity on every control cycle, selecting deterministically among minimally invasive projection, closed-loop position holding, controlled deceleration, or complete torque removal. The name records an ordering by how much control authority each response retains, from a corrected proposal down to unpowered restraint, not a sequence to descend. The arbiter never climbs down the rungs one at a time; it jumps directly to the one whose prerequisites still hold.

Definition 12.3: Dynamic fallback ladder
Dynamic fallback ladder is the set of resident protective responses (\(\ControlInput \in \{\SafeSetProjection(\NominalControlCommand), \PoweredHoldCommand, \ControlledStopCommand, \TorqueCutoffCommand\}\)). A deterministic arbiter selects one of them on every tick according to the check that failed (an invariant violation, a timing overrun, or a hardware fault) and the measured state of the plant. One trigger can therefore select different rungs in motion and at standstill.

Significance: Physical AI systems cannot treat all faults identically. Cutting actuator power on dynamic, underactuated, or high-momentum plants (for example, legged robots mid-stride or multirotors in flight) precipitates immediate catastrophic falls or tumbling. These platforms require state-matched active deceleration before executing terminal torque removal.
Distinction: Unlike software exception handlers that unwind the call stack or terminate a user-space thread, a dynamic fallback ladder operates against physical momentum. The arbiter matches each rung to the remaining valid sensor channels, surviving control authority, and available stopping clearance.
Common pitfall: Treating the rungs as an escalation sequence where lower rungs, such as safe torque off (STO), inherently provide faster or safer arrest. Each rung possesses distinct entry prerequisites; invoking an unpowered torque inhibit on an airborne drone or an unbraked mobile base allows the machine to coast freely without arresting motion.




12.8.1 The four rungs of the fallback ladder
Walking down protective responses one step at a time like a software exception cascade fails on physical hardware: commanding a standstill position hold while the base is rolling at 1.3 m/s saturates the drives, while cutting drive torque before active braking completes lets the vehicle coast into the obstacle. The dynamic fallback architecture therefore organizes protection across four resident responses (PROJECT, HOLD, STOP, and INHIBIT). The deterministic arbiter samples measured plant state (velocity, position, payload loading) and fault severity on every millisecond tick to dispatch the response whose compute, sensing, and actuation prerequisites still hold:

PROJECT, minimal-intervention projection in MCU firmware. The primary safety filter executes on every control cycle while the feasible control set is nonempty (\(\SafeControlSet \neq \emptyset\)), the proposal lease is fresh, and tracking error remains within bounds (\(\|\TrackingErrorDistance(\TimeInstant)\| \le \TrackingErrorBound\)). It computes the minimal-intervention torque \(\CertifiedControlAction = \arg\min_{\ControlInput} \|\ControlInput - \NominalControlCommand\|^2\) subject to active barrier half-spaces within its 150 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) cycle allocation. It makes the smallest feasible effort correction under the stated invariance assumptions; the planner must still account for any changed task-space path.
HOLD, powered hold at standstill in MCU firmware. When the machine is stationary, the arbiter selects an energized position hold, analogous to an IEC 60204-1 Category 2 stop: safe stop 2 (SS2) followed by safe operating stop (SOS), the drive function that monitors standstill.15 Its protective validity stems from that certified standstill monitor rather than the position loop gain. Because IEC 60204-1 permits only Category 0 or Category 1 for an emergency stop, HOLD can never serve as an E-stop response (International Electrotechnical Commission 2016a). The drives maintain coordinate \(\PoweredHoldState\) under closed-loop position control, modulating inverter phase currents against gravity and static loads. While this rung incurs continuous Joule heating in motor windings, it eliminates friction brake wear and preserves kinematic calibration, enabling instantaneous task resumption when a valid trajectory proposal arrives. On the warehouse mobile manipulator, this rung handles lapsed leases or lost host heartbeats specifically when the platform is already at standstill.
STOP, controlled dynamic stop in MCU firmware. When a machine in active transit loses proposal authority, tracking error diverges, or an obstacle breaches the stopping envelope, the response is a resident, state-matched controlled stop, analogous to an IEC 60204-1 Category 1 stop (safe stop 1, SS1). Its certified counterpart is the ramp-monitored variant (SS1-r), which checks deceleration against a bounded profile throughout the arrest; the unmonitored, time-controlled variant (SS1-t) merely removes torque after a fixed delay without verifying that the planned ramp actually decelerated the load (International Electrotechnical Commission 2016b). The resident jerk-limited S-curve stop suffix of section 12.2 serves this role provided the entry state falls within its validated domain. Executed autonomously by bare-metal MCU firmware directly from local SRAM, this stop peaks at the credible deceleration \(\CredibleBrakingDeceleration\), returning kinetic energy through motor inverters to the DC bus for absorption by the qualified regeneration path. Power removal and mechanical brake clamping occur only after confirmed zero velocity.
INHIBIT, torque inhibit and spring-brake clamping by hardware interlocks. When the safety microcontroller suffers a brownout, clock loss, or watchdog timeout, all software decision logic ceases. Dedicated, out-of-band hardware interlocks trigger STO to de-energize gate drive power supplies and drop hold current to electromechanical spring-applied brakes. This terminal rung removes motor torque without software intervention; the mechanical brakes provide only their independently qualified holding or dynamic stopping capacity.

15 Machine Stop Categories: IEC 60204-1 distinguishes uncontrolled power removal (Category 0), controlled stopping followed by power removal (Category 1), and controlled stopping with power retained (Category 2). A category defines electrical power status rather than stopping distance; every rung therefore requires its own empirically validated stopping measurement.
International Electrotechnical Commission. 2016a. IEC 60204-1:2016: Safety of Machinery, Electrical Equipment of Machines, Part 1: General Requirements. International Electrotechnical Commission.
When a machine in motion loses proposal authority or violates a tracking bound, the arbiter engages a controlled dynamic stop, operating analogously to an IEC 60204-1 Category 1 stop. On the warehouse mobile manipulator base, this rung executes the resident stop suffix pre-admitted alongside the motion trajectory, rather than attempting to synthesize a stopping trajectory on the fly during a fault. In steady-state cruising with zero acceleration, this pre-computed profile matches the operating state at fault onset directly; nonzero acceleration states require their own qualified state-matched suffixes. From an aisle cruise velocity of 1.3 m/s, the jerk-limited S-curve suffix sustains a credible peak deceleration of 2 m/s² between its jerk transitions. The entire maneuver spans 931.25 ms and traverses 605.31 mm, the stop-suffix travel the stopping budget of section 12.2 reserves at this speed. Because the deceleration phase channels kinetic energy back through the inverter into the DC bus, bus capacitance and braking choppers must absorb this regenerative surge without triggering a bus overvoltage fault. Complete electrical power removal, if mandated by protocol, occurs only after sensors verify standstill.
Beyond firmware-driven stops, a separate out-of-band circuit can inhibit motor torque generation entirely. Drive STO cuts gate-drive bias to isolate inverter FETs, but it does not disconnect the DC bus, energize mechanical friction brakes, or actively decelerate a moving rotor; an unbraked motor will simply coast under its existing momentum. In robust architectures, an external safety controller simultaneously drives a separately rated contactor and spring-applied mechanical brakes. Engineers must evaluate the dynamic stopping distance of this combined pathway as an integrated system, because dropping drive torque while an arm is under gravitational load or while a vehicle is at speed can exacerbate the hazard. For the warehouse mobile manipulator, this pathway, STO combined with nine spring brakes that engage between 30 ms and 80 ms after coil flux decay, constitutes the unbudgeted INHIBIT rung. It serves exclusively as a hardware backstop for MCU cycle failure, and the primary stopping envelope claims do not rely on it.
An undervoltage fault on the shared drive bus can invoke the STOP rung only while inverter gate drives, angular encoders, and control logic retain adequate voltage for closed-loop deceleration. The isolated permission rail maintains power to logic circuits, transceivers, and brake coils for 2 s, but it does not supply the motor currents required for braking torque. Consequently, timing guarantees for powered stopping assume a surviving drive bus. Under this condition, dynamic braking begins within 22 ms of the fault flag; the hold-up hypothetical uses the pre-dispatch inspected-floor ceiling of 1.23 m/s, rather than an admitted operating configuration, and its stop requires 1211.4 ms. Mechanical brake engagement at standstill adds at most 80 ms. This entire sequence completes within 1313.43 ms, preserving a 686.57 ms buffer of control logic hold-up.


↩︎ The isolated permission rail and its capacitive hold-up are established in Cross-budget coupling and permission rail isolation.
This analysis confirms the control-supply duration budget, whereas the electrical drive-energy budget requires separate qualification. Systems engineers must prove through empirical testing that the DC bus capacitance, inverter power stages, and regenerative dump resistors sustain controlled deceleration under worst-case electrical fault conditions. If the drive stage cannot guarantee this power integrity, the system must either adopt an unpowered dynamic braking configuration or restrict its operational safety envelope; INHIBIT cannot be credited with standard Category 1 stopping performance. Similarly, at standstill, an undervoltage fault must trigger verified mechanical brake engagement before the logic supply decays, rather than attempting to maintain an active HOLD indefinitely on finite capacitance.
Physical AI systems engineers must distinguish between fail-safe and fail-operational plants when configuring terminal fallbacks. In a machine already at a mechanically restrained standstill, removing drive torque is safe once mechanical engagement is verified. On underactuated, open-loop unstable, or high-momentum platforms, however, abruptly removing actuator torque directly initiates a catastrophic failure mode:

Aerial platforms (multirotors and eVTOLs): Cutting motor torque drops aerodynamic thrust to zero instantly, transforming an airborne vehicle into an uncontrolled ballistic projectile.
Dynamic legged systems (bipedal humanoids): During dynamic locomotion, the robot’s center of mass frequently falls outside the support polygon; stability depends on active ground-reaction forces and momentum exchange. Suddenly removing joint torques causes an unrecoverable fall, with impact severity governed by gait phase and available compliance.
High-speed autonomous vehicles: De-energizing steering actuators or electric traction motors at highway speeds strips away the control authority required to execute a coordinated deceleration, leaving the vehicle at the mercy of passive road friction.

The physical channel that dispatches a hardware torque-removal request is the out-of-band interlock that Actuation Authority traced (Illustrative out-of-band interlock and STO path). In it, dual linked emergency-stop contacts, two force-guided relays whose external device monitoring (EDM) contacts block a restart after a weld, and two STO inputs on the drive leave no single fault able to defeat the trip. What the INHIBIT rung needs from that circuit is its third stage, drawn again here with the brake in its own loop (figure 9), because removing drive torque (\(\CommandedJointTorque = 0\)) and arresting physical momentum are distinct functions that need separate validation:

Torque removal (Stage 3, drive side): De-energizing the safety relays drops the drive’s STO inputs, which de-energize the gate drive power supply for the three-phase inverter bridge, rendering the power MOSFETs or insulated-gate bipolar transistors (IGBTs) high-impedance, so the motor can no longer produce electromagnetic torque. STO alone does not apply mechanical braking. An unbraked motor carries momentum and may coast freely.
Mechanical restraint (Stage 3, brake side): A separate coil circuit powers the spring-applied electromechanical friction brake. When power is removed, coil magnetic flux decays, allowing internal springs to physically clamp friction pads against the motor shaft, applying the brake without electrical power. A holding-brake rating does not establish the ability to arrest a moving load; dynamic stopping requires separate energy, torque, and response qualification.







Figure 9: Illustrative emergency-stop circuit: Stages 1 and 2 are the out-of-band interlock circuit (Chapter 4); Stage 3 maps to the numbered list above. Two linked contacts each hold a force-guided relay, the relays’ enable contacts hold the drive’s two Safe Torque Off (STO) inputs, and their EDM contacts in series block a restart after a weld. The spring-applied brake runs on its own supply, and a supply contactor, if fitted, provides galvanic disconnection. A moving motor can coast after STO, so the brake’s set time and the physical stopping distance must be measured for the load and state.



That separation between software control and hardwired, out-of-band trip circuits is not a stylistic preference. When the processor running the control loop stalls or corrupts its own state, only a physically independent path can still remove drive enable and clamp the brakes. The precedent that the lineage table of The Four Bedrock Laws attaches to the third law shows the cost of removing that hardware path and trusting software logic to gate a high-energy actuator on its own (war story 12.1).

War Story 12.1: Therac-25 software interlock eliminationContext: Between 1985 and 1987, the Therac-25 medical linear accelerator administered massive radiation overdoses to six cancer patients after system designers eliminated the electromechanical interlocks used in previous models, assigning safety-critical beam containment entirely to software (Leveson and Turner 1993).
Mechanism: Software race conditions and shared memory corruption in the operator interface allowed the machine to fire its high-current electron beam (25 MeV) without rotating the tungsten target and beam-flattening filter into position. Because the physical microswitches that previously interlocked beam activation had been removed, the underlying hardware possessed no independent means to detect that the operational mode conflicted with the turntable state.
Impact: Six patients received radiation doses estimated between 4,000 and 20,000 rads (up to 100 times the therapeutic level), causing severe tissue necrosis and three direct fatalities (Leveson and Turner 1993).
Response: Investigators mandated the restoration of independent hardware interlocks, requiring positive electromechanical verification of turntable configuration prior to beam generation, alongside formal software safety lifecycle standards.
Systems lesson: A software-based protection layer cannot serve as its own independent backstop. A runtime barrier filter may exercise binding authority over nominal control proposals, but the architecture still requires an out-of-band, physically independent trip mechanism to survive processor lockups, memory corruption, and firmware bugs. Moreover, because torque removal alone does not guarantee deceleration, the surviving physical response must match the plant’s dynamic envelope.


The four rungs run on two paths (figure 10). PROJECT, HOLD, and STOP run in safety MCU firmware at the 1 kHz tick and reach the drives through one arbiter, which selects a single actuation command \(\SelectedActuationCommand\); INHIBIT bypasses the firmware on a hardware path that removes gate-drive supply (STO) and drops spring-brake holding current when the processor itself fails. The rungs trade response latency, control authority, and recovery cost, and the arbiter selects directly among those whose entry prerequisites still hold. A controlled stop demands verified drive electronics and sufficient stopping clearance; losing drive integrity forces unpowered mitigation with strictly weaker physical guarantees. Selection is also only as sound as the state evidence behind it. The 2023 Cruise pullover, which When the Responsibilities Fail Together set beside Tempe as a failure after impact, selected a motion fallback on the strength of a missing track (war story 12.2).






Figure 10: Fallback responses and the paths that run them: The plant state and the failed check select one response directly; the four are alternatives, not steps of an escalation. PROJECT, HOLD, and STOP run in the safety MCU’s firmware and reach the drives through its arbiter, which here passes the projected command. INHIBIT is the one response that survives loss of the MCU itself, so it bypasses the arbiter on a hardware path that removes gate-drive supply and lets the spring brakes set. On a moving machine that path also removes motor braking, and the machine coasts until the separately qualified brakes take hold.




War Story 12.2: Cruise post-impact fallback (2023)Context: In October 2023, an autonomous Cruise robotaxi in San Francisco encountered a pedestrian who had been struck by an adjacent human-driven vehicle and propelled into the robotaxi’s travel lane (Exponent, Inc. 2024).
Mechanism: The autonomous vehicle initiated an immediate emergency stop upon detecting the impact. However, the collision-classification subsystem erroneously localized the pedestrian to the side of the vehicle rather than under the chassis, categorizing the event as a side collision. The operational design domain for side collisions specified a secondary pullover maneuver to clear traffic. Because the perception pipeline had tracked the pedestrian only intermittently before the collision, the tracker marked the lane ahead as clear, prompting the vehicle to accelerate from standstill into the pullover (Exponent, Inc. 2024).
Impact: Executing the pullover dragged the pedestrian, who remained pinned beneath the vehicle’s floorpan, approximately 20 ft (6.1 m) at speeds reaching 7.7 mph (3.4 m/s), causing severe trauma (Quinn Emanuel Urquhart and Sullivan, LLP 2024). The California DMV subsequently suspended Cruise’s autonomous testing and deployment permits, prompting Cruise to halt fleet operations nationwide and recall software across 950 vehicles (California Department of Motor Vehicles 2023; Exponent, Inc. 2024).
Response: A post-collision fallback must prohibit renewed motion whenever state uncertainty persists. In this scenario, retaining a locked standstill and mandating physical inspection prevents the system from treating missing perceptual tracks as free space. Teleoperation feeds cannot substitute for verified local sensor coverage.
Systems lesson: An embodied fallback cannot infer free space from the absence of sensor tracks. Every transition across fallback states requires positive evidence verifying that assumed physical invariants hold, paired with failsafe physical restraints while state ambiguity remains unresolved.

12.8.2 Industrial stop categories and the safe torque off trap
On a moving mobile base or a gravity-loaded arm, Safe Torque Off (STO) is not an active brake: removing drive torque immediately leaves the base coasting on wheel momentum and lets the arm drop during the milliseconds before its mechanical friction brakes clamp. Decelerating the mobile manipulator safely instead uses closed-loop motor torque during the active braking phase and engages mechanical holding brakes only once the plant reaches confirmed standstill. Industrial standards distinguish machine-level stop categories from drive-level safety functions across this sequence. IEC 60204-1 classifies whether electrical power remains connected during and after deceleration. Functional safety standards such as IEC 61800-5-2 define the drive functions, including STO, SS1, and SS2, that execute individual stages of a response, and the HOLD and STOP rungs borrowed their names from them. Table 3 maps these formal classifications to their concrete physical obligations.

12.8.3 Certified safety functions beneath the permission path
Citing an unrated numerical QP solver or software evidence-age check as the primary hazard control in a safety case fails certification audit immediately, because complex solver code without formal tool qualification and hardware diagnostic coverage cannot carry a safety integrity claim. In an embodied deployment, not all firmware executing the fallback ladder carries formal functional safety certification, so a certification engineer partitions software claims by the integrity of the underlying hardware substrate. On a production machine, formal guarantees rest primarily on a second, lower layer: dedicated safety functions in the motor drives, the optical safety scanner, and the arm’s safety controller, each architected and validated to a Performance Level (PL) under ISO 13849-1 (International Organization for Standardization 2023a). A Performance Level grades a safety function rather than a component, by the architecture category of its channels, their mean time to dangerous failure, their diagnostic coverage, and their defenses against common-cause failure (The Independence Requirement and the Two-Processor Hypothesis); IEC 61508 grades the same functions by Safety Integrity Level (SIL) (International Electrotechnical Commission 2010). These hardened functions substantiate the certified protective envelope. Above them, the MCU permission path operates primarily as an unrated performance layer designed to keep the learned policy inside the admissible set, preventing unnecessary trips of the hard safety floor. Only one narrow component of this MCU layer carries a safety rating, the watchdog that revokes authority when the chunk lease expires or the host heartbeat falls silent.

International Organization for Standardization. 2023b. ISO 3691-4:2023: Industrial Trucks, Safety Requirements and Verification, Part 4: Driverless Industrial Trucks and Their Systems. International Organization for Standardization.

International Organization for Standardization. 2025a. ISO 10218-1:2025: Robotics, Safety Requirements, Part 1: Industrial Robots. International Organization for Standardization.
Table 4 maps each response and speed channel onto its certified industrial counterpart. The core drive functions derive from IEC 61800-5-2 (International Electrotechnical Commission 2016b): safe torque off (STO), safe stop 1 (SS1), safe stop 2 (SS2), safe operating stop (SOS) (which monitors standstill), safely limited speed (SLS), and safe brake control (SBC) (which drives the mechanical brake coil through a monitored output). For the mobile base, ISO 3691-4 assigns required performance level (PLr) d to braking system control and personnel detection within the travel path, while assigning PLr b to the electromechanical parking brake (International Organization for Standardization 2023b; TÜV Rheinland 2021). For robotic manipulators, ISO 10218-1:2025 classifies systems into Class I (manipulator mass under 10 kg with strictly limited force and velocity) and Class II, mandating PL d (or SIL 2) across all safety functions on Class II arms (International Organization for Standardization 2025a; Hartmann et al. 2026). Because the warehouse arm weighs 18 kg, it is governed by Class II mandates.

As the first row of table 4 indicates, the online CBF-QP, feasibility tests, and sensor evidence-age checks operate without formal safety ratings. Consequently, safety cases cannot cite these complex numerical filters as certified protective measures; instead, the enforcement record treats their correct execution as an operational premise. System architects face two choices when structuring this boundary. An engineering team can treat all MCU-level admission checks strictly as an unrated performance layer, relying entirely on the certified hardware floor to prevent harm. Alternatively, the team can certify the entire MCU firmware stack to functional safety standards (such as IEC 61508 or ISO 26262), subjecting matrix solvers and barrier algorithms to exhaustive formal methods, tool qualification, and deterministic execution bounds.
The running machine assumes the hybrid path. Its qualified watchdog, the table’s second row, independently commands STO or SS1 at the drive level when the chunk lease expires or the host heartbeat falls silent. Its bounded scope reduces the qualification burden, while isolation, failure behavior, timing, and lifecycle evidence remain necessary. Meanwhile, the complex admission checks remain unrated, leaving the certified optical scanner and drive-integrated safety functions to handle primary hazard mitigation. This split architecture demands strict physical and temporal isolation between the rated watchdog and unrated solver routines to eliminate common-cause faults.


↪ How the release case treats the certified watchdog as a rated safety function and the unrated admission checks as empirical premises is developed in The standards map for the running machine.
