Once a slow microcontroller clock lags by more than the 0.2 ms allowance, the uncompensated clock lag subtracts directly from the measured elapsed age, so the age check can no longer certify that an admitted frame lies within budget. A frame held back by an F2 stall then passes as fresh whenever the uncorrected drift exceeds the stall’s extra age. Because drift keeps accumulating for as long as synchronization stays lost, the stall the check can miss grows with the blackout. The permission path may then admit proposals computed from obstacle coordinates older than the budget allows while the loaded base moves at 1.3 m/s.



A five-period blackout spends half the clock-conversion bound.
Every physical fault injection trial concludes with a rigorous evidentiary burden. The test harness must simultaneously record the trip signal from the internal detector, the precise timestamp of proposal rejection, the actuation takeover at the motor drives, and the final physical stopping trajectory. All measurements must be captured by external, fault-isolated instruments synchronized to a single master reference clock. If a trial fails to record any of these intermediate transitions, it fails to produce actionable verification evidence. Physical fault injection campaigns do not yield simple pass/fail tallies; they generate auditable execution traces binding each trial to its architectural claim, its exact operating envelope, its software build artifacts, and its physical sensor waveforms.


↪ How these trial traces enter a safety case as evidence for a claim is developed in Safety Cases and Claims.

title: Adversarial Verification
text:
15.9 Searching Beyond the First Trial
A single successful fault trial demonstrates that the safety path can arrest the vehicle under one declared set of operating conditions. Physical machinery, however, rarely fails under tidy nominal conditions; subtle vulnerabilities hide in the narrow corners of the state space where timing jitter, payload shifts, and degraded surface traction align against the enforcer. Exhaustive testing across this continuous operational envelope is physically impossible, yet uniform random sampling requires an intractable number of runs to uncover rare edge-case failures. Searching beyond isolated trials requires systematically steering disturbances toward the boundary conditions that drive the system closest to its safety limits. Rather than replacing the formal coverage record, automated search routines prioritize which candidate executions deserve empirical evaluation on the physical test track or dynamometer.

15.9.1 Signal temporal logic and quantitative robustness
A binary PASS or FAIL verdict tells an automated search algorithm nothing about whether a passing stop cleared the rack by 15 cm or by 1 mm, leaving the optimizer blind to near misses. Classical temporal logic (Pnueli 1977) checks whether a sequence of states satisfies a property. Signal Temporal Logic (STL) extends the specification to continuous time and real-valued physical signals (such as staying inside a spatial corridor or halting before a deadline (Maler and Nickovic 2004)), and it equips every formula with quantitative robustness semantics (Fainekos and Pappas 2009). Instead of returning a boolean flag, quantitative robustness computes a real-valued signed margin \(\StlRobustness(\StlFormula, \SignalTrajectory, \TimeInstant) \in \mathbb{R}\) that measures how far a trajectory \(\SignalTrajectory: \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \to \mathbb{R}^{\SignalDimension}\) sits from violating or satisfying the temporal property \(\StlFormula\) at time \(\TimeInstant\).

↪ The syntax and semantics of signal temporal logic are developed in Signal Temporal Logic and Continuous Robustness.

For an atomic physical predicate \(\pi \equiv (\StlPredicateFunction(\SignalTrajectory(\TimeInstant)) \ge 0)\) (such as spatial clearance \(\ObstacleSeparationDistance(\TimeInstant) - \SafeSeparationDistance \ge 0\)), quantitative robustness evaluates the signed predicate margin: \(\StlRobustness(\pi, \SignalTrajectory, \TimeInstant) = \StlPredicateFunction(\SignalTrajectory(\TimeInstant))\). Across temporal operators, safety invariants evaluate worst-case (minimum) margins, whereas reachability deadlines evaluate best-case (maximum) margins: \[\StlRobustness(\square_{[0, \FiniteTimeHorizon]} \StlFormula, \SignalTrajectory, 0) = \min_{t \in [0, \FiniteTimeHorizon]} \StlRobustness(\StlFormula, \SignalTrajectory, \TimeInstant), \qquad \StlRobustness(\lozenge_{[0, \StlEventuallyDeadline]} \StlFormula, \SignalTrajectory, 0) = \max_{t \in [0, \StlEventuallyDeadline]} \StlRobustness(\StlFormula, \SignalTrajectory, \TimeInstant). \tag{3}\] Here \(\square_{[0,\FiniteTimeHorizon]}\) denotes “always on \([0, \FiniteTimeHorizon]\)” and \(\lozenge_{[0,\StlEventuallyDeadline]}\) denotes “eventually within \(\StlEventuallyDeadline\).”
The sign and magnitude of \(\StlRobustness\) in equation 3 establish an immediate operational interpretation: \[\StlRobustness > 0 \implies \text{satisfied with positive margin } \StlRobustness, \qquad \StlRobustness < 0 \implies \text{violated with shortfall depth } |\StlRobustness|.\] For example, if the spatial clearance margin is \(\StlRobustness = +0.15\text{ m}\), the minimum clearance observed along the trajectory exceeded the safety threshold by 15 cm. Conversely, if \(\StlRobustness = -0.04\text{ m}\), the machine breached the prescribed clearance boundary by 4 cm, with physical collision depending on whether the safety limit included an explicit standoff buffer.
This signed value margin constitutes space robustness, quantifying how far the signal’s physical magnitude can perturb before the verdict flips. Space robustness captures amplitude margins rather than timing margins: a delayed brake actuation represents a temporal shortfall rather than an instantaneous spatial error. Capturing temporal slack requires time robustness, a complementary semantics that evaluates how far a signal trajectory may shift along the time axis before the verdict changes (Donzé and Maler 2010). Because spatial and temporal margins govern different physical dimensions, combining them into a single unweighted formula introduces semantic ambiguity. For the F1 specification, the cleanest engineering formulation isolates the onset deadline outside the Signal Temporal Logic expression as an explicit scalar predicate on measured reaction time, while evaluating stopping distance via spatial robustness.

Donzé, Alexandre, and Oded Maler. 2010. “Robust Satisfaction of Temporal Logic over Real-Valued Signals.” Formal Modeling and Analysis of Timed Systems (FORMATS), Lecture notes in computer science, vol. 6246: 92–106. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-15297-9_9.
For this reason equation 1 keeps its two predicates apart. The onset predicate, deceleration within 82 ms of the last valid renewal, is a scalar check on measured reaction time, and the travel predicate, at most 751.9 mm at aisle speed, is a space-robustness predicate on vehicle position. Both are measured from the same reference event, so neither can silently absorb slack from the other; a different reference event would change the elapsed timing and require a correspondingly adjusted distance bound.
To illustrate this dual evaluation numerically, consider an F1 trace at aisle speed, timed channel by channel in figure 4, where powered deceleration begins 30 ms late, occurring 112 ms after the last valid renewal. The onset margin against the 82 ms bound evaluates to -30 ms. Because the mobile base travels 39 mm further before braking engages, total travel from renewal to rest reaches 750.9 mm, yielding a distance margin of 1 mm against the 751.9 mm oracle. The onset predicate fails, while nominal travel remains within the distance allowance. The verification results retain both margins in their native physical units; the tracking inset belongs in the oracle and is not additional travel in the plotted speed integral. Because taking an unweighted minimum across milliseconds and millimeters produces an uninterpretable quantity, synthesizing them into a unified score via min requires normalizing each margin by a predeclared positive scale in its corresponding unit. Logging both the raw margins and their normalization factors ensures the synthesized verdict remains physically meaningful. Choosing scales equal to the verification bounds themselves yields normalized margins of -0.366 for onset timing and 0.001 for stopping distance, making the onset predicate the governing term in the combined score. When several predicates have negative margins, alternative scales can change which one governs the compound score, so test engineers must fix normalization factors before executing verification runs. In this nominal trace only onset fails, so positive rescaling cannot make distance the governing predicate. These numerical values reflect model arithmetic over a stipulated reference trace rather than empirical physical measurements.














Figure 4: One F1 trace against its oracle: Model timelines, not measurements, of the channels an F1 trial must witness at 1.3 m/s, timed from the last valid renewal. The chunk lease expires at 60 ms, the next permission tick commands the stop, the fieldbus delivers it, and powered deceleration must begin by 82 ms; a proposal probed after expiry is refused. The dashed trace brakes 30 ms late, so its onset margin is -30 ms and its 750.9 mm of nominal travel retains 1 mm against the 751.9 mm oracle. The on-time curve travels 711.9 mm; the tracking inset is an allowance in the oracle, not extra travel in either curve.



Recording every monitored channel on one timeline, as illustrated in figure 4, helps localize a failed trial to a stage of the response path when the independent witnesses remain valid. A lease that expires on schedule and a stop command issued at the next tick, followed by a late braking onset, direct the investigation toward command delivery, drive execution, or physical brake response rather than the lease-expiry check.
By producing a continuous, signed margin rather than a binary pass/fail flag, quantitative robustness transforms verification from passive testing into temporal logic falsification as adversarial optimization. In classical computer vision and deep learning, adversarial attacks such as the fast gradient sign method (FGSM) (Goodfellow et al. 2015) and projected gradient descent (PGD) (Madry et al. 2018) search for an input perturbation \(\AdversarialPerturbation\) bounded within an \(\AdversarialPerturbationBudget\)-ball (\(\|\AdversarialPerturbation\|_\infty \le \AdversarialPerturbationBudget\)) that maximizes task loss: \(\max_{\|\AdversarialPerturbation\|_\infty \le \AdversarialPerturbationBudget} \LossFunction(\ParameterizedPredictor(\ModelInput + \AdversarialPerturbation), \ExampleLabel)\). In cyber-physical systems, temporal logic falsification provides the continuous dynamic counterpart. Rather than perturbing static feature vectors, an adversarial optimizer searches over initial state spaces and time-varying physical disturbance trajectories within a bounded physical disturbance envelope to minimize quantitative Signal Temporal Logic robustness. The robustness metric \(\StlRobustness\) acts directly as the adversarial objective function. Whereas uniform random sampling across a high-dimensional operational state space requires an intractable number of physical trials to expose rare corner-case collisions, an adversarial falsification engine actively steers disturbance sequences toward trajectories that drive the system closest to violating its safety invariants.

Goodfellow, I. J., J. Shlens, and C. Szegedy. 2015. “Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

Madry, Aleksander, Aleksandar Makelov, Ludwig Schmidt, Dimitris Tsipras, and Adrian Vladu. 2018. “Towards Deep Learning Models Resistant to Adversarial Attacks.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).


15.9.2 Formulating falsification as trajectory optimization
An unconstrained mathematical search over arbitrary disturbance signals can easily invent discontinuous spikes that no real actuator, sensor, or contact surface can physically produce, wasting the search on impossible counterexamples. To restrict the search to physically realizable disturbances, let \(\MechanicalPlantState_0 \in \FalsificationInitialStateSet\) represent the machine’s initial state vector (translational speed, payload mass, heading angle, and battery state-of-charge), and let \(\DisturbanceTrajectory(\TimeInstant) \in \AdmissibleDisturbanceSet\) denote an adversarial disturbance trajectory spanning the test horizon \([0, \FiniteTimeHorizon]\). Because physical hardware has finite bandwidth, mechanical inertia, and thermal limits, disturbance trajectories are parameterized over a compact parameter space \(\DisturbanceParameterVector \in \DisturbanceParameterSet\) using smooth basis functions, such as B-splines, cubic splines, or Fourier series: \[\DisturbanceTrajectory(\TimeInstant; \DisturbanceParameterVector) = \sum_{k=1}^{\DisturbanceBasisCount} \DisturbanceBasisCoefficient_k \DisturbanceBasisFunction_k(\TimeInstant)\] where \(\DisturbanceBasisFunction_k(\TimeInstant)\) are time-dependent basis functions and \(\DisturbanceBasisCoefficient_k\) are bounded parameter coefficients.
The temporal logic falsification problem finds the worst-case parameter combination that minimizes quantitative robustness: \[\min_{\MechanicalPlantState_0 \in \FalsificationInitialStateSet, \, \DisturbanceParameterVector \in \DisturbanceParameterSet} \StlRobustness(\StlFormula, \SignalTrajectory(\MechanicalPlantState_0, \DisturbanceTrajectory(\DisturbanceParameterVector)), 0) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|\DisturbanceTrajectory(\TimeInstant; \DisturbanceParameterVector)\|_\infty \le \DisturbanceBudget, \quad \forall \TimeInstant \in [0, \FiniteTimeHorizon]. \tag{4}\]
The disturbance budget \(\DisturbanceBudget\) in equation 4 bounds the peak magnitude of optical, acoustic, contact, and execution disturbances derived from the operational envelope. Yet magnitude bounds alone do not guarantee that a test bench can deliver the waveform. The basis functions, coefficient bounds, and experimental test fixtures must also respect realistic rates of change and duration limits. For example, a programmable load bank that cannot slew fast enough to replicate a steep simulated voltage transient leaves that synthesized counterexample untested on hardware.
A verification campaign must therefore log both the synthesized disturbance command and its independently measured physical trace. If the test fixture fails to deliver the precommitted disturbance trajectory within specified tolerances, the trial is INVALID for that test condition even if the machine comes to a safe stop. Conversely, while an empirically realized counterexample refutes a safety claim outright, a search that finds no violation within a restricted parameter family leaves arbitrary disturbances outside that basis open to question.


15.9.3 Selecting a search method
Frictional contact transitions and discrete controller state jumps often make the quantitative robustness landscape nonsmooth and non-convex, causing gradient descent to stall or step in the wrong direction unless those transitions are smoothed or handled explicitly. Derivative-free optimizers avoid this trap. The Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) (Hansen and Ostermeier 2001) updates a multivariate normal distribution over disturbance parameters across generations, discovering correlated failure modes across speed, surface friction, and execution timing. When physical trials dominate the cost because each run requires mechanical resets, hardware inspection, and thermal cool-down, Bayesian optimization10 fits a probabilistic surrogate model to previous runs to choose the next test point. Neither method guarantees convergence to a global minimum over a finite campaign, so the verification record must preserve search parameter bounds, random seeds, evaluated test vectors, and fixture limits so that auditors can see exactly which regions were challenged.

Hansen, Nikolaus, and Andreas Ostermeier. 2001. “Completely Derandomized Self-Adaptation in Evolution Strategies.” Evolutionary Computation 9 (2): 159–95. https://doi.org/10.1162/106365601750190398.
10 Bayesian Optimization: Originally developed for computationally expensive engineering simulations, Bayesian optimization fits a Gaussian-process surrogate across completed trials and selects the next sample point by maximizing expected improvement (Jones et al. 1998). Physical fault-injection rigs face the same cost structure, because each trial requires mechanical resets, hardware inspection, and thermal stabilization delays. Still, the surrogate’s confidence is only a model prediction: a region it estimates to be safe has not been physically tested simply because the surrogate predicts a positive margin.
Jones, Donald R., Matthias Schonlau, and William J. Welch. 1998. “Efficient Global Optimization of Expensive Black-Box Functions.” Journal of Global Optimization 13 (4): 455–92. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1008306431147.

Lee, Ritchie, Ole J. Mengshoel, Anshu Saksena, Ryan W. Gardner, Daniel Genin, Joshua Silbermann, Michael Owen, and Mykel J. Kochenderfer. 2020. “Adaptive Stress Testing: Finding Likely Failure Events with Reinforcement Learning.” Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 69: 1165–201. https://doi.org/10.1613/jair.1.12190.
Two software toolboxes implement this search loop for cyber-physical models: S-TaLiRo (Annpureddy et al. 2011) and Breach (Donzé 2010). Both ingest a formal Signal Temporal Logic requirement and a simulation model, compute quantitative robustness on each simulated rollout, and steer stochastic or local optimizers toward negative robustness. A related family of algorithms treats the disturbance sequence as a sequential decision process. Adaptive stress testing (Lee et al. 2020) explores the disturbance sequence via Monte Carlo tree search or reinforcement learning to find the most probable path to failure rather than an arbitrary, physically improbable edge case, ranking counterexamples by operational plausibility. A survey of these black-box methods groups them by their output (Corso et al. 2021): finding an isolated counterexample, finding the most likely failure trajectory, or estimating an aggregate failure probability. Only the third output measures operational risk, using the estimation procedure developed in section 15.10.2. Whatever search method is chosen, it returns candidate counterexamples and measured robustness margins; when those margins come from a simulator, counting them toward a physical safety claim requires bounding how far the simulator’s trajectories can drift from the real machine’s.


15.9.4 Bounding the sim-to-real transfer gap
A simulator that passes every fault-injection rollout can still hide a physical crash if its modeled trajectories differ from the real machine’s by more than the simulated safety margin. While high-throughput software-in-the-loop simulation is indispensable for exploring combinatorial corner cases, an unvalidated simulator can confirm only what its underlying model assumes. To use simulation sweeps as evidence in a safety case, the engineering team must validate and bound the sim-to-real transfer gap \(\TransferDiscrepancyBound\).
Let \(\SimulatedStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant; \SimulationParameterVector, \ControlInput) \in \TrajectoryStateSpace\) and \(\PhysicalStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant; \SimulationParameterVector, \ControlInput) \in \TrajectoryStateSpace\) denote the system state trajectories in simulation and on target physical hardware under matched declared conditions \(\SimulationParameterVector\) (initial speed, payload mass, floor friction) and control input history \(\ControlInput\). Replaying identical open-loop input sequences establishes a baseline comparison of plant dynamics, but certifying a deployed closed-loop policy requires bounding discrepancy under autonomous execution, where perturbed sensor observations produce divergent actuator commands. The continuous transfer discrepancy is the supremum state error across the test horizon \([0, \FiniteTimeHorizon]\) under a task-weighted physical norm: \[\TransferDiscrepancyBound = \sup_{t \in [0, \FiniteTimeHorizon]} \|\PhysicalStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant) - \SimulatedStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant)\|_{\StateNormWeighting} \tag{5}\] where \(\|\cdot\|_{\StateNormWeighting}\) normalizes position, velocity, and actuator torque errors by predeclared positive reference scales in meters, meters per second, and newton-meters, respectively, before applying dimensionless task weights. The verification plan fixes those scales and weights in advance; the resulting discrepancy \(\TransferDiscrepancyBound\) is dimensionless, while the Lipschitz constant \(\PredicateLipschitzConstant\) carries the physical units of the predicate margin.
A sound safety warrant requires a discrepancy bound that holds across all trajectories in the claimed operational envelope, not just the largest error observed in a small test sample. That modeling error must be deducted directly from the simulated robustness margin. Consider a Signal Temporal Logic safety requirement \(\StlFormula\) whose atomic predicates \(\StlPredicateFunction(\SignalTrajectory(\TimeInstant)) \ge 0\) are Lipschitz continuous with constant \(\PredicateLipschitzConstant = \sup_{\SignalTrajectory_1 \ne \SignalTrajectory_2} |\StlPredicateFunction(\SignalTrajectory_1) - \StlPredicateFunction(\SignalTrajectory_2)| / \|\SignalTrajectory_1 - \SignalTrajectory_2\|_{\StateNormWeighting}\). Here \(\PredicateLipschitzConstant\) is the maximum rate at which the predicate margin degrades per unit of normalized state discrepancy. For a spatial clearance predicate evaluated in meters against position error normalized by a 1 m reference scale with unit task weight, \(\PredicateLipschitzConstant\) is 1 m per unit of normalized discrepancy. By Lipschitz continuity, the physical predicate error is bounded pointwise by the state discrepancy: \[|\StlPredicateFunction(\PhysicalStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant)) - \StlPredicateFunction(\SimulatedStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant))| \le \PredicateLipschitzConstant \|\PhysicalStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant) - \SimulatedStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant)\|_{\StateNormWeighting} \le \PredicateLipschitzConstant \TransferDiscrepancyBound\] which guarantees that at every instant \(\TimeInstant \in [0, \FiniteTimeHorizon]\): \[\StlPredicateFunction(\PhysicalStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant)) \ge \StlPredicateFunction(\SimulatedStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant)) - \PredicateLipschitzConstant \TransferDiscrepancyBound.\] Taking the infimum across the temporal horizon \(\TimeInstant \in [0, \FiniteTimeHorizon]\) for an invariance property \(\StlFormula \equiv \square_{[0, \FiniteTimeHorizon]} (\StlPredicateFunction(\SignalTrajectory(\TimeInstant)) \ge 0)\), the guaranteed lower bound on physical robustness in the real world is: \[\PhysicalStlRobustness \ge \SimulatedStlRobustness - \PredicateLipschitzConstant \TransferDiscrepancyBound. \tag{6}\] The term \(\PredicateLipschitzConstant \TransferDiscrepancyBound\) in equation 6 acts as a sim-to-real robustness discount. If simulated robustness \(\SimulatedStlRobustness\) does not exceed \(\PredicateLipschitzConstant \TransferDiscrepancyBound\), the simulation pass guarantees no physical margin at all: the real machine can breach the safe invariant set (\(\PhysicalStlRobustness < 0\)) even when every simulated rollout returns a positive margin.
The rack-end claim makes this discount concrete. Scoring the distance predicate in meters and normalizing position error by a 1 m reference scale with unit task weight gives a Lipschitz constant of 1 m per unit of normalized discrepancy. Suppose a simulated stop finishes with the entire 131.0 mm reserve intact. The lower bound in equation 6 certifies a positive physical margin when \(\TransferDiscrepancyBound <\) 0.131, meaning the justified position-error bound is smaller than the reserve under this normalization. A larger discrepancy bound leaves the actual physical margin unresolved. A simulator whose stopping position is experimentally validated to within a few centimeters transfers nearly all of its verified margin; a simulator that has never been calibrated against physical stopping runs transfers none of it.
Coupled cyber-physical dynamics determine what this discount must cover: drivetrain compliance and gear backlash alter delivered torque, surface contamination and tire wear change braking traction, and real-time execution jitter shifts braking onset time. A discrepancy bound calibrated on an unloaded, cool machine cannot be silently extended to a loaded vehicle operating under thermal throttling. The verification record must state the operational envelope across which the discrepancy bound holds, keeping that justified bound distinct from the empirical maximum error observed during paired test runs.
Measuring the empirical discrepancy \(\EmpiricalTransferDiscrepancy\) builds on the paired probing protocols used to qualify simulation models for policy training. These protocols drive identical command histories into both simulated and physical hardware and score channel residuals against precommitted tolerances (The sim-to-real contact exploit). They are the same measurements that bound a simulator’s screening validity in Simulation as a conditional proxy. Verification adapts this qualification procedure in two ways. First, excitation inputs are tailored to the specific safety invariant under test, such as full-rate deceleration from aisle speed for the rack-end claim rather than low-speed docking maneuvers. Second, physical trajectories must be captured with external instrumentation independent of the robot’s onboard sensor suite, so that shared sensor calibration errors or estimator drift cannot cancel out of the residual. The resulting empirical discrepancy \(\EmpiricalTransferDiscrepancy\) is archived in the test records alongside the environmental conditions under which it was gathered. If the sim-to-real safety case relies on domain randomization distributions \(\DomainRandomizationDistribution\) to cover hardware variations, it must justify set inclusion across all declared operational conditions: \[\PhysicalTrajectorySet(\SimulationParameterVector) \subseteq \bigcup_{\SampledSimulationParameterVector \sim \DomainRandomizationDistribution} \SimulatedTrajectorySet(\SampledSimulationParameterVector).\] Finite paired measurements can falsify this inclusion by exposing an outlier, but they cannot prove it globally. If unmodeled physical effects such as fieldbus latency jitter, magnetic stator saturation, transmission backlash, or Coulomb stiction cause physical trajectories to escape the randomized simulation bundle, the sim-to-real transfer guarantee fails, and software-in-the-loop simulation passes cannot serve as evidence in the release safety case.

Checkpoint 15.3: Search, robustness, and transfer
A signed margin turns testing into search, and a simulated margin counts toward a physical claim only after its transfer discount.

Quantitative robustness interpretation: Can you explain how Signal Temporal Logic replaces binary pass/fail assertions with a signed predicate margin, and how its units and reference limit determine the meaning of a negative score?
Adversarial optimization of disturbance trajectories: Can you describe how black-box optimizers use quantitative robustness scores to discover worst-case combinations of latency, noise, and friction?
Test invalidation vs. failure criteria: Can you distinguish between an execution that falsifies a safety invariant and an invalid trial where testbed preconditions or fault injection mechanisms failed?
Normalization scale estimate: For the late F1 trace of section 15.9.1, suppose the record had fixed the distance scale at the 40 mm tracking inset while keeping the 82 ms onset scale. Can you estimate both normalized margins and say whether the governing predicate changes for this trace?
Transfer discount: A simulated F1 stop keeps 131.0 mm of reserve. Can you state the largest discrepancy bound that still guarantees a positive physical margin, and explain why a bound measured on an unloaded, cool machine cannot certify a loaded, throttled one?

title: Adversarial Verification
text:
15.10 Interpreting Campaign Statistics
Counting passed trials in an adversarial campaign can easily mislead a release review into treating a test-bench success rate as an operational reliability number. Any statistical summary describes only the specific population sampled by the test harness, and conditions that were never tested remain missing evidence no matter how sophisticated the statistical model applied afterward.
When \(\ZeroFailureTrialCount\) independent Bernoulli trials sampled from a declared fault distribution yield zero missed mitigations, the outcome puts a one-sided upper confidence limit on the miss probability for that specific distribution. This is the zero-failure trial sizing of Sample size requirements per empirical claim, applied here to an injected hardware fault population rather than closed-loop policy rollouts; at a 95 percent confidence level, it requires about \(3/\TrialFailureProbability\) consecutive successful injections to bound the miss probability below \(\TrialFailureProbability\). To turn these injection counts into a hardware coverage claim weighted by each component’s failure rate in FIT (failures in time, one per \(10^9\) operating hours; notebook 15.3 gives the component weights \(\ComponentFailureRate_i\)), the injection harness must sample faults in direct proportion to their raw failure rates \(\ComponentFailureRate_i\). Otherwise, the verification pipeline must apply an explicitly justified stratified weighting across each fault stratum.11
11 Trial sampling and aging: The binomial count assumes independent, identically distributed Bernoulli outcomes under the declared injection distribution; it does not require Poisson event arrivals. Repeated heating, mechanical wear, or contact changes can break independence and require a state-stratified experimental design.This statistical bound holds only when the physical trials satisfy the declared independence and sampling assumptions. On real hardware, repeated high-energy stops produce Joule heating (\(\WindingCurrent^2\ElectricalResistance\)) in the drive motor windings and mechanical brake linings. That heat buildup changes winding resistance and lining friction coefficients, coupling successive trials. As a result, a test campaign run on a dry aisle at room temperature cannot support a confidence bound for a contaminated floor or for the operating envelope’s 5 °C thermal extreme.
Notebook 15.3 draws its rates from four component strata (sensors, compute, transceivers and power management, gate drivers), and each stratum maps onto rows of table 2. Sensor faults are injected as F2 and as the physical transducer disturbances, compute faults as F1, transceiver and power-management faults as F3 and F4, and gate-driver faults as the drive that keeps producing torque after a stop command (section 15.6.2). Sampling in proportion to those rates therefore fixes how the campaign’s trials divide among the rows.

Napkin Math 15.3: The coverage countProblem: Illustrative component fault rates and a chosen ceiling on the unmitigated rate fix the diagnostic coverage the machine needs. How many zero-miss injections, sampled in proportion to those rates, would demonstrate that coverage?
Variables:

Component fault rates \(\ComponentFailureRate_i\) in FIT, one fault per \(10^9\) operating hours (Illustrative): sensors 1,500, compute 1,000, transceivers and power management 2,500, and gate drivers 4,800.
Target unmitigated rate \(\TargetHazardRate =\) 100 FIT, with a stricter 10 FIT alternative, at confidence \(\ConfidenceLevel =\) 95 percent (Chosen).
Diagnostic coverage \(\DiagnosticCoverage\), the \(\ComponentFailureRate_i\)-weighted fraction of faults whose hazardous effect is mitigated, so that \(\UnmitigatedHardwareFaultRate = \RawHardwareFaultRate(1 - \DiagnosticCoverage)\) and a single injection misses with probability \(\TrialFailureProbability = 1 - \DiagnosticCoverage\).

Math:
Required coverage. \[\lambda_{\text{raw}} = 1500 + 1000 + 2500 + 4800 = 9800\ \text{FIT}, \qquad C_{\text{diag}} \ge 1 - \frac{\lambda_{\text{target}}}{\lambda_{\text{raw}}} = 1 - \frac{100}{9800} = 0.9898\]
Injections to demonstrate it, from the zero-failure count of Sample size requirements per empirical claim. \[n \ge \frac{\ln(1 - C)}{\ln C_{\text{diag}}} = \frac{\ln 0.05}{\ln 0.9898} = 292.1 \;\Rightarrow\; n = 293, \qquad \frac{3}{p} = \frac{3 \lambda_{\text{raw}}}{\lambda_{\text{target}}} = \frac{3 \times 9800}{100} = 294\]
Sensitivity. The count scales as \(3\RawHardwareFaultRate/\TargetHazardRate\), so the 10 FIT target needs 99.90 percent coverage and 2,935 injections, against a rule-of-three estimate of 2,940.
Result: A 100 FIT target needs 98.98 percent coverage, which 293 zero-miss injections demonstrate at 95 percent confidence.
Systems insight: The target unmitigated failure rate, not the number of entries in the fault list, governs campaign size. Every tenfold tightening of the target rate demands roughly a tenfold increase in physical injection runs. Furthermore, this sample size holds only when injections are drawn in proportion to each component’s raw failure rate \(\ComponentFailureRate_i\). Injecting uniformly across components with disparate failure rates tests a distorted distribution unless the harness weights the empirical outcomes and gathers enough trials within every stratum. Every trial must therefore log the exact injected mode, whether hardware detection triggered within the deadline, and whether the safety controller brought the plant to a verified safe state.


Even within the declared fault strata, a campaign rarely reaches every combination of load, floor friction, and temperature. The fault-record set must therefore catalog omitted test cases as carefully as completed runs, recording every parameter region skipped because of testbed physical limits, sensor bandwidth limits, or destructive testing costs. Unprobed regions cannot count as verified safety margins in the release case, nor can passive operational hours accumulated outside the test cell fill those gaps.

15.10.1 Exposure and the population a statistic describes
Logging thousands of incident-free fleet hours in normal warehouse aisles cannot bound rare safety-critical faults or substitute for targeted fault injection, because passive operation samples a different distribution from deliberate fault trials. Fleet exposure runs into the exposure wall of equation 7.9: bounding a hazard rate \(\TargetHazardRate\) at 95 percent confidence requires about \(3/\TargetHazardRate\) failure-free operating hours, which Butler and Finelli (1993) showed is unreachable at safety-critical rates such as \(10^{-9}\) failures per hour. Pooling those hours across a fleet adds exposure time but not environmental diversity, so the bound covers only the conditions the pooled machines share (Verification Ceilings and the Exposure Wall), and normal fleet traffic rarely triggers the corner-case hardware faults this chapter injects. Verification also has to ask which configuration those hours describe. Any change to a safety filter, control policy, or actuator driver can alter the sampled outcomes, so earlier fleet hours count toward the updated configuration only when an explicit engineering argument shows that the change left the counted events unaffected. When a rare failure rate must be estimated across a high-dimensional disturbance space without waiting for billions of passive rollouts, the campaign must steer samples toward the failure region and weight them back to the operational distribution.

Butler, Ricky W., and George B. Finelli. 1993. “The Infeasibility of Quantifying the Reliability of Life-Critical Real-Time Software.” IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 19 (1): 3–12. https://doi.org/10.1109/32.210303.


15.10.2 Estimating a rare failure rate by importance sampling
Naive Monte Carlo sampling from nominal operating conditions cannot estimate rare safety-critical failure rates because nearly every rollout ends in an unremarkable, safe stop, requiring billions of runs to observe even a handful of violations (section 15.10.1). While adversarial falsification finds whether an unsafe trajectory exists, release decisions also need to know how often such failures occur under nominal operating conditions. Importance sampling12 breaks this bottleneck by drawing rollouts from an alternative proposal distribution that concentrates samples near the failure boundary and then weighting each sample by its likelihood ratio to recover an unbiased estimate under the operational distribution.
12 Importance Sampling: The technique originated in Monte Carlo calculations of nuclear radiation shielding in the early 1950s, where the few particles that penetrated dense shielding were exceptionally rare yet critical to safety. Kahn and Marshall (1953) formalized importance sampling alongside correlated sampling and statistical estimation to cut required sample counts. The method carries a sharp failure mode of its own: a proposal distribution that omits a valid failure path reports tiny sample variance and an erroneously low failure probability, a support failure that diagnostic checks must catch.
Kahn, Herman, and Andrew W. Marshall. 1953. “Methods of Reducing Sample Size in Monte Carlo Computations.” Journal of the Operations Research Society of America 1 (5): 263–78. https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.1.5.263.
Let the operational distribution of uncertain input parameters \(\UncertainScenarioParameters\) be denoted by \(\OperationalScenarioDistribution(\UncertainScenarioParameters)\), and let \(\FailureRegion\) define the subset of conditions leading to a safety violation. Standard Monte Carlo estimation evaluates the failure probability \(\OperationalFailureProbability = \Pr_{\OperationalScenarioDistribution}(\UncertainScenarioParameters \in \FailureRegion)\) by computing the empirical failure fraction across \(\EstimatorDrawCount\) independent draws from \(\OperationalScenarioDistribution\). Importance sampling instead draws samples from an engineered proposal distribution \(\ImportanceProposalDistribution(\UncertainScenarioParameters)\) and weights each outcome by the likelihood ratio \(\LikelihoodRatioWeight(\UncertainScenarioParameters) = \OperationalScenarioDistribution(\UncertainScenarioParameters)/\ImportanceProposalDistribution(\UncertainScenarioParameters)\): \[\ImportanceSampledFailureProbability = \frac{1}{\EstimatorDrawCount}\sum_{i=1}^{\EstimatorDrawCount} \mathbb{1}[\UncertainScenarioParameters_i \in \FailureRegion]\, \LikelihoodRatioWeight(\UncertainScenarioParameters_i), \qquad \UncertainScenarioParameters_i \sim \ImportanceProposalDistribution. \tag{7}\] This estimator remains mathematically unbiased as long as \(\ImportanceProposalDistribution(\UncertainScenarioParameters) > 0\) whenever \(\OperationalScenarioDistribution(\UncertainScenarioParameters)\mathbb{1}[\UncertainScenarioParameters \in \FailureRegion] > 0\), since the likelihood weight corrects for the shift in sampling probability (Owen 2013). The variance of \(\ImportanceSampledFailureProbability\) depends entirely on the geometry of \(\ImportanceProposalDistribution\). The theoretically optimal zero-variance proposal is the operational distribution \(\OperationalScenarioDistribution\) conditioned on the failure region \(\FailureRegion\) (\(\ImportanceProposalDistribution^*(\UncertainScenarioParameters) = \OperationalScenarioDistribution(\UncertainScenarioParameters)\mathbb{1}[\UncertainScenarioParameters \in \FailureRegion] / \OperationalFailureProbability\)). Constructing \(\ImportanceProposalDistribution^*\) directly is impossible because its normalizing constant is the very quantity \(\OperationalFailureProbability\) under estimation. Practical verification pipelines must therefore construct parametric approximations to \(\ImportanceProposalDistribution^*\).
The cross-entropy method (Rubinstein and Kroese 2004) systematically discovers such an approximation within a parameterized distribution family \(\ParametricProposalDistribution\) by solving a sequence of intermediate rare-event problems. Beginning with an initial proposal aligned with the operational profile (\(\InitialProposalDistribution = \OperationalScenarioDistribution\)), the algorithm iteratively draws a sample batch from the current proposal and evaluates the performance metric. It then selects an intermediate threshold at the \((1-\EliteSampleFraction)\) quantile so that a fraction \(\EliteSampleFraction\) of the batch qualifies as elite runs. The parameter vector \(\ProposalParameterVector\) is then updated by maximizing the likelihood-weighted log-density of these elite samples, which minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence (a measure of how far one probability distribution lies from another) to the optimal proposal on that intermediate slice. As the threshold steps forward across iterations, the proposal gradually shifts its probability mass toward the true failure boundary. For an exponential proposal parameterized by its mean, or a fixed-variance Gaussian proposal parameterized by its mean, this update admits an exact closed form: the updated mean is the weighted empirical mean of the elite draws.
Consider this method applied to the rack-end deceleration scenario. Traveling at nominal aisle velocity, the mobile base consumes its 131.0 mm stopping reserve from section 15.2 in \(\FallbackDeadline =\) 100.8 ms, the latest-fallback deadline of equation 14.4 at aisle speed. Any unbudgeted message queue delay exceeding \(\FallbackDeadline\) exhausts this safety buffer, causing the physical vehicle to breach the clearance boundary. To establish an analytical baseline, assume an illustrative operational distribution where queue delays \(\MessageQueueDelay\) follow an exponential distribution with mean \(\MeanMessageQueueDelay =\) 5 ms (in production verification, latency measurements gathered under the declared load must justify or replace this model). Under this formulation, the analytical failure probability is \(\OperationalFailureProbability = e^{-\FallbackDeadline/\MeanMessageQueueDelay} =\) 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ per stopping event. This closed-form quantity serves as an exact ground truth against which to benchmark competing sampling estimators. The threshold is deliberately the uncharged ceiling of section 15.2, which makes the example optimistic. Charging the dispatch-to-admission allocation leaves only 37.5 ms, and the same delay model then gives \(\OperationalFailureProbability =\) 5.6 × 10⁻⁴, about 3 × 10⁵ times larger. The comparison below keeps the uncharged threshold because there the failure is rarest and the gap between estimators widest; at the charged threshold even plain Monte Carlo would need far fewer runs.
The sample sizing required across these estimators stems directly from the variance of sample averages. When an estimator averages \(\EstimatorDrawCount\) independent draws with mean \(\OperationalFailureProbability\) and per-sample variance \(\EstimatorDrawStandardDeviation^2\), the estimator’s standard deviation is \(\EstimatorDrawStandardDeviation/\sqrt{\EstimatorDrawCount}\), yielding a relative standard error \(\RelativeStandardError = \sqrt{\EstimatorDrawStandardDeviation^2 / (\OperationalFailureProbability^2 \EstimatorDrawCount)}\). Achieving a target relative precision \(\RelativeStandardError\) requires \(\EstimatorDrawCount = (\EstimatorDrawStandardDeviation^2 / \OperationalFailureProbability^2) / \RelativeStandardError^2\) trials, where \(\EstimatorDrawStandardDeviation^2 / \OperationalFailureProbability^2\) denotes the per-draw relative variance. For naive Monte Carlo, each trial is an indicator variable with variance \(\OperationalFailureProbability(1 - \OperationalFailureProbability)\), demanding approximately \((1 - \OperationalFailureProbability)/(\OperationalFailureProbability \RelativeStandardError^2)\) simulated runs. Under the illustrative delay model, securing an estimate with \(\RelativeStandardError =\) 10 percent relative error requires 5.7 × 10¹⁰ trials. By comparison, a zero-failure qualification campaign requires 1.7 × 10⁹ consecutive incident-free runs to establish an upper bound at the \(\OperationalFailureProbability\) threshold (equation 7.4). Under importance sampling for this exponential model, the per-draw variance equals the weighted failure indicator’s second moment minus \(\OperationalFailureProbability^2\), which stays finite as long as the proposal rate is less than twice the operational rate.
The cross-entropy method using exponential proposals with an elite fraction of \(\EliteSampleFraction =\) 10 percent demonstrates how adaptive sampling overcomes this barrier. The initial threshold is set at the 90th percentile of the operational delay distribution (\(\MeanMessageQueueDelay\ln 10\), or 11.5 ms). Because the exponential distribution is memoryless, the conditional distribution of delays exceeding any threshold \(\CrossEntropyLevelThreshold\) is identical to the original distribution shifted by \(\CrossEntropyLevelThreshold\). The likelihood-weighted mean of the elite samples is therefore simply \(\CrossEntropyLevelThreshold + \MeanMessageQueueDelay\), which immediately defines the mean for the next proposal. Because the parametric proposal family consists of unshifted exponential distributions supported on the positive real line rather than truncated distributions starting at \(\CrossEntropyLevelThreshold\), matching this conditional mean stretches the exponential scale across the entire positive axis rather than shifting the lower support boundary. Successive iterations lift the intermediate threshold to 38.0 ms and 99.1 ms. By iteration 4, the intermediate quantile surpasses the critical threshold, clamping the final level at \(\FallbackDeadline\) with a proposal mean of 105.8 ms, the conditional expectation of the delay given a boundary violation. Under this adapted proposal, 38.6 percent of the generated rollouts land in the failure set, and their small likelihood weights scale each observed failure back to the operational probability. The resulting per-draw relative variance drops to 27.1. Consequently, only 2,709 simulation runs are needed to reach the target 10 percent relative error, a factor of 2 × 10⁷ fewer runs than plain Monte Carlo and within 0.1 percent of the best exponential proposal. These numerical counts derive from the assumed exponential model; testing against an empirical delay histogram will yield distinct run requirements.



Weighting runs near failure cuts the runs by about 2 × 10⁷ times.
Two statistical diagnostics safeguard the integrity of importance sampling estimates. The first is the effective sample size, defined as \(\EffectiveSampleSize = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{\EstimatorDrawCount} \LikelihoodRatioWeight_i\right)^2 / \sum_{i=1}^{\EstimatorDrawCount} \LikelihoodRatioWeight_i^2\) (Owen 2013). This metric diagnoses concentration of the likelihood weights; it does not by itself establish the precision of the weighted failure estimate, which depends on the variance of the weighted failure indicator. For the 2,709 runs above, the expected effective sample size is approximately 250; a degenerate value approaching 1 would warn that a few outlying weights dominate the summation, rendering the estimate unstable. The second diagnostic is distribution support and tail coverage. Omitting a subregion of \(\FailureRegion\) with positive operational probability violates the support condition and biases the estimate. A proposal that retains support but samples the operational tail too rarely can instead produce unstable or infinite variance, with deceptively small observed variance in a finite run. Sample variance cannot reveal an omitted failure path that generates no samples, so the campaign must justify coverage independently of its weight diagnostics. O’Kelly et al. (2018) applied adaptive importance sampling to end-to-end verification of autonomous driving software stacks and obtained speedups of several orders of magnitude over naive Monte Carlo in estimating rare collision rates.
This structure separates importance sampling from adversarial falsification. Although an adversarial search engine also concentrates runs near the system’s safety boundaries, its sampling density is unknown. Because falsification runs lack likelihood-ratio weights, the fraction of falsification runs that fail says nothing about real-world failure frequency; in the illustrative example, 38.6 percent of the proposal runs fail even though the modeled operational failure probability is only 1.8 × 10⁻⁹. A quantitative failure-probability estimate belongs in a safety case only when paired with its declared operational model \(\OperationalScenarioDistribution\), proposal distribution \(\ImportanceProposalDistribution\), weight history, effective sample size, and confidence intervals. It remains a statement about that declared operating model rather than a direct physical measurement of the deployed hardware. Estimating how often a boundary is crossed still leaves a second question open: when a near-miss or excursion occurs, how far can the worst-case physical overshoot reach?


15.10.3 Extreme value theory and heavy-tailed safety distributions
Binary pass-fail tallies throw away the margin history of near-miss stops, while fitting a Gaussian curve to nominal bus traffic or stopping-distance data underestimates the heavy tails caused by sporadic bus arbitration contention or contact slips. Deployment qualification often has to bound the physical magnitude of worst-case excursions across continuous telemetry streams: spatial clearance \(\ClearDistance - \BaseTravelDistance(\TimeInstant)\), onset slack \(\HazardOnsetBound - \HazardOnset\), and actuator torque headroom \(\JointTorqueLimit - \DeliveredActuatorTorque\). Extreme value theory (EVT) provides limiting distributions for these tail excursions, playing a role for extreme deviations similar to that of the central limit theorem for sample means (Coles 2001). Even so, engineers must check that the data belong to the assumed tail regime rather than treating a fitted mathematical endpoint as a physical barrier. While the block-maxima formulation (which yields the Generalized Extreme Value distribution) is developed in Extreme Value Theory and Tail Risk, cyber-physical verification primarily uses the threshold-exceedance formulation, which keeps every observation that crosses a high safety threshold rather than discarding all but the block maximum.

Coles, Stuart. 2001. An Introduction to Statistical Modeling of Extreme Values. Springer.

Peaks over threshold and the Generalized Pareto Distribution: Let \(\TailPerformanceMetric\) denote a continuous performance metric (such as stopping-distance error), and let \(\ExceedanceThreshold\) represent a high baseline threshold. We model the exceedances \(\ThresholdExcessVariable = \TailPerformanceMetric - \ExceedanceThreshold\) conditional on \(\TailPerformanceMetric > \ExceedanceThreshold\). For distributions in an appropriate extreme-value domain of attraction, the Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem gives an asymptotic Generalized Pareto approximation to the conditional excess distribution as \(\ExceedanceThreshold\) approaches the upper endpoint. Balkema and Haan (1974) and Pickands (1975) proved this result independently: \[\GpdCumulativeDistribution(\EvaluatedExceedance; \GpdScaleParameter, \TailShapeParameter) = 1 - \left( 1 + \frac{\TailShapeParameter \EvaluatedExceedance}{\GpdScaleParameter} \right)^{-1/\TailShapeParameter}, \quad \EvaluatedExceedance > 0, \tag{8}\] defined for scale parameter \(\GpdScaleParameter > 0\) on the support \(1 + \TailShapeParameter \EvaluatedExceedance/\GpdScaleParameter > 0\), with the exponential distribution recovered as the continuous limit \(\TailShapeParameter \to 0\). The shape parameter \(\TailShapeParameter\) governs tail thickness: \(\TailShapeParameter > 0\) indicates a heavy, power-law tail; \(\TailShapeParameter = 0\) corresponds to an exponential tail; and \(\TailShapeParameter < 0\) defines a bounded tail with finite endpoint \(\ExceedanceThreshold - \GpdScaleParameter/\TailShapeParameter\).
Return level: For a chosen return period13 \(\ReturnPeriodTrialCount\) calibrated to the sampling interval, the return level \(\ReturnLevel_{\ReturnPeriodTrialCount}\) is the threshold exceeded on average once every \(\ReturnPeriodTrialCount\) periods: \[\ReturnLevel_{\ReturnPeriodTrialCount} = \ExceedanceThreshold + \frac{\GpdScaleParameter}{\TailShapeParameter} \left[ (\ReturnPeriodTrialCount \ThresholdExceedanceRate)^{\TailShapeParameter} - 1 \right] \tag{9}\] where \(\ThresholdExceedanceRate = \Pr(\TailPerformanceMetric > \ExceedanceThreshold) = \ThresholdExceedanceCount / \TotalExecutedTrialCount\) is the empirical exceedance rate across \(\TotalExecutedTrialCount\) trials, with \(\ReturnPeriodTrialCount\) expressed in equivalent trial counts. This expression follows from multiplying the conditional Generalized Pareto survival probability \(\left(1 + \TailShapeParameter(\ReturnLevel_{\ReturnPeriodTrialCount} - \ExceedanceThreshold)/\GpdScaleParameter\right)^{-1/\TailShapeParameter}\) by the threshold exceedance probability \(\ThresholdExceedanceRate\) and setting the resulting unconditional tail probability equal to \(1/\ReturnPeriodTrialCount\). In this subsection \(\ReturnPeriodTrialCount\) is therefore a count of trials, not the test horizon of equation 4. Equation 9 holds for \(\TailShapeParameter \ne 0\); its continuous limit at \(\TailShapeParameter = 0\) is \(\ReturnLevel_{\ReturnPeriodTrialCount} = \ExceedanceThreshold + \GpdScaleParameter\ln(\ReturnPeriodTrialCount\ThresholdExceedanceRate)\). Expressing a return period in calendar operating hours requires scaling by an independently justified hourly event arrival rate under a verified temporal dependence model. The product \(\ReturnPeriodTrialCount\ThresholdExceedanceRate\) is dimensionless, and valid extrapolations must evaluate return levels at or above the conditioning threshold \(\ExceedanceThreshold\).

13 Return Period: The term comes from civil hydrology, where a “hundred-year flood” means a discharge level with a 0.01 probability of being exceeded in any single year (Gumbel 1958). The hydrological caveat applies directly to robotics: because return levels extrapolate beyond observed records, they hold only when the threshold choice and sampling distribution are physically justified. Counting return periods across synthetic fault-injection runs gives no operational safety assurance until the hourly arrival rate in service is established.
Gumbel, Emil J. 1958. Statistics of Extremes. Columbia University Press.

Connecting adversarial falsification to EVT tail sampling
Under nominal operation, exceedances past a conservative margin threshold occur far too rarely to fit an empirical tail; the exposure wall of section 15.10.1 starves extreme-value fits just as severely as binary failure counts. Adversarial falsification gets around this scarcity by concentrating rollouts near violation boundaries, solving the search problem of equation 4 over initial plant states and disturbance parameters. Let \(\KnownComponentStopDistance\) denote the design budget at the trial speed, 969.0 mm at aisle speed, so that \(\ClearDistance - \KnownComponentStopDistance\) is the 131.0 mm spare. For the braking-distance overshoot metric \(\TailPerformanceMetric = \StoppingDistance - \KnownComponentStopDistance\), the search populates the exceedance set \[\ExceedanceSampleSet = \{ \ThresholdExcessVariable_i = \TailPerformanceMetric_i - \ExceedanceThreshold \mid \TailPerformanceMetric_i > \ExceedanceThreshold \}\] with dense observations near the failure frontier. Those samples, however, reflect the adversary’s search policy rather than the operational environment. Fitting a Generalized Pareto Distribution directly to unweighted falsification runs models the optimizer’s search behavior, not the reliability of the physical plant. To inform operational risk, the runs must come from a declared proposal distribution and carry the likelihood-ratio weights of equation 7, so that both the exceedance probability \(\ThresholdExceedanceRate\) and the fitted parameters reflect weighted operational likelihoods.
A fitted shape parameter serves as an engineering diagnostic rather than a standalone safety verdict:

Positive shape (\(\TailShapeParameter > 0\)): The fitted model extrapolates a heavy upper tail, warning of sensitivity to extreme deviations. This fit does not prove that physical overshoots are truly unbounded, but it requires the engineering team to check whether threshold choice, sensor noise, or unmodeled delays drive the heavy-tailed behavior.
Negative shape (\(\TailShapeParameter < 0\)): The fitted distribution implies a finite modeled upper endpoint at \(\ExceedanceThreshold - \GpdScaleParameter/\TailShapeParameter\). That mathematical endpoint must never be mistaken for a certified hardware stop or taken as proof that a runtime safety filter will always contain motion. Verifying real-world containment requires auditing the filter’s dynamical assumptions and measuring its hardware response latencies under adversarial load.



Sim-to-real transfer bounds on EVT return levels
When high-throughput campaigns run on the software-in-the-loop and processor-in-the-loop (PIL) rungs of the qualification ladder, extreme value modeling produces a simulated return level \(\SimulatedReturnLevel\). As shown in section 15.9.4, physical trajectories can diverge from simulated trajectories by up to the sim-to-real discrepancy bound \(\TransferDiscrepancyBound = \sup_t \|\PhysicalStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant) - \SimulatedStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant)\|_{\StateNormWeighting}\). When simulated and physical trials describe the same operational population and the overshoot metric obeys the pathwise discrepancy bound with constant \(\PredicateLipschitzConstant\), that bound also limits the physical return level (equation 10): \[\PhysicalReturnLevel \le \SimulatedReturnLevel + \PredicateLipschitzConstant \TransferDiscrepancyBound. \tag{10}\] To support a stopping-distance claim, this widened return level must fit inside the available physical reserve: \[\SimulatedReturnLevel + \PredicateLipschitzConstant \TransferDiscrepancyBound \le \ClearDistance - \KnownComponentStopDistance. \tag{11}\]
The margin inequality in equation 11 is a necessary sanity check rather than a sufficient release rule. Using it requires distributional consistency between simulation and physical testbeds, proper importance weighting when quoting operational return periods, confidence intervals on the fitted parameters, and a transfer bound \(\TransferDiscrepancyBound\) justified across the entire operating domain. A small trajectory discrepancy across a handful of bench tests does not establish an envelope-wide sim-to-real bound.
In the rack-end deceleration scenario, the physical safety margin is 131.0 mm, and only 48.7 mm once the dispatch-to-admission allocation is charged, so a return level of a few centimeters, widened by a transfer bound of a few centimeters more, already consumes it. Any proposed tail bound must state its sample population, proposal weights, parameter uncertainties, and transfer error bounds before being compared against this reserve. When a fault mode (such as mode F1) has zero measured physical trials, it supports neither an empirical tail fit nor a return-level estimate; a fitted mathematical endpoint cannot stand in for missing physical test evidence.
Every statistical metric in this section is conditional. A zero-miss count describes only the declared fault injection distribution. An exposure bound reflects only the exact hardware and software configuration that accumulated those hours. An importance-sampling estimate holds only under its declared operational model. An extreme value return level holds only relative to its fitted tail and sim-to-real discrepancy bound. Because any of these premises can fail, a verification campaign never hands release an isolated scalar margin; instead, it packages fault records that bind each empirical margin to the physical, environmental, and statistical conditions that support it.

title: Adversarial Verification
text:
15.11 Fault Records for Release
A raw telemetry trace sitting on a testbench digitizer cannot certify an autonomous machine for release if nothing proves which safety claim, envelope corner, or software and hardware build produced it. In an adversarial campaign, a completed F1 trial records the full event chain across independent physical channels: the final proposal renewal, the watchdog lease expiration, the active braking response, and the final mechanical stop. The release authority can credit that trial only when the measured trace is verifiably bound to the safety claim, the tested envelope point, and the exact software and hardware builds under evaluation. The fault record establishes this link by binding the structured test header to the retained evidence bundle through a cryptographic digest.
The release authority receives these claim-specific fault records together with the coverage records needed to judge their physical scope. Combined, they form an auditable fault-record set that joins the individual fault records, qualification environments, justified sim-to-real transfer bounds, statistical tail estimates, and known coverage gaps. Rather than silently omitting unmeasured or inapplicable fields, the schema marks them explicitly so that untested operating regimes cannot pass for verified boundaries. This fault-record set feeds directly into the operational safety case for release, though its schema and cryptographic signatures carry no authority beyond the physical evidence recorded inside them.
Along with design contracts, the motion-authority cases A1–A4, and the placement allocations established during system staging, the fault records draw on two upstream records: the omission log of the policy manifest (The Policy Manifest) and the coverage-gap catalog of the evaluation record (The Evaluation Record). Those upstream records list the operating conditions, sensor degradation modes, and environmental disturbances that the learned policy proposer never saw during training. By pairing the record header with its evidence bundle, each fault record preserves the full provenance of the trial: the asserted claim, physical operating point, fault injection mechanism, hardware and software revisions, raw high-speed telemetry, detection mechanisms, response latencies, physical stopping outcomes, and any secondary anomalies observed during the run.

15.11.1 The fault-record set specification
A pile of individual pass verdicts leaves a release review unable to tell which top-level safety claims have been substantiated across the envelope and which operating conditions remain untested. Every record in the fault-record set therefore exists to support one named assurance claim \(\AssuranceClaim\) within the release safety case, and its header names that claim explicitly. In the safety case structure developed in Claims, arguments, and warrants, the top-level assurance claim \(\AssuranceClaim_0\) states a core physical invariant, such as halting within the clearance corridor (\(\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance\)), and splits into sub-claims \(\AssuranceClaim_i\) covering specific operating envelopes, hardware fault classes, and fallback behaviors. The F1, F2, and F3 records support that stopping bound across communication and timing faults, showing that the safety permission path halts the loaded mobile base within its travel bound once proposal renewals cease (F1), when sensor observations arrive stale (F2), or when fieldbus frames drop in transit (F3). Where F1–F3 test information and timing loss, the F4 and actuator-jam records test electrical and mechanical survival. F4 shows that the held-up auxiliary power rail keeps the permission path alive through a primary supply collapse long enough to complete an emergency stop and set all mechanical holding brakes. The actuator-jam records show that the chassis stays within its lateral clearance corridor during a wheel-lock fault without driving the stator windings into thermal runaway. At the control boundary, the A1–A4 records support the claims that motion authority keeps a single writer, blocks control bypass, runs a deterministic fallback when supervisory handovers stall, and rejects forged command tokens. Alongside them, the proposer-injection records show whether tested adversarial proposals were caught by the runtime permission checks. Extending that result to every possible proposal still requires an architectural or formal argument that no source can bypass the permission path.
A physical trace supports an assurance claim \(\AssuranceClaim\) only through a structured engineering argument. In a rack-end deceleration claim, for instance, a raw brake-onset trace supplies empirical evidence, but the accompanying argument must explain why the digitizer clock synchronization, fault-injection timing, payload distribution, and floor traction conditions test the claimed physical response. Gathering evidence across the qualification ladder (formal reachability bounds for the permission filter, bounded sim-to-real falsification campaigns, and hardware fault-injection trials on the rig) lets each assurance claim \(\AssuranceClaim\) rest on complementary legs of evidence rather than a single isolated trial. How claims, arguments, and evidence fit together into an auditable assurance case, and the notation used to write that hierarchy down, are developed in Claims, arguments, and warrants.
The fault records also separate three failure domains, because each asks a different engineering question about the same physical machine, even when a compound fault spans more than one domain:

Functional safety: hardware and software component faults inside the safety-related control system, such as encoder failures, dropped fieldbus frames, or auxiliary power brownouts.
Safety of the intended functionality (SOTIF): hazards that arise without hardware faults from algorithmic blind spots or sensor limits, such as perceptual occlusions, out-of-distribution optical flare, or corner-case proposer errors.
Security: deliberate adversarial tampering with physical sensors, communication buses, or cryptographic tokens.

The consensus engineering standards covering each subsystem of the machine, along with their publication editions, are mapped in The standards map for the running machine. Passing an adversarial fault-injection campaign does not by itself establish regulatory compliance or justify operation in unmodeled environments; instead, the release argument weighs exactly which claims the assembled records substantiate and where residual operational risks remain. To support that review, the individual fault records, the per-rung coverage of the qualification ladder, the empirical sim-to-real discrepancy bounds, and the extreme value theory (EVT) tail parameters assemble into one cryptographically signed set. This fault-record set is the thirteenth record in the record chain, after the authority record and before the release manifest, and it carries verification evidence to the release gate.


↪ The record chain, numbered from the limit record to the residual-claims register, is developed in The record register.
The signed fault-record set defines the evidentiary handoff between adversarial testing and operational release, with its full data schema specified in table 5:

Consumes the authority record (The Authority Record) to check handover deadline timers (\(\HandoverTimeout\), Clearance-derived fallback deadlines), duplicate-writer rejections (A1), and supervisory token integrity.
Consumes the placement record (The Placement Record) to check bus contention limits, power-rail droop tolerances, and thermal dissipation thresholds.
Consumes the enforcement record and its admitted commands (The Enforcement Record) to check control barrier function (CBF) invariant sets, quadratic program (QP) filter execution deadlines, and fallback ladder transitions.
Consumes the evaluation record (The Evaluation Record) to cross-check offline covariate drift and simulation test catalogs against physical target-hardware runs.

Downstream Release Deliverables:

Delivers to the release manifest and its safety case (Safety Cases and Claims) the empirical, claim-specific evidence and operational bounds needed by the release argument.
Delivers to the residual-claims register (A residual-claims register) the explicit list of unverified operating regimes, test-fixture bandwidth limits, and coverage gaps.
