Capturing these eight fields in a signed record set prevents post-hoc threshold tuning and silent omission of failed or unobservable trials. Even a complete, cryptographically signed fault-record set, however, can be undermined if hidden electrical, bus, or clock couplings on the test bench corrupt the trials or blind the witnesses that score them. Four recurring pitfalls illustrate how shared resources across watchdogs, fieldbuses, power rails, and loggers can subvert a verification campaign before a single record reaches release.

title: Adversarial Verification
text:
15.12 Fallacies and Pitfalls
A physical machine can pass every isolated component fault test yet catastrophically fail in deployment when a shared power rail, communication bus, or reference clock couples multiple subsystems or blinds their diagnostic monitors. These failures stem from unintended causal, electrical, and temporal coupling across architectural boundaries. Compound verification tests catch such cross-domain hazards only when enough galvanically and logically independent instrumentation survives the fault to establish the ground-truth sequence of events.

Fallacy: Independent local watchdog timers guarantee end-to-end physical deadline compliance.
A perception front-end, the chunk policy, and the safety permission monitor can each execute comfortably within their local scheduling slices while an unmonitored inter-process queue buffers stale observations between them. Local watchdog timers confirm only that isolated tasks kick their respective heartbeats within software deadlines; they reveal nothing about the total age of the physical state traversing the distributed pipeline.
Consider an asynchronous buffer that inserts delay into the machine’s 133.6 ms pre-deceleration budget. The importance-sampling example of section 15.10.2 already priced this queue. At 1.3 m/s it exhausts the spare after 100.8 ms, only 75.4 percent of the nominal pre-deceleration interval, and once the dispatch-to-admission allocation is charged it does so after 37.5 ms. The fallacy lies in what the watchdogs report while it happens. Every task-level watchdog shows nominal health as the queue expands, because no task has missed its own slice. To detect this silent failure, verification experiments must isolate each stage of the causal chain: target appearance, optical capture, message dispatch, bus admission, lease expiration, and actuator torque onset. Without stage-by-stage timestamping, latency intervals are easily overlooked or double-counted.
Local watchdogs verify component execution, not end-to-end physical propagation.
Architect’s countermeasure: Enforce monotonic capture-to-torque evidence epoch timestamps across all processing nodes. Compare the sensor’s physical capture timestamp directly against the safety monitor’s decision tick, discarding any control proposal whose total elapsed latency exceeds the safety budget regardless of healthy local thread heartbeats.


Pitfall: Allowing diagnostic logging and high-throughput telemetry to share fieldbuses with real-time safety loops.
Real-time fieldbuses in physical AI (such as CAN FD and EtherCAT) are engineered for deterministic, low-latency control: EtherCAT cyclic Process Data Objects (PDOs) and CAN FD priority-arbitrated frames carry microsecond-accurate torque targets and lease-renewal heartbeats. When engineering teams attempt to capture rich diagnostic traces by multiplexing high-throughput telemetry (diagnostic core dumps, raw LiDAR point clouds, uncompressed camera debug streams) through Ethernet-over-EtherCAT (EoE) or bulk CAN FD payloads, they risk overflowing communication channels and starving safety-critical control loops.
On CAN FD networks, message arbitration is non-preemptive: once a low-priority diagnostic frame begins transmission on the physical layer, a newly ready high-priority emergency-stop or torque-command frame cannot preempt it. The resulting blocking latency depends on frame length, arbitration and data bit rates, and bit stuffing. Unregulated diagnostic bursts therefore inflate queueing jitter and exhaust hard timing budgets, even though every frame on the bus is structurally valid. Because CAN controllers do not register arbitration delays or link saturation as electrical errors, hardware error counters remain clean while safety deadlines expire. Similarly, while an EtherCAT master partitions cyclic process data from acyclic mailbox traffic, shared host network interface cards, protocol stack buffers, and slave microcontroller processing pipelines can still experience severe resource contention under heavy mailbox load. If mailbox servicing delays PDO packet processing or causes host-side scheduling jitter, safety heartbeats fail.
When unbudgeted telemetry delays a safety lease renewal or drive update past its deadline, the affected watchdog must invoke its qualified local fail-safe response. Furthermore, if a physical emergency-stop command travels across that same saturated bus, transmission delays directly consume stopping clearance. Verification trials must capture synchronized electrical communication traces alongside physical vehicle trajectories; observing a software timeout in isolation cannot prove that the machine arrested motion within its certified clearance envelope.
Unbudgeted diagnostic traffic can delay the commands and evidence needed for a bounded response.
Architect’s countermeasure: Physically isolate high-bandwidth diagnostic telemetry from real-time safety buses on separate network media, or enforce rigorous protocol-specific traffic shaping. On CAN FD, this means strict frame-length caps, reserved identifier priorities, and rate-limiting ingress filters. On EtherCAT, it means dedicated cyclic and mailbox schedule partitioning with strict execution time budgets. Ethernet Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) scheduling and frame preemption standards (IEEE 802.1Qbv and 802.1Qbu) apply only to compliant Ethernet hardware; they do not provide preemption across CAN FD or standard EtherCAT links.


Pitfall: Relying on software anomaly detectors that share electrical power or failure modes with monitored actuators.
Actuator dynamics, including rapid motor acceleration, locked-rotor stall currents, and sharp regenerative braking transitions, cause severe electrical disturbances on shared power rails and analog ground references. Inverter switching produces steep inductive voltage transients (\(\InductiveVoltage = \PowerRailInductance\,d\ConductorCurrent/d\TimeInstant\)), while wiring harnesses and internal battery impedance introduce substantial voltage drops that can pull unregulated bus voltages below the minimum dropout threshold of downstream DC-DC converters. Adversarial testing campaigns (such as fault category F4) inject calibrated rail transients to measure whether these disturbances propagate into supposedly isolated sensor and safety controller supplies.
When digital transducers monitoring actuator velocity or position share a power distribution board, ground plane, or non-isolated buck regulator with motor gate drivers, supply dips and ground bounce propagate directly into sensor microcontrollers. A common failure mode is a frozen peripheral register: the transducer continues transmitting cyclically valid bus frames whose measurement payload has stopped updating. System behavior depends on representation: if an encoder freezes its cumulative position counter, a downstream velocity estimator that computes numerical derivatives will incorrectly deduce that the motor has reached zero velocity. Conversely, if the sensor freezes an internally computed velocity register, it may continuously report a nominal cruising speed.
For example, if a frozen velocity register continues reporting 1.3 m/s while the motor drive erroneously executes a full-throttle acceleration command, the telemetry frames will carry valid cyclic checksums and plausible values even though they no longer reflect physical reality. A software anomaly detector that monitors only motor telemetry cannot identify the divergence without an independent physical motion witness, such as a secondary wheel encoder, an inertial measurement unit, or optical flow sensors. The adversarial verification suite must explicitly inject both the electrical transient and the resulting register freeze, using external ground-truth tracking to monitor vehicle kinematics through the commanded stop.
A power fault that disrupts an actuator can simultaneously blind the sensor tasked with detecting it.
Architect’s countermeasure: Power safety-critical transducers and monitor microcontrollers from galvanically isolated, held-up auxiliary supplies equipped with sufficient energy-storage capacitance to ride through worst-case bus transients. Transducers must be configured so that internal hardware faults cannot masquerade as plausible measurements. For analog transducers, pulling an output to 0 V fails this requirement whenever 0 V represents a valid physical reading (such as zero speed or minimum distance). Reliable systems employ a “live zero” architecture with out-of-band diagnostic voltage levels, patterned after the NAMUR NE 43 standard for industrial transmitters (NAMUR 2021). For digital fieldbuses, enforce end-to-end communication protections featuring monotonic rolling sequence counters, timestamp freshness checks, and payload CRCs to detect repeated or corrupted frames (AUTOSAR 2024). A frozen measurement register can still travel in a fresh, correctly sequenced packet, so detecting that failure also requires monitoring physical acquisition progress and cross-checking the reported state against an independent motion witness.

NAMUR. 2021. NE 43: Standardization of the Signal Level for the Failure Information of Digital Transmitters. NAMUR, User Association of Automation Technology in Process Industries.

AUTOSAR. 2024. E2E Protocol Specification. No. 849. AUTOSAR.


Fallacy: Treating an unobservable test outcome where diagnostic loggers dropped packets as evidence of safety.
High-severity fault injection, such as short-circuiting an inverter drive phase, opening a contactor under full load, or coupling high-voltage electromagnetic interference (EMI) onto fieldbus cabling, generates intense radiated and conducted electrical transients within the test cell. Ground bounce and high inductive kickback routinely couple into the external data acquisition (DAQ) harness, desynchronizing high-speed digitizer clocks, overflowing PCIe frame-grabber ring buffers, or crashing host logging daemons into kernel panics.
Meanwhile, the physical mobile base comes to rest: either its spring-applied mechanical brakes engaged, its drive back-drove the gearbox to a stall, or it drifted into the test cell’s mechanical end-stop buffer. In an undisciplined test campaign, observers look at the stopped machine and declare the run a “PASS” (“no crash occurred and the system reached rest”), while dismissing the missing telemetry as an irrelevant “instrumentation glitch” or repeating the trial until the logger manages to survive.
This practice introduces survivorship bias. The trials in which the logger crashes are often those with the most violent electrical transients, which are the conditions most likely to cause the safety microcontroller to hang in an exception handler without commanding deceleration. An unrecorded trial cannot reveal which mechanism stopped the base, and an operational warehouse aisle has no end-stop buffer. Under a rigorous qualification methodology, any test run lacking continuous, verifiable telemetry must be classified as UNOBSERVABLE and treated as an immediate test defect. The campaign must report the explicit count of each verdict alongside all untested configurations. Summary ratios such as \(\PassedTrialCount / \TotalExecutedTrialCount\) serve as test-suite execution statistics rather than empirical failure-probability estimates derived from valid, independently scored trials. Before repeating that condition, the team must establish why the witnesses failed and qualify evidence capture under the injected environment.
Discarding unobservable trials conceals the exact vulnerability under test through survivorship bias.
Architect’s countermeasure: Categorize any test run with dropped, incomplete, or corrupted evidence as UNOBSERVABLE, retaining it as an evidence deficit whose cause must be investigated. Report all four verdict counts. Credit a required trial toward a protective claim only when its required evidence is complete and verified; repeated observable runs do not erase missing evidence from earlier trials.

title: Adversarial Verification
text:
15.13 Summary
The rack-end stopping claim begins as a physical distance and timing budget. Adversarial verification transforms this kinematic budget into a concrete, testable engineering contract by declaring the operating envelope across which it must hold, including the coupled corners that one-variable-at-a-time sweeps miss. A five-part test contract (bounded claim, declared conditions, precommitted oracle, stated injection procedure, provenance) decides whether any trial counts as evidence. Within it, each postulated fault is built from a five-element chain: the negated nominal condition, the injection point, the expected detector, the bounded physical response, and an observable pass condition scored on an independent witness. For example, when the chunk policy stalls while its host processor continues transmitting nominal heartbeats, the verification harness evaluates powered deceleration onset and travel to rest referenced strictly from the timestamp of the last valid lease renewal. An automated oracle fixed before the trial classifies each run into one of four mutually exclusive outcomes: PASS, FAIL, INVALID, or UNOBSERVABLE. Test coverage is then reported dimension by dimension, and the campaign is judged by its weakest dimension rather than by one aggregate percentage.
Developing a comprehensive fault catalog requires combining multiple analytical perspectives: inverting nominal design assumptions, tracing causal failure paths forward through physical mechanisms, evaluating authority boundaries, identifying shared root causes that induce coupled failures, and modeling adversarial disturbances at physical transducers. Some failure modes bypass communication buses and hardware sensors entirely. An adversarial physical patch, an optical spoof, or a maliciously crafted task instruction steers the learned proposer directly, testing the boundary of the proposal subsystem. Because the deterministic permission path monitors physical safety invariants rather than the semantic origin of a proposal, it intervenes only when an actuator command threatens a measured envelope limit. Consequently, such trials score strictly against the physical oracle. If an adversarial proposal induces an erratic or sub-optimal action that nonetheless remains entirely within the safe physical envelope, the physical predicates may pass, while the verification harness records the wrong action as a task-level coverage deficit rather than crediting it as a passed proposer-injection case.
Verification evidence must be gathered on the qualification rung that faithfully models the underlying physical mechanism. A software simulation cannot sag a power rail it does not model, whereas formal methods can verify compact, deterministic safety filters under explicit premises without establishing a closed-loop guarantee for the running machine’s learned proposers. On physical test benches, hardware fault injectors operate directly at interface boundaries, while instrumentation towers record ground truth using independent clocks and isolated power supplies to prevent observer coupling. During falsification, Signal Temporal Logic provides signed robustness margins that direct search algorithms toward worst-case counterexamples. However, simulated margins cannot transfer directly to physical claims without applying a discrepancy bound justified over the claimed conditions. Similarly, importance sampling converts targeted failure searches into operational failure rates only when the sampling proposal distribution is explicitly declared, covers the entire failure domain, and applies proper likelihood weights. In rare-event analysis, extreme value models support safety claims only to the extent justified by their distributional assumptions. A counterexample refutes a safety claim, whereas the absence of one leaves the unsearched domain open rather than certified. Eight relations formalize this quantitative framework, and table 6 summarizes what each bounds or decides.

Key Takeaways: Adversarial verification and fault injection

A fault tests a physical claim: Derive the injection, detector, response, and independent witness from the stopping or contact bound. Successful task execution alone does not exercise the protective response.
The environment bounds the evidence: Select each qualification rung for the mechanism it exercises. Simulation, processor execution, electrical benches, and physical rigs contribute complementary evidence with different blind spots.
Search finds counterexamples, not universal passes: Signed temporal margins help prioritize disturbances near a violation. An unsuccessful search does not establish a global minimum, and a fitted tail does not prove a hard physical limit.
Precommitment preserves the meaning of a pass: Fix conditions and predicates before injection. Keep FAIL, INVALID, and UNOBSERVABLE distinct, because missing or invalid evidence cannot support the stopping claim.
Verification hands release bounded evidence: Bind each fault record to its claim, builds, conditions, and raw measurements. Coverage gaps and model assumptions remain part of the fault records, so release can restrict authority where evidence ends.



Under the fourth law, permission must be earned (principle \(\ref{pri-vol4-evidence-bounds-authority}\)), and adversarial verification produces much of the evidence that earns it. Each fault record names the claim it supports, the envelope point it covered, and the oracle fixed before the run. The authority that the release decision can grant therefore reaches exactly as far as the passing records and stops at every INVALID, UNOBSERVABLE, or untested cell. The F1 record of this chapter shows the rule in its plainest form. Its timing path, candidate envelope point, and witnesses are specified, while its loaded braking premise remains unqualified and its outcome field is empty. Until measured trials on a physical rig with independent instrumentation fill that field, the stopping claim it describes grants no authority at all.

title: Adversarial Verification
text:
15.14 Historical Perspective and Further Reading
Deliberate fault injection originated in the dependability community of the 1980s, where researchers applied electrical transients, pin-level shorts, and radiation directly to working microprocessors to determine whether fault-tolerant architectures could detect and contain hardware errors. Arlat et al. (1990) formalized this methodology with the MESSALINE tool, structuring each verification campaign around four operational dimensions: the injected faults, the workload activating them, the readouts captured across system boundaries, and the dependability measures derived from observations. This four-part taxonomy serves as the foundational template for the fault records developed throughout this chapter. As systems scaled in complexity, fault injection transitioned from physical pin manipulation to software instrumentation. The comprehensive survey by Hsueh et al. (1997) framed the defining engineering trade-off: hardware-implemented injection manipulates internal signals and electrical states unreachable by software, whereas software-implemented injection offers programmatic repeatability and lower operational cost at the expense of ignoring low-level hardware faults. This trade-off reappears at every rung of the cyber-physical qualification ladder. Early practitioners also discovered that monitoring hooks and profiling code unavoidably perturb execution timing and cache states, a distortion Gait (1986) termed the probe effect. Because sub-millisecond timing shifts can destabilize physical feedback loops, high-assurance verification architectures isolate witness observers onto independent power supplies and dedicated clock domains.

Hsueh, Mei-Chen, Timothy K. Tsai, and Ravishankar K. Iyer. 1997. “Fault Injection Techniques and Tools.” Computer 30 (4): 75–82. https://doi.org/10.1109/2.585157.

Pnueli, Amir. 1977. “The Temporal Logic of Programs.” 18th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (SFCS), 46–57. https://doi.org/10.1109/SFCS.1977.32.

Maler, Oded, and Dejan Nickovic. 2004. “Monitoring Temporal Properties of Continuous Signals.” Formal Techniques, Modelling and Analysis of Timed and Fault-Tolerant Systems (FORMATS/FTRTFT), Lecture notes in computer science, vol. 3253: 152–66. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-30206-3_12.

Annpureddy, Yashwanth, Che Liu, Georgios Fainekos, and Sriram Sankaranarayanan. 2011. “S-TaLiRo: A Tool for Temporal Logic Falsification for Hybrid Systems.” International Conference on Tools and Algorithms for the Construction and Analysis of Systems (TACAS), Lecture notes in computer science, vol. 6605: 254–57. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-19835-9_21.

Donzé, Alexandre. 2010. “Breach, a Toolbox for Verification and Parameter Synthesis of Hybrid Systems.” Computer Aided Verification (CAV), Lecture notes in computer science, vol. 6174: 167–70. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-14295-6_17.

Rubinstein, Reuven Y., and Dirk P. Kroese. 2004. The Cross-Entropy Method: A Unified Approach to Combinatorial Optimization, Monte-Carlo Simulation and Machine Learning. Information Science and Statistics. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-4321-0.

O’Kelly, Matthew, Aman Sinha, Hongseok Namkoong, John Duchi, and Russ Tedrake. 2018. “Scalable End-to-End Autonomous Vehicle Testing via Rare-Event Simulation.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 31.

Balkema, August A., and Laurens de Haan. 1974. “Residual Life Time at Great Age.” The Annals of Probability 2 (5): 792–804. https://doi.org/10.1214/aop/1176996548.

Pickands, James, III. 1975. “Statistical Inference Using Extreme Order Statistics.” The Annals of Statistics 3 (1): 119–31. https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1176343003.
Search-based falsification and continuous verification followed a parallel lineage rooted in formal methods and statistical physics. Pnueli (1977) first introduced linear temporal logic to prove correctness properties over discrete program executions. To verify continuous and hybrid physical trajectories, Maler and Nickovic (2004) generalized temporal assertions into signal temporal logic (STL). Fainekos and Pappas (2009) subsequently equipped STL with quantitative spatial semantics, replacing binary true-false verdicts with a continuous signed distance margin. This formulation transformed the falsification problem from an intractable combinatorial search into continuous gradient-free or gradient-based optimization. Cyber-physical falsification frameworks such as S-TaLiRo (Annpureddy et al. 2011) and Breach (Donzé 2010) packaged these continuous margins to automate the discovery of safety violations in nonlinear dynamical models. Statistical rare-event estimation has an even older heritage. Importance sampling emerged from early Monte Carlo radiation shielding calculations by Kahn and Marshall (1953), the cross-entropy method introduced adaptive proposal distributions (Rubinstein and Kroese 2004), and O’Kelly et al. (2018) synthesized both techniques to quantify catastrophic collision probabilities across autonomous driving stacks. When safety analysts must characterize worst-case physical excursions without imposing restrictive global distribution assumptions, they draw on extreme value theory. It entered engineering through the flood-frequency analyses of Gumbel (1958) and was rigorously established in its modern peaks-over-threshold form by Balkema and Haan (1974) and Pickands (1975).
Formal verification of learned neural controllers is the most recent strand. Reluplex (Katz et al. 2017) proved that modified simplex constraint solvers could formally verify input-output safety properties on small piecewise-linear networks. Subsequent bound-propagation frameworks, including α,β-CROWN (Wang et al. 2021), scaled formal guarantees to million-parameter vision networks using branch-and-bound techniques and convex relaxation. However, formal solvers remain computationally bounded; the cited results do not establish guarantees for multi-billion-parameter vision-language-action foundation models operating in closed feedback loops. The verification architecture developed in this chapter unifies these historical lineages into a cohesive systems discipline. Each trial executes against an explicit operational claim, evaluates trajectories with an oracle declared before the run, isolates observational telemetry within uncorrupted witness hardware, and exports fault records that carry measured coverage deficits into deployment safety cases.

Katz, Guy, Clark Barrett, David L. Dill, Kyle Julian, and Mykel J. Kochenderfer. 2017. “Reluplex: An Efficient SMT Solver for Verifying Deep Neural Networks.” International Conference on Computer Aided Verification (CAV), 97–117. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-63387-9_5.

Wang, Shiqi, Huan Zhang, Kaidi Xu, Xue Lin, Suman Jana, Cho-Jui Hsieh, and J. Zico Kolter. 2021. “Beta-CROWN: Efficient Bound Propagation with Per-Neuron Split Constraints for Neural Network Robustness Verification.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 34.
Six foundational works trace the trajectory from classical hardware dependability to modern cyber-physical validation algorithms:

Arlat et al. (1990) establishes fault injection as a controlled experimental science, defining the four-factor schema of faults, activation workloads, readouts, and derived measures that governs the fault records in section 15.4.2.
Leveson (2011) introduces Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) and System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA), establishing the forward hazard methodology in section 15.6.2 that identifies systemic safety violations emerging from unsafe control interactions rather than isolated component failures.
Fainekos and Pappas (2009) formulates the continuous spatial robustness degree for temporal logic specifications over real-valued signals, providing the signed optimization margin evaluated throughout section 15.9.1.
Owen (2013) provides a definitive mathematical foundation for importance sampling and rare-event estimation, detailing effective sample size diagnostics, weight degeneracies, and failure modes where unrepresentative proposals yield falsely optimistic variance estimates.
Corso et al. (2021) surveys algorithmic safety validation for black-box autonomous systems, categorizing falsification approaches according to whether they target counterexample discovery, most-likely-failure trajectories, or rare failure probabilities.
Kochenderfer et al. (2026) synthesizes trajectory falsification, failure-probability estimation, reachable set analysis, and runtime monitoring into an algorithmic discipline for validating complex autonomous systems.


Arlat, Jean, Martine Aguera, Louis Amat, Yves Crouzet, Jean-Charles Fabre, Jean-Claude Laprie, Eliane Martins, and David Powell. 1990. “Fault Injection for Dependability Validation: A Methodology and Some Applications.” IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 16 (2): 166–82. https://doi.org/10.1109/32.44380.

Fainekos, Georgios E., and George J. Pappas. 2009. “Robustness of Temporal Logic Specifications for Continuous-Time Signals.” Theoretical Computer Science 410 (42): 4262–91. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tcs.2009.06.021.

Owen, Art B. 2013. Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples. Online book.

Corso, Anthony, Robert Moss, Mark Koren, Ritchie Lee, and Mykel J. Kochenderfer. 2021. “A Survey of Algorithms for Black-Box Safety Validation of Cyber-Physical Systems.” Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 72. https://doi.org/10.1613/jair.1.12716.

Kochenderfer, Mykel J., Sydney M. Katz, Anthony L. Corso, and Robert J. Moss. 2026. Algorithms for Validation. MIT Press.

What’s Next: From verification to release decisionsVerification delivers to the release gate a signed set of fault records, the per-rung coverage of the qualification ladder behind them, and an explicit account of the operating regimes no trial reached. For each safety claim, the set binds the corresponding fault records to any sim-to-real transfer bound (\(\TransferDiscrepancyBound\)) or rare-event tail estimate on which the claim depends, keeping measured margins, conditional model estimates, and untested regimes strictly apart. Verification records supply behavioral evidence under fault conditions, but they do not make deployment policy, and no individual fault record decides whether the machine may operate in production aisles. In Deployment Release, the release process writes each claim as a physical inequality and joins these fault records with the authority record, the placement record, and the evaluation record in a safety case. It then judges which claims are substantiated, which release verdict applies (UNCOND, COND, or REFUSE), and which standing conditions must govern live operation.

title: Responsible Physical AI
text:
Purpose



Physical AI stack focus for this chapter.
Who answers for a machine that moves on its own when its motion harms someone?
A machine’s logs can show, tick by tick, what it sensed, proposed, and admitted, and still not show who decided that it could travel at that speed, among those people, with that person as its only backup. When harm arrives, blame settles on whoever stood closest to the event, often an operator handed a duty no person could have carried out, while the decisions that set the machine’s limits stay spread across engineering teams, suppliers, site managers, and regulators. The machine’s effects also reach people who never chose it: pedestrians and coworkers whose detection rate was never measured for people like them, workers whose jobs shift to rescuing and watching it, and bystanders whose faces fill the records kept to explain its mistakes. A machine is fit to be given authority only when each decision behind its actions names the person who answers for it, each human role it relies on is one a person can actually perform, and each group that bears its risk or its recording has been counted. Assigning responsibility after a collision cannot take back the energy the machine has already delivered across the causal boundary, so it has to be assigned before the machine moves.


Learning Objectives

Explain why reconstructing what a machine did does not establish who answers for it, and trace an admitted action back to the decisions that allowed it
Evaluate whether a human role gives its holder the time, information, and authority to act, using the takeover budget and supervisor utilization
Specify the stages of operating permission, what each stage allows and must report, and what withdraws it
Calculate how a gap in per-frame detection between groups of people becomes a gap in stopping distance and impact energy
Size a per-group evaluation whose confidence interval can resolve a detection gap of a stated size
Distinguish risk borne by people who chose the machine from risk borne by people who did not, and specify exposure reporting for each group
Design an approval record that names an owner for every decision behind an admitted action, so that a missing owner blocks release

title: Responsible Physical AI
section: 17.1 Who Answered for the Cruise Collision
text:
17.1 Who Answered for the Cruise Collision
Release left the running machine with a signed manifest: a verdict, the records it binds by digest, and the standing conditions that withdraw it. The manifest names the lead systems adjudicator who signed it. It does not name who decided the aisle speed the warehouse would accept, who decided that one remote assistant would serve every machine on the floor, or who would report an incident, to whom, and how fast, if the machine hurt someone. Those decisions shape what the machine does once a command crosses the causal boundary as surely as the enforcer’s thresholds do, and none of them appears in a per-tick log.
The Cruise collision in San Francisco on the night of October 2, 2023 shows what happens when they are left unassigned. A human-driven car struck a pedestrian in a crosswalk and threw her into the path of a driverless Cruise robotaxi, which braked hard, ran over her, and stopped. With her still beneath it, the vehicle then began a pullover toward the curb and moved about 20 ft (6.1 m) at up to 7.7 mph before it stopped (Quinn Emanuel Urquhart and Sullivan, LLP 2024). The engineering failure belongs to the permission path. A post-collision classifier placed the pedestrian at the side of the vehicle rather than in front of it, and the fallback it selected moved the vehicle without any evidence that the space beneath it was clear.

Quinn Emanuel Urquhart and Sullivan, LLP. 2024. Report to the Boards of Directors of Cruise LLC, GM Cruise Holdings LLC, and General Motors Holdings LLC Regarding the October 2, 2023 Accident in San Francisco. Quinn Emanuel Urquhart; Sullivan, LLP.

↩︎ The fallback rule that forbids renewed motion while the space beneath a vehicle is unverified is established in The four rungs of the fallback ladder.

The machine’s own records were enough to reconstruct that motion. The engineers who analyzed the event for the company’s boards rebuilt it from the vehicle’s logs and video, including the dropped pedestrian track before impact and the pullover after it (Quinn Emanuel Urquhart and Sullivan, LLP 2024). What failed after the collision was the account given to the people who had licensed the vehicle. On October 3, a Cruise representative told an analyst at the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) by telephone that the vehicle had stopped on impact and contacted remote assistance; the description left out the pullover and the dragging. The commission later counted 15 days, October 3 through 18, in which Cruise withheld a full account, and it received the full video on October 19 (California Public Utilities Commission 2024). Cruise’s crash reports to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) also omitted the dragging (U.S. Attorney’s Office, Northern District of California 2024). On October 24, the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) suspended Cruise’s permits for driverless testing and driverless deployment, citing among its grounds that the company had misrepresented information related to the safety of its autonomous technology (California Department of Motor Vehicles 2023). A review commissioned by Cruise’s boards found no evidence that anyone intended to mislead regulators, but it described a “passive, non-transparent approach” to disclosure and a leadership focused on correcting media coverage of the crash (Quinn Emanuel Urquhart and Sullivan, LLP 2024).
Each group involved held one piece of the outcome: the engineers who designed the classifier and the fallback, the remote-assistance staff, the people who drafted the reports, and the executives who managed the response. Each could describe its own piece truthfully, and none of those descriptions said who had decided the whole. The CPUC had granted Cruise commercial driverless service in San Francisco at any hour seven weeks earlier (California Public Utilities Commission 2023). The logs answered what the vehicle did. They did not answer who had decided that a driverless vehicle should pull over after a side impact without checking beneath itself, who decided what regulators would be told, or who answered for either decision. Five years earlier, after the Uber test vehicle killed a pedestrian in Tempe, the person who answered in court was the vehicle’s backup operator, who pleaded guilty to endangerment in 2023 (Maricopa County Attorney’s Office 2023).

Maricopa County Attorney’s Office. 2023. Driver of Uber Vehicle Involved in Death of Woman in Tempe Pleads Guilty.
Responsibility for a physical machine therefore has to be engineered like any other premise of its authority: written down before the machine moves, attached to the decisions that set its limits, and checked when it is released. The same questions arise on the warehouse machine without a public road in sight. A remote assistant answers for takeovers, facility management for the crossing rule that keeps people out of the aisle, a data team for the camera traces the black box keeps, and someone, so far unnamed, for the decision that one person can watch every machine on the floor. The sections that follow take these decisions in turn: the links behind one admitted action, the human roles the design relies on, the stages of permission to operate, the detection of different groups of people, the people who bear the machine’s risk and appear in its records, and the labor it moves rather than removes. The approval record collects these decisions in one place that the release gate reads, so that a decision with no named owner blocks operation the way an unknown premise does.

title: Responsible Physical AI
text:
17.2 Decisions Behind an Admitted Action
Consider one command the enforcer admitted in the aisle: a base velocity of 1.3 m/s toward a rack end. The enforcement record shows that it passed the stopping check at that tick, under the thresholds in force, yet behind that single log line stand at least six decisions made by different people at different times. Four of them leave traces in the engineering records built in earlier chapters. The learning team trained and approved the policy weights that proposed the command. The safety engineering team built and signed the enforcer and its thresholds. The intervention design and the remote assistant on shift set the authority state at that tick. The lead systems adjudicator signed the operating envelope into the release manifest, including the aisle speed and the floor-friction premise beneath it. The other two decisions govern the site rather than the machine: facility management wrote the crossing rule that lets people enter the aisle only at marked points, while operations decided how many machines one remote assistant would serve. Figure 1 draws the six links and the record, if any, that holds each one.


↩︎ The lead systems adjudicator, whose signature binds the release verdict to a named person, is established in The Three Verdicts.






Figure 1: Six decisions behind one admitted command: An aisle command admitted at one tick traces back to decisions made weeks earlier by six different parties. Four of them land in a record the book has built (the policy manifest, the enforcement record, the authority record, and the release manifest); the crossing rule and the staffing ratio land in none, so no log can name who made them. The approval record lists each decision with its owner and refuses operation while any link has no owner.



When each of these decisions belongs to a different party, every party can truthfully say that the harm came from someone else’s part. Thompson called this the problem of many hands in his study of public officials, where responsibility for a policy that many people shaped ends up resting on no one (Thompson 1980). Nissenbaum showed that computer systems make it worse: they are built by many people, they fail in ways no single person caused, and their failures are easily excused as bugs that no one could have prevented (Nissenbaum 1996). A learned proposer adds a further excuse. Its behavior was learned rather than written, so no engineer wrote the rule it followed, and Matthias argued that machines which learn create a real gap in who can be held responsible for what they do (Matthias 2004). The architecture of this book closes that gap at the point where it matters. The model proposes and never admits (principle \(\ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission}\)), so every admitted action passed a check that someone designed, under an envelope that someone signed, and “the model did it” is never a complete answer.

17.2.1 Decisions that leave no trace in a log
When an incident investigator opens a machine’s runtime logs, the decisions that made the incident possible are missing because those logs capture only runtime events: an observation and its age, a proposal, an admission, a change of authority, or a fault trial. The choices that shaped those events happened weeks or months earlier in meetings and documents, long before a command crossed the causal boundary. A safety engineer approves an operating envelope, an operations manager sets a staffing ratio, a team disables a protective function, a company applies for a permit, and a data team declares what its camera traces may be used for. In the Cruise case, the rule that a side impact should trigger a pullover was a design decision made long before October 2, and the choices about what to tell regulators were made in the days after. Neither could appear in the vehicle’s log, because the vehicle did not make them.
Such decisions have to be recorded on purpose, and a chain of them is less complete than any one of its links. Suppose each of the 6 links behind the aisle command can be retrieved when an investigator asks with probability 0.99, independently of the others. The whole chain then resolves with probability \(0.99^{6} = 0.94\). At 0.95 per link it resolves with probability 0.74, and at 0.90, roughly what a decision held only in memory and email achieves once its author has changed jobs, with probability 0.53. An investigator would then find the full chain in about 53 percent of incidents. The same arithmetic makes a conjunctive release argument weaker than any one of its premises, and the remedy is also the same: each link has to be written down as part of the design, not left to accumulate.


↩︎ The conjunctive arithmetic that makes an argument no stronger than its weakest premise is established in Contextual assumptions and the weakest link.
These links are held in the decision block of the approval record (section 17.9). For each decision it names the type of decision, the role that owns it, the signed approval, the evidence it relied on, and the date after which it must be made again. A link with no owner is not a gap in paperwork; it is a premise of the machine’s authority that no one has accepted. Even when every link has a named owner, however, many of those approvals rest on a further premise: that a human operator in the loop can step in when the machine’s own case runs out.

title: Responsible Physical AI
text:
17.3 Oversight a Person Can Perform
Naming a human operator in that decision chain, whether a safety driver behind the wheel, a remote assistant at a console, or a spotter walking beside a robot during commissioning, often shifts blame onto that person without adding any real protection. A person in the loop provides genuine oversight only if three conditions hold: the person must have the time to act before the hazard arrives, the information to understand what the machine is doing, and the authority to change what it does, not only to report it. Santoni de Sio and van den Hoven state the same requirement in two parts: the system must respond to the reasons of the people meant to control it, and every outcome must trace back to someone who understood both the system and their own role in it (Santoni de Sio and Hoven 2018).

Definition 17.1: Human oversight role
A human oversight role is a duty that a design assigns to a person, such as stopping the machine, taking over a channel, or approving a motion, and that the safety argument relies on. The role counts as a countermeasure only if its holder has the time, the information, and the authority to carry it out within the time the hazard leaves.

Significance: A role that fails any of the three conditions adds no protection, yet it moves blame onto the person who holds it, so every role the safety case cites must be tested like any other premise.
Distinction: The takeover budget measures how long a person needs; the oversight role asks whether the design leaves that much time, gives that person what they need to see, and lets them act on it.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that adding a person to the loop makes a design responsible. A person who cannot act in time is a place to put blame, not a safety layer.



When a role fails any of these conditions, the person in it absorbs responsibility for control they never had. Elish calls the person in that position a moral crumple zone. Like the crumple zone of a car, the person absorbs the impact, except that here the impact is blame, and what the crumpling protects is the reputation of the system rather than the person (Elish 2019). The three conditions give a design team a test it can apply before the machine moves.

17.3.1 Time to act
Time is the condition most often violated, and it is the easiest to check. At the 1.3 m/s aisle speed, a person who steps out 1.10 m ahead of the machine leaves 0.85 s before the rack end. A remote assistant who has been monitoring rather than driving needs about 4.5 s to take over, the design out-of-loop takeover time, during which the machine travels 5.8 m. The person needs about 5× the time the hazard leaves. No training, attention, or diligence closes a gap of that size, so a design that names the remote assistant as the countermeasure for a person stepping out at a rack end has not added a layer of protection. It has recorded in advance who will be blamed.


↩︎ The out-of-loop takeover time and its price in the stopping budget are established in Human reaction time and travel before braking.
The engineering consequence is already in the book’s design. The machine stops itself first and asks for help from standstill, where waiting costs time but not clearance. What the time test adds is the duty to write that choice down. For every human role the safety case relies on, the approval record lists the response time the role requires, the time the hazard leaves, and a verdict of FEASIBLE, INFEASIBLE, or UNKNOWN. A role marked INFEASIBLE may stay in the design as a productivity resource; it may not appear in the safety argument as a countermeasure.


17.3.2 One person, many machines
A remote assistant who serves many machines is a server in a queue, and queueing theory says how busy that person is. If help requests arrive from the whole fleet at rate \(\ArrivalRate\) and each holds the assistant for a mean time \(\IntervalMean\), the share of time the assistant is busy, the utilization, is \[\ServingUtilization = \ArrivalRate\,\IntervalMean. \tag{1}\] A request that arrives while the assistant is busy waits. Under the simplest queueing model, with random arrivals and random service times, the mean wait before service begins is \[\QueueWaitTime = \frac{\ServingUtilization\,\IntervalMean}{1-\ServingUtilization}. \tag{2}\] The wait grows without bound as \(\ServingUtilization\) approaches one. Moreover, a request arriving while the assistant is busy, which happens with probability \(\ServingUtilization\) in this model, gets no human attention at all until the request ahead of it is finished.

Napkin Math 17.1: One assistant, twenty machinesProblem: A site plans to run 20 mobile manipulators with one remote assistant. Each machine asks for help 0.5 times per operating hour, and each request holds the assistant for 3 min on average. How busy is the assistant, and how long does a request wait?
Variables:

Requests per machine: 0.5 per operating hour (Illustrative); mean service time \(\IntervalMean =\) 180 s (Illustrative).
Machines served: 10, 20, or 32 (Illustrative).

Math: By equation 1, 20 machines give \(\ServingUtilization =\) 0.50, and equation 2 gives a mean wait \(\QueueWaitTime =\) 180 s. One request in a hundred waits longer than 23 min. With 10 machines the figures are 0.25 and 60 s; with 32 they are 0.80 and 720 s, about 12 min.
Result: The assistant is busy 50 percent of the time, and a typical request waits minutes. Adding machines past that point makes the wait grow much faster than the fleet.
Systems insight: Every one of these waits is longer than the 0.85 s a person stepping out at a rack end leaves. The ratio of machines to assistants is therefore a productivity budget and never a safety layer. A staffing plan that caps utilization at 0.5 limits this assistant to 20 machines, and the approval record lists that cap as the decision of whoever set it.




↩︎ Admitting a remote-assistant session only when the machine is in a state where waiting costs no clearance is established in Admitting the remote-assistant session.
The queue shows why the staffing ratio is a decision someone must own. A manager who adds machines to one assistant’s load is not changing a number in a spreadsheet; that manager is deciding how long a stranded machine, and the people working around it, will wait for a person. If that decision is written down with the utilization it implies and an owner, it can be reviewed when the fleet grows. If it is not, it changes silently every time a machine is added.


17.3.3 Information and authority
Time is necessary but not enough. A person with time to act must also know what the machine is doing and be able to change it. A console that shows the camera feed but not which channel the machine still owns leaves the operator guessing about the most important fact of a handover, and an operator who believes they hold a channel they do not hold can make a takeover worse. A role whose only output is a report, a flag raised to a supervisor or a note in a log, gives its holder no authority over the motion at all. The test for authority is mechanical. The person must be able to stop the machine, through a channel the permission path honors within the time the hazard leaves, without asking anyone else.


↩︎ Mode confusion, and the per-channel annunciation that keeps an operator’s picture of who owns each channel current, are established in Authority Handover Failure Modes.
For each human role, the approval record therefore holds three fields beside the timing verdict: the information channel the person reads, the authority channel the person can act through, and whether that channel reaches the permission path. A remote assistant on the running machine passes the information and authority tests for a stranded machine at standstill and fails the time test for a person stepping out at a rack end. Both facts belong in the record, because they assign that one person two different duties.

Checkpoint 17.1: Oversight a person can perform
A design names three people in its safety argument: the remote assistant, a teach-pendant operator during commissioning, and a floor supervisor who watches the fleet dashboard.

Time: Can you state, for each role, the time the role requires and the time the relevant hazard leaves, and mark the role FEASIBLE, INFEASIBLE, or UNKNOWN?
Load: A site runs 24 machines with one assistant; requests arrive at 0.8 per machine-hour and take 75 s. Can you compute the assistant’s utilization and mean wait, and say whether the assistant may be listed as a countermeasure for any hazard faster than a minute?
Authority: Can you say which of the three roles can stop the machine through a channel the permission path honors, and which can only report?

title: Responsible Physical AI
text:
17.4 Permission in Stages
Granting a machine full operating permission on day one exposes the public or the workforce before the configuration has accumulated the field evidence needed to support that exposure. Regulators of driverless vehicles therefore grant permission in stages. California’s rules separate testing with a safety driver, testing without one, and deployment to the public, each under its own permit and conditions (California Department of Motor Vehicles 2018a, 2018b). The CPUC adds a second ladder for carrying passengers. Before August 2023, Cruise could carry paying passengers without a safety driver only in limited areas of San Francisco between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., could carry paying passengers anywhere in the city at any hour only with a safety driver present, and could give free driverless rides anywhere at any hour. On August 10, 2023, the commission removed the time limit on driverless fared service (California Public Utilities Commission 2023). Each rung named a configuration, a place, a time, and who could be aboard.

California Department of Motor Vehicles. 2018b. California Code of Regulations, Title 13, Article 3.8: Deployment of Autonomous Vehicles.

California Public Utilities Commission. 2023. CPUC Approves Permits for Cruise and Waymo to Charge Fares for Passenger Service in San Francisco.

Definition 17.2: Permission stage
A permission stage is a grant, made by the party entitled to grant it, that allows a named configuration of a machine to operate in a named domain, among named groups of people, on named evidence, and under named reporting duties. A machine moves to the next stage only on evidence gathered at the current one, and a stage can be withdrawn for a configuration change, an incident, or a withheld record.

Significance: Exposure grows one stage at a time, so the evidence for the next stage is gathered under the protection of the current one, and a failure at one stage costs only what that stage exposes.
Distinction: A release verdict is the engineering decision about whether a configuration’s claims are supported; a permission stage is the grant that decides who may be exposed to that configuration and what must be reported about it.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that a stage, once reached, belongs to the company. It belongs to a configuration, and it carries duties that, if broken, withdraw it.



Each stage carries reporting duties, and the duties grow with the stage. California requires a manufacturer testing on public roads to report, within ten days and on a set form, any collision that causes damage, injury, or death, and to file an annual report of every disengagement, each transfer of control from the automation to the safety driver (California Department of Motor Vehicles 2018a). Since 2021, a federal order has required companies operating automated driving systems to report crashes to NHTSA. Under the version in force in 2023, a crash that involved a death, an injury treated at a hospital, or a pedestrian or other vulnerable road user had to be reported within one day, with an update at ten days (National Highway Traffic Safety Administration 2021). The disengagement reports are the data behind A decade of reported takeovers, whose two series come from two different stages, testing with a driver and testing without one.
A warehouse has no public permit office, but the same ladder exists. The machine is commissioned with a spotter walking beside it, then allowed to run unattended in a zone people cannot enter while it operates, and only then released onto an open floor among workers. The facility owner, the integrator, and the workers’ representatives grant these stages, and the approval record names who granted each one, for which configuration, on what evidence, and with which reporting duties. The stage and the verdict are recorded separately. A COND verdict for restricted inspected-route delivery says which claims the evidence supports; the stage says whether that restricted service may run on the open floor yet.

17.4.1 Leaving a stage on evidence
A stage is left on evidence, not on a calendar date, and the evidence a lower stage produces is partly hidden by the protection that stage provides. A safety driver or a spotter masks failures: when the person intervenes, the machine’s own error never reaches its consequence, and the stage records an intervention rather than a collision. Counting failures at the supervised stage therefore means reconstructing, for each intervention, whether the machine would have failed without it, which is why the disengagement reports matter and why they must say why control was transferred.


↩︎ Interventions that end a trial before its outcome is known, and how they are counted, are established in Confidence from a Finite Campaign.
The exposure arithmetic sets how long a stage must run. Under the zero-failure Poisson exposure bound of Verification Ceilings and the Exposure Wall, ruling out an intervention rate at 95 percent confidence with zero observed events requires an exposure of \(\ln(1/0.05)\), or nearly three times the target mean interval between interventions, so claiming fewer than one safety-relevant intervention per 1,000 operating hours after observing none requires the machines to accumulate about 2,996 failure-free operating hours. A fleet of 10 machines running 16 hours a day reaches that in 19 days. Those hours support the claim only for the configuration that ran them. A new policy, a new enforcer build, or a new site layout starts its own count, because the evidence belongs to a configuration, and so does the stage it supports.


17.4.2 Withdrawal and disclosure
Permission is withdrawn the way it is granted, one stage at a time. The DMV’s October 2023 order suspended Cruise’s driverless testing and deployment permits but left in place its permit to test with a safety driver (California Department of Motor Vehicles 2023), stepping the company back down the ladder rather than off it. The grounds the DMV cited show what a permit protects. One was that the vehicles were not safe for public operation, a finding about the motion. Another was that the company had misrepresented information related to the safety of its technology, a finding about the record.

California Department of Motor Vehicles. 2023. DMV Statement on Cruise LLC Suspension.

California Public Utilities Commission. 2024. Decision 24-07-004: Presiding Officer’s Decision Approving Offered Settlement Terms and Granting Deferral of the Order to Show Cause Proceedings.

National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. 2024. NHTSA Announces Consent Order with Cruise After Company Failed to Fully Report Crash Involving Pedestrian.

U.S. Attorney’s Office, Northern District of California. 2024. Cruise Admits to Submitting a False Report to Influence a Federal Investigation and Agrees to Pay $500,000.
The regulatory fines that followed were for the record. The CPUC counted the 15 days in which it lacked a full account, applied its daily maximum of $7,500 to each, and fined Cruise $112,500 (California Public Utilities Commission 2024). In September 2024, NHTSA imposed a consent order with a $1.5 million penalty for crash reports that omitted the dragging (National Highway Traffic Safety Administration 2024). In November 2024, Cruise entered a deferred prosecution agreement and paid a $500,000 criminal fine for submitting a false record to influence the federal investigation (U.S. Attorney’s Office, Northern District of California 2024). Regulators withdrew authority from the company because of what its vehicle did and because of what the company did not tell them about it.
The incident disclosure duty is the obligation, attached to an operating permit, to report an incident completely and on time to the parties the permit names. It is a decision with an owner like any other: someone decides what an incident report contains, someone signs it, and someone decides when a record has been withheld long enough to break the permit. The permit block of the approval record therefore lists, for each stage, the regulator or grantor, the configuration the stage covers, the reporting duties with their deadlines, and a disclosure log of every report sent, with its author and the evidence attached. A release manifest that binds raw traces to the configuration that produced them, and that an assessor can open, is the engineering half of that duty. The disclosure log is the other half, because it shows what was actually sent, to whom, and when. Once a machine enters an open-floor stage among coworkers or pedestrians, however, its safety case rests on a sensor premise that aggregate stage-exit hours can hide: whether its detectors see every group of people in its path equally well.


↩︎ The release manifest that binds raw traces to the configuration that produced them is established in The Release Manifest.

title: Responsible Physical AI
section: 17.5 When Detection Depends on Who Is Detected
text:
17.5 When Detection Depends on Who Is Detected
A machine that earns open-floor permission on aggregate obstacle-detection metrics can still fail systematically on specific groups of people sharing the aisle or roadway. Buolamwini and Gebru found that commercial face-analysis systems misclassified darker-skinned women far more often than lighter-skinned men, and that the benchmarks used to evaluate them contained few of the people they failed on (Buolamwini and Gebru 2018). Pedestrian detection shows the same pattern. Wilson, Hoffman, and Morgenstern annotated pedestrians in a driving dataset by skin type and found that standard detectors reached an average precision of 67.1 percent on lighter-skinned pedestrians and 55.9 percent on darker-skinned ones under a strict overlap criterion. Time of day and occlusion did not explain the gap (Wilson et al. 2019). Testing widely used pedestrian detectors, Li and colleagues found the proportion of children left undetected 20.14 percent higher than that of adults, and significant gender bias at night (Li et al. 2025).
A warehouse has its own groups. A detector trained mostly on people walking upright may see a kneeling worker, a person carrying a carton that hides the torso, a wheelchair user, or a worker without a high-visibility vest later or less often. Where the machine relies only on its certified safety scanner, which stops for any object above its resolution without deciding what it is, these differences do not matter. They matter wherever the design relies on a learned detector to recognize a person: to slow down when a person is near, to keep a wider separation from people than from pallets, or to predict where a person will walk. In those places, a difference in detection becomes a difference in how close the machine comes to each group before it begins to brake.

17.5.1 From a detection gap to a stopping gap
When a detector sees one group of people less reliably than another, the machine travels farther before braking begins and can strike a person in the less-detected group even when the stop was sized to clear the best-detected group. The conversion from a detection rate to a stopping shortfall runs through the camera’s frames. Suppose a design requires that the chance of missing a person in every frame of a window be no more than \(\DetectorMissProbability\), and that a detector reports a person in view in each frame with probability \(\PerFrameDetectionProbability\), independently from frame to frame. Because independent misses multiply across frames so the probability of missing the person in all \(\ReliableDetectionFrameCount\) frames is \((1-\PerFrameDetectionProbability)^{\ReliableDetectionFrameCount} \le \DetectorMissProbability\), the number of consecutive frames the person must be in view before the design may count on detection is \[\ReliableDetectionFrameCount = \left\lceil \frac{\ln \DetectorMissProbability}{\ln\left(1-\PerFrameDetectionProbability\right)} \right\rceil. \tag{3}\] A group the detector sees less often needs more frames, and each extra frame is travel before the machine can count on knowing the person is there. If the stop was sized for the best-detected group, a group that needs \(\FiniteChange\ReliableDetectionFrameCount\) more frames, at camera frame period \(\CameraFramePeriod\) and speed \(\SpeedAtDetection\), loses a distance \[\DetectionRangeShortfall = \SpeedAtDetection\,\CameraFramePeriod\,\FiniteChange\ReliableDetectionFrameCount \tag{4}\] before braking begins. A stop that would have ended just short of a person in the reference group now ends at the person, and the machine is still moving when it gets there. Because the reference braking distance \(\SpeedAtDetection^2/(2\,\CredibleBrakingDeceleration)\) was sized to shed all of the initial squared speed \(\SpeedAtDetection^2\) just as the machine reaches the person, losing a distance \(\DetectionRangeShortfall\) before braking begins leaves that final \(\DetectionRangeShortfall\) of braking uncompleted. While the shortfall is smaller than the braking distance, braking at \(\CredibleBrakingDeceleration\) over the remaining distance therefore leaves an impact speed and an impact energy of \[\ImpactSpeed = \sqrt{2\,\CredibleBrakingDeceleration\,\DetectionRangeShortfall}, \qquad \KineticEnergy = \tfrac{1}{2}\Mass\ImpactSpeed^2 = \Mass\,\CredibleBrakingDeceleration\,\DetectionRangeShortfall. \tag{5}\] The last form says that the energy delivered to the person grows in direct proportion to the distance lost to late detection. Fairness for a moving machine is therefore measured in meters and joules, not only in percentage points of recall.

Napkin Math 17.2: Two frames lateProblem: The running machine slows near people only after its learned detector reports a person. Its stop is sized for a group the detector sees in 95 percent of frames. A second group, kneeling workers, is seen in 75 percent of frames. At the aisle speed, what impact speed and energy does the second group receive from a stop that would have just cleared the first?
Variables:

\(\DetectorMissProbability =\) \(10^{-3}\) (Chosen); \(\PerFrameDetectionProbability =\) 0.95 and 0.75 (Illustrative).
\(\CameraFramePeriod =\) 16.7 ms (Datasheet, navigation camera); \(\SpeedAtDetection =\) 1.3 m/s (Chosen); \(\CredibleBrakingDeceleration =\) 2 m/s² (Illustrative); \(\Mass =\) 368 kg (Derived, loaded).

Math: By equation 3, the first group needs 3 frames and the second 5, so \(\FiniteChange\ReliableDetectionFrameCount =\) 2, or 33.3 ms. By equation 4, \(\DetectionRangeShortfall =\) 43 mm, well inside the 0.42 m braking distance. By equation 5, \(\ImpactSpeed =\) 0.42 m/s and \(\KineticEnergy =\) 32 J.
Result: A stop designed to end short of a standing worker ends in contact with a kneeling one at 0.42 m/s.
Systems insight: A few centimeters of late detection become a collision because the stop was sized with no margin for the slower group. The result also assumes the detector’s misses are independent from frame to frame; a detector that systematically fails on a pose misses it in many frames in a row, and the shortfall grows well beyond this best case.


Table 1 repeats the calculation for three lower-detection groups. The relationship is steep at the low end: a group seen in 60 percent of frames needs 5 extra frames and receives a 0.66 m/s impact carrying 80 J. Figure 2 plots the speed of the machine against distance for the reference group and for that group.
