That group is detected after 3 frames; a group seen in 60 percent of frames is detected after 8, so braking begins later and the same deceleration leaves the machine still moving when it reaches the person. The impact speed and energy follow from the distance lost, not from the recall gap alone.





17.5.2 Sample sizes for each group
A detection gap can be managed only if it can be measured, and measuring it per group takes more data than measuring it overall. Suppose an evaluation set holds 10,000 people, of whom 2 percent belong to a smaller group, 200 people, and the detector finds 0.95 of both groups. The exact 95 percent interval for the larger group runs from 0.945 to 0.954. For the smaller group it runs from 0.910 to 0.976, about 8× wider, too wide to tell a detection rate of 0.95 from one of 0.92. A pooled detection rate reported for “pedestrians” or “workers” hides exactly the group the machine serves worst.


↩︎ The exact binomial bound, and why a few observed failures drop it sharply, are established in Bounds when failures occur.
Telling a detection rate of 0.95 from one of 0.92 with 80 percent power takes about 1,059 people in each group, about 11 percent of the whole evaluation set for every group the evaluation must resolve. A group that makes up a few percent of the people a site employs will not reach that count by chance; the evaluation has to recruit it deliberately. The same arithmetic sets how long field monitoring must run before a per-group detection rate can be trusted, and it is why the sample size for each group belongs in the plan before data collection begins, not in the report after it.


17.5.3 Where the measurement lives
If per-group detection rates live only in a research benchmark report, the release gate cannot check them before admitting the machine to an open floor. Tracking them does not need a new pipeline; it needs a new dimension in records the book already keeps. The observation contract states its detection qualification for each group the machine must slow down for. The fault list adds a coverage dimension that seeds kneeling, carrying, and seated people as deliberately as it seeds stale frames. The evaluation record reports detection per group with its confidence interval rather than only in aggregate. From those qualified measurements, the exposure block of the approval record stores, for each group the machine relies on detecting, the sample size, the rate, its interval, and the distance shortfall it implies at the operating speed. A group with no entry is an unknown premise, and the release gate treats it as one.


↩︎ The observation contract, which states what each measurement may be relied on for, is established in The Observation Contract.

Checkpoint 17.2: Detection gaps and sample sizes

Conversion: A detector reaches a person kneeling between racks two frames later than a standing person. Can you compute, at the running machine’s aisle speed, loaded mass, and credible deceleration, the impact speed and energy if the stop was sized for standing workers?
Remedy: Can you compare three remedies (a lower speed near racks, a sensor that does not depend on the person’s pose, and a zone rule that keeps the machine out while people kneel there) by what each costs and what evidence each needs?
Sample: Can you size an evaluation that distinguishes 0.95 from 0.92 detection at 80 percent power, and say what share of a 10,000-person test set each group must be?

title: Responsible Physical AI
text:
17.6 Who Bears the Risk
The people a machine puts at risk are not only the people who chose it. The facility operator chose to buy the machine and the integrator chose how to configure it; a rider chooses to take a robotaxi. The pedestrian in the crosswalk, the coworker at an aisle crossing, and the visitor walking through a loading area made no such choice. An aggregate comparison, such as a fleet’s injury rate against a human benchmark, can improve while the remaining risk concentrates on people who never agreed to carry it. The risk such people carry without having chosen it is unconsented risk, and it has to be counted separately because no aggregate figure reveals it.


↩︎ Fleet crash rates reported outcome by outcome, each with its own interval, are established in Fleet evidence and accountable release.
Choices that look purely operational move that risk around. The site crossing rule, which lets people enter the aisle only at marked points, buys the machine its speed by asking pedestrians to wait and to comply. Suppose 80 percent of the encounters between machines and people happen at three crossings used by 10 percent of the workforce. Those workers then carry 8× the site’s average exposure per person, while everyone else carries 22 percent of it, and the site-wide encounter rate looks the same either way. Routing, the boundaries of the operating domain, and the hours a machine runs all shift exposure among groups in the same way.


↩︎ The site crossing rule, and the access restriction it places on pedestrians, are established in Restricted operation and access boundaries.
The requirement that follows is a reporting one. The exposure block of the approval record lists each group exposed to the machine, whether its members chose that exposure, how their exposure is measured (encounters per person-hour, near misses, close passes), and the routing and domain decisions that changed it. A group that bears risk it did not choose is owed two things a fleet-wide statistic cannot give it: a measurement of its own exposure, and a way to see the machine coming.

17.6.1 Legible intent
People protect themselves from a moving machine by predicting where it will go and getting out of the way. Yet a machine that follows an efficient path until the last moment leaves nearby coworkers unable to tell whether it will continue straight or turn across their path. Dragan, Lee, and Srinivasa distinguish two properties of robot motion: motion is predictable when it matches what an observer who knows the goal expects, and legible when it lets an observer who does not know the goal infer it quickly (Dragan et al. 2013). A mobile base that drifts toward the side of the aisle it will turn into, or an arm that moves toward the shelf it will reach before it reaches, is legible. A machine that moves along the efficient path until the last moment is predictable only to someone who already knows its plan.

Dragan, Anca D., Kenton C. T. Lee, and Siddhartha S. Srinivasa. 2013. “Legibility and Predictability of Robot Motion.” 2013 8th ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction (HRI), 301–8. https://doi.org/10.1109/HRI.2013.6483603.

Lee, John D., and Katrina A. See. 2004. “Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance.” Human Factors: The Journal of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society 46 (1): 50–80. https://doi.org/10.1518/hfes.46.1.50_30392.
Explicit signals add to legible motion. A light that projects the planned path on the floor, a sound before a reversing move, or a display that shows which way the machine will turn at a crossing lets a coworker begin to yield earlier. A person who yields earlier approaches the machine more slowly, which shrinks the approach-speed term of the separation the enforcer must keep. Signals help only if people’s trust follows what the machine can actually do. Lee and See showed that people rely on automation in proportion to their trust in it. Trust miscalibrated in either direction causes harm: too much leads to people stepping in front of a machine that will not stop for them, too little to people ignoring a machine that would (Lee and See 2004). A signal that the machine slows for people should therefore be shown only where the machine’s detection of people has been measured, group by group, to support it. Physical motion in the aisle is not the only burden the machine places on the people around it; the cameras and logs that verify that motion also record everyone who shares the floor.


↩︎ The human separation distance, whose approach-speed term a person who yields earlier reduces, is established in Stopping Envelopes.

title: Responsible Physical AI
text:
17.7 Data About People
When the warehouse machine logs a near miss at a rack end, its sensors and audit trails capture the people in and behind the cell alongside the telemetry of the base and arm. The records that make a machine answerable are also records about people, and the same evidence that settles who answers for an incident can, if kept forever and read by anyone, become a tool for watching the people it was meant to protect. How those records are declared, kept, and read is therefore part of the design, not an afterthought to it.

17.7.1 Recorded people as a standing condition
Three of the release records carry personal data directly: the authority record of The Authority Record names the operator behind each takeover tick by tick, the event-triggered traces of the black box hold camera frames of whoever stood in the aisle (including coworkers who never touched the console), and the demonstration archive of The Dataset Schema binds each episode to the operator who produced it. If those traces are retained indefinitely or opened to unrestricted browsing, the safety evidence store turns into continuous workplace surveillance. A release must retain the evidence needed for incident reconstruction while keeping identifying data to a minimum and within justified retention limits. The release therefore carries one more premise, and it is administrative rather than physical: each record that identifies a person declares its purpose, its retention period, and who may read it, and the site operates within those declarations.
Where the machine runs in the European Union, the General Data Protection Regulation makes that premise law (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016). Article 5(1) requires personal data to be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner incompatible with them (point b), to be limited to what those purposes need (point c), and to be kept in identifiable form no longer than they require (point e). Article 25(2) makes the minimum the default, in the amount collected, the extent of processing, the storage period, and accessibility. Article 35 requires a data protection impact assessment before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to the people concerned. Article 88 lets member states and collective agreements set more specific rules for employee data, naming monitoring systems at the workplace among the safeguards those rules must address. Other jurisdictions differ in detail; the engineering premise does not.
Each declaration becomes a standing condition of the kind The Verdict's Standing Conditions defines, with a detector and a response. Incident reconstruction sets the retention of the black-box and authority logs: the traces around an intervention are kept for a declared, justified review period, with any extension documented under the applicable retention rules, and routine ticks with no event roll off the ring buffer as they already do. Access follows the purpose, so an incident reviewer may read a trace and an operator’s supervisor may not score from it. A trace promoted into the experience pipeline carries its purpose and retention with it, which is what the consent and retention field of Demonstration dataset provenance schema records. The detector is an access and retention audit on the evidence store. Its response follows from the rule that a verdict stands only while its premises are known-true, so a record used outside its declared purpose, or held past its period, suspends that use and returns the premise to the adjudicator. Stated this way, the premise keeps the traces an investigator needs to reconstruct a stop and bars their use for watching workers.


17.7.2 Keeping less
Continuous video recording keeps every frame of every worker’s shift, creating a permanent surveillance archive when an incident investigation needs only the seconds around a fault. The first way to protect recorded people is therefore to record less of them. Event-triggered retention keeps only the window around an intervention or a boundary excursion: the 5 s before the trigger that the authority record needs to reconstruct a takeover, and the response after it, 30 s in all. At 20 such events per machine over a 16-hour operating day, the machine keeps about 1 percent of its footage, a 96× reduction, and everything else rolls off the ring buffer within seconds.


↩︎ The pre-trigger window the black box must hold to reconstruct a takeover is established in Trustworthy Operational Logs.
The event window and the records retained from it have different lifetimes. Figure 3 follows the bounded capture history into incident review and separates that use from a possible training use.






Figure 3: The Lifetime of Incident Evidence: A trigger selects the declared pre-trigger and response window while routine frames roll off the capture buffer. The incident record carries its purpose, retention, and readers. A training copy requires a separate review of consent, eligibility, and purpose; selection as incident evidence does not itself authorize training. The window and retention periods are those declared for the deployment, not universal durations.



Retention limits apply to each copy, including a copy admitted to training. Deleting a routine capture frame does not remove a retained incident record, and approving incident access does not approve every later use of that record.
Two further steps reduce what the kept footage reveals. Faces and badge numbers can be blurred on the machine before a frame is stored, provided the investigation does not need them. The declaration then records which fields stay identifiable and why, for example that the operator’s identity is kept in the authority record but not in the camera trace. People whose demonstrations train the policy are a separate case: they are recorded on purpose and at length, so their consent, what their episodes may be used for, and how long those episodes are kept travel with the data from the moment of collection. The data block of the approval record lists each record class, the people it records, its purpose, its retention, what is removed before storage, who may read it, and the result of the last access and retention audit.


17.7.3 When safety records become performance scores
The records most likely to be misused are the ones that measure workers. The machine’s authority logs and black-box recorders capture the identity of every operator who initiates a manual takeover, how long each takeover took, and how often each operator intervened. If an employer uses those records to score employee performance, the records have crossed from safety into monitoring. Conformity assessment under the European Union Machinery Regulation addresses the machinery safety requirements for the declared use; it does not govern every later use of the machine’s records. One such use falls under a different law, the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act. Its Annex III lists AI systems intended to monitor and evaluate the performance and behavior of people at work among the employment uses subject to the high-risk classification rules of Article 6. Article 26(7) requires an employer deploying a high-risk system in the workplace to inform workers’ representatives and the affected workers before putting it into use (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024).
The declarations of section 17.7.1 are where the line is drawn. A record declared for incident reconstruction may not be read to rank operators, and an access audit that finds such a read suspends that use and returns the premise to the adjudicator. If a site does want to evaluate workers, that is a separate system with its own declaration, its own legal classification, and its own owner, and the approval record lists it as a separate decision rather than letting it grow out of the safety records. Protecting workers in the machine’s records still leaves the physical work the machine shifts onto them during daily operation.

title: Responsible Physical AI
text:
17.8 The Labor the Machine Moves
Automating a task does not remove the labor the task needs. It moves that labor to the people who take over a machine when its planner stalls, the technicians who sweep and inspect the corridors the machine’s restrictions depend on, the crews who keep the floor in the state the release assumed, and the operators who record demonstrations for the next policy. The intervention frequency logged during release testing defines the human work the deployment creates: how often a technician is dispatched, how fast that person must arrive, and where on the floor that person must be stationed.


↩︎ The authority record that logs each takeover, its actor, and its timing is established in The Authority Record.

Napkin Math 17.3: Where the tote's labor wentProblem: The site of notebook 17.1 runs 20 machines for 16 hours a day with one remote assistant, and sweeps the restricted corridors 4 times a day. How many person-hours of work does the fleet create each day?
Variables:

Assistant utilization: 50 percent (Derived, notebook 17.1); operating day: 16 hours (Illustrative).
Corridor sweeps: 4 per day of 20 min each (Illustrative).

Math: The assistant must be staffed for all 16 h of operation, of which 8 h go to requests and 8 h to watching and waiting. Sweeps add 1.3 h. The fleet creates 17.3 person-hours of work a day, about 2.2 full-time shifts.
Result: The fleet needs more than two people’s working days of human labor every day it runs, before counting maintenance, charging, or the collection of new demonstrations.
Systems insight: The waiting hours are labor too. A person paid to watch a console for half of every shift, ready to act within seconds, does a job that monitoring research has long shown people perform poorly (Bainbridge 1983), and the design that creates the job owns its conditions.



Acemoglu, Daron, and Pascual Restrepo. 2020. “Robots and Jobs: Evidence from US Labor Markets.” Journal of Political Economy 128 (6): 2188–244. https://doi.org/10.1086/705716.

Burtch, Gordon, Brad Greenwood, and Kiron Ravindran. 2025. “Lucy and the Chocolate Factory: Warehouse Robotics and Worker Safety.” ILR Review 78 (4): 587–613. https://doi.org/10.1177/00197939251333754.

Gihleb, Rania, Osea Giuntella, Luca Stella, and Tianyi Wang. 2022. “Industrial Robots, Workers’ Safety, and Health.” Labour Economics 78: 102205. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.labeco.2022.102205.
The burden is not only hours. Across United States local labor markets, greater exposure to industrial robots between 1990 and 2007 lowered both employment and wages (Acemoglu and Restrepo 2020). Inside warehouses, the effect on safety cuts both ways. Burtch, Greenwood, and Ravindran found warehouse robotics associated with a 40 percent decrease in severe injuries and a 77 percent increase in non-severe ones, an increase they attribute at least partly to the faster pace of work at robotic facilities (Burtch et al. 2025). Across United States commuting zones, Gihleb and colleagues found that greater exposure to industrial robots lowered work-related injury rates while raising other harms, including drug- and alcohol-related deaths (Gihleb et al. 2022). A deployment can make the most dangerous injuries rarer and the work around the machine harder at the same time. Whether mobile manipulators in logistics follow either pattern has not yet been measured at scale. The task, takeover, and technician-hour records built in the book can inform that measurement; estimating causal effects on workers also requires comparison sites and labor-market data that no single deployment holds.
The labor block of the approval record therefore lists the work a deployment moves: takeover hours, technician dispatches, sweep hours, staffed monitoring hours, and the pace targets set for workers who share the floor. It also states the uses of worker data that the deployment bars, so that the labor the machine creates is not measured with records collected for safety. A site that cannot fill these fields does not know what its machine costs the people who work beside it.


↪ The cost of an operating restriction in throughput, against the cost of the test campaign that would lift it, is developed in What a restriction costs.

title: Responsible Physical AI
text:
17.9 The Approval Record
Left scattered across emails, slide decks, and meeting notes, the human and organizational premises behind a machine can lapse without blocking release: a staffing ratio changes on the night shift, a subgroup detection test is deferred, or a data-retention declaration expires while the robot keeps running. The approval record collects these premises in a single gate-checked artifact: it binds by digest the authority record, the enforcement record, the fault records, and the release manifest, and it adds the decisions behind them, each with a named owner.

Definition 17.3: Approval record
The approval record is the signed record that names, for each decision behind a machine’s admitted actions, the person who approved it and answers for it, and that declares the human roles the design relies on, the permission stage and its reporting duties, the groups exposed to the machine, the records kept about people, and the labor the deployment moves.

Significance: The release gate reads the approval record as a standing condition, so a decision with no named owner refuses operation exactly as an unknown physical premise does.
Distinction: The authority record shows who held each channel at each tick; the approval record shows who decided that the machine could be in that situation at all.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that a complete runtime log makes someone answerable. A log reconstructs events; only a record of decisions and their owners says who answers for them.



The approval record has seven blocks, a header that binds it to the release and one block for each kind of decision this chapter has set out (table 2). Each block names the decision owner alongside the specific evidence, bounds, or reporting duties that keep the release valid.



Table 2: The approval record: Each block holds a kind of decision the runtime records cannot hold, and each entry names an owner. The header binds the record to the release it governs by digest, so a new release requires a new approval record.










Block
What it holds

section 17.5, section 17.6

↪ Byte layout: The approval record’s fields, their encodings, and the check the release gate applies to each are given in Approval record.
The approval record gates release because the release gate reads it as a standing condition of the manifest. Four findings refuse operation the way an unknown premise does: an admitted action class has a decision link with no named owner, a human role cited as a countermeasure carries a verdict of INFEASIBLE or UNKNOWN, an exposed group the machine relies on detecting lacks a per-group entry, or a declaration about recorded people has expired or failed its audit. Each finding returns the premise to the adjudicator with its cause logged. A decision whose owner leaves the organization expires with that person’s role, so the approval record is kept current the same way the standing conditions are: by checking, on a declared schedule, that every premise still holds.


↩︎ Standing conditions, each with a detector, a cadence, and a response that withdraws the grant, are established in The Verdict's Standing Conditions.
Not every open entry can be closed before release. A decision may wait on a regulator, a per-group sample may still be filling, a staffing plan may depend on a hire. Those entries do not vanish into a footnote. Each one leaves the approval record with an operating restriction that holds until it closes, such as a lower speed near the group not yet measured or a zone the machine may not enter. It also enters the residual-claims register with an owner and a closure test, alongside the physical premises no sensor can check.


↪ The residual-claims register, which carries each open premise with its restriction, owner, and closure test, is developed in A residual-claims register.

Checkpoint 17.3: An approval record for the Cruise configuration

Decisions: Using section 17.1, can you list the decisions behind the October 2023 pullover (the post-collision response rule, the operating domain, the commercial stage, the reporting duties) and name the role that should own each?
Unknown fields: Which of those fields could have been marked UNKNOWN before the collision, and which would have refused operation under the gate rule of this section?
Disclosure: Can you write the disclosure-log entry that the permit block requires for the first report after the collision: who sends it, to whom, by when, and with what evidence attached?

title: Responsible Physical AI
text:
17.10 Fallacies and Pitfalls
Responsibility for a machine fails in predictable ways, and most of them come from treating it as something settled after an incident rather than designed before one. Each misconception below assumes that a record, a person, or an average carries a responsibility that no one has actually accepted.

Fallacy: A complete runtime log makes someone answerable for what the machine did.
The logs of the Cruise vehicle were complete enough for engineers to rebuild the pullover in detail, and still the question of who had decided the vehicle should pull over, and who decided what regulators would hear, took months and an outside investigation to answer. A log records events. The decisions that made an event possible (the operating envelope, the response rule, the staffing ratio, the permit application) were made earlier, by people who appear in no tick. Six such links, each retrievable with probability 0.90, form a chain an investigator can follow to the end only 53 percent of the time.
Reconstruction is not attribution: only a record of decisions and their owners says who answers for an admitted action.


Pitfall: Naming a person as the countermeasure for a hazard faster than a person can act.
A design that lists the remote assistant as the response to a person stepping out at a rack end asks for a takeover that needs about 4.5 s when the hazard leaves 0.85 s. The person in that role adds no protection and absorbs the blame for an outcome the design controlled. Utilization makes it worse: at 20 machines per assistant, a request waits 180 s on average before anyone looks at it.
Architect’s countermeasure: Test every human role the safety argument cites for time, information, and authority, mark it FEASIBLE, INFEASIBLE, or UNKNOWN, and let only feasible roles count as countermeasures.


Fallacy: One detection rate for “people” describes how safe the machine is for everyone.
A pooled rate is dominated by the largest group. At 200 people, a smaller group’s exact interval is about 8× wider than the rest of the set’s, too wide to resolve a gap of three points in detection. A group detected two frames later at the aisle speed loses 43 mm of clearance and is struck at 0.42 m/s.
Detection must be reported per group, with a sample large enough for its interval to resolve the gap that matters, and converted into meters and joules.


Pitfall: Justifying a deployment for everyone exposed with a favorable fleet-wide comparison.
An aggregate injury rate can fall while risk concentrates on the people who never chose the machine. When 80 percent of encounters happen at crossings used by 10 percent of workers, those workers carry 8× the average exposure, and the site-wide rate does not show it.
Architect’s countermeasure: Report exposure per group and per location, record whether each group chose it, and treat routing and operating-domain choices as decisions about who bears the risk.


Fallacy: Keeping every recording is the safe choice, because an investigation might need it.
Continuous recording keeps every frame of every worker for as long as the storage lasts. Event-triggered retention keeps the windows an investigation actually uses, about 1 percent of the day, and lets the rest roll off within seconds. Records kept without a declared purpose and period drift into uses no one approved, such as ranking operators by their takeovers.
Each record about people is kept only for a declared purpose and period, and read only by the readers that purpose names.


Pitfall: Carrying a permission stage across a configuration change.
A stage authorizes a configuration in a domain under reporting duties. A new policy, a new enforcer build, or an expanded operating domain is a different configuration, and the failure-free hours that supported the old stage, about 2,996 for the claim in section 17.4.1, do not transfer to it. A withheld or incomplete incident report breaks the stage as surely as the motion does.
Architect’s countermeasure: Bind each stage to a configuration digest in the permit block of the approval record, so an update reopens the stage along with the release claims it touches.


Fallacy: Automation removes the work it automates.
A fleet of 20 machines with one remote assistant creates about 17.3 person-hours of rescue, sweeping, and monitoring every operating day, and warehouse robotics has been associated with more minor injuries even as severe ones fell. The work moves to fewer, different people, often under a faster pace.
A deployment accounts for the labor it moves and bars the use of its safety records to measure the people who do it.

title: Responsible Physical AI
text:
17.11 Summary
A machine’s records can reconstruct every admitted action and still leave open who decided that the machine could be in that situation at all. The decisions that set a machine’s limits (the operating envelope, the response rules, the staffing ratio, the permission stage, the uses of its data) are made by different people, before any command crosses the causal boundary, and they appear in no runtime log. Each party can truthfully point to another. The Cruise collision showed the consequence: a record good enough to rebuild the motion, an account to regulators that left out the part that mattered, and penalties imposed for the record rather than the motion. Responsibility therefore has to be designed like any other premise of the machine’s authority, written into a record before the machine moves and checked when it is released.
The same discipline applies to the people around the machine. A human role counts as a countermeasure only if its holder has the time, information, and authority to act; a remote assistant whose takeover needs several times the time the hazard leaves, or whose queue makes requests wait minutes, adds blame rather than protection. Permission to operate is granted in stages, each for a configuration, a domain, and reporting duties, and is withdrawn for a withheld record as well as for unsafe motion. A gap in detection between groups of people becomes a gap in stopping distance and impact energy, and it can be managed only with per-group samples large enough to resolve it. Risk falls on people who did not choose the machine, records about people must be declared and kept no longer than their purpose needs, and the labor a machine moves must be counted. The approval record collects all of these with named owners, and the release gate refuses operation while any of them is missing.
Table 3 collects the chapter’s equations.



Table 3: Key equations of responsibility for physical AI: Each equation, what it bounds or decides about a person’s role or a group’s exposure, and where it is derived.

Key Takeaways: Responsibility for a machine that acts

Reconstruction is not attribution: A log shows what was admitted. Only a record of decisions, each with a named owner, shows who made the admission possible, and those decisions must be recorded on purpose because the machine does not make them.
A role no person can perform assigns blame, not protection: Test every human role the safety argument cites for time, information, and authority, including the queue one person serves, and let only feasible roles count as countermeasures.
Permission is staged and can be withdrawn: Each stage covers a configuration, a domain, and reporting duties. It is left on evidence gathered at that stage and withdrawn for a configuration change, an incident, or a withheld record.
Measure fairness in meters and joules: Convert per-group detection into the distance lost before braking and the impact it causes, and size each group’s sample so its interval can resolve the gap.
Count the people who did not choose the machine: Report exposure per group and per location, and give the people who bear the risk legible motion and signals backed by measured detection.
Records and labor about people carry their own premises: Declare each record’s purpose, retention, and readers, and account for the work a deployment moves onto people and the uses of their data it bars.
A missing owner refuses like an unknown premise: The approval record is a standing condition of release; entries that cannot close go to the residual-claims register with a restriction and an owner.



The fourth law, permission must be earned (principle \(\ref{pri-vol4-evidence-bounds-authority}\)), lets a machine operate only as far as its evidence supports, and the earlier chapters of this part applied it to channels, faults, and claims. Responsibility applies it to the decisions behind them: an envelope is supported only if someone accepted it, a human safeguard only if a person can perform it, and a detection claim only if it holds for each group the machine meets. The approval record makes those conditions checkable by the same gate that checks friction and timing, so the release that admits the running machine to an open floor also names who answers for each of its decisions. No assignment of responsibility after a collision returns the energy the machine has already delivered across the causal boundary, which is why every one of these decisions has an owner before the first command is admitted.

title: Responsible Physical AI
text:
17.12 Historical Perspective and Further Reading
The question of who answers for an outcome that many people produced is older than computing. Thompson (1980) named the problem of many hands in public administration, where officials who each contribute a small part to a harmful policy can each disclaim it. Nissenbaum (1996) carried the problem into computing and identified the barriers specific to software: the many hands that build it, the treatment of failures as unavoidable bugs, the use of the computer as a scapegoat, and the ownership of software without liability for it. Matthias (2004) argued that machines which learn make the gap wider, because their behavior is not fully determined by any rule their makers wrote. The field’s founding case remains Therac-25, the radiation therapy machine whose software removed the hardware interlocks that had protected patients (Leveson and Turner 1993).

Matthias, Andreas. 2004. “The Responsibility Gap: Ascribing Responsibility for the Actions of Learning Automata.” Ethics and Information Technology 6 (3): 175–83. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10676-004-3422-1.

Leveson, Nancy G., and Clark S. Turner. 1993. “An Investigation of the Therac-25 Accidents.” Computer 26 (7): 18–41.

Sheridan, Thomas B. 1992. Telerobotics, Automation, and Human Supervisory Control. MIT Press.

Bainbridge, Lisanne. 1983. “Ironies of Automation.” Automatica 19 (6): 775–79. https://doi.org/10.1016/0005-1098(83)90046-8.
A second line of work asked when a person placed in the loop actually controls the outcome. Sheridan (1992) laid out supervisory control, in which a person sets goals and monitors while the machine acts, and Bainbridge (1983) showed why the person left to handle only the rare emergency is the one least prepared to handle it. Santoni de Sio and Hoven (2018) turned the debate over autonomous weapons into general conditions for meaningful human control, and Elish (2019) named the moral crumple zone after tracing how blame was assigned in accidents from aviation to nuclear power.
A third line measured who the machine serves well. Buolamwini and Gebru (2018) showed that the benchmarks used to evaluate face analysis left out the people the systems failed on, Wilson et al. (2019) and Li et al. (2025) found the same pattern in pedestrian detection. Nissenbaum (2009) recast privacy as the question of whether information flows in the way its context expects, which is the question a declaration about recorded people answers. Regulation followed the same arc, from the General Data Protection Regulation (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016) to the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024) and the state and federal reporting duties for driverless vehicles (California Department of Motor Vehicles 2018a; National Highway Traffic Safety Administration 2021).

Buolamwini, Joy, and Timnit Gebru. 2018. “Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial Gender Classification.” Conference on Fairness, Accountability and Transparency, 77–91.

Li, Xinyue, Zhenpeng Chen, Jie M. Zhang, Federica Sarro, Ying Zhang, and Xuanzhe Liu. 2025. “Bias Behind the Wheel: Fairness Testing of Autonomous Driving Systems.” ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology 34 (3): 1–24. https://doi.org/10.1145/3702989.

European Parliament, and Council of the European Union. 2016. Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016. Official Journal of the European Union.

European Parliament and Council of the European Union. 2024. Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 Laying down Harmonised Rules on Artificial Intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act). Official Journal of the European Union, L series, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024.

California Department of Motor Vehicles. 2018a. California Code of Regulations, Title 13, Article 3.7: Testing of Autonomous Vehicles.

National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. 2021. Standing General Order 2021-01: Incident Reporting Requirements for Automated Driving Systems and Level 2 Advanced Driver Assistance Systems.
Six works reward careful study:

Thompson (1980) defines the problem of many hands and the forms of responsibility that survive it, the starting point for recording decisions with their owners.
Nissenbaum (1996) names the four barriers to answering for computer systems, each of which reappears in a physical machine’s chain of decisions.
Elish (2019) introduces the moral crumple zone and shows, case by case, how blame settles on the person nearest the event.
Santoni de Sio and Hoven (2018) states the conditions under which human control of an autonomous system is real rather than nominal.
Wilson et al. (2019) measures how pedestrian detection differs across skin types, the evidence behind measuring detection per group.
Nissenbaum (2009) explains privacy as appropriate flow, the frame for declaring what each record about people may be used for.


Thompson, Dennis F. 1980. “Moral Responsibility of Public Officials: The Problem of Many Hands.” American Political Science Review 74 (4): 905–16. https://doi.org/10.2307/1954312.

Nissenbaum, Helen. 1996. “Accountability in a Computerized Society.” Science and Engineering Ethics 2 (1): 25–42. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02639315.

Elish, Madeleine Clare. 2019. “Moral Crumple Zones: Cautionary Tales in Human-Robot Interaction.” Engaging Science, Technology, and Society 5: 40–60. https://doi.org/10.17351/ests2019.260.

Santoni de Sio, Filippo, and Jeroen van den Hoven. 2018. “Meaningful Human Control over Autonomous Systems: A Philosophical Account.” Frontiers in Robotics and AI 5. https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2018.00015.

Wilson, Benjamin, Judy Hoffman, and Jamie Morgenstern. 2019. “Predictive Inequity in Object Detection.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1902.11097.

Nissenbaum, Helen. 2009. Privacy in Context. Stanford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1515/9780804772891.

What’s Next: From responsibility to engineering judgmentWhat do the release verdict and its approval record say about the question this book opened with? On the book’s own records, the warehouse mobile manipulator is refused. The stipulated branch earns it only a restricted mission, and the approval record adds entries that cannot close before release: a per-group detection sample that is still filling, a staffing plan that depends on a hire, and a crossing rule that no sensor checks. Engineering Physical AI reads this verdict as the answer to why a better prediction can still produce a worse physical action. It transfers the same four-law method to an unfamiliar machine. It also gives each premise left open, whether physical or human, an owner, a restriction, and a closure test in the residual-claims register.
